artigo.texto: Zelestra and EDP strengthened their collaboration in Spain with two new hybrid PPAs that will incorporate 462 MWh of battery storage to 181 MWdc of solar capacity. The agreements pertain to the Pedroso project in Seville and the Valkyria project in Castilla-La Mancha. In both cases, additional measures will be added BESS systems to existing photovoltaic installations, which will allow part of the solar generation to be stored and its delivery shifted to other times of the day. Zelestra will own the projects while EDP will act as the energy buyer through new long-term power purchase agreements. The hybrid PPAs will incorporate four-hour batteries. In Pedroso, Zelestra will combine a 31 MWdc solar plant with a 25 MW BESS system and a 100 MWh battery storage capacity. Valkyria, meanwhile, will have 150 MWdc of photovoltaic generation and a 90.45 MW battery storage system with a 362 MWh capacity. The two systems will have approximately four hours of storage capacity. Together, they will provide the additional 462 MWh included in the new hybrid PPAs. This configuration allows the electricity produced during peak solar generation hours to be harnessed and stored for later use. In this way, batteries can increase the flexibility of power plants and reduce their reliance on production tied solely to hours of sunlight. Zelestra and EDP exceed 1 GWh of contracted storage The Pedroso and Valkyria agreements bring to four the number of solar energy and storage projects included in the collaboration between Zelestra and EDP in Spain. In 2025, the companies agreed a PPA for the Trujillo project in Extremadura, which combines 170 MWdc of solar capacity with 400 MWh of battery storage. Subsequently, in 2026, both companies expanded their collaboration through Pizarroso, a 50 MW solar plant in Cáceres where a 160 MWh BESS system will be incorporated. With Pedroso and Valkyria, the storage capacity linked to the four agreements reaches approximately 1,022 MWh. Unlike Trujillo, developed as a new solar project with storage, Pedroso, Valkyria and Pizarroso take advantage of photovoltaic plants existing ones to incorporate batteries. Batteries increase the flexibility of solar plants Hybridizing operational facilities allows for the addition of storage using existing infrastructure such as land, generation, and grid access. In addition, the model makes it easier for some of the renewable electricity produced during the day to be shifted to the late afternoon, evening, or other periods of higher demand. For independent power producers, this capacity opens up new commercial opportunities within PPAs. solar generation it is no longer strictly linked to the moment it occurs and can be better adapted to the buyer’s consumption profile. Zelestra has transferred to Europe some of the experience gained in markets such as Chile, where contracts combining renewable generation and storage have a longer track record. Likewise, the company is expanding this type of commercial structure in other European markets through hybrid PPAs and long-term storage contracts. Spain gains energy storage capacity The new operation also reinforces the role of BESS systems within Spanish renewable growth. Jaime Burguete, head of Zelestra in Spain, pointed out that the four joint projects demonstrate the viability of energy storage in the country and predicted that this segment will have a growing importance in the coming years. For its part, EDP seeks to use the combination of renewable generation and storage to provide a more flexible electricity supply and make better use of the energy produced by renewables solar installations. With the new agreements, Zelestra and EDP are expanding a strategy that links long-term supply contracts with large-scale batteries, a formula that can facilitate greater integration of solar energy within the Spanish electricity system. artigo.texto: China’s industry ministry and six other agencies set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of all-solid-state batteries, though CATL’s chairman rates the technology four out of nine and calls million-vehicle use before 2030 very unlikely. ProLogium’s Dunkirk plant, the largest new European cell project since Northvolt went bankrupt, is staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and will be certified against a Chinese standard. China has set 2030 as the date for the first large-scale use of solid-state batteries. Its biggest battery maker rates the technology four out of nine. A plant in northern France broke ground in February. The plan came from the industry ministry and six other agencies on 28 September and covers 2026 to 2030, as CnEVPost reported. It also targets lithium cells good for 15,000 charge cycles. The ministry acknowledged weaknesses in innovation and imbalances between supply and demand. CATL is promising less than the plan does. Its chairman, Robin Zeng, put all-solid-state at four out of nine in June, on a scale where nine means ready for vehicle production. He called the chance of fitting it to a million cars before 2030 very small. CATL intends limited production in 2027. LG Energy Solution expects the technology to reach smartphones a decade before EVs. Its North America president says large cells are where manufacturers struggle. Europe is further along than that timetable suggests, though not by much, and not on its own technology. ProLogium already makes 6,000 packs a year in Taiwan, which is half a gigawatt hour, at 381 Wh/kg on TUV Rheinland’s measurement. That is roughly 30% above the cells in most electric cars today. The company is now building the same thing in France, with subsidies agreed in 2023 and permits granted the year after. The Dunkirk plant started construction in February beside the Gravelines nuclear station, staged at 0.8 GWh in 2028 and 12 GWh by 2032. Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Mercedes are separately working with Factorial on cells of their own. None of it is close to Chinese volume, and the gap is not narrowing. Chinese and South Korean makers supply 90% of Europe’s batteries, and Northvolt went bankrupt after raising $15bn. Dunkirk is the largest new European cell project since. The standard is Chinese as well. ProLogium’s cells are certified against GB/T 43568-2026, the all-solid-state specification Beijing introduced in July, and were separately tested by UL Solutions. China took 70% of global electric car production under the previous five-year plan. The new one says initial large-scale use rather than mass production, and even that is a target rather than a promise. artigo.texto: A Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada, mais conhecida por MEX, pretende tirar partido das vantagens oferecidas por Macau para promover a negociação de activos ambientais – incluindo de créditos de carbono, certificados de energia verde e outros instrumentos similares – entre a China e os Países de Língua Portuguesa. Meng Meng, Directora-Geral da entidade, revela que a plataforma de negociação operada pela MEX já listou mais de 30 projectos ligados a países lusófonos e de língua espanhola, envolvendo uma redução total de emissões de carbono superior a 14,13 milhões de toneladas Como foi criada a Macau Internacional Troca de Emissões de Carbono Limitada (MEX, na sigla inglesa)? Quais são os seus objectivos estratégicos? A MEX foi criada a 30 de Outubro de 2024. Recorrendo a tecnologias de informação avançadas e padrões de referência no sector, integra produtos e oportunidades relacionados com o clima a nível global, proporcionando à China uma solução específica com características de Macau para se conectar aos mercados internacionais de finanças verdes. A Região Administrativa Especial de Macau (RAEM) é um porto franco, com regras financeiras alinhadas com as normas internacionais. Além disso, a cidade situa-se na confluência de duas importantes estratégias nacionais – o projecto da Grande Baía Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau e a Zona de Cooperação Aprofundada entre Guangdong e Macau em Hengqin. Neste sentido, possui um conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas que lhe permite posicionar-se como um “superconector” no mercado internacional de carbono. A nossa tarefa é transformar gradualmente esse conjunto de vantagens intrínsecas numa realidade concreta. A nível nacional, trabalhamos no sentido de apoiar as metas de “duplo carbono” estabelecidas pelo país [atingir o pico das emissões de dióxido de carbono antes de 2030 e alcançar a neutralidade carbónica antes de 2060], proporcionando um canal mais aberto para que o mercado de carbono da China possa estabelecer ligações com capital, tecnologia e regulamentações internacionais. A nível global, estamos a construir uma plataforma de cooperação no campo da acção climática, ao mesmo tempo que promovemos o alinhamento de padrões com as normas internacionais e a sua implementação prática, divulgando o progresso alcançado pelo mercado de carbono da China. Em paralelo, a MEX encara o comércio de carbono como um motor para alcançar a neutralidade carbónica e desenvolver as finanças verdes. Oferecemos também a diversos sectores-chave em Macau soluções ligadas à neutralidade carbónica, ferramentas associadas a certificados verdes de absorção de carbono e instrumentos de financiamento verde, transformando a transição para a neutralidade carbónica numa vantagem competitiva para as indústrias da RAEM. Qual é o modelo operacional da MEX? A nossa plataforma pode ser entendida como um mercado digital de negociação de activos ambientais. Os produtos listados na MEX incluem créditos de carbono, certificados de energia renovável e outros itens similares. Apoiamos a negociação de certificados verdes internacionais e chineses e somos a única bolsa do género na China a disponibilizar contratos padronizados de créditos de carbono de elevada qualidade com cobertura global. Nas áreas não directamente relacionadas com a negociação de activos, prestamos serviços de dados e estudos, formação, consultoria e outras soluções. Publicamos regularmente relatórios sectoriais para ajudar os participantes no mercado a compreenderem melhor tendências, a identificarem oportunidades e a mitigarem riscos. Além disso, disponibilizamos programas de capacitação que ajudam as empresas a aprofundarem o seu conhecimento sobre os desafios associados à acção climática. Prestamos igualmente serviços personalizados ao longo de toda a cadeia, desde o inventário de emissões de carbono e o planeamento de trajectórias de redução de emissões até à definição de soluções de compensação. Através deste modelo integrado, que combina actividades de negociação e serviços não transaccionais, procuramos criar um ecossistema sustentável de activos ambientais e serviços verdes, permitindo que as empresas que necessitam de soluções nesta área as encontrem na MEX. Quais os principais marcos já alcançados pela MEX? Em primeiro lugar, concretizámos o nosso posicionamento estratégico de utilizar Macau como ponto de apoio para ligar a China ao mercado internacional de carbono. Macau tem vindo, gradualmente, a afirmar-se como um centro activo do mercado de carbono na Ásia. Até Agosto deste ano, o volume acumulado de créditos de carbono negociados através da MEX tinha ultrapassado 1,17 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO2-e). Já o volume de certificados de energia renovável negociados ascendia a 2,07 milhões de certificados. Contamos actualmente com 146 membros registados na nossa plataforma. Logo no dia da nossa inauguração, concluímos as primeiras negociações envolvendo cerca de 870 mil toneladas de créditos de carbono, abrangendo uma dezena de sectores em cinco países. Esperamos que, através da adopção de um conjunto de normas rigorosas e de uma governação sólida, os produtos disponibilizados através da MEX se tornem sinónimo de elevada qualidade. Somos a única instituição de Macau que é membro da Associação Internacional de Comércio de Emissões. Estabelecemos igualmente parcerias com outros membros e organizações internacionais e mantemos uma cooperação aprofundada com diversas instituições académicas e industriais de referência a nível mundial no sector. Estas colaborações, ao promoverem o reconhecimento mútuo de activos, a integração de sistemas e a harmonização de normas, posicionam Macau como um verdadeiro pólo de ligação entre os vários mercados de carbono da Ásia e do mundo. artigo.texto: Uma das maiores empresas de auditoria e consultoria do mundo, a PWC, projeta US$ 11,4 bilhões em investimentos em data centers no Brasil em 2026. O valor é 49,3% maior em relação a 2025, que foi de US$ 7,6 bilhões. A informação foi publicada no jornal ‘Folha de S. Paulo’. No entanto, o mercado ainda aguarda a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenters (Redata), sancionado pelo governo no dia 15 de setembro. Há indefinições com relação a impostos estaduais na implantação de projetos de centro de dados. O cálculo é que o Redata abra caminho inicialmente para planos de investimento de R$ 20 bilhões no Brasil. Entre as empresas que devem fazer esse aporte incluem as americanas Ascenty e Scala, a britânica Terranova e a brasileira Takota. O Brasil é o quinto maior destino de recursos em datacenters no mundo em 2026. Os investimentos são liderados pelos Estados Unidos (US$ 448,4 bi), seguidos da China (US$ 48,9 bi), Índia (US$ 28,2 bi) e Alemanha (US$ 16,7 bi). No mundo, os investimentos devem chegar a US$ 828,4 bilhões só este ano. Um estudo recém-divulgado da FGV Projetos estima que a implantação de um único datacenter, incluindo a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, mobiliza cerca de R$ 25 bilhões em investimentos totais. A instituição calcula que aproximadamente 12.560 empregos diretos e indiretos são gerados durante a fase de construção e implantação. Desse total, cerca de 1.860 postos são permanentes, incluindo equipes de operação, manutenção e serviços de apoio ao empreendimento. O setor calcula investimentos de R$ 500 bilhões até 2030 em centro de dados. A capacidade atual dos datacenters no Brasil gira em torno de 730 MW, mas a previsão é de saltar para 3,2 GW em quatro anos, com foco em atender o processamento de inteligência artificial.

artigo.texto: Nigeria is set to strengthen the integrity and credibility of its emerging carbon market through the deployment of robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) systems, as the Federal Government seeks to attract large-scale private investment into climate action. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs. Omotenioye Majekodunmi, disclosed this at a high-level roundtable on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) Protocols,” convened under the European Union Climate Dialogues programme in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. Represented by the Director, Energy, Transportation & Infrastructure of NCCC, Mr. Michael Ivenso, the Director-General said Nigeria was determined to ensure that carbon markets translate the country’s climate commitments into tangible economic opportunities while preventing greenwashing and protecting the interests of communities, investors and project developers. According to the Director-General, “carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits,” stressing that Nigeria would not accommodate a carbon market that lacked transparency, credibility and environmental integrity. Mrs. Majekodunmi said the country’s objective was to ensure that carbon projects delivered real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes, while contributing to community development, environmental protection and fair returns for project developers and investors. READ ALSO: Nigerian President Approves Carbon Market Framework The Director-General said carbon markets were not a panacea for Nigeria’s climate and development challenges, but argued that, when supported by transparency, credible MRV systems and effective stakeholder collaboration, they could become a major catalyst for sustainable development. The NCCC Boss, therefore, urged participants at the roundtable to move beyond discussion and develop an actionable and time-bound roadmap capable of positioning Nigeria as a leading destination for high-integrity carbon investment in Africa. “A major component of the new approach is the operationalisation of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry. “The registry is expected to provide a digital record of carbon credits generated, issued, transferred and retired in Nigeria, thereby helping to prevent double-counting and strengthening the integrity of carbon transactions.” She explained. The NCCC also plans to accelerate the adoption of digital Measurement, Reporting and Verification (dMRV) technologies, including remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies. The technologies are expected to reduce the cost and time required to verify carbon projects while improving the accuracy and reliability of emissions data. The Director-General explained that without effective MRV systems, buyers would be unable to determine whether claimed emissions reductions were genuine, regulators would face difficulties tracking emissions and safeguarding against double-counting, while communities could struggle to monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. The NCCC called for stronger collaboration among federal ministries, state governments, private-sector operators, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. Head of section, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms. Yolanda San Jose, said carbon markets are playing an increasingly important role in supporting emissions reductions, mobilising finance, and encouraging investment. According to her, this is why Nigeria took a very important step last year by adopting its National Carbon Markets Framework. It established a structured legal and institutional system for domestic and international carbon trading under the Climate Change Act (2021) and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The Framework is the foundation for confidence, trust, and effectiveness in Nigeria’s emerging carbon market system. Ms. Jose noted that, for Nigeria, the development of a strong national carbon market system is both imperative and a significant opportunity, and would help align climate targets with development priorities, support investment, and create an enabling environment for a low-carbon future. “Today’s event is intended to help shape that pathway. In particular, we aim to align stakeholder views around Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework and to discuss a preliminary roadmap for its operationalisation. We will do so by emphasising the robustness of so-called Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) practices, to ensure that this market mechanism delivers credible results for both the Nigerian people and the environment.” She added that the European Union is pleased to support this process in partnership with Nigeria. Representing the Ministry of Environment, Mrs Halima Bawa-Buhari said the ministry is working towards a partnership that will lead to a robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system and a high-integrity carbon market, contributing significantly to the Securing Nigeria’s Forest Future (SNFF) financing roadmap. One of the development partners, UKPACT Officer, Ms Folakemi Aletan, said a well-functioning carbon market in Nigeria represents more than a climate policy instrument. She said it provides an opportunity to mobilise investment, support sustainable development, strengthen competitiveness and ultimately mobilise climate finance. The representative of the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), Mrs Nifesimi Ogunkua, said; “the organisation is supporting the National Council on Climate Change through a partnership agreement to strengthen the operationalisation of Nigeria’s carbon market framework.” She said the support includes the design and deployment of a digital portal for managing the lifecycle of carbon credit projects. Please enter the email address you use for your account so we can send you a link to reset your password: Local opposition has exacted a much higher cost for developers than has been previously understood, according to new Heatmap Pro survey of public records and financial information. The country’s largest technology companies are expected to spend more than $800 billion this year investing in data centers and artificial intelligence. But new data suggests the local backlash to data centers may be taking a meaningful bite out of that boom. At least $260 billion of data center investments were canceled this year after sustained local opposition, according to new Heatmap Pro data. The pace and size of those cancellations is picking up. About $130 billion in data center investment — or about half of the total — was canceled in the three months ending on September 30. And in dollar terms, the size of canceled projects in the third quarter of 2026 exceeded the size of all data center projects canceled last year. Roughly $1 trillion in data center investment now faces some kind of sustained or meaningful local opposition, according to Heatmap Pro data. About half of all projects that have met local backlash this year were ultimately canceled, our data suggests. Our market intelligence service Heatmap Pro tracks local projects and regulations affecting clean energy, batteries, and data centers. We run a continuous survey of public officials, regulatory filings, and local media to monitor energy and data center cancellations nationwide. Our investment figures, which have not been previously published and are larger than other estimates, are likely an undercount. Only about 60% of data center projects disclose the size of their planned investment, especially during a proposal’s early stage when it is most likely to run aground. These figures also do not include every project currently stalled because of state-level data center moratoriums in Texas and New York. But the totals show that the surging backlash to data centers is beginning to kill a sizable share of large computing projects. In August, a Heatmap Pro and Embold Research poll found that 75% of Americans would oppose a data center getting built near where they live — a striking change from a year earlier, when Americans were roughly split over the projects. “The number of canceled data centers speaks to the vast and growing grassroots opposition to these projects in communities across the country. The fact that many of these projects were defeated in just the past few months speaks to the upward trajectory of this opposition movement,” Mitch Jones, a policy director at Food and Water Watch, an environmental group that opposes AI data centers, said in a statement. A spokesperson for the Data Center Coalition, which advocates for the industry, did not respond before press time. Most canceled data center projects in our database are terminated because they fail to secure a local permit or face a hostile local government action. Hundreds of U.S. counties and towns now maintain a ban or moratorium on data center construction, our data shows. The Senate’s bipartisan permitting reform proposal would not affect towns or counties’ ability to prohibit data center development under their jurisdiction.

artigo.texto: Amazon abandona NDAs em data centers: o que muda na prática A AWS aboliu os acordos de confidencialidade com governos locais para tentar frear mais de 100 moratórias contra data centers nos EUA. A Amazon Web Services decidiu parar de usar acordos de confidencialidade (NDAs) nas negociações com governos locais para aprovação de novos data centers nos Estados Unidos. O anúncio foi feito por Matt Garman, CEO da AWS, em uma publicação que tenta responder à crescente resistência de comunidades americanas contra a expansão dessas instalações. A medida não é um gesto de boa vontade espontâneo. É uma reação calculada a um movimento que está ganhando corpo: mais de 100 moratórias contra data centers estão sendo discutidas em diferentes localidades dos EUA. O estado de Nova York já aprovou uma suspensão de um ano em licenças para grandes data centers. A Amazon está, na prática, tentando conter um incêndio regulatório antes que ele se espalhe. Por que as comunidades americanas estão rejeitando data centers A raiz do problema é a falta de transparência. A ativista ambiental Erin Brockovich resumiu o padrão que gera revolta: projetos anunciados depois que as licenças já estão garantidas, desenvolvedores que não retornam ligações e autoridades locais que assinaram NDAs antes que os vizinhos soubessem que um projeto estava sendo considerado. Esse ciclo corroeu a confiança pública. Como analisamos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a corrida por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial acelerou drasticamente a construção de data centers, mas as empresas trataram a expansão como uma operação sigilosa, e não como um projeto que afeta diretamente a vida de milhares de pessoas. O CEO da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, classificou a situação como “fundamentalmente uma crise de confiança”, em que as pessoas assumem que governos e big techs estão sempre tramando alguma forma de prejudicá-las. É um diagnóstico que vale para todo o setor, não apenas para a Amazon. Os quatro mitos que a Amazon tenta derrubar Garman tentou desmontar quatro críticas recorrentes aos data centers: consumo excessivo de água, aumento nos custos de eletricidade, poluição e ausência de benefícios para as comunidades locais. Sobre a água, a Amazon apontou que o consumo direto de seus data centers representa apenas 0,5% de todo o uso industrial de água nos EUA, volume descrito como “ordens de magnitude menor” do que campos de golfe ou o cultivo de amêndoas. A Nvidia, por sua vez, afirmou recentemente que seu novo sistema de refrigeração elimina “praticamente todo o uso de água” dentro dos data centers. Há um problema nesses números, no entanto. Tanto a Amazon quanto a Nvidia parecem ignorar o consumo mais amplo de água envolvido na geração de eletricidade e na fabricação de chips. Cientistas alertaram que precisam estudar o uso de água e energia dos data centers de forma independente, já que não existem exigências federais ou estaduais sobre como as empresas de tecnologia reportam esses dados. Em outras palavras: as big techs estão pedindo que acreditemos nos números que elas mesmas compilam, sem auditoria externa. Quanto à eletricidade, Garman argumentou que as tarifas só subiram em alguns estados com grande concentração de data centers, enquanto em outros caíram ou cresceram mais lentamente. Ele atribuiu os aumentos à falta de investimento prévio na rede elétrica. Mas um órgão de fiscalização independente apontou recentemente que os data centers foram os principais responsáveis por um aumento de 76% nos preços de energia, em base anual, na maior rede elétrica dos Estados Unidos. Os dados contam uma história diferente da narrativa corporativa. A questão da poluição e o caso Texas O ponto mais delicado talvez seja a poluição. Um data center planejado pela Amazon no Texas tem licença para emitir até 33 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono por ano, volume superior ao de qualquer outra usina de energia do país. Garman contra-argumentou dizendo que os geradores ficam ociosos 99,9% do tempo, funcionando em média apenas 10 horas por ano para testes de manutenção. A resposta, embora tecnicamente válida, não aborda o ponto central da crítica: se os geradores quase nunca funcionam, por que solicitar uma licença tão permissiva? O limite alto na licença cria uma percepção de risco que alimenta a desconfiança, como já discutimos ao analisar o impacto energético da IA. O caso do Texas é emblemático porque ilustra como o setor opera na prática: pede o máximo possível de margem regulatória, argumenta que usará uma fração mínima e espera que a comunidade confie nessa promessa. É uma estratégia que funcionava em um ambiente de baixa fiscalização, mas está sendo desafiada agora. Um bilhão em contribuições é suficiente? Garman também destacou que, nos últimos três anos, a Amazon contribuiu com mais de 1 bilhão de dólares para comunidades onde mantém presença significativa de data centers. É um número expressivo, mas que precisa ser colocado em perspectiva: a AWS gerou cerca de 105 bilhões de dólares em receita apenas em 2024. O investimento comunitário representa menos de 1% desse faturamento. O abandono dos NDAs é um passo concreto, mas provavelmente insuficiente para reverter o sentimento anti-data center. Como observou a escritora Jasmine Sun, quando opositores dos data centers são confrontados com os argumentos das empresas de tecnologia, a resposta costuma ser simples: “Eu não acredito neles.” Para a indústria de tecnologia como um todo, o episódio é um alerta. A expansão da infraestrutura de IA depende de licenças locais, apoio comunitário e redes elétricas que consigam absorver a demanda. Se as moratórias avançarem, Garman avisa que “os EUA podem estar escrevendo seu próprio bilhete perdedor nessa corrida, e as consequências durariam gerações.” O argumento de competitividade global pode funcionar em Washington, mas não convence moradores que veem seus custos de energia subir e caminhões de construção passarem pela porta todos os dias. artigo.texto: Côte d’Ivoire has shortlisted developers for two 100MW solar photovoltaic plants, each paired with 33MWh of battery storage, as the country moves to close the gap between its 45% renewables target by 2030 and a grid that currently runs on thermal power for roughly two thirds of its installed capacity. The two sites — Dabakala in the north east and Niakaramandougou in the centre of the country — will each be awarded as 25-year independent power producer (IPP) concessions covering design, financing, construction, operation, and maintenance. The concessions run through Ci-Energies, the state electricity utility, and the procurement was launched last year before advancing to shortlist stage, according to Africa Energy. The scale of the ambition is thrown into relief by the starting point. The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) counted just 40MW of installed solar capacity in Côte d’Ivoire at the end of 2024. Thermal generation accounted for approximately 69% of the country’s 2,907MW of installed capacity as of 2023 — a grid profile that makes absorbing intermittent solar generation difficult without storage. The 33MWh of battery storage specified at each site addresses that integration problem directly. A predominantly thermal grid has limited tolerance for the midday surges that solar produces; battery systems capture that output and release it when demand rises after dark, smoothing the load curve and reducing curtailment risk that would otherwise undermine the economics of new solar investment. The procurement sits within the Pacte National Énergie, the government’s overarching framework for reaching 45% renewables — including hydropower — in the national electricity mix by 2030. The framework also encompasses Côte d’Ivoire’s ambition to position itself as a power exporter to neighbouring countries, giving the grid stability question a regional dimension: reliable, dispatchable renewable capacity is a prerequisite for cross-border supply agreements. West Africa’s power interconnection landscape makes that export ambition credible. Côte d’Ivoire already supplies electricity to several neighbours through the West African Power Pool (WAPP), the regional body coordinating grid integration across the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Adding dispatchable solar-plus-storage capacity strengthens the country’s ability to honour export commitments regardless of time of day or weather conditions. For developers shortlisted on the two concessions, the 25-year contract horizon and the involvement of Ci-Energies as the offtake counterparty provide the long-term revenue visibility that project finance for utility-scale renewables typically requires. The move to award stage will be closely watched as a signal of how quickly Côte d’Ivoire can translate procurement ambition into contracted capacity.

artigo.texto: BETHLEHEM, Pa. — Bethlehem City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday to give initial approval to the city’s first zoning rules for data centers, which face a final vote Oct. 20. Bethlehem’s zoning code currently treats a data center like any other industrial use, with no added limits, Planning and Zoning Director Cathy Fletcher told council. The new rules would add a public hearing, require studies on water, power, noise and heat, and keep data centers at least 1,000 feet from homes and schools. The rules will not cover the one data center already proposed in the city, a project on Industrial Drive that could not be built under them. During the nearly three-hour hearing, Councilwoman Jo Daniels said the rules fall short in the areas that matter most to residents. Other council members argued that passing them now is better than leaving data centers unregulated. Get the latest laws & regulations news and updates from across the Valley. By subscribing, you agree to our Privacy Policy and consent to receive updates. Most of the 24 people who spoke during public comment urged council to pass the rules and strengthen them over time. Daniels and Councilman Bryan Callahan both said during the hearing that they did not expect to vote for the rules. Both voted yes. The Industrial Drive project The proposed data center is a two-story building with a 65,000-square-foot footprint at 2184 Industrial Drive, replacing the former Crowder Service Center building along Route 22. Boyle Construction and Paxos, both of the Lehigh Valley, and Tensor IQ of Newark, Del., proposed the project. The site is in the city’s Planned Industrial district, where the ordinance would not allow data centers. City zoning and parcel maps also show every part of the 6.75-acre lot is within 1,000 feet of residentially zoned property. Because its application was filed before the amendment, it will be reviewed under the current code, Fletcher said. The project goes before the city Planning Commission at 5 p.m. Nov. 12 in the Town Hall Rotunda, where the public can comment, Council President Rachel Leon said. Get the latest laws & regulations news and updates from across the Valley. By subscribing, you agree to our Privacy Policy and consent to receive updates. That local review carries added weight under a state order. Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order on data centers on Aug. 18. Under it, the state Department of Environmental Protection will not issue a permit unless the project “has received all required local approvals.” The order also bans nondisclosure agreements, which keep project details secret, on data center projects. What the rules do State law requires every municipality’s zoning to allow every legitimate land use. That means Bethlehem cannot ban data centers or write rules so strict that one could never be built. Under the amendment, data centers would be allowed only in the city’s Industrial district, not its Planned Industrial district, and only by special exception. That means an applicant would need approval from the Zoning Hearing Board at a public hearing, in addition to the usual Planning Commission review. The city Planning Commission voted 4-0 on Aug. 25 to recommend the rules. In a review letter, the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission called them “a thoughtful and intentional response to a complex land use.” Applicants would have to submit several studies and plans with their application, including an environmental study, water and sewer approvals, an energy plan, an emergency plan, a decommissioning plan, a heat plan, a lighting study, and noise studies before and after construction. Noise would be measured at the property line. The post-construction noise study would be due one to 12 months after the city clears the building for use. Buildings would have to sit at least 80 feet from property lines, up from 20 feet for other industrial uses. The setback grows to 200 feet next to any non-industrial lot. It grows to 1,000 feet from a residential district or an existing home, school, day care, park, hospital, or recreation center. That is 50 times the current 20-foot minimum. Larger buildings would also require larger lots. Fletcher said a data center under 50,000 square feet could cover no more than 50% of its lot, down from 65% for other industrial buildings. The limit tightens as buildings grow, she said. Councilwoman Hillary Kwiatek later returned to the rule to walk the audience through it. The rule means “the bigger the building gets, the even huger the lot size has to be,” Kwiatek said. Under the ordinance, each square foot of building between 50,000 and 250,000 square feet needs 3 more square feet of land. Above 250,000 square feet, each added square foot needs 5 more. By that math, a 250,000-square-foot data center would need a lot of about 16 acres, and a 500,000-square-foot one would need about 45 acres. Where the rules stop Fletcher said the city cannot require yearly reports once a data center opens. Zoning Officer David Taylor said post-approval inspections would largely be driven by complaints. Councilman Justin Amann said a zoning fine of $500 a day “is not going to be an issue” for a data center operator. City Solicitor Jack Spirk said the city could also seek a court injunction to stop a violation. Jill Seitz, chief community and regional planner for the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission, said state law limits what zoning can cover. The state Department of Environmental Protection oversees air quality, and the Public Utility Commission oversees electric service, she said. artigo.texto: DeepSeek is close to raising at least 80 billion yuan, or about $12bn, in a new funding round, Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday. Tencent and the battery maker CATL have committed some of the largest sums, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Bloomberg. The Chinese AI lab had first set out to raise about 50 billion yuan. Demand grew after the launch of its latest model, Bloomberg said, and the final total could approach 100 billion yuan. DeepSeek has not announced the round. At these levels, it would top the company’s first outside funding earlier this year. That round raised about 50 billion yuan at a valuation of $52bn to $59bn. Founder Liang Wenfeng was the largest investor in that first round, putting in about 20 billion yuan of his own money. Tencent added roughly 10 billion yuan and CATL about 5 billion yuan, alongside JD.com, NetEase and China’s national AI investment fund. Those same two backers now lead the new round. Tencent runs the WeChat messaging app and a large cloud business. CATL makes batteries for electric cars and is working on solid-state batteries. For Tencent, becoming more closely associated with DeepSeek could enable it to keep up with its domestic competitors. This was reported by Reuters in June when the first round of the comparison was being prepared. Last month, Reuters reported that DeepSeek had secured CITIC Securities to prepare for a possible initial public offering on Shanghai’s STAR Market, a market board for technology companies. However, they said that the timing, valuation and scale of the listing had not yet been determined. DeepSeek originated from High-Flyer, the quantitative hedge fund which Liang set up. The laboratory attracted widespread attention around the beginning of 2025 due to its R1 open-source model and launched its V4 models this year. artigo.texto: Google has been ordered to halt work on two data centers it's developing in Finland, a month after the tech giant committed to investing $15 billion in AI infrastructure in the country. Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency (LVV) on Tuesday issued a notice to Google subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend building work for data center projects planned for Muhos and Kajaani until the environmental impact assessments have been completed. The suspension request applies, among other things, to the removal of trees, removal of topsoil, excavation, quarrying, crushing, transfer of soil masses, ditching and the construction of roads and storage areas, according to a Google translation of an LVV press release. "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance," a Google spokesperson told CNBC, adding that they would follow the LVV's guidance. "We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas," the spokesperson said. "As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos." The LVV ordered Google to halt work no later than Oct. 23. The request does not apply to planning, measurements, soil surveys, or other measures with minor impacts that can be easily restored. "In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure," Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at the Finnish licensing and supervision authority, said in the statement. 'Texas of Europe' Finland has emerged as a key location for data centers amid the AI boom, with hyperscalers and developers eyeing its available land and power, which is in short supply throughout most of Europe. Several data center projects with potential capacities of hundreds of megawatts have recently been announced in the country. The rise in demand has led to Finland being dubbed the "Texas of Europe." The U.S. state has become one of the leading locations for AI data centers globally, with a number of huge projects announced by hyperscalers and AI labs, including Google, Meta, Microsoft and Anthropic. Google's $15 billion plan for Finland will mark its largest investment in Europe. The capital will be deployed through 2028 into data centers and other supporting investments like energy projects, the company said in a statement at the time.

artigo.texto: The tech industry would build data centers twice as fast without the supply constraints they face, the CEO of Nokia told CNBC, underscoring continued demand for AI even as top executives debate slowing down the pace of development. "I don't think you can say in any manner we're overbuilding today because reality is that if we could build 2x faster, our customers could build 2x faster, they probably would," Justin Hotard told CNBC's "The Tech Download" podcast. "So that gives me confidence that we're still in the early days" of the AI buildout, Hotard added. Shortages of key memory chips and energy are among the supply constraints facing the sector. Nokia, one of the world's biggest telecommunications equipment makers, has pivoted to become a key player within the AI infrastructure space. It sells the technology required to connect racks of chips within data centers as well as technology that interconnects data centers across different locations. Nokia's growing role as a "picks and shovels" player in the AI boom appears to have won over investors, with the stock up around 130% over the past year. But there's been continued debate over whether the industry is building data centers too fast and whether demand will be there to sustain it. Investments in the AI buildout from data centers to chips and related infrastructure will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032 — an average of 3.63% of U.S. gross domestic product per year, according to research presented at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity. Companies are using debt, joint ventures and other complex financing mechanisms to raise investment for these projects, which depend on sustained demand for AI services over the long term. Concerns about the pace of the AI buildout were exacerbated by safety worries sparked by an Anthropic researcher's warnings on the existential threat of the technology, which prompted the company's CEO Dario Amodei to call for a slowdown in the development of the most advanced models. That sparked a knee-jerk sell off in AI-related stocks last month. Hotard said that demand for AI is not just predicated on frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI releasing new models. "I think the reality is that we're even where we are today is so early in the deployment, and the power of these models is so massive that there's a lot of there's a lot of demand to run in just deploying," Hotard said. "Even if we didn't have another frontier model released in the next three years, we could probably make tremendous progress just deploying the technology that's there today."

artigo.texto: LG Energy Solution Targets EV Commercialization on 2029, Focusing on Cost and Application-Specific Designs While Samsung SDI Pushes Faster Mass Production With Supply Chain Deals and Sulfide-Based Technology As the commercialization of solid-state batteries comes into sight, technological competition within the domestic battery industry is also beginning in earnest. While Samsung SDI is accelerating efforts up to establishing a material supply chain with the goal of mass production next year, LG Energy Solution puts more weight on securing technological differentiation and cost competitiveness rather than the timing of commercialization. According to the industry on Oct. 7, LG Energy Solution is aiming for the commercialization of graphite-based solid-state batteries for electric vehicles (EV) in 2029, and the commercialization of anode-free solid-state batteries for next-generation applications such as humanoid robots in 2030. A solid-state battery is a battery that changes the electrolyte, the pathway through which lithium ions move, from the existing liquid to a solid. It is also called a ‘dream battery’ as it does not use a flammable liquid electrolyte, thereby lowering the risk of fire and increasing energy density. However, complex manufacturing processes and high production costs are considered challenges that need to be solved for mass production. Rather than rushing commercialization, LG Energy Solution has chosen a strategy of subdividing its technology to fit actual applications. The plan is to secure competitiveness by varying the battery structure according to the required performance, rather than targeting all markets with a single solid-state technology. The company is also developing dry electrode technology to lower high manufacturing costs. This is interpreted as a strategy to lower equipment and process costs as well as production time by reducing the organic solvents and drying processes required in the existing wet process. This comes from the judgment that securing both mass producibility and economic feasibility is important for solid-state batteries to compete in price with existing lithium-ion batteries. In comparison, Samsung SDI is stepping up to establish a supply chain with the goal of commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries faster around next year. It recently signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with EcoPro BM and agreed to cooperate from the development of core materials such as sulfide-based solid electrolytes and cathode materials for solid-state batteries, to quality evaluation and the establishment of a mass production system. EcoPro BM is operating a sulfide-based solid electrolyte pilot plant with an annual capacity of 40 tons. The two companies, which had previously been cautious about disclosing their specific cooperative relationship, have formalized their collaboration for the commercialization of solid-state batteries through this MOU. An industry official said, “The solid-state battery is a market where technological prowess determines competitiveness,” and added, “Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution will engage in a competition for dominance with differentiated strategies that utilize their respective strengths.”

artigo.texto: Carbon credits not only open up additional revenue streams but also help businesses improve their emissions management capabilities, meet market demands, and create added brand value. The value of a credit lies in one ton of carbon reduced. The Vietnamese carbon market is entering an operational phase with many opportunities but also places higher demands on businesses. Investing in carbon credits requires costs for technology, measurement, inventory, verification, and data management, while revenue from selling credits in the initial stages may not be large enough to provide direct financial incentives. However, the value of carbon credits lies not only in transaction revenue. The credit creation process is also linked to improving emission management capacity, meeting market standards, expanding access to green finance, and building the business's position in the supply chain. The story of Thanh Thanh Cong - Bien Hoa Joint Stock Company (AgriS) is a case in point. The company has recorded 4,375 carbon credits from its Verra (VCS) organic fertilizer project, which adheres to international standards, and has issued 25,000 I-REC renewable energy certificates. The Ba Tra plant, specializing in processing agricultural by-products, is expected to provide approximately 9,600 carbon credits annually. AgriS has also signed a bilateral carbon credit transfer agreement with a Singaporean partner under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. According to the company, direct revenue from selling carbon credits currently does not contribute significantly to its financial structure. So what motivates businesses to continue investing? Speaking at the Vietnam Carbon Forum 2026 “From Policy to Action,” Mr. Tran Tan Viet, a member of the Board of Directors of AgriS, stated that early participation in the carbon market contributes to enhancing the reputation and position of businesses in the international market. Several investment funds and financial institutions have proactively explored this, thereby opening up more opportunities for businesses to access green credit sources. The key point is that not all emission reduction activities automatically generate carbon credits. Mr. Nguyen Tuan Quang, Deputy Director of the Climate Change Department, Ministry of Agriculture and Environment , stated that projects must meet requirements for complementarity, integrity, and sustainability; the amount of emission reduction must be measured, validated, and supported by sufficiently reliable data. This requirement lays the foundation for the quality of the carbon market. When credits are used in domestic transactions or international cooperation mechanisms, the ability to measure and verify emission reductions is a crucial factor determining market acceptance. Requirements for sustainable development, environmental responsibility in supply chains, and new trade mechanisms are increasingly impacting production and export activities. According to Mr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, Deputy Head of the Carbon Market Department, Climate Change Agency, Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, processes related to carbon credits need to ensure transparency, rigor, and conformity with international practices. Regarding international cooperation under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, the Climate Change Agency is coordinating with partners to develop detailed forms, guidelines, and procedures. Dr. Nguyen Hung Minh, Deputy Head of the Carbon Market Department, Climate Change Agency, Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, stated that Vietnam is perfecting its system of policies and laws on climate change response. The 2020 Environmental Protection Law, in which Article 139 provides the legal basis for organizing and developing the carbon market, along with subsequent regulations, has gradually concretized the inventory of greenhouse gases, measurement, reporting, assessment, allocation of emission quotas, and operation of the carbon market. Meanwhile, demands from international markets are becoming increasingly clear. The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) directly impacts several sectors such as steel, cement, aluminum, electricity, and hydrogen. In the aviation sector, CORSIA also creates additional demand for carbon credits. These changes make the ability to manage and provide emissions data increasingly an integral part of the requirements for production, business, and export activities. For businesses participating in international supply chains, the ability to demonstrate environmental performance can affect their ability to meet partner requirements and expand cooperation. According to estimates, Vietnam could face a carbon deficit of approximately 2.3 million carbon credits by 2028, equivalent to a financing need of around $92 million if the price per credit remains at $40 per ton. These figures demonstrate that the carbon market is increasingly integrated into many sectors of the economy , from industrial production and exports to aviation and finance. At the enterprise level, early preparation can therefore offer certain advantages. TH Group is a case in point, having started measuring carbon emissions throughout its entire production chain in 2018, before Vietnam made its commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 at COP26 in 2021. Speaking with a reporter from the Industry and Trade Newspaper, Associate Professor Dr. Nguyen Thuong Lang, an economic expert and senior lecturer at the Institute of International Trade and Economics, National Economics University, argued that the value of carbon credits needs to be viewed more broadly than their transaction value. Businesses must invest in technology, improve energy and raw material efficiency, process by-products, control emissions, and build data systems. artigo.texto: Créditos de carbono: Não olhe apenas para o preço. Os créditos de carbono não só abrem novas fontes de receita, como também ajudam as empresas a melhorar suas capacidades de gestão de emissões, atender às demandas do mercado e criar valor agregado à marca. O valor de um crédito corresponde a uma tonelada de carbono reduzida. O mercado de carbono vietnamita está entrando em uma fase operacional com muitas oportunidades, mas também com maiores exigências para as empresas. Investir em créditos de carbono requer custos com tecnologia, medição, inventário, verificação e gestão de dados, enquanto a receita da venda de créditos nos estágios iniciais pode não ser suficiente para fornecer incentivos financeiros diretos. No entanto, o valor dos créditos de carbono não reside apenas na receita das transações. O processo de criação de créditos também está ligado à melhoria da capacidade de gestão de emissões, ao atendimento aos padrões de mercado, à ampliação do acesso ao financiamento verde e ao fortalecimento da posição da empresa na cadeia de suprimentos. A história da Thanh Thanh Cong - Bien Hoa Joint Stock Company (AgriS) é um exemplo disso. A empresa registrou 4.375 créditos de carbono provenientes de seu projeto de fertilizante orgânico Verra (VCS), que segue padrões internacionais, e emitiu 25.000 certificados de energia renovável I-REC. A planta de Ba Tra, especializada no processamento de subprodutos agrícolas, deverá gerar aproximadamente 9.600 créditos de carbono anualmente. A AgriS também firmou um acordo bilateral de transferência de créditos de carbono com um parceiro de Singapura , nos termos do Artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris. Segundo a empresa, a receita direta proveniente da venda de créditos de carbono atualmente não contribui de forma significativa para sua estrutura financeira. O que motiva as empresas a continuarem investindo? Em sua apresentação no Fórum de Carbono do Vietnã 2026 “Da Política à Ação”, o Sr. Tran Tan Viet, membro do Conselho de Administração da AgriS, afirmou que a participação precoce no mercado de carbono contribui para fortalecer a reputação e o posicionamento das empresas no mercado internacional. Diversos fundos de investimento e instituições financeiras têm explorado essa possibilidade de forma proativa, abrindo assim mais oportunidades para que as empresas acessem fontes de crédito verde. O ponto crucial é que nem todas as atividades de redução de emissões geram automaticamente créditos de carbono. O Sr. Nguyen Tuan Quang, Diretor Adjunto do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente , afirmou que os projetos devem atender aos requisitos de complementaridade, integridade e sustentabilidade; a quantidade de redução de emissões deve ser mensurada, validada e comprovada por dados suficientemente confiáveis. Esse requisito estabelece a base para a qualidade do mercado de carbono. Quando os créditos são utilizados em transações domésticas ou em mecanismos de cooperação internacional, a capacidade de mensurar e verificar as reduções de emissões é um fator crucial para a aceitação no mercado. Quando a demanda do mercado impacta a produção Você também pode gostar A pressão para reduzir as emissões já não provém apenas das políticas ambientais. Os requisitos para o desenvolvimento sustentável, a responsabilidade ambiental nas cadeias de abastecimento e os novos mecanismos comerciais estão a impactar cada vez mais as atividades de produção e exportação. De acordo com o Sr. Nguyen Thanh Cong, Chefe Adjunto do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono da Agência de Alterações Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e do Ambiente, os processos relacionados com os créditos de carbono precisam de garantir transparência, rigor e conformidade com as práticas internacionais. No que diz respeito à cooperação internacional ao abrigo do Artigo 6.2 do Acordo de Paris, a Agência de Alterações Climáticas está a coordenar com os parceiros o desenvolvimento de formulários, diretrizes e procedimentos detalhados. O Dr. Nguyen Hung Minh, Vice-Chefe do Departamento do Mercado de Carbono da Agência de Mudanças Climáticas do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, afirmou que o Vietnã está aprimorando seu sistema de políticas e leis de resposta às mudanças climáticas. A Lei de Proteção Ambiental de 2020, cujo Artigo 139 estabelece a base legal para a organização e o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono, juntamente com as regulamentações subsequentes, concretizou gradualmente o inventário de gases de efeito estufa, a medição, a comunicação, a avaliação, a alocação de cotas de emissão e a operação do mercado de carbono. Entretanto, as exigências dos mercados internacionais estão se tornando cada vez mais claras. O Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) da União Europeia impacta diretamente diversos setores, como aço, cimento, alumínio, eletricidade e hidrogênio. No setor da aviação, o CORSIA também gera demanda adicional por créditos de carbono. Essas mudanças tornam a capacidade de gerenciar e fornecer dados de emissões cada vez mais parte integrante dos requisitos para atividades de produção, negócios e exportação. Para empresas que participam de cadeias de suprimentos internacionais, a capacidade de demonstrar desempenho ambiental pode afetar sua capacidade de atender aos requisitos de parceiros e expandir a cooperação. Segundo estimativas, o Vietnã poderá enfrentar um déficit de carbono de aproximadamente 2,3 milhões de créditos de carbono até 2028, o que equivale a uma necessidade de financiamento de cerca de US$ 92 milhões, caso o preço por crédito se mantenha em US$ 40 por tonelada. Esses números demonstram que o mercado de carbono está cada vez mais integrado a diversos setores da economia , da produção industrial e exportações à aviação e finanças. Em nível empresarial, o planejamento antecipado pode, portanto, oferecer certas vantagens. O Grupo TH é um exemplo disso, tendo começado a medir as emissões de carbono em toda a sua cadeia

artigo.texto: Chinese Battery Makers Grab 34% Share Outside China; South Korea's Big Three Slump to 27% Chinese battery manufacturers are rapidly expanding their market share in the global EV market outside China. From January through August this year, usage volumes for Chinese players including CATL and BYD surged sharply in non-China markets, while the combined share of South Korea's three major battery makers—heavily reliant on North America—fell below 30%. According to data released on October 7 by SNE Research, a specialized energy market research firm, total battery usage in battery electric vehicles (BEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), and hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) registered outside China from January through August reached approximately 360.5 GWh. That represents a 23.7% increase year over year, outpacing the global overall growth rate of 19.7% by 4.0 percentage points. However, the monthly growth rate for August alone slowed to 9%. SNE Research attributed this to the impact of the North American demand vacuum becoming more pronounced in monthly figures. Broad-Based Growth for Chinese Players CATL solidified its No. 1 position with 121.3 GWh of usage, up 43.3% year over year. Its market share climbed 4.7 percentage points from 29.0% to 33.7%. In Europe, usage rose 30.4% from 61.8 GWh to 80.6 GWh, while in Asia it more than doubled to 24.0 GWh. BYD maintained third place with 39.7 GWh, up 66.5%. Its share rose 2.8 percentage points from 8.2% to 11.0%. Usage grew broadly across Europe (14.5 GWh, +65.6%), Asia (13.2 GWh, +41.7%), and South America (6.2 GWh, +138.5%). Growth among later-entrant Chinese players was even steeper. Gotion High-tech surged 147.2% to 14.4 GWh, SVOLT jumped 105.2% to 11.4 GWh, and CALB rose 77.6% to 8.4 GWh. EVE posted the highest growth rate among the top 10 companies at 185.6%, reaching 7.5 GWh. South Korea's Big Three Fall Across the Board on North American Weakness The combined market share of South Korea's three major battery makers dropped 11.1 percentage points from 37.9% to 26.8%. The decline in usage was concentrated in North America. The trio's North American usage fell 46.5% from 47.4 GWh to 25.3 GWh, while Europe rose 5.2% from 49.9 GWh to 52.5 GWh and Asia increased 33.0% from 11.2 GWh to 14.8 GWh. LG Energy Solution posted 58.1 GWh, down 5.8% year over year, but held onto the No. 2 spot in non-China markets. European usage rose 9.8% to 31.3 GWh and Asia grew 44.4% to 9.2 GWh, but North American usage tumbled 42.3% from 25.2 GWh to 14.6 GWh, dragging down overall results. Its market share fell 5.1 percentage points from 21.2% to 16.1%. SK On remained in fifth place with 24.8 GWh, down 14.4%. Its share slipped 3.0 percentage points from 9.9% to 6.9%. North American usage fell 41.8%, and Europe also declined 1.5%. Samsung SDI posted the steepest decline among the top 10 companies, falling 32.0% to 13.6 GWh. Its share contracted 3.0 percentage points from 6.8% to 3.8%. European usage was roughly flat year over year at 8.3 GWh, but North American usage plummeted 62% from 10.4 GWh to 3.9 GWh. Japan's Panasonic ranked fourth with 29.7 GWh, up 1.8%. Tesla's North American volume underpinned its performance, but with growth well below the non-China market average, its share fell 1.7 percentage points from 10.0% to 8.3%. Non-China Market Usage and Share by Major Player Note: January–August 2026, excluding China market. Share change is versus the same period last year. Gotion High-tech's share was not disclosed. Policy and Supply Chain Capabilities Will Be Decisive SNE Research projected that regional policies and customer diversification will determine supplier competitiveness going forward. The research firm said, "Local production capacity, price competitiveness, and supply chain traceability capabilities in preparation for the battery passport regime taking effect next February will be the key variables determining market position." The rise of Chinese players reflects simultaneous penetration of the European market and expansion across Asia. South Korean manufacturers, by contrast, took a direct hit from slowing North American EV demand driven by policy shifts including the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Given their heavy North American exposure, the shock of market contraction was proportionally severe. Investors and industry observers see the key question for South Korean battery makers as how quickly they can capture the timing of a North American demand recovery while sustaining growth in Europe and Asia. Given the pace of Chinese players' price competitiveness and production capacity expansion, securing next-generation battery technology and supply chain transparency—beyond simply defending market share—is expected to be the crux of long-term competitiveness. artigo.texto: For nine months, the Rev. Edward Moultrie of St. Paul CME Church and his congregation filled county meetings, urging officials to reject a proposal for a massive data center near their church and homes. They warned that the project near Walterboro, South Carolina, would threaten the waterways they rely on and bring pollution to their doorstep. On Monday, they won. In January, two weeks after Capital B first wrote about the proposal, residents sued Colleton County over its effort to change the zoning code to allow data centers in rural areas. This week, the Southern Environmental Law Center reached an agreement with the county to resolve that lawsuit. The fight in Colleton County underscored a pattern in where these facilities are proposed. Last year, after a majority-white county in Georgia blocked a data center, the data center developer, Eagle Rock Partners, proposed a similar project in Colleton County, where the share of Black residents is nearly twice as high. Analyses have found that communities closest to U.S. data centers regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency are “overwhelmingly” nonwhite. Moultrie said the settlement “is a relief.” “I can’t preach to my people that God is making a way for them and offering them hope, and then have something like this come into the community to take people’s hope away,” he said. “Black people here have worked hard all their lives to survive and thrive and protect their land. It gives us some kind of sense of pride knowing that we’re not going to go by the wayside or be destroyed or taken for granted — for now.” With the settlement, the county has agreed to establish a “Data Center Exclusion Area” that prohibits data centers across the majority of the ACE Basin in Colleton County, which is a rural area home to ecologically sensitive animals and some of the most important waterways in South Carolina. The exclusion area includes the land where the data center was proposed in December 2025. The data center would have been over 800 acres, making it one of the largest in the South, which has become the epicenter of data center development. “I have lived in the ACE Basin my entire life, right here in Colleton County. My family has been here for generations. The original data center complex that was proposed would have surrounded my property on three sides and completely changed the area,” said Miles Crosby, one of the residents who brought the lawsuit. “I’m thankful we could reach an outcome that not only prevents data centers from surrounding my home but also protects the majority of the ACE Basin in Colleton County from data center development.” In the first half of 2026, at least 115 data centers nationwide were blocked by local residents. The blocked projects’ price tags totaled roughly $200 billion, according to Data Center Watch, a group tracking data center development. At the same time, data center development continues to climb. August saw the most money ever spent on data center construction in the U.S., up more than 73% over the past 12 months. The struggle for local Black communities is not over. A new fossil fuel plant, partially proposed to keep this and other data centers running, is moving forward in a majority-Black area located in Colleton County. The methane gas power plant would result in more than $30 million in local health care costs as residents begin to struggle through respiratory illnesses, according to a pollution analysis by the Southern Environmental Law Center. The pollution from gas power plants — fine particulate matter known as PM2.5 — can penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. It is linked to asthma attacks, strokes, dementia, and cancer. Black Americans have the highest death rate from such pollution in the U.S. Chris DeScherer, the South Carolina office director for the Southern Environmental Law Center, said the group will continue to “help ensure that any data center projects in Colleton County and beyond are developed responsibly with respect to surrounding communities and natural resources.” Read More:

artigo.texto: BYD Sealion 6 Adds All-Wheel Drive in South Korea…Dual-Motor Setup Hits 100 km/h in 5 Seconds BYD Korea has added an all-wheel-drive (AWD) trim to its plug-in hybrid (PHEV) SUV, the Sealion 6 DM-i, and began taking pre-orders on the 6th. The strategy is to broaden choices beyond the existing front-wheel-drive (FWD) single configuration to respond to diverse driving environments and consumer preferences. The newly unveiled Sealion 6 DM-i AWD places electric motors with peak output of 150 kW (204 horsepower) on both the front and rear axles. The front motor produces 300 Nm of maximum torque, while the rear motor delivers 340 Nm, giving the rear axle greater rotational force. The vehicle accelerates from a standstill to 100 km/h in 5.0 seconds, a configuration that emphasizes the instant acceleration response characteristic of electric motors. Along with the AWD system, dedicated Mud and Sand terrain modes have been applied to ensure driving stability on rough surfaces such as unpaved roads. The goal is versatility that spans urban commuting as well as weekend leisure and outdoor activities. Battery and Charging Performance The vehicle is equipped with a 26.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery. It can travel 93 km in pure electric mode under South Korea's Ministry of Environment certification, allowing daily short-distance driving to be operated like a fully electric vehicle. On the charging front, it supports approximately 18 kW DC fast charging and features V2L (Vehicle-to-Load) capability with up to 3.3 kW of external power output. This allows the vehicle battery to power electronic devices during outdoor activities such as camping. Convenience features have also been upgraded compared to the existing trim. The audio system uses HARMAN's premium brand Infinity sound system, with a total of 10 speakers including a subwoofer. A head-up display (HUD), multi-color ambient lighting, metal door sill plates, and dynamic ceremony lighting have been applied to elevate the interior ambiance. The driver's seat supports 8-way power adjustment with memory function. Pricing and Market Strategy The Sealion 6 DM-i AWD starts at ₩41.9 million (approximately $31,000). BYD Korea stated, "By adding AWD, we have broadened the range of choices according to customers' driving environments and preferences," adding, "We plan to continue introducing products that consider the diverse lifestyles of South Korean consumers and to continuously strengthen product and service experiences." The addition of this trim is interpreted as BYD's intent to compete head-on with existing hybrid SUVs in the South Korean market not only on price competitiveness but also on driving performance and convenience features. The Sealion 6 was previously launched with a single FWD trim, and the addition of this AWD version has further thickened the lineup in South Korea's PHEV SUV market. In another statement, a BYD Korea representative said the AWD trim, which combines dynamic driving performance with premium convenience features, now allows the company to meet the expectations of customers seeking diverse PHEV options. As the presence of Chinese-made PHEVs grows in the South Korean market, the Sealion 6 AWD — offering dual-motor all-wheel drive and 93 km of electric range at a starting price in the low ₩40 million range (approximately $30,000) — is expected to appeal to value-conscious consumers. However, South Korea's PHEV market remains small compared to the EV segment, and factors such as consumer perception of Chinese-made vehicles and changes in government subsidy policies are expected to serve as variables in actual sales performance. artigo.texto: South Korea's Big Three Battery Material Makers Counter China with LFP, LMR, and Solid-State Push — Cathode Supremacy Battle Reignites Chinese battery makers are rapidly encroaching on the global market with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries as their weapon, forcing South Korean cathode material producers to overhaul their product strategies. POSCO Future M, EcoPro BM, and L&F — which had concentrated on high-nickel ternary chemistries — are now racing to close the gap with China by strengthening their LFP response while simultaneously broadening their portfolios to include lithium-manganese-rich (LMR) and solid-state battery materials. According to SNE Research on October 5, global EV battery usage excluding China reached 316.2 GWh in the first seven months of this year, up 25.8% year over year. During the same period, the combined market share of CATL and BYD climbed to 44.6%, up 7.0 percentage points from a year earlier. Chinese companies that once relied heavily on their domestic market are now rapidly seizing the non-China market by expanding supply to global automakers, establishing overseas production bases, and leveraging the price competitiveness of LFP batteries. By contrast, combined battery usage by South Korea's three major cell makers — LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI — in the non-China market fell 8.9% year over year to 86.1 GWh. Their combined share tumbled 10.4 percentage points from 37.6% to 27.2%. While the overall non-China market grew more than 20%, the South Korean trio actually contracted, widening the gap with Chinese rivals. The decline in North American usage was a particularly significant drag on their performance. South Korea's materials industry is strengthening its LFP response beyond its traditional high-nickel focus while preparing LMR and solid-state technologies as next-generation counteroffensive cards. The growing share of entry-level EV models and the explosive growth of the AI data center-driven energy storage system (ESS) market are creating structural demand for low-cost, high-safety materials. Defending with LFP, Counterattacking with LMR POSCO Future M is placing the most aggressive bet on LMR cathode materials. The LMR cathode jointly developed by POSCO Holdings' Future Technology Research Center and global automakers and battery companies has successfully completed pilot production, and the company is now working to secure mass-production technology. LMR reduces the use of expensive nickel and cobalt while increasing manganese content, lowering costs while maintaining high energy density. It also has the advantage of being compatible with existing NCM cathode production facilities, relatively reducing the burden of new factory investment. At the same time, the company is rapidly expanding its LFP footprint in Pohang. It plans to convert part of its existing Pohang NCM cathode lines to LFP and begin supply by the end of this year, while its joint venture CNP New Material Technology is building a dedicated LFP plant with a maximum annual capacity of 50,000 tons at the Pohang Yeongilman Industrial Complex, targeting mass production in 2027. It is a two-track strategy: defending the current market with LFP while targeting the next mid-to-low-priced EV market with LMR. SK Securities analysts Park Hyung-woo and Jung Young-hwan noted, "Precursors and anode materials are expected to become bottlenecks in the LFP landscape next year. POSCO Future M is well positioned to respond flexibly to this." EcoPro BM is raising its commercialization readiness on both the LMR and solid-state fronts. Its LMR cathode has entered the final validation stage targeting mass production for key customers. The company has optimized its processes so that existing ternary cathode production lines can be used as-is, enabling rapid conversion to mass production once orders are confirmed. For solid-state batteries, the company is operating a solid electrolyte pilot line, and its products are undergoing quality verification by major battery makers. The mass-production line design is also complete, with construction to begin once customer demand is confirmed, targeting mass production as early as 2027. Eugene Investment & Securities analyst Han Byung-hwa said, "Next-generation materials including solid-state and LMR have advanced to the stage just before mass production. Once the market recovers from the EV chasm, the company will be able to secure growth engines simultaneously in both existing high-nickel and new battery chemistries." L&F Builds the Broadest Portfolio L&F, based in Daegu, is pursuing the broadest portfolio strategy. Building on its experience as the world's first to mass-produce ultra-high-nickel 95% cathodes, the company has entered LFP mass production and is expanding its next-generation product lineup to include high-voltage mid-nickel, LMR, all-solid-state battery (ASSB), and sodium-ion battery (SIB) cathodes. It unveiled next-generation materials at major exhibitions this year and is in concrete discussions with select customers on mass production of solid-state battery cathodes. Its current primary focus is LFP. The company is pursuing commercialization of LFP cathodes at a level unprecedented in South Korea in the second half of this year, while developing proprietary iron phosphate (FP) technology and a precursor-free manufacturing process to build a supply chain with reduced dependence on China. The plan is to add LMR and solid-state cathodes going forward, transitioning to a structure that addresses everything from high-nickel to mid-to-low-priced and next-generation markets. L&F recently signed a mid-to-long-term LFP cathode supply contract with Samsung SDI worth 1.6067 trillion won (approximately $1.2 billion), followed by a 160 billion won (approximately $119.0 million) supply deal with SK On.
