artigo.texto: Berlin-based ebike startup Lemmo has been shaking up the European market with a small selection of handsome mid-range models since 2022. It's now got something in the works for families and more adventurous riders with a versatile SUV ebike that promises to take you places while delivering an exceptionally comfortable ride. The Lemmo 3 is a long-tail ebike with room for cargo in the front and rear, plus pannier bags and up to two child seats. It sports a full suspension setup, a hydraulic seatpost, and all-terrain tires to soak up bumps and make it a breeze to cover all kinds of surfaces. The brand says this model is three years in the making, and includes plenty of tech for safety, performance, and convenience that you'd expect to see on the latest ebikes. It's also capable of covering longer distances than just your usual city commutes. Let's talk suspension first. A high-load spring for the rear suspension affords 80 mm of travel to ensure your little passenger is comfortable. Up front, you've got hydraulic forks that deliver 80 mm of travel too. Meanwhile, the seatpost offers 20 mm of travel as well. Closer to the asphalt, 65 mm wide all-terrain tires offer cushioning and stability while riding with heavier cargo. Lemmo's gone with a 960-Wh semi-solid state battery, which reportedly allows for up to 110 miles (180 km) of range and won't go up in flames from punctures or thermal runaway incidents. This pairs with a rear hub Bafang H720 motor that's rated for 750 W of continuous power in the US (500 W in Canada, and 250 W in Europe), and a three-speed automatic gearbox. This setup allows for a pedal assist up to 28 mph (45 km/h). With this kind of kit, the Lemmo 3 should be up to the task of tackling steep inclines and all manner of rough terrain. The brand says its direct steering makes it easier to maneuver than conventional cargo bikes, despite its long wheelbase. Riders ranging from 5ft1 (155 cm) to 6ft5 (195 cm) can enjoy a comfy upright riding position thanks to the adjustable stem and seat. If you plan to take this out on the trail on camping trips, it'll happily handle up to 176 lb (80 kg) of gear in the rear, and an additional 44 lb (20 kg) on the front rack. There's some neat tech on here too, including GPS tracking and a motion detection alarm for security, a 3.5-inch touchscreen displaying your riding metrics, a rear-approaching radar with automatic brake lights, and keyless start. That makes this a compelling option for people looking for a more versatile ebike than the vast range available for riding only around town. Lemmo is scheduled to crowdfund this model on Kickstarter later this month, during which the Essential model will be available at about US$2,155. That's discounted down from its expected MSRP of €3,390 ($3,890) – but it requires an early reservation on Lemmo's site with a refundable $45 deposit. You can add on a belt drive for an extra $193. There are also a couple of bike bundles which include accessories like a passenger guardrail, seat pads and foot boards, pannier bags, and a front rack. With that, Lemmo's set to go up against the Amflow TL Carbon we saw earlier this year. That's another capable SUV ebike, with a powerful motor and swappable add-on battery – at a slightly higher price above the $4,000 mark. Check out the Lemmo 3 on the company's site, and head here for the Kickstarter campaign that's yet to go live at the time of writing (you can sign up to be notified when it takes off). If all goes as expected, orders are estimated to begin shipping next April in the aforementioned regions. Source: Lemmo

artigo.texto: China’s Gotion High-Tech has secured 6GWh of battery storage capacity in Saudi Arabia’s first utility-scale battery storage programme, accounting for around 75% of the total tender. Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) awarded the company three core sites of Al Muwayah, Haden and Al Kahafa, under the G1 project. Each site will provide 500MW/2GWh, giving the project a combined capacity of 2GW/8GWh and a value of around $1.16 billion. The award represents the first international large-scale deployment of Gotion Grid, the company’s utility-scale energy storage system. Gotion says the system has been engineered for extreme environmental conditions, with an operating range from -30°C to 55°C. Its thermal management system is designed for desert conditions and maintains full output during sandstorms, while reducing high-temperature degradation by 40% compared with conventional systems. The ESS has a stated design life of 25 years, compared with an industry average of 15–20 years. The company says this can avoid mid-life equipment replacement, an important consideration for build-own-operate contracts requiring more than 20 years of operation. The system also incorporates an AI-powered battery management system for intelligent dispatch, proactive safety warnings and lifecycle diagnostics. All three Gotion sites can be remotely operated and connected to Saudi Arabia’s 380kV backbone grid. The award adds to the company’s growing presence across the Middle East and North Africa, where it says its regional footprint is around 9GWh. This includes a 1.5GWh BESS in Egypt alongside a planned 3GWh local manufacturing base, and a 1.2GWh project in Morocco with ACWA Power. Globally, the company’s cumulative system-level storage projects exceed 10 GWh, including a 281MW/843MWh solar-storage project under construction in Australia that is expected to enter commercial operation in the first half of 2027. With G1 awarded and G2 underway, the Saudi programme could provide further opportunities as renewable deployment and grid stability requirements increase. Image: Gotion BESS. Credit: Gotion

artigo.texto: Elon Musk's data centers are pushing out a family that's owned land since "before people of color were allowed to" On a 2-acre property in Mississippi, 52-year-old Krystal Polk's family lived off the land for generations, raising chickens and pigs, growing onions and herbs and trading their peaches for pears. The land, on the border with Tennessee in the city of Southaven, was her family's survival, Polk said. "We lived a very simplistic life," she told CBS News. While life there may have been simple in Polk's view, the circumstances surrounding her home rarely ever were. Her family acquired the property "before people of color were allowed to have land," she said, and it's been passed down for four generations. When Polk's parents first moved in, they discovered "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill of their property, she said. Holding on to the land was made more difficult a year ago when a noisy neighbor appeared across the street — a power plant so loud, it drove the family away. Since then, the land has sat mostly empty, occupied only by an unrelenting hum. The plant, which is powering Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the Memphis area, has sparked backlash from Southaven residents concerned about noise and air pollution. A petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plant has over 1,400 signatures. Polk said she remembers when she could hear the birds chirping at her family home. Now, she said the plant's "constant roaring" lingers in her ears even after she leaves. "It's like you're in the middle of the airport where the planes are taking off, but they never take off," she said. SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, recently said in a July press release that it is investing millions of dollars in sound walls and silencers with "advanced quieting technologies" around the plant. Southaven residents have told CBS News that one sound wall installed so far has provided little reprieve from the noise. "We gathered there" Over the course of two years, Musk has expanded his footprint in the Memphis region starting with the construction of his Colossus 1 data center just north of Southaven in 2024. By January 2026, two more data centers were announced. This July, Musk quietly confirmed the construction of another local data center, "Minihard," in a reply to a post on his platform X. Musk's SpaceXAI projects will total more than $20 billion in investments to Southaven, which Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a press release will "bring amazing opportunities to its residents for generations." But for Polk, the development has meant a new kind of strain on her family. "We don't know the future," she said. "So we're not sure what to invest into it." Polk moved away from the family home after getting married, and for years, it bounced between relatives. It was where Polk churned her own ice cream as a child, held her rehearsal dinner when she got married and hosted the holidays each year. "We gathered there and we thanked God for what we had," she said. "It was always a celebration." She planned to return as a retiree and eventually pass the property down to her children. But now, those plans have been put on hold. Apart from the "24/7" noise, Polk said she and her family have asthma and are concerned about fumes from the gas turbines at the plant. "I'm afraid that we will be the ones that everyone looks back on and says, 'Hey, remember they tried to tell us that these things were hazardous to our health and causing harm,'" Polk said. "I'm afraid that we're going to be those casualties." The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and other groups sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in April, alleging that the plant "emits significant amounts of harmful pollutants." In June, SpaceXAI filed a motion to dismiss the case, and the Department of Justice also moved to intervene and dismiss the case. The Justice Department said in a statement that the matter "concerns national security and Mississippi's lawful action regarding permitting" and that the NAACP's lawsuit "could hinder the War Department's use of AI for national defense." CBS News reached out to SpaceXAI multiple times for comment and has not heard back. The company has entered into an agreement with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality that includes removing the 69 temporary turbines at the plant and replacing them with 41 permanent turbines over the course of a year. But a study conducted by EmPower Analytics Group found that the plan to install dozens of gas turbines would increase air pollution in the area and would be concentrated in communities that are disproportionately Black. The study was commissioned by the Southern Environmental Law Center, which is co-counsel for the plaintiffs in the NAACP's lawsuit against xAI and MZX Tech. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said in a statement that it doesn't comment on "third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation" and that it "remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations." MDEQ said that as part of the permitting process, MZX Tech was required to demonstrate that the proposed facility would not violate air quality standards. Still, residents are not convinced. Shannon Samsa, a 27-year-old physician assistant living in Southaven, is concerned about the plant's impact on her community's health. She's become an outspoken advocate against the plant, speaking up at city meetings and leading the Safe and Sound Coalition as its director. "It's not just my neighbors, it's not just my family and friends, it's my future patients," she said. "It's also a huge healthcare issue." artigo.texto: A moratorium on the facilities that enable artificial intelligence would last 45 days and could be extended to 22 months. The data centers powering artificial intelligence technology — and the accompanying public outcry — are officially something San Francisco city leaders can’t ignore. The San Francisco Board of Supervisors on Tuesday unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on data centers that would pause city approvals of the facilities and task the Planning Department with studying their impacts and developing long-term controls. The moratorium now awaits action from the mayor. “During this period, we are looking at issues including energy, water, air quality, land use, and community impacts, while working toward stronger protections and meaningful community input, as well as a data center definition that is clear to everyone,” said Supervisor Shamann Walton, who authored the moratorium. Tuesday’s vote is a significant step as city leaders grapple with the wider land use and infrastructure impacts of one of the city’s biggest exports. By November, city leaders will convene a hearing about progress by the Planning Department and its findings on data centers. The moratorium could be extended to 22 months, but it’s unclear whether city leaders would entertain the idea. Walton represents District 10, which stretches from Visitacion Valley and Bayview Hunters-Point to Potrero Hill and Dogpatch. His district has two of the six data center sites in San Francisco, according to market intelligence firm Data Center Map (opens in new tab). His district may have been eyed for a third one. In August, a lobbyist for a private equity firm advertising a 1.6-acre data center (opens in new tab) met with two of Mayor Daniel Lurie’s policy chiefs about planning and building permits for a waterfront plot of land in Dogpatch. The cities of Oakley, Richmond, and Gilroy already have moratoriums on data centers, while Oakland and Hayward are considering it. The Land Use and Transportation Committee advanced Walton’s proposal to the full board. At the committee’s Monday meeting, more than a dozen people showed up in support of the moratorium on new data centers. Among them was Arieann Harrison, a Bayview resident and executive director of the Marie Harrison Community Foundation (opens in new tab). She said her community already deals with worse health outcomes than other parts of the city, triggered by the industrial facilities located in District 10. “We need for this committee right here to stand on business when it comes to the health outcomes of our districts,” Harrison said at the Monday meeting. Walton’s proposal is among his final priorities in office. He was first elected in 2018 and will term out in January. All three of the frontrunners in the race to replace him on the Board of Supervisors are supportive of a data center moratorium. “Transparency about water and energy demands enforceable community benefits and a real opportunity for residents to weigh in before projects are approved, not after,” Walton said at the Monday committee meeting. Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the moratorium takes effect immediately. It awaits action from the mayor. More about the author Omar Rashad reports on San Francisco government and politics.

artigo.texto: First Look: West Feliciana’s data center Parish president says tax revenue and transparency were priorities in deal WEST FELICIANA PARISH, La. — A data center under construction in West Feliciana Parish will serve as a processing hub for Anthropic’s Claude artificial intelligence model when it opens in just over a year. Water usage and energy consumption are top concerns as Louisiana positions itself for a national A.I. build-out. Size and scope The data center will measure roughly 10 football fields long once completed. Projects of similar size elsewhere in the country have raised concerns over groundwater usage and rising electric bills for nearby residents. Parish President Kenny Havard said protecting the community against those issues was part of his goal. The developer Hut 8 is partnering with Entergy for a new substation on site that will power the project, fully funded by the company. On top of that, the data center will be using a closed-loop coolant system that replaces the need for tapping groundwater. “One was water and the other was taxes, we wanted to make sure everyone in West Feliciana Parish pays the same taxes whether you’re big industry or the local grocery store,” Havard said. Tax revenue and community funding Havard said the data center will bring in $90 million in tax revenue every year. That money will go back into the community through funding, infrastructure projects and rebates on property taxes. “We would have to build 6,000 houses to pay for one mile of road the way the taxes are distributed so this allows us to keep the quality of life that makes West Feliciana such a special place,” Havard said. Transparency in the deal process The agreement was made without non-disclosure agreements or private negotiations, according to Hut 8’s Hailey Miller. “Working with the parish president and parish council, a deal was done in public view, in open, transparent and for everyone to have input and consideration,” Miller said. State and political reaction Gov. Jeff Landry has pointed to more than $200 billion in industrial development during his time in office. Landry pushed back against critics of transparency in deals, who say secrecy is sometimes necessary to attract large projects. “Everything we’ve done to change policy in this state has been in the public so the public gets to grade us on that, this just says when these companies come in we don’t tell anybody they are coming in. Why? Because we want to keep them here!” Landry said. Many of Hut 8’s data centers across the country mine bitcoin rather than power artificial intelligence models like the one at River Bend. That connection brought bitcoin investor Donald Trump Jr. to the site. “People understand generally that you need AI, its the space race of 2026, its a really big deal there’s another reason why China is funding 200,000 bots on Twitter trying to vilify AI, its not because its bad for America, its because America leading is bad for China and we need to do that while still addressing the needs of the community,” Trump Jr. said. Construction timeline About 1,200 construction employees are working day and night to complete the project. The data center is expected to be operational by the end of 2027. artigo.texto: Em Brasília, a CNA recebeu na terça-feira (6) integrantes da Nuffield, rede global de produtores e especialistas do agro voltada à formação de lideranças e ao intercâmbio de conhecimento. O grupo reuniu representantes de Brasil, Holanda, Irlanda, Malaui, Zimbábue e Austrália. Elena Castellani, responsável pela área internacional da CNA, destacou o perfil produtivo brasileiro e explicou frentes da CNA, do Senar e do Instituto CNA, como inteligência técnica, capacitação, defesa de interesses, representação e apoio gerencial e técnico a produtores. A comitiva passou ainda pelo Instituto CNA, onde viu tecnologias voltadas ao setor agrícola. A ferramenta de dados da CNA despertou dúvidas sobre como as informações são coletadas, analisadas e implementadas. PSA, sigla de pagamento por serviços ambientais, e mercado de carbono regulado foram apontados como desafios comuns a vários países. Para Jackie Morrison, da Nuffield Austrália, o encontro ampliou a leitura que o grupo fez do Brasil. Segundo ela, os participantes entenderam que o país pode ser concorrente e parceiro de cooperação. Criadora de mel em parceria com o marido, ela investiga desde 2023 o Manejo Integrado de Pragas (MIP) para apoiar a apicultura australiana diante do ácaro Varroa destructor. Luciana Kliemann, que integra a Nuffield Brasil e cultiva grãos em Mato Grosso do Sul, considerou relevante apresentar a CNA ao grupo após uma programação internacional voltada a soluções, inovação e contato com produtores. Além do Brasil, o roteiro passou por Austrália, França, Romênia, China e Cingapura, com atividades em setembro e outubro de 2026. No período, os participantes analisaram modelos de produção, políticas, inovações e desafios ambientais e comerciais do campo.

artigo.texto: Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson’s recent defense of data centers presents a fundamentally flawed economic development narrative (“When judging data center incentives, don’t ignore the revenue,” Sept. 30). While he touts short-term revenue, his ledger ignores the long-term, structural costs these facilities impose on local communities. First, using job creation to justify data center subsidies is a sleight of hand. While $1.2 billion in construction permits is impressive, they’re short-term bumps in revenue. This masks the reality that data centers are essentially ghost towns once operational. They consume prime industrial real estate but employ only a small number of permanent staff members, meaning taxpayers are often subsidizing millions of dollars per permanent job. Furthermore, major tech companies rely on specialized, traveling construction crews. The economic multiplier effect largely leaves town when the concrete dries. Second, the mayor’s claim that Class 6B incentives don’t harm homeowners ignores the basic math of Illinois property taxes. When a data center’s assessed value is artificially slashed, the local tax levy doesn’t shrink. The burden simply shifts onto everyone else, driving up residential tax bills for 12 to 24 years. This is compounded when tax increment financing districts are used, such as the one Elk Grove Village created for the Vulcan Construction Materials site in 2022. While the mayor suggests schools stand to benefit, it should be noted TIFs divert new tax revenue to pay for project costs for up to 23 years, meaning schools and municipal services wait decades for the promised windfall. Worse, once operational, these operators frequently deploy aggressive legal teams to appeal their property assessments year after year, forcing municipalities to spend taxpayer dollars defending their own revenue. Finally, while data centers don’t add students to classrooms, they place enormous, invisible strains on our infrastructure. Their construction increases wear and tear on local roads from construction vehicles. Once completed, they are massive consumers of municipal water for cooling and place unprecedented demands on the electrical grid. These upgrades are eventually paid for by everyday ratepayers. Subsidizing heavily automated server farms that hollow out industrial parks, generate negligible employment and strain our grid is not the “pro-growth” policy our region needs. — Donald Guisinger, Strong Towns Oak Forest Will data centers pay fair share? Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig B. Johnson in his op-ed completely ignores the higher cost of water and electricity that his constituents will face subsidizing these monstrosities. Will he demand that data centers pay their fair share for the high volume of water and electricity they use? Or is it too late? — Ken Perez, Wood Dale Department of Justice’s credibility I am hopeful that with the recent focus on the “Broadway Six,” in particular due to the reporting of Tribune reporter Jason Meisner, the public will begin to understand that when prosecutors go unchecked, victims face extreme consequences for which they have very little redress. In recent years, the credibility of the U.S. Department of Justice has fallen to all-time depths as it has been weaponized against those with whom it disagrees, both political and nonpolitical, taking up positions not supported by the facts or even the law. This is on full display in Chicago. U.S. District Judge April Perry is being asked to consider disciplinary action against the U.S. attorney’s office for alleged misconduct in the grand jury investigation and prosecution of the “Broadview Six.” No justice system can function effectively if there are components within it that disregard the rules and mechanisms of checks and balance. The public relies upon this system to keep prosecutors in line, to punish misconduct and to send a message that misconduct cannot be tolerated. Misconduct is anathema to justice. — Michael Segal, U.S. National Title Services, Chicago Celebrate parking meter deal? No. Regarding Chicago’s parking meter deal, what a demonstration of ineptness and buffoonery — this is the 2026 edition of the 2008 disaster. As a Chicago resident and motorist, I have one simple question: Will it cost me less to park? Nothing I’ve read about this deal — a transfer fee, percentages of a future sale and net income, a “city wallet” program and 25- to 50-cent-per-hour surcharges for non-Chicagoans — suggests that it will benefit the great majority of drivers in Chicago. And as for the City Council’s self-congratulation over the deal: same-o, same-o. A final question: Where’s Mayor Brandon Johnson? — John Mjoseth, Chicago I support the arts in the city Thank you for the editorial regarding suburbanite parking in Chicago ( “Chicago may charge suburbanites more to park. How neighborly,” Oct. 1). I am a suburbanite who supports the Joffrey Ballet, the Chicago Architectural Center and the Art Institute with subscriptions to their events. I do attempt to take public transportation when I can, but that is not always feasible, since as the editorial mentions, timing for public transportation is sparse on the weekends. For example, a friend and I have Joffrey season tickets for its Sunday matinees, but trying to coordinate Metra and “L” train times with that is difficult. Although driving into town is stressful, we brave it by going down early to enjoy a great lunch at Italian Village before the show. And yes, we look for cheap parking because we’re already supporting businesses and cultural events. Also, because we are both in our 70s, we cannot park too far from the venue just to find an extremely cheap parking lot; we would then need a taxi to get to the Lyric Opera House. In short, considering our generous monetary contributions to the city of Chicago, asking us to pay more for parking really takes the cake! — Dianne Casuto, Lake Forest Naperville’s welcoming vibe Thank you for say

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações (MCom) planeja avançar nas políticas para data centers, cabos submarinos, rodovias e inclusão digital ainda neste ano, afirmou nesta terça-feira, 6, o secretário de Telecomunicações, Hermano Tercius, durante o evento Futurecom, em São Paulo. Um passo importante nesse sentido deve ocorrer na quinta-feira, 8, quando o secretário vai apresentar a política nacional de data center e de cabos submarinos à Casa Civil. A expectativa é de que os planos saiam do papel ainda em 2026. Tercius deixou claro que "apenas o Redata não resolve" as demandas do setor de data center. O anseio do MCom é estimular a instalação de infraestruturas pelo território brasileiro, tanto data centers de borda como complexos para hyperscalers. No caso dos cabos submarinos, o secretário afirmou que a política setorial deve ampliar os pontos de ancoragem pela costa brasileira – atualmente, ainda estão bastante concentrados em Fortaleza, Rio de Janeiro, Salvador e litoral de São Paulo. Segundo exemplificou Tercius, a implantação do cabo Malbec em Porto Alegre já atraiu mais de R$ 4 bilhões em investimentos para a região Sul. Desse modo, a ideia é viabilizar pontos de ancoragem para cabos em outras localidades do País, como Belém e Recife. "Já mandamos para a Casa Civil a política pronta. Uma parte pode vir por portaria, outra tem que ser pelo Congresso", disse o secretário. "Com isso, a gente espera atrair para o Brasil mais data centers e fazer um cinturão digital nos próximos quatro anos", pontuou. Inclusão digital e rodovias O secretário ainda afirmou que a Política Nacional de Inclusão Digital (PNID) deve ser lançada em novembro – no mais tardar, no início de dezembro. A pasta ainda avalia se a política será implementada via portaria ou decreto. Em conversa com jornalistas, Tercius adiantou que o plano prevê um voucher para contratação de banda larga fixa ou móvel, de modo a subsidiar parte dos custos com o serviço, e medidas de letramento digital. Já a Política Nacional de Conectividade de Rodovias (PNCR) deve ser publicada ainda este mês, após alinhamento com o Ministério dos Transportes. Cada pasta deve publicar uma portaria, indicou o secretario. "A política vem sendo executada desde o início do ano. O que a gente vai fazer é uma portaria para dar um salto, levando em conta a questão do roaming, que queremos liberar e obrigar. [O ministério dos] Transportes vai pôr isso em concessões para ter cobertura nas rodovias federais", sinalizou.

artigo.texto: O ministro das Comunicações (MCom), Frederico Siqueira, afirmou que a etapa mais difícil do Redata (15.504/2026) já foi superada: a aprovação do seu texto na Câmara e no Senado. Em conversa com a imprensa nesta terça-feira, 6, o representante do Executivo afirmou que a próxima fase é a regulamentação, que envolve ajustes finos, principalmente na área de energia. Durante o Futurecom Leaders Congress 2026, Siqueira explicou que esses ajustes estão em discussão com outros ministérios, como Desenvolvimento, Indústria e Comércio, Minas e Energia e Casa Civil. Para Juscelino Filho (PSDB-MA), deputado federal reeleito e presidente da Frente Parlamentar Mista de Telecomunicações e Soluções Digitais, a aprovação do Redata foi uma grande vitória para o País. O parlamentar lembra, contudo, que a regulamentação é indispensável para destravar as negociações do ICMS no Confaz e atrair investimentos aos estados. São Paulo no Redata Para o vice-governador reeleito de São Paulo, Felicio Ramuth, há risco de a Reforma Tributária impactar em parte o Redata, uma vez que a implementação do IBS e da CBS unificará as alíquotas, o que pode tornar os benefícios do ICMS obsoletos. Ramuth afirmou ainda que o estado de São Paulo defende conceder incentivos de ICMS a equipamentos específicos de alta tecnologia para inteligência artificial sem similar nacional, como processadores e computadores. Por outro lado, o gestor não defende a redução do imposto para itens genéricos, como ar-condicionado. O vice-governador afirmou também que o estado não foi contra o ICMS, mas acusou o Rio Grande do Sul e o Ceará de atuarem contra a proposta e de articularem para incluir itens genéricos na isenção do imposto estadual no escopo do Redata. artigo.texto: Silicon anodes can store around ten times more charge per gram than graphite and can support faster charging, but silicon swells by 300–400% as it charges, which has historically wrecked its cycle life. The silicon anodes now reaching EVs are silicon-graphite (or silicon-carbon) hybrids that deliver around 20% more range than graphite equivalents, with fewer charge cycles and a higher cost. Graphite remains the industry standard, but silicon is now in production cars. Lithium-ion batteries are the cornerstone of EV technology and most consumer electronics, and their basic architecture hasn't changed dramatically for decades. While cathode chemistries have evolved to give batteries different properties, the anode has almost always been graphite – sometimes with a few percent of silicon oxide blended in for a small capacity boost. Graphite became the staple anode material because it is stable and low cost, but there are other anode materials with a much higher specific capacity that could make EV batteries far more energy dense. The problem has been commercialising them. Related:Volkswagen and Gotion plan flexible LFP cell production across EV and energy storage applications Silicon is the best example of an anode material with huge potential that has been difficult to commercialise. It has around ten times the specific capacity of graphite and could enable faster-charging, more energy-dense EV batteries with a much longer driving range. However, silicon undergoes large volumetric expansion during charging that has historically degraded cells very quickly and made them unsuitable for commercial use. That is now changing. We're still not seeing pure silicon anodes in EVs, but hybrid anodes that combine silicon with graphite or other carbon materials have reached the market, and Mercedes-Benz has become the first carmaker to offer a high-silicon anode battery in a production vehicle. Silicon vs graphite anodes at a glance How do silicon and graphite anodes work? The silicon vs graphite anode debate has been running for a long time. The anode is a critical part of any battery: it stores lithium ions while the battery charges and releases them when it discharges, sending electrons through the external circuit that powers the EV. Silicon's theoretical specific capacity is roughly ten times that of graphite, which on paper makes it an ideal EV battery anode material. Depending on the material and form, silicon's theoretical specific capacity sits between 3,400 and 4,200 mAh/g, whereas the top end of battery-grade graphite is 372 mAh/g. In theory, a pure silicon anode could hold up to ten times more charge than a graphite anode of the same weight. That doesn't mean a battery with ten times the energy, though, because the cathode and the rest of the cell stay the same – and today's silicon hybrid anodes sit well below silicon's theoretical limit, somewhere between graphite and pure silicon. Related:Geely, NIO partner for Chinese battery swapping network However, specific capacity doesn't tell the whole story, and there's a reason graphite has been the industry standard since the 1990s. Graphite's inherent safety and stability have been key to its longevity, whereas silicon anodes have suffered from rapid degradation as they expand and contract during cycling. Battery safety is paramount to avoid EV fires. Graphite anodes also form a very stable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer, while silicon's is less stable – one of the reasons current silicon anodes also contain carbon as a stabilising material. Even so, graphite is nearing its practical capacity ceiling, and as demand for longer-range EVs grows, new chemistries are needed to push further. Enter silicon, which offers higher energy density – translating into longer driving range – and the potential for faster charging. Silicon itself is a relatively cheap and abundant material, and there is already a large global silicon supply chain serving the electronics and solar sectors, even if a dedicated silicon anode supply chain is still small. However, making silicon anodes is currently more complex and expensive than making battery-grade graphite, which benefits from decades of high-volume production that have driven costs down. Silicon is already used safely in many high-power electronics, so the main barrier to battery safety and lifespan is the anode's expansion. Related:UK to invest over US$9 billion into EV batteries, but must make up 55GWh supply gap Energy density: How much better is silicon than graphite? Because silicon's theoretical specific capacity is so much higher (3,400–4,200 mAh/g against graphite's 372 mAh/g), its potential energy density is much higher too. But today's cells use silicon-graphite hybrids rather than pure silicon, so they don't come close to silicon's theoretical limits. Most practical hybrid anodes have a specific capacity of 600–1,500 mAh/g – still well above graphite, but the real-world gains are smaller than the headline figures suggest. At cell level, that currently means around 20% more energy density, with up to 40% expected as the technology matures. The gain comes from making the anode smaller. In a lithium-ion cell, the cathode supplies the lithium, and the anode has to be large enough to store it. Graphite's relatively low capacity means the anode takes up a large share of the cell. Silicon offers about ten times graphite's capacity by weight and roughly three times by volume, so a much thinner anode can store the same amount of lithium – freeing space for more cathode material, and therefore more energy, in the same cell. At the upper end, silicon alloys with lithium so that several lithium ions can be stored per silicon atom. The highest theoretical capacity (4,200 mAh/g) comes from the Li22Si5 phase, but the more practical figure demonstrated in studies (3,579 mAh/g) comes from the Li15Si4 phase. artigo.texto: Evanston Councilmember Krissie Harris is proposing a formal one-year moratorium on data centers across the city following vocal backlash to a proposal in her Second Ward, telling the RoundTable she wants to complete “due diligence” to understand data centers’ potential impacts before any are approved. Harris’ plan calls for a one-year halt on any city-level zoning approvals and incentives for data centers “pending infrastructure and grid audits,” and will go to the council’s Referrals Committee on Monday, Oct. 12. The measure is co-sponsored by Councilmembers Clare Kelly (1st Ward), Bobby Burns (5th), Parielle Davis (7th) and Matt Rodgers (8th), immediately giving it majority support from the nine-member council. Property owner Reed Beidler submitted a zoning analysis application last month to establish a “computer processing center” at 1265 Hartrey Ave. in the Second Ward. Beidler proposes filling about 20,000 square feet of space in the former factory building and envisions a large organization renting out most of the data center’s processing power alongside other businesses with smaller needs. Like other data center projects around the country, the Evanston proposal drew intense backlash from residents and local organizations, including at Second Ward and City Council meetings last month. Harris said in a phone interview Sunday she hasn’t met with Beidler about his proposal, but that she felt the city could be “bombarded with requests” in the near future and feels an official pause is warranted. “I don’t want it to be one of those [situations] like we say yes because it’s small, looks like it’s … not a big deal, and then it just balloons into this thing that we cannot control,” Harris said. “I want to make sure … we’ve investigated that thoroughly.” While Beidler argued the data center should be approved as a permitted use under existing zoning, city staff disagreed and found it doesn’t fit under any use already listed in the city code, meaning a zoning amendment is necessary for approval. City Manager Luke Stowe called this a “de facto moratorium” during the last council meeting and invited council direction to “pursue an official moratorium,” which Harris is now taking up. previous coverage Harris said she’s particularly concerned about the center’s potential impact on water and power use, sharing that she has a stake in the outcome since she lives just a few blocks away. “If I get more information and we, as a council, feel good about it, we can change that moratorium,” Harris said. “But it gives us, at least, time to just breathe and figure it out.” She also referenced potential state legislation that could impact projects in Evanston and elsewhere. The Illinois General Assembly failed to pass a comprehensive data center bill during its spring session, and Gov. JB Pritzker is pushing hard for lawmakers to take action during the veto session, which will run from Nov. 17 to 19 and Dec. 1 to 3. Asked if the four councilmembers co-sponsoring her proposal feel the same as her, Harris said some are less sure a moratorium is needed but are trusting her judgment, especially since the current proposal is in her ward. “Some people are kind of like, ‘Oh, I don’t know, but I’ll follow your lead on this,’ and so I’m appreciative of my team members saying OK,” Harris said. “I’ve got to be accountable for this, and if it’s going somewhere else [in another ward], I got to trust if somebody says, ‘I need more time to really make a good decision.'” The moratorium will need to be approved by City Council before it can officially take effect. Depending on how much time staff need to develop the proposal into full legislation, it could advance as soon as the council’s next meeting on Oct. 12 or at a future meeting in the coming months. As of Oct. 1, staff are still waiting for Beidler to submit additional information about his proposal before directing him to propose a zoning amendment.

artigo.texto: Nigeria will not allow carbon markets that lack integrity or amount to greenwashing, the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) has warned. The director-general of the NCCC, Omotenioye Majekodunmi, yesterday at the European Union Climate Dialogue programme organised by the NCCC in partnership with the EU Global Gateway and funded by the European Union. Majekodunmi, represented by the NCCC director of Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, Michael Ivenso, said the country was determined to ensure that carbon projects delivered measurable environmental and economic benefits. He said global carbon markets offered a major opportunity to mobilise private capital for climate action, but warned that the market would collapse without credible systems for verifying carbon credits. “Global carbon markets present one of the most promising avenues to mobilise this private capital. “However, as I have repeatedly stated, carbon markets are only as strong as the integrity of the underlying credits. “A carbon market without rigour is merely an exercise in greenwashing—a scenario that Nigeria will not accommodate,” he said. Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon projects must deliver “real, additional, and permanent mitigation outcomes” while benefiting communities, protecting ecosystems and ensuring fair returns for investors and project developers. She said climate finance was critical to powering clean energy transitions, restoring degraded lands, modernising agriculture, improving waste management and expanding access to clean technologies across the country. The NCCC boss said the operationalisation of Measurement, Reporting and Verification systems was central to building confidence in Nigeria’s emerging carbon market. “Frameworks on paper do not trade carbon—transparent and verifiable data does. This brings us to the core theme of today’s roundtable: Operationalising Measurement, Reporting, and Verification,” he said. “MRV is the backbone of market credibility.” He explained that without credible MRV systems, buyers could not determine whether carbon reductions were genuine, regulators could not properly track emissions, and communities could not ensure fair benefit-sharing. Majekodunmi disclosed that the government was operationalising a unified national carbon registry to prevent double-counting and ensure the integrity of carbon credits generated in Nigeria. “Every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred, or retired in Nigeria will carry a digital footprint to prevent double-counting and guarantee baseline integrity,” he said. He added that Nigeria was moving towards digital MRV using remote sensing, Internet of Things sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to reduce verification costs and improve accuracy. The NCCC identified three immediate regulatory priorities, including finalising carbon market regulations, publishing sector-specific MRV guidelines and establishing local capacity-building hubs for Nigerian auditors and technical experts. Also speaking, the Director-General of the European Commission’s CLIMA Task Force on International Carbon Pricing and Markets, Jop Watering, said the European Union was prepared to deepen its engagement with Nigeria on high-integrity carbon markets. Watering said the EU had 20 years of experience with domestic carbon pricing and was now opening its climate strategy to high-quality international carbon credits. He warned that carbon markets would not succeed if issues surrounding integrity, transparency and accountability were not properly addressed. “If you don’t get the integrity right, the market will just not take off. It will just not be there,” he said. Watering said international carbon-crediting mechanisms had so far failed to fully realise their potential because of accounting loopholes and weak checks and balances. He said the EU wanted stringent methodologies, transparent registries, fair transactions and equitable benefit-sharing to underpin the international carbon market. The Head of Section, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms Yolanda Josaid, credible systems were necessary to ensure transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. She said Nigeria’s National Carbon Market Framework, adopted last year, provided the foundation for domestic and international carbon trading under the Climate Change Act and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The official said a credible carbon market could align Nigeria’s climate targets with development priorities, attract investment and support the country’s transition to a low-carbon economy. The Director of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa Buhari, said Nigeria’s forests remained central to the country’s climate response. She said forests served as carbon sinks, temperature buffers and sources of livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. Buhari warned that carbon market development must support forest conservation rather than create incentives for further exploitation. She called for stronger forest inventories, remote sensing, satellite monitoring and the use of appropriate artificial intelligence technologies to improve carbon measurement. “Forestry, I’d like to remind us all that the forest sector is central to Nigeria’s climate response because forests are both carbon sinks, temperature buffers, reducing natural disaster risk, livelihoods, humans’ primary food source, and famine, among several others,” she said. She also called for stronger coordination among institutions responsible for collecting, managing, validating and reporting forest carbon data. Meanwhile, the UK PACT Officer and Programme Manager at the British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, Folakemi Aletan, said carbon markets could mobilise investment and strengthen Nigeria’s sustainable development. artigo.texto: There's A Big Problem With Building Data Centers Underground Data centers have become the necessary evil we all have to deal with for the sake of rapid AI advancements. However, they're problematic, and most regular people are very much against them for obvious reasons. Data centers are so loud that their noise may carry for a mile, and they may also drive up local utility costs, take up precious land, and waste water reserves. So, why not put them underground? That would theoretically solve most of these issues. If only it were that easy. Though the UAE has considered fortifying its own data centers with guns and burying some underground, that's basically a means-to-an-end solution due to the dangers of Iranian attacks. In normal circumstances, the project would just end up costing more, as you'd need to create a strong shell that can take the weight of all the soil above. That's not even accounting for drilling, insulation, and waterproofing. Then, these facilities wouldn't be easy to scale up because it would require additional blasting or drilling, meaning companies are unlikely to put down the cash for something that will make people happy at an additional cost and loss of scalability. The biggest challenge, though? Maintaining solid air quality. When you're underground, complications with the air can add up quickly. As such, the data center would require some expensive systems to get the same environment that's practically a given above ground, so add the expensive humidity control and ventilation system to an already hefty bill. In the end, it's all much more feasible than making orbital data centers, but far too tricky for companies to seriously consider it. In which case can building underground work? The good thing about underground data centers, theoretically at least, is they'd save operators money on cooling because there's no sunlight. They could also resort to geothermal energy, so it wouldn't waste as much electricity. It truly seems like a magic bullet when you lay it all out — if only the construction costs weren't so high. Well, new AI data centers can be built inside existing underground structures, which automatically solves the brunt of the issues, and we have real-world examples that attest to how well it can work. For instance, there are a few data centers operating out of abandoned mines in the U.S., which makes them super secure by design. The best part is, they're not expensive to build and maintain. Plus, the temperature in the mines, and more importantly, the humidity, are sometimes bordering on perfection. Unfortunately, there aren't that many mines that are both close to a power source and already have the necessary connections, so it's not as if companies can move to the mines in droves, Fallout style. In a perfect world, profits would be secondary to preservation of our natural resources. Ultimately, the reason why there isn't a huge push to find better solutions is that it's simply more expensive than just taking a piece of land and constructing a data center. Plus, the alternatives we have so far are all difficult to pull off. Data centers aren't built in Antarctica because it's too remote and doesn't have a power grid, despite the naturally cool air making it seem like a perfect solution for the AI boom. Until we figure something out, we'll all probably have to contend with effects of new facilities popping up, sadly.

artigo.texto: AI infrastructure is reshaping more than the servers inside data center racks. As GPU-intensive workloads push rack densities higher, Eaton, NVIDIA, Google, Microsoft and others are advancing direct-current power architectures designed to deliver more power with fewer conversion stages and less physical infrastructure. For solution providers, integrators and infrastructure partners, that shift could broaden the scope of AI infrastructure projects. Moving from traditional AC designs toward rack-level 48/50V DC and, eventually, 800 VDC affects not only power distribution but also backup systems, cooling, rack design and serviceability â forcing partners to think about those systems as an interconnected architecture rather than separate infrastructure purchases Why AI is pushing data centers toward DC power The broader demand curve explains why power architecture is receiving so much attention. The International Energy Agency projects global data center electricity consumption will roughly double from 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh in 2030, with consumption from AI-focused data centers growing even faster. Inside the facility, higher density creates another challenge: current. Delivering more power at lower voltages requires greater current, which can mean larger conductors, greater losses, and more heat. Higher-voltage DC distribution can reduce current while eliminating some power-conversion stages between the utility feed and IT equipment. 48V, 50V and 800 VDC architectures take shape The transition is already visible at the rack level. Open Compute Projectâs Open Rack V3 ecosystem uses 48V DC busbar architectures, while Eatonâs upcoming 50V DC system is designed for both conventional 19-inch racks and 21-inch ORV3 racks, with power ratings ranging from 33 kW to 132 kW per rack. Eaton specifically identifies system integrator builds, enterprise and colocation environments, AI/HPC deployments and OCP migration projects among its intended applications. The next step could be significantly larger. NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft are collaborating through OCP to establish 800 VDC as an open architecture for next-generation AI data centers. NVIDIA says moving from todayâs lower-voltage rack architectures toward 800 VDC reduces current, copper requirements and cable bulk while allowing fewer power-conversion stages. More than 80 equipment and infrastructure companies are participating in the ecosystem. Eaton is among them and is developing 800 VDC infrastructure alongside its current ORV3 and 50V DC offerings. DC power creates a broader infrastructure role for partners That does not mean every enterprise data center is about to switch to 800 VDC. In fact, the emerging market is better understood as a continuum. Existing facilities can continue operating AC infrastructure while introducing DC closer to high-density compute. Rack-level 48/50V systems offer another path, while 800 VDC is being positioned for future AI environments with substantially greater density. NVIDIAâs own roadmap explicitly includes hybrid architectures designed to introduce 800 VDC power racks into facilities with existing AC infrastructure. For the channel, architectural knowledge is increasingly important. Partners accustomed to selling servers, UPS systems, racks and power distribution as relatively discrete infrastructure categories may need to approach AI projects more holistically. Power density affects distribution, backup requirements, cooling, physical rack design and serviceability, meaning infrastructure decisions become interconnected earlier in the design process. Eaton similarly argues that power and cooling need to be planned together as AI densities rise. The opportunity, then, isnât simply selling a different power product. It is helping customers determine when existing AC infrastructure remains sufficient, when rack-level DC makes sense, how to design hybrid environments, and when future workloads justify a more fundamental architectural shift. Hyperscalers may be setting the direction today. Channel partners should be watching closely for when their customers begin following it.

artigo.texto: Lightstar is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage footprint across the state As the solar energy industry continues to advance, there is an abundance of companies that are looking to be involved in shaping the sector and future energy production strategies. The United States continues to be among the leading solar energy-producing countries in the world, competing with other powerhouses like China. The big advantage that the U.S. has over most nations is its access to great wealth and resources, which increases its chances of producing the most sophisticated energy projects. As of late, Lightstar expressed that it is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage footprint across the state. Lightstar continues to advance the United States solar energy sector Lightstar’s approach to project execution means that it is in a position where it is likely to always be in the running to be appointed to spearhead massive projects. Its reputation and previous success also mean that it is in a good position to be selected by countries other than the U.S.A., where it is based. The company’s current commitment is to building sustainable, high-value assets that support local economies and farming legacies for decades to come. Lightstar is doubling down on Illinois, expanding its community solar and battery-storage A recent press release from Lightstar Renewables, a national leader in community solar generation, announced that it is set to continue the expansion of its active Illinois portfolio across three service lines: community solar, agrivoltaic solar, and battery energy storage systems (BESS). Lightstar is known for contributing to Illinois not just in terms of energy facilities but also toward the economic progression of the state. The company develops these projects on private land throughout Illinois, guiding landowners through an origination-to-cooperation process that preserves land ownership, delivers fixed long-term lease income, and keeps land in productive use. Lightstar’s permitted, market-ready project pipeline offers an answer for landowners, municipalities, and clean energy partners looking for companies that develop community solar and battery energy storage in Illinois. Interestingly, Illinois has become one of the most active clean energy markets in the Midwest, driven by the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) and its target of 100% clean energy by 2050. Supportive programs continue to quicken deployment: the Illinois Shines Adjustable Block Program opens its 2026-2027 cycle on June 1, 2026, and the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA) expands community solar while permitting co-location of projects up to 10 MW on a single parcel or adjacent properties. A general overview of Illinois’ clean energy landscape as of 2026 With the year now coming to an end, industry experts are expecting it to be a record-breaking year for Illinois, considering the number of projects that have materialized. In 2026, Illinois enacted statewide energy storage legislation establishing new storage projects, emphasizing demand for reliable, grid-responsive infrastructure. Lightstar actively monitors these programs and evaluates every Illinois project for eligibility. This track record has positioned the company as one of the state’s most determined and experienced community solar and battery storage developers. Gaining an insight into the future of community solar and battery storage There has been a common theme of community and battery storage projects leading the charge in the solar sector in recent years. Kyle McAdam, Senior Development Manager at Lightstar, stated the following: “We believe that clean energy development must work hand-in-hand with the local community. By protecting the land, engaging with incredible students right here in Fulton County, and now investing directly in the VIT athletic field, we ensure this project leaves a positive, lasting mark on the region for decades to come.” Lightstar is well respected as a trailblazing community solar developer that was founded on the principles of advanced design and strategic project development. As a proud American company, Lightstar is a trusted partner for landowners, focusing on community solar and agrivoltaics projects that preserve agricultural land while generating energy. artigo.texto: The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said the measures establish rules covering the development, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon projects and lay the groundwork for a credible domestic carbon market. Environment Assistant Secretary for Integrated Management System and Information Systems Daniel Darius Nicer presented the policies at a high-level roundtable on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York. Market roadmap The first policy adopts the Philippines’ Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market Roadmap for 2026 to 2030. The roadmap sets the national direction for policy development, measurement, reporting and verification systems, data management and registry readiness—all considered important in determining whether carbon credits can be reliably measured and tracked. “To date, the Philippines, through its Department of Environment and Natural Resources, issued two major policy instruments that establish the foundations of a credible forest carbon market directly addressing private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways,” Nicer said. He spoke during the “Shaping High-Integrity Carbon Markets” session convened by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development during Climate Week NYC. Project safeguards The second policy establishes national guidelines for the creation, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon credit projects. The rules require environmental safeguards, compliance with Free, Prior and Informed Consent and benefit-sharing with communities. They also mandate transparent project registration, which the DENR said would help reduce reputational and delivery risks for carbon credit buyers. “For the Philippines, carbon markets—both voluntary and compliance pathways—are central to our strategy for accelerating mitigation and unlocking climate finance,” Nicer said. “But for markets to function, the private sector needs clarity, predictability, and confidence that the credits they purchase are real, additional, and backed by strong governance.” Carbon framework The forest policies form part of wider government efforts to develop the country's carbon market infrastructure. Nicer cited Department of Energy guidelines for renewable energy projects, the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework and the rollout of the Philippine National Carbon Registry. The registry is intended to provide accounting and traceability of carbon credits and prevent double counting. Nicer said Philippine policies are also being aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement through bilateral arrangements, including an implementation agreement with Singapore and the Joint Crediting Mechanism with Japan. Looking ahead to the COP31 climate summit, he called for stronger international guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. “High-integrity markets should not only accelerate global ambition, but also deliver real, measurable mitigation outcomes that directly benefit and reach the communities, ecosystems, and sectors that need them most,” Nicer said. — Ed: Corrie S. Narisma

artigo.texto: Origin plans a 500 MW, 4,942 MWh battery at Eraring Origin proposes adding a 500 MW storage system at the Eraring power station site. The project, which still has to clear the approval stages, would target commercial operations between early and mid-2031. Origin is proposing Eraring BESS North, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with a discharge capacity of 500 megawatts (MW) and an accessible energy storage capacity of approximately 4,942 megawatt hours (MWh). The project would require up to 22 hectares on Origin-owned land at the Eraring power station site in New South Wales. It is located in the suburb of Eraring, within the Lake Macquarie local government area. A combined facility of about 1,200 MW The project would operate alongside the existing Eraring BESS, part of Origin's generation portfolio. The existing project received State Significant Development consent SSD-15950052 on 10 May 2022. According to the project document, the two facilities together would provide a combined maximum registered active power capacity of around 1,200 MW and an accessible storage capacity of approximately 8,600 MWh, subject to detailed design. The storage sector is drawing other projects from Europe to Asia. ML System secured two energy storage contracts in Poland worth â¬4.1 million, while Vena Energy won a 46.8 MW battery storage contract in Japan. In power transmission, Iberdrola expanded its alliance with GIC in Brazil. Company Origin Energy: company profile ORG A regulatory pathway ahead Origin expects the project to qualify as a State Significant Development (SSD) under Section 2.6(1) of the 2021 Planning Systems state environmental planning policy. It would be subject to Part 4, Division 4.7, Section 4.36 of the 1979 Environmental Planning and Assessment Act, as an electricity generating works development whose estimated cost exceeds the set thresholds. An environmental impact statement will have to be prepared in line with the Secretary's Environmental Assessment Requirements. The existing BESS received a "not controlled action if undertaken in a particular manner" decision on 19 July 2021 under the federal Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 [2021/8956]. The new project includes approximately 11 hectares of vegetation clearance outside the previously assessed disturbance area. Origin says it reviewed alternative locations and consulted key stakeholders and the community to limit impacts. Components and timeline The project covers construction, operation, decommissioning and rehabilitation as far as reasonably practicable. It would include transmission works to connect the BESS to TransGrid's switching station, along with an extension of the existing substation. It also provides for extended water supply infrastructure, new electricity buildings, internal access roads and new operation and maintenance compounds. Construction is expected to start in 2028 and last about 2.5 years, with commercial operations anticipated in early to mid-2031, subject to approvals. Operations would run for up to 25 years, with a possible extension. Works would be staged, including site establishment, then earthworks for the battery compound and transformer yard, and finally civil and foundation works. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 % Origin presents the project as a response to the National Electricity Market's shift from coal toward variable renewables, supported by dispatchable storage capacity. The New South Wales roadmap targets at least 12 gigawatts of renewable generation and 2 gigawatts of long-duration storage by 2030. The Australian Energy Market Operator's 2024 Integrated System Plan forecasts that the market must triple grid-scale variable renewable capacity by 2030.

artigo.texto: Após dobrar a área de manufatura em fevereiro, a Adata prepara nova operação industrial em Manaus para montar e testar servidores de alta potência, enquanto avalia projetos para automação e setor automotivo em 2027 também A fábrica da Adata em Manaus vai ganhar uma nova frente industrial em dezembro de 2026, quando a companhia pretende iniciar a montagem e os testes de servidores, incluindo equipamentos de alta potência destinados a data centers. Fábrica da Adata em Manaus dobrou área de produção em 2026 A expansão faz parte de uma estratégia que vem sendo colocada em prática desde 2021, quando a Adata iniciou sua operação industrial na capital amazonense. Desde então, a unidade recebeu investimentos para ampliar capacidade, automatizar processos e aumentar o portfólio produzido localmente. Um dos movimentos mais recentes ocorreu em fevereiro de 2026. A empresa dobrou sua área de manufatura ao incorporar um segundo galpão industrial à planta de Manaus. - Gigante americana Sukup coloca Mato Grosso no radar e avalia instalar fábrica em Lucas do Rio Verde para produzir sistemas de armazenagem de grãos em um dos maiores polos do agronegócio brasileiro - Duas gigantes chinesas negociam novas fábricas de geladeiras e lavadoras no Brasil enquanto setor supera R$ 7 bilhões em investimentos e amplia corrida pela produção local de eletrodomésticos - Grupo Michelin amplia presença industrial no Brasil com nova fábrica da Fenner em Guarulhos e projeto prevê aumento de 40% na capacidade para atender mineração, cimento, siderurgia e outros setores pesados - Indústria da soja acelera no Brasil, capacidade cresce 13% em um ano e setor prepara R$ 7,65 bilhões em novas fábricas e expansões para adicionar 7,4 milhões de toneladas ao processamento nacional Segundo Nivaldo Gagliardo, vice-presidente de Operações da Adata Technology Brasil, essa nova estrutura começará a contribuir com o crescimento das operações locais ainda no último trimestre de 2026. A companhia não informou, na entrevista, o valor aplicado na ampliação nem divulgou a capacidade de produção que será acrescentada pelo segundo galpão. Unidade já monta módulos DRAM e SSDs Hoje, a operação de Manaus realiza a montagem eletrônica completa de módulos de memória DRAM e SSDs utilizando tecnologia SMT, além dos testes desses produtos. Os principais componentes utilizados, como circuitos integrados de memória DRAM e Flash destinados aos SSDs, são fornecidos pela fábrica da própria Adata localizada em Santo Antônio de Posse, no interior de São Paulo. A produção ocorre em ambiente com controle de temperatura e umidade. A planta também utiliza equipamentos automatizados para manipulação e inspeção de produtos e ferramentais. Parte dessas soluções emprega inteligência artificial e foi desenvolvida no Brasil em parceria com institutos de Manaus, dentro de projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Servidores para data centers entram na linha em dezembro O próximo salto será a entrada no mercado de servidores. A partir de dezembro de 2026, a Adata pretende começar, em Manaus, uma operação destinada à montagem e aos testes desses equipamentos. A fabricação será realizada em regime de manufatura sob contrato. Entre os produtos previstos estão servidores de alta potência voltados à utilização em data centers. Com isso, a planta amplia suas competências para além de memórias e unidades de armazenamento, entrando em uma área ligada diretamente à infraestrutura de processamento de dados. A expansão ocorre após a empresa ter um projeto de diversificação aprovado pelo Conselho de Desenvolvimento do Estado do Amazonas, o Codam. Automação e setor automotivo estão no radar para 2027 A Adata também avalia novos caminhos para sua estrutura industrial em Manaus. As equipes de engenharia da companhia estudam, junto às engenharias de clientes, oportunidades para produzir outros equipamentos eletrônicos. Entre os segmentos citados estão automação e indústria automotiva. Segundo a empresa, essas possibilidades estão sendo analisadas para produção a partir de 2027. Na avaliação da companhia, a Zona Franca de Manaus oferece previsibilidade para investimentos industriais devido à manutenção constitucional dos incentivos, além de contar com cadeia eletrônica consolidada e mão de obra especializada. A empresa afirma ainda que recebe apoio da Suframa, da Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação do Amazonas e de institutos locais desde 2021. Para a Adata, a continuidade dessas políticas e a redução de gargalos operacionais são pontos considerados importantes para acelerar novos projetos e aumentar a eficiência das empresas instaladas no Polo Industrial de Manaus.

artigo.texto: O setor elétrico brasileiro vive um momento de transformação acelerada com a crescente demanda por infraestrutura digital de alto desempenho. A aprovação do regime de incentivos fiscais (Redata) aqueceu o mercado, mas acendeu um alerta sobre a capacidade da rede em suportar a carga exigida pelos novos centros de processamento de dados. Segundo a redação do Imprensa 24h, o desafio atual não é a falta de geração, mas sim a eficiência no escoamento dessa energia para os polos de consumo. Resumo da Notícia - Investimento previsto de R$ 120 bilhões em linhas de transmissão até 2035. - Projetos de data centers somam 10 GW em contratos e pedidos firmes de conexão. - Brasil desperdiçou 33 milhões de MWh em 2025 por falta de malha para escoar energia. - Descompasso temporal: obras de transmissão levam 7 anos, enquanto data centers ficam prontos em 18 meses. Para quem acompanha as notícias de Sergipe, o estado se posiciona estrategicamente nesse cenário, dada sua relevância na matriz energética nacional. A integração de fontes renováveis, especialmente as vindas do Nordeste, depende diretamente da robustez do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). As informações de Aracaju reforçam que a estabilidade elétrica é o principal atrativo para indústrias que buscam se instalar na região, transformando a infraestrutura em um motor de desenvolvimento local. O papel estratégico da transmissão no cenário nacional A malha de transmissão é o elemento que conecta a abundância de energia renovável produzida no Nordeste aos grandes centros industriais e tecnológicos do Sudeste e Sul. Sem essa conexão, o potencial de geração solar e eólica acaba subutilizado. Em 2025, o fenômeno conhecido como curtailment — a limitação da geração por falta de espaço na rede — resultou no corte de 33 milhões de MWh, volume comparável ao consumo anual de todo o estado do Rio Grande do Sul. A expansão da rede é, portanto, a solução para evitar esse desperdício e garantir que a energia limpa chegue aos novos polos de tecnologia. O mercado de data centers, que exige alta confiabilidade e grandes volumes de carga, monitora de perto os leilões de transmissão. Para mais detalhes sobre como esses movimentos impactam a economia regional, acompanhe no portal Imprensa 24h. Descompasso entre demanda tecnológica e obras de infraestrutura Um dos pontos críticos identificados pelo setor é a diferença de ritmo entre a construção de um data center e a entrega de uma linha de transmissão. Enquanto uma unidade de processamento de dados pode ser erguida em cerca de um ano e meio, o ciclo completo de uma obra de transmissão — que envolve planejamento, licenciamento ambiental pelo Ibama e construção — leva, em média, sete anos. Esse intervalo exige uma coordenação fina entre órgãos como a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) e investidores privados. A sinalização antecipada da demanda é fundamental para que os traçados das linhas sejam definidos antes que a necessidade se torne uma urgência crítica, garantindo que o crescimento tecnológico não seja freado por gargalos logísticos de energia. Planejamento decenal e aportes bilionários na rede O governo federal, por meio do Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), já traçou a rota para mitigar esses riscos. A previsão é de que sejam investidos aproximadamente R$ 120 bilhões na próxima década. Esse montante será destinado à construção de 30 mil quilômetros de novas linhas e ao acréscimo de 82 mil MVA em capacidade de subestações em todo o território nacional. Onde há linha de transmissão, há crescimento econômico e geração de empregos. A consolidação dessa infraestrutura permitirá que o Brasil não apenas atenda sua demanda interna, mas se torne um hub global para serviços de inteligência artificial e armazenamento de dados em nuvem. Fique por dentro das últimas notícias em Sergipe e no Brasil acessando nossa página inicial. Mantenha-se atualizado com as principais movimentações do setor de energia e tecnologia. Continue bem informado navegando pelas editorias do Imprensa 24h, o seu portal de referência para notícias de Sergipe e do mundo.

artigo.texto: San Francisco’s Board of Supervisors today passed a temporary, 45-day moratorium on data centers citywide, halting the construction of new centers including one proposed in Dogpatch. The move follows increased fears surrounding the potential environmental impacts of data centers, many of which are planned or already exist in District 10, the city’s industrial southeast. The measure, first proposed by District 10 supervisor Shamann Walton and co-sponsored by supervisors Connie Chan, Jackie Fielder and Cheyenne Chen, will take effect immediately. Sources close to Walton’s office say the supervisor hopes the moratorium will result in a permanent ban. The San Francisco Planning Commission will assess during the ensuing 45 days whether the several data centers throughout San Francisco, including larger facilities in District 10 and smaller, regional ones downtown, pose an environmental threat to nearby residents. During the moratorium, the planning department will study the data centers’ impact on water, energy, air quality, land use, and the surrounding community. In the legislation, data centers are broadly defined as any “facility, or part of a facility, that houses computing infrastructure, including graphics and central processing units, servers, storage devices, networking equipment, and associated power and cooling systems, for the primary purpose of processing, storing, or distributing electronic data.” If the data centers are found to have a significant environmental impact, the moratorium could be extended up to 22 months — or alternatively, result in permanent controls or restrictions. At the conclusion of the 45-day period, the planning department will hold a hearing to present its findings. The moratorium will pause the expansion of NOVVA, a 7.6-acre data center at 400 Paul Ave. in Bayview, which was slated to increase output from nine to 36 megawatts by 2028. Though permits have been filed for an additional, 160,000 square foot datacenter in the Dogpatch at 1215 Michigan St., no construction has yet taken place — though an extended moratorium could put plans to expand data centers in San Francisco on hold for an undetermined period. Walton’s term will end in January 2027, potentially before the end of a moratorium if it is extended beyond four months. But strong regulations on data centers — and potentially an all-out ban — has gained increasing support among the candidates racing to replace Walton. Each of the front-running candidates, Theo Ellington, J.R. Eppler, and Dion-Jay Brookter, have expressed support for a moratorium. Brookter was, at first, the only candidate to propose a permanent ban, but during a recent candidate forum, all the others said they would support one, too. District 10’s Bayview-Hunters Point, which has two of the city’s largest data centers, has experienced a disproportionate level of air pollution for decades, including from increased truck traffic and a since-shuttered PG&E power plant. “We need to know what these impacts are,” said Walton, at the time he announced his plans to introduce the moratorium. “Until we know what that is, it needs to stop.”
