artigo.texto: Maryland nets 440 MW/1,760 MWh in first bulk energy storage procurement This story was originally published on Utility Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily Utility Dive newsletter. Dive Brief: - Two transmission-connected energy storage projects are slated to receive awards in the first round of the Maryland Next Generation Energy Act energy storage procurement, the state public service commission said on Thursday. - The finalists are Flatiron Energy's 400 MW/1,600 MWh Chalk Point Storage Project in south-central Maryland and REV Renewables's 40 MW/160 MWh Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in the far western part of the state. Both will receive flat pricing for 15-year terms at a combined cost of 6.98 cents/month for the average Maryland residential customer, the public service commission said. - The award will help address the PJM Interconnection's capacity woes, which Federal Energy Regulatory Commission chair Laura Swett last week called a "mess." The grid operator faces a capacity shortfall of 6.8 GW for the 2028-2029 delivery year, up 300 MW from the previous period, as capacity prices remain at the $325/MW-day cap. Dive Insight: Passed in 2025, the Next Generation Energy Act requires Maryland to conduct at least two solicitations for a combined 1.6 GW of energy storage capacity. Eligible projects must be designed to discharge at full power for at least four hours. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced the awards for the first solicitation round on Thursday, the statutory deadline. By law, it must open bidding for the second round by Jan. 1, 2027, and announce project awards by Oct. 1, 2027. Evan Vaughan, executive director of the regional clean energy group MAREC Action, said Thursday's selections will help mitigate the effects of PJM's high capacity prices. "These projects can help meet growing electricity demand while reducing exposure to volatile capacity prices that ultimately affect customers' bills," Vaughan said in a statement. Also known as the Mid-Atlantic Renewable Energy Coalition, MAREC Action consists of more than 50 developers and manufacturers serving the region's utility-scale solar, wind and battery storage industry. Flatiron Energy and REV Renewables are both members. Flatiron's project will be located at NRG's oil- and gas-fired Chalk Point power plant in the southeastern corner of Prince George's County, according to the Maryland Public Service Commission. REV will site its project on a portion of a reclaimed coal mine in mountainous Garrett County, near Maryland's border with West Virginia and Pennsylvania. The commission said it chose not to award the 500-MW/3,000-MWh Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project nor a 135-MW/540-MWh expansion Flatiron requested for the Chalk Point project in a revised filing after the first-round application window closed. The commission said Flatiron could reapply for the Chalk Point expansion and "invited [Oystercatcher] to consider participating" in round two, citing the "desirable electric grid location and characteristics" of the project's northeastern Maryland site while noting "the need for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County if the project is pursued further." In addition to near-term cost pressures due to PJM's capacity crunch, Maryland has ambitious clean energy goals, including a statutory 2045 target for statewide net-zero emissions and a 2035 goal for 100% carbon-free electricity set by gubernatorial order. In a statement, Maryland Public Service Commission Chair Kumar Barve called the first-round award a milestone in the state's effort to meet its energy policy goals, while acknowledging its relatively modest contribution. "While we are disappointed that these awards are below our 800-MW target for Round 1, our Round 2 solicitation is expected to attract many more offers due to a pool of over 40 additional energy storage projects from PJM's Cycle 1 interconnection process," Barve said.

artigo.texto: Sistemas de armazenamento de energia elétrica, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, estão vendendo como nunca no País. Enquanto o leilão do Governo para contratar grandes projetos de baterias continua agendado para dezembro mas enfrenta incertezas, o mercado encontrou seu caminho no varejo. Instalações menores em indústrias, comércios, condomínios e residências, muitas vezes associadas a sistemas solares em telhados, têm movimentado a indústria num ritmo recorde. Em 2025, o volume vendido e contratado atingiu 730 MWh, mais do que o acumulado dos cinco anos anteriores. E só no primeiro semestre deste ano foram mais 504 MWh, a caminho de uma nova marca histórica para o setor, segundo um levantamento da consultoria Greener. “O leilão é importante, claro, mas o BESS de uma forma distribuída, vamos chamar assim, vai ser em minha visão uma das grandes fontes de flexibilidade para o sistema elétrico no País,” Marcio Takata, o CEO da Greener, disse ao Brazil Journal. Ele fez uma comparação com a indústria de energia solar, que começou a se movimentar com leilões do Governo para grandes projetos e nos anos seguintes teve uma disparada puxada pelo mercado de pequenas instalações em telhados e miniusinas. A capacidade em geração solar distribuída hoje soma mais de 53 gigawatts, contra 23,6 gigawatts em usinas de geração centralizada, segundo dados da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). No momento, o acumulado em sistemas de baterias no País representa 1,9 GWh, com empresas incluindo WEG e Grupo Moura apostando no setor. O leilão programado para dezembro deve contratar pelo menos 2 gigawatts para operação durante 4 horas diárias, segundo sinalizações de Brasília, o equivalente a 8 GWh – embora parte do mercado já espere volumes maiores. O Ministério de Minas e Energia também programou leilões anuais, até 2029, para contratação de reserva de capacidade, nos quais haverá espaço para sistemas de baterias. Esses certames, porém, vão promover uma disputa da tecnologia com termelétricas e hidrelétricas, incluindo as chamadas hidrelétricas reversíveis – que na prática funcionam como uma bateria, ao guardar água para produzir mais nos momentos em que o sistema precisa. A contratação dessa reserva de capacidade é vista como importante para que a rede elétrica possa lidar com a variação da geração eólica e solar, que por vezes resulta num excesso de energia, obrigando usinas a paradas forçadas, conhecidas como curtailment. “Hoje o tema mais quente no setor são as baterias. E as hidrelétricas reversíveis. Até por essa necessidade do sistema,” disse o diretor da consultoria Thymos Capital, André Millions. Apesar do intenso interesse de investidores, o leilão de dezembro está sob risco devido a discussões sobre quem vai pagar o custo dos projetos de armazenamento, segundo diversas fontes do setor. A legislação atual define o rateio dos custos entre todas empresas de geração, uma regra que gera ameaças de judicialização. No momento, empresas do setor se movimentam para convencer o Governo a trabalhar pela aprovação de um projeto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim que alteraria a lei para repassar a conta aos consumidores, como ocorre nos demais leilões do mercado de energia.

The upper compartment consists of a dry chamber housing vehicle electronics, key electrical equipment, and connectors, while the lower compartment is designed as a liquid chamber where multiple battery cell modules are fully submerged in dielectric cooling fluid. The core engineering challenge of this structure—electrical connections at the liquid-sealed interface—was resolved by safely routing wiring and connection points outside the liquid volume through the upper dry chamber. The crux of the patent lies in a design that actively leverages the excellent insulating and cooling properties of the coolant while thoroughly separating and maintaining the insulation and operational stability of electrical components and contacts that must not come into direct contact with the coolant, through the physical layout of the cabinet. This patent should be viewed not merely as a method of using individual cooling fluids, but as an emphasis on enclosure cabinet structure design that physically isolates liquid cooling environments from electrical equipment. With this patent, BYD has gained a key to further refreshing its image as a technology company. The Raton City Commission has voted down a proposed one-year moratorium on new data centers. Raton resident Pat Walsh, who has helped lead the charge against a data center in Raton, says she is disappointed by the City Commission's recent decision to vote down a proposed one-year moratorium on such projects. An attempt to pump the brakes on data center development in Raton went down in defeat last month after members of the City Commission voted 3-2 against a proposed ordinance that would have put a one-year moratorium against such projects. The Sept. 22 vote came after commissioners were presented with a petition signed by nearly 500 Raton residents expressing opposition to data centers in the Colfax County community of about 6,000 residents just south of the Colorado border. The City Commission’s decision stands in contrast to an August vote by the Colfax County Commission to adopt a one-year moratorium on data centers in unincorporated parts of the county. That made Colfax the fourth county in New Mexico to adopt such a restriction, joining Santa Fe, Sierra and Socorro counties. Raton Mayor Lori Chatterley and City Commissioners Daniel Campbell and Mark Honeyfield voted against the moratorium, while Commissioners Linde Schuster and Sally Hoger, who proposed the measure, voted for it. Campbell, who did not respond to a request for comment from The New Mexican, said at the meeting last month he saw no point in adopting the measure. “I can’t see that it gains us anything to be the first municipality in New Mexico that does this,” he said. Campbell noted Raton lacks the electrical power and water necessary to operate a data center, and the city’s ownership of the utilities that control those commodities serves as an adequate hedge against any potential development. “The data center issue was never going to happen to the degree that that’s been discussed because we don’t have the power to do that,” Campbell said. Hoger, however, described it as a commonsense measure and dismissed the idea the city already has adequate safeguards in place. “I don’t agree with that,” she reiterated in a recent interview. How it got started The issue arose in Raton earlier this year after leaders of Atterix LLC, a Denver-based company incorporated in late 2025, signed a memorandum of understanding with Raton officials to conduct a feasibility study for a data center project. That agreement, signed in February, gave the company six months to conduct the study; during that time, the city was prohibited from soliciting a similar project from another company. Atterix officials had floated the idea of creating a three-phase project in Raton that would have been constructed over several years, vastly increasing the city’s consumption of electricity. The company has not submitted the results of the feasibility study to the city, Hoger said. Chatterley said at the Sept. 22 commission meeting there was no project for the city to consider. She did not respond to The New Mexican‘s request for additional information. Kimberle Burke, owner and operator of a local ice cream shop, presented a petition to the commission Sept. 22 opposing a data center, warning against negative impacts a project might bring to the city when it comes to water, noise, the economy and “long-term repercussions that we may not know about right now.” Burke said people who signed the petition are anxious to understand what value a data center would provide to the community and who would benefit from it. “We want a moratorium so the community’s concerns can be addressed and we can all be aware of what’s going on, when and why,” she said. “Something of this magnitude should be decided by the community by the majority, not just a few.” Another resident who spoke in favor of the moratorium, Max Holland, reminded commissioners the adoption of a one-year moratorium would not permanently ban data centers from Raton. “A moratorium is not a no,” he said. “A moratorium is a timeout. Let’s utilize that time to inform ourselves and make sure we are doing the right thing.” Raton resident Pat Walsh, who co-founded Protect Our Resources, residents who oppose a data center in the city, said last week she was disappointed but not surprised by the commission’s action. She believes the issue is a long way from being dead in Raton. “We are going to keep an eye on various parts of city government to stay vigilant to see if any applications come through for power, utilities or water, or planning and zoning so we don’t get blindsided,” Walsh said. “I don’t want to take a chance on it being done,” Walsh said. “Nothing I can see would prevent someone else from coming in.” Hoping for a remedy Walsh and Hoger said they are more optimistic an ordinance regulating data center operators will get the commission’s approval, especially after the mayor has spoken in favor of such a measure. “I’m still very much in support of an ordinance of having strong guardrails,” Chatterley said Sept. 22. Hoger said she is part of a committee that has drafted an ordinance, which has been submitted to the city’s legal staff for review. She said it includes provisions that would require data center operators to work with local utilities to determine how much water and power they could use, establish minimum distances between such facilities and the nearest residence, and set limits on the amount of noise they could generate. She said the measure is based on similar ordinances adopted in other communities across the country. Hoger said she isn’t sure how to assess the data center battle in Raton with the defeat of the moratorium and the regulatory measure awaiting legal approval. artigo.texto: Renewable energy company Zelestra has entered into two new power purchase agreements (PPAs) with EDP to add four-hours of battery storage to existing solar plants in Spain. The deals will bring about 462MW-hours (MWh) of battery capacity to 181MW-direct current (MWdc) of solar power across two sites, Pedroso in Seville and Valkyria in Castilla-La Mancha. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. Under the new agreements, Zelestra will install a 25MW battery energy storage system (BESS) with around 100MWh of capacity at Pedroso, which already operates a 31MWdc solar plant. At Valkyria, a 90.45MW (approximately 362MWh) BESS will be added to the existing 150MWdc solar facility. EDP serves as the current offtaker for both sites. EDP global energy management CEO Pedro Neves Ferreira said: “At EDP, innovation goes beyond deploying renewable generation. We are continuously developing new solutions that combine technology, market expertise and flexibility assets to unlock greater value from clean energy. “By integrating storage with renewable generation, we can enhance system resilience, improve efficiency and accelerate the electrification and decarbonisation of the economy.” With these transactions, Zelestra and EDP’s joint portfolio in Spain now comprises four hybrid projects, with more than 1GW-hour of contracted storage capacity. The companies’ cooperation began in 2025 with the country’s first combined solar and BESS PPA, involving a 170MWdc solar installation and 400MWh of storage at Trujillo, Extremadura. Earlier, in 2024, the companies signed another agreement for a 160MWh BESS at the 50MW Pizarroso plant in Cáceres, reportedly the first PPA in Spain to hybridise an operational solar plant. Zelestra Spain CEO Jaime Burguete said: “Zelestra and EDP have built something together that is unique in the Spanish market: a commercial partnership that is unlocking large-scale storage capacity that will benefit the wider energy system. “These four hybrid projects show that energy storage is bankable in Spain, and we expect this segment of the market to be the main growth area in the years ahead. “It also means that every megawatt-hour moved into the evening or early morning is clean power the system would otherwise have had to find elsewhere.” In July 2026, Zelestra and EnBW signed a long-term tolling agreement for a 300MW share of a planned battery energy storage project in Emilia-Romagna, Italy.

artigo.texto: CATL in Debrecen is expanding its workforce CATL’s Chinese battery factory in Debrecen is increasing its workforce: now that trial production of battery cells has begun following the ongoing production of modules, the workforce will be expanded from the current 2800 to 3300 by the end of the year. Qin Liang, the chief operating officer of the Debrecen battery factory, said at a press event showcasing the plant that the third production line has already been launched in the module manufacturing operation that began in 2024; since then, more than 500.000 modules have been produced, powering approximately 10,000 vehicles across Europe. Module production has generated 100 billion forints in revenue for the company to date, on which taxes were paid in Hungary, the director noted. The Debrecen plant is designed to meet the needs of European automakers, producing nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, the director said, adding that the Debrecen plant ensures long-term stability, jobs, and new business opportunities for the region. Qin Liang noted that the cell factory received its operating permit in August, fulfilled all the conditions specified in the permits, and began trial production of battery cells on the first two production lines on September 22. Production will expand soon Following a few technical adjustments, the company will begin cell production on the other two lines as well. During the trial run, CATL experts are continuously monitoring the equipment, the quality and safety of the products, and full compliance with regulatory requirements. The new cell factory has a maximum annual capacity of 40 gigawatt-hours, all of which has already been fully reserved by customers. It was also announced at the press conference that the first phase of the project has now been completed at a cost of approximately 900 billion forints, and that once full capacity is reached, 4000 people will be employed at the plant. In response to a query from MTI, however, they confirmed that the entire project is planned in three phases; the total investment of 3000 billion forints will provide jobs for 9000 people and have an annual capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours. They added that they are open to negotiations with the government regarding the project, noting that they had an agreement for 129 billion forints in state subsidies to implement the first phase. They plan to rely on local labor Shen Feng, CATL’s managing director responsible for European operations, said at the press conference that cell production began in Germany in 2022; initially, the ratio of Chinese to German workers was 40 to 60 percent, but today 90 percent of the workforce is German. In Debrecen, the ratio of Chinese to local workers is currently 50–50 percent; according to their plans, the proportion of Hungarian workers will reach 90 percent by 2030. Qin Liang added that they will launch a supplier campaign in October to increase the involvement of local businesses in production. He noted that they currently have more than 300 local suppliers, 80 percent of whom are from Debrecen and the surrounding region. The plant manager also addressed the Debrecen plant’s water consumption, which is a particularly sensitive issue in Debrecen. He noted that they have developed water-saving technology—specifically, a cooling tower—that drastically reduces the plant’s water requirements. It was announced at the press event that the company will continuously provide the authorities with information on the plant’s water and energy consumption as well as its emissions, and that monitoring data will be published every two months so that the public can also access it. artigo.texto: In Festus, Missouri, a town that gave Donald Trump 67 percent of its vote, residents have filed to recall the mayor and three council members over a $6 billion data center. In New York, a Democratic governor has signed the first statewide moratorium on new ones. Across seven states, at least 33 recall campaigns are targeting as many as 58 local officials for the same reason, and the reason is not a party. It is a building. That makes data centers the rarest thing in American politics right now: an issue where the folding chairs in a red county and a blue one are filled with people saying the same words. They are not saying "no technology." They are saying the box across the road raises their power bill, drains their water, takes the farm, and was negotiated behind a nondisclosure agreement before anyone in town knew its name. In Luther, Oklahoma, the moratorium passed only after word leaked that the mayor had been in closed talks with a developer for months. The anger is not about servers. It is about being handed a decision that was already made. Here is what almost nobody in those rooms has been told, and what both sides would want if they knew it. Every data center is a furnace. Nearly all the electricity that goes in comes out as heat, and in every facility in America that heat is thrown into the sky through cooling towers, at the owner's expense. The newest liquid-cooled halls release it as warm water, exactly what a greenhouse wants in January. A two-and-a-half-acre greenhouse on that water grows on the order of 695,000 pounds of fresh produce a year with no boiler and nothing burned. Write into the rezoning that at least 15 percent of it is covenanted to the host community, to the schools, the food bank, the farm store on the road, and one building's waste feeds about 400 of its neighbors, year-round, in towns where the nearest winter tomato has traveled 1,500 miles. Put the fish house on the same loop and homes on radiant floors at the end of it, and the campus that was going to bury the farmland has built a farm. Notice what that covenant is. It is the opposite of an NDA. It is a promise, written into a public document, that a resident can read at the county clerk's office and hold the developer to at every hearing for the life of the project. The reason people in Festus and Luther and Prince William County feel the technology is being forced on them is that the terms were hidden. A heat covenant puts the terms on the wall. And it is the one proposal that does not ask either side to give up what it wants. Conservatives want the tax base, the jobs, and the AI race won; Loudoun County, Virginia, collected $1.2 billion in data-center property taxes this year and cut its residential rate for the tenth straight year, so the money is real. Progressives want communities protected, ratepayers held harmless, and food grown close to home; a farm on the fence line does all three. Michelle Obama and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. agree on almost nothing, but they agree that Americans should eat real food grown nearby. A data center that powers the cloud and feeds the town is not a compromise between the two camps. It is both of them, in one site plan. Virginia noticed first. This spring its General Assembly passed the first law in the country directing the state to put data-center waste heat to use, and the Senate vote was 39 to 0. In a legislature that spent the same session at war with itself over data-center tax breaks, that is what an issue looks like when it belongs to no one. Wall Street has noticed too. Lenders now weigh local opposition and permitting status before financing a campus, and local resistance blocked or delayed some $130 billion in projects in the first quarter of this year alone. The developer who arrives with a public covenant and a farm in the first phase of the site plan is not being generous. He is de-risking his loan. So, to the organizers running recall petitions and the officials facing them, to the governors weighing a pause and the developers hoping they don't: there is a yes here that both of you can sign. Put one question in every rezoning, in public, in writing: where does the heat go, and what share of what it grows stays here? A moratorium buys a town a year. A covenant buys it a farm. The fight in Festus and the fight in Albany are the same fight, and this is the same answer. Andrew Potter is the founder and CEO of Intelligent Harvest, a Lynchburg, Virginia company that develops greenhouses and community farms powered by data-center waste heat.

artigo.texto: Just days after Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman declared that a gigantic proposed data center in the city “must be stopped,” a spokesman for the company behind the project said the 860,000-square-foot facility should be “evaluated based on verified facts.” Coffman posted his thoughts about Vantage Data Centers’ Trident project late last week on Facebook, saying the project “must not go forward.” His post followed a City Council meeting last week during which hundreds of people living in neighborhoods near the site came out to decry the data center, which would be among Colorado’s largest. Residents voiced concerns about the facilities’ large water use and electric consumption, along with worries about noise. Several cities in the state, including Denver, Thornton and Commerce City, have imposed temporary bans on new data centers as larger and larger — or hyperscale — facilities have sprouted. Hyperscale data centers are engineered for large-scale workloads and are at the heart of the burgeoning data-hungry artificial intelligence sector. The Aurora council narrowly rejected a moratorium on data centers in August, but the city is hammering out rules for the facilities, including a just-passed ban on the use of water-hungry evaporative cooling systems by any business across the city. Aurora, Coffman wrote, “must explore every available option, to include my calling the proposed Trident data center up for a public hearing and then asking the members of City Council for a ‘no’ vote to stop it from being built.” The mayor said he would do this regardless of any litigation Vantage might level against the city. Mark Freeman, vice president of global marketing for the Denver-based company, wouldn’t answer a question from The Denver Post about whether Vantage might take legal action against Aurora should the city kill its project. Freeman said the company’s proposed data center on a 108-acre site just inside the E-470 beltway at East 48th Avenue would use a closed-loop system that would require one initial 600,000-gallon injection of water and 2,200 gallons a day as part of ongoing operations — “about half the amount used by a similarly sized office building.” It would be designed to use 334 megawatts of electric power, he said, to run both “cloud and (artificial intelligence) workloads.” By comparison, nearby Denver International Airport uses 45 megawatts of electric power. Freeman also said the site plan will comply with all noise ordinance standards in the city, with sound levels from the facility expected to be “similar to a typical office building or a dishwasher running in the next room.” Aurora Councilwoman Amy Wiles, whose ward covers the proposed Trident site, recognizes the city is in a tricky position given that Vantage has been following the city’s approval process for more than a year and the site where it wants to build its center is zoned for that use. “I wish this had been done sooner — I brought it up months ago,” she said Monday. “Ideally, when (the area) was first re-zoned, I wish it had been looked at a bit more closely to balance the need for business while also prioritizing our residents.” Wiles said she still has questions about low-frequency noise and vibrations from data centers and how those might affect nearby neighbors. Coffman, in his Facebook post, said the project received preliminary administrative approval without a public hearing “because a data center is a permitted use under the current zoning.” The parcel Vantage wants to develop was zoned “airport district” by the city four years ago — a designation that permits businesses like data centers. The mayor is not against data centers per se, but he said more scrutiny needs to be applied in terms of where they are built. “We need to update our development code so that we have realistic distances between residential developments and data centers,” he told The Post in a text response to questions Monday. “The city of Aurora has a land mass a little larger than Denver and about a third of our city is undeveloped, so there definitely are suitable locations for data centers that are far enough away from homes.” Get more Colorado news by signing up for our daily Your Morning Dozen email newsletter.

artigo.texto: How AI is Reshaping Data Center Financing The race to build computing capacity for artificial intelligence is reshaping data center financing in the United States. As projects become larger, more capital-intensive and increasingly developed in phases, sponsors need financing that can adapt to changing capital requirements while still providing certainty of execution on increasingly compressed timelines. Some of the largest developments now represent multi-billion-dollar investment programs encompassing multiple buildings and years of construction. Rather than financing a single asset with a defined completion date, sponsors may be funding a campus that grows in stages as new capacity is added. The result is a financing model that increasingly needs to evolve alongside the project itself. Financing a project built in phases A large data center campus is rarely developed all at once. Sponsors may begin with land and site infrastructure before moving into the first buildings, then add capacity over time as customer demand develops. Each phase can bring different capital requirements, construction milestones and operating considerations. That makes flexibility increasingly important. “Five years ago, you were looking at a very different type of data center project,” says Michael Lardieri, Managing Director, Institutional Client & Financial Sponsors at BBVA USA. “Today we're talking about campuses that can require billions of dollars of investment and are being developed in multiple phases. That changes how sponsors think about capital and what they need from their banks.” Financing can therefore become part of a longer development strategy rather than a single transaction. Sponsors and lenders need to consider when capital will be required, how later phases relate to earlier ones and how the financing may need to evolve as a project moves from construction into operation. Speed is changing the equation At the same time, the expansion of AI infrastructure is putting greater pressure on development timelines. Suitable land, power capacity, equipment and construction resources are all in demand. Once those elements have been secured, delays elsewhere in the development process can become costly. Financing is no exception. For sponsors, having access to capital is essential, but so is knowing that financing can be executed within the project's timetable. Large transactions may require substantial underwriting commitments and coordination among multiple institutions, often while other parts of the development are moving simultaneously. “Clients don't only want to know whether the capital is available,” Lardieri says. “They want confidence that it can be delivered on the timeline the project requires. As the market has accelerated, that certainty has become increasingly important.” The asset cannot be viewed in isolation The infrastructure surrounding a data center is also becoming more relevant to financing decisions. Power is the most visible example. Large AI-oriented facilities require significant electricity capacity, and the timing of that capacity can influence when a project is built and when capital needs to be deployed. "The challenge is not simply the amount of capital required." But the same principle extends to other parts of a development, from connectivity and construction to customer commitments and the timing of future expansion. For lenders, that means understanding the financing increasingly requires understanding how the project itself will develop. Financing the next phase of growth AI is expected to continue driving significant investment in digital infrastructure. As it does, the financing supporting that expansion will have to keep pace with a sector that is changing quickly. The challenge is not simply the amount of capital required. It is matching that capital to projects that are being developed at greater scale, in multiple phases and under increasingly demanding timelines. For sponsors and financial institutions alike, that is making data center financing a more dynamic part of the infrastructure landscape.

artigo.texto: A agenda climática deixou de ser um capítulo isolado dos relatórios de sustentabilidade e passou a orientar decisões de investimento, contratos com fornecedores e a reputação de marcas inteiras. Nesse cenário, dois termos se tornaram onipresentes nos comunicados corporativos — Carbono Neutro e Net Zero. Embora sejam tratados como sinônimos, eles descrevem compromissos com profundidade, prazo e rigor bem diferentes. Segundo o Monitor do Mercado, entender essa distinção não é apenas uma questão semântica: é o que separa uma meta climática consistente de uma promessa sem lastro ou, em casos mais graves, de greenwashing. O que diferencia Carbono Neutro de Net Zero Ser Carbono Neutro significa que uma empresa equilibra a quantidade de dióxido de carbono que emite com uma quantidade equivalente removida ou evitada em outro lugar. Na prática, funciona como uma conta que precisa fechar em zero: de um lado ficam as emissões medidas; do outro, as compensações. Essas compensações costumam vir da compra de créditos de carbono ligados a projetos de preservação florestal, energia renovável ou captura de metano, de investimentos em reflorestamento — que aproveitam a capacidade das árvores de absorver CO₂ durante a fotossíntese — ou ainda de aportes em fontes de energia limpa. O ponto central é que a neutralidade de carbono não exige, necessariamente, que a empresa reduza suas próprias emissões antes de compensá-las. Ela pode manter o nível atual de emissão e simplesmente pagar pela compensação em outro ponto da cadeia. Trata-se de um modelo mais acessível e mais rápido de alcançar, o que o torna útil como primeiro passo, mas limitado quando tratado como meta final. Net Zero: escopo mais amplo e exigência de corte real O conceito de Net Zero representa uma evolução desse compromisso e parte de uma lógica bem mais exigente. Em vez de olhar apenas para o CO₂, a meta abrange todos os gases de efeito estufa, incluindo metano, óxido nitroso e hidrofluorcarbonetos. Além disso, a compensação só entra em cena depois que a empresa tiver cortado a maior parte possível de suas próprias emissões ao longo de toda a cadeia de valor. Isso envolve normalmente três frentes de emissão, conhecidas como escopos. O escopo 1 cobre as emissões diretas geradas por fontes controladas pela própria empresa, como frota própria, caldeiras e processos industriais. O escopo 2 está ligado à energia elétrica comprada. Já o escopo 3 abrange as emissões indiretas espalhadas por toda a cadeia de valor, da matéria-prima ao descarte do produto, e costuma ser a fatia mais difícil de endereçar. Só depois de reduzir drasticamente essas três frentes — e não apenas uma parte delas — é que se admite compensar a fração remanescente, considerada tecnicamente inevitável no estado atual da tecnologia. O que a SBTi considera uma meta Net Zero legítima A Science Based Targets initiative, conhecida como SBTi e principal referência internacional para validar metas corporativas de clima, reforça essa distinção. De acordo com a avaliação apresentada, uma meta Net Zero só é considerada legítima quando a empresa demonstra uma trajetória de corte real de emissões, geralmente entre 90% e 95% do total, antes de recorrer a qualquer compensação para o restante. O Carbono Neutro não segue esse mesmo nível de exigência. Esse padrão vem sendo continuamente aperfeiçoado. Em 2026, a SBTi atualizou seu padrão internacional de metas Net Zero corporativas, reforçando critérios sobre como as empresas devem comprovar, monitorar e reportar essa redução real ao longo do tempo — um sinal de que o mercado está fechando o cerco contra metas anunciadas sem lastro técnico. Hoje, milhares de empresas ao redor do mundo já têm metas climáticas validadas por esse tipo de padrão, número que cresce ano a ano à medida que reguladores, investidores e consumidores cobram mais transparência. Por que a diferença importa para quem investe É essa diferença de rigor, alcance e prazo que explica por que uma empresa pode se declarar carbono neutro já hoje, com relativa facilidade, comprando compensações suficientes para equilibrar suas emissões de CO₂ em um recorte específico da operação. Uma meta Net Zero, por outro lado, costuma levar décadas de reestruturação de processos, fornecedores e tecnologia para se tornar realidade. Justamente por essa diferença de complexidade e percepção pública, quanto mais a sustentabilidade influencia decisões de compra, contratação e investimentos, maior é a tentação de usar esses termos de forma solta. Uma empresa pode anunciar neutralidade de carbono comprando créditos de projetos de qualidade duvidosa, sem nunca reduzir de fato sua produção — o que, na prática, não resolve o problema climático, apenas o desloca no papel. O que observar além do rótulo Por isso, especialistas recomendam observar não o rótulo usado pela empresa, mas o plano por trás dele. Existe uma meta de redução real, com etapas intermediárias verificáveis? A compensação é usada como complemento ou como substituto da redução? Há transparência sobre os escopos 1, 2 e 3? Segundo a análise, essas perguntas dizem mais sobre o compromisso climático de uma empresa do que qualquer selo isolado. Na prática, os dois conceitos não são excludentes e costumam ser etapas de uma mesma jornada. Em um mercado onde compromissos ambientais se multiplicam, entender a diferença entre Carbono Neutro e Net Zero tornou-se essencial para interpretar o que as empresas realmente estão fazendo para enfrentar as mudanças climáticas. A neutralidade pode representar um ponto de partida relevante, mas o Net Zero é o que revela o grau de ambição e transformação envolvido. No fim, a pergunta mais importante não é qual termo aparece no relatório, mas quais ações concretas estão sendo implementadas para tornar essa promessa uma realidade. O texto é assinado por Renata G. Moreno, especialista em Direito Ambiental e Regulatório, sócia e fundadora do escritório Renata Franco Sociedade de Advogados, e por Luara Teixeira, estagiári

artigo.texto: Stevens Point starts data center conversation STEVENS POINT, Wis. (WSAW)— The city of Stevens Point added an item to Monday’s planning commission meeting for a public discussion on data centers, with city leaders saying they want the community to drive how the city reacts if or when a data center looks to move in. Current zoning rules “At this point, if a data center wanted to build one of those massive things, what safeguards would there be for the community?” said Alder Mary Kneebone, Stevens Point Planning Commission. The planning commission says there isn’t much. As of now, data centers can’t be built in residential or commercial zoning districts. They would be allowed in the city’s industrial zoning districts. Developer interest While the city hasn’t had conversations about constructing a data center, data centers have reached out to the city about interest levels. “It was a conversation that, we didn’t talk about it,” said Jarod Kivela, director of community development, Stevens Point. “They have been, I guess not responded to until we have this conversation.” Public concerns During public comment, many expressed concerns over the environmental impacts in a city built on the outdoors. “If I saw that there was a data center being built in Stevens Point and I was a prospective college student...like, if I went back to when I was looking just out of high school...I would’ve said no. I wouldn’t have come here,” Reemus said, an environmental studies student. Other concerns were lack of economic impact after data centers are built, as well as want of transparency between the city and the people if a project were to start. Federal candidates weigh in The issue of data centers is more of a city and state-level policy, but it can be influenced at the federal level. Both candidates for the 7th Congressional District are hearing from voters about them. “We are way behind in regulating this entire sector,” said Fred Clark, (D) 7th Congressional District candidate. “We need to treat AI like we treated nuclear energy in the 1950s. And, and the federal government is the only game in town to make that happen.” “This is where I think it’s so important to have young faces involved in this rise of AI,” said Michael Alfonso, (R) 7th Congressional District candidate. “You know, AI has the ability to put out of work so many workers. But I actually think if done properly, it can actually empower workers.” Clark says the state needs to regulate how they’re built. Alfonso adds that should include supplying their own power, not use up waterways and let local leaders make the decision. artigo.texto: Northfield council moves away from data center ban, toward tiered regulation After more than two hours of public comment and council discussion, the Northfield City Council voted 7-0 Tuesday night to reduce the required setback between data-processing facilities and parks or trails from roughly three-quarters of a mile to 200 feet. But the setback change was only part of the story. In a separate motion, the council also directed staff to explore a tiered regulatory framework for data-processing facilities as part of the upcoming Land Development Code update, looking beyond just power consumption to include water use and other emerging concerns. The change to the setback had been in the works since 2024, when the city passed an ordinance regulating data-processing facilities. That ordinance required a 3,950-foot setback from any existing or planned park, trail, or recreational feature. It also required a 200-foot setback from residential structures. Community Development Director Scott Wopata acknowledged the moment was about more than one number. “This one's going to be hard,” he said. “In any example I look at around Minnesota or the Midwest or nationally, there aren't a lot of examples where communities have figured out a way to have this conversation and learn from each other and to empathetically see things from different perspectives. There's a lot of negative examples of how elected officials and staff members in different cities have signed NDAs, dismissed the public, not listened to public concerns.” Wopata framed the night as an effort to rebuild public trust after a year of conversations that started long before any application existed. "In 2024, we put a moratorium on all data-center development so that we could develop policies before we had a project application," Wopata said. "That is what we did. We have been following those best practices." The city's regulations include 17 performance standards covering noise, water use, glare, vibrations and more. They also require a conditional use permit triggered by any water use. “If we read anywhere anything about data centers, [there] is a very well documented track of negative externalities,” Wopata said. “There are water quality issues. There's water quantity issues. There are stories of communities losing water pressure. There's stories of communities where residents have seen significant spikes in their utility bills because the data centers moved in and this corporate development has happened.” But he also drew a distinction between prohibition and regulation. "Regulating is often a more strategic and sophisticated and just successful approach than prohibition," Wopata said, listing alcohol and cannabis prohibition as negative examples from history. "Bringing something into the light and regulating it can often help ameliorate some of the biggest harmful negative externalities." City Planner Mathias Hughey explained the rationale for the change. The 3,950-foot setback made every industrial parcel in the city undevelopable, and it was originally drafted without a clear rationale. "This is still much more restrictive than other industrial uses," Hughey said. Hughey said the planning commission had separately recommended that data-processing facilities be prohibited outright and that staff research a tiered regulatory framework. Because that recommendation was not part of the published public hearing notice, the council had to proceed with the setback item as written. Competing priorities More than a dozen residents spoke during public comment, most urging the council to keep the moratorium or reject the setback change. One Northfielder, Trisha Brunk, even led the room through a song. Councilor Kathleen Holmes acknowledged the volume of opposition in the room but said the council has to weigh competing priorities. “While there is a high number of people who have spoken out against data centers, we, those of us decision makers, policymakers up here, have to hold many priorities,” she said. “And while we have heard the thoughts, the feedback, the opinions on data centers, I would say probably all of us here more often and more frequently hear 'Lower our taxes.’ … I take this as the belief that the path forward is through regulation and not prohibition.” Councilor Jessica Peterson White said she saw parallels to hog feedlot debates from the early 2000s. "But when we were talking about hog feedlots, the scale was a really important part of the conversation," she said. "I don't have a clear sense myself of what scale of data center or other types of development is where we should set a regulation, but I believe that the regulations that we have make it vanishingly unlikely that we will get a hyperscale data center, and that seems good." She also addressed the equity dimension. "There is a history in this country of affluent white communities sort of offshoring their industrial needs to communities that don't have the same resources, don't have the same organizing power, and those industrial uses are then underregulated and create issues for poorer and less white communities," she said. "And I hope we don't play a role in that." No one is saying ‘Let’s build a huge data center’ Councilor Davin Sokup said he was voting yes despite his own uncertainty. "But I just really want to highlight that what we're considering here tonight, I think, in my opinion, does show an openness to having a data center in Northfield," he said. "I'm not willing to say that it couldn't possibly be that in the future." Councilor Chad Beumer said he understood the distrust but believed the city's regulations were already strong. “I don't think there's a single person sitting up here that is saying, ‘Let's build a huge data center out there that's going to burn up all kinds of energy and waste a whole bunch of water,’” he said. “I think our ordinance 1098 clearly dictates that that's not going to happen.” Mayor Erica Zweifel closed the discussion by noting the s

artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL has reached a key milestone in proving the durability of its technology, demonstrating impressive laboratory analysis results. The prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells tested, which have been operating without interruption for almost fourteen years, have retained about 85 percent of their original energy capacity. The cells analyzed are part of the world's first large-scale energy storage facility, the 63 MWh Zhangbei, which began operation in 2011 and even provided clean energy for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The complete decommissioning of the facility in the summer of 2025 has allowed engineers to subject the components to detailed chemical and physical destructive testing. Over 50 samples taken from the original cells reveal remarkable material durability: the anode and cathode layers have retained perfect geometry, and the graphite shows no structural defects or critical signs of aging. An interesting detail is the fact that not a single cell from this manufacturer had to be replaced over the entire 14-year cycle. The test results open up new perspectives for the so-called “second life“ of industrial batteries. According to the company's experts, the retired cells have a resource for about 1,000 more complete charge and discharge cycles. This makes the components fully suitable for reintegration into smaller secondary storage systems for at least another decade. The current findings reconfirm the expectations from the control tests carried out on the ninth year of the facility's launch. LFP technology is also gaining in importance in the automotive sector. While these chemistries are inferior in specific energy density to nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) alternatives, they offer significantly lower manufacturing costs and unrivaled durability under extreme temperature and operating conditions. The achieved lifespan solidifies the technology's position as a key pillar for the future of sustainable mobility and green energy.

artigo.texto: Climate experts and other stakeholders yesterday gathered in Abuja for the European Union Climate Dialogues programme ( EUCDs2) for Nigeria’s carbon market roadmap. The event, which focuses on “Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets Through Robust Monitoring, Reporting And Verification (MRV) Protocols,” brought together government officials, development partners, private-sector operators, investors, civil society organisations and other stakeholders. The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi said Nigeria’s carbon market must be built on integrity, transparency and credible data, warning that the country would not tolerate practices capable of undermining confidence in carbon credits generated in Nigeria. Represented by the Director, Energy , Transportation and Infrastructure, Mr Michael Ivenso, l she said that the council had issued about 26 million carbon credits so far from projects previously executed in Nigeria, describing the development as evidence of the country’s capacity to participate in international carbon markets. According to her, Nigeria’s objective is to ensure that carbon projects deliver “real, additional and permanent mitigation outcomes” while protecting communities, ecosystems and the interests of investors and project developers. The Director-General said the operationalisation of the National Carbon Markets Framework would provide the institutional foundation for a credible carbon market capable of mobilising private capital for clean energy, agriculture, forestry, waste management and other climate interventions. The NCCC boss said a key component of the strategy was the establishment of a unified and interoperable national carbon registry through which every carbon credit generated, issued, transferred or retired in Nigeria would have a digital record. “This will help prevent double-counting and strengthen the integrity of carbon transactions,” she said. She added that Nigeria was also moving towards digital MRV, leveraging remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to improve the accuracy of carbon measurement while reducing the cost and time required for verification. Majekodunmi said effective MRV would also enable regulators to track emissions trajectories, assure buyers that claimed emission reductions were genuine and help communities monitor benefit-sharing arrangements. She called for stronger coordination among federal ministries, state governments, project developers, development partners, financial institutions, civil society organisations and academic institutions. She said the Council was working with relevant stakeholders to ensure that future carbon credit transfers under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were supported by credible national systems. The Director, Federal Department of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, said the forestry sector remained central to Nigeria’s climate response and could become one of the country’s biggest opportunities in the carbon market. She said forests served as carbon sinks and temperature buffers while providing biodiversity, soil protection, water regulation and livelihoods for millions of Nigerians, particularly rural and forest-dependent communities. “We must therefore ensure that carbon-market development supports forest conservation rather than creating pressure for further forest exploitation,” she said. Bawa-Bwari stressed that credible carbon markets could not be built without credible data, particularly in the forestry sector. She said Nigeria needed reliable information on forest cover, degradation, deforestation, biomass and carbon stocks to determine how much carbon was being stored or removed and how those changes occurred over time. She called for continued strengthening of the National Forest Inventory and forest monitoring systems, as well as increased use of satellite imagery, remote sensing and artificial intelligence. However, she cautioned that satellite information must be complemented with ground-based measurements and field verification. The director also called for increased capacity among federal and state forestry institutions to collect and manage forest data. “MRV should not be developed as a stand-alone carbon-market activity. It should build on existing national systems for forest monitoring, greenhouse-gas accounting, REDD+ data, land-use planning and climate reporting,” she said. Bawa-Bwari urged relevant agencies to avoid establishing parallel systems that collect similar information, calling instead for clear institutional responsibilities for the collection, management, validation and reporting of forest-carbon data. On it part, the European Union said Nigeria’s efforts to develop a credible carbon market could help attract much-needed finance for climate action while supporting sustainable economic growth. Mr Jop Weterings, a member of the Task Force on International Carbon Pricing And Marketing Diplomacy at the EU said the bloc had stepped up cooperation with Nigeria on carbon markets over the past year, describing the roundtable as an important milestone in the partnership. The EU said its shared interest with Nigeria was to scale up high-integrity carbon markets capable of strengthening global climate action, channeling resources into Nigerian initiatives and driving sustainable economic growth. It noted that Nigeria’s adoption of the National Carbon Markets Framework had provided an important foundation for building confidence and trust among investors, buyers and other market participants. The EU representative said the focus should now be on operationalising the framework, particularly through strong MRV systems that would ensure carbon credits generated in Nigeria represented credible climate outcomes. artigo.texto: The Public Utility Commission of Texas is asking a Travis County judge to block the release of information showing where data centers and virtual currency mines operate, saying those details could aid terrorists. The lawsuit filed Monday pits the state agency responsible for regulating utilities against Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office over the scope of Texas’ public-records law and the state’s protections for critical infrastructure. At the center of the dispute are two seemingly basic geographic details: the county where a facility is located and the regional water planning area in which it sits. The PUC argues that those details are “privileged information” and become sensitive when combined with other information collected through its survey of the industry, including electricity demand, actual electricity consumption, projected peak demand, water consumption, water sources, cooling technology and the utilities and infrastructure serving a facility. The commission is not asking the court to declare the entire survey confidential. Instead, it wants the court to rule that the two geographic fields are exempt from disclosure under the Texas Homeland Security Act, which is meant to “protect against homeland security threats and hazards . . . and prevent significant criminal and terrorist attacks.” The lawsuit does not represent a final ruling on whether the information ultimately must be released. But it does come as Texas officials are seeking more information about the state’s data center industry. Gov. Greg Abbott has ordered state agencies to conduct additional reviews of data centers seeking to connect to the state’s electric grid, including reviews of electricity and water use, cooling systems and other information. He has also directed the Texas Water Development Board to take enforcement action against data centers that fail to comply with required water use reporting. What’s in the PUC water and energy use survey? In 2025, Texas lawmakers directed the PUC to collect information about water and energy consumption at data centers and virtual-currency-mining facilities to better understand the growth of the industry. The effort reflects a growing concern among state officials and Texans about the resources required by large computing facilities. Data centers can consume enormous amounts of electricity because of the thousands of servers operating inside them. Depending on their cooling systems, they can also require substantial quantities of water to help keep their servers cool during operation. The PUC developed its survey in cooperation with the Texas Water Development Board, the state agency tasked with overseeing the state’s water planning process. The information was intended to help state officials better understand the relationship between electricity demand and water consumption and to inform future planning. The Legislature also directed the PUC to share information with other state agencies and produce a report on its findings. The survey was sent to 377 facilities and sought information including a facility’s location, county and regional water-planning area, electricity load and consumption, projected future peak demand, cooling technology, water consumption and sources and information about the facility’s connection to the electric grid. The response was limited and called “pathetic” by one state representative during a June legislative hearing where PUC officials said 28 companies representing 92 facilities had responded to the survey. Lawmakers questioned whether the resulting data would be sufficient to support long-term policy decisions. The PUC later reopened the voluntary survey for an additional 10 days in July. As of August, 13 virtual currency mining and 77 data center facilities had filled out the survey, according to an email from a PUC spokesperson. The PUC lawsuit The PUC dispute with the attorney general’s office began after a resident from McLennan County and four journalists, including a reporter at The Texas Tribune, sought the survey responses through open records requests. The PUC denied those requests, saying that the information should be protected from disclosure in its entirety. Those requestors have an opportunity to participate in the open records dispute if they choose. Under Texas law, when a governmental agency believes requested records aren’t open to the public, it can ask the Attorney General’s Open Records Division for a ruling. That is what the PUC did. The commission argued that at least some of the survey information was protected under the Texas Homeland Security Act, which makes certain information concerning vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure confidential. But the PUC, the government entity seeking to withhold records, must establish that the statutory exception applies. That distinction is at the heart of the dispute. The Attorney General’s office issued two rulings concluding that the PUC had not sufficiently established that the disputed information identified the kind of technical vulnerabilities covered by the Homeland Security Act. The PUC is now challenging those rulings by asking a court to reach a different conclusion. The agency argues that the individual pieces of information in the survey cannot be considered in isolation. A county name, for example, ordinarily would not reveal much about a facility’s security. But the commission argues that the county and regional water planning area can be combined with information about a facility’s electricity consumption, water use and the infrastructure that supplies those resources. artigo.texto: Tech giants are trying to win over communities that oppose data centers as they pour billions into the infrastructure powering their AI ambitions. Amazon’s latest approach is to invest more than $1 billion over five years in job training, free community college, and energy efficiency upgrades. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman announced the Built Together program in an Oct. 2 corporate post that also defended the company’s data center build-out. He compared the build-out to public benefit projects such as the interstate highway system, and wrote that Amazon understands communities’ “apprehension” about data centers. Still, he wrote, the more than 100 proposed data center moratoriums under construction could sideline the U.S. from the AI race. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman wrote. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.” Amazon isn’t the only hyperscaler trying to make the data center boom easier for host communities to accept. Microsoft pledged in January to cover the electricity and grid costs tied to its facilities, and Meta said it invested more than $550 million in water and wastewater infrastructure in its data center communities. What Amazon is offering Built Together targets common complaints dogging data center projects—that they raise energy bills, strain local infrastructure, and don’t deliver enough lasting benefits to residents. Those concerns have become harder for hyperscalers to ignore. New York imposed a statewide moratorium on new large data centers in July, and opposition spread to major data center markets like Virginia, where only 35% of people said in March that they’d be comfortable with a new facility being built there, according to a Washington Post and Schar School poll. Amazon itself is facing resistance in Loudoun County, Va., where officials are objecting to a proposed 800,000-square-foot data center project on the former George Washington University Virginia Science and Technology campus. Built Together is Amazon’s attempt to answer those objections with more direct benefits for host communities. Amazon said it will cover students’ remaining community college costs after financial aid for certain certificates and associate degrees, including programs in HVAC, fiber optics, and IT, and estimates more than 300,000 students could gain access over five years. The company also said its skilled trades centers plan to train up to 100,000 workers a year for jobs with Amazon and its construction partners by the end of 2028. The company also plans to fund energy efficiency upgrades for more than 30,000 homes and more than 300 schools and community buildings. Local officials and community groups will help steer funding toward projects such as roads, parks, fire equipment, affordable housing, and food assistance. “Working with county officials and trusted community organizations, we will identify the highest-impact investments and provide annual funding with transparent reporting on outcomes,” Garman wrote. “This is not Amazon deciding what communities need—it is Amazon providing resources and letting communities decide.” Amazon is also using the Built Together announcement to push back on some causes of the backlash. Garman wrote that data centers are unfairly blamed for higher electricity bills and water use, and that aging grids are at fault for rising energy bills in some states. “In instances where energy rates are going up, it’s primarily because the grid is old and hasn’t been invested in and expanded before the demand arrived,” he wrote. He also said Amazon’s average data center uses less than 13,000 gallons of water per day and said the facilities deliver tax revenue and construction jobs to host communities. In St. Joseph County, Ind., Amazon estimates it will pay more than $3 billion in taxes over the same period, compared with $1.2 million that the land’s previous use would have generated.

artigo.texto: Adani Green Energy Ltd. (AGEL), one of India’s largest renewable energy company, increased its operational battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity to 6.63 GWh at Khavda, Gujarat. The company expanded the capacity from 3.55 GWh in June 2026 and now accounts for more than half of India’s approximately 12.6 GWh of operational BESS capacity. According to AGEL, the milestone establishes Khavda as the world’s largest operational battery energy storage installation at a single location, with 6.63 GWh of operational capacity. BESS Expansion Supports Khavda Renewable Energy Project AGEL achieved the 6.63 GWh milestone within 14 months of starting BESS construction at Khavda. The latest capacity addition took just 10 months to commission from the beginning of construction. The battery storage system forms an integral part of AGEL’s renewable energy development at Khavda, where the company is developing a 30 GW renewable energy plant across 538 sq km of barren land. The company said its 6.63 GWh BESS can store enough clean energy to power around two million homes for a day. It can also support peak electricity demand in cities such as Nagpur, Patna and Vizag for several hours. Moreover, the storage capacity is equivalent to the battery capacity of more than 150,000 mid-sized electric vehicles and can store enough energy each day to meet almost twice the estimated daily electricity requirement of the Delhi Metro. Battery Storage Strengthens Renewable Power Reliability “Reaching 6.63 GWh of operational battery storage in just 14 months is a significant milestone for AGEL and India’s clean energy transition,” said Sagar Adani, Executive Director, Adani Green Energy Ltd. He added that storage at this scale can make renewable power firmer, more reliable and dispatchable when the electricity grid requires it. The BESS uses lithium-ion battery technology, supported by energy management systems (EMS) and automated telemetry. These systems manage charging and discharging, optimise battery performance and enable the facility to provide grid services. AGEL Targets More Than 10 GWh of BESS Additions Looking ahead, AGEL plans to add more than 10 GWh of BESS capacity during FY 2026–27. The company is also targeting 50 GWh of energy storage capacity over the next five years. In addition, AGEL is pursuing pumped storage projects (PSPs) as part of its broader strategy to develop large-scale renewable power that can deliver firm and dispatchable electricity. AGEL Expands Renewable Energy Portfolio AGEL develops, owns and operates utility-scale grid-connected solar, wind, hybrid and energy storage projects. The company currently has an operating renewable energy portfolio of 20.76 GW, along with 6.63 GWh of operational BESS capacity across 12 states. As reported by pv-magazine-india.com, AGEL aims to reach 50 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030, supporting India’s broader decarbonisation and clean-energy transition goals.

artigo.texto: Sistema de armazenamento de energia solar para varanda com duas tomadas de alimentação de reserva: análise do SigenMate 2700 Ultra Sistema complexo de armazenamento para varanda e casa. O SigenMate 2700 Ultra é um sistema de armazenamento tudo-em-um para instalações solares em varandas, oferecendo até 18,8 kWh e 4.000 Wp. A nossa análise revela o desempenho do sistema na prática e onde surgiram problemas. Marcus Schwarten (traduzido por DeepL / Ninh Duy) Publicado 🇺🇸 🇩🇪 ... Veredito do teste do SigenMate 2700 Ultra: Controle rápido, mas também problemas Com base nos nossos testes, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra da Sigenergy oferece uma interessante solução tudo-em-um para sistemas solares de varanda. No nosso teste, gostámos particularmente da elevada potência de entrada fotovoltaica distribuída por quatro MPPTs, da construção de alta qualidade e do assistente de IA na aplicação abrangente. O controlo da injeção na rede também é rápido e preciso - quando a ligação ao contador inteligente funciona. Também nos deparámos com alguns outros problemas menores, mas estes deverão ser corrigíveis com uma atualização de software. No geral, um sistema de armazenamento tudo-em-um mais do que sólido para sistemas solares de varanda, cuja capacidade pode aumentar até 18,8 kWh ao longo do tempo, mas que não oferece qualquer margem para além dos seus 800 W de potência de injeção na rede. Pro Contra Preço e disponibilidade Na Alemanha, o preço de venda recomendado do SigenMate 2700 Ultra é de 1.199 euros (com IVA de 0% na Alemanha). O preço de venda recomendado da bateria de expansão SigenMate BAT 2700 é de 899 euros. Os produtos estão disponíveis diretamente no fabricante, mas também podem ser encomendados em retalhistas como a Amazon ou a Tepto. Com o crescimento dos sistemas solares para varandas e dos pequenos sistemas fotovoltaicos, cada vez mais fabricantes estão a lançar no mercado soluções tudo-em-um que combinam inversores, MPPTs e armazenamento. Além dos nomes habituais, como Anker Solix, EcoFlow e Zendure, existem também soluções de fabricantes menos conhecidos. Entre estas encontra-se o SigenMate 2700 Ultra, que está disponível há alguns meses. A empresa por trás deste produto, a Sigenergy, não é uma recém-chegada, mas até agora tem atuado sobretudo na área dos sistemas fotovoltaicos de maiores dimensões. A nossa análise do SigenMate 2700 Ultra revela como o seu sistema compacto de armazenamento de energia para todos se comporta na prática e como se compara com a concorrência. Specifications Equipamento e instalação: Sistema de armazenamento para sistemas solares de varanda Uma análise das especificações acima mostra que o SigenMate 2700 Ultra tem muito em comum com o Anker Solix Solarbank 3 Pro do ano passado. Também oferece uma capacidade de bateria LiFePO₄ de pouco menos de 2,7 kWh (6.000 ciclos de carga, garantia de 10 anos). Se necessário, esta capacidade pode ser ampliada até 18,8 kWh com seis baterias de expansão BAT2700. Isso deve ser mais do que suficiente para a grande maioria dos lares - não só para sistemas solares de varanda, mas também para armazenamento de energia doméstico. Com uma potência de entrada fotovoltaica de 4.000 W, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra supera até ligeiramente o Solarbank 3 Pro, oferecendo também 4 MPPTs. Isto é vantajoso, pois não só permite ligar até oito painéis solares sem qualquer problema, como também proporciona condições ideais para painéis com diferentes orientações e sombreamento. A potência de saída é limitada a 800 watts, como é habitual num sistema solar de varanda. Além disso, estão disponíveis diretamente no dispositivo duas tomadas de alimentação de emergência com uma potência de saída contínua de 1,400 W e uma potência de pico de 1,800 W. Estas funcionam independentemente da rede elétrica e, por isso, também funcionam durante uma falha de energia (se a bateria estiver carregada). Quando ligado à rede elétrica, é possível atingir até 3,600 W (bypass). Além da entrada solar, o SigenMate 2700 Ultra também pode ser carregado a partir da rede elétrica com uma potência de até 1,400 W. Alguns outros sistemas no mercado oferecem potências máximas de saída e de entrada superiores. No entanto, estas capacidades são suficientes para um sistema solar de varanda. Tudo isto está alojado numa robusta estrutura metálica. A qualidade de construção da unidade que testámos é excelente e transmite uma impressão de produto de gama alta, inclusive em termos de design. Graças à classificação IP66 e à proteção contra corrosão C5-M o sistema está bem equipado para utilização no exterior. Foi concebido para suportar temperaturas entre -20 °C e 55 °C e pode ser aquecido através de uma manta de aquecimento, de acordo com uma programação ou automaticamente, se necessário. No entanto, já gera uma quantidade considerável de calor por si só sob carga. O dispositivo pesa cerca de 29 kg e exige alguma força para o deslocar até ao local de instalação. As duas pegas embutidas à esquerda e à direita facilitam o transporte. As dimensões de 46.0 x 27.5 x 22.5 cm são bastante compactas para um sistema com cerca de 2.7 kWh. Quando combinado com uma ou mais baterias adicionais, a torre torna-se proporcionalmente mais alta. O material de montagem para o fixar a uma parede não está incluído. A embalagem inclui apenas um cabo de alimentação com ficha Schuko, uma chave para desligar os painéis solares e um manual. To get started, simply connect the power cable to the corresponding port on the side of the SigenMate 2700 Ultra and to a power outlet. The system can then be switched on. To generate your own solar power, at least one solar panel must also be connected to the four inputs (MC4 sockets). These are located on the top under a somewhat cheap-looking plastic cover, rather than on the side (as with many competitors). This makes access and cable management easier (the cables run out toward the back). However, the spacing between the individual connectors is quite tight. App & operation: AI assistan

artigo.texto: Technology group Wärtsilä has secured an order to supply a 282 MW onsite power solution for a data center project being developed by a major US independent power producer in the United States. The power plant will operate with 15 Wärtsilä 50SG engines. The order demonstrates the growing need for fast-deployable onsite power solutions as grid constraints, lengthy connection timelines, and accelerating AI-driven electricity demand create power availability challenges for new data center developments. The order was booked by Wärtsilä in Q3 2026. The project further strengthens Wärtsilä's proven position in the rapidly growing U.S. data center power market. It marks the company's seventh data center-related order in the United States, bringing the total power capacity sold by Wärtsilä for U.S. data center applications to more than 3 GW. The customer selected Wärtsilä engine-based solution for its ability to provide large-scale power capacity on efficient timelines while enabling phased expansion as computing demand grows. The Wärtsilä 50SG engines provide high efficiency in demanding operating conditions, feature a closed-loop cooling system that minimises water consumption compared with conventional thermal power alternatives and offer flexibility to convert the engines to run on future fuels. For data center developers, these features translate into dependable power availability, scalable growth, and greater long-term optionality. “The U.S. data center market is moving faster than traditional power infrastructure can support,” says Risto Paldanius, Vice President, Americas at Wärtsilä Energy. “This order shows how flexible onsite power can help developers secure reliable power, reduce deployment risk, and scale their operations with confidence. Our growing portfolio of data center projects to date demonstrates the critical role flexible engine technology can play in solving one of the sector’s most urgent growth challenges.” The Wärtsilä equipment is scheduled for delivery in 2028, and the project is expected to become fully operational in 2029. Wärtsilä Energy in brief Wärtsilä Energy is at the forefront of the transition towards a 100% renewable energy future. We help our customers and the power sector to accelerate their decarbonisation journeys through our market-leading technologies and power system expertise. Our solutions include flexible engine power plants and services for the whole lifecycle of our installations. Our engines are future-proof and can run on sustainable fuels. Our track record comprises 81 GW of power plant capacity in 180 countries around the world. About 35% of our operating installed base is under service agreements. www.wartsila.com/energy Wärtsilä in brief Wärtsilä is a global leader in innovative technologies and lifecycle solutions for the marine and energy industries. We emphasise innovation in sustainable technology and services to help our customers continuously improve environmental and economic performance. Our dedicated and passionate team of 17,900 professionals in 199 locations in 78 countries shape the decarbonisation transformation of our industries across the globe. In 2025, Wärtsilä’s net sales totalled EUR 6.2 billion. Wärtsilä is listed on Nasdaq Helsinki. www.wartsila.com
