artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media Households and the power grid run on alternating current. Batteries — including those in electric vehicles — run on direct current. That AC-DC divide has complicated the prospect of EVs as home backup batteries. Today, almost every commercially available vehicle-to-home (V2H) backup power system in the U.S. requires a pricey DC bidirectional charger: a device that converts direct current from the vehicle to home-ready alternating current. The only exception is Tesla’s. Over the past few years, the major EV and home battery manufacturer has been working out how to get its vehicles to do the job of sending AC power to homes and the grid. Tesla’s Cybertruck has had this ability for more than a year, and on Tuesday, the firm announced it is expanding the capability to its new Model 3 and Model Y EVs — as long as your home has a Powerwall 3 battery, that is. “This is us bringing the whole ecosystem together and allowing our products to complement each other,” said Colby Hastings, head of Tesla Energy’s residential energy business. Instead of relying on a DC bidirectional charger to do the power conversion, AC bidirectional charging does the job with hardware in the vehicles themselves. The Powerwall 3 retails for $8,200 and costs several thousand dollars more to install, but it’s a complete home backup system. The only additional equipment Tesla requires to add between two and three days of additional V2H backup power from an EV battery is its standard Wall Connector charger, which retails for $595. It’s cheaper to set up a Cybertruck for home backup power, since those vehicles don’t require homes to have a Powerwall. Customers simply need to pay for a V2H hardware package that retails for $1,990, plus about $1,800 to $2,200 for installation. Either way, these prices are a good deal compared to the $6,500 to $10,000 and up it typically costs to buy a DC bidirectional charger — a price that doesn’t include a home battery. That’s largely because it’s a lot cheaper to convert DC to AC power within an EV — which already has to convert incoming AC to DC for its battery — than to buy a separate power conversion system that attaches to your house, Hastings said. “We’ve been very focused on what we think is the more long-term scalable pathway,” she said. “That’s what led us to this architecture.” To be clear, Tesla EVs and Powerwall batteries still cost a lot of money. And arguably, Tesla could be seen as something of a latecomer to the V2H game, which other automakers have offered for years with DC V2H backup systems. But in terms of establishing a means for lower-cost AC hardware to turn EVs into home batteries, Tesla’s latest development is a big deal, said Zach Woogen, executive director of the Vehicle-Grid Integration Council. “Many in the industry expect AC bidirectional charging equipment will be economical for customers and manufacturers alike at a lower price point,” he said. “This is an exciting proposition for a technology space that’s been limited by relatively high up-front costs.” Woogen’s group represents EV and charging manufacturers working with utilities and regulators across the country to streamline the use of EVs as backup batteries and as grid assets. The cumulative impact of millions of EVs could be huge. A recent study found that California could get one-third of its grid energy storage needs from tapping just 10% of the 9.7 million EVs it expects to have by the mid-2030s. Automakers have been touting the potential of EVs to back up homes during power outages for years, from the first Nissan Leaf EVs to the discontinued Ford F-150 Lightning. General Motors’ GM Energy business offers home battery and EV charger-power conversion systems that currently retail for just under $12,000 to more than $20,000. Kia markets its EV9 with V2H charging, and electric truck maker Rivian is working on similar capabilities. But beyond Tesla, automakers selling EVs in the U.S. haven’t publicly announced that they have embedded the technology so that the cars can provide AC backup power on their own. That’s partly because adding such tech tacks on complexity and cost to the vehicle manufacturing process. Things get even more complicated when you start talking about sending EV battery power back into utility grids. That’s called vehicle-to-grid, or V2G. Utilities have been running V2G pilot projects for decades, and a handful have started to expand into standard programs that pay customers who let the utility tap their EV batteries. But right now, only California and Maryland have established utility regulations that allow for AC bidirectional charging outside of pilot projects, although other states are working on it. Pacific Gas & Electric, California’s largest utility, has been running V2G pilots for years now and is now testing V2H capabilities with EVs from GM, Kia, Nissan, Polestar, and Volvo using bidirectional DC chargers. But the cost of the gear required for households to sign up has been daunting, said Eli Darby, part of PG&E’s clean energy transportation team. “We’ve had decent participation from DC systems,” Darby said. “But we’ve seen there’s a ceiling to the amount of money customers are willing to spend. The $10,000 to $15,000 it takes to pay for equipment and also installation and interconnection is a barrier.” That’s why PG&E has been working to certify the technology combos that can supply AC power directly from EVs to home chargers, and from there to the grid. So far, “Tesla is the lead product to market,” he said. “We’re technically piloting interconnecting their systems today.” Tesla has been enrolling Cybertrucks in programs with PG&E as well as with Texas utilities CenterPoint Energy and Oncor to tap their battery power to send back to the grid, Hastings said. artigo.texto: Crise energética nos EUA ameaça IA, mas poupa Nvidia e Broadcom Déficit de 34% na energia para data centers até 2028 pode travar a expansão da IA nos EUA, mas as duas maiores fabricantes de chips seguem blindadas, segundo análise do Morgan Stanley. O boom da inteligência artificial criou um problema que dinheiro, sozinho, não resolve: falta energia elétrica. Os bilhões de dólares despejados na construção de data centers nos Estados Unidos esbarram numa infraestrutura energética que não acompanha o ritmo da demanda. E o gargalo começa a redesenhar o mapa de vencedores e perdedores na cadeia de semicondutores. Um relatório do Morgan Stanley publicado nesta segunda-feira estima que os desenvolvedores de data centers nos EUA enfrentarão um déficit líquido de energia de 34% até 2028, o equivalente a 32 gigawatts. Para colocar em perspectiva, isso representa mais do que toda a capacidade instalada de geração eólica do Brasil. O número evidencia que o problema não é marginal: é estrutural. A conclusão central do banco, porém, surpreende pelo otimismo seletivo. Nvidia e Broadcom, as duas maiores fornecedoras de chips de alto desempenho para IA, estão relativamente protegidas contra esse cenário. O risco real recai sobre os elos secundários da cadeia: fabricantes de chips de memória, componentes ópticos, gerenciamento de energia e processadores analógicos. Por que Nvidia e Broadcom escapam do gargalo energético A lógica do Morgan Stanley é relativamente simples. Nvidia e Broadcom têm visibilidade privilegiada sobre a alocação de seus chips, a expansão geográfica dos clientes e a coordenação entre centros de dados, fornecedores e a cadeia de abastecimento de energia. Isso significa que essas empresas conseguem antecipar onde haverá capacidade de instalação e direcionar sua produção de acordo. Na prática, os maiores compradores de GPUs da Nvidia, como Microsoft, Google, Amazon e Meta, são justamente os operadores de data centers com maior poder de negociação junto a concessionárias de energia e governos locais. Esses hyperscalers já garantiram contratos de fornecimento de longo prazo e estão diversificando geograficamente suas operações, inclusive para fora dos EUA. O banco afirmou que não vê os gargalos energéticos colocando em risco as previsões de receita da Nvidia ou da Broadcom para 2027. A análise reforça uma tese que o mercado financeiro já precifica parcialmente: essas duas companhias operam num nível de demanda tão elevado que mesmo restrições de infraestrutura não reduzem a fila de pedidos, apenas redistribuem onde os chips serão instalados. Quem paga a conta: os elos frágeis da cadeia de IA Se a capacidade de produção de chips não puder ser implantada por falta de energia nos data centers, os clientes poderão adiar entregas ou cancelar pedidos. E os componentes mais expostos a esse risco são justamente os que dependem de volumes elevados para manter margens saudáveis. Fabricantes de chips de memória, como Micron e SK Hynix, operam com margens mais estreitas e dependem do ritmo de construção de novos data centers para manter a demanda aquecida. O mesmo vale para fornecedores de componentes ópticos, essenciais para a conectividade entre servidores, e para empresas de gerenciamento de energia e chips analógicos. Como analisamos na cobertura de tecnologia do portal, a cadeia de semicondutores funciona como um ecossistema integrado, e o atraso num elo propaga efeitos em cascata. O Goldman Sachs também sinalizou restrições crescentes à expansão dos data centers nos EUA, embora com uma leitura levemente diferente. O banco espera impacto limitado no curto prazo, em parte pela resistência política a medidas que freiem investimentos em IA. Já o Morgan Stanley enxerga desafios mais concretos, ligados a mão de obra, fornecimento de energia e entraves regulatórios. O déficit de 32 GW e o que isso significa para investidores O número de 32 GW de déficit projetado para 2028 não é apenas uma curiosidade técnica. Ele tem implicações diretas para quem investe em empresas de tecnologia e infraestrutura. A construção de novas usinas de geração, linhas de transmissão e subestações leva anos. Mesmo com o incentivo bilionário dos governos federal e estaduais, a oferta de energia não se expande na mesma velocidade que a demanda por computação. Esse descompasso já está gerando movimentos concretos. Empresas como Microsoft fecharam contratos para reativar usinas nucleares. Amazon investiu em geração solar e eólica dedicada a seus data centers. Google assinou acordos de compra de energia geotérmica. Como acompanhamos na editoria de finanças, o setor de energia virou talvez o maior beneficiário indireto do boom de IA, com ações de concessionárias e empresas de infraestrutura elétrica acumulando altas expressivas nos últimos 12 meses. Para o investidor, a leitura é que a tese de Nvidia e Broadcom permanece intacta no médio prazo, mas o risco migrou para a segunda e terceira camadas da cadeia. Empresas que pareciam apostas seguras no ciclo de IA, como fabricantes de memória HBM e fornecedores de equipamentos de rede, agora carregam um risco adicional de atraso na implantação que não estava no radar há seis meses. IA e energia: um gargalo que veio para ficar O cenário descrito pelo Morgan Stanley não é temporário. A demanda energética da IA generativa cresce exponencialmente a cada nova geração de modelos. O treinamento do GPT-4 consumiu estimados 50 GWh de eletricidade. Modelos futuros devem demandar ordens de magnitude a mais. E a inferência, o uso cotidiano dos modelos por bilhões de pessoas, adiciona uma camada contínua de consumo que não existia antes. A questão energética, portanto, deixou de ser um risco periférico e se tornou o principal limitador da velocidade de expansão da IA nos Estados Unidos. Países que conseguirem resolver essa equação primeiro, seja por abundância de recursos naturais, seja por agilidade regulatória, tendem a capturar uma fatia desproporcional dos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›SECI Invites Bids for 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS SECI Invites Bids for 800 MW/3,200 MWh BESS Solar Energy Corporation of India has issued a tender for supplying energy from 800 MW/3,200 MWh standalone battery energy storage system in India. Bid submission ends on October 30, 2026. October 05, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) has floated a tender for the supply of energy from 800 MW/3,200 MWh ISTS-connected standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in India. The projects must be set up under the build, own, operate (BOO) model. Bidders must pay INR 59,000 as a tender document fee. They also need to deposit INR 20,000/MW (plus GST) as a bid processing fee, subject to a maximum amount of INR 20 lakh (plus GST). Further, they need to furnish INR 7.184 lakh/MW as an earnest money deposit (EMD). Selected bidders must deposit INR 17.96 lakh/MW as a performance bank guarantee (PBG). The last date for submission of bids is October 30, 2026. The techno-commercial bids will be opened on November 4, 2026. The minimum capacity for bidding will be 50 MW/200 MWh. The BESSD must set up, operate, and maintain a BESS, with the primary objective of providing stored energy from the BESS to the buying entities on an “on-demand” basis. Identification of land, installation and ownership of the project, along with obtaining connectivity and necessary approvals and interconnection with the ISTS network/ STU or InSTS network (as applicable) will be under the scope of the BESSD. The charging power for the BESS project must be arranged by the BESSD such that at least 51 percent of the energy used for charging the BESS is procured from renewable energy sources. The BESSD must guarantee a minimum system availability of 85 percent on a monthly basis. The net worth of the bidder must be at least INR 71.84 lakh/ MW, as on the last date of FY26, or as on the day at least 7 days prior to the bid submission deadline. artigo.texto: India's battery storage demand to hit 236.22 GWh by FY32, require Rs 3.49 trillion investment: Report Synopsis India's battery energy storage system market is expected to reach 236.22 GWh by FY2031-32. The country will require Rs 3.49 trillion in investments for this growth. Significant advancements in BESS deployment were noted between early and mid-2026. The government is providing extensive support through various initiatives and schemes. These measures aim to enhance project viability and stimulate private-sector participation in the energy storage sector. Furthermore, as of August 2026, 9.08 GWh of BESS capacity was operational, while 79.92 GWh was under construction, with 79.92 GWh under construction, 24.13 GWh awarded, and 63.53 GWh under tendering, taking the total operational and identified project capacity to 176.66 GWh, with the current CEA project pipeline scheduled for commissioning till FY2029-30. In capacity terms, the report noted, this represents approximately "75% of the NEP's projected FY2031-32 requirements, although the identified capacity is at different stages of development and is not yet fully operational." "The share of BESS in India's total energy storage requirement is expected to increase from ~42% in FY2026-27 to ~57% in FY2031-32," it said. The report estimated that India will require around Rs 3.49 trillion in investment in the sector by FY2031-32. Separately, the broader energy storage sector is expected to attract about Rs 4.79 trillion in investments by 2032. The report expects India's BESS market to expand strongly, supported by investments in domestic battery manufacturing, a sizeable project pipeline and government initiatives. Measures including Viability Gap Funding (VGF), the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage and interstate transmission system (ISTS) charge waivers are expected to improve project viability and encourage private-sector participation. The government is also stepping up support for the sector. The Union Cabinet has approved the Rs 1.86 trillion PM-DHARA (PM-Developing Harmonized and Accelerated Renewable-energy Access) Scheme, which includes Rs 500 billion for the deployment of 50 GWh of BESS capacity by FY2032-33, it noted. artigo.texto: Data Center Design in the AI Era The unprecedented performance demands of AI workloads require a reimagined approach to data center design toward fully autonomous operations. October 5, 2026 Sponsored by HPE It wasn’t long ago that organizations thought their data centers would play a less central role in IT service delivery. Virtualized infrastructure, cloud computing, colocation, SaaS applications, and other factors pointed to more computing being done off-premises. But the rapid acceleration of compute-intensive workloads, generative AI, and ever-increasing network complexity is driving organizations to reimagine and, in some cases, completely re-engineer their data centers. The same is true for third-party data centers leveraged by so many organizations, often in tandem with their on-prem facilities. AI training and inference, combined with a rapid swing toward agentic AI, is intensifying pressure on data centers. Even with the impressive advances in compute and storage density, enterprises are realizing that incremental component refreshes cannot solve operational complexity; they require a modern fabric design and shift toward self-driving networks to improve IT agility, increase reliability, and optimize the end user experience. The trends have been exacerbated by huge demands for power and cooling, which data centers have struggled to meet. Research from Uptime Institute notes that 82% of data center operators report their highest-density racks are still below 30 kilowatts, a level unlikely to meet the growing demands of AI-level performance as rack densities increase. New Challenges Force Changes to Data Center Design The harsh reality is that traditional data centers were never designed for the performance, scalability, security, and resilience demands of the AI era. The massive growth in data volumes has created important opportunities for new insights, but also requires a fundamentally different approach to network design. Servers, networks, storage, end-user devices, cloud gateways, applications, security tools, and other sources generate unprecedented amounts of data, making it more difficult for networks to discern whether an alert indicates a potentially serious failure or a minor problem elsewhere. But it’s not just the proliferation of data sources that renders legacy data centers inadequate for the AI era. Traditional data center traffic usually had a fair amount of entropy, making it easier to design for capacity and accommodate occasional demand spikes that could impact network performance. AI has changed that in a big way. Modern AI workloads running on GPUs require deterministic, low-latency, higher-bandwidth networks, and massively scalable storage infrastructure, meaning that both existing and greenfield data centers need to support significantly higher performance. In addition, the traditional siloed approach to IT infrastructure that reflects organizational boundaries rather than end user needs—compute, storage, and networking—has given way to new design principles that promote tighter cross-domain integration for better overall data center and application performance. Shifting the Data Center to Autonomous Operations Although data centers have increasingly embraced automation, the next step is for data center design to progress toward autonomy. Data center personnel are simply too hard-pressed to address the increasing telemetry volume and complexity in real time without tools that provide full-stack, cross-domain visibility across the entire enterprise. AI agents should be an important element in the move toward autonomous operations because they enable lightning-fast assessments, analysis, and decision-making across the full spectrum of infrastructure and data sources. Management should focus not just on automating operations to reduce headcount, but on autonomous operations that improve the quality of application and user experience. The Importance of a Self-Driving Framework AI-era data centers now have the potential for unsurpassed levels of intelligence, autonomous operations, observability, and contextually aware decision-making. This is where self-driving frameworks coordinate data center operations with AI-era requirements. The emphasis has swung decisively away from historically fragmented management frameworks in favor of approaches that collect information from all available sources and put them into an actionable context across infrastructure. A key first step is intent-based networking, which defines the desired state of the network based on operator-intent and continuously validates its conformance to that standard. Problems are identified faster and with greater precision, relieving the data center team of tedious, time-consuming, and often inaccurate triage to avoid failures and downtime. A well-planned and meticulously executed approach to building the right data center architecture helps organizations establish validated topologies, automate deployment, improve visibility, automate remediation, and balance the strengths of AI tools with human experience. artigo.texto: EP Cube displayed its EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 for new or existing residential and Three-Phase Light C&I Solution for small commercial PV-plus-storage systems The residential system supports a maximum PV capacity of 15 kW and lists its storage capacity range of 5 to 40 kWh with a rated 10 kVA full-load power It also integrates with the company’s upcoming 7.4 kW AC EV charger, updated EP Cube App, and a new HMI for a connected and smarter home energy ecosystem EP Cube, an independent subsidiary and residential energy storage brand of Canadian Solar Inc., introduced its residential EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 and Three-Phase Light C&I Solution at Solar & Storage Live UK 2026 in Birmingham. The company's booth also displayed an EV charger, a Human Machine Interface (HMI) display, and a new dynamic tariff pricing AI mode as part of a smart home energy ecosystem. Both energy storage systems (ESS) feature an 'All-in-One' configuration, which combines a hybrid inverter and modular battery packs, stacked on one another. They use lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery units, each measuring 600 × 266 × 200 mm and providing 5 kWh of storage capacity at a 51.2 V rated voltage. While the configuration and battery pack are identical, their inverter and total storage capacities vary. The EP CUBE Single-Phase 2.0 features a 10 kVA hybrid inverter and a storage capacity range of 5 to 40 kWh by connecting to eight battery packs. With 4 built-in MPPTs, the inverter supports up to 15 kW of PV capacity with a 600 V maximum PV input voltage. In comparison, the Three-Phase Light C&I Solution combines a higher-capacity hybrid inverter (12 kVA) and storage capacities of 10 to 40 kWh using the same 5 kWh battery packs mentioned above. Its inverter lists a higher PV capacity of 24 kW and a maximum input voltage of 1,000 V, though the MPPT numbers remain the same. The product datasheets specify compatibility with new and existing PV arrays to make an AC-coupled PV-plus-storage system. The residential ESS supports up to 10 kVA (single-phase) emergency backup within 10 ms of a grid outage, while this function is optional for the C&I product. It switches to off-grid mode in less than 20 ms of a grid blackout and delivers up to 12 kVA (3-phase) backup power. Backup duration varies based on total connected storage capacity, rated discharge limit, and operational conditions, among others. EP Cube also introduced its new AC EV chargers in two variants – 7.4 kW single-phase and 11 kW 3-phase. According to the company, it planned to launch the 3-phase charger by the end of September 2026, while the launch of its single-phase counterpart is slated for Q4 2026. The single-phase charger supports direct connection with the EP Cube Single-Phase 2.0 through a dedicated built-in port, enabling a connected home energy ecosystem. These ESSs (mentioned above) integrate with the EP Cube App (installed on the user's device) and help monitor and support multiple applications, including PV self-consumption maximization and time-of-use (TOU) tariffs, among others. It also enables smart EV charging from excess PV generation during peak hours and use of low-priced electricity at night or during low solar generation periods. This increases PV self-consumption and optimizes charging costs. The company says it has updated the app with features that support the UK's dynamic electricity tariff management services. It added that these features will soon be embedded in a new Dynamic Pricing AI mode for more accurate low-price capturing and battery charging/discharging decisions. EP Cube is also expecting to include new Open APIs with the app. This will enable the home ESS platform to integrate with an existing third-party home energy management system (HEMS), like Home Assistant, to make the connected energy ecosystem smarter. In addition to remote monitoring and data visualization, the booth displayed the new 7-inch HMI for local data accumulation and visualization with local data storage, supporting data independence for end users.

artigo.texto: German Sodium-Ion Battery Tech Gains EU Funding Support ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: German startup Revolta AG received €264,200 in EU co-financing for its sodium-ion AC battery project, designed for grid-charging in residential apartments. - Why it matters: This development highlights the growing viability of lithium-free storage solutions that can operate independently of on-site PV generation. - Watch: The impact of new German grid regulations that allow storage systems to arbitrage grid power with reduced levies and fees. Background and Context As the global energy transition accelerates, the development of sodium-ion battery technology is emerging as a critical alternative to traditional lithium-ion systems. German startup Revolta AG has secured significant funding from the German state of Hesse, supported by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), to advance its “Highly Efficient AC Salt Battery” project. This initiative aims to deploy residential-scale storage systems that do not rely on lithium or cobalt, addressing supply chain vulnerabilities and material cost volatility. Key Details The project, which runs from August 1, 2026, to December 31, 2029, involves eligible costs totaling €660,545, with the EU providing a 40% co-financing rate of approximately €264,200. The core innovation lies in the system’s ability to connect directly to the grid, allowing users to charge during periods of low electricity prices and discharge when costs peak. This model is specifically targeted at rental apartments that lack the space or infrastructure for rooftop solar PV installations. Furthermore, the regulatory landscape in Germany has evolved to support this business model. Since October 1, the national grid regulator has implemented rules allowing storage systems to draw power from the grid and feed it back later, benefiting from reduced grid fees and levies. This shift effectively opens a new market segment for storage providers. Beyond Revolta AG, the ERDF is also supporting broader sodium-ion manufacturing, including a €2.52 million grant for a 1 GWh sodium-ion battery plant in Bavaria. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the rise of grid-charging sodium-ion systems represents a shift toward decentralized energy management. While currently focused on the residential sector, the underlying technology—sodium-ion—offers a scalable, safer, and more sustainable alternative for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications. Developers should monitor these advancements as they provide a pathway to integrate storage in locations where solar generation is physically constrained. What Happens Next The industry will closely monitor the performance of these pilot projects as they move toward the 2026 launch window. As India continues to expand its renewable energy sector, the lessons learned from European regulatory frameworks—specifically regarding grid-charging arbitrage and non-lithium storage chemistries—will become increasingly relevant. India’s push for indigenous battery manufacturing under various PLI schemes may eventually incorporate these sodium-ion advancements to diversify the national energy storage portfolio.

artigo.texto: Nvidia e Broadcom se isolam de impacto de crise de energia em data centers dos EUA, diz Morgan Stanley Nvidia e Broadcom estão protegidas da crise energética em data centers nos EUA até 2027, segundo o Morgan Stanley, devido ao forte planejamento e alocação de chips. Contudo, o setor enfrenta um déficit de energia projetado em 34% até 2028, impulsionado pela alta demanda da inteligência artificial. Se a infraestrutura atrasar por gargalos elétricos, fabricantes de componentes secundários, como chips de memória, óptica e analógicos, serão os mais impactados por cancelamentos e adiamentos. Nvidia e Broadcom estão relativamente protegidas contra o agravamento da crise de energia nas centrais de processamento de dados dos Estados Unidos, afirmou o Morgan Stanley em relatório nesta segunda-feira. Porém, qualquer atraso resultante nas implantações de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial pode afetar os fabricantes de chips de memória, componentes ópticos e outros processadores secundários. O banco estimou no mês passado que os desenvolvedores de data centers nos EUA enfrentarão um déficit líquido de energia de 34% até 2028, equivalente a 32 GW. O boom da IA gerou bilhões de dólares em investimentos em data centers, mas as enormes necessidades de computação e eletricidade da IA generativa estão cada vez mais esbarrando nos problemas de fornecimento de eletricidade nos EUA. Tanto Morgan Stanley quanto Goldman Sachs sinalizaram restrições crescentes à expansão dos data centers nos EUA; o GS espera um impacto limitado no curto prazo devido à resistência política, enquanto o MS vê desafios relacionados à mão de obra, energia e política. O Morgan Stanley afirmou que não vê os gargalos colocando em risco as previsões da Nvidia ou da Broadcom para 2027, citando a visibilidade dessas empresas quanto à alocação de chips, à expansão geográfica e à coordenação entre centros de dados, fornecedores de chips e a cadeia de abastecimento de energia. Se a capacidade de produção de chips não puder ser implantada, os clientes poderão adiar entregas ou cancelar pedidos, sendo que componentes de memória, óptica, gerenciamento de energia e analógicos são os mais expostos a problemas de fornecimento, afirmou o Morgan Stanley.

artigo.texto: O mercado brasileiro de sistemas de baterias para armazenar energia elétrica, conhecidos no setor como BESS, vive um boom de vendas puxado por instalações de menor porte em comércios, indústrias, condomínios e residências, segundo reportagem de Luciano Costa no Brazil Journal. Enquanto o leilão federal para grandes projetos segue previsto para dezembro sob incertezas, o segmento encontrou no varejo a via para crescer em ritmo recorde. Conforme levantamento da consultoria Greener citado na reportagem, as vendas e contratações de BESS somaram 730 MWh em 2025, mais do que a soma dos cinco anos anteriores. Nos seis primeiros meses de 2026, foram outros 504 MWh, caminho de um novo recorde histórico. Muitos desses projetos vêm acompanhados de painéis solares em telhados. O CEO da Greener, Marcio Takata, afirmou ao Brazil Journal que o leilão é relevante, mas que o BESS distribuído deve se firmar como um dos principais vetores de flexibilidade da rede elétrica. A trajetória lembra a da geração solar, que decolou com grandes usinas contratadas pelo governo e depois com telhados e miniusinas. Segundo a Aneel, a geração solar distribuída já soma mais de 53 GW no País, contra 23,6 GW das usinas centralizadas. O armazenamento acumulado no Brasil chega a 1,9 GWh, com companhias como WEG e Grupo Moura apostando no segmento. O leilão de dezembro deve contratar pelo menos 2 GW para operar quatro horas por dia, o equivalente a 8 GWh, segundo sinalizações de Brasília, ainda que parte do mercado espere volumes maiores. O Ministério de Minas e Energia também programou certames anuais até 2029 para reserva de capacidade, nos quais as baterias disputarão espaço com termelétricas e hidrelétricas reversíveis. Para André Millions, diretor da Thymos Capital, baterias e hidrelétricas reversíveis são hoje os temas mais quentes do setor. A reserva é considerada importante para a rede absorver a oscilação da geração eólica e solar, mas o certame está sob risco por causa do impasse sobre quem paga a conta dos projetos, conforme fontes do setor ouvidas pelo Brazil Journal. A regra atual divide o rateio entre todas as empresas de geração, o que ameaça levar o tema à Justiça, e o setor pressiona o governo a aprovar um projeto do deputado Arnaldo Jardim que transfere o custo aos consumidores.

artigo.texto: Cindy O’Neil understands the boom-and-bust cycles of industry. Her husband spent years working in Carbon County’s namesake coal mines. In this pocket of central Utah, energy and the economy have long been intrinsically linked, at great sacrifice to county residents. “We’ve had the coal. We’ve dealt, the whole community, with black lung,” O’Neil said. “The explosions, the fires and all the things that came along with it.” But a new industry and type of energy production is about to move near her rural home. And she says it has her and her neighbors even more worried than they were about the dangers that came from their long history with coal. “It’s all descending, these data centers,” said O’Neil, who tracks mysterious new projects in the works and shares updates on Facebook community pages. “They’re setting these things within a couple of miles of homes.” Her latest updates involve a lot of chatter about Valar Atomics, a nuclear startup. The company plans to build a mega-complex of 456 small modular reactors — a still largely untested and unproven technology in the United States — on the vast tracts of Bureau of Land Management land in the county. The project will store radioactive waste, according to a report from National Public Radio, and power an array of industrial activities, including data centers. “Project Beehive” has support from the state of Utah, and will include a square mile of state-owned trust lands. Another data center complex planned for the county, Altigen Energy’s “Jurassic Spark,” will cover hundreds of acres and include a massive natural gas plant. It’s an abrupt shift. Carbon County’s coal mines produced nearly 10 million tons of coal in 2006. But a shift to cheaper energy sources, like renewables and natural gas, along with depleted supplies in the coal seams, sank the region’s main economic engine in just a few decades. Since 2023, not a single pound of coal has been mined in Carbon County. “They say everything’s left us, and if we don’t grab these table scraps we’re not going to get anything,” said O’Neil. “I don’t think our county has to take the table scraps.” None of Carbon County’s new data center plans call for coal. The Utah Trust Lands Administration recently agreed to lease a square mile of its state-owned land for up to 100 years to Valar Atomics. The nuclear startup intends to use that lease to run some of its SMRs, process its uranium TRISO-fuel to feed the reactors, build water desalination, manufacture steel, refine critical minerals — and support data centers. The Valar site is expected to generate $35 million in lease rents over 50 years, according to information the Trust Lands Administration staff presented to its board last month. Revenue collected from the project benefits Utah schools. (The state agency declined to comment on the Valar project.) During that September board meeting, three Carbon County residents who are employed or expected to be employed by Valar spoke in favor of the project. All three of the Carbon County Commissioners also voiced their support. “[We] realize that this topic is a hot button now, along with data centers,” said Larry Jensen, one of the commissioners. “It’s important that you understand that the Carbon County Commissioners are committed to allowing these things to move forward. Even with the pushback — we realize that there are a few in our community who will push back — but the silent majority are the ones that we really represent.” Cheryl Lupo, a longtime resident of the county, balked at that assertion. She is running for a seat on the county commission this year. As an unaffiliated candidate, she had to collect 300 signatures to land on the ballot. She said the opinions she heard during that process were overwhelmingly opposed to data centers and nuclear plants. “People are up in arms,” Lupo said. “Torches and pitchforks. Because they’re not being heard.” Governor Spencer Cox, U.S. Senator John Curtis and other high-ranking Utah officials welcomed Valar to the state earlier this year, allowing it to test its “Ward250” microreactor at the San Rafael Energy Lab in neighboring Emery County. Valar announced it had achieved “self-sustaining criticality” in June – a process where atoms split and maintain a steady fission chain reaction without being fed more neutrons. The company has plans to power a 30-megawatt nuclear-powered AI data center in Emery County, too, in partnership with the computer-chip giant Nvidia. Small modular reactors have yet to be deployed for commercial use in the United States. During last week’s Trust Lands Administration meeting, Mike Nelson, the board’s chair, seemed to acknowledge that the deal with Valar came with some unknowns. “We weren’t always sure what to ask about,” Nelson said, while offering praise for the nuclear startup, “and probably still aren’t sure of everything to ask about because this is a first, right?” Utah has a troubled history with nuclear testing. Lupo’s mother was 38 years old when she died, and Lupo believes the cause was downwind effects from radioactive weapons testing in nearby Nevada during the 1950s. Her mother lived in Carbon County at the time. She believes the fallout caused her grandfather’s death, too. “I will never, ever be a proponent of nuclear,” Lupo said. Even before the proposal to build Valar’s complex started causing a stir, rumors swirled about the possibility of another data center campus in Carbon County. Altigen, a company that builds natural gas-power plants for data centers, has selected an area east of Wellington for its 1,200-acre “Jurassic Spark” project — nearly double the size of the Valar campus, according to meeting minutes from the local Community Economic Development Board. Plans call for building a 250-megawatt gas plant to power the complex initially, but it could eventually produce 3 gigawatts of electricity, according to Jensen. artigo.texto: Data Center World estreia com foco em energia e Redata Edição brasileira começa nesta terça-feira, em SP, com debates sobre tributação, capacidade energética, financiamento e conectividade. A primeira edição brasileira do Data Center World começa nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro, no São Paulo Expo, com debates sobre os principais condicionantes para a expansão dos data centers no país. Tributação, disponibilidade de energia, financiamento, conectividade e aumento da demanda computacional estão entre os temas centrais do encontro. Realizado simultaneamente à Futurecom, o evento prevê a participação de mais de 2,5 mil líderes e 300 congressistas. Um dos destaques do primeiro dia será o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata). O tema entra na discussão sobre competitividade, atração de investimentos e ambiente regulatório, ao lado dos efeitos do ICMS e de decisões do Confaz sobre a implantação de novos projetos. Oferta de energia concentra debates A disponibilidade de energia aparece como um dos principais fatores para a expansão do setor. O aumento da capacidade computacional exigida por novas aplicações amplia a demanda elétrica dos empreendimentos e afeta decisões sobre localização, escala e continuidade operacional. Os debates vão tratar de oferta efetiva, intermitência, geração, armazenamento e alternativas para reduzir riscos associados ao fornecimento. O crescimento da densidade dos racks também pressiona a infraestrutura elétrica e térmica dos data centers. Esse movimento tem ampliado a discussão sobre novas arquiteturas e sobre tecnologias de refrigeração, incluindo liquid cooling. Financiamento e viabilidade O acesso a capital será outro eixo do congresso. Representantes do Ministério das Comunicações, BNDES, Brasscom e Patria Investments participam de um debate sobre crédito, financiamento e condições para viabilizar novos empreendimentos. A análise de grandes projetos passa também por fatores como localização, custo, latência, segurança e continuidade dos serviços. Esses critérios serão discutidos sob a perspectiva de empresas que contratam infraestrutura de data center. Conectividade e capacidade A conectividade completa o conjunto de fatores que condicionam a expansão do mercado. O congresso terá discussões sobre rotas internacionais, latência e edge computing, relacionando a localização dos data centers ao desempenho das aplicações. O planejamento de capacidade por hyperscalers também estará em pauta, diante da dificuldade de projetar demanda em um ambiente de crescimento acelerado das cargas computacionais. A agenda inclui ainda debates sobre continuidade operacional, preparação para falhas e eventos extremos, além de investimentos e expansão da infraestrutura na América Latina. Serviço Data Center World Brasil 2026 (DCW) Data: 6 a 8 de outubro de 2026 Local: São Paulo Expo – São Paulo (SP) Horário: das 10h às 20h Endereço: Rodovia dos Imigrantes, km 1,5 – Vila Água Funda – São Paulo

artigo.texto: Telcomp cobra agilidade nas licenças para data centers Entidade relata demora superior à construção de empreendimentos e aponta impasses na regulamentação do Redata como entrave. A demora na emissão de licenças e as pendências na regulamentação do Redata estão entre os obstáculos à implantação de data centers no Brasil, segundo o presidente da Telcomp, Luiz Henrique Barbosa. Durante a abertura do Data Center World, nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro, o dirigente defendeu maior previsibilidade para atrair investimentos e integrar o país às cadeias internacionais de infraestrutura digital. Barbosa relatou o caso de uma associada que aguardou dois anos por uma licença para atravessar uma rodovia no interior de São Paulo. Segundo ele, o prazo foi superior ao necessário para construir o próprio data center. Para o dirigente, situações desse tipo comprometem a segurança jurídica dos projetos. Ele afirmou que investidores estrangeiros comparam as condições brasileiras com as de outros mercados e que o país precisa considerar essa concorrência ao definir regras, tributos e procedimentos de licenciamento. A Telcomp reúne aproximadamente 60 empresas de diferentes segmentos, incluindo operadores de cabos submarinos, satélites, data centers e redes de transmissão de longa distância e metropolitanas. Impasse sobre equipamentos Barbosa também cobrou a conclusão da regulamentação do Redata. Segundo o presidente da Telcomp, há divergências com fabricantes nacionais de equipamentos, preocupados com o alcance dos benefícios para importações. Na avaliação do dirigente, a indefinição mantém investimentos parados. Ele defendeu que o regime seja entendido como uma forma de aproximar a tributação brasileira das condições oferecidas em outros países. No mesmo painel, Walter Wolff, diretor de projetos da Brasscom, afirmou que a regulamentação envolve discussões sobre os equipamentos contemplados e sobre o fornecimento de energia aos empreendimentos. Já o presidente da Equinix, Victor Arnaud, alertou que o detalhamento das regras pode comprometer os resultados do incentivo caso imponha burocracia excessiva aos projetos. Cabos submarinos e segurança jurídica Para exemplificar os efeitos internacionais de decisões sobre infraestrutura, Barbosa citou a proposta de instalação de uma usina de dessalinização na Praia do Futuro, em Fortaleza, nas proximidades de cabos submarinos. Segundo ele, a discussão gerou preocupação entre agentes de outros países porque as conexões que passam por Fortaleza também atendem ao tráfego internacional. O dirigente citou as ligações com a África, a Europa, os Estados Unidos e a Argentina para defender que decisões locais considerem o papel dessas redes. A relação entre data centers e telecomunicações também foi destacada pelo diretor jurídico da Conexis, Bruno Cavalcanti. Ele afirmou que a atração de investimentos em processamento depende de redes de fibra, backbones e conectividade de alta capacidade. Cavalcanti defendeu uma regulação responsiva, com espaço para atuação do mercado, e segurança jurídica para os investidores. Na avaliação do representante da Conexis, regras antecipadas que burocratizem a implantação dos empreendimentos podem prejudicar o crescimento do setor e a competitividade brasileira.

artigo.texto: An industrial park in Irvine, California, may seem an odd spot to show off technology that wouldn’t be out of place in Dune, but that’s what’s happening on a sweltering September morning. The temperature is already over 80 degrees Fahrenheit as the sun rises on a 20-foot-tall, metal-clad machine in the parking lot of Atoco, an Irvine, California-based startup. Engineers open panels to check systems and an iPad that shows a steadily ascending line that reveals the device’s purpose: harvesting water from thin air using special materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs. The materials won Omar Yaghi, the company’s founder, the Nobel Prize for chemistry in 2025, and Atoco has shown they work in prototypes capable of producing gallons of water per day. What’s unique about this iteration of Atoco’s technology is what it doesn’t require. No grid connection or even electricity is needed to grab water from the air at the microscopic level, nor is it required to in turn wring the water out of the materials in a form useful for humans. Instead, all that’s needed is low-level industrial heat. That, Atoco says, makes them a perfect candidate to hook up with AI data centers, which throw off loads of waste heat as servers churn out everything from math proofs to virtual editors while also often requiring massive amounts of water. “We were not really thinking of AI data centers,” four or five years ago, says Atoco CEO Samer Taha. But the massive buildout has created an opportunity for the startup that could allow it to get a step closer to its larger goal of ensuring people living in water-stressed regions have control over an increasingly precious resource. When Yaghi was a PhD student, he says, creating something like MOFs was “every chemist’s dream.” Part of his Nobel-winning work over the past 20 years has been taking theoretical research into the real world, creating a stable molecular structure that links organic material with metal ions. The structure of a MOF looks somewhat “like a jungle gym on a playground,” says Seth Cohen, the dean of the School of Physical Sciences at UC Irvine. MOFs are essentially “molecular sponges—they’re a solid material that’s very, very good at absorbing other molecules,” says Cohen, who is not involved with Atoco. Like a sponge, the materials can also be wrung out using methods including heat to release whatever they’re holding onto. These jungle-gym-like frameworks create open spaces on the microscopic level that can hold an unbelievable amount of material, and small tweaks can yield even more interior space. “The footage of a gram of MOF could cover two football fields,” Yaghi explains. “They can store hydrogen in there to make clean energy, or you could store CO2 in there to make clean air. Or, in this case, you can store water.” Atoco has developed what Taha calls “precision materials” with a specific objective of being able to harvest water, release it, and then do it over again and again. He quips that, as vice president of R&D Benjie Limketkai puts it, the material has to like water but not love it. To succeed commercially, it also has to use as little energy as possible. “The scientists reach a level of precision [where] we really know even the angle of the atom,” in a given material, Taha says. In Atoco’s technology, air passes through the MOF, which has been specially tailored to attract water molecules. Those molecules adhere to the pores. But the material feels completely dry to the touch even when saturated, and squeezing it doesn’t release a single drop. (Taha was kind enough to let WIRED try our hand at it.) Instead, the company relies on heat to release the captured molecules. There are other means of harvesting water. Cohen notes that silica, a popular desiccant, can also pull water out of air, but it doesn’t hold as much moisture and requires you to “heat the heck out of it to get the water back out,” he says. The monolith in the parking lot of the company’s Irvine facility is the culmination of decades of precision development. Atoco’s materials and approach allow its off-grid system to work even when relative humidity is in the teens. The MOFs in the device can harvest and release water with heat as low as 100 degrees Fahrenheit, Taha says. With no data center nearby, Atoco’s team simulated it by piping heat from a source that was around 150 degrees Fahrenheit. A solar panel powers various systems but not the water-harvesting operation itself, making the metal-clad machine eerily quiet. Cars pulling into the adjacent businesses create more of a sonic disruption, but Taha is ready to show the device has been working hard. It’s a little after 9 am, and the temperature is over 90 degrees Fahrenheit when he pushes a button on the side and turns a spigot. Out tumbles a clear stream of water that looks good enough to drink. Unfortunately it’s not on offer for legal liability reasons, though Taha notes it’s the equivalent of distilled water, because Atoco’s MOFs aren’t built to gather air pollution. Tossing it in the bushes, Taha retreats to an air-conditioned conference room where he lays out the company’s vision for its new machine. “Roughly 70 percent of the industrial waste heat is low-grade, unutilized, thrown into oceans or into the air,” he says. “If you convert that waste heat to clean water using our technology, you're talking about trillions of liters of clean water.” Data centers are an increasingly big source of that waste heat, with a single facility capable of pumping out as much heat as tens of thousands of homes. Operators are forced to disperse that heat into the surrounding environment, creating heat islands, while also paying for various types of cooling systems. Many of those cooling systems also rely on water, and some can consume millions of gallons per day. Atoco’s technology would thus address two of data centers’ biggest problems. artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL has reached a key milestone in proving the durability of its technology, demonstrating impressive laboratory analysis results. The prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells tested, which have been operating without interruption for almost fourteen years, have retained about 85 percent of their original energy capacity. The cells analyzed are part of the world's first large-scale energy storage facility, the 63 MWh Zhangbei, which began operation in 2011 and even provided clean energy for the 2022 Winter Olympics. The complete decommissioning of the facility in the summer of 2025 has allowed engineers to subject the components to detailed chemical and physical destructive testing. Over 50 samples taken from the original cells reveal remarkable material durability: the anode and cathode layers have retained perfect geometry, and the graphite shows no structural defects or critical signs of aging. An interesting detail is the fact that not a single cell from this manufacturer had to be replaced over the entire 14-year cycle. The test results open up new perspectives for the so-called “second life“ of industrial batteries. According to the company's experts, the retired cells have a resource for about 1,000 more complete charge and discharge cycles. This makes the components fully suitable for reintegration into smaller secondary storage systems for at least another decade. The current findings reconfirm the expectations from the control tests carried out on the ninth year of the facility's launch. LFP technology is also gaining in importance in the automotive sector. While these chemistries are inferior in specific energy density to nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) alternatives, they offer significantly lower manufacturing costs and unrivaled durability under extreme temperature and operating conditions. The achieved lifespan solidifies the technology's position as a key pillar for the future of sustainable mobility and green energy.

artigo.texto: Opponents of a proposed Brighton data center development will push the City Council for a moratorium Tuesday night, as the populist backlash against the resource-hungry megacenters spreads across Colorado. Weld County data center opponents are also launching a signature drive to get a moratorium on a future countywide ballot. Questions about transparency from government officials, how much water and energy the data centers will use, and how much noise they will generate for nearby subdivisions are bringing unusual coalitions together to fight growth, said Jordan Forsyth, a Democratic Socialists of America activist in Adams County. “To see me, a very vocal member of DSA, and my neighbor who is very Republican and voted for Trump, being able to have a conversation on this issue and actually be united … it’s been really cool to see everybody be able to put politics aside and just engage for the good of the community,” Forsyth said. A nonpartisan Weld County group says it is circulating two data center petitions in coming weeks. One, requiring 10,000 signatures in 45 days, would petition the Weld County commissioners to refer their approval of Global AI’s proposed data center to all voters in a special election sometime after the November general elections. The second Weld County petition, also needing 10,000 signatures according to the coalition, would create a separate ballot measure that if approved would require a public referendum on any newly proposed data center or data center expansion. “This referendum puts power back in the hands of the people of Weld County,” said community advocate Patricia Garcia-Nelson, who also works as a fossil fuels transition advocate for GreenLatinos. “We have the right to decide what happens to our community, not just on this project, but on the ones that come next. Over the next 30 days, we’re going to make sure every voter in Weld County has that chance,” Garcia-Nelson said, in a statement announcing the petition drives. More chances for referendums on data centers arise as candidate positions on the controversial developments become a litmus test from city council races to U.S. Senate campaigns. Colorado Springs recently delayed approval of a proposed data center near Garden of the Gods after protesters were arrested at the public hearing. Aurora’s City Council rejected a moratorium on data centers but put in place new requirements on how much water projects might use. Seeking info in Brighton Activists in Brighton are organizing, and studying documentation filed with the city for a 2.5-million-square-foot, eight-building data center mapped out on farm land near 50th Avenue and Weld County Road 4, about 25 miles northeast of downtown Denver. The development would be in a portion of Brighton that is in Weld County, according to BizWest. Former Chicago TV anchor and current Brighton resident Stacey Baca has compiled the documents and explanations of the developer’s plans on her YouTube channel, and activists say they want answers from City Council on why the project has moved forward without public debate. Nondisclosure agreements or other proprietary negotiations might get in the way, Forsyth said, ““but I think they had the option for community involvement and input, and it doesn’t seem that they’re interested in it,” Forsyth said. Council members should have looked around Colorado and seen that data centers would be coming for the ample open space on co-op United Power’s grid, the activists say. A moratorium would give the community time to develop standards, from whether they want data centers at all, to whether they should be supported with tax breaks, to how water and power will be supplied, opponents say. Representatives of Dewberry engineers, the firm that has filed paperwork for the Brighton development, did not return calls seeking comment about the project. Activists say the developer is California-based Raeden, which did not return messages seeking comment. In addition to concerns about data centers’ cooling-water use amid historic drought conditions, activists also question how the centers’ massive power needs will be supplied. Data centers come with large fossil-fueled backup generators that emit pollution when fired up; their everyday needs require hundreds of megawatts of power. If the data centers are powered by new fossil-fuel generation such as natural gas, Colorado’s progress in switching to clean, renewable energy could stall further, opponents say. A United Power spokesperson said the co-op power supplier cannot talk about individual customer projects or proposals. United Power said it works with large-load prospective customers to ensure adequate supply will be available. Some Brighton City Council members have supported consideration of a 90-day moratorium on data center approvals. Forsyth said another council member will support a 180-day freeze at the Oct. 6 meeting. Weld County activists will be at the Brighton meeting, in neighboring Adams County, to gather signatures for their data center petitions, a campaign spokesperson said. Political leaders haven’t listened so far, said Matt Cheroutes, who is the campaign manager for the Weld County activists calling themselves Protect Our Water and Energy Resources, or POWER. “So now we’re taking this to the voters. The commissioners had their vote. Now it’s the people’s turn,” Cheroutes said.

artigo.texto: A Alibaba Cloud inaugurou seus primeiros data centers no Brasil em São Paulo em agosto de 2026, prometendo reduzir o tempo de resposta de sites e sistemas de pagamento. No entanto, especialistas do Grupo HRZ destacam que a infraestrutura só será útil se integrada a um planejamento completo de CRM, estoque e atendimento, evitando falhas em campanhas de alto volume. A Alibaba Cloud, divisão de computação em nuvem do grupo chinês Alibaba, anunciou em 27 de agosto de 2026 a inauguração dos seus dois primeiros data centers no Brasil, ambos localizados em São Paulo. A chegada dessa infraestrutura aproxima os servidores das empresas e dos consumidores brasileiros, o que pode melhorar significativamente o desempenho de sites, sistemas de pagamento, consultas de estoque e plataformas de atendimento. Essa expansão faz parte do compromisso global de US$ 53 bilhões da companhia com inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem. Com a chegada dos novos data centers da Alibaba Cloud no Brasil, a latência deve cair, mas será que a tecnologia sozinha salva uma operação de vendas instável Especialistas debatem o tema e analisam os desafios de integração de CRM, estoque e e-commerce para aproveitar ao máximo essa nova infraestrutura. - A Alibaba Cloud abriu dois data centers em São Paulo para reduzir o tempo de resposta dos sites brasileiros. - A infraestrutura faz parte de um investimento global de US$ 53 bilhões em inteligência artificial. - Especialistas alertam que servidores rápidos não resolvem falhas de estoque ou atendimento desatualizado. - Campanhas de grande volume, como a Black Friday, exigem estabilidade total de todos os sistemas. - É necessário diagnosticar a operação antes de migrar para garantir que os dados fluam entre canais. Proximidade de servidores reduz tempo de resposta Hugo Silveira, cofundador do Grupo HRZ, holding especializada em crescimento empresarial e estruturação comercial, avalia que a entrada de mais um grande fornecedor amplia as opções para empresas que dependem de sistemas digitais para vender. Ter servidores mais próximos pode diminuir o tempo que a informação leva para ir e voltar. Mas isso, sozinho, não resolve os problemas de uma operação. É preciso analisar o site, as integrações, o estoque, o atendimento e o CRM para entender onde a nova infraestrutura realmente pode trazer ganho, afirma o estrategista. Na prática, essa distância entre o usuário e o servidor influencia a chamada latência, que é o intervalo entre uma ação e a resposta do sistema. Quando um consumidor abre uma página, consulta um produto, tenta finalizar uma compra ou realiza um pagamento, diferentes sistemas precisam trocar informações em poucos segundos. Esse ponto ganha importância em operações que conectam loja física, e-commerce, aplicativo e WhatsApp. O Grupo HRZ atua em projetos nos quais estoque, vendas, CRM e atendimento precisam compartilhar dados para que o consumidor consiga iniciar uma compra em um canal e continuar em outro sem perder o histórico. A Alibaba Cloud informa que sua estrutura em São Paulo conta com duas zonas de disponibilidade. Em termos simples, são ambientes separados, com redes e fontes de energia independentes, criados para reduzir o risco de uma única falha afetar toda a operação. A própria companhia recomenda que as empresas utilizem estruturas próximas de seus usuários quando o objetivo é diminuir o tempo de resposta. Estabilidade é crucial em picos de vendas A capacidade de aumentar recursos rapidamente se torna especialmente importante em períodos que concentram muitos acessos em poucas horas, como Black Friday, lançamentos de produtos e grandes campanhas promocionais. Nessas situações, uma falha pode atingir diferentes etapas da compra, da abertura da página até a aprovação do pagamento. Iury Borges, estrategista de vendas e sócio-diretor do Grupo HRZ, afirma que uma infraestrutura mais próxima pode ajudar, mas precisa fazer parte de um planejamento mais amplo. Uma campanha com milhares de pessoas acessando ao mesmo tempo exige que toda a operação esteja preparada. Não adianta o site responder rápido se o estoque estiver desatualizado, o pagamento apresentar falhas ou a equipe não conseguir atender a demanda. A nuvem é uma peça dessa estrutura, ressalta. O desafio, portanto, não termina na velocidade do site. Sistemas de vendas, estoque, CRM e atendimento precisam trocar informações de forma organizada. Quando essa comunicação funciona, a empresa consegue atualizar a disponibilidade dos produtos, identificar a origem das compras e manter o histórico do consumidor ao longo do relacionamento. João Vinas, engenheiro e sócio do Grupo HRZ, onde atua em projetos de CRM, automação comercial e inteligência artificial aplicada a vendas, afirma que a migração para uma nova infraestrutura deve começar por um diagnóstico. O varejista precisa saber onde seus dados estão armazenados, quais sistemas dependem uns dos outros, quais serviços estão disponíveis no Brasil e quanto uma mudança custaria. Só depois desse levantamento é possível saber se a migração faz sentido, aponta. Privacidade de dados e diagnóstico prévio A presença dos servidores no Brasil também pode ser considerada por negócios que desejam manter parte do processamento de informações no território nacional. Isso, porém, não substitui as demais obrigações de proteção de dados. A Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados estabelece responsabilidades para empresas que coletam e utilizam informações pessoais, enquanto transferências internacionais seguem regras específicas da Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados. Antes de trocar de fornecedor ou transferir sistemas, a recomendação é medir o desempenho atual. O primeiro passo pode ser verificar, principalmente pelo celular, quanto tempo uma página de produto leva para abrir, como o checkout responde e em quais pontos o consumidor encontra demora. artigo.texto: Nevada data centers promise big power demand. Who will pay the bill? As Nevada faces unprecedented demand for electricity from the data center industry, developers are pushing back against some of NV Energy’s proposed safeguards designed to prevent the cost of serving their projects from shifting to other customers. But as the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada weighs agreements with future data center customers, confidentiality claims and redactions are preventing the public from seeing project-specific information needed to determine whether those safeguards are sufficient. Many data center developers currently seeking electric service from NV Energy are requesting 300 to 500 megawatts of electricity, six to 10 times the roughly 50 megawatts a major casino or mine might use, said Shawn Elicegui, NV Energy’s senior vice president of regulatory and resource planning. “What we see from data centers is unprecedented,” Elicegui said in a recent interview. “There’s really nothing comparable to data center load.” Unlike most customers — such as households or small businesses, which typically receive a monthly bill based largely on how much electricity they use — data centers typically commit in advance to how much power they expect to need. If they take service under terms approved by the PUC, they can be required to make minimum payments based on those commitments, even if they ultimately use less electricity. The stakes are significant. NV Energy’s plans for future electricity needs account for the enormous demand expected from data centers and other large customers, as well as the infrastructure needed to serve them. If a data center ultimately uses less power than expected, the utility could be left with costs it expected the large customer to help cover, potentially shifting some of those costs to other ratepayers. NV Energy wants some of its largest new customers to pay minimum charges tied to at least 90 percent of the power demand and energy use they sign up for. At least one data center developer, however, wants that minimum set at 70 percent, according to PUC regulatory filings. The disagreement is a test of NV Energy’s promise that Nevada’s growing data-center industry will pay the costs it creates rather than shift them to other customers. Guardrails — but not enough information to test them A Las Vegas Review-Journal investigation found several guardrails in regulatory filings designed to support NV Energy’s repeated promise that data centers will pay their own way. They generally include proposed minimum payments, charges for new generation, financial guarantees and penalties if a customer leaves early. But simply having those protections does not show whether they are sufficient to prevent the costs of serving data centers from shifting onto other ratepayers, energy and utility-regulation experts told the Review-Journal. Sarah Wang, a researcher who studies massive customers called large loads, said regulators can calculate the minimum revenue a customer must provide and compare it with the costs the utility would not otherwise incur. “Without modeling, or some set of calculations, it’s really hard to figure out what 70 percent or 90 percent really mean,” said Wang, a senior associate at energy policy research organization RMI. Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, said the key question is whether the service agreements between utilities and data center developers cover all the infrastructure costs created by the new demand, rather than only some of them. “I believe that large loads should be required to pay for 100 percent of the incremental costs,” Peskoe said. Utilities around the country are confronting similar questions as they plan new power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure to accommodate rapidly growing data center demand. New large-load customer rules increasingly use minimum payments, long-term contracts, financial guarantees and exit charges to reduce the risk that other customers are left paying for infrastructure built for projects that arrive late, use less power than expected or never fully develop. The Review-Journal examined proposed agreements between data center customers and NV Energy, utility testimony and power plans, and submitted multiple public records requests to the PUC. The public filings and records obtained for several data center projects the newspaper reviewed do not contain enough project-specific information to compare the minimum revenue those data centers would provide with the costs NV Energy would not otherwise incur — and determine whether any of those costs could shift to other ratepayers. What 90 percent vs. 70 percent really means The minimum-billing dispute is playing out in a pending commission case over proposed large-load electric service agreements between NV Energy and industrial real estate company Prologis for at least one data center project under development in North Las Vegas. The agreements would govern how NV Energy supplies data centers’ enormous power needs. Prologis argues that a 70 percent minimum better reflects how data centers actually operate, saying their electricity use does not consistently reach 90 percent of capacity in every billing period and can vary as tenants move in. Prologis did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The reverse, she said, is also possible: Even requiring minimum billing at 100 percent of contracted demand would not guarantee full cost recovery if the rates or the way costs are assigned are inadequate. The goal, Wang said, should be 100 percent recovery of the total cost to serve — both the properly assigned new costs and the large customer’s share of existing infrastructure it uses. artigo.texto: Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) has committed €1.2 billion to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ (CIP) sixth flagship renewable energy fund, CI VI. NBIM said CI VI will primarily invest in renewable power generation and energy storage projects across OECD countries in North America, Western Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region. The investment builds on NBIM’s partnership with CIP, following a €900 million commitment to CIP’s fifth flagship fund in 2024 (see Norway Commits €900 Million To CIP’s Renewable Energy Fund). In March 2025, CIP said its CI V fund exceeded the target of €12 billion to support grid connection of 30 of new energy capacity (see Danish Fund Manager Exceeds €12B Target For New RE Fund). The renewable energy business of Australia’s Igneo Infrastructure Partners, Atmos Renewables, has reached financial close on two projects backed by Australia’s Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS). The projects comprise the 400 MW/1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Queensland and the 470 MW Parron Maam Marang Wind Farm in Western Australia. Together with the 100 MW/400 MWh Merredin BESS, which reached financial close in June 2025, Atmos says it has now taken 970 MW of CIS-backed capacity through financial close. Teebar BESS will provide 4 hours of storage, storing electricity when supply is abundant and dispatching it during periods of higher demand. Atmos will retain ownership of both projects through construction and operate them once completed. Austrian independent power producer (IPP) Renalfa IPP and Danish renewable energy developer Eurowind Energy have inaugurated the Tenevo hybrid renewable energy complex in southeastern Bulgaria. The project combines a 242 MW solar PV plant with two co-located BESS totaling 311 MW/773 MWh. The Tenevo complex is expected to generate around 332 GWh of clean electricity annually. The solar plant and the first phase of the BESS have been operational since 2025, while the project has now reached its full announced storage capacity. The duo calls it one of Europe's largest hybrid renewable energy projects. Financed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Raiffeisen Bank International, with support from an InvestEU guarantee, the project is located next to a coal region undergoing transition. The Tenovo site is planned to expand with more than 250 MW of wind capacity, with total investment across all phases expected to exceed €500 million. US-based developer and manufacturer of iron-sodium battery systems Inlyte Energy and CutPeak Energy have announced plans for an 80 MWh long-duration BESS at Berkshire East Mountain Resort in western Massachusetts. CutPeak Energy develops battery storage projects at ski resorts. The project is targeted to come online in 2028. The project is one of two long-duration storage demonstrations selected under Massachusetts’ $40.3 million Advancing Massachusetts Power (AMP) Energy Storage Grant Program. The battery will help the resort manage electricity demand from snowmaking, which can reach about 4 MW during peak periods, while also providing backup power during grid outages. Inlyte says the project is designed to charge during periods of lower electricity demand and discharge during snowmaking peaks. European BESS projects operator GIGA Storage has achieved ready-to-build (RTB) status for its 350 MW/1.4 GWh Albatross battery energy storage project near Neuenkirchen in Lower Saxony, Germany. It is developing the project with Isenau Projects and will connect directly to Amprion’s 380 kV high-voltage grid. The project will comprise 264 battery units and is expected to supply electricity equivalent to the daily consumption of approximately 193,000 households. With the development phase completed, GIGA Storage plans to take the final investment decision (FID) in Q4 2026, start construction in H1 2027, and commission the project in 2028. Albatross is GIGA Storage’s first large-scale energy storage project in Germany. It is one of three projects being jointly developed by GIGA Storage and Isenau, with the three projects together representing more than 1 GW of power capacity and 4 GWh of storage capacity. Global energy infrastructure manager Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) has taken the FID on the Kilmarnock South BESS in southern Scotland. The company is investing more than €270 million in the 350 MW/1,400 MWh lithium-ion project. Construction is already underway, and it is expected to begin commercial operations in Q1 2028. The 4-hour BESS will store surplus wind power and discharge electricity to the grid when network capacity is available. CIP said this project is its fourth transmission-connected BESS investment in Scotland. It has an optimization agreement with Shell Energy Europe, ensuring long-term contracted revenue. Together, CIP shared that its four Scottish projects are expected to provide 1.85 GW of power capacity and 4.4 GWh of storage when fully operational. Excelsior Energy Capital-backed Lydian Energy has closed a $300 million holding company credit facility with Infranity, an infrastructure asset manager. Lydian will use the proceeds for the development, construction, acquisition, and operation of its utility-scale battery energy storage and solar projects across the US. Lydian said its portfolio includes about 6 GW of operating, construction-ready and development-stage projects. In April 2026, Lydian acquired 1.5 GW Atlas North solar-plus-storage portfolio from Hanwha Renewables (see Lydian Energy Acquires Hanwha’s 1.5 GW Atlas North Portfolio).
