artigo.texto: Em uma manhã ensolarada de agosto, Bob Clark visita o novo Obama Presidential Center, no Jackson Park, zona sul de Chicago. Fundador da gigante da construção Clayco, ele ajudou a erguer o complexo, avaliado em US$ 850 milhões (R$ 4,23 bilhões). Clark faz uma rápida inspeção no “Obamalisk”. É assim que chama, carinhosamente, a torre central de oito andares, feita de granito, vidro e concreto. Depois, cumprimenta Valerie Jarrett, ex-assessora sênior da Casa Branca e atual CEO da Obama Foundation. A visita é rápida. Clark entra no banco traseiro de um Escalade branco e segue pela Lake Shore Drive. O destino é outro de seus projetos, que pode ter uma importância ainda maior para Chicago e para o mundo. Às margens do Lago Michigan, o “Quantum Shore” ocupa uma área onde funcionava uma fábrica da U.S. Steel. Quando for inaugurado, no fim de 2027, será um dos maiores campi de computação quântica dos Estados Unidos. Entre os ocupantes estarão a IBM e a PsiQuantum, empresa de Palo Alto, na Califórnia. A companhia pretende construir no local um computador quântico de 1 milhão de qubits. Uma máquina desse porte teria uma capacidade difícil de imaginar. Poderia quebrar os tipos tradicionais de criptografia que protegem grande parte dos computadores — e das contas bancárias — do mundo. No futuro, também poderia acelerar o aprendizado de sistemas de inteligência artificial. Isso ocorreria por meio da redução do tempo de treinamento de determinadas arquiteturas complexas de aprendizagem profunda. O Quantum Shore é um empreendimento complexo — e caro. A primeira fase está sendo desenvolvida pela CRG, subsidiária imobiliária de Clark, em parceria com o escritório do Meio-Oeste da gigante imobiliária Related Companies. O projeto custará US$ 12 bilhões (R$ 59,76 bilhões). Desse total, US$ 500 milhões (R$ 2,49 bilhões) serão aportados pelo estado de Illinois. Os bits quânticos, conhecidos como “qubits”, são extremamente sensíveis às condições ambientais. Por isso, a estrutura terá uma instalação criogênica. Ela fornecerá hélio e nitrogênio líquidos super-resfriados aos computadores. “A única maneira de estabilizar o chip é mantê-lo mais frio do que o espaço sideral”, diz Clark, enquanto guindastes de 550 toneladas passam pelo local. A complexidade da obra impressiona até mesmo o empresário. Ele se lembra de quando o CEO da PsiQuantum lhe disse que projetaria um edifício que iria “mudar tudo”. O negócio Clark, de 67 anos, parece adequado para comandar um projeto dessa dimensão. Ele constrói data centers desde a década de 1980. Somente no ano passado, concluiu 16. Outros 77 estão em andamento em 13 estados americanos. Os centros de dados devem responder por 75% da receita de quase US$ 12 bilhões (R$ 59,76 bilhões) da Clayco em 2026. A expansão do segmento deve ajudar a companhia a elevar o faturamento em 43% na comparação com 2025. “Trabalho no setor de data centers durante a maior parte da minha carreira, mas nunca teria imaginado o que está acontecendo hoje”, afirma. Quando Clark começou, há quatro décadas, um data center era algo bem mais simples. Eram apenas algumas salas de computadores instaladas nos fundos de um banco. Hoje, o cenário mudou. Sediada em Chicago, a Clayco ergue estruturas que equivalem a cidades autossuficientes de bilhões de dólares. Elas praticamente não têm presença humana e podem abrigar 100 mil ou mais das GPUs mais avançadas do mundo. Entre os clientes estão Amazon, Microsoft e Oracle. Para construir esses complexos com eficiência e em grande escala, a Clayco controla suas próprias empresas de arquitetura, concreto, compras e logística. É uma máquina criada para alimentar as máquinas insaciáveis da inteligência artificial. Corrida dos data centers Os gastos dos Estados Unidos com a construção de data centers mais do que triplicaram desde 2023. Neste ano, devem chegar a US$ 75 bilhões (R$ 373,5 bilhões), segundo dados do Census Bureau. O montante nem sequer inclui a compra dos computadores. Esses equipamentos podem representar 40% do custo total de um projeto. Jeff Blau é CEO da Related e parceiro de Clark no Quantum Shore. Os dois também trabalham em um data center de US$ 1,2 bilhão (R$ 5,98 bilhões) para a CoreWeave, em Cheyenne, no Wyoming. Segundo Blau, a forte demanda por centros de dados, somada aos juros elevados, tirou espaço de muitos outros grandes projetos de construção. “Isso não tem precedentes. Nunca tivemos algo com uma demanda tão forte e, ao mesmo tempo, em uma escala tão grande”, afirma. A Related Digital, comandada por Blau, tem US$ 55 bilhões (R$ 273,9 bilhões) em projetos de data centers em desenvolvimento. Para as construtoras, é uma ótima notícia. Quase 1.300 data centers já estão em funcionamento nos Estados Unidos. Essas colmeias de concreto e aço consomem aproximadamente 70 milhões de galões de água por dia. Também precisam de um fornecimento constante de 62 gigawatts de energia. Para efeito de comparação, a cidade de Nova York utiliza, em média, seis gigawatts. E a expansão está longe de terminar. Outros 2.142 centros estão planejados ou em construção, segundo a empresa de inteligência em infraestrutura Cleanview. Sem medo de uma bolha O boom da IA também tornou Clark muito mais rico. Seu patrimônio líquido quadruplicou nos últimos três anos e chegou a US$ 7 bilhões (R$ 34,86 bilhões). A fortuna garantiu ao empresário uma estreia na lista Forbes 400 deste ano. Ele aparece na 245ª posição. Mas a expansão dos data centers também trouxe outro efeito: uma oposição cada vez maior. Uma pesquisa recente do Annenberg Public Policy Center mostrou que 61% dos americanos são contrários à construção dessas instalações em suas comunidades. Quatro meses antes, eram 49%. Segundo o Data Center Watch, projetos avaliados em US$ 18 bilhões (R$ 89,64 bilhões) foram bloqueados. Outros US$ 46 bilhões (R$ 229,08 bilhões) em construções sofreram atrasos. Clark não se intimida com a reação. Prefere manter o foco nos resultados. “Não vemos nenhum sinal de alerta no horizonte”, afirm

artigo.texto: Reduce emissions to 'profit': New opportunities from the carbon market. (CLO) Officially operational from the end of June 2026, the carbon exchange in Vietnam is considered a significant step towards a low-emission economy. Although the market is still in its nascent stages, Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung - Director of VinaCarbon Investment Fund - believes that Vietnam has sufficient potential to transform emission reduction into a real source of economic value, attracting large capital flows into forestry, clean energy, and agriculture. The carbon exchange in Vietnam officially began operations at the end of June 2026. To date, the number of products and transactions on the market remains quite limited. However, the potential for development is considered significant as Vietnam is accelerating its emission reduction goals, promoting green transitions, and gradually improving the legal framework for the carbon market. Regarding this issue, a reporter from the Journalists and Public Opinion Newspaper had a private interview with Mr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung, Director of VinaCarbon Investment Fund, about the prospects of the carbon market in Vietnam. The Vietnamese carbon market has many favorable conditions for strong growth. + Sir, the official launch of the carbon exchange in June 2026 is considered the starting point for the carbon market in Vietnam. From an investment perspective, how do you view the opportunities and growth potential of this market in the coming years? - It can be said that the Vietnamese carbon market has many favorable conditions for strong development, especially given that our country is in a favorable position thanks to the convergence of four factors: international demand, natural supply, legal framework, and international institutions ready to cooperate. The pilot operation of the domestic carbon exchange, despite its limited number of products and transactions, is a significant step forward, as it lays the foundation for a transparent market, moving towards a low-emission economy and fulfilling Vietnam's climate commitments. The potential for growth in Vietnam's carbon credit market stems primarily from demand. Domestically, the need to reduce emissions and transition to green is being concretized through quota mechanisms, starting with high-emission industries such as thermal power, steel, and cement, and will be tightened to more industries in the future. Globally , the trend of greening supply chains is gaining momentum, with many new requirements for reducing emissions. From the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for Aviation (CORSIA), the net-zero commitments of multinational corporations, to the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), exporting businesses are being forced to manage their emissions more tightly. This creates a significant demand for high-quality and integrity carbon credits in the future. To meet that demand, Vietnam has potential supply sources in many sectors such as agriculture , renewable energy, waste management, and especially forestry, where there are clear and sustainable advantages. Vietnam has a large forest area, with planted forests accounting for a significant proportion, along with years of experience in forest management and established forest product value chains. Furthermore, forest carbon already has its own legal framework. Projects for forest protection, restoration, and sustainable management can both generate substantial emission reductions and support community livelihoods if appropriate benefit-sharing mechanisms are in place. And because forests are a long-term asset, with project cycles spanning decades, forestry is also best suited to the medium- and long-term development narrative of the market. However, having both supply and demand is not enough, because a market can only develop sustainably when it has the necessary infrastructure. In just about a year and a half, Vietnam has built almost the complete "framework" necessary for a carbon market, from a domestic emissions trading mechanism, an official exchange, a national registration system, to regulations for transferring credits internationally and a separate decree on forest carbon. Furthermore, Vietnam has also established bilateral cooperation channels with Japan and Singapore. In summary, Vietnam has all the necessary conditions for carbon market growth in the coming years. However, the pace of development will depend on the completeness of the legal framework and trading infrastructure, the quality and integrity of the credits, and the ability to meet international standards. You may also like + In your opinion, what are the biggest difficulties and challenges hindering the development of Vietnam's carbon credit market, in terms of credit supply, credit quality, trading mechanisms, and the ability of businesses to participate? - The biggest challenge currently is the limited supply of high-quality carbon credits. Generating a carbon credit requires a relatively long and expensive process, from project development and evaluation to registration, making it generally difficult for investors to access. Furthermore, buyers of carbon credits are becoming increasingly demanding regarding quality. Criteria such as complementarity, risk of reversal, and risk of double counting are receiving more attention. Therefore, the market will tend to prioritize credits certified by reputable standards. This requires Vietnam to improve its measurement, reporting, and assessment capabilities, while gradually harmonizing domestic standards with international practices. Another challenge lies in the legal framework and market infrastructure. Regulations, credit standards, data systems, and supervisory mechanisms still need further improvement to increase transparency, build confidence, and reduce uncertainty for investors. artigo.texto: ESS, an opportunity for K-batteries A new current is reshaping the global battery market. In the first half of 2026, global shipments of lithium-ion batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) reached 461 gigawatt-hour (GWh), up 71 percent from 270 GWh in the same period a year earlier, according to SNE Research. This represents a remarkable leap for the ESS market, especially compared with the 20 percent year-on-year growth in global battery demand for electric vehicles (EVs), which reached 609 GWh over the same period. Key drivers include rising energy demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, where speed and reliability are critical, and growth in renewable power generation, which requires solutions to address its intermittency. The expansion of AI data centers and the transition to renewable energy are powerful trends unlikely to reverse in the short term. As a result, the global ESS market is forecast to reach 1,870 GWh in annual shipments by 2035, roughly twice this year’s level. The Korean government is also stepping up efforts to develop the domestic ESS industry through a range of policy measures. On the technology front, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced its Battery Industry Technology Roadmap on Sept. 22. The road map’s main elements are to position sodium-ion and solid-state batteries as new growth engines: The government will invest more than 250 billion won in next-generation battery technology development; the country’s three cell manufacturers will collaborate on research and standardization in noncompetitive areas; and the industry as a whole will invest approximately 8 trillion won ($5.97 billion) through 2030 in manufacturing-process innovation and the localization of materials. On the production front, the government has pledged tax support. On Aug. 3, the Ministry of Finance and Economy announced its 2026 Tax Reform Proposal, which introduced a domestic production tax credit to expand local manufacturing capacity in industries of strategic importance to the green transition and economic security. Rechargeable batteries are among the eligible products. On the deployment front, the government is expanding the market through auctions under the Central Contract Market. On Sept. 23, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment announced the third ESS Central Contract Market in which it would select ESS project developers with a record-high total capacity of 1,180 megawatts. By the auction, the Korea Power Exchange competitively tenders the ESS capacity needed to stabilize the grid and enters into 15-year contracts with successful bidders. This is an encouraging development, as it creates substantial new demand for a battery market that has slowed amid moderating growth in EV demand. For K-batteries to build on these policies and strengthen their position, however, they must increase their share of the rapidly expanding global ESS market. This presents both significant challenges and important opportunities. The fact that China has already established a strong lead in the ESS market is a challenge for Korea. The top four companies in the global ESS market in the first half of this year were all Chinese, and together, they accounted for nearly 55 percent of the market. Korean companies have also recorded strong year-on-year growth, but the gap in absolute volume with China remains substantial. Moreover, with global ESS supply capacity exceeding demand — 900 GWh against the actual demand of 612 GWh at the end of 2025 — price competition is intensifying. Competing with Chinese companies, which have maintained operating margins through economies of scale, can seem like an uphill battle. At the same time, several factors create opportunities. First, regional imbalances between battery supply and demand mean that key export markets for Korean companies are likely to face shortages. For example, battery supply in China is expected to exceed demand by about 90 percent in 2030, while Europe is projected to face a supply shortfall of 40 percent. North America is also expected to face a shortage from 2035. This presents an opportunity for Korean companies, which have established production bases in Europe and North America, to increase their market share. Second, in Europe, capacity for facilities combining renewable energy and batteries is expected to rise by more than 450 percent, from 6.3 GW in 2025 to around 35 GW in 2030. In parallel, the region is working to reduce its reliance on battery supply chains from any one country. For example, it is preparing an Industrial Accelerator Act that would encourage greater use of components and batteries manufactured within Europe when awarding public procurement contracts and subsidies. Korean battery companies are well positioned to benefit, as they already have a substantial manufacturing footprint in Europe. Third, the U.S. market is also opening up significant opportunities for Korean companies. ESS demand is growing rapidly as AI data centers proliferate, while U.S. policies to reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains are being strengthened. The ESS market is expected to grow by an average of 16 percent annually to reach 320 GWh by 2035, while the uninterruptible power supply market for AI data centers is projected to expand at an average annual rate of 47 percent to 135 GWh. Meanwhile, tariffs on Chinese ESS products are rising under measures such as Washington's Section 301 of the Trade Act and forced labor standards under the environmental, social and governance (ESG) pillars. The Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit and restrictions concerning prohibited foreign entities are also creating additional opportunities for K-battery companies with U.S.-based manufacturing operations. artigo.texto: SEATTLE — Amazon.com Inc. is pledging $1 billion or more over five years to communities where it builds and operates data centers. The company last week unveiled the “Built Together” investment framework for communities where the tech giant operates data centers across the United States. The increased investment will fund free community college for local residents, energy upgrades for homes and businesses, job training and protecting local water resources, the company said. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run,” Matt Garman, chief executive officer for Amazon Web Services, wrote in an October 2 post. “The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so.” Amazon is a leading player in the tech industry’s massive AI buildout that relies, in part, on finding communities willing to host data centers. Garman noted that there are more than 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the United States. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race,” he said, “and the consequences would last generations.” Added Garman, “There are clearly areas in which the technology and energy industries can be doing better (along with their government partners) but just like in the past when the country has banded together to accomplish something that’s critical for our national security and economic prosperity — we should approach this as a long-term mission that the private and public sectors pursue together.” Amazon said it is responding to apprehension over the data center buildout by codifying a series of tenets in what the company is calling its “Amazon Data Center Commitment.” The company commits to “protect and enhance communities,” “provide jobs and economic opportunities,” “engage communities,” and “build and operate responsibly.” Submit Your Press Release Have news to share? artigo.texto: Reduzir emissões para 'lucrar': Novas oportunidades no mercado de carbono. (CLO) Oficialmente operacional a partir do final de junho de 2026, a bolsa de carbono no Vietnã é considerada um passo significativo rumo a uma economia de baixas emissões. Embora o mercado ainda esteja em seus estágios iniciais, o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung, Diretor do Fundo de Investimento VinaCarbon, acredita que o Vietnã tem potencial suficiente para transformar a redução de emissões em uma fonte real de valor econômico, atraindo grandes fluxos de capital para os setores florestal, de energia limpa e agrícola. A bolsa de carbono no Vietnã iniciou oficialmente suas operações no final de junho de 2026. Até o momento, o número de produtos e transações no mercado permanece bastante limitado. No entanto, o potencial de desenvolvimento é considerado significativo, visto que o Vietnã está acelerando suas metas de redução de emissões, promovendo a transição para energias limpas e aprimorando gradualmente o arcabouço legal para o mercado de carbono. A respeito desse assunto, um repórter do jornal Jornalistas e Opinião Pública realizou uma entrevista particular com o Sr. Nguyen Ngoc Tung, Diretor do Fundo de Investimento VinaCarbon, sobre as perspectivas do mercado de carbono no Vietnã. O mercado de carbono vietnamita apresenta muitas condições favoráveis para um forte crescimento. Senhor, o lançamento oficial da bolsa de carbono em junho de 2026 é considerado o ponto de partida para o mercado de carbono no Vietnã. Do ponto de vista de investimento, como o senhor vê as oportunidades e o potencial de crescimento desse mercado nos próximos anos? Pode-se afirmar que o mercado de carbono vietnamita possui muitas condições favoráveis para um forte desenvolvimento, especialmente considerando que o país se encontra em uma posição privilegiada graças à convergência de quatro fatores: demanda internacional, oferta natural, arcabouço legal e instituições internacionais dispostas a cooperar. A operação piloto da bolsa de carbono doméstica, apesar do número limitado de produtos e transações, representa um avanço significativo, pois estabelece as bases para um mercado transparente, caminhando rumo a uma economia de baixas emissões e cumprindo os compromissos climáticos do Vietnã. O potencial de crescimento do mercado de créditos de carbono do Vietnã decorre principalmente da demanda. No âmbito interno, a necessidade de reduzir as emissões e fazer a transição para energias limpas está sendo concretizada por meio de mecanismos de cotas, começando com indústrias de alta emissão, como energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento, e será estendida a mais setores no futuro. Globalmente , a tendência de tornar as cadeias de abastecimento mais ecológicas está ganhando força, com muitos novos requisitos para a redução das emissões. Do Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação (CORSIA), aos compromissos de emissões líquidas zero das empresas multinacionais, ao Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira (CBAM) da União Europeia, as empresas exportadoras estão sendo obrigadas a gerenciar suas emissões com mais rigor. Isso cria uma demanda significativa por créditos de carbono de alta qualidade e integridade no futuro. Para atender a essa demanda, o Vietnã possui fontes de suprimento potenciais em diversos setores, como agricultura , energia renovável, gestão de resíduos e, principalmente, silvicultura, onde existem vantagens claras e sustentáveis. O Vietnã possui uma vasta área florestal, com florestas plantadas representando uma proporção significativa, além de anos de experiência em gestão florestal e cadeias de valor de produtos florestais já estabelecidas. Além disso, o carbono florestal já possui seu próprio marco legal. Projetos de proteção, restauração e gestão sustentável de florestas podem gerar reduções substanciais de emissões e apoiar os meios de subsistência das comunidades, desde que existam mecanismos adequados de compartilhamento de benefícios. E como as florestas são um ativo de longo prazo, com ciclos de projetos que se estendem por décadas, o setor florestal também se adapta melhor à narrativa de desenvolvimento de médio e longo prazo do mercado. No entanto, ter oferta e demanda não é suficiente, pois um mercado só pode se desenvolver de forma sustentável quando possui a infraestrutura necessária. Em apenas um ano e meio, o Vietnã construiu praticamente toda a "estrutura" necessária para um mercado de carbono, desde um mecanismo doméstico de negociação de emissões, uma bolsa oficial, um sistema nacional de registro, até regulamentações para a transferência internacional de créditos e um decreto específico sobre carbono florestal. Além disso, o Vietnã também estabeleceu canais de cooperação bilateral com o Japão e Singapura. Em resumo, o Vietnã possui todas as condições necessárias para o crescimento do mercado de carbono nos próximos anos. No entanto, o ritmo desse desenvolvimento dependerá da completude do arcabouço legal e da infraestrutura de negociação, da qualidade e integridade dos créditos e da capacidade de atender aos padrões internacionais. Você também pode gostar + Na sua opinião, quais são as maiores dificuldades e desafios que impedem o desenvolvimento do mercado de créditos de carbono do Vietnã, em termos de oferta de crédito, qualidade do crédito, mecanismos de negociação e capacidade das empresas de participar? O maior desafio atualmente é a oferta limitada de créditos de carbono de alta qualidade. Gerar um crédito de carbono requer um processo relativamente longo e caro, desde o desenvolvimento e avaliação do projeto até o registro, o que geralmente dificulta o acesso para investidores. Além disso, os compradores de créditos de carbono estão cada vez mais exigentes em relação à qualidade. Critérios como complementaridade, risco de reversão e risco de dupla contagem estão recebendo maior atenção. Portanto, o mercado tenderá a priorizar créditos certificados por padrões reconhecidos. artigo.texto: Good morning. Andrew Nusca here, back in action after a week in New York for our inaugural AIQ Summit about putting AI to work in large companies. (Many thanks to Alexei Oreskovic for steering the ship while I was away.) Miss the AIQ festivities? No sweat—you can watch the entire thing here or view a session of your choosing here. If you’re in the business of deploying AI in the enterprise, there are lots of good insights to be had. And today’s tech news? Well, let’s get right to it. —Andrew Nusca Thoughts? Suggestions? Hot tip? Drop me a line. THE BIG STORY Meta is building one of the world’s biggest undersea cable networks While data centers dominate headlines amid mounting local opposition over electricity bills, water use, and zoning fights, Meta has been expanding its infrastructure somewhere far less visible: the bottom of the ocean. On Sept. 21, the company announced Petal, a roughly 4,300-mile subsea cable connecting the U.S. and France. Meta says the cable, expected to enter service in 2029, will be the first to deliver petabit-scale capacity across an ocean—double what today’s most advanced transoceanic cables can handle, thanks to “two-core fiber” that fits two light paths inside each strand. Projects like this rarely make headlines in an industry fixated on AI models and apps, but they’re what make those products run. Products like Meta’s personal AI agent Muse depend on moving enormous volumes of data between its data centers and its users around the world. Subsea cables aren’t new territory for Meta, which is now valued at roughly $1.85 trillion. The company has spent the past decade building its presence on the seafloor and says it has invested in more than 20 subsea cable projects. Taken together, those projects touch every continent except Antarctica. The most ambitious is Project Waterworth, announced in February 2025. Meta says the system will stretch more than 31,000 miles, longer than the Earth’s circumference. It will connect the U.S., Brazil, South Africa, India, and other regions across five continents. Meta hasn’t built all of this alone. Petal is being developed with Japan’s NEC and Sumitomo Electric Industries, and French telecom Orange is handling the landing on France’s Atlantic coast. Meta has even partnered with rivals: The MAREA cable between Virginia and Spain, completed in 2017, is jointly owned with Microsoft and telecom company Telxius. These projects don’t come cheap. TechCrunch estimates that the Waterworth project could top $10 billion. —James LaForge THE BLIND BOX “Just because you are using AI, that is not a proxy for your productivity or you doing a good job at work.” THE RUNDOWN —Trump forms “Super Intelligence Force” led by National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. —OpenAI CEO Sam Altman: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” —Meta's Muse compiles “a page for every person in the user's life,” per Wired. —Firmus IPO: Investor demand far exceeds the offer size, one of Australia's largest. —Schneider Electric may buy PTC, the U.S. engineering software firm, for $20 billion. —Apple CEO John Ternus is in the design studio “several times per week,” per Bloomberg. —McKinsey: AI and automation will eliminate 36 million U.S. jobs by 2035 but add 41 million elsewhere. —U.K. neobank Monzo may sell a 15% stake to CVC and Advent after a Nubank deal fell apart. THE PARTING SLOP Sam told Mark not to say anything. Mark can't go in there, brazenly flaunt the rules and then think Sam’s gonna share his CUDA with him. Sorry! artigo.texto: Cygni Energy and Indus Towers will explore BESS manufacturing capacity of up to 1.5 GWh for telecom applications The companies will evaluate higher-capacity and emerging battery technologies for telecom infrastructure Cygni currently operates a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS facility in Hyderabad and plans to expand its overall capacity beyond 10 GWh Indian energy storage manufacturer Cygni Energy and telecom infrastructure company Indus Towers have joined hands to explore up to 1.5 GWh of battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing in India to serve telecom infrastructure. The duo has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) and plans to establish manufacturing capacity to meet the ‘evolving energy requirements’ of telecom infrastructure in India. The partnership will also evaluate advanced battery technologies for telecom applications. Formed by the merger of Bharti Infratel Limited and Indus Towers, Indus Towers Limited had over 267,611 towers and 432,250 co-locations as of June 30, 2026. It is present across 22 telecom circles. While Cygni's official statement does not reveal details about the MoU, telecom companies have been exploring energy storage as a backup power strategy to improve operational efficiency. According to Battery Council International (BCI), batteries can help provide stable power for data centers and telecom systems. Incubated at IIT Madras, Cygni Energy develops energy storage products for telecom, stationary energy storage, mobility, and other applications. Its battery portfolio currently includes 100 Ah solutions and could expand to higher-capacity systems, including 314 Ah. “We plan to develop capacity of up to 2 GWh, while building a portfolio that can evolve from today’s 100Ah solutions to higher-capacity 314Ah systems and emerging battery technologies,” said Cygni Energy Founder & CEO Venkat Rajaraman. In 2025, Cygni Energy opened a 4.8 GWh cell-to-container BESS Gigafactory in Hyderabad’s Maheshwaram, with plans to scale it up to exceed 10 GWh in the future. “Our ambition is to combine scale, reliability and Indian engineering to create future-ready energy storage solutions that can evolve alongside India’s rapidly expanding digital infrastructure,” added Rajaraman. According to Crisil, India could see up to 50 GWh of BESS installations by FY2028 as the technology helps improve power availability during peak demand. However, reducing reliance on overseas suppliers remains important to limit exposure to global supply disruptions and procurement uncertainties (see Crisil Projects India To Add 50 GWh BESS Capacity By FY2028).

artigo.texto: Frederico prevê regulamentação do Redata até o fim do ano Ministro das Comunicações diz que pendência está concentrada na questão energética e diverge da estimativa de seis meses apresentada pelo governo paulista O ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, afirmou nesta terça-feira, 6, que o governo trabalha para concluir até o fim de 2026 a regulamentação do Redata, regime tributário destinado aos investimentos em data centers. A declaração foi dada a jornalistas durante a Futurecom 2026, em São Paulo, após o vice-governador paulista estimar que o processo poderia levar aproximadamente seis meses. Segundo Frederico, a etapa considerada mais difícil — a aprovação do regime pelo Congresso — já foi superada. Agora, disse, restam questões de regulamentação. “A questão da regulamentação agora são ajustes finos”, afirmou. Segundo ele, “com relação à infraestrutura digital está resolvido” e permanece em discussão a questão energética. “A expectativa é que sim, a gente consiga resolver até o final do ano.” A declaração estabelece uma diferença de expectativa entre o governo federal e o paulista sobre o calendário necessário para que o regime possa produzir efeitos sobre novos investimentos. São Paulo trabalha com prazo maior Pouco antes, o vice-governador de São Paulo havia afirmado que a regulamentação poderia levar cerca de seis meses e associado a conclusão desse processo ao avanço da discussão estadual sobre ICMS. No discurso de abertura, ele disse que São Paulo pretende acompanhar a regulamentação federal para posteriormente adequar a legislação estadual, “principalmente em tópicos do ICMS”. Questionado pelos jornalistas sobre essa diferença de calendário, Frederico sustentou a possibilidade de concluir o processo ainda em 2026. O ministro não anunciou, entretanto, uma data para publicação dos atos nem detalhou quais instrumentos normativos ainda serão necessários. Também questionado sobre a possibilidade de os efeitos do Redata perderem relevância diante da entrada em vigor de etapas da reforma tributária, Frederico afirmou que o governo está concentrado no efeito econômico final para os investidores. “O que vale no final do dia é qual é o benefício que toda essa solução vai trazer ao investidor. Se vai ser o Redata ou se vai ser reforma tributária, o importante é a gente discutir o benefício”, disse. Governo discute regulamentação entre ministérios Frederico afirmou que o Ministério das Comunicações mantém discussões com outras áreas do governo, citando Minas e Energia, Casa Civil e outros ministérios envolvidos no tema. Questionado se algum projeto poderia utilizar os benefícios ainda em 2026, respondeu que o governo trabalha para acelerar as definições no período posterior às eleições. A regulamentação também apareceu no discurso oficial do ministro na abertura da Futurecom. Na ocasião, Frederico afirmou que o governo trabalha para dar previsibilidade ao setor produtivo e evitar a perda de investimentos. O Redata também foi citado pelo vice-governador paulista e pelo deputado federal e ex-ministro das Comunicações Juscelino Filho durante o evento, indicando convergência entre União, governo estadual e Congresso quanto à utilização do regime como instrumento de atração de data centers. A diferença está, neste momento, no calendário e nas etapas complementares necessárias para que os incentivos sejam operacionalizados. ICMS será próxima frente O ICMS aparece como uma dessas etapas. Como o tributo é estadual, sua eventual redução depende de decisões dos estados e das regras aplicáveis à tributação estadual. O governo paulista afirmou que pretende atuar nessa frente, mas depois de conhecer a regulamentação federal. Além da tributação, autoridades presentes à Futurecom relacionaram a expansão dos data centers à disponibilidade de energia, redes de fibra óptica, cabos submarinos e infraestrutura de conectividade. Frederico afirmou que data centers dependem de uma rede capaz de transportar os dados processados e armazenados. Essa combinação entre incentivos tributários, energia e telecomunicações deverá determinar a capacidade do Redata de efetivamente destravar novos projetos.

artigo.texto: Just outside Toledo, Ohio, Meta is building an $800 million data center campus. Annually, the data center will use only as much water as two full-service restaurants using a technology known as a closed-loop system. The Great Lakes region offers an unmatched set of resources ripe for data center development, including an abundance of fresh water for cooling; longer, colder winters than the South or Sunbelt; and former industrial lands ready for redevelopment. But in Illinois, a polarizing data center debate has heated up in recent weeks. I agree with Gov. JB Pritzker’s recent statement at New York’s America is All in Conference. When asked whether we should be welcoming data centers into Illinois, he said that we need to ensure that data centers are bringing their own energy, and they are using their own closed-loop water systems. There are still very valid public concerns about letting these data centers develop projects untethered to government accountability. I hear them weekly on the campaign trail from Chicagoans who voice concern that we could damage Lake Michigan by exploiting its resources too heavily and that our electricity bills could skyrocket. I have two solutions for those main two concerns. Regarding the first concern — water usage — many Chicagoans I speak with hear “data center” and picture a server farm drinking up the lake. My vision is to build a massive geothermal heat sink coil system in Lake Michigan. This system is closed loop and filled with liquid coolant. This loop would be miles, perhaps tens or hundreds of miles, long and coiled far offshore at or near the bottom of the lake (the deeper, the better, as it’s colder). This system would consume water over time, thus taking a data center’s water consumption to virtually zero. The second concern I have heard is that with this new architecture, we would cook the lake. But Lake Michigan holds about a quadrillion gallons of water, so adding data centers is like setting a sealed coffee thermos in a swimming pool — it wouldn’t change. From a thermodynamics perspective, even with miles of coils and loops constantly cooling themselves in Lake Michigan, we likely could not even marginally increase the temperature or create an environmentally noticeable impact. But “it’s fine, trust me” is not good enough for a lake this city drinks from, so I propose a water and environmental study before a single pipe goes in, with the results and data published where anyone can read it. On top of closed-loop infrastructure at the bottom of the lake, data centers should have windows. It may sound basic, but right now, data center construction typically creates hard cases of primarily concrete with no ability to leverage the outside cold air. They are basically heat-trapping boxes, and, as we now know, they produce a massive amount of heat. When a house is hot, open the windows. When a data center is hot, open the windows. Chicago’s cooler fall, chilling winter and brisk spring climates all lend themselves to a basic idea of circulating cold air into the data center itself and hot air out. With windows open, they essentially have natural air conditioning three-quarters of the year. The marginal cost to put in windows and natural cooling systems in northern and colder climates such as Chicago far outweighs the risk of continuing to use billions of gallons of water and energy to sustain these operations. The potential savings are not marginal; they are massive. Cornell University has cooled its campus from a Finger Lake for 25 years and reports saving roughly 85% of the energy conventional refrigeration would burn. Toronto has cooled more than a hundred downtown buildings with Lake Ontario since 2004, saving about 90,000 megawatt hours a year, enough to power a town of 25,000 people. Its system is nearly full, and it is spending $100 million to expand it. A massive, closed-loop coil system in Lake Michigan could cool much more than data centers; it could provide air conditioning and cooling for hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of households and buildings across the city as climate change increases the overall temperature throughout the year. None of this is theoretical anymore because the demand is already here. Chicago’s data center vacancy rate is under 2%. There is not a single block of 5 megawatts or more available to lease anywhere in this market, and developers asking ComEd to connect new projects are being told 2032 and beyond, which is why they are now buying land based on where the power is rather than where they want to be. The real question is whether we shape our response or let it shape us. We are constantly told we have to pick. Jobs or the lake. Investment or affordable power bills. The artificial intelligence economy or the environment. I have never accepted that framing, and my entire plan for Chicago when I am mayor argues against it. This is not a “this or that.” It is both creating more jobs while protecting the lake and environment. Chicago has an answer, and it is sitting a few miles off Michigan Avenue at the bottom of the lake. Joe Holberg is a Chicago mayoral candidate. He was a math teacher on the West Side, then a small business owner and entrepreneur helping Chicagoans work toward financial goals. artigo.texto: Developers have legitimate business interests to protect. Minnesotans deserve a meaningful say in projects that could reshape their communities. In my hometown of Inver Grove Heights, a proposed data center has generated intense public debate. City Council meetings have been packed with concerned residents who feel left out of the process, and the city enacted a one-year moratorium before ultimately exempting the proposed project amid litigation. The tension is only increasing across Minnesota, and now we are throwing secrecy into the mix. Across our state, data-center developers and tech companies have asked local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements. In Pine Island, discussions surrounding the development now known as “Project Skyway,” which involves Google, began in late 2023. Residents were not let in on those discussions until September 2025, only months before city approval, leaving little time for public input on this major project. In Hermantown, an NDA prevented city officials from sharing information about Google’s proposed 1.8-million-square-foot data center until a Data Practices Act request finally brought the information to light. To be clear, businesses have legitimate reasons to seek confidentiality, but within reason. Revealing the identity of a prospective developer can fuel land speculation. And businesses considering multiple sites understandably do not want competitors learning every detail of their plans, but that still leaves a question: Why have NDAs become so prevalent in data-center development? “There should be 100% transparency with the public,” said Rep. Drew Roach (R-Farmington), co-author of HF 4077. Both Republican and DFL lawmakers have backed measures aimed at limiting their use. Interestingly, Minnesota law already protects legitimate business secrets. Under the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act, Minn. Stat. § 13.37, legitimate trade-secret information held by the government is already protected from public disclosure. The real problem here is that these NDAs go much further. They tend to prevent members of the community from participating in decisions about massive projects coming into their own neighborhoods until the process is already almost wrapped up. Whether that is the intention or not, it sure looks that way to the people being stonewalled. Developers may think these NDAs are helping them get projects built. But the secrecy may actually be doing the opposite, turning communities against them. That is never a good idea here in Minnesota. Imagine discovering that your local government had been discussing a big, intrusive development planned for your backyard for years, and officials agreed not to tell you about it until the process was already nearing the final signature. Even people who support data centers have to wonder: Why all the secrecy? What else are they hiding? It’s not a good look, and it is costing these developers what little support they may have had. Secrecy creates suspicion. Suspicion creates questions. Leave those questions unanswered long enough, and you may be surprised by how hard the people of the North Star State will push back. Some Minnesota lawmakers have gotten the message. HF 4077 would restrict local governments from signing NDAs that keep information about these development projects from the public. Of course, information already protected by state or federal law would remain protected. The bill has bipartisan authors, although some lawmakers remain hesitant about the extent of these restrictions. It’s a tough spot for lawmakers. They have to find a way to keep communities from being shut out of monumental decisions while also respecting free enterprise and rightful business interests. As tempting as it may be to target data centers, the same transparency rules should apply to every industry. They must protect developers from government overreach, and they must protect the people of these communities from being kept in the dark. The debate over where that balance should be drawn is just getting started. I am not calling for our state to be especially hostile toward data centers, but I understand why that hostility is growing. If developers believe in these projects, why hide the details? We have simple questions: How will they affect our water supply? What about our power grid? How much noise will they create? Too often, we aren’t getting answers. We as Minnesotans welcome entrepreneurship, but we also demand the opportunity to judge these projects on their merits. Transparency is all we are really asking for. AJ Gubash is a Minnesota legal professional working in nonprofit public-interest law, a graduate legal studies student at Hamline University, and a candidate for the Minnesota House of Representatives.

artigo.texto: Scale Microgrids, the corporation behind Nodaway County’s proposed data center project, is partnering with another company to operate the facility, though that end user is not yet known. While the Nodaway County Commission said the company is close to announcing the details of the partnership, not everyone is so sure this is true. Missouri allows data center developers in the state to receive tax exemptions on their facilities. Scott Wilson is an independent candidate running for Nodaway County presiding commissioner this November. He said he feels like Scale Microgrids is waiting for the commission to give the company a tax abatement before the public receives more information. Last week, Wilson took these concerns to a Nodaway Says No informational meeting in Graham, Missouri, which saw around 100 attendees. He said he feels apprehensive about how a hyperscale data center could affect environmental safety and the local ecosystem. “There’s a lot of different ways that people talk about it, and a lot of the people, the citizens, have had to try to prove to the commissioners that the things that are being said are actually true, and I don’t know that that’s a 100% fair way to do it,” Wilson said. “It would seem more like that data center developer and the commissioners would have to prove to the citizens that it is safe, not the citizens having to prove to them that it’s not safe.” He said he has heard many people talk about the impact data centers have on livestock due to the sound pollution it causes. Particularly, he heard it can reduce reproduction and increase stillbirths in cattle populations. Cows are not the only animals at risk. Horses, sheep — and even insects — are sensitive to sound. “They’ve talked about the bees, and they communicate with sound, and they can’t hear this,” Wilson said. “Someone mentioned just the other day, it’s like being at a loud party, and they can’t figure out what’s going on, so they can’t even get back to their hives, and it could drive the wildlife out of that area,” Wilson said. Nodaway County, he said, has a lot of land that is tilled up and farmed. He said adding a data center into such an agriculture region feels invasive — both to people and animals. “They talk about a heat dome…I think someone said it could raise the temperature within six miles of 16 degrees, like, average four to 16 degrees, just because of the massive amounts of concrete and all the cooling systems,” Wilson said. Another major concern for many residents is water. Scale Microgrids will need at least 1.5 million gallons of water to operate its facility, but not all residents see how it is feasible. “Of course, the river, if they suck too much water, they’re going to run the river lower than it already is at times,” Wilson said. The water Scale Microgrids uses would routinely filter through the 102 River every three years. However, many data centers add synthetic compounds — known as forever chemicals — into their water supplies. These can take hundreds or thousands of years to break down, and they are harmful to the ecosystem, according to the World Economic Forum. The Missourian reached out to the Nodaway County Public Water Supply District No. 1, which would supply water to the data center, and received a message in response. “When the project particulars are agreed to by all entities public and private maybe we could give a story with background on the whole thing,” the message said. “However since the district is in the middle of contract negotiations with suppliers and customers, we really say can’t speak to much.” Along with water stress and rising temperatures, emitted light from the facility can also be an issue, as it can disturb humans and confuse animals. People living within a half-mile of Scale Microgrids’ project, called White Cloud Acres, may be most heavily affected by the light. “They say that the critters need to have time at night to where they know it’s night and day, and if the lights are on all the time, it bothers them, but some of this can be mitigated,” Wilson said. “They can have different dimming type of lights or different ways to help all these problems along the way, but again, all that costs more for the developer, and it makes the return on investment less, but that really shouldn’t be our problem.” He said officials at hand should strive to make the best decision possible regardless of money. “I believe that the commissioners should strive to make this as safe as possible, and it doesn’t really matter what the developer’s return on investment is,” Wilson said. “If it doesn’t work out for them, it just doesn’t work out.”

artigo.texto: [Photo: MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND CLIMATE CHANGE/ FACEBOOK] Fiji has launched a five-year $5.2 million plan aimed at preparing the country to enter international carbon markets by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan was launched yesterday during the opening of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan sets out the regulatory, technical and institutional systems Fiji needs before its first international carbon trade under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. It focuses on sectors including energy, transport, agriculture, waste and forestry, with strong emphasis on forests, mangroves, wetlands and other nature-based solutions. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu says carbon markets must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners.” The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre, with provisions for fair benefit-sharing, social and environmental safeguards and Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Fiji will also establish a Fijian Transactional Registry and a National Carbon Market Inter-Agency Technical Working Group to manage and track carbon market activities. The Government will use the plan to engage development partners, donors and potential carbon buyers to secure the finance and technical support needed for implementation. Conservation International says the plan could help Fiji attract high-integrity carbon finance while protecting ecosystems and supporting resilient livelihoods.

artigo.texto: Tighter data center rules on Fort Smith Board agenda The Fort Smith Board of Directors is set to vote Tuesday (Oct. 6) on an ordinance that would give the city more oversight of any planned data center development within the city. The ordinance, if approved, also would require more information from utilities about energy availability and potential energy load. Board members on Aug. 11 asked city staff to craft new rules or amend existing rules around water use, zoning and other areas to discourage data center construction in the city and the metro. According to the city, there are no known data centers being considered in the Fort Smith metro. Tim Allen, president and CEO of the Fort Smith Regional Chamber of Commerce, said chamber staff are ânot actively working a data center project.â There are five large announced data center projects in the state. The facilities are either planned or in some stage of construction in Clarksville, Conway, Little Rock, Pulaski County, and West Memphis. The proposed ordinance the board will consider Tuesday would require a development plan review by the Planning Commission and then full board approval of a data center project in the cityâs industrial zoning districts. The ordinance also would require an eight-foot opaque wall surrounding the property, 500 feet setbacks from each property line, and âletters from applicable public utilities regarding capacity and proposed load.â The cityâs Planning Commission voted unanimously for the proposed ordinance, according to a memo from Deputy City Administrator Maggie Rice. The ordinance does not include any language about water rates and access to the cityâs regional water system. At the Aug. 11 board study session, Director Kevin Settle suggested the city consider significantly higher water rates for data centers. Settle also said he would support language that gives the board authority over certain water connections outside city limits. âTo me, the water, Iâve said many times, is our commodity, and we should be able to choose what is the price for it,â Settle said at the Aug. 11 meeting. BACKGROUND Arkansas officials, with support from Gov. Sarah Sanders, have restricted local government actions on data centers. Arkansas Act 851 of 2023 prevents local governments from banning data center development. The law does not prevent local governments from adopting rules that create delays or significant restrictions with data center projects. The cities of Fayetteville and Little Rock have approved more stringent data center development rules. The development of data centers nationwide and in Arkansas has become controversial, with pushback often resulting from local grassroots efforts. Concerns include the potential for massive water use, rising utility rates, excessive noise, and groundwater pollution. The state of New York recently implemented a one-year moratorium on data center construction. According to reporting from CNBC and other outlets, more than 500 local governments nationwide have enacted bans, moratoriums, and other restrictions on data centers. âData centers sit at the intersection of economic development, energy policy and state fiscal health,â according to a report from the National Conference of State Legislatures. âWhile 38 states currently offer dedicated tax incentives to attract data centers, lawmakers across the country are working to balance economic development priorities with sustainable development goals. These capital-intensive projects can generate significant tax revenue for localities, yet data centers also contribute to surging energy demand across the country.â

artigo.texto: Battery Energy Storage Trends: Shorter PPAs and Market Growth ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: Battery energy storage developers are pushing for shorter PPA tenures, while the MNRE updated ALMM List-II to 37,394 MW and Chhattisgarh approved a ₹2.98/kWh tariff for a 125 MW/500 MWh BESS project. - Why it matters: Shorter, more flexible PPAs are essential for the bankability of BESS projects, which currently face rigid 20-25 year contract structures similar to solar and wind. - Watch: Further regulatory shifts regarding transmission charges for open access customers and the progress of upcoming pumped hydro and solar tenders. Background and Context The Indian energy storage market is undergoing a significant evolution as stakeholders call for more flexible contractual frameworks. While solar and wind projects have traditionally relied on 20-25-year Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), battery energy storage developers are increasingly advocating for shorter tenures to better align with the operational lifecycle of battery technology. This shift is critical as the country integrates larger volumes of variable renewable energy into the grid. Key Details Regulatory activity remains high across the sector. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) has revised its standardized nomenclature for solar cells under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II. The 11th revision has expanded the total enlisted capacity to 37,394 MW, mandating that module model numbers clearly identify the country of origin for both cells and modules. In the storage segment, the Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission (CSERC) has set a benchmark by adopting a tariff of ₹2.98 (~$0.031)/kWh for a 125 MW/500 MWh standalone battery energy storage system. Meanwhile, in Karnataka, Sumitomo Corporation has committed to investing in a 500 MW solar and wind project with a co-located 200 MWh BESS, being developed by Hero Future Energies in Bidar. Other notable developments include the rejection of MP Power Transmission Company’s petition on transmission charges by the Madhya Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission, and NTPC Renewable Energy’s call for bids for interstate transmission system-connected pumped hydro projects. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the push for flexible PPAs signals a maturing market where risk-sharing is becoming more sophisticated. The standardization of ALMM nomenclature provides greater transparency in the supply chain, which is vital for procurement planning. Furthermore, the adoption of competitive tariffs for BESS projects suggests that storage is becoming increasingly cost-competitive, opening new avenues for large-scale infrastructure projects. What Happens Next The industry is closely watching the outcome of the NTPC Renewable Energy pumped hydro tender, with bids due by November 3, 2026. As the India renewable energy sector continues to scale, the interplay between regulatory policy, such as the ALMM updates, and commercial innovations in PPA structures will define the next phase of growth for developers and EPC firms alike.

artigo.texto: Director-General, National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi, has called for a stronger carb on verification to enhance the credibility and integrity of Nigeria’s carbon market. Majekodunmi, who was represented by Mr Michael Ivenso, Director, Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, NCCC, made the call at an NCCC/European Union Climate Dialogues High-Level Roundtable on carbon markets in Abuja on Tuesday. Majekodunmi said Nigeria must turn its climate ambition into tangible, bankable and verifiable action to support sustainable economic growth and attract climate finance. She said Nigeria’s National Carbon Markets Framework had established the institutional and regulatory architecture required to govern carbon activities, including Article 6 cooperation, voluntary markets and national oversight. She said the NCCC was operationalising a unified national carbon registry while promoting digital Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) through remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, geospatial data and distributed ledger technologies to enhance accuracy. The director-general called for stronger collaboration among government agencies, private developers, financial institutions, development partners, civil society and academia to establish bankable projects and strengthen local verification capacity. Majekodunmi said priorities included finalising carbon market regulations, publishing sector-specific MRV guidelines and establishing local capacity-building hubs to position Nigeria as a destination for high-integrity carbon investments. Jop Weterings, Policy Professional and Team member at the DG CLIMA’s Task Force on International Carbon Pricing and Markets, European Commission, said the EU adopted legally binding target to cut emissions 40 per cent by 2040. Weterings said the target includes at least 85 per cent domestic reductions and up to five per cent high-quality international carbon credits under Article 6, from 2036. He said quality, transparency and robust accounting were essential to scaling carbon markets, and urged stronger methodologies, fair transactions, equitable benefit-sharing and national strategies protecting domestic climate priorities. Weterings said that EU support for carbon pricing and international markets was increasing, while cooperation with Nigeria offered opportunities to operationalise its framework and strengthen high-integrity markets. Mrs Halima Bawa-Bwari, Director of Forestry, Ministry of Environment, urged Nigeria to strengthen forest inventories, monitoring systems, remote sensing, satellite technology and artificial intelligence for carbon monitoring. Bawa-Bwari said satellite information should complement ground measurements and field verification, while forestry institutions require stronger capacity to collect, manage and utilise reliable data for carbon markets. She called for coordinated, transparent and independently verifiable forest-carbon data, warning against parallel systems and stressing clear responsibilities, accountability, technical credibility and stakeholder partnership for high-integrity markets. Ms Yolanda Jose, Head, Green and Digital Economy, EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, said that credible carbon markets require robust systems ensuring transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. Jose said Nigeria’s adoption of its National Carbon Markets Framework established a structured legal and institutional sytem for domestic and international carbon trading under relevant climate agreements. She said the EU Climate Dialogues roundtable would align on operationalising Nigeria’s framework, strengthen MRV practices, mobilise investment and support Nigeria’s low-carbon development pathway. Mr Huzi Mshelia, Country Facilitator, Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) partnership said robust MRV systems were essential for building trust and investor confidence, welcoming the dialogue’s convergence of stakeholders to establish common national standards and understanding. He stressed partnership among NCCC, Finance, Budget and National Planning institutions, ensuring climate actions align with development priorities, while technical support strengthens Nigeria’s MRV system globally.

artigo.texto: The e SKY, Suzuki’s first electric kei car, is expected to undercut BYD’s Racco as Japan’s cheapest mini EV, starting at around $13,500. Suzuki launches its first mini EV using BYD batteries Suzuki is entering Japan’s competitive electric mini car segment with the e SKY set to launch on November 16. The e SKY will start at around 2.12 million yen, or about $13,500, according to Nikkei, making it the lowest-priced EV in its class. BYD currently holds the title with the Racco EV priced from 2.145 million yen ($13,600). Suzuki said the e SKY offers a WLTC driving range of up to 310 km (192 miles) and a “class-leading” AC energy consumption rating of 97 Wh/km. Suzuki developed a dedicated kei EV platform and electric drive system for the e SKY to optimize efficiency. Interestingly, Suzuki’s mini EV uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries supplied by BYD’s battery unit to cut costs. Government subsidies have yet to be announced, but if it qualifies for the same 568,000 yen subsidy as its commercial kei EV, the e-Every, the e SKY would cost about the same as the Spacia. The Spacia is Suzuki’s most popular gas-powered kei car. It starts at 1.53 million yen, or slightly under $10,000 in Japan. BYD’s cheapest Racco 200 model uses a 22.4 kWh LFP battery, providing a WLTC driving range of 210 km (130 miles). High-priced trims, including the Racco 300 Plus and Premium models, use a larger 35.84 kWh battery with a range of up to 320 km (199 miles). BYD said it was the first kei EV to offer over 300 km range. BYD’s Racco and the Suzuki e SKY will be more affordable and offer a longer driving range than the Nissan Sakura, which starts at ¥2,448,600 ($15,000). BYD aims to sell 10,000 Racco models by the end of 2026. In its first two weeks on the market, BYD’s mini EV secured 1,000 orders. On Monday, BYD Japan also celebrated reaching 10,000 domestic cumulative registrations.

artigo.texto: ROX Capital Launches Gulf Energy Storage Platform ROX Capital has launched a platform to develop utility-scale and commercial energy storage projects in Gulf. October 06, 2026. By EI News Network ROX Capital Group has launched the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform to develop utility-scale and commercial energy storage projects in the UAE and Oman, as the Gulf region expands its large-scale solar capacity. The UAE-based real assets investor and developer said that the platform will assess multiple energy storage technologies, including vanadium redox flow batteries, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and sodium-ion batteries. It will also evaluate long-duration energy storage technologies such as CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage. ROX said that it will partner with selected technology providers based on their track record in deploying large-scale storage projects, expertise in long-duration energy storage, financial and operational capabilities, and ownership or control of core technology intellectual property. The platform will prioritise technology providers offering bankable systems, established manufacturing capabilities, long-term technical support, performance guarantees and warranties, according to the company. ROX and its technology partners will participate in upcoming energy storage tenders in the UAE and Oman. The platform will also examine opportunities for local assembly and manufacturing in the region where commercially viable. Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group, said the Gulf’s growing deployment of large-scale solar projects was increasing the need for energy storage to make renewable power available after sunset and during periods of peak electricity demand. Antony said that no single storage technology would be able to address all energy storage requirements in the region. The platform will therefore seek to match different technologies with the specific requirements of individual projects while also exploring opportunities for local manufacturing. ROX said that lithium-ion batteries will remain an important part of the Gulf’s energy storage mix, but regional conditions could create demand for a wider range of technologies. High summer temperatures in the Gulf can increase cooling requirements for battery systems, while power systems with a high share of solar generation require longer-duration storage to supply electricity after sunset. Against this backdrop, ROX said that technologies including vanadium flow batteries, CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage and thermal storage could complement lithium-ion systems in the Gulf market. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Voters in eight states have faced, or are soon to face, local ballot measures over data center development, as the infrastructure powering AI becomes an increasingly important issue in the midterm elections. According to the latest Ballotpedia count, at least 39 measures have been scheduled across California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin. Of those, 35 will be decided during the November 3 general election, while four were put to voters earlier in the year. The proposals range from outright bans on new data centers to advisory questions supporting the development. Others would require voter approval, introduce zoning protections or place conditions on companies receiving tax incentives. Data centers have become a major midterm issue because of concerns about their demands on electric grids, water supplies and land, as well as questions about tax breaks and whether residential customers could be left paying for infrastructure upgrades. At the same time, supporters argue that the facilities are essential to America’s AI ambitions and can generate construction work, investment and local tax revenue. The debate is affecting midterm races, even when data centers don’t appear directly on the ballot. Candidates are increasingly being judged on whether they do or don’t support tax incentives or projects, or whether they have or haven't called for restrictions and greater protections for ratepayers. In Ohio, for example, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has sought to make Republican Senator Jon Husted's role in the growth of the state's data center industry a central campaign issue, arguing that Husted was a leading advocate for the projects during his time as lieutenant governor. Brown told the Statehouse News Bureau in August: "I've made clear from the beginning that Jon Husted is the point man for these 230 or 240 new data centers in Ohio," labeling him “the face of data centers in Ohio.” During his time in office, Husted did publicly celebrate projects from technology companies including Google and Amazon Web Services, arguing that they would help establish Ohio as the "tech capital of the Midwest" and strengthen the state's role in the AI economy. More recently, however, Husted has emphasized consumer protections around data center growth, introducing the Ratepayer Protection Act, which seeks to ensure large electricity users such as data centers pay for the infrastructure needed to serve them rather than shifting costs onto households and small businesses. That evolution is reflected in Newsweek's AI Policy Scorecard, an interactive tool that evaluates where members of Congress stand on AI-related issues including regulation, data centers and energy, jobs and the economy, safety and privacy, and national security. Lawmakers are ranked from "AI Skeptic" to "AI Booster" based on their voting records, legislation, and public statements. While Brown continues to focus on Husted's previous support for bringing data centers to Ohio, the scorecard currently categorizes Husted as a "Lean Skeptic" on data centers and energy, indicating a more cautious approach to large-scale expansion and its impact on communities and utility customers than lawmakers classified as "boosters." Here are all 39 measures tracked by Ballotpedia, including the 35 scheduled for November and four decided earlier in 2026. California Voters in Alhambra will settle on a measure that would prohibit data centers within the city. It’s one of the most straightforward measures on the November ballot, as it simply asks residents whether the facilities should be banned rather than regulated through additional conditions. A second California measure has already been decided. In June, 88 percent of voters in Monterey Park supported a policy that amended the city’s land-use framework to prohibit data centers. Florida In Edgewater, voters will consider an amendment prohibiting new data centers from being approved, built, expanded, or operated within the city. The measure goes beyond preventing new projects by also addressing the expansion and operation of data center facilities, giving voters a broader choice over how they want the industry to operate within the community going forward. Illinois Seven measures are being put before Illinois voters, although several are advisory and would communicate residents’ preferences rather than automatically changing local law. In Bloomington, voters will determine whether to advise the city to impose a moratorium on the construction of large-scale data centers. Four measures are concentrated in Madison County. Voters in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki, and Venice will be asked whether officials should permit the construction and operation of new data centers. In Joliet, in Will County, voters will consider an advisory question asking whether the city should approve the construction of AI data centers. Meanwhile, voters in Morgan County will decide whether to advise county officials to impose restrictions on the construction and operation of data centers. Together, the Illinois measures show that not every data center vote is designed to block development: Five ask whether officials should support or permit projects, while two seek a moratorium or additional restrictions. Kansas Three Kansas cities will vote on proposed data center prohibitions. In El Dorado, an initiative would prohibit the construction of “high-impact” data centers, as well as certain Type 2 and Type 3 battery energy storage systems. Voters in Emporia will also consider a measure prohibiting the construction of high-impact data centers within the city. In Ottawa, the proposed ban is tied to electricity consumption. It would prohibit data centers using more than 25 megawatts of power, a threshold also used by several measures in Ohio. artigo.texto: Canadian Solar Inc. (NASDAQ:CSIQ) said its energy storage subsidiary, e-STORAGE, has signed an agreement to supply and commission a 100 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system for OX2's Muswellbrook Solar Farm and Battery project in New South Wales, Australia. The system will use e-STORAGE's SolBank 3.0 battery containers alongside Power Conversion Systems, plant controls and the company's EQ-S Energy Management System. e-STORAGE will also provide a hybrid power plant controller to coordinate the battery storage system with the co-located solar farm. The company will be responsible for overall system integration and commissioning. Shipments Scheduled to Begin in Third Quarter of 2027 Shipments for the project are scheduled to start in the third quarter of 2027, with commercial operations targeted for the third quarter of 2028. Canadian Solar said the battery cells and SolBank system will be manufactured at its own facilities. The agreement also includes a 20-year long-term service arrangement covering hardware, software and system performance. Project Located at Former Coal Mine Site The Muswellbrook project is located approximately 2.5 kilometres east of Muswellbrook on land at a former coal mine within the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. Once operational, the battery system will support a long-term hybrid power purchase agreement that OX2 has signed for the project. "Australia's energy transition is being decided in regions like the Hunter, where storage now has to carry the load that retiring coal once did. We control this project from the cell through to our own energy management software and 20 years of service, which means OX2 has one partner accountable for how the system performs over its full life," said Jeff Roy, President of e-STORAGE. artigo.texto: DENR sets forest carbon market regulatory foundations Nicer called for stronger global guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) recently disclosed that the Philippines has already established the regulatory foundations of a credible forest carbon market by issuing two major policy instruments designed to directly address private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways. Atty. Daniel Darius M. Nicer, DENR assistant secretary for integrated management system and information systems, spoke at the High-Level Roundtable convened in the sidelines of 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York last week, and declared that these regulatory milestones position the country to attract high-integrity private investments in nature-based carbon projects. Addressing international ministers, climate envoys and business executives at the session titled “Shaping High-Integrity Carbon Markets,” Nicer emphasized that corporate buyers require predictability and environmental rigor before deploying capital at scale. “To date, the Philippines, through its Department of Environment and Natural Resources, issued two major policy instruments that establish the foundations of a credible forest carbon market directly addressing private sector expectations for clear rules, credible safeguards, and transparent project pathways,” he said during the meeting convened by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development at Climate Week NYC. The first policy instrument is the adoption of the Philippines’ Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market Roadmap (2026 to 2030). The strategic framework sets out national direction for policy development, measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) systems, data management, and registry readiness — key elements corporate investors evaluate when assessing market reliability. The second instrument is the national guidelines for the establishment, registration and monitoring of voluntary forest carbon credit projects. These rules enforce environmental integrity, Free, Prior and Informed Consent compliance, and guaranteed community benefit-sharing, while mandating transparent project registration to significantly reduce reputational and delivery risks for corporate buyers. “For the Philippines, carbon markets — both voluntary and compliance pathways — are central to our strategy for accelerating mitigation and unlocking climate finance,” Nicer said. “But for markets to function, the private sector needs clarity, predictability, and confidence that the credits they purchase are real, additional, and backed by strong governance.” Beyond forestry, Nicer highlighted broader national carbon governance efforts, including the Department of Energy’s guidelines for renewable energy projects, the overarching Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework, and the rollout of the Philippine National Carbon Registry to ensure full accounting traceability and prevent double counting. He added that domestic policies are aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement through bilateral partnerships, such as the Implementation Agreement with Singapore and the Joint Crediting Mechanism with Japan. Looking ahead to the COP31 climate summit, he called for stronger global guidance on market infrastructure and supply-side integrity for forest and blue carbon ecosystems. “High-integrity markets should not only accelerate global ambition, but also deliver real, measurable mitigation outcomes that directly benefit and reach the communities, ecosystems, and sectors that need them most,” Nicer said.
