artigo.texto: A WEG prepara uma expansão industrial de US$ 165 milhões na América do Norte, com novas estruturas no México e nos Estados Unidos e uma meta de multiplicar por cinco sua capacidade global de geradores até 2030. A brasileira WEG anunciou um plano de investimento de US$ 165 milhões, aproximadamente R$ 840 milhões pela conversão divulgada pela própria companhia, para ampliar a fabricação de geradores na América do Norte. O projeto será executado em duas fases e pretende elevar a capacidade global da empresa dos atuais 10 para cerca de 50 geradores por dia, avanço relacionado ao aumento da demanda por infraestrutura crítica nos Estados Unidos, especialmente para data centers. Anunciada em 28 de setembro de 2026, a expansão combina uma nova operação no México e a construção de outras duas instalações industriais na América do Norte. A primeira etapa deverá entrar em operação já no segundo trimestre de 2027, enquanto a segunda está prevista para ser concluída até 2030. - Gigante chinesa prepara fábrica de R$ 200 milhões em Minas Gerais para dobrar produção de cabos ópticos - Brasil pode perder empregos e valor da sucata porque Repetro facilita operação de plataformas, mas deixa desmantelamento e reciclagem fora da mesma lógica tributária - Fábrica de semicondutores no RS recebe R$ 84,86 milhões para produzir memórias avançadas usadas em smartphones e inteligência artificial - Após 64 anos no Rio, Limppano investe R$ 50 milhões para ampliar fábrica, comprar novas áreas e modernizar produção O investimento ocorre enquanto grandes centros de processamento de dados ampliam a demanda por equipamentos capazes de sustentar operações que não podem ficar sem eletricidade. No caso da WEG, os geradores são destinados a aplicações críticas e podem integrar sistemas de energia de emergência e continuidade de fornecimento. O próprio presidente da companhia, Alberto Kuba, relacionou recentemente o movimento à aceleração desse mercado. Em entrevista à Exame, o executivo afirmou que a empresa “não imaginávamos que teria esse boom”, ao comentar o ritmo da demanda associada aos data centers. México receberá primeira etapa da expansão A expansão começará no México. Dos US$ 165 milhões previstos, US$ 24 milhões serão destinados à compra e adaptação de um prédio industrial localizado ao lado do atual Parque Industrial de Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula. A nova estrutura será voltada à montagem de geradores e deverá começar a operar no segundo trimestre de 2027. A escolha do local aproveita uma presença industrial que a WEG já mantém no município mexicano. Em janeiro de 2025, a companhia havia inaugurado a ampliação de uma fábrica de produtos de automação em Atotonilco de Tula, com aproximadamente 4,9 mil metros quadrados de área construída. A estrutura passou a concentrar atividades de produção, engenharia, projetos de painéis e treinamento. Segunda fase concentra US$ 141 milhões No novo projeto de geradores, porém, a maior parte dos recursos ficará para a segunda fase. A WEG prevê desembolsar US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais em território norte-americano. Até o anúncio, a empresa ainda não havia definido publicamente onde essas duas unidades serão construídas. Essa segunda etapa terá uma configuração mais verticalizada. Em vez de concentrar a operação apenas na montagem, as novas fábricas deverão incorporar processos como fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças. Segundo a WEG, a internalização dessas etapas busca aumentar a eficiência operacional e a competitividade da produção. O projeto também reduz a quantidade de processos industriais que precisam ser executados fora da nova estrutura antes da montagem final dos equipamentos. A diferença de escala entre as duas fases aparece também na distribuição dos investimentos. Os US$ 141 milhões previstos para a segunda etapa representam aproximadamente 85% dos US$ 165 milhões anunciados para todo o programa de expansão. Capacidade global pode saltar de 10 para 50 geradores por dia Quando o projeto estiver concluído, a mudança deverá ser significativa na capacidade industrial da companhia. Hoje, a WEG informa capacidade global de aproximadamente 10 geradores por dia. Até 2030, a previsão é alcançar cerca de 50 unidades diárias, considerando as fábricas localizadas no México, Estados Unidos, Brasil e China. Isso representa uma capacidade cinco vezes maior que a atual. O número, contudo, deve ser entendido como capacidade global de fabricação prevista depois da conclusão da expansão, e não como produção efetivamente realizada hoje ou como volume destinado exclusivamente aos data centers. A WEG também não informou que todos os 50 geradores diários serão produzidos nas novas instalações da América do Norte. A projeção considera o conjunto das operações da companhia nos quatro países citados. Expansão está ligada ao negócio incorporado com a Marathon O movimento industrial está ligado à Marathon, marca incorporada ao portfólio da WEG após uma aquisição anunciada em setembro de 2023. Na ocasião, a companhia brasileira fechou a compra dos negócios de motores elétricos industriais e geradores da Regal Rexnord por US$ 400 milhões, operação que envolveu as marcas Marathon, Cemp e Rotor. A transação trouxe para a WEG aproximadamente 2.800 funcionários e dez fábricas distribuídas por sete países: Estados Unidos, México, China, Índia, Itália, Países Baixos e Canadá. Também foram incorporadas estruturas comerciais em outros mercados. Três anos depois, a companhia associa diretamente os novos US$ 165 milhões ao crescimento desses negócios. João Paulo Gualberto da Silva, vice-presidente da Unidade de Energia da WEG, afirmou no anúncio que a expansão aumenta a capacidade produtiva e reforça a integração das operações incorporadas com a Marathon. artigo.texto: What does the data say about data centers? People everywhere are talking about data centers, the high-tech facilities that house our nations growing digital infrastructure. Illinois is a Top 10 state for data centers, with a history dating all the way back to the 1970s, initially as a central repository to meet the technology needs of state agencies. More recently, however, data centers have become the foundation of a global technology race in the private sector, housing large computer servers, storage, and networking equipment necessary to support cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI). In Illinois, they comprise 7% of total electricity demand (and climbing). Many rely on water for cooling. And new data centers often come seemingly out-of-nowhere, as major technology companies use of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with elected officials instead of committing to public transparency. All of which has contributed to a public backlash against construction of these facilities that is playing out in statehouses and electoral campaigns around the country. Developments have been canceled or postponed, and Gov. JB Pritzker paused Illinois tax exemption for data centers. But data centers now are a fixture of the modern economy. Understanding their costs and benefits and identifying the guardrails needed to mitigate risk to our communities is of paramount importance. It is with these factors in mind that the Illinois Economic Policy Institute and the Project for Middle Class Renewal at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign recently undertook the most robust analysis of Illinois data centers to date. Specifically, we looked at 75 completed and ongoing projects and related reports culled from state, county, and industry data, and integrated industry-standard economic modeling to forecast potential impacts of $57 billion in planned data center projects across our state over the next decade. Here’s what we found. First, data centers mean jobs. More than 120,000 of them over the next 10 years, to be exact. About a third of these will be in skilled construction occupations or IT, engineering, and operations jobs that pay well into the six figures, and the other two-thirds in the supply chain or as a result of related increases in consumer spending across the economy. This investment will grow the Illinois economy by $5 billion a year during the construction phase, and about $2 billion per year thereafter. The facilities would also mean $300 million in new property tax revenue going to local communities each year nearly two-thirds of which will support public schools. When it comes to protecting communities from potential costs, the picture is more complex. By 2035, new data centers could use the same electricity as 4.5 million Illinois homes. Without any sort of requirements that data centers produce or otherwise offset their power demands, this would increase average Illinois household electric bills by $12 per month. Water resources can also be strained, unless new data centers use the air-cooling or closed-loop systems which recycle water instead of constantly drawing on new resources that are becoming commonplace. In both cases, there are tools available to policymakers to mitigate the risk and ensure responsible development of data centers. First, they can be required to pay for 100% of their energy, transmission, and interconnection costs and to use closed-loop or air-cooling systems to reduce water usage. The currently suspended sales tax exemption could be reformed to promote stronger energy and environmental standards, rewarding only those facilities that install Illinois-based clean energy. New data centers can be required to have battery storage. And policymakers can improve public disclosure around energy usage, water usage, and contact with elected officials. Even though the data on data centers shows they can be a net positive for our economy and our communities, there is a trust deficit. With commonsense guardrails, Illinois can modernize our energy system, protect workers and ratepayers, and improve transparency around an industry that too many people believe has been operating in the dark. Frank Manzo IV, MPP is an economist at the nonpartisan Illinois Economic Policy Institute.

artigo.texto: By PACNEWS Fiji has launched a FJD$5.2 million (US$2.6 million) five-year plan to develop its carbon market and position the country to undertake its first international carbon trade by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan 2026–2030 was launched by the Government on the opening day of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan, developed by the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change in collaboration with the Ministry of Forestry and Conservation International, sets out the systems and frameworks Fiji needs to participate in international carbon markets. Carbon markets allow verified reductions in greenhouse gas emissions to be traded, creating opportunities for Fiji to attract climate finance for projects that reduce emissions and protect natural ecosystems. The Government said the plan could help attract new investment into renewable energy, sustainable forestry, waste management and the protection of forests, mangroves and other ecosystems. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu said Fiji’s carbon market must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners,” Bulitavu said. The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre of Fiji’s carbon market development, with a focus on fair benefit-sharing, safeguards and resilient livelihoods. The Government said the framework would prepare Fiji to access emerging sources of climate finance while ensuring communities and resource owners share in the benefits. It has also called on development partners to support implementation of the plan. The plan forms part of Fiji’s broader efforts to mobilise climate finance and strengthen its capacity to respond to climate change while protecting the country’s natural ecosystems.

artigo.texto: A Motorola anunciou nesta terça-feira (6) o lançamento do novo Moto G37 para o mercado brasileiro, focado em apresentar características mais básicas ao mercado de entrada. O novo aparelho da companhia traz um conjunto de câmeras suficiente, com principal de 50 MP, e bateria para 43 horas, mas pouca memória RAM. Com características mais básicas, o Moto G37 aposta em uma tela HD+ e tamanho de 6,7 polegadas. O painel é simples, de LCD, com taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho máximo de 1.050 nits, mas sem grandes funcionalidades além da profundidade de cores em 8-bits. Em termos de bateria, a fabricante explica que a capacidade do componente é de 5.200 mAh, proporcionando uma autonomia de 43 horas. Vale notar que no site estrangeiro da companhia esse número vai para 63 horas. Já o carregador é padrão de 20W. Câmera de 50 MP e chip MediaTek Por ser um produto bem inclinado ao mercado de dispositivos de entrada, o Moto G37 possui um conjunto traseiro de câmeras bem básico, mas aparentemente suficiente. Esse sensor principal trabalha com resolução de 50 megapixels, mas acompanha um sensor de ambiente dois em um. - Quando o assunto são as especificações internas desse celular, o chip escolhido pela Motorola é o Dimensity 6300, da MediaTek; - A plataforma foi lançada no fim de 2024, fabricada em um processo de 6 nanômetros e compatível com a rede 5G; - A parte mais complicada é o fato de esse aparelho ter somente 4 GB de memória RAM, embora a marca cite os 8 GB de memória virtual; - Além disso, há opções de 64 GB ou 128 GB para o armazenamento interno, mas há compatibilidade com cartão microSD para expansão de até 1 TB; - O modelo possui certificação militar MIL-STD 810H e proteção IP64 contra respingos d’água e poeira; - As possibilidades de gravação incluem resolução 2K a 30 fps na frontal e traseira; - Por ser um modelo de entrada, a conexão de 3,5 mm para fone de ouvido está disponível; - Tecnologias como o Gemini e o Circule Para Pesquisar são integradas ao aparelho. O novo Motorola Moto G37 já pode ser oficialmente adquirido no mercado brasileiro, através do site da fabricante, pelo preço de R$ 899 na versão de 64 GB e R$ 1.079 na variante de 128 GB. É possível adquirir o produto nas cores grafite, azul turquesa, azul náutico e rosa com certificação Pantone. Ficha técnica - Tela: LCD de 6,67 polegadas, resolução HD+ (1604 x 720), taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho de até 1.050 nits - Processador: MediaTek Dimensity 6300 (octa-core de até 2,4 GHz, 6 nm) - Memória RAM: 4 GB LPDDR4X (expansível via RAM Boost) - Armazenamento interno: 128 GB (expansível via cartão microSD de até 1 TB) - Câmeras traseiras: 50 MP (f/1.8, PDAF, Quad Pixel) e sensor 2 em 1 de luz ambiente e detecção de cintilação - Câmera frontal: 8 MP (f/2.0) - Gravação de vídeo: até 2K a 30 fps (frontal e traseira) - Bateria: 5.200 mAh com carregamento TurboPower de 20 W e recarga reversa com fio de 6 W - Sistema operacional: Android 16 - Construção e durabilidade: vidro frontal Gorilla Glass 7i, proteção IP64 contra poeira e respingos d’água, e certificação militar MIL-STD-810H - Áudio: alto-falantes estéreo com Dolby Atmos e entrada P2 (3,5 mm) para fone de ouvido - Conectividade: 5G, Wi-Fi dual-band (2,4 GHz e 5 GHz), Bluetooth 5.4, NFC e porta USB-C 2.0 - Segurança: leitor de digitais na lateral e reconhecimento facial - Dimensões e peso: 166,23 x 76,50 x 7,85 mm; 191 g Compre o Moto G37 - Moto G37 de 128GB por R$ 1.079,10 no site da Motorola - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 899,10 no Magazine Luiza - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 999,00 na Amazon - Moto G37 de 64GB por R$ 999,00 no Mercado Livre Por falar em produtos, a Motorola lançou os novos Moto Watch Ultra recentemente no Brasil com especificações bem robustas. artigo.texto: Cheyenne and Arapaho tribal citizens voted Saturday to impose a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands. During the tribal meeting, the floor was opened for anyone to speak about the topic. The primary concerns related to environmental, economic and transparency issues. Key Takeaways - Cheyenne and Arapaho tribal citizens voted Saturday for a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands. - Of 351 votes cast, 261 supported the moratorium, 83 opposed it and seven abstained. - Tribal citizens raised concerns about water use, environmental effects, potential economic benefits and transparency surrounding future data center proposals. - Cheyenne and Arapaho Gov. Reggie Wassana said no data center agreement has been signed and said any potential project would undergo further study and community discussion. Environmental Concerns “We have a spiritual responsibility because we are Cheyenne and Arapaho people and our traditional values respect this water of life,” said Kyle Spotted Horse, a member of the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes. He brought up Mní Wičóni at Standing Rock, the location of a protest against an oil pipeline that crosses Sioux land in the Dakotas. In 2016, a vocal protest against the Dakota Access Pipe Line took place, creating the Mní Wičóni movement to protect water and tribal lands. Spotted Horse said a data center would require 300,000 gallons of water per day, adding up to 100 million gallons per year. RELATED: Oklahomans Gather In Downtown OKC In Support Of Standing Rock Sioux Tribe A group of Oklahomans gathered at downtown Oklahoma City’s Kerr Park to show support for the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe in their fight against the Dakota Access Pipeline. “Until we adjudicate our water rights, how do we move forward with such a massive amount of consumption of water?” Patrick Kincaid said. According to Oklahoma State University, water right adjudication is the process through which groups can establish who has ownership of which bodies of water. “You know what would be a dealbreaker for me is that through this whole process, there is 100% transparency. No NDAs and a full impact study, especially on our buffalo,” said another woman. “We’ve spent years building our herds. How will this affect our buffalo herd? And as good neighbors, what impact will this have on surrounding farms and farmland and animals? I want us to be informed all along the way.” Damon Dunbar raised the question of fracking and its comparable water usage to a potential data center. “They’re draining Canton Lake right now to feed Oklahoma City. That’s not funny, that’s very deadly. We’re not going to be having anything. We’re going to be looking like south Texas or the desert.” Another man was concerned about the effects of drought and further water usage on the community and environment. “I don’t get up and say much at these meetings, but this part is very important,” he finished, a sentiment echoed by another speaker. “Water is our way of life. If we don’t protect our lands, who’s going to? If we don’t stand up for our kids, who’s going to?” A woman said, supporting the moratorium. RELATED: How much water does AI really use? Governor’s Response Governor Wassanna responded to these concerns, saying a potential data center would use a closed loop system, challenging earlier estimates of 300,000 gallons of water per day being used. “The water usage has developed to where there’s little to none except filling it up because it’s a closed loop,” he said. Wassanna further clarified that data centers are now capable of using cooling coils which do not use as much water as previous facilities. “It won’t be 300,000 gallons a day. Actually, cities use more water on their golf courses than people would actually use probably for data centers.” Economic Concerns “I feel like it’s the old days of the old cattle barons, oil barons, people wanting to exploit our resources, snake oil salesmen,” Spotted Horse said of the economic impact of a potential data center. He questioned who would receive the profits from the facility. Governor’s Response “Data centers are huge profit making projects. They make over $1 billion a year. 20%, 30%, $200 million. Somebody told us the other day, ‘Reggie, we make $90 million a day.’ $90 million a day,” said Wassanna. “If you want to look at the tribe’s share, you look at elders, you look at per cap, you look at housing, renovations, all these things we talk about that we’re hurting. Food, gas, these things.” Wassanna further stressed that if a data center was built on tribal lands, those in the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes wouldn’t have to worry about financial issues. “You’d be comfortable, the most comfortable tribe around in western Oklahoma.” Transparency Concerns “We have a responsibility not only to ourselves and this water and Mother Earth, but we also have a responsibility to our community. How many have heard about Yukon voting out their mayor because he did an NDA? Kudos to them for doing that,” Spotted Horse said in reference to the recent recall motion against Yukon mayor Brian Pillmore in Aug. “How would they feel if we just ripped right behind their back in their backyard and did our own thing, potentially causing water pollution, air pollution, not to mention electrical grid cost impacts.” RELATED: Yukon certifies recall petition against Mayor Brian Pillmore “If we make this decision today, in 3 years, we’ll have a better idea of how this is going to impact our future, our children,” said a woman named Vera. The moratorium would halt any data center construction for three years. Governor’s Response “I just want to say something. Before, there was going to be community meetings. This resolution came up, but there was going to be community meetings. Nothing’s been signed, there is a feasibility study that was going to be done. The legislators all acknowledged it. We ain’t done nothing yet. This is up to you guys to say yes or no.” RELATED:

artigo.texto: I’ll admit that I’m the Computer Village Idiot when it comes to using technology like personal computers and smartphones; I still struggle. And I’m in over my head trying to figure out this whole AI (artificial intelligence) thing that some Anthropic research experts believe could ultimately destroy mankind. Are you thinking about artificial intelligence? AI is in the news everywhere these days, and the subject of AI data centers popping up in one’s town or city is enough to freak out most people. There are many unknowns about artificial intelligence, and we need to learn as much as we can about this new technology. Here in the Granite State, there are multiple traditional data centers, but they aren’t the same as AI data centers. There’s often confusion about the two, and unfortunately, AI has become the catch-all term for modern tech infrastructure. For instance, data center space is available for lease in Nashua Technology Park off Exit 1 near the NH/MA border. The campus offers dedicated data center space equipped with heavy-duty corporate infrastructure, but it lacks the capacity and available land for a huge hyperscale or large-scale AI build. And the same could be said for my city’s Millyard Technology Park in the historic district. The tech park leases general office space to companies of all sizes under one roof, featuring “software firms, various service businesses, more than one corporate headquarters, and a few computer hardware companies,” its website says. I know of no AI data center proposals in Nashua, and that’s good news to me. However, a warehouse-sized data center using 40 acres of land on Old Turnpike Road was proposed for the town of Nottingham last May. Residents were up in arms, blasting Granite State developer Tom Moulton. He later withdrew his application because of heavy community opposition. Nottingham residents recently voted overwhelmingly on a 12-month moratorium on any data center development within town limits. That enormous proposal wouldn’t sit well with most people. Massive data centers consume tons of energy, thereby placing a significant strain on water infrastructure and the power grid. These facilities are also seen as a threat to residents’ income, quality of life and the environment. In Bow, residents have come out fighting hard against Granite Shore Power, which owns the shuttered Merrimack Station. The owners had filed a request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to discuss connecting a 350-megawatt project to the regional power grid for a potential hyperscale AI data center. No data center development proposal has been submitted to the town yet, but that was enough to draw outraged locals to the Bow municipal building. Some of us also wonder about the harm AI could do to the journalism industry. Generative AI is considered a time-and-money-saving newsroom tool that can handle diverse data types like documents, videos and social media at speeds unmatched by traditional processing. But it could also eliminate jobs. However, AI has limitations and cannot replace human reporting, as Mike Reilley explained in an essay for the Red Line Project. Reilley is a University of Illinois Chicago digital journalism professor and an expert in artificial intelligence and data visualization within newsrooms. “Specifically, AI cannot: physically enter a courtroom or interview a defendant behind bars; cultivate trust with a whistleblower; brave the front lines of a war zone; provide the critical thinking, original reporting and smart editorial judgment that humans do.” Innovation should always be welcomed with responsibility. On that note, here’s to a free press!

artigo.texto: Trending VANDALIA, Ohio --- President Donald Trump defended data centers that power artificial intelligence projects but have become a contentious campaign issue nationwide, as he took his midterm tour to Ohio this weekend to insist his party will keep its majorities in Congress despite steep political headwinds. Trump took several minutes during his campaign rally in southwestern Ohio near Dayton late Saturday night to promote his administration's action on data centers, saying he was seeking to ensure they "benefit local communities" and praising Republican Sen. Jon Husted for an ill-fated attempt to push forward legislation on the issue. "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China," Trump said, repeating his defense of data centers that he had made before. The massive warehouse campuses generating energy for AI projects have become a toxic political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies. It's become especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centers to Ohio when he served as lieutenant governor. Trump is embarking on what he says will be a 32-day blitz ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, hitting the deep red states of Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama last week before pivoting to Ohio, a battleground state once again that's home to one of the top-tier Senate races this cycle. Husted -- who was appointed to fill the Senate vacancy left by now-Vice President JD Vance -- is running to win the seat outright. There is likely no path to a Senate majority for Democrats without flipping Ohio, where former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the Senate after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno two years ago. Polls show that race is extremely tight. Since last year, Democrats have listed Ohio, along with states such as North Carolina and Maine, as key races to win control of the Senate. And this past week, the head of the Senate GOP's campaign arm said Ohio is among 10 battleground races that are "within striking distance." "The good news for us is that Jon Husted is a closer," Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told reporters. "We're seeing the gap that was there between the two candidates, which was just a few points, now it is right at a dead-even race. So this is as tight as ticks, as we say in South Carolina." DATA CENTERS At his rallies, Trump has been trying to convince voters that the economy is better than they feel it is, even though polls show Americans are frustrated with the way he's handled it. The high cost of living, including gas prices elevated by Trump's war on Iran, is a top issue in the Dayton area, too. And just days before Trump's rally, nearly 1,400 people were laid off from a truck factory in nearby Springfield. "Your state is booming. Every -- I hate to say it -- every state is booming," Trump said Saturday. "They're all booming." Trump's rally comes as Republicans worry that Husted's campaign has failed to adequately catch fire with voters in the state. Brown and allied groups have hammered Husted for his data-centers role, and the NRSC has pinpointed it as a political vulnerability. The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats. "You got to remember, Sherrod Brown was for data centers, and Jon Husted is for data centers being responsible," Scott told reporters this week. "If a community doesn't want them, he doesn't want them either." But Trump has become one of data centers' most vocal proponents, shrugging aside voter concerns and arguing that the U.S. cannot cede advancements in AI to China. "Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio," Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump's visit. "Now, he's making Ohioans foot the bill." Brown's campaign also has hammered Husted for donations he's received from retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Husted has donated remaining Wexner contributions to an anti-human trafficking charity. There were several Epstein-themed signs outside the Vandalia school where the rally was being held, as more than a hundred protesters lined the road with a slew of anti-Trump and anti-Husted signs. But inside the school's gymnasium, the boisterous crowd -- decked out in red "Make America Great Again" hats and "Trump 47" jerseys -- greeted each Republican candidate enthusiastically as they awaited the president's arrival. From the stage, Husted said the state had been through "hard times," noting his dad had worked at a factory that closed down. But he said Republicans in the state had turned it around. "We now have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate we've ever had in the history of Ohio," he said. Meanwhile, in the governor's race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director. A wealthy biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate, Ramaswamy's star appeal among conservatives led to quick backing by Ohio Republicans and hopes of an easy victory in the Republican-dominated state. However, despite a massive fundraising lead and more than $12 million spent in campaign advertising, he is now locked in a close fight with Acton with weeks to go until Election Day. "I'm so grateful to this state and to this country for giving a kid like me opportunities that would not have been available to my family in any other country on planet earth," Ramaswamy said at the rally ahead of Trump's arrival, as he underscored the American dream for his Indian immigrant family.

artigo.texto: 2 min leitura Mercado Voluntário de Carbono alarga projetos florestais Duas novas metodologias juntam-se à de Novas Florestações, aumentando as oportunidades para projetos de sequestro de carbono em Portugal. Carbono azul e pradarias marinhas vão seguir-se, 06 Out 2026 - 07:45 2 min leitura O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passa a contar com três metodologias para projetos florestais, abrindo novas oportunidades à mobilização de investimento privado para o sequestro de carbono e a gestão sustentável da floresta. Foram aprovadas duas novas metodologias de carbono dedicadas à Reflorestação e à Gestão Florestal Melhorada, que se juntam à metodologia já existente para Novas Florestações. As novas metodologias permitem abranger um conjunto mais diversificado de intervenções florestais, reforçam o potencial de geração de créditos de carbono em Portugal e incentivam práticas de gestão sustentável com benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática. Ao alargar as metodologias disponíveis, reforçamos a credibilidade e a capacidade de crescimento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono e mobilizamos financiamento privado para projetos que contribuem simultaneamente para a neutralidade carbónica, a valorização do território e a resiliência das nossas florestas”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, numa nota enviada às redações. Atualmente, o MVC conta com dois projetos registados na tipologia de Novas Florestações e um terceiro projeto está em fase de validação inicial. Estão ainda disponíveis 977 créditos de carbono para venda, a plataforma conta com 29 utilizadores registados e existem 10 verificadores qualificados para assegurar a validação inicial e a verificação periódica dos projetos, segundo o ministério. “O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono está a ganhar escala e maturidade. Depois das metodologias florestais, estamos já a trabalhar em novas abordagens para valorizar o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, para colocar também os ecossistemas costeiros no centro da ação climática e da valorização do capital natural”, acrescenta a ministra.

artigo.texto: Battery energy storage is moving from a supporting role in the energy transition to one of its central pillars. IDTechEx puts figures on that shift in its newly updated report Batteries for Stationary Energy Storage 2027–2037, forecasting that the global lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) market will reach $135 billion by 2037, with cumulative installations exceeding 10.5 TWh worldwide. It traces this growth to the rising share of renewables in electricity grids, new demand from data centre build-out and a shift in policy from headline storage targets towards bankable revenue frameworks and more sophisticated routes to market. A rapid shift in battery demand Lithium-ion remains the dominant chemistry for stationary storage, supported by broad availability, falling costs and steady performance gains. Total lithium-ion battery demand continues to climb, but the application mix is changing quickly. Electric vehicles still account for the largest share of global demand, although their portion fell from 84 percent in 2023 to 78 percent in 2025, while the BESS share rose from 10 to 19 percent over the same period. Policy shifts in the EV market have contributed to this change, but the main driver is the faster growth of stationary storage as grids integrate more variable renewable generation and require greater flexibility. AI turns storage into a multi-revenue asset for industry Within lithium-ion, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) continues to extend its lead over nickel manganese cobalt (NMC), reflecting lower cost, longer cycle life and better thermal stability. Sodium-ion is also gaining ground as developers improve performance and cut production costs, but LFP is expected to remain the chemistry of choice for most BESS applications over the forecast period. Deployments triple in two years IDTechEx estimates that annual global Li-ion BESS deployments across grid-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential segments rose from 92 GWh in 2023 to 318 GWh in 2025, an increase of more than threefold. China accounted for 58 percent of 2025 deployments at 183 GWh, with the United States contributing 57 GWh, or 18 percent. China is likely to retain its lead over the coming decade, supported by intense domestic competition, growing grid flexibility requirements and expanding LFP cell and BESS manufacturing capacity. The US market, by contrast, is being reshaped by industrial policy aimed at reducing reliance on Chinese cells and systems. That policy is accelerating the localisation of the domestic supply chain, with several players expanding LFP cell and BESS manufacturing capacity in the country, while most Chinese suppliers have scaled back or exited the market. Beyond the two leaders, countries previously absent from the global top tier are now entering it at scale. Saudi Arabia emerged as the third-largest market in 2025, boosted by several gigawatt-hour-scale projects, and Chile also broke into the top ten. IDTechEx expects more countries to follow, with leading suppliers already securing projects of several hundred megawatt-hours up to gigawatt-hour scale in markets where deployment had previously been limited. Europe scales up through policy and procurement Europe is emerging as one of the most dynamic regions in the global BESS market, with the report covering Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Spain and Poland in detail. Two policy schemes stand out. The UK’s cap-and-floor framework for long-duration energy storage is designed to unlock projects that struggle to secure financing on merchant revenues alone, while Italy’s MACSE auction establishes a central procurement route for large-scale storage. Europe hits 100 GWh as utility-scale takes over the storage market Beyond these schemes, Germany continues to anchor Europe’s residential and commercial storage segments, and markets such as Bulgaria, Spain and Poland are moving quickly from early projects to structured pipelines. Together, these developments are shaping Europe into a region where storage deployment is increasingly underpinned by predictable revenue mechanisms rather than merchant exposure alone. Procurement, revenue models and bankability The same shift is under way well beyond Europe. Governments and system operators are moving beyond headline targets towards mechanisms that can carry large waves of BESS projects through tendering and commissioning. Examples include Australia’s Capacity Investment Scheme and the New South Wales Long-Term Energy Service Agreements, as well as state-backed tenders in the Middle East. Overstated battery availability puts investor returns at risk Project financing is also becoming more sophisticated. Revenue floors, capacity contracts, tolling agreements and stacked revenue models combining arbitrage, ancillary services and capacity payments are improving bankability and enabling a broader pipeline of projects to secure investment. In the residential segment, subsidies continue to play a decisive role, as shown by the strong uptake under Australia’s Cheaper Home Batteries Program. When such schemes are phased out, however, activity can drop quickly. Technology trends: larger cells, denser systems At the technology level, developers are increasingly launching containerised grid-scale systems built around higher-capacity cells, with a growing number of units rated at 6.5 MWh or more. Larger cells can improve system-level energy density by reducing the number of cells, interconnections and casings per megawatt-hour, allowing a greater share of the container to be occupied by active battery material. The approach also simplifies manufacturing and can lower project-level costs, as fewer units are needed for a given site capacity. Although energy density has traditionally mattered less for stationary storage than for EVs, it is becoming a point of differentiation. artigo.texto: MONTGOMERY, Ala. – The Alabama Public Service Commission unanimously adopted a procedure Tuesday allowing automatic approval of Alabama Power’s contracts with large load data centers if the commission fails to take a vote within 90 days of submission. Chief Administrative Law Judge Luke Bentley had recommended that the PSC adopt a policy requiring a vote on every large load data center contract but did not include a time window for a vote, which is standard for PSC procedures. Following legislation, the PSC defines large load data centers as facilities that require 150 megawatts or more of electricity and operate on one piece of land. Commissioners Chris Beeker and Jeremy Oden expressed concerns about contracts potentially falling through because of the PSC not acting in a timely manner. Oden called the automatic approval procedure a “consequence” for the PSC not voting. “I want the commission to vote, but then again, I understand if they do not vote, then it’s not on the company and it’s not on the data center. It’s really and truthfully back on the commission …” Oden said. “Saying, ‘Well, since we just didn’t bring it up and vote, it’s gone,’ I don’t think that’s a good move, I don’t think it’s a good economic presentation for the state if we do that.” Though she ultimately introduced an amendment setting up an automatic approval in the case of the PSC’s inaction, PSC President Cynthia Almond said she felt strongly that the commission should take a public vote on data centers because of the public’s concern about the massive facilities that power artificial intelligence. She included the 90-day window for voting in her amendment. “We should not follow the ‘deemed approved’ process that we’ve been following for a number of years,” Almond said. “The current (rate) FCR deals with industry that is one megawatt or greater, and we’re talking about industry now that is at least 150 megawatts, and those are some of our smaller data centers. So these are just to me different animals, and it should be a very public process that we go through.” Data centers previously fell under the general rate flexible contract rate docket – rate FCR – like all commercial and industrial customers with accounts of at least one megawatt. The rate FCR for data centers temporarily had a turnaround time of 45 days, up from the standard 10, while the commission established new procedures. Under Almond’s amendment, the commission is supposed to vote on the contracts within 90 days. If it doesn’t, the contract will automatically be approved. The new procedure does not mandate a public hearing about proposed data center contracts. Tuesday’s vote came after a monthslong general proceeding seeking input from members of the public about how the commission should evaluate Alabama Power’s contracts with data centers. Legislation requiring data centers to pay for the additional electricity they need and refining the longstanding public interest standard sparked the proceeding. Nineteen people and organizations submitted initial comments in the proceeding, while 10 offered reply comments, Bentley said. The newly approved procedure for evaluating contracts also establishes specific reporting requirements for Alabama Power and its data center customers, including a public petition naming the entities behind the facility, its maximum electric capacity and the municipality or county where the center will be. Alabama Power, the state’s largest utility, will now also be required to submit a full copy of its contracts to the PSC and the attorney general’s office. This submission will be confidential. The company must also include in the confidential submission an estimate of impacts on other customers’ costs, how much revenue the project would generate for the company and the cost of the incremental capacity required. It also has to provide a detailed explanation of how the contract meets the public interest standard expanded in Senate Bill 270. That legislation, which established that data centers are in the public’s interest only if they “promote positive benefits” to other customers, went into effect Oct. 1. Lowering the cost for other customers, increasing the efficiency of the power system and contributing to economic growth in the community where a data center is located are examples of positive benefits the bill lays out. The new procedure also forbids the utility from informally submitting information to the PSC or attorney general’s office before filing the public petition. Alabama Power told Alabama Daily News that it is committed to complying with all applicable regulatory requirements, including the one approved Tuesday. “Alabama Power will continue to require large load data center customers to pay the full cost to serve their energy needs, so costs are not shifted to existing customers,” the company said in a statement. “Alabama state law affirms that same standard and the Alabama Public Service Commission approves contracts that meet that standard while promoting positive benefits for other customers.” Though Energy Alabama and the Southern Environmental Law Center celebrated some of the new transparency requirements created by the PSC on Tuesday, the advocacy groups said in statements that they wished the commission had done more to loop the public into its future decision-making. artigo.texto: A Navitas Semiconductor (NASDAQ:NVTS) e a Microchip Technology (NASDAQ:MCHP) desenvolveram em conjunto um projeto de referência de 800V CC para 6V CC para aplicações de alimentação de racks de data centers com inteligência artificial, anunciaram as empresas em 5 de outubro de 2026. A plataforma combina os controladores de sinal digital dsPIC33AK da Microchip e o dispositivo de criptografia TA100 com os dispositivos de potência de nitreto de gálio GaNFast da Navitas. O projeto está alinhado com o padrão Open Compute Project 800V DC e combina estágios de conversão de 800V DC para 50V DC e de 50V DC para 6V DC em um único conversor. O projeto visa atingir uma eficiência máxima de 96% Segundo as empresas, a plataforma de referência visa uma eficiência máxima de até 96% em plena carga, uma frequência de comutação de 1 MHz e uma densidade de potência de 2.100 watts por polegada cúbica. O lado primário utiliza 16 FETs GaNFast Navitas NV6034 de 650V em uma topologia de meia ponte empilhada. A família de controladores dsPIC33AK256MPS306 da Microchip inclui um núcleo de 32 bits de 200 MHz, moduladores de largura de pulso de alta resolução de 78 picossegundos e conversores analógico-digitais de 12 bits operando a até 40 MSPS. Os controladores também são compatíveis com algoritmos de criptografia pós-quântica do pacote Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0. O dispositivo TA100 CryptoAuthentication da Microchip oferece funções de segurança baseadas em hardware, incluindo inicialização segura, geração de código de autenticação de mensagens, atualizações de firmware confiáveis e suporte a Transport Layer Security (TLS). “À medida que o ecossistema avança em direção a sistemas de alimentação de rack de alta tensão, os desenvolvedores precisam de componentes básicos comprovados que ajudem a reduzir o risco de projeto e acelerar a inovação”, disse Joe Thomsen, vice-presidente corporativo da unidade de negócios de controladores de sinal digital da Microchip. Plataforma de referência será apresentada em outubro As empresas planejam apresentar a solução no evento OCP da Microchip em San Jose, Califórnia, agendado para 12 a 15 de outubro de 2026. O projeto de referência será disponibilizado juntamente com uma placa de referência, software e documentação de apoio. artigo.texto: Utah Survey Uncovers Why Residents Oppose New Data Centers LOGAN — A new Utah State University statewide survey examines Utah residents’ views on data centers. The results indicate that 75.8% of respondents oppose or strongly oppose building new or additional data centers in Utah. The survey offers insights about what drives this opposition. The findings appear in the first executive summary from a broader research project led by Gina Gilson, Stacia Ryder, and Jessica Schad of USU’s Community and Natural Resources Institute (CANRI). The project will examine data centers’ water and energy demands, Utah residents’ views on data centers, and generate information that could help state and local leaders evaluate proposed development. The August 2026 survey gathered responses from nearly 900 Utah residents and is representative of the state adult population. “We are excited to share some of the initial results from our statewide survey on data centers,” said Schad, CANRI director and administrator of the survey. “One of the most important findings in my view is that public participation in decision-making processes is nearly as important as the amount of energy and water projects consume, meaning that government and business leaders may want to consider how they can engage communities throughout the planning process.” The results show that water and energy use, location, and opportunities for public participation are important considerations for residents evaluating data center projects. The survey predominantly measured reported views of hypothetical project features; it only asked about whether residents support or oppose the Stratos data center in Box Elder, which 60.7% strongly opposed. More than half of respondents (57.2%) strongly oppose data center development, and opposition rises when proposed projects are closer to where respondents live. Residents’ responses also vary with the characteristics of a proposed project. Asked how specific features would affect their views of a data center within 3 miles of home, 54.1% said usage of recycled or other non-potable water would make them more likely to support it. Renewable energy infrastructure had a similar effect for 51.2%, while 43.4% said a project that built or paid for new energy infrastructure would increase their likelihood of support. By comparison, 61.3% said using nonrenewable energy would make them more likely to oppose a local project. The use of nuclear energy increased the likelihood of opposition for 41.4%. Responses to a proposal for public reporting of annual water and energy use were more mixed. “Similar to what we have seen in the context of other energy infrastructure project siting processes, like for shale gas, residents in our survey indicate the continued importance of processes creating avenues for meaningful community participation in these decision-making processes,” said Ryder, assistant professor of sociology. "Additionally, the type of energy and water used to support data centers matters to residents, as respondents were likely to respond more positively to the use of renewable energy and recycled or non-potable water. These are important considerations for shaping planning and public reception." Gilson, assistant professor of environment and society and interim director of USU’s Center for Colorado River Studies, said: “Our survey findings underscore the concern that Utahns feel about our water resources. I think it’s important for us to better understand where the water comes from, how much water is used on-site, and how much is used to generate the electricity that powers data centers. Our research will gather information to help answer these questions." The survey is one part of an ongoing project. CANRI researchers also want to examine public documents and media coverage to assess what information is available about data centers’ water and energy use, and to interview policymakers, developers, community leaders, and residents of select Utah communities affected by data center development. A follow-up survey in 2027 is planned to assess whether residents’ views change over time. To learn more, read the executive summary: https://artsci.usu.edu/canri/projects/data-center-development-in-utah. artigo.texto: Oakland City Council approves 45-day moratorium on new data centers OAKLAND, Calif. - The Oakland City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to place a 45-day temporary moratorium on all new data center development across the city. Oakland Enacts Temporary Moratorium on Data Center Construction The urgency measure, sponsored by Councilmember Carroll Fife, pauses new approvals to allow city leaders time to study the potential environmental and operational impacts of data centers on local water supplies, electrical grids, and air quality. Before the vote, protesters rallied outside Oakland City Hall to demand a pause on data center developments, expressing concerns over natural resource consumption. Inside council chambers, community members and activists offered mixed testimony on the proposal. Opponents of data centers highlighted the massive water demands required for cooling systems. "My concern about it being in Oakland is that we have limited water from the Mokelumne River, and that’s in the Sierra Nevada, and we’re already taking up to 60 to 70 percent of that river out of the river," said Dr. Elizabeth Dougherty. "If we increase water use here, that would take more and more out, so what would be impacting not just our ecosystem, but also up river in the Sierra Nevada." Other residents voiced fears regarding daily utility volume, with one speaker noting that "a large data center can use up to 5 billion gallons of water a day," while another called on the council to implement a permanent ban. Conversely, supporters urged the council to reject the moratorium, emphasizing the economic potential and job creation tied to technology infrastructure. "I oppose the moratorium on data centers," one resident told council members. "Data centers will bring jobs. They will not take jobs away," another resident added. Concerns Over Non-Disclosure Agreements and Downtown Proposal Councilmember Fife, who proposed the moratorium, has criticized developers for using non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to shield specific project details from city officials and the public. The vote followed growing scrutiny over plans announced by Behring Companies to convert the ground floor of a building near 20th and Franklin streets in downtown Oakland into a data center. The developer stated that the other floors of the facility would serve as office space for artificial intelligence research. Mayor Barbara Lee noted that the pause would provide necessary time for public engagement. "This is a moment to have the public weigh in, and the public will be able to weigh in during this 45-day moratorium to see exactly what people here in Oakland want," Mayor Lee said. Next Steps and Public Forum The 45-day moratorium takes effect immediately. City officials will use the interim period to analyze policy options and development standards for future data center projects. Councilmember Fife has scheduled a community conversation for Oct. 24 at 10 a.m. at the Beth Eden Baptist Church at 1183 10th Street in West Oakland to allow residents to further discuss the future of data centers in the city.

artigo.texto: Hallam Village Board approves zoning rights for data center HALLAM, Neb. (KOLN) - The village of Hallam is now one step closer to getting a data center. The village board approved zoning rights in a vote on Monday. It was about an hour of discussion between board members, the public, and a representative from Crusoe Technologies, who signed a special permit alongside Monolith Materials back in July to get the data center plan started. People had questions about fire safety and noise, but Steve Buster, a Crusoe Technologies representative, said they have a fire plan just in case something does happen. A handful of people from Hallam were invited to a data center to help calm worries about excessive sounds. Even though there wasn’t much drama during the vote, some weren’t happy with the decision. “Well at first I thought that’s okay, you can just move somewhere but everywhere you look they are fighting data centers,” said a woman at the discussion. “So where will you move where there won’t be another data center.” While a number of people were disappointed, a reporter said about half the room applauded when the zoning rights were approved. artigo.texto: Três carros para comprar com valor do novo BYD Sealion 7 O BYD Sealion 7 tem 531 cv de potência, 70,3 kgfm de torque e roda 360 km de autonomia com uma carga completa A BYD lançou um novo modelo elétrico para o mercado brasileiro chamado de Sealion 7. O SUV 100% elétrico tem mais de 4,80 metros de comprimento e desempenho de esportivo. Com preço de R$ 339.990, a reportagem da CNN Brasil separou algumas opções de carros para comprar com esse valor. O BYD Sealion 7 tem 531 cv de potência, 70,3 kgfm de torque e pode rodar 360 km com uma carga completa. Com essa mecânica, o SUV atinge os 100 km/h em 4,5 segundos e a velocidade máxima é de 215 km/h. Com esse valor do SUV, uma opção semelhante é o Volvo EC40. O modelo da marca sueca parte de R$ 334.950. A configuração perde na potência, que conta com 238 cv e acelera de 0 a 100 km/h em 7,3 segundos. A vantagem fica por conta da autonomia. Segundo o Inmetro, o Volvo EC40 pode rodar 385 km com uma carga completa, superando o número do BYD Sealion 7. Em termos de tamanho, contudo, a vantagem fica para o modelo chinês. Um outro SUV chinês que é posicionado no mesmo patamar do Sealion 7 é o GAC Hyptec HT. Com preço de R$ 314.990, o modelo entrega mais autonomia elétrica. Na versão Elite, de entrada, são 431 km de autonomia elétrica com uma única carga. O SUV da GAC também é superior em algumas dimensões. Tem 4,93 metros de comprimento (+10 cm), 1,92 de largura e 2,93 metros na distância entre os eixos. O porta-malas tem 670 litros — O BYD tem 500 L. Com R$ 10 mil a mais no bolso, uma outra alternativa é o Chevrolet Equinox EV. O SUV elétrico tem 304 cv de potência (menos que o Sealion 7), mas ganha com grande vantagem no alcance elétrico. Segundo dados do Inmetro, o Equinox EV consegue rodar 443 km com uma única carga de bateria completa. Com os 443 quilômetros de autonomia, a velocidade de recarga é de até 22 kW (AC) e 150 kW (DC). Em apenas 10 minutos nesta última, o motorista pode somar 130 km de autonomia. No porte, o Equinox é bem semelhante ao Sealion 7. São 4.840 mm de comprimento, 1.954 mm de largura, 1,64 metro de altura e 2.336 kg. O entre-eixos tem 2,95 metros.

artigo.texto: A BYD, uma das principais empresas no setor de carros elétricos, está desenvolvendo uma solução inovadora para combater o superaquecimento das baterias, problema recorrente nestes veículos. A empresa estuda a imersão das baterias em um líquido especial, que não conduz eletricidade, para dissipar o calor de forma mais eficiente e segura. Uma nova patente publicada em 5 de outubro de 2026 na China detalha este projeto. A ideia é utilizar um fluido dielétrico em contato direto com os módulos das baterias, sem a necessidade do uso de placas ou canais de refrigeração, métodos mais tradicionais de resfriamento. A tecnologia ainda é voltada para baterias de carros e sistemas estacionários de armazenamento de energia. O inovador sistema ainda não foi anunciado como solução oficial para os modelos da BYD. No entanto, destaca-se o avanço contínuo da empresa para aumentar a eficiência das suas baterias. Recentemente, em março, a BYD apresentou a segunda geração de sua bateria Blade e o sistema Flash, que possibilita carregar a bateria de 10% a 70% em apenas cinco minutos. Isso reflete o compromisso da empresa em acelerar os processos de recarga, oferecendo melhores experiências para os usuários de veículos elétricos. O sistema de imersão em líquido propõe compartimentar a bateria de forma que os conectores fiquem em uma área seca, enquanto as demais partes do módulo fiquem submersas no líquido dielétrico. Este fluido, por estar em contato direto, proporciona um resfriamento mais homogeneizado. Além disso, a BYD planeja posicionar as conexões da bateria na parte superior do compartimento, onde a pressão exercida pelo líquido é menor, minimizando as chances de vazamento e outros problemas de segurança. O desenvolvimento dessas tecnologias ainda não tem previsão de utilização nos veículos elétricos da marca, embora represente um passo significativo na melhoria dos sistemas de armazenamento de energia e segurança das baterias automotivas. A empresa continua a investir pesadamente em inovação tecnológica para se manter na vanguarda do setor, almejando atender às crescentes demandas por eficiência energética e segurança em seus produtos.

artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons shares hit a day high of Rs 226.99 on 5 October, up 1%, after the firm won a Rs 100 crore battery storage order in Uttarakhand. The company told exchanges about the win at around 13:30 pm. Jupiter Wagons, better known for building railway wagons, landed the job through JEM Energy, its clean energy arm. Madhav Infra Projects Limited is its partner on the project. The customer is Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL). The project is essentially a giant battery. It stores electricity when demand is low and sends it back to the grid when demand peaks. The system is rated at 41 MW and can hold 102.5 MWh of energy. Jupiter and its partner will supply and set it up, and the work is worth about Rs 100 crore. The two firms won by quoting the lowest price in a competitive bidding round run by UPCL. It is JEM Energy’s first project in Uttarakhand. This is not the only recent win. In August 2026, the company also received a formal award letter from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited. That job is a 50 MW/200 MWh battery project at the Jeerat substation in North 24 Parganas. Managing Director Vivek Lohia called both wins important steps in turning JEM Energy into a bigger business. Jupiter Wagons still aims to build a battery storage order book of about Rs 1,000 crore by FY27. Lohia also said the electric mobility arm, Jupiter Electric Mobility, should start making an operating profit in the October to December quarter of FY27. He expects it to turn profitable overall by FY28. The orders follow the Union Cabinet’s approval of Green Energy Corridor Phase-III, which includes 50 GWh of battery storage. The early rally did not hold. Jupiter Wagons closed at Rs 223.44 on the NSE, down 0.22%, after swinging between a low of Rs 218.61 and its high of Rs 226.99. artigo.texto: Fayette County residents push back on data center zoning plan Opponents call for extended moratorium, stricter limits on hyperscale facilities LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Fayette County residents voiced opposition Tuesday to hyperscale data centers and current zoning recommendations put forth earlier this year by the planning commission. “I expect for my council, my representatives to represent me. Not big industry,” one resident said. Opponents cite risks, demand moratorium extension Opponents said that if the draft moves forward, anticipated noise, water, energy, financial and air quality impacts will put communities at risk. Those opposed overwhelmingly demanded a two-year extension of the moratorium and a complete ban of centers larger than 25 megawatts if evidence discovered in those two years points to negative impacts. “Other safety critical industries such as transportation, energy, medicine and weapons are regulated and monitored. AI needs to be treated the same,” one speaker said. Other demands included a cap on data center license issuances, incentives to use lower carbon emission fuels, cutting the decibel limit to 25, and changing zoning rules to limit a center by its utility intake rather than square footage. Some also called for a one-year extension of the data center moratorium. Some see economic opportunity Others in attendance Tuesday said they see AI and data centers as drivers of economic growth in the future and do not wish to jeopardize it. “Data infrastructure is critically important. Data technology, having that infrastructure here is as essential to economic development today as sites and buildings, as water and sewer, and broadband capacity,” one speaker said. Developer addresses concerns Several speakers noted data center developer DART Point’s recent acquisition of more than 300,000 square feet of property to create a data center campus. A DART Point representative addressed resource-based concerns. “We’re not a threat on the noise factor, the water system we use will be a closed loop system, and the power, we already have it,” the representative said. Urban County Council members said they will continue discussions on data centers at the next meeting, including where any potential projects could be developed and how the data centers would be used. The possibility of a one-year extension of the moratorium will also be discussed. Copyright 2026 WKYT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA atNorth planeja o Data Center FIN05 em Salo, Finlândia, com caminho para 230 MW Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google O operador nórdico de data centers atNorth, em 5 de outubro de 2026, anunciou planos para desenvolver o FIN05, um novo data center em Salo, Finlândia. A empresa espera investir aproximadamente €2 bilhões no site de 28,6 hectares, onde a energia para a primeira fase planejada de 75 MW está garantida, com um caminho para até 230 MW para o desenvolvimento mais amplo. Especificações do Site e Planos de Investimento A atNorth afirmou que Salo oferece uma localização forte para infraestrutura crítica que atende clientes com exigentes requisitos de conectividade e resiliência. A empresa citou a proximidade da cidade com Helsinque e o pool de talentos digitais da Finlândia como fatores adicionais que sustentam o desenvolvimento, e posicionou o FIN05 como parte de seu objetivo contínuo de atender à demanda por infraestrutura digital de alto desempenho de maneira responsável. O site será conectado por meio de uma subestação da Fingrid. O investimento esperado de €2 bilhões da empresa não inclui servidores de propriedade dos clientes ou sua instalação, o que a atNorth estima que pode representar um investimento adicional de até €10 bilhões. A empresa planeja celebrar acordos de compra de energia de longo prazo com fornecedores locais para apoiar a produção de energia na região, juntamente com soluções de flexibilidade que, segundo ela, podem apoiar a operação eficiente da rede de transmissão da Fingrid. A atNorth também trabalhará com partes interessadas locais para explorar oportunidades de uso do calor gerado pelo data center, que a empresa afirma ter como objetivo gerar valor além da própria instalação. Esse esforço baseia‑se em colaborações existentes de reutilização de calor com a Kesko Corporation na Finlândia, a Stockholm Exergi na Suécia, e a Vestforbrænding e a Selected Group na Dinamarca. Declarações da atNorth e Parceiros Locais “O FIN05 é uma oportunidade de desenvolver infraestrutura digital crítica enquanto trabalhamos com a região para criar valor local duradouro”, disse Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson, CEO da atNorth. Ele afirmou que a empresa está explorando como parcerias energéticas locais, soluções de flexibilidade e reutilização de calor podem contribuir para o sistema energético mais amplo e para a comunidade, e espera trabalhar com Salo e parceiros regionais à medida que o projeto avança. Anna‑Kristiina Korhonen, prefeita de Salo, disse estar encantada em receber o investimento na região. Ela afirmou que o novo data center criará oportunidades de emprego valiosas tanto durante a construção quanto nas operações contínuas, gerando benefícios econômicos mais amplos para os negócios locais, acrescentando que o desenvolvimento reforça a posição de Salo como um destino atraente para indústrias inovadoras e apoia o crescimento sustentável de longo prazo da comunidade. Matti‑Juho Ervasti, sócio da Regant Oy, afirmou que o projeto demonstra o potencial de Salo como local para investimentos significativos em infraestrutura digital. Ele disse que a Regant trabalhou de perto com a atNorth e a municipalidade para oferecer um site pronto para desenvolvimento, com a escala, prontidão de planejamento e roteiro energético necessários para grandes projetos de data center. Cadeia de Valor Nórdica e Histórico de Propriedade A atNorth descreveu o FIN05 como parte de seu investimento contínuo nos países nórdicos, juntamente com desenvolvimentos em Estocolmo e Sollefteå, na Suécia, Haugaland, na Noruega, Ølgod, na Dinamarca e Kouvola, na Finlândia. O projeto de Kouvola, FIN04, foi anunciado em dezembro de 2023 como um mega site em um terreno de 21 hectares, a 139 km a nordeste de Helsinque e a 52 km da cidade de Hamina, atendendo tanto clientes de colocation quanto projetos build‑to‑suit. A atNorth disse na época que o FIN04 teria um fornecimento de energia imediato de 60 MW, uma primeira fase pronta para operação no segundo semestre de 2025, e um caminho para potência de várias centenas de megawatts quando totalmente construído, descrevendo‑o como o décimo data center da empresa nos países nórdicos e seu quarto campus na Finlândia. Trabalhando com a cidade de Kouvola e o parceiro energético KSS Energia, o site foi projetado com capacidades de reutilização de calor, permitindo que o excesso de calor do data center fosse reciclado para possível reutilização na comunidade local. O projeto de Salo também segue uma mudança na propriedade da atNorth. A CPP Investments e a Equinix concluíram a aquisição de US$4 bilhões da atNorth em 2 de setembro de 2026, com a CPP Investments detendo uma participação controladora de cerca de 51 % com um compromisso de US$1,3 bilhão, a Equinix detendo cerca de 34 % com um compromisso de US$895 milhões, e a Partners Group detendo cerca de 10 % com um compromisso de US$260 milhões. O restante está nas mãos dos acionistas internos da atNorth, que mantiveram uma parte substancial de sua participação acionária. A transação envolveu um pacote de financiamento de US$4,1 bilhões (€3,6 bilhões) garantido por um grupo de credores europeus e canadenses, e a atNorth continua a operar de forma independente sob sua marca existente.

artigo.texto: Data center moratorium vote postponed after fight, protests MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC/Gray News) — Chaos ensued during Tuesday night’s data center moratorium vote by the city council in Memphis, Tennessee. More than 100 people showed up to the meeting to hear the outcome on the proposed ordinance. “This is just a total hazard. We’ve basically been invaded by strangers, by people that have gotten paid, and they have not communicated with us in any way,” said Amber Lowe, a local community member. “This is hurtful, and I’m rethinking where I need to be living at.” The decision to delay the vote until Oct. 20 led to a fight breaking out in the lobby and tense exchanges among city council members. A fight between two women spilled into the lobby, with punches thrown while protesters chanted inside the meeting. One woman had her hair pulled and was slapped seconds later. Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton was pulled out of the meeting after arguing with protesters and council member JB Smiley. “You could’ve came to see me like I asked you to... I ain’t no coward; you pipe down, baby, I clap back,” Cooper-Sutton said. The city council halted the meeting amid the turmoil and subsequently delayed the vote. Crowds chanted “this is our city” and “show me what democracy looks like” as the demonstration moved from the chamber into the halls of the building. Protesters said they are not done pursuing the issue. Memphis police were called to the disturbance at city hall, but a department spokesperson says no one was detained and no one was harmed. artigo.texto: An ambitious ETS can strengthen European competitiveness The Commission’s Emissions Trading System (ETS) proposal maintains the pathway towards decarbonisation by 2050 but risks slowing down industrial renewal in Europe. Co-legislators should keep the supply of allowances in check to enable frontrunner investments in decarbonisation. In her State of the European Union speech, President Ursula von der Leyen correctly noted that our dependence on fossil fuels has led to over 90 billion euros in additional costs, “without a single molecule of energy added”. A large part of that amount flowed outside of Europe. She also set out the alternative: an electrified Europe that could cut the fossil fuel import bill by 260 billion euros a year. She also reiterated her support for the EU’s climate targets, which are the basis for flagship energy and climate legislation of this mandate: namely, the revision of the EU Emissions Trading System, which the Commission adopted in mid-July this year. It’s not just the destination that matters The Commission’s proposal does indeed align the ETS with the EU’s emission reduction target. But in addition to the destination, the journey there matters: the Commission’s proposal and the alternative option included in the Parliament’s draft report would increase the volume of allowances released by roughly 30–40 percent between 2030 and 2040. Furthermore, free allocation would continue for several years longer. These changes would weaken the incentives for the deployment of clean technologies in Europe. In practice, a significantly less ambitious trajectory for cutting emissions would affect European companies investing in the development of clean technologies and production of near-zero emissions materials. Manufacturers like Metso, Andritz and Valmet provide state-of-the art solutions for industrial processes such as clean steelmaking and hydrogen production. Metal producers such as SSAB, Outokumpu and Boliden offer low-carbon metals for customers globally, with plans to go even further. Furthermore, all of this is supported by a strong grid technology sector, whose ranks include companies like ABB and Prysmian. In many of these sectors, European companies remain global leaders and the EU, with ambitious policies like the ETS, has built an excellent environment for deploying their technologies. A large number of countries and regions are following Europe’s example, with the share of global emissions covered by carbon pricing on the rise. The IEA estimates the global market for clean technologies to grow rapidly from the current 1.2 trillion to 2–5 trillion USD by 2035. There is also significant untapped potential in the market for near-zero emissions materials such as clean steel, that will, according to the IEA, remain unrealised without a strong policy push. Taking a giant leap requires trust To take the next step in decarbonisation, gradual change is not enough: we need frontrunner investments in ground-breaking technologies, such as steelmaking based on clean electricity and hydrogen. Trust in the system is crucial for turning plans into reality: the ETS works not only because it encourages companies to cut emissions here and now but also in the long run. That helps companies plan long-term and make investments in innovative new technologies instead of only making their existing processes more efficient. Keeping the increase in in the volume of released allowances more modest than in the Commission’s proposal is important for securing that trust. Similarly, sticking to the previously agreed timeline for phasing out free allocation is crucial. Putting revenues to work The ETS does come with costs. But unlike the money spent on imported fossil fuels, ETS revenues stay in the coffers of the EU and the Member States. Yet only around 5 percent of them are currently channelled back to industry to speed up decarbonisation. This needs to change: smarter use of the revenues and free allocation can help kickstart the switch to clean steelmaking, fuels and feedstocks. The need to develop and tune the EU ETS has been part and parcel of the journey from the beginning. The revision of the ETS is an opportunity to prove that we can also persist, by holding the agreed course on the cap and free allocation, and by putting the system’s own revenues to work. In doing so, we can also show that climate action and competitiveness can go hand in hand. TIF recommendations for the revision of the EU ETS - Align the cap with the 90 % emissions reduction target while keeping the cumulative number of issued allowances in check: an ambitious LRF in the early 2030s is crucial for achieving this goal. - Ensure that the revenues collected are channelled back to the sectors affected by the EU ETS - Shape free allocation into an instrument for speeding up the decarbonisation in Europe, especially in energy-intensive industry - Allocate EU funding to projects based on excellence - Include a broad range of permanent carbon removal technologies in the EU ETS

CleanChoice Energy has secured more than US$166 million in financing for two solar photovoltaic projects in the US Northeast, the Dolan project in New York at roughly 27MW and the Kylertown project in Pennsylvania at roughly 28MW. The package included a US$105 million construction loan from Investec Bank, which acted as lead arranger, green loan structuring agent and collateral agent. BHI, the US branch of Bank Hapoalim, BM and Stifel Bank served as coordinating lead arrangers. Advantage Capital supplied a US$61 million tax equity commitment for the portfolio. Both projects are expected to reach commercial operations in 2027. Separately, distributed energy company Maxwell Power has closed an US$800 million investment from private equity firm Fairtide Partners to acquire battery storage and solar PV power projects. The deal follows investments of US$250 million and US$750 million in 2024 and June 2026, lifting Fairtide's total commitment to US$1.8 billion for projects developed by Maxwell. Maxwell said it has helped its consumer and small commercial customers achieve US$100 million in future energy savings so far this year. The company also relocated its headquarters from San Diego, California, to Salt Lake City, Utah, a move it described as fulfilling a promise to Utah Senator John Curtis. In a third transaction, independent power producer Lydian Energy and infrastructure asset manager Infranity agreed on a US$300 million holding company credit facility intended to support expansion of Lydian's 6GW portfolio of solar PV and utility-scale battery energy storage systems. The bespoke facility is based on Lydian Energy's existing operating and construction-ready assets and is designed to give the company added flexibility to accelerate build-out of its business pipeline. Lydian said the financing will help it advance projects from development through construction and retain ownership of operating assets. Lydian Energy is backed by Exelsior Energy Capital. Sacha Kamp, global head of debt investment at Infranity, characterized the transaction as resting on a portfolio of high-quality contracted projects and a strong pipeline of energy infrastructure assets developed and owned by Lydian, adding that the support of an experienced and committed sponsor provides a foundation for long-term growth.
