artigo.texto: Amazon Commits $1 Billion to US Data Center Communities Amid AI Backlash - Amazon will invest more than $1 billion over five years in US communities hosting its data centers, targeting education, workforce training, energy affordability and water preservation. - AWS says it is 75% of the way toward its 2030 water-positive goal, as scrutiny grows over the electricity and water demands of AI infrastructure. - More than 100 data center moratoriums are under consideration across the US, raising political and investment risks as technology companies accelerate AI infrastructure spending. Amazon is committing more than $1 billion over five years to communities hosting its US data centers. The investment comes as the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure faces growing resistance over energy costs, water consumption and local impacts. Amazon Web Services will direct the funding through its new Built Together framework. It will support education, job training, energy affordability, water preservation and other community priorities. The initiative adds a community investment component to one of the largest private infrastructure expansions underway in the United States. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025. Large projects or expansions are now underway across several states, including Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia and Mississippi. AI growth collides with local infrastructure concerns Data centers provide the computing capacity required to train and operate AI models. Their rapid expansion has also intensified questions about who bears the infrastructure costs. Communities across the US have raised concerns about electricity demand, utility bills, water use and pressure on local infrastructure. More than 100 data center moratoriums are currently being considered nationwide, according to Amazon. That opposition creates a growing governance challenge for technology companies and policymakers. It also adds a political dimension ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. AWS CEO Matt Garman framed continued construction as an economic and national security priority. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it,” Garman said. Amazon compared the current expansion of digital infrastructure with the construction of the US interstate highway system. However, the company stressed one major difference. Private companies, rather than taxpayers, are financing much of today’s infrastructure buildout. AI infrastructure is increasingly tied to healthcare, education, financial services, cybersecurity, defense and scientific research. That broadening role has strengthened the case for investment while increasing scrutiny of its environmental footprint. RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Adds 50+ Mercedes Electric Trucks in Germany Water and energy move higher on the agenda Amazon’s investment framework seeks to address some of the most contentious environmental issues surrounding data centers. AWS has committed to becoming water positive across its data center operations by 2030. The company said it is now 75% of the way toward that goal. Water positive means returning more water to communities than its operations consume. The commitment has become increasingly relevant as new data centers expand into regions facing competing demands for water and electricity. Energy affordability is another focus of the $1 billion program. Rising data center demand has prompted questions about grid investment and whether households could face higher costs as utilities build infrastructure to serve large technology customers. For Amazon, addressing those concerns has become part of maintaining community support for continued expansion. Community acceptance becomes an investment risk The scale of proposed data center development means community relations are moving from corporate philanthropy into core infrastructure strategy. Moratoriums, permitting disputes and public opposition can delay projects and raise development costs. They can also complicate the long-term power procurement and grid planning needed to support AI investment. Amazon’s Built Together framework gives communities a role in determining how funds are allocated. That approach could help companies align investments with local concerns rather than applying a uniform national model. For executives and investors, the broader issue extends beyond Amazon. AI growth depends on physical infrastructure that requires land, power, water and political approval. The next phase of the AI investment cycle will therefore depend on more than access to capital and computing technology. Developers will need credible plans for resource use, community benefits and energy affordability. As governments compete for leadership in AI, those local constraints are becoming part of the global race for digital infrastructure. The companies that manage them effectively may gain an advantage in securing the permits, power and public support required for continued expansion. artigo.texto: MONTEZUMA COUNTY, Colo., Oct. 5, 2026 (SEND2PRESS NEWSWIRE) — NoValleyRange, a neighborhood group located near Mesa Verde (a UNESCO World Heritage site and National Park), are fighting a Texas developer proposing a $240 million dollar solar and lithium battery development. The proposed project consists of 900 acres of solar panels and 8 acres of lithium battery storage at the base of Colorado’s only UNESCO world heritage site. This project is comparable in size to the 500,000-panel Cleve Hill Solar Park, the largest solar field in the UK. The neighbors are fighting the project for the same reasons that many other rural communities across the US are fighting similar projects. Namely, that the solar field and BESS facility will degrade property values, harm tourism, and put small businesses out of business. However, the Valley Range Energy Park presents unique problems. It will dominate the views from the northside overlooks from Mesa Verde National Park and degrade the park visitor experience. Mesa Verde is not only a cultural treasure, but also the economic tourism engine that supports the entire community. Even more alarming is the potential for a catastrophic battery fire. According to Lillian Wakeley, Board Director at Mesa Verde Association, in a recent social media comment, “The solar array will overwhelm the views from every overlook on the north escarpment in Mesa Verde National Park. Large battery storage means fire risk and also huge security lights. One of Mesa Verde’s major drawing points is the dark night sky, and ranger programs with new night-scopes are hugely popular. Please think about the impact on our tourist industry if we encroach on our national park with overwhelming lights, noise, and nearly a thousand acres of solar panels.” Mesa Verde National Park is also a huge driver of the local economy. According to a National Park Service report, in 2023 505,000 visitors came to Mesa Verde National Park and spent $59.5 million in communities near the park. That spending in the local area had a cumulative benefit to the local economy of $75.6 million (*see note 1). Park visitation was directly responsible for approximately 8% of total employment in Montezuma County (*2). The Valley Range solar project also includes 8 acres of lithium battery storage commonly referred to as a BESS. BESS facilities are new technology with a dismal safety record. Most of the BESS systems in the US have been installed since 2020 (*3) Unlike conventional fires, BESS fires produce their own oxygen and are nearly impossible to extinguish (*4). BESS fires also produce poisonous gasses including hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen fluoride. Most troubling, is the ability of a BESS fire to produce carcinogenic fallout in the form of aerosolized exotic metals (*5). In the 2025 Moss Landing battery fire, 55,000 pounds of carcinogenic metals were aerosolized into the neighboring tourist town and surrounding marshes (*6). BESS installations present unique economic problems when located near a major tourist attraction, such as Mesa Verde National Park. According to KAZU News, the 2025 lithium-ion battery fire in the popular tourist town of Moss Landing California (and the accompanying repeated evacuation orders and national news coverage) devastated the local tourism industry (*7). According to neighboring business owner, Bryan Davis, “Anything negatively effecting Mesa Verde National Park is a critical economic issue here. This community relies on the National Park for a huge percentage of the local economy.” In recent weeks the Valley Range project has become a local political issue in Montezuma County with Republican commissioner candidate Rodney Cox saying “There is a solar farm being proposed now, and I’m against everything about that.” Rodney Cox’s opponent Democrat Rebecca Busic has said she supports the solar project and lithium battery installation (*8). ABOUT NOVALLEYRANGE: NoValleyRange is a local community activism group made up of two neighborhoods located near Mesa Verde National Park. We are sheep farmers, chocolate shop owners, campground owners, retirees and ordinary folks. NoValleyRange is not a partisan group, our members span the political spectrum. However, we are united in our effort to stop this project. Sign the petition and learn more at https://www.novalleyrange.com/. artigo.texto: Investimento da Amazon em Data Centers em Ohio Enfrenta um Novo Teste para os Consumidores de Energia A Amazon comprometeu bilhões de dólares com data centers em Ohio, mas sua expansão em IA agora enfrenta contratos de energia mais rigorosos, escrutínio tributário e oposição local organizada. O investimento da Amazon em data centers em Ohio deixou de ser uma história simples de capacidade de nuvem. Tornou-se um teste sobre quem paga pela infraestrutura por trás da inteligência artificial. Um resumo recente do TradingView descreveu uma expansão plurianual em Ohio até 2030, sem identificar novos locais, número de projetos ou um novo compromisso de investimento. Esse resumo trazia um importante aviso: foi gerado por IA e poderia conter imprecisões. O registro verificado é mais específico, mas aponta principalmente para investimentos já anunciados, e não para um novo projeto divulgado em Ohio. A AWS opera sua região de nuvem em Ohio desde 2016. A Amazon anunciou outra grande expansão em dezembro de 2024, com base em compromissos assumidos em 2023 e em construções anteriores. Desde então, o ambiente político mudou. Ohio impôs compromissos mais fortes de eletricidade aos data centers e suspendeu novas concessões sob um valioso incentivo tributário. A Amazon ainda tem capital e demanda para construir. A questão mais difícil é se as comunidades de Ohio, os reguladores e os clientes das concessionárias aceitarão os termos. Esse conflito agora importa tanto quanto o número de servidores que a AWS pode instalar. O Que o Investimento da Amazon em Data Centers em Ohio Realmente Abrange A história verificada é um programa contínuo de infraestrutura, não uma coleção recém-detalhada de campi de IA. A AWS anunciou em dezembro de 2024 que planejava outro grande investimento em infraestrutura de nuvem em Ohio. A empresa afirmou que a expansão poderia incluir até oito novos locais de data centers até 2030. Ela não identificou todos os locais. O anúncio seguiu um compromisso anterior, feito em junho de 2023. Na época, a AWS disse que pretendia expandir suas operações no centro de Ohio até 2029. A empresa já havia investido em instalações que atendem sua região de nuvem US East Ohio. Os compromissos combinados colocaram a Amazon entre os maiores investidores em data centers de Ohio. Uma ficha informativa atualizada da Amazon afirmou que a empresa investiu US$ 19,7 bilhões em infraestrutura de IA e nuvem em Ohio desde 2011. Essa categoria incluía data centers e redes de fibra. O plano de investimento em Ohio mais amplo da Amazon descreve instalações com servidores, sistemas de armazenamento, hardware de rede e equipamentos de suporte. Esses ativos atendem clientes convencionais de nuvem, além de cargas de trabalho mais recentes de inteligência artificial. A distinção importa. Nem todo data center da AWS é exclusivamente uma instalação de IA, mesmo quando a demanda por IA ajuda a justificar sua construção. A mesma região de nuvem pode oferecer suporte a bancos de dados, sites, aplicações empresariais, treinamento de modelos e inferência. Inferência é o processo de executar um modelo de IA treinado para gerar uma resposta ou previsão. O treinamento cria o modelo, enquanto a inferência entrega suas capacidades aos usuários. Ambas as atividades exigem capacidade computacional, embora seus perfis de hardware e energia possam ser diferentes. A AWS lançou a região de Ohio em outubro de 2016 com três zonas de disponibilidade. Uma zona de disponibilidade é um grupo de instalações fisicamente separadas, projetadas para isolar falhas. Os clientes usam várias zonas quando precisam que aplicações permaneçam disponíveis durante uma interrupção de equipamento ou instalação. A expansão da Amazon, portanto, faz mais do que adicionar espaço físico. Ela aumenta a oferta regional de capacidade de computação, armazenamento e rede disponível aos clientes da AWS. Também pode oferecer às empresas mais opções para manter cargas de trabalho geograficamente próximas aos usuários. O anúncio da empresa em 2024 afirmou que as futuras construções dependiam de acordos de serviço de energia de longo prazo. Essa condição tornou-se central para a história. Terrenos e edifícios têm pouco valor como infraestrutura de IA sem eletricidade confiável na escala necessária. A Associated Press informou que o investimento adicional elevaria o compromisso total da Amazon em Ohio até 2029 acima do patamar anterior. Sua cobertura do investimento também observou que os locais futuros ainda não haviam sido definidos quando o plano foi anunciado. Isso deixa uma lacuna entre um compromisso de capital em nível estadual e um cronograma de construção por projeto. A Amazon pode descrever a escala pretendida sem prometer que todos os campi potenciais serão concretizados. Contratos com concessionárias, licenças, aprovações de terrenos e resistência local ainda podem alterar a sequência. A manchete recente não elimina essa lacuna. Ela reembala a expansão já estabelecida da Amazon enquanto investidores reavaliam a exposição da empresa a data centers. Os leitores devem tratá-la como um resumo conciso de investimentos, e não como prova de uma expansão adicional em Ohio. Essa interpretação também explica por que as contagens exatas de projetos parecem inconsistentes entre diferentes resumos. A Amazon discutiu locais potenciais, investimentos históricos e compromissos futuros em documentos distintos. Essas medidas descrevem atividades relacionadas, mas não são intercambiáveis. A conclusão confiável é mais restrita. A Amazon continua expandindo sua presença de nuvem em Ohio por meio de um programa que avança em direção a 2030. O tamanho final e a localização de cada componente continuam sujeitos a decisões de infraestrutura e regulação. Por Que a Expansão de IA em Ohio Agora É uma História de Energia A demanda por computação criou o argumento para a expansão, mas a disponibilidade de eletricidade agora determina quais projetos se tornam reais. artigo.texto: As AI moves from experimentation into production, data centers face growing demands for power, cooling, and space. Real-time inference and other AI workloads require infrastructure that can scale without adding unnecessary complexity. Conventional rack designs may not provide the density, or flexibility operators need, while proprietary designs can limit hardware choices and make expansion more complex. Cisco helps operators integrate and scale networking into ORv3 environments while maintaining a consistent operating model. What ORv3 changes for high-density AI data centers Open Rack Version 3 (ORv3) is designed for high-density environments. Developed through the Open Compute Project (OCP), it defines an open rack architecture with mechanical and serviceability specifications and supports power designs suited to modern AI, machine learning, and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. ORv3 racks use a 21-inch equipment bay and Open Units (OU); traditional enterprise equipment commonly uses 19-inch racks and Rack Units (RU). One OU measures 48 mm, while one RU measures 44.45 mm. Some ORv3 designs accommodate 19-inch equipment with mounting adapters, but rack dimensions and usable space vary. That flexibility can help organizations introduce high-density infrastructure while continuing to support compatible equipment and existing deployment strategies. The value of ORv3 comes down to efficiency and scale. ORv3 delivers several important advantages: - Standardized interoperability: Components from different manufacturers can work together more seamlessly, enabling a more open, plug-and-play approach and reducing concerns about hardware compatibility. - Higher power and cooling: A 48V DC busbar power distribution system can reduce power loss and support higher power densities compared to traditional designs. It also offers built-in support for direct liquid cooling (DLC) manifolds and blind-mate connections to manage the intense heat of AI servers. - Sustainability benefits: Reusable components and standardized hardware help reduce waste, lower carbon footprints, and minimize operational inefficiencies. - Operational Efficiency: Features tool-free, “click-in” assembly for IT gear and power rails, allowing for faster maintenance and reduced cabling complexity. It also supports hybrid mounting for both 21-inch OCP (OU) and traditional 19-inch (RU) equipment within the same frame. These features make ORv3 more than a rack specification. They offer a practical foundation for aligning infrastructure density, operational needs, and future growth. How Cisco is supporting the transition Cisco is preparing its data center networking portfolio for evolving rack designs. Cisco offers ORv3- compatible trays for Cisco N9000 Series switches. The trays align networking hardware with open-rack mechanical and power designs, giving operators more flexibility as they build or expand high-density data centers. Customers can choose a bundle with the switch preinstalled on the tray or purchase a spare tray for self-installation, depending on their deployment needs. Cisco N9000 ORv3 compliant trays for operational choice Key capabilities include: - Compatibility with ORv3 rack environments for Cisco N9000 Series switches. - Support for 48V DC power architectures aligned to modern high-density requirements. - Mounting kits for existing 19-inch equipment, enabling traditional gear to fit into the 21-inch ORv3 environment. Cisco power trays are designed to connect at different busbar positions, helping ensure the hardware receives the power it needs in supported rack configurations. This design readiness is essential in high-density environments, where small physical differences can have a significant operational impact. Together, these options give organizations a path to adopt ORv3-based infrastructure while maintaining continuity in network operations, accommodating compatible existing equipment, and aligning the rack with AI’s power, cooling, and density demands. Cisco accelerates AI infrastructure with new liquid-cooled switches: the ORv3-native N9364F-SG3-RL and the purpose-built N9164F-NS6-ML for NVIDIA MGX accelerated-computing rack deployments. These platforms deliver the critical thermal and connectivity efficiency required for modern, high-density AI fabrics. Cisco Nexus switches are part of Cisco Nexus One, a data center networking architecture for AI and modern workloads. With Cisco Cloud Control, Nexus One supports a unified AgenticOps experience for managing infrastructure from silicon to workloads. Who benefits most from an ORv3-ready approach ORv3 is especially relevant for hyperscale and enterprise data centers with roadmaps that include large-scale AI or machine learning workloads. For these organizations, the move to ORv3 is not simply about following the latest hardware standards. It is about creating a data center foundation that can scale with the performance, density, and efficiency requirements of modern workloads. - Simplify the deployment of a high-density fabric. - Maintain environmental goals as infrastructure grows. - Future proof existing investments and extend their longevity. - Reduce total cost of ownership. Building the foundation for what comes next As AI shifts into production and real-time inference, the physical design of the data center becomes a strategic consideration. ORv3 introduces an open, high-density architecture built for the power and thermal realities of AI, machine learning, and HPC. Cisco N9000 support for ORv3 helps organizations adopt that architecture with greater confidence, while preserving proven networking performance and management consistency. Data centers need a smarter, more scalable infrastructure foundation to support continued compute growth. artigo.texto: Enduro 4 smartwatch redefines ultraperformance with extreme battery life and advanced training features Comprehensive power modes, enhanced stamina metrics, a ComfortFit Fabric Band and Garmin Epic help endurance athletes and multiday adventurers train, race and explore even farther OLATHE, Kan. , Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Garmin (NYSE: GRMN) today announced Enduro™ 4, its longest-lasting GPS smartwatch with solar charging, which includes dynamic features and capabilities to take endurance enthusiasts farther on their next expedition. Utilizing an energy-efficient 1.4" MIP display in combination with a solar lens, Enduro 4 has up to 320 hours of battery life in activity mode1 or up to 90 days of battery life in smartwatch mode2. It also leverages innovative updates like grade-adjusted pace-based workout targets, grade-adjusted rolling pace, stamina zones, stamina curve and Garmin Epic multiday activity logging. "As interest and participation in ultra-endurance activities continue to grow, Enduro 4 is designed for athletes and adventurers who want gear they can trust to perform through every mile, every climb and every challenge . Intuitive features like comprehensive power modes make the most of the long-lasting battery life, while grade-adjusted metrics add a new dimension to preparing for hilly or mountainous terrain." —Susan Lyman, Garmin Vice President of Consumer Sales and Marketing Grade-adjusted features, stamina metrics and more In addition to 100+ activity profiles, Enduro 4 introduces new capabilities to the Enduro line, optimized for trail runners, multiday hikers and backpackers, and endurance athletes. - Comprehensive power modes provide preset options to optimize battery life and performance based on the needs of the user. Configurations include Max Accuracy, which offers full-feature tracking for shorter efforts, and Max Battery, ideal for extended activity recording (up to 320 hours with solar charging). - Grade-adjusted pace-based workout targets help athletes maintain the right effort range on hilly terrain, while grade-adjusted rolling pace provides a real-time view of pace over varying terrain. - Stamina zones show athletes how their stamina impacts an activity, and stamina curve helps users understand how their endurance changes over time based on fitness and training history. - With 50% more RAM than Enduro 3 and a more powerful, updated map engine, navigation is easier than ever with 30% faster panning and a smoother, more intuitive map interface for built-in routable maps. Perspective view provides more detail, both close-up and further away, allowing users to better anticipate what comes next. - Garmin Epic allows athletes to combine multiple activities into one cohesive story in Garmin Connect™. Activities can be grouped together over days, weeks or months to create an "Epic", which enables users to add photos and share with family and friends, as well as see health and performance data aggregated during that period. - Enhanced rowing tools provide additional training insights like VO2 max and power curve for indoor rowing activities, while expanded rucking features let users adjust pack weight during an activity and set target metrics like calories burned. Premium design for maximum versatility Enduro 4 weighs in at an incredible 66 grams, making it one of the lightest ultraperformance smartwatches on the market. With a 51mm case, Power Sapphire™ scratch-resistant lens, titanium bezel and lightweight fiber-reinforced polymer case, it is built for the demands of the longest races and most taxing adventures, remaining remarkably light on the wrist. An integrated LED flashlight includes both white and red-light options, while a 10 ATM water resistance rating enables confident use in challenging environments. New to Enduro 4, the ComfortFit Fabric Band combines exceptional comfort, durability and moisture-wicking performance with QuickFit™ functionality, making adjustments and swapping bands even simpler. 64 GB of memory gives users more room for onboard maps, music and data, making it easier to stay prepared for extended adventures away from home. Available now, Enduro 4 has a suggested retail price of $899.99. Learn more at Garmin.com. artigo.texto: Since the Iran-US military conflict began earlier this year, disrupting global oil markets, Australia’s electric vehicle (EV) market has experienced an unprecedented boost. With motorists facing sharp increases at the bowser and continuing uncertainty about fuel prices, many drivers have decided to go electric. EVs accounted for 25.8% of total car sales in the first half of 2026. One brand in particular is capitalising on this trend, and that’s the Chinese carmaker BYD, whose name was previously spelled out as “Build Your Dreams”. It is now outselling many far older and more established competitors in Australia. Fifteen years ago, Elon Musk poked fun at BYD, saying it was not a serious competitor in the electric vehicle business. And until just a few years ago, hardly anyone in Australia had even heard of the brand. So how did BYD become such a formidable competitor in the EV market so quickly? BYD’s origin story BYD’s story began not with cars, but batteries. In 1995, 29-year-old battery specialist Wang Chuanfu founded the company in Shenzhen with a small team. BYD initially manufactured rechargeable nickel-cadmium batteries, before moving into lithium-ion batteries. The company grew quickly, and by 2000, BYD had become Motorola’s first Chinese supplier of lithium-ion batteries. Nokia followed in 2002, and the same year BYD listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. In 2003, BYD entered the automotive industry by acquiring a struggling Chinese manufacturer. Its first model, the petrol-powered F3, arrived in 2005. By then, BYD was already looking towards electrification. In 2008, it launched the F3DM plug-in hybrid. That same year, legendary US investor Warren Buffett backed the company with an investment of about US$230 million for a 9.9% stake, which he later sold. When Bloomberg asked Tesla chief executive Elon Musk in 2011 about BYD as a potential competitor, he laughed. “Have you seen their car?” he asked, before saying he did not see BYD as a competitor. But, by 2023, his assessment had completely changed: “Their cars are highly competitive these days.” What do the sales numbers say these days? Sales figures both in Australia and overseas show just how rapidly BYD has become a formidable name in the automotive industry. Globally, BYD went from selling about 190,000 battery or hybrid vehicles in 2020 to 4.6 million in 2025 – a roughly 24-fold increase in just five years. Of the 2025 sales, 2.26 million were fully electric, enough to overtake Tesla’s 1.64 million deliveries. Its rise in Australia has been similarly striking. In the first eight months of 2026, BYD sold more than 68,000 vehicles, making it Australia’s second-highest-selling car brand behind Toyota. In the month of June, just 243 sales separated the two. Among electric vehicles, over the same period, BYD sold more than 39,000 cars, overtaking Tesla to become Australia’s highest-selling electric vehicle brand. What is BYD’s secret sauce? BYD’s rise from a relatively unknown battery maker to a global automotive giant cannot be attributed to any single factor. But four factors have likely been instrumental to its success. First, BYD makes an unusually large proportion of its cars itself. This includes batteries, electric motors, power electronics and even some of the semiconductors its vehicles need. This high degree of “vertical integration” reduces its reliance on outside suppliers and gives BYD greater control over both its supply chain and production costs. The company even owns and operates its own ships to transport the vehicles to Australia and other markets. Second, BYD did not bet everything on fully electric vehicles. It also sells a large range of plug-in hybrids. This gave buyers who are not yet ready to rely entirely on battery power another route into electrification. Third, BYD took a different approach to battery technology. Its Blade Battery uses lithium iron phosphate chemistry, which is generally cheaper than nickel-based alternatives and requires neither nickel nor cobalt. Fourth, BYD has benefited substantially from China’s long-running support for its electric vehicle industry. This has included direct subsidies to manufacturers as well as subsidies and tax incentives for consumers buying electric vehicles. A history of controversy BYD’s rapid expansion has not been without controversy. Despite its global success, BYD has never established passenger-car sales in the United States. More recently, high tariffs and national-security concerns about Chinese vehicles have created prohibitive barriers to entry to the US market. Cybersecurity concerns have also attracted scrutiny in Australia. This was highlighted in a recent ABC Four Corners investigation showing a cybersecurity expert remotely accessing functions in a BYD Shark 6. Safety concerns have emerged too. While safety regulator ANCAP awarded the Shark 6 five stars, it also applied a penalty score for posing a greater risk to oncoming vehicles due to its size, weight and front-end design. The Shark 6 is larger than many of Australia’s largest utes, including some variants of the Ford Ranger. A new global order for autos For decades, Australia’s car market has been dominated by Japanese brands, with US, Korean and European manufacturers also prominent. Chinese brands are now challenging that order remarkably quickly. China made becoming a global leader in electric vehicles an industrial priority. It has largely achieved that ambition. If current momentum continues, the badges Australians see on their roads over the coming decade could look very different from those they grew up with. BYD is one name they are likely to see much more often.

artigo.texto: The technology industry can’t afford to ignore a growing AI data center backlash - Summary: - Concerns over environmental impact but also higher bills for their neighbors is starting to build to real social resentment Just weeks away now, the US midterms have a new factor beyond American voter cost of living or forever war concerns: whether they want what more than a few see as a potential blight on their neighbourhoods - those awful data center things. It seems a lot don't. A recent national Gallup survey reported 70% of Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities, while three-quarters of the 375 data center bills introduced in US state legislatures in 2026 seek to restrict their development in some way. Surprisingly, perhaps, it’s not just the ‘Dumocrats’ doing this: Republican candidates in states including Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania but most notably Texas, are pushing back on the President’s ‘drill, baby, drill’ pro-AI agenda. You may indeed be a 'socialist dupe’ for not loving all this new compute, but when even Erin Brockovich has set her sights on you, this is not a welcoming climate. There does seem to be a growing case file for the prosecution here: on an almost daily basis, more evidence seems to come out about the downsides of this infrastructure. Meta may be using its US data center buildout as a way to avoid paying at least £4 billion so far in Federal taxes as they are “really” R&D projects, for example, while the push for more and more data center power is driving up fossil fuel demand, nearly tripling gas-fired capacity in the United States in 2025 alone. According to at least one report, Elon Musk is even getting into the turbine-making business himself to keep up. It might not just be the environment that takes a hit from data center building frenzy; investors might soon be feeling the pain as well, given leaked Anthropic IPO plans that suggest it thinks it needs to spend a staggering $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure in coming years, despite possibly losing $42 billion last year - with it spending three times on infrastructure in 2025 versus 2024, $7.3 billion. Here, the AI lab’s far from being an outlier: all these guys say they want more and more data centers and more and more juice to run them. But while at least some of the public say they dislike data centers for their perceived negative impact on the water table or pumping out of carbon dioxide, it’s actually their pocketbooks that the real pushback is happening - with headlines about how Google’s proposed data center in West Memphis may ‘have’ to be paid for by a 20-year $6 utility rate hike for locals, as just one example. AI firms and some almond-based whataboutery As so often, the AI firms’ response can seem very tone deaf - like Sam Altman’s claim that 38,000 ChatGPT queries only use as much water, 0.000085 gallons, as “the production of one Californian almond;” the actual figure for the latter, say commentators, is more like 1 to 3.2 gallons, so the ratio is more like 1,000 to 11,000 queries “per almond.” Well, maybe he’s right - but the data center-AI industry isn’t being believed when it says there’s nothing to fear here. Not believed, in fact, to such an extent that, according to a September analysis by Bloomberg, local opposition “blocked or delayed” 45 U.S. data center projects worth approximately $68 billion during the second quarter of 2026. It’s not just US residents raising green fears about all this - UK citizens are also noticing, with reports of how two planned Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire data centers potentially having higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil - and with 315 more in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, the argument here, as in the US, is that fossil fuel power is the only thing available so must be used. Last month the Scottish Parliament voted to pause decisions on new AI data centers for up to a year while stricter environmental assessments and national planning guidance are developed - evidence, say activists, of a wider national UK push back against such sites. Which may or not be true, but the sector is in the spotlight. Ofgem, the national UK energy regulator, says applications in the connections queue jumped from 41 GW to 125 GW in less than a year, with data center projects accounting for at least 80 Gigawatts of that. Demand is rising so fast it’s proposing a commitment fee specifically for large data centers so speculative projects don't clog up the grid. The data center industry response So, what to make of all this? Last time we looked in depth at the “AI data centers = the burning up of Planet Earth” equation, the IT industry told us that this was a short-term problem, as renewables would end up being the main power source for all these servers and NVIDIA chips, and anyway, AI would tell us how to run these places more efficiently anyhow. Two years on and in the face of the data center backlash, what is the verdict now? The response falls into two categories: one, that the economic needs for all this are so pressing that we just need to push on, and two, well, we still need to trust that we’ll figure out how to do this more efficiently. In the words of Gary Watson, MD of Stellanor Datacenters: Some level of debate around the growth of data centers is inevitable, particularly as the scale of AI investment increases, but we shouldn’t lose sight of what these facilities actually enable; they are the backbone behind the digital services we use every day, from banking and healthcare to transport and now AI. The answer to concerns about data center growth isn’t to step back from the infrastructure needed to support the digital economy but to think carefully about where they are located and how they connect with the communities around it. artigo.texto: Novacium Delivers First Batch of Prototype Batteries to STAT with Twice the Energy Capacity of Batteries Currently in Service - The first batch, delivered to STAT in the third quarter of 2026, integrates GEN3 21700 cylindrical cells in place of the 18650 cells currently in service - With this first delivery, Novacium achieved two key project objectives: - Doubling the energy capacity of the batteries - Limiting geometric modifications to meet dimensional and connector requirements. MONTREAL and SOLAIZE, France, Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HPQ Silicon Inc. (TSX-V: HPQ) (OTCQB: HPQFF) (FRA: O08) is pleased to inform its shareholders that its strategic partner, NOVACIUM SAS, a French deep-tech company specializing in green engineering of materials for energy applications, announces that it delivered to the French Army Technical Section ("STAT"), in the third quarter of 2026, a first batch of prototype batteries intended for tactical radio sets. Using its high-capacity cells, Novacium designed batteries offering twice the energy capacity of the batteries currently in service. This delivery follows the award, at the end of June 2026, of a contract by STAT to develop and supply, in successive batches, these high-capacity prototype batteries. Transition to 21700 Cells: Double the Capacity While Preserving Compatibility To achieve this objective, Novacium integrated GEN3 21700 cylindrical cells in place of the previously used 18650 cells. This format offers higher capacity but integrating it required preserving compatibility with existing equipment. Through an optimized cell arrangement and adapted enclosure geometry, Novacium's teams limited dimensional changes to meet STAT's dimensional and connector requirements while doubling the battery's energy capacity. A patent application has been filed for this design. Through the integration of these 21700 cells, the new battery pack reaches an onboard energy capacity of 144 Wh, twice the 72 Wh of the reference battery currently in service, and an energy density of 261 Wh/kg, compared with 160 Wh/kg for the existing solution, representing a 63% increase. An adapted battery management system (BMS), combined with this patent-pending enclosure assembly system, makes the new battery fully compatible with existing connectors, chargers, and interfaces, with only minor changes to its dimensions and mass (42.6 × 98.63 × 74.35 mm; 551 g). Under a comparable usage profile, this doubled energy capacity is intended to provide up to twice the operating time of the reference battery while retaining existing connectors and chargers. STAT will evaluate the operating time actually achieved under operational conditions. An Evaluation Campaign and User Feedback Expected in the Coming Weeks The first batch of prototype batteries delivered in the third quarter of 2026 will undergo an evaluation campaign under operational conditions conducted by STAT. At the end of this phase, detailed feedback (RETEX) will be prepared jointly by STAT and Novacium in the coming weeks. Lessons learned from this field evaluation will allow Novacium to make the necessary design, ergonomic, and parameter-setting adjustments before producing and delivering a second batch that better reflects a production configuration. "Doubling the onboard energy of a tactical radio battery while retaining the existing connectors and chargers represented an engineering challenge that our teams successfully addressed. The transition to 21700 cells enabled us to double the battery's energy capacity, and we worked to limit geometric modifications to preserve compatibility with equipment currently in service. The delivery of this first batch for evaluation under operational conditions is a key milestone: user feedback will guide the adjustments to be made before production of the second batch," said Dr. Jed Kraiem, Ph.D., Chief Operating Officer of Novacium. "The delivery of this first batch illustrates Novacium's ability to transform its anode-material expertise into batteries designed for critical applications," said Bernard Tourillon, President and CEO of HPQ Silicon Inc., which is itself President of Novacium. "If the evaluation phase confirms the expected performance, this program could provide a technical basis for offering the solution to other allied forces with comparable requirements. For HPQ, this program also illustrates the strategic value of our 36.8% interest in Novacium and of its activities in the defence sector." Next Step: A Second Batch Representative of a Production Configuration Following the evaluation campaign and RETEX, Novacium will begin production of a second batch of batteries incorporating lessons learned in the field and better representing a production configuration. This second batch will integrate Novacium's new GEN4 cells, with a capacity exceeding 6,500 mAh, with the objective of increasing the battery's energy capacity at the same mass and therefore its energy density and potential operating time. This stage aims to evaluate the solution's robustness, ergonomics, and reproducibility for potential larger-scale deployment. This first delivery forms part of the expansion of Novacium's activities in the defence and autonomous-systems sectors, notably including the order for battery packs intended for French Army drones, announced on August 19, 2026 through LN'INNOV, and the order for 100 drone battery packs from Alta Ares announced on September 17, 2026. About Novacium SAS Novacium is a French deep-tech company based in Solaize, specializing in developing and producing silicon-based anode materials for lithium-ion batteries through a proprietary process. Novacium also designs custom battery cells and packs for demanding applications, particularly in the defence, aerospace and portable-energy sectors. artigo.texto: e‑STORAGE to Supply and Commission 100 MW/200 MWh Battery Storage System for OX2 in New South Wales KITCHENER, ON , Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canadian Solar Inc. (the "Company" or "Canadian Solar") (NASDAQ: CSIQ) today announced that e‑STORAGE, its energy storage solutions business, has signed an agreement to supply and commission a 100 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) for OX2's Muswellbrook Solar Farm and Battery, a solar-plus-storage project in New South Wales, Australia. Shipments are scheduled to begin in Q3 2027, with commercial operation targeted for Q3 2028. The battery cells and SolBank system will be produced in-house at Canadian Solar's manufacturing facilities, giving the customer end-to-end supply chain visibility and ensuring strict quality control across the product. e‑STORAGE will deliver an integrated solution built on SolBank 3.0 battery containers, paired with Power Conversion Systems (PCS), plant controls, and the Company's proprietary EQ-S Energy Management System (EMS) developed and built in-house by e‑STORAGE's North American software team. e‑STORAGE will be responsible for the R1 grid connection studies, supply the hybrid power plant controller that coordinates the battery with the co-located solar farm, and lead the overall integration and commissioning of the hybrid project. The arrangement is backed by a 20-year long-term service agreement (LTSA), placing hardware, proprietary software, and long-term performance under a single accountable partner. The project sits roughly 2.5 kilometers east of Muswellbrook, on land at a former coal mine within the Hunter-Central Coast Renewable Energy Zone. The location is significant: as the region's aging coal generators wind down toward retirement in the early 2030s, the dispatchable capacity they once provided must be replaced. Two-hour storage fills that gap directly, holding midday solar output and releasing it into the evening demand peak when supply from retiring thermal plants tightens. Once operational, the system will support the long-term hybrid power purchase agreement OX2 has signed for the project, converting variable solar output into firm, contracted supply. By storing and dispatching solar energy on demand, the BESS strengthens grid reliability in a region transitioning away from coal and helps deliver firm renewable power to the communities in the Hunter Region. Steve Symons, Vice President, OX2 Australia, said: "This battery storage system is what turns Muswellbrook into a true hybrid facility — pairing solar generation with storage so we can capture energy when the sun is shining and deliver it when the grid needs it most. It's a key step in providing firm, reliable renewable power to the Hunter region." Jeff Roy, President of e ‑ STORAGE, said: "Australia's energy transition is being decided in regions like the Hunter, where storage now has to carry the load that retiring coal once did. We control this project from the cell through to our own energy management software and 20 years of service, which means OX2 has one partner accountable for how the system performs over its full life." About Canadian Solar Inc. Canadian Solar is one of the world's largest solar technology and renewable energy companies. Founded in 2001 and headquartered in Kitchener, Ontario, the Company is a leading manufacturer of solar photovoltaic modules; provider of solar energy and battery energy storage solutions; and developer, owner, and operator of utility-scale solar power and battery energy storage projects. Over the past 25 years, Canadian Solar has successfully delivered nearly 180 GW of premium-quality solar photovoltaic modules to customers across the world. Through its energy storage solutions business e-STORAGE, Canadian Solar has shipped over 23 GWh of battery energy storage solutions to global markets and had a contracted backlog of $3.5 billion as of June 30, 2026. Since entering the project development business in 2010, Canadian Solar has developed, built, and connected approximately 12.4 GWp of solar power projects and 6.4 GWh of battery energy storage projects globally. Its geographically diversified project development pipeline includes approximately 22 GWp of solar and 84 GWh of battery energy storage capacity in various stages of development. Canadian Solar is one of the most bankable companies in the solar and renewable energy industry, having been publicly listed on the NASDAQ since 2006. For additional information about the Company, follow Canadian Solar on LinkedIn or visit www.canadiansolar.com. About e-STORAGE e-STORAGE is a subsidiary of Canadian Solar and a leading company specializing in designing, manufacturing, and integrating battery energy storage systems for utility-scale applications. e-STORAGE offers proprietary battery energy storage systems (BESS) spanning battery cells, battery PACKs, power conversion systems (PCS), energy management systems (EMS) and system integration. It also provides comprehensive EPC services and full-lifecycle station operation and asset management, helping customers improve grid operations across the project lifecycle. For more info, please refer to the Media&PR section of www.csestorage.com and follow our LinkedIn page. artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Sets November 12 as Investor Day to Discuss Michigan AI Expansion and Strategic Alternatives Across Its Portfolio Company reiterates 2027 guidance of $300–$350 million in revenue and $60–$80 million in consolidated Adjusted EBITDA LAS VEGAS , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that it will virtually host an investor day (the "Investor Day") on November 12, 2026, from 1:15 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. Pacific Time, to discuss the Michigan AI data center campus (the "Michigan Campus"), the status of its other portfolio businesses and strategic alternatives intended to enhance stockholder value. Participation details for Investor Day will be provided at a later date. During the Investor Day, management will provide an update as to the progress on, and expansion of, the Michigan Campus and the executed master services agreement (the "MSA") with a California-based neocloud provider (the "Customer"). As previously disclosed, the MSA contemplates the deployment of an initial 20 megawatts ("MW") of critical AI compute capacity and, if the Customer exercises all of its options to extend the term, and rights to an additional 32 MW of critical AI compute capacity, the MSA could generate more than $3.0 billion in total contract revenue from the potential 52 MW deployment over a 20-year period. The Company has previously announced that it believes the Michigan Campus could ultimately support more than 300 MW of total power capacity. The development of any capacity beyond the initial 20 MW covered by the MSA is subject to financing, regulatory approvals, engineering, utility agreements, infrastructure availability, customer demand and other conditions. There can be no assurance that additional capacity will be developed, financed, contracted or placed into service. Additionally, management is expected to provide a review of the Company's various portfolio businesses within its various sectors, including: defense; energy and infrastructure; hotel operations and commercial real estate holdings; technology and finance; and commercial lending and trading and activist investing. In addition, the Company will be discussing ongoing initiatives, including, without limitation, the AI software platform by the Company's subsidiary askROI, Inc. ("askROI") and blockchain and digital technology initiatives by Ault Markets, Inc., another subsidiary. Management anticipates discussing the Company's evaluation of strategic alternatives, including potentially selling the Michigan Campus, taking public the Company's wholly owned subsidiary, Sentinum, Inc. ("Sentinum") through an initial public offering or the Company's continued ownership and development of the Michigan Campus. The discussion will also address options involving askROI, including a potential sale, strategic partnership or divestiture, and the possibility of combining askROI with a broader technology business. Transactions under evaluation could include equity consideration, which would allow Hyperscale Data to retain an ownership interest in the combined business and participate in its potential upside. "We are focused on delivering the contracted capacity in our Michigan Campus and turning that investment into cash flow," said Milton "Todd" Ault III, Executive Chairman. "Investor Day will also provide an update on the strategic alternatives we are evaluating for the Michigan Campus and our other portfolio businesses. Our objective is to place these businesses in structures that support their development and make their value more identifiable to our stockholders." The Company reiterates its preliminary consolidated financial guidance for the year ending December 31, 2027, of $300 million to $350 million in revenue and $60 million to $80 million in Adjusted EBITDA. Based upon known and reasonably calculated projections, including management's current operating plans, anticipated customer deployments, expected financing activities, projected digital-asset initiatives and the anticipated performance of the Company's portfolio businesses, this guidance reflects management's current projections. The Company cannot provide a quantitative reconciliation of its projected Adjusted EBITDA to the most directly comparable measure calculated under GAAP, which in this case, would be net income or loss, because certain components required to calculate net income or loss cannot presently be reasonably estimated without unreasonable effort. These components include future interest expense, income taxes, depreciation and amortization, stock-based compensation, impairment charges, acquisition-related expenses and changes in the fair value of financial instruments. These items are likely to be material to the Company's future GAAP results. No definitive decision has been made regarding any strategic alternatives under evaluation. Any discussions or considerations remain preliminary, and no assurances can be given that any definitive terms will be agreed upon or result in any transaction. Any transaction would be subject to further negotiation, due diligence, execution of definitive agreements and applicable corporate and regulatory approvals, including, as applicable, approval by the Company's Board of Directors. There can be no assurance that an agreement will be reached or that, if an agreement is reached, any transaction would ultimately be consummated. No transaction timetable is assured. These reports highlight service providers excelling in private cloud, hybrid cloud and data center infrastructure management. This marks the sixth consecutive year Unisys has been recognized as a Leader with an increase in 2026 to five Leader designations from four in 2025. ISG defines Leaders as companies with comprehensive portfolios, strong market presence, established competitive strategies and a demonstrated commitment to innovation. "Organizations are looking for infrastructure environments that can support growing AI demands while remaining secure, resilient and cost-efficient," said Chris Arrasmith, chief operating officer, Unisys. "Being recognized by ISG as a Leader for the sixth consecutive year reflects the strength of our AI-driven operations, depth of our hybrid cloud expertise and commitment to enabling clients by modernizing their infrastructure and improving their resilience, so they can operate with greater confidence and efficiency." Unisys was recognized as a Leader in five market quadrants: - U.S . AI-ready Infrastructure Managed Services for Midmarket: for connecting infrastructure transformation with ongoing operations, enabling organizations to modernize data centers and build AI-ready hybrid cloud environments. - U.S . Managed Cloud Hosting and Resilient Infrastructure Services: for delivering integrated cloud hosting, disaster recovery and infrastructure optimization services for complex enterprise environments. - U.S . Public Sector AI-ready Infrastructure Managed Services: for taking a pragmatic approach to modernizing hybrid cloud environments across state, local and education organizations while balancing governance requirements and operational accountability. - U.S . Public Sector Managed Cloud Hosting and Resilient Infrastructure Services: for delivering secure, resilient cloud and data center services that strengthen continuity and control across public sector environments. - U.K. AI -ready Infrastructure Managed Services for Midmarket: for using AI-driven operations and rapid value assessments to identify modernization opportunities and optimize hybrid cloud environments for midmarket organizations. In the report, Unisys was also recognized as a Product Challenger in several quadrants, including U.S. AI-ready Infrastructure Managed Services — Large Accounts, U.K. AI-ready Infrastructure Managed Services — Large Accounts, andU.K. Managed Cloud Hosting and Resilient Infrastructure Services. Product Challengers are providers that demonstrate strong technology capabilities, broad service offerings and continued investment in expanding their market presence. "Unisys differentiates itself through its ability to translate hybrid infrastructure transformation into a governed operating model by addressing hosting, recovery and optimization as a single service, making it highly relevant for complex U.S. enterprise environments," said Shashank Rajmane, senior manager and principal analyst, ISG. artigo.texto: Commentary: Data Centers Aren’t the Only Threat to Farmland by Tim Gibbons / National Family Farm Coalition and Dena Hoff / Northern Plains Resource Council, The Daily Yonder Protests against data centers have exploded across the US, with communities revolting against a multitude of proven damaging effects on energy prices, clean air and water – and the devastation of tens of thousands of acres of agricultural land. Recent headlines in national publications report that farmers and rural communities are rejecting multimillion-dollar bids from institutional investors and tech companies to buy their farmland to build data centers. A farmer in Kentucky rejected $33 million for her farmland; another in Pennsylvania turned down a $15 million offer; and one farmer in Wisconsin even reportedly refused a whopping $70+ million bid. Land has become the next big asset class for investors, especially billionaires and private equity firms, to hide and protect their wealth. It is seen as a safe, low-risk way to park money to hedge against inflation – at the expense of farmers and local communities alike. These investors aren’t just seeking out farmland to build data centers. Just like they’re targeting housing, investment firms are buying up land and renting it back to farmers for a hefty profit. The 2024 Tenure, Ownership, and Transition of Agricultural Land (TOTAL) Survey, released this March, shows that 87% of the more than 2 million landowners renting out farmland are non-operators – that is, they are not actively farming, and the majority of these landowners never have. While these landlords raked in more than $34 billion in rent combined, the total value of farmland held for rent is $1.7 trillion – up 47% since 2014. We are watching in real time the emergence of a long-term, non-farming rural landlord class. While the TOTAL survey provides a useful indicator of farmland ownership trends, it doesn’t give us the full picture. Farmland ownership has never been effectively tracked in the US with regularity, and what limited data exists is difficult to find. The data we do have shows that investment in farmland has risen dramatically over the past two decades. Companies like AcreTrader, Farmland Partners, and others that allow individuals to invest in farmland have become increasingly popular. The most alarming growth has come from institutional investors, like pension funds, private equity firms, and wealth management groups. The value of farmland held by institutional investors has more than doubled over the past three years up to $16.6 billion dollars by 2024, an eightfold rise since 2008. Based on publicly available data alone, the largest corporate owners of US farmland control more than 2 million acres. But why are farmers selling their land in the first place? The hard truth is that farming just isn’t working as a viable livelihood anymore, and hasn’t for years. In just five years from 2017-2022, we lost 159,000 US family farms. The Farm Crisis didn’t go away in the 1980s – it’s just become quieter and less visible to most. Chronic low and volatile prices across sectors, coupled with a handful of multinational corporations tightening their iron grip over global agriculture, have pushed farmers to the brink of existence. With farm debt at an all-time high, selling the farm for the best offer possible is often the only feasible way to escape dire financial straits. And when the farm is for sale, companies with billions in assets are primed to outbid new and beginning farmers seeking land to start their own businesses. The best opportunity we have to protect farmland comes from strong federal policies that safeguard land for multiple generations of working farms and ensure farmers make a living wage. Right now, the Farmland for Farmers Act is one of the boldest pieces of federal legislation to combat this worrying trend. Modeled after anti-corporate farming laws in Midwestern states, the bill would stop large corporate entities from being able to purchase farmland only to let it lie fallow in the hopes that its value will skyrocket over time, or to rent it back to farmers at a premium price. With policies like it, coupled with a Farm Bill that allows farmers to pay their bills and sustainably grow their businesses, farmers might stand a chance. It’s long overdue for policy solutions championed by federal representatives not afraid to stand up against deep pocketed special interests. We need Congress to enact policies like the Farmland for Farmers Act that fight back against the profiteering on the backs of farmers, communities, and our natural resources. The first step in protecting farmland means supporting the next generation of farmers to enter the business with confidence and without having to compete with billionaires. We need to ensure that farmers now and in the future actually have the land they need to feed us all. Tim Gibbons is the Executive Director of the National Family Farm Coalition, a national coalition representing 30 grassroots farm, ranch, and fishing organizations in Washington, DC. A life-long Missourian, Tim has spent decades organizing family farmers, ranchers, and rural residents in support of fair, healthy and thriving rural economies, fair markets, and clean water and air. Dena Hoff represents the Northern Plains Resource Council on the NFFC Board. Since 1979, she’s raised sheep, cattle, alfalfa, corn, and edible dry beans, among other crops, on her farm in Glendive, Montana. She is an active member of and advocate for her rural community. This article first appeared on The Daily Yonder and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

artigo.texto: Juscelino põe postes, Fust e data centers na agenda do novo mandato Deputado e ex-ministro das Comunicações diz que pretende avançar com regras de compartilhamento de postes, recursos do Fust e infraestrutura para data centers O deputado federal Juscelino Filho, ex-ministro das Comunicações, colocou a regulamentação do compartilhamento de postes, a proteção dos recursos do Fust e a infraestrutura necessária à expansão dos data centers entre as prioridades de sua atuação no Congresso nos próximos anos. Reeleito para o quarto mandato, Juscelino afirmou na abertura da Futurecom 2026, nesta terça-feira, 6, em São Paulo, que pretende manter a agenda de telecomunicações e infraestrutura digital como uma das frentes de atuação parlamentar. O deputado preside a Frente Parlamentar de Telecomunicações e Soluções Digitais e disse que o grupo pretende atuar para dar continuidade às políticas do setor independentemente das mudanças no comando do governo federal. “É muito importante a gente ser vigilante”, afirmou ao tratar da continuidade dos investimentos. Segundo ele, a frente deverá trabalhar para garantir que políticas de Estado tenham sequência “independente de presidente que seja”. Relatório sobre postes deve ser apresentado Entre as pautas legislativas citadas está o PL 3.220/2019, que trata do compartilhamento de postes entre os setores elétrico e de telecomunicações e tem Juscelino como relator na Câmara. O deputado afirmou que ouviu empresas, entidades e especialistas dos dois setores e que pretende apresentar “em breve” seu relatório. A regulamentação dos postes é uma discussão de longa duração entre telecomunicações e distribuição de energia, envolvendo ocupação, preço, regularização das redes e responsabilidades das empresas que utilizam a infraestrutura. Fust volta ao centro da disputa orçamentária Juscelino também voltou a defender mecanismos que impeçam o contingenciamento dos recursos do Fundo de Universalização dos Serviços de Telecomunicações. Em seu discurso, lembrou que o Fust passou a financiar projetos de infraestrutura depois de mais de duas décadas de existência e citou aplicações em redes de fibra, escolas, áreas rurais e comunidades. O ex-ministro defendeu a continuidade dessa utilização e afirmou que o Congresso precisa garantir os recursos necessários aos investimentos. A questão também apareceu no quebra-queixo com Frederico. O atual ministro confirmou que existe uma discussão dentro do governo sobre restrições aos recursos e disse estar negociando com outras áreas do Executivo para preservar investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Redata é apenas uma etapa, diz Juscelino Na agenda de data centers, Juscelino afirmou que a aprovação do Redata representa um passo para atrair novos investimentos, mas relacionou o desenvolvimento desse mercado a uma infraestrutura mais ampla. Em sua intervenção, mencionou a necessidade de redes robustas, cabos submarinos, fibra óptica, energia e instrumentos de financiamento. “Não adianta você só ter o data center em algum lugar se você não tiver uma rede robusta, se você não tiver conectividade, velocidade, para esses dados estarem trafegando”, afirmou. O deputado também apontou a regulamentação do Redata como a próxima etapa e observou que, depois dela, haverá a discussão do ICMS com os governos estaduais. A avaliação converge com a posição apresentada pelo governo de São Paulo na Futurecom: o estado pretende discutir a adequação de sua tributação depois da regulamentação federal. Continuidade das políticas entra no debate A diferença entre a fala de Juscelino e as manifestações mais institucionais da abertura está na preocupação explícita com a continuidade das políticas públicas após a próxima mudança de ciclo político. O deputado defendeu que investimentos em conectividade e infraestrutura digital sejam tratados como políticas permanentes, independentemente de quem ocupe a Presidência. A agenda apresentada por Juscelino reúne, assim, questões que estão em diferentes estágios: o Redata já passou pelo Congresso e depende de regulamentação; o compartilhamento de postes continua em tramitação; e a proteção dos recursos do Fust permanece vinculada às decisões legislativas e orçamentárias. Para o setor de telecomunicações, essas três frentes deverão ocupar parte relevante da agenda do Congresso no encerramento de 2026 e no início da próxima legislatura.

artigo.texto: EcoPro BM (247540) is strengthening its strategic partnership with Samsung SDI (006400) with the aim of commercializing sulfide-based solid-state batteries in 2027. EcoPro BM said on the 6th that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Samsung SDI to cooperate on materials development for solid-state batteries. The two companies will pursue joint research and development in solid-state batteries, a core next-generation battery technology. EcoPro BM and Samsung SDI plan to strengthen their cooperation framework from the early development stage through quality evaluation and the establishment of mass-production systems, raising both technological maturity and business competitiveness. They will also widen the scope of cooperation across core materials, including cathode materials for solid-state batteries as well as electrolytes for cathodes and for separators. Samsung SDI will work on solid-state battery cell development and the advancement of mass-production technology, while EcoPro BM will handle the development of core materials for solid-state batteries. Solid-state batteries can improve safety and performance at the same time, making them a key technology for future industries such as electric vehicles and humanoid robots. EcoPro BM has secured proprietary process technology in sulfide-based solid electrolytes, a core material for solid-state batteries, and operates a pilot plant with annual capacity of 40 tons. In August, the company was selected for the "Super Eul Project," a government program supporting materials, parts and equipment companies run by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, in recognition of those research and development results. Through the program, it will receive 20 billion won in research and development support over more than seven years. In July, EcoPro BM unveiled a full value chain roadmap for solid-state batteries at an investor briefing for retail investors. "We are currently reviewing trial production with leading customers, and we expect the earliest mass-production timing to be 2027," said Kong Bo-hyun, an executive director in charge of research and development at EcoPro BM. "We have completed the design of the mass-production line and are preparing so that construction can begin immediately in line with customer demand."

artigo.texto: Judge dismisses lawsuit challenging $2.8B Valara data center in S.C. SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (WRDW/WAGT) - A judge has thrown out a lawsuit that sought to block permits for Valara Holdings’ $2.8 billion data center in South Carolina. The group Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County argued the county broke its own rules by approving the project as a “minor” development, which gets staff-only review with no public hearing. They said a project this big should have gone through “major” review, with public notice, public comment and a Planning Commission vote. Judge J. Derham Cole Jr. threw the case out Oct. 6 for two reasons: - No specific harm shown: The judge said concerns about noise, dust, traffic, transparency and health were too general. Under state law, neighbors must show they were “specially damaged” to block a project. - Wrong process: The judge said the group should have appealed to the county’s Board of Zoning Appeals within 10 days first, before going to court. He also said the fight over the second permit is too early because the county hasn’t decided on it yet. That second application — for four new buildings, a power yard and cooling systems, is still pending. The first permit to redevelop the old Kohler plant was approved in August 2025. The ruling also ends the group’s bid to pause construction. A judge heard that pause request Sept. 17 and took it under advisement. In August, state regulators dismissed a separate challenge over Valara’s plans for gas turbines to power the site. In June, Spartanburg County paused new data center applications for one year, but that does not stop Valara, which was already underway. Read the order in full: Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. artigo.texto: Key Stats for Amazon Stock - Price change for Amazon stock in last 6 months: 18% - $AMZN Stock Price as of Oct. 2: $252 - 52-Week High: $287 - $AMZN Stock Price Target: $331 What Happened? Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) said its cloud unit will invest more than $1 billion over the next five years. The money will go to US communities that host its data centers. Amazon Web Services made the announcement on Friday. The plan covers education, job training, and energy affordability. It also covers water and energy preservation. AWS also promised to tackle the impact of its data centers on electricity and water use. The move makes sense. Data centers power and run AI models. But communities across the US have pushed back. They worry about electricity demand and utility costs. AWS noted that more than 100 data center moratoriums are being considered nationwide. The backlash is also a political issue ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025. It has large projects or expansions planned in Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia, and Mississippi. AWS CEO Matt Garman said the buildout is urgent. He said other countries also see the benefits of AI. He added that the countries leading in AI will shape it. AWS also said it will be water positive by 2030. That means it will return more water to communities than it uses. It says it is 75% of the way there. What the Market Is Telling Us About Amazon Stock $1 billion is small compared with what Amazon spends. On the Q2 call, management said it expects about $220 billion in cash capex this year. Most of that supports AI and AWS. So this pledge is more about public trust than cost. That trust matters for Amazon stock. AWS is the growth engine. Revenue rose 36.7% last quarter, its fastest pace in 18 quarters. Backlog reached $496 billion. AWS also posted $16.6 billion in operating income. Management says demand is higher than capacity. It expects that to stay true in 2027. New data centers are how Amazon meets that demand. If local opposition slows approvals, that could hold back growth. That is the real risk for Amazon stock. Amazon also said it plans to double its power capacity by the end of 2027 from 2025 levels. Community support will help make that possible. For now, the market will likely stay focused on AWS growth and capex returns. Still, rising local pushback is worth watching. Any new moratoriums could affect how investors view Amazon stock. A clear community plan may ease some of that worry for Amazon stockholders.

artigo.texto: Amazon warns $68 billion in blocked data centers threatens US AI lead — AWS CEO decries 100 proposed bans, pledges $1B community fund Various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down - AWS CEO Amazon has issued grave warnings to communities opposing data centers, stating that their actions could cause irreversible damage to the U.S. economy and national security. In a lengthy 3000-word post earlier today, October 2, CEO of Amazon Web Services (AWS), Matt Garman detailed the many benefits of Artificial Intelligence, comparing the technology’s impact on the economy to those of modern transportation systems and the Internet, before attempting to debunk “myths” around data centers and calling on local communities to be more receptive to build-outs as a matter of national urgency. The post also details Amazon's plans to do more for data center host communities through its “Built Together” community investment frameworks. After outlining AI’s impact and the need for data center buildouts, Garman explained why it was imperative for the U.S. to lead the AI race. “The countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run. The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so,” he wrote, presenting urgent buildouts as a key factor in leading that race. Next, Garman addressed growing anti-data center movements that have reportedly blocked data center projects worth $68 billion in the second quarter of 2026 alone, warning that if the 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country should go through, “the US could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations.” He also pointed out that unlike transportation infrastructure, the comparably critical data center buildout is not funded by taxpayer money, but by private firms. The post dismissed many of the concerns about the buildouts as myths, then proceeded to attempt to debunk them. Garman said that, contrary to popular belief, “Data centers actually use very little water relative to other industries,” a position many hyperscalers have repeated. Amazon earlier claimed that its data centers consume only 0.075% of the water Americans use to water their lawns and gardens. Garman also claims the narrative that data centers are driving up energy bills is “misleading and convenient scapegoating.” He argues that AI is simply precipitating an expansion of power infrastructure that was always bound to happen. “Once we collectively build out this new capacity, again funded by the private sector, it should lead to flat or lower rates in the future for residents living in communities with these expanded grids,” he said. On the other hand, contradictory reports claim that AI data centers trigger a "massive irreversible" 76% electricity price spike. The U.S. House also recently passed a bill that directed regulators to consider making AI data centers pay for grid upgrades to minimize the impact on residents. The bill was eventually rejected in the Senate, with opponents saying it was "toothless" and didn't do enough to protect residents. Speaking on pollution, Garman says that data centers emitting huge amounts of pollution with their large backup diesel generators is a myth. He claims that while data centers have rarely used backup power in case of a power outage, this is only necessary because many industries depend on the facilities. This claim doesn’t exactly address growing concerns of pollution from gas turbines powering off-grid data centers. Elon Musk recently came under fire for using unlicensed gas turbines at the Colossus data center. Lastly, Garman said claims that communities do not benefit from data centers are false, citing “considerable tax revenue, positive economic impact, large numbers of good jobs, and education programs” as some of the benefits to the communities where data centers are built. Microsoft pledged to invest $1 billion in local infrastructure improvements in its Hyperion data center community and had reportedly awarded $1.6 billion in contracts to local businesses since construction began, in addition to paying teacher bonuses. As benefits specifically on Amazon’s part, Garman listed an estimated $3 billion in taxes to St. Joseph County, Indiana, over time; more than $1 billion already contributed to communities across the U.S.; thousands of jobs created in building and running the data centers; and education programs with over 10,000 educators and learners enrolled.
