artigo.texto: Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) delivered more vehicles than Wall Street expected in the third quarter of 2026, giving investors a reason to turn more positive on the electric vehicle maker’s near-term outlook. Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles in Q3, beating the company-compiled analyst consensus of 461,974. Deliveries also rose 1.3% from 480,126 vehicles in Q2. However, they remained 2.1% below the 497,099 vehicles delivered in Q3 2025. The stronger-than-expected result helped Tesla stock rebound. Shares closed at $370.59 on October 2, up 4.7% in the session. Reuters reported that the stock gained more than 5% earlier in trading after the delivery figures were released. Still, Tesla faces a growing challenge from Chinese EV giant BYD. BYD’s battery-electric vehicle sales continued to pull further ahead of Tesla during the quarter. Tesla Q3 Deliveries Beat Estimates Tesla’s Q3 delivery result came in well above the latest company-compiled consensus. Analysts surveyed by Tesla had expected 461,974 deliveries, with a median estimate of 463,406. Tesla ultimately delivered 486,532 vehicles, exceeding the consensus by about 24,600 vehicles. The Model 3 and Model Y remained the company’s main volume drivers. Tesla delivered 478,237 Model 3/Y vehicles during the quarter, compared with just 8,295 deliveries across its other models. Production, meanwhile, reached 464,391 vehicles. Tesla also deployed 13.7 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage products during Q3. That figure was below the 15.9 GWh analyst consensus, highlighting that Tesla’s energy business remains an important part of the company’s broader growth story. The delivery beat is significant because analysts had entered the quarter expecting a decline. FactSet estimates cited by MarketWatch had pointed to roughly 461,000 vehicles, or a 7% year-over-year decline. Instead, Tesla limited the decline to about 2%. Tesla vs. BYD: The EV Gap Is Growing Despite Tesla’s better-than-expected quarter, its competition with BYD is becoming more intense. BYD sold 762,478 battery-electric passenger vehicles during Q3, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. That was up nearly 31% from a year earlier and 37% from Q2. As a result, BYD sold about 275,946 more battery-electric vehicles than Tesla during the quarter. The comparison needs some context. Tesla reports deliveries of its vehicles, while BYD sells both battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids under its broader new-energy vehicle category. BYD sold 1.32 million new-energy vehicles in Q3, including both types. Total NEV sales rose 18.8% year over year. BYD also recorded 463,561 new-energy vehicle sales in September alone, its strongest monthly result of 2026. Overseas passenger vehicle and pickup shipments jumped 153.9% year over year to 179,877 in September, Reuters reported. This international expansion could become increasingly important for the global EV market. It also shows how competition is moving beyond traditional EV strongholds as Chinese manufacturers expand into overseas markets. Sustainability Remains a Key Part of Tesla’s Story Tesla’s delivery numbers also matter from a sustainability perspective because more EV sales can accelerate the shift away from gasoline-powered vehicles. The International Energy Agency said global electric car sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, with EVs accounting for one in four new cars sold worldwide. China remained the largest EV market, accounting for six out of 10 electric cars sold globally. - Tesla says its products helped avoid 37 million metric tons of CO₂e emissions in its 2025 Impact Report. The company’s sustainability strategy also extends beyond vehicles to battery storage, solar energy, and its supply chain. The company also highlighted the emissions benefit of its electric vehicles over their operating lives. It estimates that one Tesla vehicle can avoid about 32 metric tons of CO₂ emissions over its lifetime compared with a comparable gasoline-powered vehicle. However, the actual benefit varies by factors such as electricity generation, vehicle efficiency, and driving patterns. However, EV growth does not eliminate the environmental impact of manufacturing. Batteries require minerals such as lithium, nickel, graphite, and other materials, while vehicle production and electricity generation also create emissions. That makes the growth of energy storage particularly relevant. Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of storage products in Q3, while the company-compiled analyst consensus had expected 15.9 GWh. Large-scale batteries can help integrate renewable power into electricity systems by storing electricity when supply is high and releasing it when demand rises. Can Tesla’s Q3 Delivery Beat Support Its Stock? Tesla stock entered October under pressure after a volatile year. Shares closed at $370.59 on October 2, although the latest delivery beat provided some relief. Investors are now looking beyond vehicle sales. Tesla’s valuation increasingly depends on its plans for robotaxis, AI, robotics and energy storage, while its automotive business remains critical to funding those investments. Tesla will report its full Q3 financial results on October 21. The earnings report should give investors a clearer view of vehicle margins, revenue, cash flow, and spending on its next-generation businesses. For now, the delivery beat strengthens Tesla’s near-term position. However, BYD’s growing lead in battery-electric vehicle sales highlights the competitive pressure facing Tesla as global EV adoption accelerates. The longer-term sustainability opportunity remains significant, but Tesla must balance EV growth with improving manufacturing efficiency, battery supply chains and the emissions impact of its operations.

artigo.texto: Springfield, IL-(Effingham Radio)- As more Illinois municipalities weigh moratoriums on data center construction, Gov. J.B. Pritzker is pressing state lawmakers to pass uniform regulations – despite light pushback from some who view the proposed rules as potentially misguided. The Illinois General Assembly failed to pass legislation to further regulate data centers statewide through the POWER Act before the end of the spring session on June 1. Pritzker said recently he’s not concerned about getting short-term solutions passed sooner than when state lawmakers return to Springfield. Pritzker noted there isn’t always transparency for communities when a data center project is being pitched in a locality. State Rep. Jeff Keicher, R-Sycamore, said data center non-disclosure agreements aren’t much different from privacy measures put in place when others buy a property, but there should be transparency after that. He also said there’s been benefits in his district including significant decreases to the property tax levy – though he acknowledged there are bad actors in the space. Lawmakers are set to return to Springfield for a six-day veto session from Nov. 17-19, and Dec. 1-3. The legislature is expected to return to bills that didn’t pass in May, such as the Power Act. Story from Illinois Radio Network

artigo.texto: IMPERIAL — As part of their bus tour across 28 states, conservative non-profit organization Humans First stopped at Eager Park in Imperial to spread their message against an “unaccountable AI buildout” on Friday, Oct. 3. Despite the nationwide bus tour being called “AI Data Center Revolt,” Kylie Jane Kremer, Senior Advisor for Humans First, said the movement is not anti-AI or anti-AI data centers, but rather “America first.” “We’re definitely not anti-data center, we’re not anti-AI; we’re not anti-tech, as I said. We believe we can do this in a way that is transparent and lets communities know what they’re getting into and what’s involved,” said Kremer. For Humans First, communities facing AI data center proposals should be the ones with the authority to welcome or reject the projects while having full transparency from the project developers and local officials. “If these data centers are so great, if they’re going to bring so many jobs and be so powerful in these communities and be this economic boom, why are they not being transparent?” said Kremer. ”Shouldn’t they be able to sell this to the American people very easily and tell them all the facts? Because if they’re so great, it should be an overwhelming yes. But they know that that’s not the truth, that these are not great for communities.” “People don’t want them, and so that’s why they’re having to go about it in sneaky ways where they’re doing NDAs, payouts, and that sort of thing,” explained Kremer. The bus tour transporting the Humans First team began their cross-country trip with stops at 35 different cities in Austin, Texas, and going as far east as Washington, D.C. The tour then made its way toward the West Coast, where it will reach San Francisco as its final stop on Monday, Oct. 5. Kremer explained that each city the Data Center Revolt bus tour stopped at was at different stages of an AI data center project, but their goal to elevate community voices and make them engaged stayed the same. Some cities face an uphill battle when it comes to opposing AI data centers, such as Jonesburg, Missouri, one of the stops made by Kremer and her team. Jonesburg is located in rural Montgomery County, which currently has two data centers under development, despite local opposition. “It’s a town of, I think, 640 people. They have roughly an $18 million county budget annually. Google and Amazon are going there and bringing two massive hyperscale data centers over $25 billion,” explained Kremer. “How does a town of 640 people with an $18 million annual budget even begin to fight that? So we went there; it’s about generational land, farmers, communities that really matter just like here in Imperial.” Tom Gaitens, Senior Advisor for Humans First, praised Imperial for their success in opposing the hyperscale AI data center proposed in Imperial County, which, if built, would be the largest data center in the state. “What you did here needs to be echoed around the country. What you did here, you’re heroes. You found out the process late in the game, and they tried to hide it from you,” said Gaitens. “They did not want to disclose this information in public hearings and allow you to see what your neighbors were going to be doing, but you are the heroes who stood up, faced this giant, a $10 billion giant, and you held it at bay.” Local opposition against data centers has been an issue that Democrats and Republicans find common ground on, with Kremer noting that the issue affects local communities as a whole, bringing them together against a common cause. Kremer stressed the importance of staying engaged in creating opposition to data centers, and despite meaningful victories, the issue of data centers is far from over. “We’re seeing time and time again that communities have wins, and then the people get complacent or, you know, have this victory and they kind of take a break from it. What happens when people let their guard down is that the big tech companies come back with bigger lawyers, smarter about the process,” said Kremer. “We are on track to have over 10,000 data centers in the United States by 2030. And right now we’re just roughly over 5000, so that will be doubling it. So this issue is not going away; it’s not just temporary, this is a long-term play that people need to remain engaged in,” explained Kremer.

artigo.texto: Demand for artificial intelligence data centers will continue to push shares of Vertiv higher, according to BMO Capital Markets. The firm initiated coverage of the stock on Sunday with an outperform rating and $329 price target, which implies roughly 30% upside from Friday's close. The company provinces digital infrastructure and hardware for data centers and other facilities, with data centers making up about 85% of its revenue, said analyst Daniel DiCicco. He called Vertiv a "premium data center play" that has already run up more than 900% in the last five years. Shares have pulled back from their peak in May and now offer an attractive entry point, he said. "Vertiv is well positioned as data centers are increasing in scale and intensity (more power to the rack) and demand for resilience and speed to deployment continues to increase," DiCicco wrote in a note to clients. VRT YTD mountain Vertiv year to date There are more than 4,700 data centers in the United States — and the number is growing . Some $6 billion was spent on land purchases in the U.S. for future data centers in the first half of 2026, according to commercial real estate firm Avison Young. That's a 79% increase from last year, the firm found. Vertiv's management has estimated that its $75 billion total addressable market is increasing 16% to 18% a year, with data centers growing 18% to 20% annually, DiCicco said. However, the company's long-term growth forecasts could be conservative, he noted. Plus, Vertiv has a full suite of offerings. The current rate for data center content is $3.25 to $3.75 per megawatt, but innovation, standardization, service growth and integrated systems can all push that higher, DiCicco pointed out. "VRT has positioned itself as one of the few providers capable of delivering a fully integrated power and thermal management solution across the entire data center," he said. Shares of Vertiv are up nearly 56% year to date. — CNBC's Tobias Burns contributed reporting.

artigo.texto: San Francisco approves, other cities consider bans and reviews on data center growth SANTA CLARA, Calif. - As artificial intelligence and digital services rapidly expand, several California local governments are stepping back to evaluate the footprint of data center development in their communities. Cities across the Bay Area and Southern California are considering pauses or reviewing long-standing policies to address rising concerns over energy demand, water usage, and environmental impacts. High demand prompts policy evaluation The City of Santa Clara stands as one of California's primary data center hubs. Despite its population of roughly 133,000 residents, Santa Clara currently hosts 56 data centers, with two additional projects in development. The industry has proven highly lucrative for Santa Clara, contributing $35 million annually in taxes directly into the city's general fund. However, high power demand prompted the city's municipal utility, Silicon Valley Power, to stop accepting new data center applications in 2023. Santa Clara officials are launching a year-long interdepartmental review of environmental, water, power, and quality-of-life impacts before updating local development rules. Regional moratoriums and community pushback Local perspective: In Oakland, City Council members are considering a 45-day temporary moratorium on new data center construction. Protesters gathered at Oakland City Hall ahead of a council vote scheduled for Tuesday night to voice concerns about local neighborhood impacts, high water consumption, and energy efficiency. Similarly, San Francisco supervisors unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on data center approvals, declaring an immediate threat to public health, safety, and welfare without comprehensive regulations in place. Supervisor Shamann Walton noted the pause allows the city time to study energy, water, air quality, land use, and community effects. Meanwhile, Southern California is taking a similar approach. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors received a proposal to permanently ban massive "hyperscale" data centers—frequently built to support resource-intensive AI workloads—while leaving allowances for smaller operations.

artigo.texto: Silicon has long been the tantalizing prize of lithium-ion battery research. Theoretically, it can hold roughly ten times more lithium than the graphite that dominates today’s anodes, promising batteries that last dramatically longer on a single charge. Yet silicon has a fatal flaw that has kept it out of most commercial cells: when lithium floods into the material during charging, it swells by hundreds of percent, cracking particles, fracturing electrodes, and destroying the delicate interfaces that make a battery work. A team of researchers in Qinghai, China, now reports a practical route around this problem, combining a metal-processing technique borrowed from metallurgy with a carefully tuned dose of ordinary graphite. The study, published in the journal Ionics by Zhanshou Yang, Fa-Feng Xu, and colleagues at the Qinghai Institute of Salt Lakes of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, centers on a process called dealloying. In dealloying, one element is selectively dissolved out of an alloy, leaving behind a sponge-like scaffold of the remaining element riddled with pores at the nanometer scale. The technique has a pedigree in materials science, having been used to create nanoporous gold and other architectures, and it has increasingly attracted attention as a scalable way to fabricate porous electrode materials for rechargeable batteries. Applied to silicon-bearing alloys, it produces porous silicon structures whose internal voids act as built-in expansion chambers. That architectural trick addresses the core failure mode of silicon anodes. In a dense silicon particle, the volume change that accompanies lithiation generates enormous mechanical stress. Particles pulverize, fresh surfaces are repeatedly exposed to the electrolyte, and a thick, unstable solid electrolyte interphase layer grows and rebuilds with every cycle, consuming lithium and raising the cell’s internal resistance. A porous particle, by contrast, can expand into its own empty space. The pores absorb much of the strain, the particle’s outer dimensions stay comparatively stable, and the electrode’s conductive network and binder matrix survive far longer. Porosity alone, however, does not solve every problem. Silicon is a semiconductor with modest intrinsic conductivity, and the tortuous pathways through a porous structure can slow both electrons and lithium ions. The Qinghai team therefore wrapped the porous silicon in a carbon coating, producing a composite they designate Si@C. The carbon shell serves a dual role: it provides an electron-conducting highway that connects the silicon to the current collector, and it acts as a mechanical and chemical skin that stabilizes the electrode structure and limits parasitic reactions with the electrolyte. Carbon coatings of this kind have become a standard strategy in silicon anode research, but their effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of the underlying silicon architecture and on how the composite is formulated. The second half of the team’s strategy is arguably the more pragmatic one: blending the carbon-coated porous silicon with graphite. Graphite remains the workhorse anode of the lithium-ion industry, prized for its low cost, flat voltage profile, and remarkable structural stability over thousands of cycles. By mixing silicon with graphite, researchers can trade some of silicon’s enormous capacity for graphite’s reliability, while the graphite matrix helps buffer swelling and maintains electronic contact throughout the electrode. The ratio matters enormously. Too little silicon and the energy-density gain is marginal; too much and the electrode’s mechanical integrity collapses within a few hundred cycles. Yang and colleagues systematically optimized this ratio, testing different proportions of porous silicon to graphite before settling on a mass ratio of 1:2. At that composition, the composite delivered the best combination of capacity, stability, and rate performance in their experiments. The finding underscores a broader lesson in battery engineering: the performance of a composite electrode is not simply the weighted average of its components, but emerges from how those components interact mechanically and electrochemically during cycling. The graphite appears to function not merely as a diluent but as an active structural partner for the swelling silicon. The electrochemical results reported in the paper are striking. After 500 charge-discharge cycles, the optimized Si@C anode retained a reversible capacity of 688.5 milliampere-hours per gram, corresponding to a capacity retention of 63.6 percent. For context, conventional graphite anodes typically deliver around 350 to 370 milliampere-hours per gram, so even after substantial degradation the composite still stores nearly twice as much charge per unit mass. Equally important is the coulombic efficiency, which the team reports at 99.9 percent. This figure measures how many lithium ions that enter the anode during charging come back out during discharge, and values approaching 100 percent indicate that parasitic side reactions, which slowly poison a cell, have been largely suppressed. The authors state that these results surpass previously reported data for comparable silicon-based anodes in both cycling stability and rate performance, the latter describing the electrode’s ability to deliver capacity at high charging speeds. Rate capability is often the quiet casualty of silicon anode designs, because the same structural features that buffer swelling can impede ion transport. The combination of porous silicon, a conductive carbon coating, and a graphite matrix appears to keep those transport pathways open even as the electrode ages, allowing the material to sustain fast charging without catastrophic capacity loss. The work also carries a regional and industrial dimension. artigo.texto: Data centers pedem redução de 90% do ICMS para equipamentos Brasscom relata resistência dos estados à proposta discutida no Confaz; entidades também cobram regulamentação do Redata. As entidades do setor de data centers negociam com o Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) uma redução de 90% do ICMS sobre equipamentos contemplados pelo Redata. Segundo Walter Wolff, diretor de projetos da Brasscom, a proposta enfrenta resistência dos estados e busca complementar os incentivos federais do regime. A discussão foi apresentada durante a abertura do Data Center World, nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro. De acordo com Wolff, o setor trabalha com uma lista de 25 equipamentos, concentrada em eletrônicos. A relação está em discussão com outras associações, incluindo representantes dos fabricantes brasileiros. O dirigente explicou que o foco da negociação está nos equipamentos de tecnologia, sem abranger toda a infraestrutura física dos empreendimentos. A Brasscom defende que o tratamento estadual acompanhe os benefícios federais para aumentar a competitividade do Brasil na disputa por projetos. Na avaliação de Wolff, a negociação deve considerar a concorrência com outros países pela instalação de data centers. A Conexis também participa da mobilização. Seu diretor jurídico, Bruno Cavalcanti, afirmou que a entidade assinou, com outras associações, um manifesto dirigido ao Confaz. “Não existe um Redata completo sem esse endereçamento do tema no Confaz”, declarou. Regulamentação ainda em discussão Além do ICMS, as entidades aguardam a regulamentação do Redata. Wolff afirmou que a expectativa é concluir essa etapa nas próximas semanas, mas reconheceu os obstáculos nas negociações. “Tem sido uma discussão extremamente difícil”, disse o dirigente da Brasscom. Segundo ele, as condições de fornecimento de energia aos data centers estão entre os assuntos discutidos. A definição dos equipamentos beneficiados também permanece pendente. Renan Lima Alves, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), explicou que a lista de classificações fiscais dos produtos ainda precisa ser divulgada, assim como os procedimentos para apresentação de pedidos de inclusão. Alves destacou a dificuldade de aproveitamento dos créditos tributários da aquisição de hardware na prestação dos serviços. Por isso, a entidade considera o tratamento do ICMS parte relevante da política de redução dos custos de implantação. Wolff também apontou a previsibilidade dos benefícios para os próximos cinco anos como um elemento importante para decisões de investimento de longo prazo. Incentivo à transferência de processamento Para o presidente da Equinix, Victor Arnaud, a combinação entre regulamentação do Redata, tratamento dos tributos estaduais e compatibilidade com a reforma tributária determinará as condições de aplicação do incentivo. O executivo identificou como oportunidade imediata a transferência para o Brasil de cargas de processamento que atendem ao mercado brasileiro, mas estão hospedadas no exterior. Segundo ele, a redução da diferença de custos pode estimular empresas a manter esses dados em território nacional. Arnaud ressaltou, porém, que a demanda por data centers já cresce independentemente do regime. Na avaliação do executivo, os incentivos podem ampliar esse movimento e melhorar as condições de atração de novos projetos.

artigo.texto: A Posição de Byron Donalds sobre Data Centers Entra em Choque com a Reação dos Eleitores da Flórida Byron Donalds transformou os data centers em uma prioridade econômica, apesar de uma pesquisa na Flórida apontar 79% de oposição à construção de instalações de IA no estado. Esse conflito tornou a posição de Byron Donalds sobre data centers um teste decisivo para sua campanha ao governo. Donalds argumenta que a Flórida pode receber grandes campi de computação sem transferir seus custos de eletricidade e água para os moradores. Ele apoia o controle local e proteções ao consumidor, mas rejeita uma paralisação estadual de novos empreendimentos. Seu adversário democrata, David Jolly, escolheu uma linha divisória mais clara. Jolly apoia uma moratória, enquanto Donalds afirma que construções cuidadosamente reguladas devem continuar. Essa diferença oferece aos eleitores uma escolha incomumente direta sobre quem deve arcar com os custos da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. A disputa deixou de ser um debate abstrato sobre a tecnologia do futuro. Condados e cidades da Flórida já estão suspendendo projetos enquanto estudam a demanda por eletricidade, o consumo de água, o ruído, o uso do solo e o financiamento dos serviços públicos. Para Donalds, o problema político é maior do que defender uma única política. Ele precisa convencer moradores céticos de que as proteções funcionarão, enquanto interesses ligados a data centers investem pesadamente nas eleições do estado. A Posição de Byron Donalds sobre Data Centers Enfrenta uma Revolta Local Donalds avançou em direção a salvaguardas mais fortes, mas não se juntou à campanha crescente para interromper a construção em escala hyperscale. Em um evento de campanha em julho, em Clearwater, Donalds disse que era favorável a desacelerar o desenvolvimento quando as comunidades precisassem de proteções mais robustas. No entanto, ele se opôs a uma moratória estadual que suspenderia todos os projetos qualificados. Ele também prometeu respeitar as decisões dos governos locais. Se um condado ou cidade rejeitar um data center, disse Donalds, o estado não deveria forçar essa comunidade a aceitá-lo. Essa posição o coloca entre defensores da indústria e eleitores que exigem uma pausa abrangente. Ela reconhece a oposição local sem aceitar a política central proposta por Jolly e por vários governos de condados. A distinção importa porque os projetos em debate não são simples salas de servidores. Instalações hyperscale são campi de computação concebidos para operar enormes frotas de servidores para serviços em nuvem e inteligência artificial. Suas necessidades contínuas de eletricidade podem se equiparar às de grandes operações industriais. Os equipamentos de refrigeração também podem aumentar a pressão sobre os sistemas de água, dependendo do projeto e das condições operacionais da instalação. A Flórida já tem mais de 100 data centers em operação, segundo reportagens citadas por organizações de notícias estaduais. As disputas mais intensas envolvem locais hyperscale propostos, e não todos os prédios existentes que armazenam ou processam dados. Condados em todo o estado adotaram ou consideraram moratórias temporárias. Leon, Nassau, Pasco, Sarasota e outros governos locais avaliaram pausas enquanto autoridades desenvolvem regras de zoneamento e infraestrutura. O Condado de Nassau, por exemplo, publicou uma moratória temporária que abrange o recebimento, a análise e a aprovação de pedidos para data centers. Autoridades de Pasco também consideraram uma pausa de um ano devido a preocupações com infraestrutura e recursos naturais. Essas ações revelam um movimento político de baixo para cima. Autoridades locais estão respondendo a moradores que temem custos mais altos de serviços públicos, esgotamento dos recursos hídricos, ruído persistente de geradores e construções industriais perto de suas casas. As objeções também refletem incerteza. As comunidades muitas vezes não dispõem de informações públicas suficientes sobre a demanda final de energia de uma instalação proposta, seu método de refrigeração, geração de reserva, incentivos fiscais ou empregos de longo prazo. Essa lacuna de informação oferece aos defensores da moratória uma mensagem direta. Eles argumentam que os governos devem estabelecer as regras antes de aprovar empreendimentos que podem remodelar o planejamento dos serviços públicos por décadas. Donalds propõe uma sequência diferente. Ele quer proteções aplicáveis, tomada de decisão local e continuidade das construções onde as comunidades concederem aprovação. Sua posição pressupõe que a Flórida consegue avaliar os projetos individualmente. A oposição argumenta que decisões fragmentadas deixam os moradores expostos a riscos que ultrapassam as fronteiras dos condados e das concessionárias. Esse desacordo criou a tensão central da campanha. Donalds apresenta o desenvolvimento regulado como um caminho para o crescimento econômico, enquanto críticos veem a mesma política como um subsídio público evitável. A disputa se intensificou à medida que desenvolvedores de data centers e organizações aliadas ampliaram sua atividade política. Reportagens compiladas a partir de registros estaduais de campanha estimaram seus gastos na Flórida em mais de US$ 22 milhões durante o ciclo eleitoral. Mais de US$ 5 milhões teriam apoiado Donalds ou iniciativas alinhadas à sua candidatura. Esses gastos não comprovam que doadores controlem sua política, mas intensificam o escrutínio público sobre cada promessa que ele faz. Para os eleitores, portanto, a questão central não é se Donalds reconhece as preocupações locais. É se suas salvaguardas propostas conseguem superar as pressões financeiras e técnicas criadas por projetos de dimensão sem precedentes. artigo.texto: Large-scale battery storage, life extension for Lepreau and new nuclear feature in N.B. Power’s latest plan Ramp-up of wind, solar and gas combustion turbines also figure in utility's future N.B. Power’s latest plan is calling for large-scale battery storage in the province by 2035. The utility released a new integrated resource plan on Monday, replacing a 2023 version of the plan that was criticized as out-of-date during hearings on the proposed 500-megawatt Tantramar gas plant earlier this year. The plan is N.B. Power’s roadmap for making sure it can meet energy demand over the coming decades. It calls for 500 megawatts of battery storage in the province in the next decade and also for an extension of life for the Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station that would take it beyond its estimated expiry date in 2045. The plan also calls for big build-outs of wind and solar generation, an expansion of gas turbine generation, and the possible addition of new nuclear generation on the Point Lepreau site. 'Final throes' of analysis on battery proposals Brad Coady, the utility's chief commercial officer, said he’s “hopeful that we can get to a battery here in the short run.” N.B. Power issued requests for proposals for 50-megawatt battery storage projects in 2023 and in 2025, but the utility has yet to build a large-scale project. The batteries allow energy to be saved up and used during peak times. Coady said the utility is “in the final throes of doing the analysis at our latest call for proposals.” According to the new resource plan, the first 500 megawatts of battery storage development is cost-competitive with combustion turbine technology, such as the Tantramar gas and diesel plant. But Coady said the proposals he has seen in response to N.B. Power’s December 2025 request for proposals would require government subsidies. “Based on the bids and offers that were submitted, they're not great without government help,” said Coady. “So we're working very closely with our federal government to say, 'Can we make these cost effective solutions for New Brunswickers?'” Nuclear decision has public policy angle The 2023 version of the plan named small modular nuclear reactors as a critical part of N.B. Power’s future. The 2026 plan takes a more technology-agnostic approach, which “could include large nuclear or could include small modular nuclear,” said Coady. The plan explores the possibility of adding 750 megawatts of new nuclear capacity at the Point Lepreau site by 2039 or 2040. It also calls for either another new nuclear project or the refurbishment of Point Lepreau in 2045. Coady acknowledged the conversation over nuclear power would go beyond the scope of N.B. Power’s plan. “The decision for a future nuclear plant in New Brunswick is also going to have to be a pretty strong public policy angle,” said Coady. While the utility does not include a new nuclear plant in its “base case," said Coady, it does identify “the amount of utility it brings the power system.” Lepreau costs, especially when it's down Coady acknowledged that repairs to Lepreau have been driving increased debt with N.B. Power in recent years. But he noted those investments are expected to pay off for the next 20 years. “I'd argue the larger driver to our debt is actually when [Lepreau] doesn't produce the electricity that we depend on it for,” said Coady, “and we have to turn to more expensive sources.” In addition to proposed nuclear and battery capacity, the plans also calls for big increases to wind and solar generation and more gas turbine projects. “I often describe the power system much like an orchestra,” said Coady, “and we need all parts of that orchestra performing the tune or we're not going to sound very good at the end of the day.”

artigo.texto: On Monday, 5 October, the European Commission published the price for the third quarter of 2026, which will be used to calculate the charges for importers whose products are subject to the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). The cost of 1 metric tonne of CO₂-equivalent emissions stood at €82.32. This information was revealed in updates on the European Commission’s website. By way of comparison, the price in the first quarter was €75.36, and in the second quarter €75.28 per metric tonne of embedded emissions. In other words, over the course of three months, the cost of atmospheric pollution on the European market rose by almost 10 per cent. Link to the EU ETS To determine the average quarterly price for the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), the EU uses the average price of emission allowances within the EU ETS. In this way, the EU seeks to maintain a balance between what European producers and importers pay for emissions, in order to achieve what the EU considers to be a fair environmental burden on businesses. For 2026 — the first year in which the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) will be fully operational — prices will be set on a quarterly basis. From 2027 onwards, the European Commission will publish the price of these allowances on a weekly basis. The sale of certificates under the CBAM scheme will begin on the central platform in February 2027. As a reminder, emissions calculations under the CBAM are carried out either using standardised values or actual figures. The former are usually higher than the latter, but the latter must be verified by accredited verifiers. Ukraine, which is not yet a member of the EU, is entitled to apply to the national accreditation body of any EU country. The Ministry of Economy has agreed on such cooperation with the Swedish body SWEDAC. A company from Greece was the first in the world to receive accreditation for verifying CBAM emissions. Experts noted a curious approach — granting the accrediting body the authority to assess emissions across all industrial sectors covered by CBAM. Also in September, the European Parliament extended the scope of the emissions trading scheme to include derivatives. Due to the CBAM, Ukraine has already lost more than half of its exports of certain types of products, as industry, which is trying to operate under wartime conditions, is unable to cope with the additional financial pressure.

artigo.texto: Alarm.com Extends Intelligent Video Protection to More Entryways with New Battery-Powered 781B Wire-free video doorbell brings intelligent video, relevant alerts, and proactive deterrence to entryways where traditional doorbells aren't practical TYSONS, Va.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 6, 2026-- Alarm.com (Nasdaq: ALRM), the leading platform for intelligently connected properties, today announced the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell, giving homeowners and businesses a new way to bring video security to entryways throughout their properties. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261006740792/en/ Alarm.com announces the release of the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell (ADC‑VDB781B). The 781B combines a rechargeable battery, Wi-Fi connectivity, and intelligent video capabilities in a doorbell designed for locations without existing doorbell wiring. Customers can install the 781B at a front door, side door, back door, detached garage, gate, shed, or other entryway where running new wiring may be impractical. As part of the Alarm.com platform, the doorbell works alongside the broader connected property system, unlocking a range of intelligent features that go beyond basic video coverage. "The 781B brings intelligent video, proactive deterrence, and connected actions to more entryways," said Dan Kerzner, President of Platforms Business at Alarm.com. "It gives our service providers another strong wireless option for delivering comprehensive video coverage across a property." Intelligent Awareness at More Entryways A square 1:1 view captures visitors from head to toe, while Advanced Video Analytics can identify people, animals, vehicles, and packages to help deliver more relevant alerts. As the first Alarm.com battery video doorbell to offer animal and vehicle detection, the 781B helps customers distinguish different types of activity around their property. Familiar Face Analytics can recognize up to five familiar people and support customized notifications, while Package Alerts help customers stay aware of deliveries and removals of packages. When a response is needed, customers can interact with visitors remotely through crisp two-way audio and Call Screen Actions, allowing them to unlock doors, turn on lights, and more through the Alarm.com platform without leaving the doorbell screen. For unwanted visitors, Perimeter Guard® combines attention-grabbing lights and audio alerts with the ability to trigger connected lights throughout the property. AI Deterrence can also deliver AI-generated verbal warnings when a person is detected at the door. Flexible Protection Without Doorbell Wiring The 781B is designed to make video protection possible in more locations without requiring an existing doorbell power source. Its battery-powered, Wi-Fi-connected design allows customers to install the doorbell where traditional wired models may not be an option without requiring connection to a hub or base station. Specially designed Energy Saver Video Analytics help conserve battery power during periods of inactivity. When it's time to recharge, the removable battery can be swapped out, or customers can use optional wiring for continuous trickle charging. The removable universal rechargeable battery is also compatible with the Alarm.com Volt Series™ V731B Battery Camera, giving customers a common battery solution across compatible devices and a simpler way to expand battery-powered video throughout a property. Designed for Everyday Security From monitoring a side entrance to keeping an eye on packages delivered near a garage, the 781B extends the role of the video doorbell beyond the front door. Customers can see activity, communicate with visitors, and respond to unexpected activity from the Alarm.com platform, wherever the doorbell is installed. The 781B also supports Bluetooth® Enrollment, designed to make device setup faster and easier for service providers. Availability The 781B is compatible with a range of Alarm.com residential and commercial video service packages, with feature availability varying by service package. To learn more about the Alarm.com 781B Battery Video Doorbell, visit www.alarm.com or contact an Alarm.com service provider. About Alarm.com Alarm.com is the leading platform for intelligently connected properties. Millions of homeowners and businesses rely on Alarm.com’s technology to secure, monitor, and manage their environments from anywhere. Our comprehensive suite of solutions—including security, video surveillance, access control, active shooter detection, intelligent automation, energy management, personal safety and awareness, and fire—is delivered exclusively through a trusted network of thousands of professional service providers and commercial integrators across North America and worldwide. Alarm.com’s common stock is traded on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ALRM. Alarm.com delivers serious security for serious people. To learn more, visit www.alarm.com. artigo.texto: Physical AI’s bottleneck shifts from what robots can do to whether factories trust them AI is moving beyond the data centers where models are trained and onto factory floors where machines must handle constant change. But traditional industrial robots work behind a cage, repeat a single task and were never designed for the complexities of today’s market. Manufacturers now want general-purpose machines that can switch tasks and improve as processes evolve. The hard part is deploying it, according to Adrien Gaidon (pictured, right), co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics Inc. “If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon said. “What we do is we do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.” Gaidon and John Mancuso (left), vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc., spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante at Fully Connected, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how cloud infrastructure, simulation and human assistance help robots learn and adapt on factory floors. (* Disclosure below.) Physical AI moves from data centers to the factory floor Walden spun out of Toyota Research Institute in January 2026 and launched with $300 million in July to put general-purpose robots to work in manufacturing. Its robots have worked full production shifts alongside people since May. They handle machine tending, parts kitting, and subassembly, tasks manufacturers had either failed to automate or never tried, Gaidon explained. “There’s half a million open positions for machinists in the U.S. because it’s a hard job and it requires skills,” Gaidon said. “But part of that job does not require the craft or the human creativity.” Getting a robot to that point takes serious compute long before it reaches a production line. CoreWeave, which has been betting on physical AI, also brings mechanical engineers and robotics experts into customer engagements alongside its infrastructure, Mancuso explained. “In the end, before a model is ever going to do something in the physical world, it’s going to have a tremendous amount of simulation that happens in the virtual world,” Mancuso said. “We’re providing the infrastructure.” But while simulation in data centers can make a robot useful, but it can’t make it perfect. Walden pairs autonomous robots with remote human assistants. The setup is comparable to automated looms of 120 years ago, when one person oversaw 40 machines, Gaidon noted. “Our robots are autonomous, but they know how to call for help,” Gaidon said. “They know when they need some assistance – and that assistance feeds the most valuable data to improve over time.” Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of Fully Connected: (* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Fully Connected 2026 event. The contract value is approximately $24 million. Fisk’s scope of work includes prefabrication and assembly of modular containment systems and related electrical infrastructure, including liquid-cooled components and piping, for a new ground-up data center. These units will be built at Fisk’s new 75,000-square-foot prefabrication/manufacturing facility in Houston. Electrical construction work is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 with substantial completion anticipated in the first quarter of 2027. The contract value will be reflected in the Company’s backlog for the third quarter of 2026. About Tutor Perini Corporation Tutor Perini Corporation is a leading civil, building and specialty construction company offering diversified general contracting and design-build services to private customers and public agencies throughout the world. The RTP100E005G1FL, RTP100E2P6G1FL, RTP100E1P8G1FL-DSC and RTP100E1P2G1FL-DSC low-voltage GaN FETs deliver ultra-fast switching speeds and enhanced thermal performance in efficiency-critical, high power density applications, including AI data centers, humanoid robotics, factory automation and industrial motor drives, power tools and solar microinverters. This press release features multimedia. Power converters in today's data centers generally operate at switching frequencies of a few hundred kilohertz. But as AI servers and industrial infrastructure transition to 800 VDC power distribution and 48V bus architectures, many converter stages are moving toward megahertz-class switching to shrink magnetics, increase power density and improve overall efficiency. At the system level, this translates to better efficiency, fewer thermal management requirements and lower energy and BOM costs. Broad GaN Portfolio Yields Greater Efficiency, Power Density and Design Flexibility Built on Renesas’ recently expanded low-voltage E-mode GaN technology platform, this new transistor portfolio features ultra-fast GaN switching with low total gate charge (Qg) and output charge (Qoss) to minimize the overlap between voltage and current. It reduces energy lost in each conversion cycle across AI power supply units, motor drives and DC-DC power stages. The new GaN transistors are offered in multiple standard MOSFET-compatible packages, allowing customers to quickly migrate from silicon MOSFET layouts for faster design implementation without significant PCB rework. The package options, combined with a wide RDS(on) range (5 mΩ-1.2 mΩ), enable designers to scale across power levels and applications, including synchronous rectification, multiphase buck conversion and motor drives. "Our low-voltage GaN family delivers the efficiency, switching performance and power density designers expect from GaN while making it significantly easier to transition from existing silicon MOSFET designs.” High GaN Performance in Silicon-Compatible Footprints The new GaN family is built on E-mode (normally off) GaN technology, which offers the performance advantages of GaN in a convenient silicon-compatible footprint. This helps designers capture the efficiency and power benefits of GaN and simplifies migration from existing silicon-based designs. artigo.texto: The electric vehicle revolution has a hidden Achilles’ heel, and it is not the batteries themselves but the fragile web of companies that mine, refine, and ship the minerals inside them. A new study published in iScience has mapped the entire firm-level supply network of the lithium-ion battery industry and stress-tested it against shortages of lithium, cobalt, and nickel. The results reveal a system that is far more vulnerable than its headline market size suggests, with losses cascading through unexpected pathways and recovery depending less on direct suppliers than on a handful of shared corporate hubs. The research team, led by Xuena Liu and Haibin Liu, constructed a multilayer supply chain network centered on nine of the world’s dominant battery manufacturers, including CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, SK Innovation, CALB, Samsung SDI, Gotion, and EVE Energy. Using the FactSet Revere database of interfirm supply relationships, supplemented by corporate disclosures and stock-market volatility data, they built a directed, weighted network spanning mineral extraction, intermediate materials, battery assembly, electric vehicle manufacturing, and recycling. The timing could hardly be more pressing: global electric vehicle battery demand reached 950 gigawatt-hours in 2024 and is projected to exceed 3 terawatt-hours by 2030, while the International Energy Agency expects electric vehicles and energy storage to account for more than 90 percent of future lithium demand. The network’s anatomy alone tells a striking story. All nine manufacturer-centered networks follow power-law degree distributions, meaning a few hub firms dominate connectivity while most firms maintain only a handful of relationships. The commodity trader Glencore, the Australian lithium producer Pilbara Minerals, and the Chinese materials firm CNGR each maintain business relationships with seven to nine core battery makers, forming what the authors call cross-layer super-hubs. Meanwhile, most shared nodes connect to only two manufacturers. The networks led by Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution are strongly correlated with each other and with Panasonic’s, implying that a shock at a shared supplier could transmit simultaneous damage across multiple corporate ecosystems. By contrast, the SK Innovation- and Gotion-led networks show slightly negative correlations, hinting at potential substitutability at certain supply nodes. When the researchers simulated shortages of increasing intensity, from 10 percent to a complete cutoff of supply, lithium emerged as the most damaging mineral by a clear margin, with network losses ranking lithium above cobalt above nickel under every scenario. This asymmetry reflects chemistry as much as geology. Lithium is an indispensable element in every lithium-ion battery, whereas cobalt is progressively being engineered out of newer cathode designs, and nickel benefits from abundant resources and diversified supply. At a shortage intensity of 0.9, the CATL-dominated network suffered losses of 1171.42 under lithium scarcity, compared with 909.05 for cobalt and 918.45 for nickel. The BYD-led network fared worst of all under lithium stress, reaching 2587.49, a consequence of its enormous lithium iron phosphate production volumes and vertically integrated business model. Manufacturer-level losses varied dramatically, defying any simple ranking of corporate might. CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, recorded the highest losses across all three minerals, ranging from roughly 130 to 160 under lithium shortages, a pattern the authors attribute to its simultaneous operation of both LFP and high-nickel NMC pathways, which broadens its mineral exposure and concentrates its supplier base. SK Innovation’s network proved exceptionally vulnerable to nickel because its product portfolio is dominated by high-nickel NCM811 cells, while EVE Energy’s cobalt-containing cathode materials and stringent certification requirements concentrated its dependence on upstream refining hubs. Panasonic, by contrast, recorded the lowest losses and responded only weakly to changes in shortage intensity, reflecting its comparatively low structural exposure. Tracing exactly where the damage came from produced some of the study’s most actionable findings. Under cobalt shortages, a single firm, Glencore, accounted for between 73.43 and 92.75 percent of CATL’s attributed losses, a near-single-source structure in which one disruption could rapidly amplify risk downstream. Nickel losses for CATL were dominated by Glencore and the Indonesian producer Trimegah Bangun Persada, the latter reflecting the localized supply concentration fostered by Indonesia’s nickel ore export ban. Lithium losses were far more dispersed, spread across Tianqi Lithium, Ganfeng Lithium, Yahua, and Albemarle. Path analysis of a total Tianqi Lithium shortage showed that two pathways, a direct cross-chain link to BYD and a long cascade through the midstream materials firm BTR, together accounted for roughly 70 percent of BYD’s total impact, with the cathode makers Hunan Yuneng and Ronbay emerging as the most frequently traversed intermediary nodes. Perhaps the most surprising result concerns how the industry recovers. The researchers decomposed recovery into three mechanisms: direct restoration through existing supply relationships, indirect recovery through shared nodes that connect multiple manufacturer networks, and recovery through newly established supply links. Indirect recovery dominated overwhelmingly, contributing 70 to 74 percent of total recovery, followed by new links at 15 to 18 percent, with direct recovery contributing a mere 10 to 12 percent. In other words, when a mineral shortage strikes, battery makers do not primarily heal through their own contracted suppliers; they heal through the network’s hidden cross-connections, as shared suppliers reallocate resources across tiers. artigo.texto: RALEIGH, N.C. (WTVD) -- The Raleigh City Council voted 7-1 on Tuesday to approve a six-month moratorium on new data center development, a move city leaders say will provide time to study potential effects and develop regulations for the rapidly growing industry. The temporary pause applies to data centers with footprints exceeding 10,000 square feet. City officials said Raleigh's current regulations do not include standards specifically tailored to large-scale data centers. The decision followed public debate both outside and inside council chambers, where community advocates argued the moratorium does not provide enough time to fully evaluate potential effects on utilities, communities, and the environment. "There's a lot that the city does not know. Can it get all this information in six months? That becomes a really big question," said Rania Masri of the North Carolina Environmental Justice Network. During the council meeting, advocates continued to express concerns about the scope and duration of the pause. "This moratorium doesn't have a conditionality about it. It's simply time. So in six months, whether or not the city can do what it says it's going to do, the moratorium ends," Masri said. Supporters of a longer pause said more time is needed to address unanswered questions about the effect of data centers on Raleigh communities. "What is the harm in giving Raleigh more time? We have a city, a new half a million people, and there's still a massive knowledge gap about what the center for in our communities. And somehow, six months is enough. We're asking for 32 months," said Raleigh resident Zainab Baloch. The moratorium is intended to give city staff time to study the effects of data center development and determine whether additional regulations are needed. Residents also voiced concerns about whether six months would allow for meaningful public engagement and long-term planning. "Six months is not enough time to make decisions that impact not only the major decisions, but also their lifetimes and future generations. The people of our city, especially those in southeast Raleigh, deserve to have a policy and a vision of all of the nations around the data centers. And this period will not allow that to happen," said Raleigh resident Anusha Yadav. Councilwoman Christina Jones, the lone dissenting vote, said she had concerns about the structure of the moratorium and the challenges it could present. "When you were watching different municipalities extend their moratoriums having longer ones. It's something that we are in the defensive mode to begin with, and so for me not having those laid out at this moment or voting on the moratorium is where I'm struggling to get there," Jones said. Duke Energy said data centers account for less than 1% of total peak electricity demand, but that figure is projected to rise to 13% of sales by 2030. The utility said it has been involved in discussions with Raleigh leaders about managing future growth. Lee Freedman, a Duke Energy spokesperson, said the company is focused on balancing expansion with reliability for customers. "That means protecting reliability and making sure customers benefit and not subsidize growth -- so we're working with city staff to educate them, educate council members, and if this moratorium does pass, we will continue working with them," Freedman said. Freedman also said projects under development are expected to provide financial benefits in the future. "We're talking about billions of dollars in bill relief beginning in about 2029 when the new data centers start going online in North Carolina," he said. Dustin Winkler, an AI enablement engineer and owner of the consulting company AWACS.AI, said data centers are essential to his work helping enterprise teams integrate AI technology into their operations and build applications. "I don't know where I pull from, just like no one else does," Winkler said of the network of data centers that support AI services. Despite relying on those facilities professionally, Winkler said he supports a temporary pause to assess potential effects. "It is something that can be hard to reconcile," he said. "I think it's good to take a pause and make sure that we don't limit ourselves and to what kind of a technology expansion that we want. But we also are careful about our area. Make sure that it's not overtaxed." The City said it is aware of eight data centers within Raleigh city limits, most of which are smaller-scale facilities. City officials said Raleigh does not have a hyperscale data center within its jurisdiction. There are eight hyperscale data centers in North Carolina, with others under construction. Amazon is building a $10 billion data center and AI campus in Richmond County. Raleigh Mayor Janet Cowell said city leaders are seeking a balanced approach that encourages innovation while addressing community concerns. "We want to have a very rational, careful approach that protects individuals who live in Raleigh and still be known as a tech-right, innovative city," she said. The moratorium takes effect immediately and is scheduled to continue through April. City leaders said they plan to provide nearly a dozen opportunities for public comment as they work toward developing a city ordinance. Advocates, however, said they are seeking a broader conversation about data center development in Raleigh.

artigo.texto: Hawaii County considers curbing AI data centers HILO — Two Hawaii County commissions are considering a bill aimed at prohibiting artificial intelligence data centers on the Big Island through the creation of a new definition in the county code. The Windward Planning Commission discussed the bill at its meeting on Thursday after previously deferring on Sept. 3. Introduced by Hamakua Councilperson Heather Kimball, Bill 170 distinguishes between “data processing facilities” and “data centers.” Data processing facilities are defined as places where records and other digital information are stored and are currently a permitted use under the county code in certain zoning districts, while data centers refer to the large-scale facilities being built to house the infrastructure needed to power AI. These data centers, which use significant amounts of energy, water and other resources, have drawn concern and pushback from communities across the country where they have been built or proposed. The Leeward Planning Commission will also evaluate the bill and make a recommendation to the Council. The Leeward commission’s next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 15. Kimball told the Hawaii Tribune-Herald that her goal in introducing the bill was to close a potential loophole that could allow such centers to be constructed on the island. “I think we have to preemptively prepare for an interest in developing data centers in Hawaii,” she said. “The purpose of this bill is very simple, very straightforward, from the standpoint that it defines what data centers are, and therefore, because it defines them and then does not put them anywhere in Chapter 25 (of the county code) as a permitted use, they become prohibited through that absence.” The bill defines a data center as “a facility used for the industrial-scale operation of computer systems and associated equipment for the processing, computing, transmission, or dissemination of digital data, and that requires supporting infrastructure beyond that typically accessory or incidental to office, commercial, or public institutional uses.” Kimball said this definition came from the National Association of Counties. While commissioners expressed support for the intent of the bill at the Thursday’s meeting, they voted 5-1 to send an unfavorable recommendation to the County Council, due primarily to concerns that the definition was not specific enough. “They need to come up with something better that involves expertise, opinions, and it needs to be done in a way that’s separated and in a clean way so that there’s no loopholes left,” said Commissioner JoNelle Fukushima. “That’s the biggest issue here, is that if we do this too quickly, and we don’t take our time in understanding what the definition is, we may leave with unintended consequences, pathways to them being able to come in and do the data centers.” Windward Planning Commission Vice Chair Chantel Perrin, who was the sole vote in favor of the bill, said there would be future opportunities for additions and clarifications to be made to the bill once it returns to Council. She suggested that instead of submitting an unfavorable recommendation for Bill 170, the commission instead indicate support for the intent of the bill and submit a list of the changes they would like to see made to the definition. “Bill 170 needs to happen. It needs a definition,” she said. “Nonetheless, we may not agree with what’s being written, but it doesn’t mean it’s done there. We can tell them, that’s why we can suggest recommendations as to how we want it worded.” Several members of the public who provided testimony during the meeting, expressed strong opposition to data centers and support for the bill’s goal, but also asked for additional, more specific language to be included. “Bill 170’s intent is what our hopes and dreams are as a community,” said Hilo resident Cristina Holt. “However, the only thing that we are doing with Bill 170 is creating a definition. As I’m sure you guys have seen in your own research and the testimony that has come your way, there’s a lot of confusion about what we’re even talking about, so, setting a clear definition for what we are talking about is literally the very first step.” There was also confusion surrounding recommendations submitted by the county Planning Department in response to the bill which included potential permitting regulations, which Kimball and Deputy County Corporation Counsel Jean Campbell noted are beyond the scope of this bill and would acquire additional legislation. “(The Council) would not be able to amend this particular bill in the ways that are being recommended,” Campbell said. “However, they have other options. They could withdraw this bill and introduce one that’s broader. They could pass this bill and then introduce something else that would address your recommendations.”

artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: quem vai construir, operar e crescer com eles? Em artigo à CNN Infra, Léo Oliveira explica como infraestrutura de data centers deve transformar o investimento em capacidade local no país A chegada de um data center deve levar quem lidera empresas e políticas de desenvolvimento a pensar em como transformar esse investimento em oportunidades para as pessoas e os negócios da região. Com a sanção do Redata, o Brasil reforça sua aposta na atração de data centers. Energia, conectividade e equipamentos estão no centro dessa agenda, mas a preparação das regiões para construir, operar e prestar serviços a esses empreendimentos também precisa fazer parte do planejamento. Quem vai transformar o investimento em capacidade local? Como CEO de uma plataforma de IA, Executivo de RH e Líder, vejo três prioridades. A primeira é preparar pessoas antes da inauguração, considerando que construção, operação e manutenção exigem competências diferentes. O plano de formação deve acompanhar o cronograma e prever os profissionais necessários na obra, na entrada em operação e nos anos seguintes. É preciso um planejamento rigoroso para estabelecer vagas temporárias, permanentes e explicar quais caminhos de qualificação permitem transitar entre essas etapas. Empresas, escolas técnicas e universidades devem organizar essa preparação a partir das demandas concretas. As empresas devem sinalizar as competências e os prazos para que as instituições de ensino avaliem como preparar os profissionais com antecedência. Quem já trabalha também precisa encontrar caminhos para ampliar sua qualificação através de cursos, formações e trocas para se manter relevante. Que oportunidade terá o jovem que mora perto desse investimento? Ele precisa saber quais profissões serão necessárias e encontrar condições para conciliar formação, deslocamento e renda. Os programas devem considerar essas questões para que as pessoas consigam frequentar o curso, concluir os estudos e disputar uma vaga. A segunda prioridade é criar condições para que empresas brasileiras participem da cadeia de fornecedores desses projetos. Os empreendedores precisam informar quais serviços pretendem contratar na região e os requisitos técnicos e de segurança que serão exigidos, permitindo que empresas locais se preparem para disputar contratos. Pense em uma empresa regional de manutenção elétrica interessada em atender um data center. Ela precisará conhecer as exigências da operação, qualificar profissionais e demonstrar que consegue cumprir os padrões do contratante. Um programa de desenvolvimento de fornecedores pode apoiar essa preparação, com critérios claros e sem garantia de contratação. Essa conexão pode ampliar a competência de empresas locais e abrir mercados para seus serviços. Cabe aproximar universidades e empreendimentos para pesquisar soluções para a operação. O desenvolvimento que buscamos inclui conhecimento que permaneça na região e possa ser utilizado em outros negócios. A terceira prioridade é trazer o RH e a liderança para o planejamento desde o início. Se a formação necessária leva mais tempo que o previsto para contratar, o projeto precisa reconhecer esse descompasso. Quem vai formar os gestores, organizar o trabalho e acompanhar os resultados? Essas decisões precisam estar presentes quando os investimentos e os prazos são definidos. O RH pode contribuir com o diagnóstico de competências, a formação, os caminhos de carreira e se antecipar conhecendo o negócio. As lideranças precisam traduzir a estratégia em responsabilidades, recursos e condições de execução. Essa construção exige muita articulação entre operação, finanças e compras, instituições de ensino técnico e superior, governos, lideranças locais e movimentos sociais. A articulação precisa ter responsáveis, prazos e compromissos claros. Governos podem coordenar ações de qualificação e acesso em parceria com instituições de ensino técnico e superior. Lideranças locais e movimentos sociais ajudam a identificar barreiras de transporte, renda e informação, enquanto as empresas devem explicitar suas demandas e os critérios de seleção. Essa pode ser uma chance de ampliar o emprego e desenvolver essas regiões, abrindo caminhos para as profissões do futuro. O legado que devemos buscar inclui profissionais mais preparados e empresas locais mais capazes de inovar. Quando os data centers estiverem operando, o que os brasileiros estarão mais preparados para fazer, criar e liderar? Léo Oliveira é fundador e CEO da Humanos & Inteligência Artificial*

Partilhar Duas novas metodologias juntam-se à de Novas Florestações, aumentando as oportunidades para projetos de sequestro de carbono em Portugal. Carbono azul e pradarias marinhas vão seguir-se, O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passa a contar com três metodologias para projetos florestais, abrindo novas oportunidades à mobilização de investimento privado para o sequestro de carbono e a gestão sustentável da floresta. Foram aprovadas duas novas metodologias de carbono dedicadas à Reflorestação e à Gestão Florestal Melhorada, que se juntam à metodologia já existente para Novas Florestações. As novas metodologias permitem abranger um conjunto mais diversificado de intervenções florestais, reforçam o potencial de geração de créditos de carbono em Portugal e incentivam práticas de gestão sustentável com benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática. Ao alargar as metodologias disponíveis, reforçamos a credibilidade e a capacidade de crescimento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono e mobilizamos financiamento privado para projetos que contribuem simultaneamente para a neutralidade carbónica, a valorização do território e a resiliência das nossas florestas”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, numa nota enviada às redações. Atualmente, o MVC conta com dois projetos registados na tipologia de Novas Florestações e um terceiro projeto está em fase de validação inicial. Estão ainda disponíveis 977 créditos de carbono para venda, a plataforma conta com 29 utilizadores registados e existem 10 verificadores qualificados para assegurar a validação inicial e a verificação periódica dos projetos, segundo o ministério. “O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono está a ganhar escala e maturidade. Depois das metodologias florestais, estamos já a trabalhar em novas abordagens para valorizar o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, para colocar também os ecossistemas costeiros no centro da ação climática e da valorização do capital natural”, acrescenta a ministra.

artigo.texto: Data center como obrigação reflete novo ecossistema de telecom, avalia Anatel Nilo Pasquali diz que consulta sobre 6 GHz abre discussão sobre novos compromissos de infraestrutura; agência pretende manter modelo que prioriza investimentos em vez de arrecadação A Anatel pretende discutir se investimentos em data center e outras infraestruturas digitais podem integrar os compromissos associados a futuras licitações de radiofrequência, que já aparece na consulta de futuros leilões relacionados à faixa de 6 GHz. Segundo o superintendente de Planejamento e Regulamentação da agência, Nilo Pasquali, esse é um movimento natural, diante das mudanças do ecossistema de infraestrutura digital. Ele participou de painel na Futurecom 2026, nesta terça-feira, 6. Pasquali afirmou que a inclusão de data centers na discussão não representa uma mudança abrupta de atribuições da agência, mas uma consequência da integração crescente entre telecomunicações e outras infraestruturas digitais. “Eu acho que não é uma mudança, eu acho que é uma maturidade da agência, por conta das discussões dos últimos anos”, afirmou. Segundo ele, as antigas divisões entre os segmentos deixaram de refletir o funcionamento do mercado. “A gente está agora em um ambiente digital. A gente não está mais naquele momento de divisão das cadeias, as estruturas bem divididinhas, todo mundo no seu quadrado. Quando a gente está falando de ecossistema digital, a gente está falando de telecom e mais uma série de outras coisas também.” Pasquali confirmou que a proposta submetida à consulta pública leva os data centers para a discussão sobre os compromissos associados ao espectro. O superintendente ressaltou, porém, que a proposta está em consulta e pode ser modificada. Segundo ele, essa é justamente a finalidade do processo: avaliar se a formulação faz sentido, se deve permanecer como apresentada ou se precisa de outro desenho. A discussão acontece no contexto da Consulta Pública nº 37, que trata da faixa de 6 GHz. Conectividade continua pendente Pasquali ressalvou que a incorporação de novas infraestruturas aos compromissos não significa que o problema tradicional de cobertura esteja resolvido. “O Brasil não acabou de conectar o país”, afirmou. Segundo ele, ainda existem áreas identificadas nos levantamentos da agência que demandam expansão das redes. A diferença é que a Anatel considera necessário começar a observar simultaneamente outras estruturas que compõem o ecossistema digital. “Tem que se começar a olhar para as outras infraestruturas que também fazem sentido, que compõem esse ecossistema e começam a contribuir para colocar o Brasil no futuro”, afirmou.

artigo.texto: Memphis mayor defends data center benefits ahead of moratorium vote Leaders speak ahead of highly anticipated vote MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Memphis Mayor Paul Young said his goal is to make the city better by accommodating everyone as data centers continue to be an issue for some Memphians and surrounding cities. The comment comes a day before a critical vote on a data center moratorium. “We must do it in a way where our people are protected; I think that’s really important. They need to have confidence they’re protected,” Young said. Addressing community concerns “That’s part of governance; governance is finding a way to address the potential negatives and harms that could be brought to the community and find a way to maximize the potential benefit to the community,” Young said. Groups like Memphis Community Against Pollution (MCAP) have laid out what the negatives are: - Air pollution - Nearby residents dealing with noise complaints - Effects on the water supply - Rising energy prices Tax revenue from data centers Young said significant tax dollars are generated by projects like data centers. He said Memphis is the only city with an ordinance requiring data centers to pay full taxes, with 25% of those taxes going back to the community most adjacent to them. Young said SpaceXAI alone generated $54 million between the city and county this year. He gave a comparison to help people understand the scale: “That’s the equivalent of 12,400 units of housing built in our city at $300,000 each,” Young said. The initial vote was supposed to happen September 15, but Councilman JB Smiley Jr., the ordinance’s leading sponsor, says the council wanted to factor in more community concerns. “One of the things that I heard consistently from the community is, ‘What about us? You can create laws, but you’re not talking to us,’” Councilman Smiley told Action News 5. While the council is speaking to various experts, Sarah Houston, executive director of Protect Our Aquifer, says they should also prioritize lifting up the voices of local organizations on concerns about the data centers, since they’re the ones on the ground. “There’s been a lot of confusion and a lot of listening to people with fancy titles,” says Houson. “The reality is there’s a lot of expertise in the Memphis community that city council members really need to lean on and really need to listen to.” Smiley says he believes the council likely has six votes for the moratorium and four against it, leaving the remaining three councilmembers to decide its fate. He says the point of a temporary moratorium is not necessarily to shut the door on the industry, but to make sure the city understands what it’s getting into before moving forward. “What I don’t want to happen is we allow 20, 30 more data centers to come in and in a year’s time, data centers stop being the hot thing and we have 30 empty buildings,” says Smiley.
