artigo.texto: Battery demand for stationary energy storage (ES) is set to grow as the penetration of renewable energy sources (RES) within electricity grids increases, alongside new demand created by data center build-out. Policy is also shifting from simply setting storage targets towards creating bankable revenue frameworks and increasingly sophisticated routes-to-market for battery energy storage system (BESS) deployment. As shown in IDTechEx's newly updated market report "Batteries for Stationary Energy Storage 2027-2037: Markets, Forecasts, Players, Technologies, Policy, and Projects", the global Li-ion BESS market will reach US$135B in value by 2037. Li-ion battery demand shifts across sectors Li-ion batteries (LIBs) continue to dominate the stationary battery energy storage system (BESS) market, driven by their wide availability, low cost and improvements in performance. While total cross-sector LIB demand has continued to increase, the application mix has shifted. EV batteries still dominate global demand, but their share decreased from 84% in 2023 to 78% in 2025, while the share attributable to BESS applications increased from 10% to 19%. Policy-driven changes in the EV market have contributed to this shift, alongside much faster growth in BESS demand as electricity grids integrate greater volumes of renewable energy and require increasing levels of flexibility. Li-ion BESS demand by country and key drivers IDTechEx estimates that annual global Li-ion BESS deployments increased by more than 3x between 2023 and 2025 across grid-scale, commercial and industrial (C&I), and residential sectors. This is equivalent to 92 GWh deployed in 2023 and 318 GWh in 2025. China and the US represented 58% and 18% of deployments in 2025, respectively, highlighting China's continued lead in the global market. The US BESS market is increasingly being shaped by industrial policy and efforts to reduce dependence on Chinese cells and BESS technologies. Critically, countries not previously prominent in the global BESS market have emerged within the top 10 by GWh deployed, including Saudi Arabia and Chile. IDTechEx would expect more countries to enter the market at significant scale. Key drivers facilitating BESS growth across both established and emerging markets include a growing number of procurement frameworks, routes-to-market and increasingly sophisticated financing structures that improve project bankability and help BESS projects secure investment. Examples include Australia's Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS), New South Wales' Long-Term Energy Service Agreements (LTESAs), Italy's MACSE, state-backed Middle Eastern tenders, and the UK LDES cap-and-floor framework. Future challenges, pricing, and technology trends While many future projects are being facilitated by government-backed procurement and revenue-support frameworks, often administered by regulators, system operators or designated procurement bodies, grid connection queues are emerging as a key bottleneck. Project delays and attrition may therefore be expected, while an increasingly competitive BESS developer landscape is also making it more difficult for new entrants to penetrate the grid-scale market at scale. Developers with proven utility-scale experience, strong local execution capabilities and demonstrable bankability are increasingly winning significant projects. Further upstream, raw-material prices and policy changes may also create uncertainty. China's reduction in and eventual elimination of its battery export VAT rebate could affect future cell and BESS pricing. This has encouraged some front-loading of battery production and exports and, alongside other factors, contributed to higher lithium carbonate prices in early 2026. If such prices are sustained, they could place upward pressure on cell and BESS prices, weaken project economics and increase margin pressure across the containerized Li-ion BESS supply chain. At the technology level, many players are launching containerized grid-scale BESS technologies using increasingly high-capacity cells, contributing to a growing number of systems with capacities of 6.5 MWh or greater. Higher capacity cells can improve system-level energy density by reducing the number of cells, interconnections and casings required per MWh, allowing a greater proportion of the container to be occupied by active battery material. This can also bring project-level cost benefits, as fewer BESS units are required to achieve a given site capacity. However, these designs create additional thermal management requirements and can introduce transportation weight constraints, contributing to new system-level design trends. --- Conrad Nichols, Principal Technology Analyst, IDTechEx.

artigo.texto: Escobar: Fort Bliss data center to shrink, shift site and use brackish water EL PASO, Texas (KFOX14/CBS4) — Changes to a planned data center at Fort Bliss are being touted as progress by U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, who said the Army and the Carlyle Group appear to be responding to community concerns even as key issues remain unresolved. On Monday, Escobar released a statement describing what she called “positive developments” about the project, including a smaller footprint, the use of brackish water and a move away from residential areas. She said the facility will still be located close to neighborhoods and that she will continue pushing for a different location. Escobar also said she remains concerned the data center will rely on gas-generated power. RECOMMENDED: Proposed Fort Bliss data center could use more power than all of El Paso Below is Escobar's full statement: "Today, the Army and Carlyle Group held a meeting of El Paso community stakeholders to discuss the latest updates on the Fort Bliss data center. "Since March, when my team and I first learned of this project, we have asked that the public and local representatives be kept in the loop and be allowed to voice their concerns and ask questions. I’m grateful to the Army and Carlyle for their continued engagement. "I’ve consistently had a number of requests, including that they: - Move the data center far away from any neighborhood; - Preserve our water; - Use renewable energy for the electrical generation; - Be transparent and accountable. "Today we learned that the location of the data center has indeed been moved, but it is still too close to residential areas. Close proximity to homes is not acceptable, and I will continue to advocate for a different location. "We also learned that their water use will likely be of brackish water that will be sent to the Kay Bailey Hutchison Plant for desalination, which I see as a positive development. And while the scale of the data center has also been reduced, they are still on track to utilize gas generation for their power needs. The gas generation for power remains an additional serious concern. We must protect our community’s air quality, and I will continue to push for the use of renewable energy. "As more information becomes available, my team and I will continue to keep the community updated." artigo.texto: YOU.ON e HyperStrong firmam acordo para leilões de baterias Parceria busca unir as capacidades das empresas para disputar projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias no Brasil SBT News Sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias da Hyperstrong instalados na Europa Foto: Hyperstrong As empresas YOU.ON Energia e HyperStrong International USA Corp. anunciaram nesta terça-feira (6) a assinatura de um acordo vinculante para atuar conjuntamente nos Leilões de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (LRCAP 2026), previstos para ocorrer no Brasil. O acordo foi firmado no fim de setembro. A parceria prevê cooperação exclusiva entre as empresas nos dois leilões previstos no LRCAP 2026, identificados como Leilões A e B. O objetivo é integrar as capacidades das duas companhias para disputar oportunidades de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de grande escala no país. Para o Leilão A, a YOU.ON obteve credenciamento junto ao Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e está avançando no processo para obter o código de identificação CFI. Acompanhe o SBT News nas TVs por assinatura Claro (586), Vivo (576), Sky (580) e Oi (175), via streaming pelo +SBT,Site e YouTube, além dos canais nas Smart TVs Samsung, LG e Roku. Segundo Martin Ding, presidente da HyperStrong, o acordo amplia a atuação da companhia no mercado brasileiro e combina sua experiência em sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) com a presença local da YOU.ON. “Estamos muito satisfeitos em anunciar que assinamos um acordo vinculante com a YOU.ON para trazer soluções de armazenamento de energia de última geração ao Brasil”, afirmou. O presidente da YOU.ON Energia, Giorgio Seigne, disse que a parceria combina a capacidade local de engenharia, prestação de serviços e assistência técnica da empresa com a tecnologia e os produtos da HyperStrong. “Essa união nos posiciona para oferecer soluções integradas, competitivas e financiáveis para os Leilões do LRCAP 2026, contribuindo para o avanço do armazenamento de energia no Brasil”, afirmou. Fundada em 2011, a HyperStrong integra sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias e tem ações listadas no STAR Market da Bolsa de Valores de Xangai desde janeiro de 2025. Sua capacidade instalada acumulada superava 70 GWh em agosto de 2026, distribuída em mais de 400 projetos. A YOU.ON é uma empresa brasileira especializada em sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A companhia atua em projetos residenciais, comerciais, industriais, de agronegócio e de grande porte para o setor elétrico. O acordo entre as empresas representa o primeiro passo de uma integração para a atuação conjunta em novas oportunidades de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de grande escala no Brasil. artigo.texto: By Chuks Oyema-Aziken Nigeria has reaffirmed its commitment to developing a credible and transparent carbon market capable of attracting climate finance and supporting sustainable economic development. This was disclosed at a High-Level Roundtable on Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV), held in Abuja on Tuesday, under the European Union Climate Dialogues Programme. Speaking on behalf of the Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs. Omotenioye Majekodunmi, the Director of Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, Michael Ivenso, said Nigeria was determined to turn its climate ambitions into tangible and bankable investments. Ivenso said climate action under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration was being viewed as an economic opportunity, particularly in clean energy, agriculture, forestry, waste management and clean technology. He said carbon markets could provide an important avenue for mobilising private capital, but stressed that their credibility would depend on reliable data, transparency and effective verification. According to him, Nigeria would not accommodate carbon markets that encourage greenwashing, insisting that carbon projects must deliver real, additional and permanent emissions reductions. He identified the National Carbon Markets Framework as a major step towards establishing a structured regulatory and institutional system for carbon-market activities in Nigeria. Ivenso said the NCCC was also working towards an integrated national carbon registry that would track carbon credits generated, issued, transferred and retired in the country, thereby helping to prevent double counting. He added that Nigeria was promoting digital MRV through remote sensing, geospatial information, IoT sensors and other technologies to improve accuracy and reduce verification costs. Representing the EU Delegation to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ms. Yolanda San Jose said the roundtable was coming at an important time as countries increasingly sought practical ways to translate climate ambitions into action. She said carbon markets were becoming important instruments for supporting emissions reduction, mobilising finance and encouraging investment, but stressed that they must be supported by credible systems that guarantee transparency, accountability and environmental integrity. San Jose commended Nigeria for adopting its National Carbon Markets Framework, describing it as an important foundation for confidence, trust and effectiveness in the country’s emerging carbon market system. She said the framework would help align Nigeria’s climate targets with its broader development priorities while creating an enabling environment for investment in a low-carbon economy. She explained that the EU Climate Dialogues programme was supporting discussions aimed at aligning stakeholders around the framework and developing a practical roadmap for its implementation, with MRV serving as a critical pillar. Also speaking, Director of Forestry at the Federal Ministry of Environment, Halima Bawa-Bwari, stressed the importance of forests to Nigeria’s climate response, calling for stronger forest monitoring, satellite technology, ground verification and institutional capacity to ensure a high-integrity carbon market.

artigo.texto: Wartsila Launches Valo Joint Venture with RCT Solutions for Energy Storage According to ESS News, Finnish technology group Wartsila has shifted its worldwide energy storage operations into Valo, a joint venture it co-owns on an equal basis with German engineering firm RCT Solutions. The company anticipates that the new entity will post losses during 2026 before returning to profitability near the close of 2027. Valo, characterized as a utility-scale battery energy storage system integrator encompassing Wartsila's Energy Storage operations, commenced on Oct. 1 following the completion of the joint venture between the two owners. Valo starts with over 20 GWh spanning more than 130 projects globally. Peter Fath, who formerly served as chief executive of RCT Solutions, heads the new venture as chief executive, while Luke Witmer holds the position of chief technology officer. Wartsila disclosed the transaction on June 15, stating it would hand over net assets amounting to under 5% of its total net assets. Finalization hinged on regulatory clearances and securing a financing package. Additional investors could enter at a later stage, possibly reducing the stakes of the two founding shareholders, and the joint venture will gain from project guarantees Wartsila has already provided on ongoing projects, according to the Helsinki-based group. Wartsila further indicated that the joint venture would operate at a loss in 2026 owing to weak recent order intake and transformation expenses, primarily a write-down of capitalized research and development. It projected the effect on its full-year 2026 operating result at EUR40 million to EUR50 million, or $45.2 million, contingent on when closing occurs. The company expressed expectations that the joint venture would deliver positive results near the end of 2027, and its Oct. 1 closing release restated the anticipated 2026 loss. Wartsila noted that the energy storage business represented its smallest segment, employing roughly 480 people. It recorded net sales of EUR694 million in 2025 with an operating margin of 3.3%, finishing the year with an order book valued at EUR719 million. Wartsila stated that RCT Solutions, established in 2012, has overseen the engineering and creation of multiple battery and solar manufacturing plants across the globe, and that one RCT entity has served as a crucial supplier to Wartsila Energy Storage for several years. It added that RCT also offers a chance for vertical integration via an existing integrated battery energy storage system manufacturing effort in the United States in the near term. Neither company has disclosed the project's name. Wartsila initiated a strategic review of the business in October 2023 and concluded it in March 2025 by separating storage into a distinct reporting segment with its own financial objectives. Following the joint venture agreement, it reclassified the unit as discontinued operations, and it will now report its stake as a share of result in associated companies. At the time it began the review, Wartsila reported net sales of EUR983 million for the business on a 12-month rolling basis through the end of the third quarter of 2023. The targets established in March 2025, low double-digit annual organic growth and an operating margin of 3% to 5%, are no longer applicable after the joint venture agreement. - 1. artigo.texto: One third of the way there: is the CATL dream lost in translation? The Orbán government had expected the transition to electric mobility to happen more quickly, but the revolution in the automotive industry was delayed. The Hungarian economy was intended to serve as a link between German premium manufacturers and Asian suppliers of key components. To that end, an extremely large amount of funding was made available — at CATL in Debrecen, roughly one in every seven forints of the investment was subsidised — in the hope of achieving economic growth, technology transfer, and job creation. CATL, the global market leader in battery technology, began producing modules at the Debrecen site in 2024, while the battery plant in the immediate vicinity of the BMW New Class factory was still under construction. Since then, BMW has been assembling the cells delivered by its partner into battery packs at its own plant, as has Mercedes at its separate battery final assembly facility in Kecskemét. CATL plant director Qin Lang, speaking during a factory tour ahead of the weekend, said that more than 500,000 modules had been built in just under two years across three production lines in the temporary facility. According to him, the company’s revenues have since totalled 100 billion forints. Both NCM and LFP batteries are manufactured in Debrecen. Nickel technology delivers greater range thanks to its higher energy density, while batteries made from lithium iron phosphate are extremely long-lasting and free of expensive raw materials such as cobalt. On 22 September, a trial run for battery cell production began at the new plant, initially on two production lines. Two further production lines are still being prepared technically for the start of operations. The battery cell plant’s capacity of 40 GWh has long been fully committed by its clients. The original site plan envisaged a total capacity of 100 GWh across three construction phases, for which CATL intended to invest a total of 7.5 billion euros. With the Tisza government taking office, however, the plant expansion appears to be under threat, as the environmental lobby is said to have strong backing within the new political movement. This would freeze the large Chinese investment at one third of its originally planned volume, amounting to a maximum of 4,000 jobs. CATL has not yet abandoned all hope of reaching an agreement with the government on the terms for the plant expansion — an expansion that involves a total of 9,000 jobs, which by 2030 would be filled to around 90% by domestic workers. Artificial intelligence was used for the translation of parts of the original German text.

artigo.texto: Supercapacitors charge in seconds and batteries store vast amounts of energy, but no single device has ever managed to do both at once. A team of researchers from India, China, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and Thailand now reports a promising step toward closing that gap. In a study published in the Journal of Materials Science, the group synthesized petal-like nanostructures of bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3) and demonstrated that these flower-shaped particles can serve as the workhorse positive electrode in a supercapattery, an emerging hybrid device that combines the battery-like ability to store large amounts of charge with the supercapacitor-like ability to deliver it rapidly. The work stands out not only for its impressive performance numbers but also for the depth of its explanation: the team paired meticulous electrochemical experiments with density functional theory (DFT) simulations to reveal, atom by atom, why the device works best in one particular electrolyte. The choice of material is deliberate. Bismuth sulfide is an earth-abundant, environmentally benign semiconductor that has attracted growing attention as an electrode material for energy storage. Its layered orthorhombic crystal structure, built from covalently bonded Bi2S3 ribbons held together by weaker van der Waals forces, offers open channels along which ions can migrate, making it naturally suited to intercalation-based charge storage. Previous studies have produced Bi2S3 in the form of nanorods, nanowires, nanoflowers and nanoflakes using solvothermal, chemical bath and spray methods, and several groups have reported respectable supercapacitor performance from composites that pair the sulfide with graphene, carbon nitride or nickel foam. What has been missing, the authors argue, is a systematic understanding of how the electrolyte itself, not just the material, controls the charge storage process. To build their electrode material, the researchers turned to hydrothermal synthesis, a technique that grows crystals from aqueous precursors inside a sealed, heated vessel. Under the right combination of temperature, time and precursor chemistry, the reaction self-assembles Bi2S3 into petal-like nanopetals, which the team abbreviates BSNP. This flower-like architecture is more than aesthetic. The petals create a high surface-area scaffold with abundant exposed active sites, short diffusion pathways for ions and open voids that accommodate the volume changes that occur as charge is stored and released. Such morphological engineering is a central strategy in modern electrode design, because electrochemical reactions happen only at surfaces and interfaces; the more accessible surface a material presents to the electrolyte, the more charge it can store and the faster it can deliver it. The heart of the experiment is a comparison across three alkaline electrolytes: 2 M solutions of lithium hydroxide (LiOH), sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and potassium hydroxide (KOH). All three contain the same charge-carrying hydroxide ion, but they differ in the size and hydration behavior of their cations, and those differences ripple through every aspect of electrode kinetics. When the team tested BSNP as the positive electrode in each solution, the results were striking. In 2 M KOH, the nanopetals delivered a gravimetric capacity of 797.9 coulombs per gram at a scan rate of 1 millivolt per second, outperforming the same material in LiOH and NaOH. In other words, simply swapping the electrolyte cation from lithium or sodium to potassium unlocked a substantially larger fraction of the material’s theoretical storage capability. Why would potassium ions give bismuth sulfide an edge? The answer, the researchers show, lies in the electronic and ionic interplay at the material’s surface. Using DFT calculations, they probed how hydroxide species interact with the Bi2S3 lattice under each electrolyte condition. Orbital hybridization analysis revealed favorable overlap between the electronic states of the surface and the adsorbed species in the KOH case, while Bader charge analysis quantified the electron transfer between them. Charge density difference maps and electron localization function analysis visualized where electrons accumulate and deplete during adsorption, painting a consistent picture: the potassium-containing environment promotes stronger, more favorable electronic coupling at the Bi2S3 surface, which lowers the energetic barriers for the redox reactions that store charge. This computational evidence aligns neatly with the electrochemical data, giving the performance claims a mechanistic foundation rather than leaving them as empirical observations. Kinetic analysis added another layer of insight. Applying Dunn’s method, a widely used technique that separates the capacitive (surface-controlled) and diffusion-controlled contributions to charge storage from cyclic voltammetry data measured at different scan rates, the team confirmed that diffusion-dominated processes govern the behavior of the BSNP electrode. That finding matters because it places the material firmly in the battery-type category rather than the purely capacitive one. Battery-type electrodes store charge through faradaic reactions, in which ions insert into the crystal lattice and electrons transfer to or from the metal centers, allowing much more charge to be packed per gram than in the electrostatic double-layer storage that characterizes carbon-based supercapacitor electrodes. It is precisely this battery-like positive electrode, paired with a capacitive negative electrode, that defines the supercapattery architecture. To prove the concept at the device level, the researchers assembled an asymmetric supercapacitor (ASC) in which the BSNP nanopetals served as the positive electrode and activated carbon, a classic high-surface-area capacitive material, served as the negative electrode. artigo.texto: Tuesday night’s Urbana City Council meeting lasted about four and a half hours, wrapping up around 10:30 p.m., with much of the meeting focused on a pending agreement involving Thor Equities and a proposed data center. Approximately 30 people addressed council during the meeting, with speakers raising concerns about the proposed settlement and a potential data center development. The proposed facility could include approximately two million square feet and would be located within the Urbana city limits along South U.S. 68. While individual comments varied, several common themes emerged. Speakers questioned whether the decision should remain a local one and raised concerns about the proposed agreement and its potential long-term effects. Some speakers said, “This should be a local choice,” “No man can serve two masters,” and “We cannot be bought.” Others described the proposal as a potential “buyout,” questioned what price Urbana could be bought for, and warned that once the city “opens Pandora’s box,” it may not be able to close it. Some members of the public also raised the possibility of recalling the entire city council. The comments followed a recent public letter released by Urbana Mayor Bill Bean regarding the proposed data center agreement. Community member Brad Winner Jr. urged council members to carefully consider any proposed settlement and asked why the matter is being handled through an executive session. The letter also raises concerns about the financial incentives that could be associated with the proposed data center, including possible cash, infrastructure, and other financial commitments. Winner alleged that the city administration and developers have been working on the project for some time and questioned the extent to which council members and the public have been informed. He also raised concerns about additional pending litigation involving property rights and affected citizens, and questioned whether approving a settlement could result in what was described as “trading one lawsuit for another.” Council Approves EMS Equipment Funding Also during Tuesday night’s meeting, Urbana City Council unanimously approved additional funding for EMS equipment replacement and service agreements. Last year, council approved a $150,000 capital allocation for three critical pieces of emergency medical equipment manufactured by Stryker. Those include a LUCAS 3 mechanical CPR device, a LIFEPAK 35 monitor and defibrillator, and a Power-PRO 2 powered ambulance cot. The equipment is used on Urbana’s frontline emergency response vehicles, including Engine 1, Medic 1 and Medic 2. According to information presented to council, the equipment currently in service includes previous-generation models that have reached, or are approaching, the end of their manufacturer-supported life cycle. The department also explained that a Medic 1 accident in late 2025 changed some of the original equipment replacement priorities. The city has since received a new chassis and a new Stryker Power-PRO 2 cot for Medic 1. The legislation approved Tuesday authorizes a purchase order of $108,464.98 to Stryker Medical for a replacement Power-PRO cot loading system and a service agreement covering the department’s Power-PRO cot loading systems. The new cot loading system will be installed in Medic 2. The service agreement provides seven years of coverage, including parts, labor, travel, per diem, maintenance, and battery service. City officials said the agreement will provide more predictable maintenance costs and help ensure the equipment remains operational and supported throughout its service life. The expense will be paid from the Police and Fire Capital Improvement Fund and is included in the 2026 budget. The council’s approval of the additional EMS funding and service agreement was unanimous. No Action Taken on Pending Litigation Toward the end of Tuesday night’s meeting, council members entered executive session for pending litigation. The executive session lasted more than an hour. Council members eventually returned to the public meeting and told those who remained that no action would be taken at this time regarding the pending litigation. Council members said they want to gather additional information so they can make an educated and informed decision. The next Urbana City Council meeting is scheduled for Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at 6 p.m., where it’s expected to be decided at that time.

artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – Indonesia is pushing ASEAN to make its emerging carbon pricing systems more compatible as countries across the region develop different national approaches amid growing pressure from carbon-related trade measures and international markets. Mari Elka Pangestu, Indonesia’s Special Envoy for International Trade and Multilateral Cooperation and Co-Chair of the Green Investment Principles (GIP) ASEAN, said ASEAN countries were no longer debating whether carbon pricing was needed, but how their systems could work together. “We are no longer now talking about whether we need carbon pricing. We know we do need it, but we need to figure out how we should be doing it, whether as each country or as ASEAN as a region,” Mari said at the GIP ASEAN research dissemination of The Emerging Carbon Pricing Landscape in Southeast Asia in Jakarta on Monday (Oct. 5, 2026). She said ASEAN countries had made progress in developing carbon pricing systems over the past decade, with each country pursuing a different model based on its own circumstances. Singapore has established a carbon tax and recently raised the price to US$45, while Indonesia and Vietnam are developing emissions trading systems. Thailand has focused on international cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, while Malaysia is moving from voluntary toward compliance carbon markets. Indonesia is also moving to implement sectoral regulations under Presidential Regulation No. 110/2025 on carbon economic value. Mari said the country had made progress on its carbon registry and forestry regulations, while energy-sector regulations were also being prepared. She identified forestry and energy as two key sectors for Indonesia’s carbon market, with further sectoral regulations expected for agriculture, marine and fisheries, and industry. Market Access Mari said differences in national systems were natural given the varying economic conditions of ASEAN countries. However, developing carbon markets in isolation could create risks if rules become disconnected, data are misaligned and carbon prices differ significantly. “This learning by doing, of course, comes with risks if we are developing our systems in isolation with disconnected rules, misaligned data, and very different price levels,” she said. Such fragmentation could make it harder for countries to trade carbon assets, attract investment and gain recognition from international partners, she added. The pressure to improve compatibility is also coming from international trade measures, including the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), as well as green standards and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Mari said businesses, particularly exporters, were increasingly aware of the need for carbon pricing as they face growing climate-related requirements in international trade. “Being competitive today means sustainability. You have to be part of a sustainable supply chain,” she said. She said the EU CBAM and similar measures being developed elsewhere could increasingly affect how carbon pricing is linked to international trade. “If we do not price our own carbon, others will price it for us, and the revenue will go to their budgets, not ours,” Mari said. GIP ASEAN Study The research dissemination was organized by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), which has served as the secretariat of GIP ASEAN since its inception in 2023. The GIP ASEAN chapter seeks to connect research and policy recommendations with financial institutions, governments, investors and other stakeholders to support Southeast Asia’s green transition. Yose Rizal Damuri, Executive Director of CSIS, said the research presented at the event examined carbon pricing in Southeast Asia and its implications for the region. Carbon pricing, he said, should not be viewed solely as a mechanism for carbon markets, but also as a way to translate sustainability principles into economic activities, including investment and emissions reductions. “When we’re talking about carbon pricing, we have to look at also on how to translate this carbon pricing into real investment and also to emission reductions, to internalize the carbon price into our economic activities,” he said. The study also highlighted the importance of ASEAN cooperation while recognizing differences in economic structures and levels of readiness among member states. Yose said regional cooperation should focus not on creating a uniform carbon pricing mechanism, but on reducing uncertainty and improving interoperability among national systems. “It will reduce uncertainty for business and investors while also strengthening their confidence in carbon market and also in internalizing the carbon price into their decision,” he said. ***

artigo.texto: How much are AI data centers adding to your electricity bill? Americans are worried AI data centers will raise their electricity bills. Congress has come up with a plan to protect ratepayers, but there's no easy way to find out what AI is costing them. ELISSA NADWORNY, HOST: The construction of huge, new AI data centers has become a political lightning rod. Communities near proposed projects are raising questions about their impact, including on electricity costs. One big question is who will end up paying for expensive new infrastructure needed to power these massive facilities. NPR's Scott Neuman has been looking into that question, and he joins me now. Hi, Scott. SCOTT NEUMAN, BYLINE: Hi, Elissa. NADWORNY: So, Scott, most of us know by now that these hyperscale AI centers require a lot of power and upgrades to the electrical grid. Who is paying for all that? NEUMAN: Well, the simple answer is everybody who buys electricity. That means people who are building and using these data centers for sure, but also local businesses and homeowners and renters, even if they don't think they're using AI. During my reporting this past week, I spoke with Ari Peskoe. He's the director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative. He says that, ultimately, everyone is shouldering the burden for the billions of dollars in new upgrades to the electrical grid. ARI PESKOE: Everyone pays those costs. They're spread across the region to every business and resident that has an electricity meter. NEUMAN: Now, in many cases, the pace and scale of the demand is coming at - it's really breakneck speed, and that makes all of this unpredictable. The demand for new transmission lines, substations and other infrastructure is ramping up faster than the utilities can keep up in many cases. And that creates an enormous planning challenge. But, you know, Peskoe brings up another interesting point. He says that the speed that all of this is happening can actually drive up the cost of these improvements. Components, things like transformers, are in short supply, and everybody wants them and wants them now. So there's a scarcity, and that makes everything more expensive. NADWORNY: OK, so we're all paying for the AI upgrades, but how are those costs divided up? NEUMAN: That's a really tough question to answer. Even if an AI data center is - in your area is the reason for these improvements, everyone is going to be getting the use of them. But Peskoe says no one has really figured out how to divvy up the costs in an equitable way. PESKOE: There's no agreement as to what infrastructure is for a data center versus for the public. That itself is a disputed point. NEUMAN: So in 2024, Maryland's Office of People's Counsel, an independent state consumer agency, forecast that new costs due to data centers would run residents as much as $216 a year. But the rapid buildout of these data centers means there's a lot of uncertainty. NADWORNY: Do individual customers get any benefit from all this new grid infrastructure? NEUMAN: Yeah, so the fact that everyone gets the use of these improvements to the grid means everyone gets the benefits too. Lucy Qiu is a professor at the University of Maryland who is looking into all of this. She says that in many places, the upgrades are long overdue. They'll be needed for AI data centers, but they'll also be needed for things like meeting the charging capacity for electric vehicles. LUCY QIU: On the positive side, you can accelerate the upgrade of the grid infrastructure. NEUMAN: Qiu says studies show that people who live near data centers where the grid has been more - made more robust to accommodate them, those residential rate payers have fewer power outages during extreme weather events. NADWORNY: All right, so some positive side too, thank you. That was NPR's Scott Neuman. NEUMAN: Thank you. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. artigo.texto: O Histórico de Jon Husted com Data Centers Transforma um Ativo de IA em um Passivo para as Eleições de Meio de Mandato O histórico de Jon Husted com data centers tornou-se um passivo, apesar de sua tentativa de proteger as famílias de Ohio dos custos de infraestrutura antes das eleições de meio de mandato de novembro. O senador republicano já promoveu os data centers como motores de investimento, emprego e força tecnológica americana. Sua campanha atual agora enfatiza responsabilização, controle local e proteção contra contas de eletricidade mais altas. Essa mudança reflete uma reversão política mais ampla. A Newsweek identificou 16 candidatos em disputas acirradas cujos históricos favoráveis a data centers agora colidem com a crescente resistência dos eleitores. A discussão já não se limita a saber se os Estados Unidos precisam de mais capacidade computacional. Agora, ela se concentra em quem paga pela eletricidade, pelos equipamentos de transmissão, pela água, pelos terrenos e pelos incentivos fiscais que sustentam essa capacidade. Husted enfrenta o ex-senador democrata Sherrod Brown em uma disputa que pode influenciar o controle do Senado. Brown usou o histórico anterior de Husted em desenvolvimento econômico para retratá-lo como excessivamente próximo dos interesses dos data centers. Outros candidatos enfrentam versões do mesmo problema. Instalações antes apresentadas como vitórias econômicas quase automáticas tornaram-se símbolos visíveis dos custos locais da IA. O Histórico de Jon Husted com Data Centers Encontra um Eleitorado Transformado O valor político de apoiar data centers se inverteu mais rápido do que muitos candidatos conseguiram reescrever seus históricos. Husted passou seis anos como vice-governador de Ohio antes de ingressar no Senado em 2025. Nesse período, Ohio buscou ativamente grandes instalações de tecnologia com incentivos fiscais e apoio ao desenvolvimento. Essas políticas antes se encaixavam em uma mensagem econômica familiar. Os data centers representavam investimento privado, empregos na construção, ampliação da base tributária e uma posição mais forte na economia da tecnologia. Essa mensagem perdeu força à medida que os projetos se multiplicaram. Os moradores associam cada vez mais as novas instalações à demanda por eletricidade, à construção de infraestrutura de serviços públicos, ao uso de água, ao desenvolvimento de terrenos industriais, ao ruído e ao número limitado de empregos permanentes. A análise da Newsweek de 4 de outubro identificou 16 candidatos em disputas competitivas com históricos favoráveis ao desenvolvimento de data centers. A conclusão insere Husted em um grupo mais amplo, em vez de tratar Ohio como uma disputa de campanha isolada. O risco exato varia conforme o distrito. Alguns candidatos apoiaram isenções fiscais, enquanto outros promoveram projetos específicos ou se opuseram a restrições ao desenvolvimento. Ainda assim, a vulnerabilidade política segue um padrão comum. A promessa anterior de um candidato de benefícios públicos amplos agora enfrenta questionamentos sobre ganhos privados concentrados e custos distribuídos entre as famílias. O histórico de Husted torna essa tensão particularmente direta. Ohio se tornou um mercado relevante de data centers enquanto ele desempenhava um papel central na estratégia de desenvolvimento econômico do estado. A Newsweek informou que a isenção de imposto sobre vendas para data centers em Ohio custou ao estado quase US$ 1,6 bilhão em receita não arrecadada durante 2025. Esse número deu aos adversários uma medida concreta para contestar os incentivos anteriores. Brown argumentou que os moradores de Ohio não deveriam subsidiar as necessidades energéticas e de infraestrutura do setor. Ele também chamou Husted de “o rosto dos data centers” no estado. Husted rejeita a sugestão de que abandonou os interesses locais. Sua campanha afirma que ele tem defendido de forma consistente o controle das comunidades sobre a decisão de os projetos avançarem ou não. No entanto, a consistência quanto à autoridade local não elimina a mudança mais ampla de ênfase. As mensagens anteriores celebravam a expansão, enquanto as atuais se concentram em impedir que os custos cheguem aos consumidores comuns. A transição é relevante porque os eleitores podem comparar a linguagem da campanha com registros criados antes da reação negativa. O reposicionamento político se torna mais difícil quando políticas fiscais, anúncios de projetos e declarações públicas continuam disponíveis. O debate mais amplo sobre data centers nas eleições de meio de mandato, portanto, envolve mais do que instalações individuais. Ele testa se os candidatos conseguem separar o apoio à infraestrutura de IA da responsabilidade por suas consequências locais. Essa distinção era mais fácil quando a maior parte dos custos parecia distante ou técnica. É mais difícil quando as famílias conectam novos empreendimentos às contas mensais de serviços públicos. A Lei de Proteção aos Pagadores de Tarifas Não Resolveu a Questão dos Custos A resposta federal de Husted colocou a proteção aos pagadores de tarifas na agenda, mas não decidiu se os data centers devem arcar com todos os seus custos de infraestrutura. Husted patrocinou a Lei de Proteção aos Pagadores de Tarifas à medida que a oposição a grandes instalações de computação se intensificava. A legislação abordava clientes de grande carga, ou seja, instalações que consomem quantidades excepcionais de eletricidade. A proposta orientava os reguladores estaduais de serviços públicos a considerar padrões que abrangessem as melhorias de geração, transmissão e distribuição exigidas por esses clientes. Seu objetivo era evitar que essas despesas fossem transferidas para famílias e pequenas empresas. A Câmara aprovou a legislação por 417 votos a 3 em 16 de setembro. artigo.texto: Power U.S. Battery-Power Kickoffs Hit $3.2 Billion in September Industrial Info Resources is tracking 11 standalone U.S. BESS projects that were scheduled to kick off in September, totaling US$3.28 billion of investment Released Monday, October 05, 2026 Written by Jesse Broehl, Editor-in-Chief, Breaking Energy News (BEN), IIR Intelligence, (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Eleven standalone BESS projects were scheduled to break ground across the U.S. in September, representing $3.28 billion in combined investment and 2,236 MW of capacity. BESS Ranks Third Among Power Plant Types for September Sixty power generation projects in the U.S. are scheduled to break ground this September, representing a total investment value (TIV) of $16.8 billion and roughly 18,083 megawatts (MW) of capacity across 10 fuel categories. Standalone battery energy-storage systems (BESS) rank third among power plant types this month for total investment, and it trails only solar in project count. Rarely built a decade ago, BESS plants are a rapidly growing market. According to Industrial Info Resources data, 11 standalone BESS projects are scheduled to break ground across the U.S. in September, representing $3.28 billion in combined investment and 2,236 MW of capacity. This story focuses on project starts in the BESS sector for September. For a look at all generation types of plants kicking off, see this accompanying overview news story by IIR Energy. Solar focus is here and natural gas here. See this data compilation for the full list of projects, all generation sources for September. Multiple Enabling Factors Drive Fast-Growing BESS Market BESS's success is driven by multiple factors: battery costs have drastically fallen, making the plants more cost-effective to build. According to BloombergNEF's annual Lithium-Ion Battery Price Survey, overall, battery pack prices have fallen 93% since 2010 -- from roughly $1,436 to $1,474 per kWh (in real 2025 dollars, per BNEF's own inflation-adjusted figures) down to $108 per kWh in 2025. Policy also has been a key factor. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) provided for the first time tax credits for standalone BESS, which before had been limited to co-located with solar. After U.S. elections in the fall of 2024 ushered in a second Trump Administration and full Republican control of Congress, wind and solar tax credits were phased out while the credits for BESS were left intact. Eleven Battery Storage Projects, 2,236 MW of Capacity Texas hosts the largest project (the 1,043-MW Zeus Armstrong BESS), while California and New Mexico each host multiple smaller projects. Minnesota, Indiana and Michigan each have one project. Every one of the 11 projects is new construction; as with solar, there is no refurbishment or life-extension activity in this category, consistent with battery storage being a fundamentally newer technology at utility scale. Ownership skews heavily nonutility, similar to solar: Nine of the 11 projects, representing $2.91 billion, are developed by nonutility/IPP entities. Only two projects are utility-owned--and, notably, both belong to the same company, Xcel Energy. Some notable projects and ownership or offtake structure include: Zeus Armstrong BESS Unit Addition (Claude, TX): At 1,043 MW and $1.57 billion, this is the largest battery-storage project in the September pipeline, and the largest planned standalone battery project in Texas overall, according to third-party interconnection-queue tracking. The project, developed by Zeus Renewable Energy Development, sits in Armstrong County, Texas -- the same county as this month's Claude Armstrong Phase I solar project profiled in IIR Energy's accompanying solar coverage for September planned starts. Armstrong County is also home to a major Crusoe Energy AI data center campus with Google as an anchor tenant, part of Google's broader $40 billion Texas AI infrastructure buildout. Becker Sherco BESS (Clear Lake Township, MN) and Shakopee Blue Lake BESS (Shakopee, MN): These two projects, together worth $549 million, are both pieces of a single, coordinated Xcel Energy clean-energy transition plan. Xcel filed a proposal with Minnesota regulators in October 2025 to double battery storage capacity at its retiring Sherco coal plant in Becker to 600 MW -- Minnesota's largest power plant, scheduled for full coal retirement by the end of 2030 -- while separately adding 135.5 MW of storage at its Blue Lake facility in Shakopee. Both projects reuse existing grid interconnections from the coal and gas infrastructure already on site. The following charts show all 11 projects in two charts, ranked by TIV value and by MW installed capacity. See this data compilation for the full list of all projects, all generation sources for September. Tax credits for BESS were added in 2022. When wind and solar tax credits were phased out by Congress in 2025, the credits for BESS were left intact. - Texas hosts the single-largest project (the 1,043-MW Zeus Armstrong BESS), while California and New Mexico each host multiple smaller projects. artigo.texto: Rethinking WUE: Data Center Water Strategy Beyond The Facitily As AI reshapes data center cooling, improving water usage effectiveness requires a system-level view. October 5, 2026 Water has always served a strategic role in hydronic applications. It carries thermal energy more efficiently than air, making it well-suited for applications where precise thermal management is critical. Today, that includes AI data centers, where rising computing densities are creating unprecedented cooling demands. But as data center development accelerates, the conversation around water is changing. Water is no longer merely a cooling input – its availability, quality and infrastructure capacity have become important considerations for siting, permitting, resilience and community alignment. That makes water usage effectiveness (WUE) an increasingly important metric, but also one that needs to be considered in context. Water as a strategic resource Liquid-based cooling isn't new. Data centers have used water for decades to absorb and remove heat generated by IT equipment. What is changing is the scale and concentration of that heat. AI and high-performance computing are driving higher rack densities that challenge traditional air-cooling approaches. As a result, direct-to-chip liquid cooling and other liquid-based architectures are moving closer to the heat source, where they can efficiently capture heat from CPUs and GPUs. Closed-loop hydronic systems can also recirculate fluid rather than continuously consuming makeup water. Together, these approaches create opportunities to reduce reliance on evaporation and improve facility-level WUE. But there's an important distinction: Using water more efficiently inside a data center doesn't necessarily tell the whole story. Look beyond WUE alone Every cooling architecture involves trade-offs. A closed-loop system, for example, may significantly reduce on-site water consumption, but the heat still has to go somewhere. Depending on the heat rejection strategy, reducing water use can increase electrical demand. Conversely, evaporative cooling can reduce cooling energy under the right conditions while consuming more water. That’s why WUE shouldn't be considered separately from power usage effectiveness (PUE). Water and energy use are closely connected, and the electricity powering a data center can carry its own water footprint depending on the regional generation mix. A cooling strategy that reduces water consumption on-site but requires more electricity may simply shift some of that water demand upstream rather than eliminate it. Liquid cooling adds another factor. Moving liquid closer to high-density computing equipment provides an effective way to manage concentrated heat loads, but liquid cooling alone doesn't determine overall water consumption. Operators and designers still need to consider the complete thermal chain, including pumping, heat exchange, heat rejection and the energy required to operate the system. The objective isn't simply to drive one metric lower. It's to find the appropriate water-energy balance for the site. That balance will look different from one data center to another. Climate, water availability and quality, workload, rack density, grid characteristics, utility capacity and local infrastructure can all influence the appropriate cooling strategy. A data center in a water-stressed region with available electrical capacity may require a different approach than a facility where water is abundant but the grid is constrained. That's where system-level thinking comes in. Instead of starting with a specific cooling technology, project teams should consider the outcomes the facility needs to achieve and consider the complete water cycle: - Where will water come from? - What quality is required? - How will it be treated and moved? - How efficiently can it be reused? - How will heat be rejected? - What happens to the water before it leaves the facility? Advanced treatment technologies can expand opportunities to use reclaimed or alternative water sources while maintaining the quality required for reliable cooling, while digital monitoring can provide visibility into water quality, flow, equipment condition and changing system performance. Meanwhile, heat recovery may create opportunities to put captured thermal energy to beneficial use rather than simply rejecting it. Collaboration outside the facility matters, too. Early coordination with water and wastewater utilities can help data center developers understand local constraints, evaluate reuse opportunities and identify infrastructure investments that strengthen long-term water resilience. Design WUE into the system As AI infrastructure scales, water strategy can no longer be something addressed after the cooling architecture is already established. While WUE provides an important measure of progress, the bigger opportunity is understanding what sits behind the metric. Water source, treatment, hydronics, cooling, monitoring, reuse, discharge and even community infrastructure are all interconnected. The goal isn't simply to use less water. It's to manage water and energy together in a way that supports thermal performance, uptime and responsible growth. For the next generation of data centers, that broader view may be the most effective way to make every drop – and every watt – count. About the Author: Steven Lucente is a business development manager for Xylem’s Applied Water business, where he leads data center business development and turns customer infrastructure challenges into scalable growth strategies and win-ready solutions.

artigo.texto: Politics & Government Operations Suspended At 2 East End Battery Storage Facilities: Romaine "Operations must cease until changes are made that will protect our drinking water." EAST HAMPTON, NY — Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine announced Monday that NextEra Energy had agreed to suspend operations at two battery energy storage facilities on the East End: the facility at Cove Hollow Road in East Hampton and the facility in Montauk near Fort Pond. Both facilities are jointly owned by NextEra Energy and National Grid. "Less than 24 hours after the town board unanimously authorized litigation to shut down the East Hampton and Montauk battery storage facilities, NextEra has temporarily shut both facilities down," East Hampton Town Supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez said. "This is the action we demanded, and I am pleased that NextEra responded swiftly to my September 29 letter and the town board’s action. The board had authorized litigation, retained counsel and taken the steps necessary to go to court to secure this shutdown. I am pleased that NextEra acted before litigation had to be commenced." Find out what's happening in East Hamptonfor free with the latest updates from Patch. She added: "The town will hold off on commencing litigation while counsel reviews the agreement. The town retains all of its legal rights should NextEra fail to follow through on removing all NOVEC 1230 from both facilities and ensuring appropriate fire safety and environmental measures are in place." The suspension, Romaine said, follows weeks of discussions between Suffolk County and NextEra. Find out what's happening in East Hamptonfor free with the latest updates from Patch. NextEra did not immediately respond to a request for comment by Patch. Under the arrangement, NextEra will suspend operations at both sites and remove the Novec 1230 fire suppression agent from both facilities by about October 9, Romaine said. "We are very grateful that this agreement has been reached," said Romaine. "The 2023 fire at the East Hampton BESS location, and the consequent contamination of the site and surrounding areas, prove that the operations must cease until changes are made that will protect our drinking water." The State Department of Environmental Conservation has determined that when water was applied to the East Hampton facility during a May 2023 fire, it mixed with Novec 1230 and broke down into PFPrA, a short-chain "forever chemical," which has since been detected in drinking water in the surrounding area, Romaine said. Two Suffolk County Water Authority wells have been taken offline, he added. The county has drilled monitoring wells to investigate the contamination and supports the Water Authority's litigation against NextEra, he said. In July, Romaine and East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen sent letters to the chief executives of NextEra Energy and National Grid urging them to suspend operations at the East Hampton facility until the investigation is completed, he said. "We need a remediation plan immediately, one approved by the DEC, so the hard work of cleaning the site can begin," said Romaine. "The community did not know for years that the 2023 fire had left behind PFPrA. They should not wait any longer for the situation to be addressed." In August, the Town of East Hampton formally directed East Hampton Energy Storage Center, NextEra Energy and National Grid to take six specific actions, at their sole expense, to address fire-water containment and other safety concerns at the battery energy storage facility on Cove Hollow Road. The demands include new engineering controls capable of containing all fire water and runoff, a revised emergency and safety plan, complete and certified technical information, a hazardous-waste management plan and an independent study of whether the facility remained necessary for the East End electric grid. The action followed questions raised by the May 2023 battery fire and came as state and county agencies continued an investigation into PFPrA and other PFAS contamination near the Suffolk County Water Authority’s Bridgehampton Road Wellfield. No source had been determined, town officials said. Earlier this year, the Water Authority detected PFPrA at the wellfield, removing three wells from service and limiting a fourth to emergency use, town officials said. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation is currently sampling the battery storage property, town officials said. The Suffolk County Department of Health Services is also conducting groundwater sampling and testing private drinking-water wells in the area. The county has identified 26 homes in the area that are not connected to public water; results are not yet available for all of those wells, and several have not yet been sampled, town officials said. When the facility was reviewed in 2017 by the town’s planning board, the town relied on technical information provided by the applicant stating that no liquid within the battery cells could spill and that the only hazardous spillable liquid at the site was oil contained in the transformers and inverters, town officials said. The approved plans therefore included containment for that oil, but not a permanent system capable of capturing the fire-suppression water generated during the May 2023 battery fire, which the Water Authority alleges exceeded 2.2 million gallons, officials added. The town required the companies to: - Submit a revised emergency and safety plan for town approval explaining how the facility would respond to a worst-case battery fire, contain all fire-suppression water and promptly notify the town and emergency agencies. artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr. e Lais Carregosa, da Agência iNFRA A diretoria da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) aprovou nesta terça-feira (6) a abertura de consulta pública sobre o rateio do encargo que vai custear a contratação de baterias via leilão. A proposta da área técnica é ratear os custos entre todos os geradores conforme a flexibilidade oferecida ao sistema. Desta forma, as usinas intermitentes, que não geram de forma firme, devem pagar 100% do encargo. Já os geradores que são mais flexíveis devem pagar menos, entre 75% e 25% do encargo. Assim, usinas eólicas, solares e nucleares pagariam mais, as térmicas um pouco menos e hidrelétricas, o menor patamar. A MMGD (Micro e Minigeração Distribuída), a princípio, não entraria no rateio. Também será discutida na consulta uma proposta do ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) para que o encargo seja reduzido no caso de fontes que entreguem mais potência na ponta de carga – janela em que a geração solar cai e o consumo aumenta, exigindo resposta rápida do sistema. As contribuições poderão ser enviadas até 9 de novembro, e, com isso, a conclusão do processo deve se dar após a realização do primeiro leilão de baterias, marcado para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro.

artigo.texto: Delphos City Council approves 18-month data center moratorium DELPHOS, Ohio (WLIO) — Delphos is joining other cities in the area that are putting a hold on new data centers. Delphos City Council voted Monday night to impose an 18-month moratorium on data centers and renewable energy projects. Each of the Ohio gubernatorial candidates has plans for data centers moving forward in the state. Delphos officials want to wait and see what Ohio lawmakers do to shape how new data center projects are addressed in the state. Council also appointed Doug Mullenhour as mayor to replace Andre McConnahea, who resigned in August. Mullenhour previously served as Delphos mayor from 2020 to 2024 and said he is glad to be back in the mayor’s seat. “Delphos is a great place to live and raise a family. I’ve done that here and we’ve made a lot of progress in the last past years and I just wanted to come back and make sure we get that progress momentum keep it keep it going. We got a safety service building to get built and we got a canal to keep pushing through to try to get it cleaned up and some development going down there. So, there’s a lot of things in the fire” says Doug Mullenhour, Delphos Mayor. During its next meeting, council will vote on a tax abatement agreement that would help establish a pharmacy in the city. artigo.texto: Four EV battery stocks with strong future roadmap New Delhi, Oct. 7 -- India's electric-vehicle (EV) revolution is creating opportunities well beyond vehicle manufacturers, with batteries emerging as a critical part of the ecosystem. As EV adoption increases, demand for lithium-ion cells, battery packs, advanced energy-storage systems and critical battery materials is expected to grow substantially. Indian companies are therefore investing in new battery technologies, manufacturing capacity, and supporting infrastructure to reduce dependence on imports and capture a larger share of this emerging market. In this editorial, we examine four listed companies with significant battery-related ambitions and clearly defined roadmaps. Their businesses span EV batteries, advanced battery technologies, and key materials used in battery manufacturing. This is not a stock recommendation. Exide Industries is one of India's largest battery companies, with more than seven decades of operating history. Its core business remains lead-acid storage batteries, but it's now investing heavily in lithium-ion technology, creating a second growth platform. Exide Energy Solutions, a wholly owned subsidiary, is engaged in lithium-ion cells, modules and battery packs, with applications across electric vehicles and stationary energy storage. The company's new plant is progressing rapidly. At the Bangalore gigafactory, equipment across all four production lines has been delivered, installed, and is fully operational. The company's first NCM cylindrical line has commenced customer sample deliveries. The LFP prismatic line has also started sample supplies for three-wheeler and telecom applications. Management says it has completed key certifications and testing requirements, including multiple BIS standard registrations. They expect revenue contribution from the Bengaluru plant to commence during FY27. According to the company, Exide is building a genuinely Indian advanced chemistry cell platform, with multiple chemistries, multiple form factors, strategic sourcing partnerships for raw materials, automation-led manufacturing, and a global technology partnership. The company's lithium-ion modules and packs are designed for two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles and commercial vehicles, among other applications. On the financial front, the company reported revenue of Rs.5,528.4 crore for Q1 FY27 vs Rs.4,695.1 crore year-on-year. Net profit at Exide Industries was Rs.350.7 crore vs Rs.274.2 crore on-year. Q1 FY27 saw broad-based growth across Exide Industries' key businesses. The automotive OEM business marked its third consecutive quarter of 25% year-on-year growth. According to the management, this reflected sustained momentum in automotive OEM demand and our strong position across key vehicle platforms. Home inverters and solar also grew over 20% on-year, aided by strong summer demand and focused market initiatives. Solar achieved its highest-ever quarterly revenue of Rs.400 crore plus. Industrial Infrastructure, excluding telecom, maintained its double-digit growth trajectory, supported by industrial UPS and traction business. However, management said government tenders remained muted during the quarter, though they expect them to pick up in the second half. The exports business, on a low base after five consecutive quarters of decline, grew revenue by more than 20%. The company says that it continues to closely monitor the evolving global macro environment, as the global situation remains volatile. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility, formerly Amara Raja Batteries Ltd, is one of India's largest manufacturers of lead-acid batteries. The company changed its name in 2023 to reflect its broader vision to lead India's energy transition in the energy and mobility space by providing comprehensive energy solutions. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility has strong brands like 'Amaron', 'PowerZone', 'Quanta', and exports to 70 countries. The company has evolved considerably over the last few years. While the lead acid battery business continues to hold a strong position across automotive and industrial applications, it now extends beyond its traditional areas of operation. Investments in battery packs, cell technologies, energy storage solutions, recycling and power electronics have broadened its presence across the energy and mobility landscape. The company has manufacturing infrastructure that has 1.5 GWh of EV battery pack capacity. Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies (ARACT) is leading initiatives across lithium-ion cell manufacturing and next-generation energy storage technologies. The business is supported by manufacturing infrastructure, R&D capabilities, strategic partnerships and a phased scale-up roadmap aligned to evolving market requirements. The new energy business has a capex plan of Rs.9,500 crore for setting up a Giga Corridor in Telangana. On the financial front, for the quarter ended 30 June 2026, Amara Raja Energy and Mobility achieved robust growth of around 24% on a consolidated basis, with revenue of around Rs.4,215 crore, with about 95% of revenue coming from the lead-acid business, which grew around 22%. The net profit for Q1 FY27 was Rs.190.9 crore vs Rs.164.8 crore on-year. The new energy business grew by more than 70%, recording revenue of around Rs.209 crore. Management said revenue has remained strong, driven by sustained volume momentum in both the aftermarket and OEM segments. Lithium-ion telecom volumes grew by around 50%, and the company maintained a combined market share of over 60% in the telecom segment during the quarter. During FY27, Amara Raja Energy & Mobility expects to spend around Rs.1,700 crore on its capex projects, with a major outlay of around Rs.1,300 crore towards the new energy business and the rest towards the lead-acid business, including recycling capex. artigo.texto: The Lansing Town Board decided to draft a ban on the construction of new data centers in the town at a special meeting on Tuesday night. The meeting was packed with over 200 concerned citizens, who voiced opposition to data center development during a public comment period. The approval process for a proposed data center on Cayuga Lake was paused in July when Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-N.Y.) signed Executive Order 62, enacting a one year moratorium on state permitting for data centers exceeding a 50 megawatt capacity. The board met to navigate uncertainty with how the state moratorium applies to the town — they were met with a crowd of frustrated residents who expressed concern for the future of their hometown in the event of data center construction. The event was lively, with loud reactions from the crowd throughout the evening, met with multiple requests for quiet from the town board. Many of the speakers and audience members wore red, signifying a “stop” to data center development and support of a data center ban. Of the over 30 people who spoke, all but one called for a data center ban in Lansing — the one dissenter being a TeraWulf employee. The draft of the ban will be presented to the public by the town’s attorney at a future meeting. If developed and passed, Lansing will join Dryden and Danby in being some of the first New York towns to ban data centers of any size. Background In August 2025, data center developer TeraWulf secured an 80 year lease to the former Milliken Station powerplant, located in Lansing, and approval for the construction of a data center with up to 400 megawatts of industrial capacity. The project, known as Lake Hawkeye Data, has been met with protest from groups such as No Data Center FLX and Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Now!. The groups sued Lansing’s Zoning Board of Appeals and TeraWulf in January 2026, challenging the zoning board’s classification of the center as a “general processing facility” — an undefined term in the code which makes it easier for development to proceed. The lawsuit is ongoing in spite of the moratorium, the lead attorney for the environmental groups told The Sun in July, because the zoning board’s decision remains in effect. No Data Center FLX has collected almost 23,000 signatures for their petition rejecting the project and has organized protests throughout the approval process. During the moratorium, the Department of Environmental Conservation is prohibited from issuing discretionary permits, which are a necessary step in the data center approval process. The moratorium, however, “does not directly impact local reviews and approval,” according to the board’s statement to open the public comment period. Therefore, it is unclear the exact impact of the moratorium on TeraWulf’s plans for the data center. Public Comments Over 200 people filled the Lansing Middle School auditorium to voice their concerns at the special meeting. This showing came after previous board meetings about the data center did not allow an open public comment period. Commenters were widely in agreement, raising concerns around noise from the proposed data center and stress on the electrical grid, along with potential costly litigation in the event TeraWulf breaches any agreements. However, most did not directly address the state’s moratorium, instead raising concerns about the data center itself. At the midpoint, the agenda called to shift from hearing comments from Lansing residents to non-Lansing residents, which was met with boos from the crowd. The board decided to allow a mix of Lansing and non-Lansing speakers to come forward, and many of the latter abdicated their allotted two minutes of speaking time to Lansing residents. The single voice in favor of the development was Pace Ralli, TeraWulf’s vice president of project development. He said he has worked in clean energy for over 20 years and “care[s] deeply about our environment and natural resources.” Ralli sees the Lake Hawkeye project as an opportunity for economic development and repurposing old industrial land. He described TeraWulf’s work with the town as “constructive and collaborative” and said TeraWulf has made “meaningful changes to the site plan in response” to local concerns. Ralli asked Lansing residents to keep an open mind and “evaluate the project on the facts.” Board Discussion After hearing public comments, some board members were split between a desire for economic development and opposition from the community. Council member Judy Drake, who expressed concern for Lansing’s economic development, said the town has a reputation as “not interested in business.” She said she wanted to explore the option of a “highly regulated data center” as a means to promote the economy. Regulations on project size “make an ugly project seem not quite as ugly,” Wetmore said. He added that supporting the data center as a means of economic development may push away other businesses. Town Supervisor Ruth Groff described the prospective data center as a “fiscal nightmare” that is “open[ing] the door for more problems,” noting that allowing data centers of any size into Lansing could be risky as the only way to hold these companies accountable in the event they breach contract is expensive litigation. The board discussed a town level moratorium due to uncertainty in how Hochul’s executive order would affect local governments, and expressed hope that the state would provide further frameworks or regulation to guide the local government through the evaluation and approval process. Drake said he does not “trust the state when it comes to deciding what happens in our town.” Within the final minutes of the meeting, board members decided to draft an all-out ban. artigo.texto: On Oct. 1, SB 484 required each of Florida’s investor-owned utilities to file a tariff for its largest customers. The law’s core is two sentences. The rules must reasonably ensure that each large-load customer, defined as one drawing 50 megawatts or more, bears its own full cost of service. And the risk that such a customer doesn’t pay may not be borne by everyone else. I published a rubric for reading those filings on Sept. 15, before any existed, and finished amending it before the first one arrived. Each filing gets one of three results: it clears, it has a shortfall to defend, or it misses a required test. Three utilities made Oct. 1 filings. Two filed new large-load tariffs, and FPL asked the Commission to deem its existing one compliant. Duke filed nothing new and relies on a petition pending since April. The scorecards are below. Tampa Electric put real numbers on the page: stated charges, a 20-year minimum term, and, in its customer contract, a termination fee covering the remaining generation, transmission, fuel transportation, and purchased-power charges for the rest of the term. Only two required tests are partly met. The tariff reaches only new or incremental load, and security for an investment-grade customer is 50% of $2.0 million multiplied by its contracted megawatts, against roughly $2.7 million per megawatt of committed plant and transmission, by my arithmetic from the company’s exhibits. The open question is year 20: a customer giving notice can leave owing nothing more, while the company’s own exhibits show about $1.07 billion of generation net plant still on the books in 2047. TECO says that plant would then serve its other customers. That may prove true; no one has agreed to pay for it if it does not. Florida Power & Light filed no new large-load tariff. It asked the Commission to find that the tariffs approved in January as part of its rate settlement, before SB 484 took effect, already comply. Those tariffs carry a 20-year term, two years’ notice, and an exit fee covering the remaining generation charges. The miss is coverage: they apply only to a customer with a projected new or incremental load of 50 megawatts or more and a projected load factor of 85% or more. A load factor can lawfully set a price; here it decides who is covered. The statute defines the customer by peak demand alone. That may describe few customers today. The rubric reads the text, not the current queue. Florida Public Utilities says it has no qualifying customers and no inquiries, and leaves every rate to customer-specific agreements the Commission must approve before service starts. That is reasonable for a small utility. But the filing states no rate, and under the rubric’s first test, a filing with no stated rate misses. Duke Energy Florida filed nothing new by Oct. 1. It relies on a petition filed in April, heard in August and briefed in September. Its president, Melissa Seixas, made the case in these pages on Oct. 2: “Floridians should never be asked to finance someone else’s business decision.” That is the right standard. The filing falls short on one required test. Duke’s policy measures the 50-megawatt threshold over 30 minutes; the statute says 15. And it reaches only firm load, so a new customer that takes interruptible service falls outside it. Duke says such customers need less capacity built for them; the statute’s definition makes no such exception. Until a large-load rate arrives in 2028, which Duke committed to in its brief, qualifying customers pay existing general-service rates, backed by a 20-year term and an exit fee. Two points for anyone following these cases. First, the statute requires the outcome and only permits the tools. The Commission may approve exit fees and minimum terms, but the full-cost result is mandatory either way. Second, FPL asked for proposed agency action, so the Commission can rule without a hearing unless an affected party asks for one. And one number belongs in every conversation about this law. SB 484 does not reach municipal utilities or rural electric cooperatives. By the Commission’s own statistics, that is about 25% of the state’s customer accounts. These are readings of the filed words, not Commission findings. Every citation is collected with the rubric. They show a promise written in mandatory terms, met unevenly. ___ Dr. Mark McNees is director of the MS in Social and Sustainable Enterprises at Florida State University’s Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship. He writes on energy cost policy.
