artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) vai colocar em uma mesma consulta pública duas alternativas para definir quanto cada gerador pagará pelo encargo das baterias contratadas nos leilões de reserva de capacidade (LRCap) de dezembro. A proposta da área técnica da agência gradua a cobrança de acordo com a flexibilidade das usinas, enquanto uma variante apresentada pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) considera a contribuição de potência de cada empreendimento na janela crítica do sistema. A consulta será realizada entre 8 de outubro e 9 de novembro e terá um workshop para apresentação e discussão das metodologias antes do término do período de contribuições. A decisão foi tomada nesta terça-feira, 6 de outubro, seguindo voto do diretor Gentil Nogueira. O prazo reduzido surgiu da preocupação de que o certame ocorra sem que haja tempo para a Aneel concluir a discussão sobre o rateio. Segundo o relator do processo, a alternativa do ONS não substitui, neste momento, a metodologia recomendada pela Superintendência de Regulação dos Serviços de Geração e do Mercado de Energia Elétrica (SGM). As duas serão submetidas ao debate para que a Aneel compare seus efeitos antes de definir o modelo de rateio. “A consulta pública é o ambiente adequado para comparar as duas réguas de graduação, examinar seus pressupostos e efeitos distributivos”, afirmou o diretor em seu voto. Ao final da consulta, a Aneel poderá decidir se o coeficiente que determinará a participação de cada gerador no encargo será baseado na flexibilidade operativa, na contribuição de potência durante a janela crítica ou em uma combinação dos dois atributos. A discussão trata do Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade associado à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (Ercap-SAE). A Lei 15.269/2025 determinou que os custos da contratação sejam rateados entre os geradores, mas deixou para a Aneel regulamentar a forma de divisão da conta. Flexibilidade reduz participação no rateio A metodologia recomendada pela área técnica mantém todos os geradores agentes da Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) na base de custeio, mas gradua a participação de cada empreendimento de acordo com sua flexibilidade. A energia gerada no mês será utilizada como base de incidência do encargo. Os empreendimentos serão distribuídos em quatro patamares. Usinas classificadas como inflexíveis, no P1, terão coeficiente equivalente a 100% do encargo; aquelas com flexibilidade baixa, no P2, 75%; as de flexibilidade alta, no P3, 50%; e as classificadas com flexibilidade muito alta, no P4, 25%. Nenhum dos geradores abrangidos pela regra ficará completamente isento. A proposta busca evitar que a retirada dos empreendimentos mais flexíveis reduza progressivamente a base de custeio e concentre a cobrança sobre os demais agentes. “Todos os geradores fazem parte do universo pagante, mas eles são diferenciados por patamar de flexibilidade. Quanto mais flexível, menos o custo arcado com o pagamento do Ercap”, explicou representante da área técnica da Aneel. A área técnica considera que a flexibilidade é o atributo que melhor representa a contribuição dos geradores para reduzir as necessidades operativas que justificam a contratação das baterias. A constatação é de que nenhum gerador entrega a flexibilidade bidirecional das baterias, e que os sistemas de armazenamento também atuam como carga durante a recarga, o que impede uma equiparação completa entre uma usina considerada flexível e a bateria contratada no leilão. Hidrelétricas ficariam com 46,2% da conta Em uma simulação apresentada pela Aneel, considerando um encargo total de R$ 1 bilhão, as hidrelétricas responderiam por 46,2% da conta, embora representem 60,5% da energia gerada considerada no cálculo. As eólicas, com 18,3% da base, ficariam com 26,8% do encargo. As termelétricas responderiam por 15%, ante participação de 13% na geração, enquanto as fotovoltaicas passariam de 5,7% da base para 8,4% do custo. As nucleares, com 2,5% da geração, responderiam por 3,6%. Nesse cenário, o encargo médio seria de R$ 1,25/MWh para as hidrelétricas, R$ 1,90/MWh para as termelétricas e R$ 2,40/MWh para eólicas, fotovoltaicas e nucleares. A média do sistema seria de R$ 1,64/MWh. O cálculo ocorre em duas etapas. Primeiro, é considerada a energia associada a cada gerador. Depois, essa base individual é ajustada pelo coeficiente correspondente ao patamar de flexibilidade da usina. As bases ajustadas são normalizadas para garantir a arrecadação integral do valor necessário para remunerar as baterias. Com isso, reduzir o coeficiente de uma usina não diminui o montante total do encargo, mas redistribui a conta entre os demais geradores, conforme a análise da área técnica. Para as hidrelétricas, a proposta mede a capacidade efetivamente demonstrada de modular a geração entre períodos de menor e maior necessidade do sistema. Nas termelétricas, são considerados atributos como tempos de acionamento e desligamento, rampas e capacidade de modulação. Já eólicas e solares sem armazenamento associado são enquadradas no patamar de menor flexibilidade. A instalação de baterias associadas ou colocalizadas poderá levar esses empreendimentos a patamares superiores, conforme o porte do armazenamento em relação à usina. Potência na janela crítica O ONS propôs manter a arquitetura geral da metodologia da Aneel e alterar o atributo utilizado para determinar o coeficiente de cada empreendimento. Todos os geradores continuariam na base pagante, a energia efetivamente gerada no mês permaneceria como base de incidência e a cobrança seguiria graduada. artigo.texto: Independence council restricts future data centers after Nebius backlash INDEPENDENCE, Mo. (KCTV) - The Independence City Council voted 6-0 Monday to approve restrictions on future data center development, following a push by opponents of the Nebius AI data center project. The new rules will not affect the Nebius facility, a hyperscale data center on 400 acres at Highway 79 and Little Blue Parkway that broke ground in May. The project drew opposition earlier this year after the previous council approved tax breaks for the company. Voters later removed two city councilors who supported the project and recalled another. Under the new rules, the city council must approve “major” data centers before they can be built. Major data centers are defined as those with electrical loads greater than five megawatts. The city’s amendment to its development ordinance also sets specific requirements, including how far such facilities must be from homes. Councilman Brice Stewart, the only remaining council member who voted against the Nebius incentives, said large-scale data centers were not anticipated when the city’s code of ordinances was last updated in 2022. “The Nebius data center, everything was zoned. They could just come in, buy the land and open the data center,” Stewart said. A planning commission report on the proposed changes said large data centers differ from traditional industrial development, citing “substantial electrical demand, water consumption backup, power generation noise from mechanical equipment, large building, footprints, visual impacts, and potential compatibility, concerns with nearby residential neighborhoods, and community facilities.” The revisions include the following requirements for major data centers: - Generator testing is limited to normal weekday business hours, no more than 10 hours per month, with required sound attenuation and generator testing records. - Closed-loop cooling systems, or similar technologies that use less water than other systems, are required. - Architectural design standards are required that are “intended to reduce their appearance of large uninterrupted building walls.” - A 1,000-foot setback, measured property-line to property-line, is required from residential areas, schools, parks, playgrounds, daycares, nursing homes, hospitals and places of worship. The setback was amended from an initially proposed 500 feet before passage Monday. Resident Daniel Morehead told the council Monday that the city has failed to enforce its current rules on light and noise at the Nebius construction site. “Several of the residents have had to find alternative ways to even exist, most of them moving to their basements, finding other locations with lower noise emissions, just so they can get some sleep,” Morehead said. The new restrictions for major data centers are part of a broader set of changes that create a tiered framework with different rules for smaller facilities. A related set of rules was also created for battery energy storage systems. A six-month moratorium on new data centers, passed by the council in July, remains in effect through Jan. 2, 2027. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no EPE adia estudo de data centers no RS para dezembro Publicado 06/10/2026 • 18:17 | Atualizado há 13 horas KEY POINTS Informe trimestral reorganiza 47 estudos de transmissão: nove estão concluídos, 28 em andamento e dez ainda serão iniciados. Alterações de prazo não significam atraso automático em obras. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) atualizou o calendário da Programação de Estudos da Transmissão de 2026. O informe trimestral de setembro reúne 47 análises: nove finalizadas, 28 em andamento e dez ainda por iniciar. Uma das mudanças alcança o estudo sobre o atendimento a grandes cargas de data centers no Rio Grande do Sul. A conclusão, antes indicada para agosto, passou para dezembro de 2026. O trabalho examina a integração dessas cargas à rede de transmissão; a nova data é do estudo e não representa, isoladamente, adiamento de um empreendimento privado ou de uma obra específica. Também foi ampliado o horizonte do estudo de compensação dinâmica de potência reativa no Sistema Interligado Nacional, de dezembro de 2026 para abril de 2027. A análise sobre controle de tensão no Norte foi dividida em duas partes: a primeira segue para outubro de 2026 e a segunda, incorporada agora à programação, tem término previsto para fevereiro de 2027. A segunda parte do trabalho do Norte está associada à consulta tecnológica da EPE sobre recursos avançados para controle de tensão e suporte dinâmico, aberta até 31 de dezembro. A separação indica que o planejamento pretende incorporar respostas do mercado antes de fechar a recomendação tecnológica. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Na comparação com junho, três estudos passaram à condição de finalizados: atendimento à região da Grande Vitória, à região de Sorocaba, Indaiatuba e entorno e ao sul do Rio Grande do Sul. A finalização do estudo significa conclusão da análise técnica e não equivale a licenciamento, contratação ou entrega das instalações recomendadas. Outros cronogramas foram estendidos. Entre eles estão as análises da ilha do Marajó, da interligação Acre–Rondônia–Mato Grosso, do noroeste de Minas Gerais e de regiões de Campinas e Curitiba, agora apontadas para dezembro. Trabalhos no Maranhão, Mato Grosso, Minas Gerais, Paraná e Rio Grande do Sul também receberam novos marcos entre outubro de 2026 e fevereiro de 2027. O documento funciona como instrumento de transparência do planejamento. Os estudos podem recomendar novas linhas, subestações, transformadores, compensadores ou soluções operativas; depois, cada alternativa ainda precisa percorrer decisões setoriais, autorização ou leilão, licenciamento, contratação e implantação conforme o caso. Para transmissoras, grandes consumidores, fabricantes e financiadores, a atualização ajuda a identificar quando soluções técnicas deverão ficar maduras para as etapas seguintes. artigo.texto: Nearly a year after they received their first data center proposal, Ransom Twp. officials are poised to adopt an ordinance regulating the facilities’ development. Supervisors will vote Monday on an ordinance updating the township’s zoning laws to include requirements for data centers’ development, according to public notices and the agenda for the meeting. The vote comes as the township is involved in litigation over its rejection earlier this year of a proposal by Scranton Materials LLC to construct a data center campus on the company’s Newton Road property. The company in November filed for a curative amendment, challenging the validity of the township’s zoning ordinance, that would have allowed the construction of six data centers — each with a 156,648-square-foot footprint — at its 251-acre quarry at 819 Newton Road. The board voted in January to dismiss the proposed changes due to lack of testimony and evidence from Scranton Materials. Under state law, municipalities are required to allow every type of lawful land use within their borders, or else face legal challenges over exclusionary zoning. The law is the focus of several legal challenges related to the supervisors’ January dismissal of the zoning change. The developer appealed the decision and filed a second lawsuit seeking a declaratory judgment against the board earlier this year. The second lawsuit is ongoing. A Lackawanna County judge ruled in July that a Scranton woman can legally oppose the plans despite not living in Ransom Twp. Officials have not said how the new ordinance would affect the litigation with Scranton Materials. Efforts to reach township Solicitor William Rinaldi about whether the ordinance would render the lawsuits moot were unsuccessful Friday. The Pennsylvania Municipal Planning Code states that no zoning changes or other governing ordinance may adversely affect an existing land development application. More recently, Mudiita Land Venture LLC, a Carbon County-based firm with a parent company in New Jersey, purchased 528.6 acres south of Ransom Road and west of South Keyser Avenue in the township to build a hyperscale data center campus. There have been no other data centers proposed in the township, officials have said. At public meetings on the ordinance, people have been receptive to the proposed law but worry about future development. The ordinance says data centers would be allowed only in the township’s general commercial/manufacturing and heavy manufacturing districts — along the southeastern part of the municipality at the Taylor border and in the southwestern part along the Susquehanna River, respectively — as a conditional use. As a conditional use, the developer would need to meet specific criteria outlined in the ordinance and receive township approval. The board of supervisors would be required to render a written decision on the application within 45 days after the final hearing. Under state law, if a governing body fails to hold a public hearing within 60 days of the application being received, the decision is deemed in favor of the applicant. The ordinance stipulates that data centers have a maximum height of 40 feet and lot area of 8 acres. Other requirements address buffering, fencing, wastewater management, air quality, odor, glare and emissions, battery and fuel storage, parking, noise and vibration, and lighting.

artigo.texto: The Baldwin County Commission passed a 180-day moratorium on all rezoning requests, new data centers and renewable energy projects within zoned areas. Commissioner Jeb Ball said the county has received many rezoning requests, and without a planning director or an updated master plan, he believes it's best to let the incoming commission and a new planning director decide future rezoning cases. "The moratorium will actually be enacted after we leave this meeting today. Is it going to cause some backlashes and rifts? It probably will. Don't care," Ball stated. "It's needed for mainly our staff and for the citizens of this county just to slow down a minute and catch our breath, let the new commission get a planning director in place, let them get the master plan set up and then if they feel like they're ready to go, the new commission can always undo the moratorium." RELATED: Foley puts six month moratorium on data centers to update ordinances, evaluate capacity Ball hopes developers will have time to consider more plans before presenting them to the new commission. "It shouldn't be controversial," he added. "It shouldn't be going against everybody's will around the area and stuff like that, and that's what this master plan, once it's solidified and a new planning director are going find." There are currently exceptions to single-family residential building permits on existing, individually owned lots that do not require a change in zoning or special exception approval. Exceptions also exist for previously approved renewable energy projects and data centers. "I don't disagree with the moratorium. The staff-they're going to get hit harder too once this 180 days is up and there's going to be a lot of rezoning cases coming in front of them," Commissioner Matt McKenzie voiced. "This helps out. I really appreciate it and I know the developers will be upset, but like I said earlier, when do we ever listen to developers?" Commissioner Billie Jo Underwood, who will serve on the next commission, believes the moratorium will allow for smarter preparation for growth as the master plan is updated. "I understand that master plans are just a guide. They're not statutory. But we're being asked more and more to put the brakes on things," Underwood said. "This is not about putting brakes on development at all. It's about making sure we have the proper framework in place to guide the development that is continuing to come." Underwood is unaware of any data center plans for Baldwin County but wants the commission to be prepared as the demand for data increases nationwide. The moratorium was imposed upon passage. The DG made the call during a High-Level Roundtable on Operationalising Nigeria’s Carbon Markets through Robust Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) in Abuja, calling on Private Sectors and Project Developers to build a robust, bankable pipeline of high-integrity projects. artigo.texto: Trending With the November midterm elections approaching, environmental and community advocates gathered at the Capitol Rotunda in Harrisburg Tuesday to protest the impacts of hyperscale artificial intelligence data centers and urge their fellow Pennsylvanians to become more civically engaged. The demonstration was organized by several advocacy groups, including the Better Path Coalition, a grassroots organization that advocates for clean, renewable energy and government policies that prioritize public health. Attendees were encouraged to sign constituent letters representing different subgroups. Organizers said the letters are intended to show lawmakers and other decision-makers opposition to the expansion of data centers while giving frustrated voters a way to engage with elected officials. Organizers said they hope that engagement will motivate voters to participate in the November elections, even if they are angry with the elected leaders on either side of the aisle. "What we're doing is launching the campaign today to encourage people to write constituent letters so that we can send them to not only the governor and our legislators, but anyone who is making decisions about data centers," said Karen Feridun, co-founder of the Better Path Coalition. "I know a lot of people are really angry because they're not seeing an alternative ... sometimes I worry that people might stay home on Election Day." The letters represented a range of concerns, including artists worried about how generative AI could affect their work, parents and guardians concerned about the effects of data centers and AI on children, health care professionals focused on potential impacts to physical and mental health and faith leaders seeking to protect God's creation and marginalized communities, according to Better Path. Though organizers said the event was not intended to rally behind a particular candidate, some attendees held signs that read "Senator Katie Muth: Write-In for Governor." Muth, a Democrat from Montgomery County, introduced Senate Bill 1349 in June. The legislation would impose a three-year moratorium on hyperscale data center development. Speakers criticized Democrat Gov. Josh Shapiro for initially "rubbing elbows" with Amazon Web Services (AWS) executives before calling for greater scrutiny of the data centers supporting AI development. AWS operates hundreds of data center facilities worldwide, though the company does not publish an official count. "Pennsylvania lawmakers, particularly Governor Shapiro, put communities across the state in a very difficult position when it came to hyperscale data center development," said Stuart Day, co-founder of Ohio Valley Allies. "The governor enthusiastically promoted the AI and data center boom, supported these companies, pushed fast track permitting and talked about Pennsylvania working at the speed of business, but while he was cheerleading for this industry, communities -- real communities like mine -- were burdened with figuring out the consequences in real time." Shapiro's administration has sought to regulate that infrastructure through its GRID standards, which set requirements for data centers related to energy, environmental protections and community engagement. A subsequent executive order signed in August requires developers to meet those standards as part of the state permitting process. Speakers at the rally raised concerns about the long-term environmental and health impacts of data centers and what their expansion could mean for future generations. "Communities across the state see the horrific consequences of these data centers on our health, including air pollution, which damages the heart and the lungs, and light pollution, which does not sleep and leads to chronic stress," said Parker Studebaker, director of the Phoenixville Liberation Center. The speakers urged lawmakers to prioritize the health and interests of Pennsylvania communities over the economic incentives driving data center development. "Our parents are not just numbers in the study. Our children are not just a profit margin. Our friends and neighbors are not just a check to be cashed," said Anneke van Rossum, advocacy and advancement coordinator at the Delaware Riverkeeper Network. "I'm tired, but more than anything, I'm angry. The people are angry, and we are not going to let them get away with it this time." Lawmakers advanced several bills last week related to data centers in both chambers ahead of the rally. The bills address issues including the facilities' energy and water use, environmental impacts and how their development is regulated, as lawmakers face increasing pressure to respond to communities concerned about the effects of these facilities.

artigo.texto: ”Agriculture and blue carbon are the next frontier; this means carbon financing will extend to farmers, fishers, and coastal communities—not just large corporations," Coordinating Minister for Food Affairs Zulkifli Hasan remarked at the Indonesia Sustainability Forum (ISF) 2026 in Jakarta, Tuesday. Hasan, who chairs the Carbon Economic Value (NEK) Steering Committee, explained that carbon economic mechanisms serve as an instrument to assign direct monetary value to environmental preservation while channeling financial benefits to grassroots community managers. Indonesia's annual carbon market potential is estimated to reach US$7.7 billion. The national carbon ecosystem is governed under Presidential Regulation No. 110 of 2025 on Carbon Economic Value, supported by six implementing regulations and the Carbon Unit Registry System (SRUK). The market framework incorporates carbon trading, carbon taxation, and result-based payments. To date, the government has issued registered carbon units for four forestry projects, representing an emission reduction capacity of approximately 30 million tons of CO2 equivalent. These four projects carry an estimated total transaction value of Rp5 trillion (approximately US$279.3 million) and have the potential to generate Rp500 billion (US$27.9 million) in non-tax state revenue. Hasan stressed that carbon market development must prioritize inclusivity, ensuring that localized agricultural and coastal conservation activities generate tangible economic improvements for rural populations. artigo.texto: Brookwood City Council backs $3.2 billion Applied Digital data center project BROOKWOOD, Ala. (WBRC) - The Brookwood City Council voted Tuesday to support a resolution backing the Tuscaloosa County Economic Development Authority’s (TCEDA) agreement with Applied Digital for the company’s “Delta Forge 2” AI data center project. The TCEDA signed off on Applied Digital’s “Project Highlands” last month. The council’s decision comes after weeks of concerns from the community about environmental impacts and a lack of transparency surrounding the project. Applied Digital says the project would bring thousands of construction jobs, just over 100 full-time jobs, and hundreds of millions of dollars over time for schools and community projects. Brookwood Mayor Joe Barger believes the project is going to be a game changer for the city. “This has been a long time coming. It’s a project that our city has long been fighting for as a community leader. We are excited about what this economic impact comes to for our police, fire, education, infrastructure and a town as a whole,” Barger said. The Alabama Public Service Commission will vote on a power agreement between Applied Digital and Alabama Power. Barger said that vote could happen within weeks. artigo.texto: Big Island Wants To Ban Big Data Centers, Once They Agree On What They Are Giant data centers have become the latest bogeyman for residents across the nation wary of industrial development. So far, none are based in Hawaiʻi. Hawaiʻi County is discussing a bill that would restrict large-scale data centers on the island. But the public, officials and state representatives can’t agree on how to define one — or whether they are even a threat. Under Big Island zoning rules, residents and businesses can only use their land in the ways outlined by the county’s code. If it’s not listed as a permitted use, then it’s not allowed. Currently, the code allows for data processing centers in an area with a mouthful of modifiers: industrial-commercial-mixed-use-zoned. Translated, that means if a data center developer wants to build in an industrial area, they would just need to apply. There aren’t any so-called “hyperscale” data centers in Hawaiʻi yet. Zoning codes for Maui, Kauaʻi and Honolulu counties also have a not-listed-not-allowed rule for land use. Some of their codes currently permit data storage and processing facilities. But no other county has put forward regulations and the state is only just beginning to study the issue. Bill 170, introduced by Councilwoman Heather Kimball, seeks to make sure data centers like the ones ruffling feathers across the continent are not permitted anywhere on the Big Island. If it passes, construction of large data centers would be banned with one caveat: they can apply for a special use permit. The bill was heard for a second time by the Windward Planning Commission on Thursday. The Leeward Planning Commission will take up the issue on Oct. 15. So far, however, the biggest hurdle is figuring out how to define what would qualify as a data center under the proposed new rules. “If we get a really good definition, I think that could solve a lot of things,” said Louis Daniele, chair of the Windward Commission. “We keep calling things data centers, data processing facilities – That’s kind of confusing for the layperson.” ‘We Don’t Want It’ Powerful technology corporations are rapidly putting up data centers across the country to power the artificial intelligence boom. The rush has sparked significant backlash from communities over concerns about the impact on the environment, the power grid and their neighborhoods. Hundreds of counties from California to Maine have already introduced regulations or instituted moratoriums on data center construction. The centers, which can cover thousands of acres and consume entire city blocks, are the latest target for those wary about new industrial development, such as Amazon megawarehouses and microwave cellphone towers. “I wanted to make sure we got ahead of the issue,” Kimball said. “I think it’s better to do it now,” she added, before developers start knocking on the door. Her primary concern is the effect a data center could have on the island’s already strained grid and aquifers. The massive centers being built across the country require equally massive amounts of energy and water. A typical hyperscale data center can use up to 100 megawatts of electricity annually, for instance. That could power 100,000 households, according to The International Energy Agency. The increased demand on the grid and the added infrastructure required to support it are raising utilities’ costs to produce electricity elsewhere, and those costs are being passed on to residents. In Maryland, customers pay $168 to $216 more per year on their electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom, according to estimates. Across Hawaiʻi and the country, residents are not only concerned about higher bills. They’re also worried that the energy demand increases the use of fossil fuels and thus pollution, which drives climate change and threatens health. Christina Holt, a Hilo resident who recently ran unsuccessfully for state representative, is leading the local charge against the centers. She’s hosted community Zoom meetings and posts regularly on social media to inform residents and urge them to speak out. Dozens of Big Island residents have shown up at planning commissions meetings. In hours and pages of testimony, residents have made clear that they support an outright ban. “We don’t want it,” Holt said, “and we, as a community, have every right to say no.” Defining ‘Data Center’ No Easy Feat For Bill 170 to be effective, advocates say, it needs to clearly define data centers and distinguish them from a data processing center. Data processing center use was added to the county code in 1996 when the council undertook numerous amendments to the zoning rules. The addition reflected emerging technologies and business activities at the time. It generally referred to office-oriented businesses that used computers to process information, maintain electronic records, or provide administrative and technical services. These types of centers don’t require much electricity and are vital to business and research operations. Today, the state has more than 20 data processing centers, two of them on the Big Island. A Hawaiian Telecom facility in Kawaihae is one of them. Jeannine Souki, manager of government and regulatory affairs for Hawaiian Telecom, testified in front of the Windward Commission, one of two planning commissions on the island, in September. Advocates have two related worries. A definition that’s too broad could exclude necessary infrastructure. Being too specific could create loopholes developers can exploit. Souki urged commissioners to consider whether the way Bill 170 defines data centers could unintentionally ban these essential telecommunication facilities Lawsuits by developers against towns elsewhere in the country that have attempted to prevent construction are adding further pressure to get the definition right. “They’re going to lie, cheat and steal to get what they want,” Chuck Flaherty, secretary of the Hawaiʻi island Sierra Club, said

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Energia nuclear vai abastecer novo data center nos EUA Publicado 06/10/2026 • 10:00 | Atualizado há 21 horas KEY POINTS Foto: AFP A Oracle planeja usar energia nuclear para atender parte da demanda de seu novo campus de data centers nos Estados Unidos. A empresa propôs comprar entre 125 MW e 250 MW da produção da usina nuclear de Point Beach, em Wisconsin. O projeto, chamado Project Lighthouse, deve ficar em Port Washington. A Oracle apresentou a proposta em 2 de outubro de 2026, mas ainda precisa da aprovação do órgão regulador de energia de Wisconsin. Leia também: Oracle fecha contrato de US$ 7 bilhões para fornecer serviços de nuvem à Tencent A quantidade negociada representa a potência que a Oracle pretende adquirir para o novo campus. A usina Point Beach possui dois reatores nucleares e fica às margens do Lago Michigan, de acordo com informações internacionais. A We Energies vendeu a usina para a NextEra Energy em 2007, mas manteve um contrato para comprar a maior parte da geração de Point Beach até 2033. A negociação envolve um fornecimento de energia mais eficaz. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC A movimentação da Oracle segue um padrão visto no mercado recentemente. Com o avanço da inteligência artificial e da construção de novos data centers, as empresas buscam um fornecimento de energia mais poderoso e eficaz. Vale destacar que uma energia contínua e sem falhas é essencial para manter o funcionamento das estruturas tecnológicas. Em especial, as usinas nucleares voltaram a receber maior atenção do mercado de tecnologia. Leia também: Entrelinhas de Mercado: IA vai eliminar negócios antes de revelar o que criará, diz VP executivo da Oracle A Public Service Commission of Wisconsin (PSC) precisa analisar e aprovar a negociação. Ainda de acordo com as informações, a vice-presidente de Capacidade e Planejamento de Infraestrutura da Oracle afirmou que a empresa esperava apresentar a proposta à comissão até o fim de 2026. O acordo também se relaciona a uma proposta de aumento de US$ 176 milhões (R$ 878,9 milhões) nas tarifas de eletricidade da concessionária para 2027. artigo.texto: Sen. Britt rallies Mobile County GOP, talks data centers and AI accountability MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Alabama Sen. Katie Britt headlined the Mobile County Republican Party meeting at Regency Church of Christ, rallying voters with less than a month until the midterms. Senator warns against complacency Britt faced a packed house. Her message: don’t get complacent. While Republicans are used to winning big in Mobile County, some polls show Democrat Doug Jones within striking distance of Republican Tommy Tuberville in the governor’s race. In May, more Mobile County voters voted in the Democratic primary than the Republican one. That hasn’t happened since 1994. Data centers divide governor’s race candidates Data centers have emerged as a top issue dividing Republican gubernatorial candidate Tommy Tuberville from his Democratic opponent, Doug Jones. Tuberville considers them essential, while Jones has called for a one-year moratorium. At the Mobile County Republican Party event, Britt sought to strike a middle ground. She said she doesn’t want to stop the construction of data centers, and she doesn’t support a national one-size-fits-all policy. But she said she favors “guardrails” to make sure data centers don’t receive special tax breaks and pay their own way when it comes to electricity and water usage. Britt warned that the U.S. can’t fall behind China. “What we have to understand is what’s good for one community may not be good for another, and that’s why I reject that we have to have a moratorium across the country because for some communities, this is the right pathway forward. And I also don’t believe that we should put one in every corner,” Britt said. “Guys, you don’t want our greatest adversary having capabilities that we do not. So we have to do that, but I think we also have to do that in a very smart and measured way,” Britt said. Britt discusses AI accountability efforts Britt also talked about her efforts to hold artificial intelligence companies accountable. She pointed to conversations she’s had with parents whose children have committed suicide after receiving encouragement to do so from chatbots. Copyright 2026 WALA. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Across the country, data centers are driving a rise in utility prices, imposing a massive demand on our electricity grid and contributing to increased noise pollution in communities large and small. They are also projected to increase both our yearly consumption of fresh water and our carbon emissions. In short, data centers are bad news: for the environment, and for all of us. So it might shock you to learn that one is rising up in Princeton’s backyard. Right this moment, a data center is being built a mere 10-minute drive from our main campus. The South Brunswick data center on Route 1 will rely on 20 diesel generators for backup power and store an estimated 400,000 gallons of diesel fuel on site. But to term these generators as “backups” is deceptive when their operation will not really be an exception or an emergency measure. As Princeton’s mayor and Council explained in a statement to the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection, “the 20 generators, misleadingly characterized as ‘minor sources’ of emissions, will run not only during power outages but also for routine testing and during periods of peak or critical demand … operating the generators will make the site a major source of emissions.” Diesel exhaust particles and gases are linked to asthma and other respiratory health issues: When running, the generators of the South Brunswick data center will send these harmful substances across Princeton’s municipal boundaries. Fortunately, there is something that the University can do about it. Princeton University should submit a statement to the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection urging them to deny the permit for the center as it runs in its current form. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection is currently considering whether to grant an air permit to the data center, which will be located on a site that was owned by Princeton University until 2024. The University may no longer own the land, but that doesn’t mean it should stand by and remain passive to the approval of an industrial project whose generators will threaten the health of all those local to the area. Air doesn’t care about municipal boundaries or campus borders; the emitted particulates and gases will affect our University community, from the student body to faculty and staff to the foxes and squirrels that live on our campus. It is understandable that universities sometimes try to skirt political hot topics to evade unwelcome attention from the media or the government. But the demand for the regulation of data centers is a rare bipartisan issue, with seven in 10 Americans opposing constructing AI data centers in their local area. Speaking out against the construction of the data center is not a political statement: It’s about standing in opposition to a direct threat to the health and safety of our community. The Princeton Undergraduate Student Government and the Princeton Municipality have both published statements to the NJDEP opposing the air permit. It’s time for the University to follow their lead. Data center construction is certainly not unique to the Princeton area. But even if we consider them an unavoidable manifestation of a technologically developing society, that doesn’t mean we can’t push for their being held to higher environmental standards. We can hold data centers accountable for generating and using electricity without poisoning our air and water, and stand against their receiving air permits until they do so. Princeton University should echo the Princeton Council in asking the Department of Environmental Protection to “take every possible measure to ensure that this data center does not become an environmental blight on our region.” That means not granting an air permit until the plan is adapted with cleaner backup energy generation solutions. Until Oct. 7, the public also has the opportunity to submit written comments to the NJDEP expressing concerns about the data center. The agency will issue a final decision soon after the deadline about whether or not it will grant the permit, or set other environmental safeguards that will need to be met before the permit can be issued. Princeton prides itself on its policy of institutional restraint. But that doesn’t absolve the University of an obligation to speak out against a direct threat to the public health of its community. In times of trouble for higher education, the University doesn’t hesitate to turn to its community to stand up for Princeton. Now, we need Princeton to stand up for us. In his 2026 Commencement address, University President Christopher Eisgruber ’83 quoted former University President Robert Goheen ’40 GS ’48: “Courage, with temperance, is always needed to hold the university to its role and mission [...] the university as a human institution can be confident not only of its past but of its present and future, ready to stand up for its aims and basic commitments, bold to make its voice heard in the land.” As the data center rises, we’re looking towards the future not merely of the University itself, but of the land it sits on and the entire community to which it belongs. Protecting that should be its most basic commitment. Princeton, it’s time to stand up with your students and their health: Say no to the South Brunswick data center. Elif Cam ’30 is a contributing Opinion writer from Princeton, N.J. Since you read this far, she thinks you might as well take a minute to submit a comment to NJDEP opposing the South Brunswick data center air permit. She can be reached by email at elif[at]dailyprincetonian.com.

artigo.texto: Scott County candidates oppose data centers, split on Flock cameras at public forum Forum held at the Scott County Public Library on Sunday GEORGETOWN, Ky. — Debate over data centers and Flock cameras dominated a candidate forum in Scott County, where candidates hoping to represent the county after the November election weighed in on the hot-button issues at the Scott County Public Library. Many were clear: no to data centers. On Flock cameras, their answers were more nuanced. Youth voice in the debate For Scott County High School senior Nate Reeves, the stakes are high. “People like me are going to grow up with a data center in our community and be impacted by the widespread use of Flock cameras. This is why I’m here. Being young only increases my passion for this issue, it doesn’t decrease it,” Reeves said. Reeves was part of a youth-driven push for harsher restrictions in the county’s data center ordinance. On Sunday, he just listened. “We’re seeing an issue here that’s really, really powerful. And it is really, really impactful to young people,” he said. Among those hoping to earn votes like Reeves’ were candidates for Georgetown City Council, state representative and Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District. Candidates say no to data centers On data centers, most candidates offered the same message — “no” in principle — citing water consumption, driving up utility rates and use of farmland. “But it’s very clear to me that going around the Sixth District that all communities are against data centers in central Kentucky,” Peter Lynch, an independent candidate for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, said. But some said they want to have rules on the books regulating data centers in case a full data center ban falls in front of the courts. “This is the first time the city council is passionate enough against something that they themselves brought it to the table for direction to planning and zoning. That’s how passionate we are about it,” Georgetown City Council member Karen Tingle Sames said. Nuance on Flock cameras Some candidates say they see the cameras as a useful tool for law enforcement, citing things like helping police locate missing people, but raised concerns over a private company like Flock owning the data and not enough parameters around who gets to access it. “If I had to vote today, I would not want Flock cameras,” Georgetown City Council member Willow Hambrick said. For Reeves, Sunday was about listening. He says November will be about action. Candidates who did not attend weigh in Three candidates who did not attend the forum provided statements to WKYT: U.S. Senate candidate Charles Booker said he backs a moratorium on data centers until water, utility and environmental impacts are clear, saying “while Kentucky is open for business, it’s not for sale.” He said he opposes Flock cameras as “a gross violation of Kentuckians’ privacy.” Republican candidate for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District Ralph Alvarado, through a spokesperson, said data center decisions “belong in the hands of local fiscal courts.” Democratic candidate for Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District Zach Dembo said he opposes special tax breaks and liability protections for data center developers and backs a ban on congressional stock trading on nonpublic information. artigo.texto: O debate sobre data centers de IA no Kansas transforma a eleição para governador em um teste de controle local O Kansas transformou seu debate sobre data centers de IA em um conflito político estadual depois que comunidades questionaram projetos por causa de eletricidade, água, incentivos fiscais e controle local. A discussão agora divide os dois principais candidatos ao governo. A candidata democrata Cindy Holscher defende a suspensão de grandes empreendimentos até que o Kansas inclua proteções mais robustas na legislação. O candidato republicano Ty Masterson afirma que as regras atuais podem proteger os moradores, ao mesmo tempo que permitem aos governos locais aprovar projetos adequados. Ambos os candidatos ajudaram a criar a política que agora debatem. Os dois votaram a favor de uma lei de 2025 que oferece aos data centers qualificados uma isenção de 20 anos do imposto sobre vendas. Holscher mais tarde mudou de posição após ouvir uma oposição crescente em reuniões públicas. Masterson apresenta essa reviravolta como inconsistência política. A disputa, portanto, vai além de uma discussão já conhecida entre desenvolvimento e conservação. Ela questiona se o Kansas deve confiar nas salvaguardas regulatórias existentes ou interromper a construção enquanto os legisladores definem padrões estaduais mais firmes. Essa escolha importa além do Kansas. Empresas de inteligência artificial precisam expandir redes de instalações de computação intensivas em energia. Ainda assim, o custo político de hospedar essas instalações recai cada vez mais sobre governadores, reguladores de serviços públicos, câmaras municipais e moradores próximos. O debate sobre data centers de IA no Kansas saiu de Topeka e chegou à Main Street O Kansas já não debate data centers como uma oportunidade econômica abstrata. As comunidades estão testando quem controla suas terras, serviços públicos e processo de negociação. A base imediata da política é o Projeto de Lei do Senado 98, aprovado em 2025. A lei criou uma isenção de 20 anos dos impostos estadual e local sobre vendas para projetos qualificados de data centers. Um operador qualificado deve se comprometer com pelo menos 250 milhões em investimentos, além de cumprir exigências de emprego e operação. O programa de incentivos do Kansas também exige um plano de compra de eletricidade de longo prazo, planejamento de conservação de água e uma análise de segurança. O Kansas proibiu as concessionárias de oferecer aos data centers qualificados tarifas de eletricidade com desconto destinadas ao desenvolvimento econômico. A lei também exige uma análise pelo Kansas Intelligence Fusion Center antes que um projeto receba benefícios públicos. Essas disposições permitem que os defensores argumentem que o Kansas não ofereceu um subsídio irrestrito. Eles descrevem a lei como uma estrutura para atrair grandes infraestruturas, ao mesmo tempo que atribui obrigações identificáveis a seus operadores. A legislação ainda criou um incentivo excepcionalmente duradouro. Vinte anos vão muito além do mandato de um governador, da vida política de uma comissão municipal ou do ciclo inicial de construção. Esse horizonte temporal mudou a conversa pública. Os moradores não perguntam apenas se um projeto gerará trabalho na construção civil. Eles querem saber quem assume o risco se a demanda de energia, o consumo de água ou a propriedade mudarem ao longo de duas décadas. Disputas locais tornaram essas questões concretas. Emporia aprovou um Distrito de Sobreposição de Infraestrutura Digital em julho de 2026, criando regras de zoneamento para o possível desenvolvimento de data centers. A cidade enfatiza que não aprovou nenhuma instalação para construção. Essa distinção não encerrou o conflito. Opositores buscaram uma iniciativa para proibir data centers de alto impacto. A comissão municipal então solicitou orientação judicial sobre a situação jurídica da petição. O processo demonstra por que estruturas de zoneamento podem se tornar politicamente relevantes antes que um operador identificado apresente um plano final de construção. Depois que terrenos são designados e as discussões sobre serviços públicos avançam, os moradores podem acreditar que as decisões decisivas já foram tomadas. Lawrence adotou uma abordagem mais cautelosa. Líderes municipais aprovaram uma suspensão temporária enquanto autoridades estudavam possíveis regras para grandes instalações. Outras comunidades debateram campi propostos, compromissos com serviços públicos e a abrangência das divulgações públicas. Independence forneceu um alerta eleitoral ainda mais claro. Os eleitores destituíram o vereador John Perkins por uma margem de 68% a 32%, depois que ele apoiou um empreendimento proposto envolvendo a empresa de infraestrutura de IA Nebius. Outro apoiador do projeto perdeu uma disputa para prefeito depois que um adversário questionou o processo de aprovação e pediu uma votação pública. Esses resultados não estabelecem um consenso estadual, mas mostram o custo político de parecer desdenhoso. A reação local transformou a localização de data centers em uma questão de consentimento. Um projeto pode cumprir os procedimentos formais de zoneamento, enquanto os moradores ainda concluem que sua escala, suas demandas por recursos ou suas negociações receberam escrutínio insuficiente. Para empresas de tecnologia, essa distinção é crucial. Obter uma licença não é o mesmo que manter o apoio de uma comunidade durante toda a construção e operação. O debate sobre data centers de IA no Kansas agora começa nessa lacuna. Líderes estaduais criaram o incentivo, mas autoridades locais e moradores precisam lidar com as consequências práticas dos locais propostos. artigo.texto: The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors will consider a proposal Tuesday to develop a zoning amendment prohibiting large-scale data centers in unincorporated parts of the county, citing concerns about the energy and water demands and potential public health effects associated with facilities used to power artificial intelligence. The motion by Supervisor Hilda Solis would direct the Department of Regional Planning to begin drafting an amendment to the county’s zoning code establishing definitions for different types of data centers based on factors including acreage, square footage, energy use and water consumption. The proposed zoning amendment would distinguish hyperscale and artificial intelligence data centers from what the motion calls “beneficial use” facilities, including enterprise, accessory or sole-source data centers used for daily computational needs. The zoning amendment would prohibit all data centers meeting the zoning amendment’s definition of “large-scale” in every zone of unincorporated Los Angeles County. “Given the pressing concerns to immediately prevent the environmental and health effects of data centers powering AI from impacting unincorporated County residents, it is imperative that the Board of Supervisors act on the recommendations to prohibit these facilities expediently,” according to the motion. The proposal comes amid growing interest in the environmental effects of the computing infrastructure required for increasingly powerful AI systems. “Data centers servicing artificial intelligence (AI) consume high rates of energy, over-utilize water resources, contribute to environmental pollution, and impact public health in ways that are still being understood,” according to Solis’ motion. The motion states that the growth of artificial intelligence has fueled development of hyperscale or large-scale data centers that can be larger and consume more resources than facilities traditionally used to service computer networks and store data. It also points to opposition to proposed data centers in the San Gabriel Valley. According to the motion, the Board of Supervisors received 101 pages of public comments, primarily calling for a moratorium on data centers. The motion cites actions by Monterey Park, Montebello, Baldwin Park and El Monte to restrict or halt data center development and notes that Alhambra voters are scheduled to consider a similar ballot measure in November. The county began examining the issue in April, when the board approved a motion directing county departments to study the potential health, environmental and safety effects of data centers, along with their impact on electrical and water resources. A subsequent county report recommended amending Title 22 of the county zoning code to define data centers and prohibit hyperscale facilities in all zones. According to Solis’ motion, the county’s director of Regional Planning on Sept. 17 invoked existing authority under Title 22 to rely on the absence of a similarly defined land use to prohibit large-scale data centers while a comprehensive zoning amendment is developed. Tuesday’s motion would direct Regional Planning to inform residents in unincorporated communities about that action. It would also direct the Department of Public Health, working with County Counsel, to determine whether the county’s noise regulations should be amended to address “low frequency and continuous noise associated with large-scale data centers.” The county’s chief executive officer would be directed to identify funding needed to prepare and implement the zoning amendment, its required California Environmental Quality Act analysis and any changes to the county’s noise regulations. The motion additionally calls for Regional Planning and County Counsel to be prepared to introduce a moratorium if a proposed data center in an unincorporated area presents what the motion describes as a “current and immediate threat to public health, safety, and welfare.” Such a moratorium would target facilities posing a serious risk or nuisance involving health, safety or environmental resources, particularly water and energy resources. The item is scheduled to be considered when the Board of Supervisors meets Tuesday.

artigo.texto: DeLAND, Fla. — The Volusia County Council is moving forward with a ban on data centers after the first reading of the proposed ordinance. Residents in favor and against them spoke out at the podium, but it wasn't easy to change commissioners' minds. As they reviewed an ordinance written by staff, county commissioners listed concerns discussed two months ago during a meeting in August — like possible sinkholes, public safety and environmental impacts, like water usage. The ordinance said the county will not review or approve any applications, permits, amendments or construction about them. “I, for one, am pleased with what we have in front of us, and unless someone can change my mind, I’ll be voting in favor of it,” District 4 Volusia County Council Member Troy Kent said. The 26-page ordinance references Florida Senate Bill 484, which went into effect in July. The bill allows local governments to regulate large-scale data centers through land development regulations. The proposed ordinance also references studies that say data centers consume large amounts of water, affect the environment and pose health risks for residents. “And if we vote for this ban, it’s not a statement that any of us up here are against data centers," Volusia County Chair Jeff Brower said. "We use them every day. It just means not here.” Council members voted unanimously to move the proposal forward. It is expected to be discussed by the Planning and Land Development Regulation Commission on Oct. 15. Then it’s up for the second and final hearing on Oct. 20. If approved, the ordinance would take effect once filed with the Florida Department of State.

artigo.texto: EU Commits KSh590 Million to Back Kenya's Carbon Market Monitoring Framework The European Union is supporting Kenya with KSh590 million to develop a robust monitoring and validation system, aligning with the country's newly launched National Carbon Registry. The European Union has committed KSh590 million (approximately 4 million euros) to support Kenya in developing a robust monitoring and validation system for its rapidly expanding carbon market. This strategic financial backing comes at a critical juncture as Kenya seeks to position itself as a continental leader in climate finance, ensuring that the revenues generated from carbon credit trading are transparent, verifiable, and equitably distributed to local communities. Strengthening Market Integrity and Transparency The EU funding is specifically earmarked for the enhancement of Kenya's National Carbon Registry, a digital platform recently launched by the government to track the issuance, transfer, and retirement of carbon credits. As the global demand for high-quality, verified carbon offsets surges, the integrity of the underlying data has become paramount. The new monitoring system will utilize advanced satellite imagery, blockchain technology, and independent third-party audits to validate the actual emission reductions claimed by project developers, thereby preventing greenwashing and ensuring that buyers receive genuine climate impact. This investment aligns perfectly with Kenya's newly published Carbon Market Engagement Guide, which established a strict national carbon budget for international transactions. The government has capped the export of carbon credits at 10 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent through 2030, a move designed to ensure that Kenya retains sufficient mitigation capacity to meet its own Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. The EU-backed validation framework will be instrumental in enforcing this cap and managing the complex accounting required under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Empowering Local Communities A central pillar of Kenya's carbon market regulations is the mandatory sharing of revenues with the communities that host the projects. Under the Climate Change (Carbon Markets) Regulations, land-based projects such as reforestation and sustainable agriculture initiatives are required to allocate a minimum of 40 percent of their net earnings to local community development funds. The new EU-funded monitoring system will include a specific module to track these financial flows, ensuring that the promised benefits actually reach the intended beneficiaries and are used for agreed-upon development projects like schools, clinics, and water infrastructure. By guaranteeing fair distribution, the government aims to secure the long-term social license for carbon projects. Historically, some carbon initiatives in Africa have faced backlash from local populations who felt excluded from the financial benefits or whose land rights were compromised. A transparent, verifiable system of revenue sharing is therefore seen as essential for the sustainable scaling of the sector, attracting high-quality impact investors who prioritize social equity alongside environmental outcomes. Positioning Kenya as a Regional Hub The EU's financial support underscores the deepening climate partnership between Brussels and Nairobi. As the European Union implements its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which places a tariff on carbon-intensive imports, African nations are under increasing pressure to decarbonize their export industries. A well-regulated, transparent domestic carbon market provides Kenyan exporters with a mechanism to offset their emissions and remain competitive in the European market. Furthermore, Kenya is laying the groundwork for a formal, regulated carbon exchange, with plans to have the platform fully operational by early 2027. This exchange will move the country away from fragmented, over-the-counter bilateral deals towards a centralized, price-discovery mechanism that reflects the true value of high-integrity African carbon credits. The EU's technical and financial assistance is providing the foundational infrastructure necessary to make this exchange a reality, ensuring it meets international standards of governance and market surveillance. Future Outlook and Global Integration As Kenya refines its regulatory framework and deploys the new monitoring technologies, it is sending a clear signal to the global market that it is open for high-quality climate business. The combination of a strict national cap, mandatory community benefit-sharing, and EU-backed verification creates a premium product that is highly attractive to multinational corporations seeking to meet their net-zero commitments with credible offsets. The successful implementation of this KSh590 million project will not only safeguard Kenya's environmental assets but also serve as a blueprint for other developing nations navigating the complex intersection of climate finance, sovereign rights, and community development. By prioritizing transparency and equity, Kenya is demonstrating that the global carbon market can be a powerful engine for sustainable development, provided it is governed with rigor and accountability. artigo.texto: Linea Energy Closes Financing for 250 MW Mesa View Battery Storage Project in Texas Linea Energy has closed project debt and a preferred equity commitment for Mesa View, a 250 MW / 500 MWh battery storage project in Upton County, with commercial operation expected in 2027. Linea Energy, a renewables developer and independent power producer sponsored by EnCap Investments L.P., has announced the closing of project debt financing and a preferred equity commitment for Mesa View BESS. The standalone 250 MW / 500 MWh battery energy storage project is located in Upton County, Texas. The announcement was made on October 1, 2026. A three-part financing structure According to the company, the debt consists of a construction-to-term loan, a tax equity bridge loan and a letter of credit facility. Norddeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale (NORD/LB) acted as coordinating lead arranger, while Texas Capital participated as a syndicate lender. D.E. Shaw Renewable Investments (DESRI) provided the preferred equity commitment. Linea Energy did not disclose the amount of the debt or of the preferred equity commitment. This type of financing comes in a market where storage projects attract varied structures, as illustrated by CIP's investment in the Kilmarnock South battery storage project in Scotland. Company Linea Energy: company profile Partners already engaged with Linea Cassidy DeLine, Chief Executive Officer of Linea Energy, says the closing illustrates the maturation of the company's platform and its ability to repeatedly deliver investable opportunities to the market. Sondra Martinez, Managing Director at NORD/LB, states that the bank led another financing for Linea, following three previous transactions. Peter Koczanski, Head of Corporate Development at DESRI, notes that the new commitment follows the preferred equity commitment made on Duffy BESS. According to him, the partnership reflects DESRI's confidence in Linea's development platform and execution capabilities. Commercial operation expected in 2027 Mesa View BESS is expected to reach commercial operation in 2027. artigo.texto: Beaufort Co. planning commission recommends a temporary moratorium on data centers BEAUFORT COUNTY, S.C. (WTOC) - Beaufort County leaders are moving forward with a temporary moratorium on data centers. The county’s planning commission voted to send the proposed ordinance to the county council. They also asked council to consider extending the pause from nine months to 12 months. If passed, it would pause acceptance, processing, approval, or issuance of certain applications, permits, and approvals for data centers in the county. County leaders say the moratorium will give them time to define what a data center is and look at the potential impacts one could bring to the county. Several residents spoke during the public comment period, and they were all against the idea of data centers in Beaufort County. They also questioned where one would go. For the moratorium to pass, it will need to go through three different votes and a public hearing. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Fort Smith Board approves data center ordinance, but seeks more restrictions An ordinance making it more difficult to build a data center in Fort Smith was approved Monday (Oct. 5) by the cityâs board of directors, but many on the board want more stringent guidelines and at least one director wants legal clarity on using water sales to limit regional data center development. The ordinance approved Monday by the board requires a development plan review by the Planning Commission and then full board approval of a data center project in the cityâs industrial zoning districts. The ordinance requires an eight-foot opaque wall surrounding the property, 500-foot setbacks from each property line, and âletters from applicable public utilities regarding capacity and proposed load.â Director Christina Catsavis expressed concern about the Fort Chaffee Redevelopment Authority (FCRA), which manages land within city limits, being able to sell land for a data center project without city oversight. The FCRA was formed in 1997 to oversee redevelopment of 6,000 acres of land released by the U.S. Army from Fort Chaffee as part of a Base Realignment and Closure downsizing. Deputy City Administrator Maggie Rice said any property within city limits fall under city development ordinances. “This board still has zoning control over the FCRA property that is in Fort Smith, so you would still have development plan approval that would be required should the FCRA sell property for a data center,â Rice said. As to concerns expressed by some board members about the proposed ordinance not being as tough as that passed by the city of Fayetteville, Rice said the Fort Smith board will have more control over data center development than the Fayetteville City Council. âIn my opinion you donât get much more control over a data center than whatâs being proposed,â Rice said. âThis has to go through two public hearings and this board can ask for anything that it wants. You can make the setback larger, you can make the wall taller, you can require certain facade requirements, you can tell them no.â Rice said the cityâs rules now allow a data center to be built in certain city industrial zones without planning commission or board review. However, Directors AndrÃ© Good and Catsavis wanted to table the proposed ordinance and consider one with more restrictions at a December board meeting. âIâd like to put more teeth in it,â Good said. âIâd like to make it a little bit more difficult.â But Directors Neal Martin and Kevin Settle said they should pass the ordinance because existing city rules now allow a data center project to be built. Martin said the proposed ordinance is a âgood initial step.â âIâd rather pass it tonight, and then have an amendment come back in December,â Settle said. âThat way weâve got protections over these next two months.â Settle, a frequent advocate for using the cityâs water system, which provides water to numerous cities and associations in the region, again pushed city administration to come back with clear and legal options about adding language in water contracts that could restrict or prevent data centers from being built outside city limits. âI want to know if we can have full control over, if they tie in a data center, we should have the right to vote on that as a board,â Settle said in a conversation with City Administrator Jeff Dingman. âYou said yes, but now Iâm hearing that it depends if itâs a contract user, wholesale user. I want this board in the future to have full autonomy that if a data center comes to any city that is connected to our water system, this board votes on that connection, yes or no.â The board voted 6-0 in favor of the ordinance. BACKGROUND Arkansas officials, with support from Gov. Sarah Sanders, have restricted local government actions on data centers. Arkansas Act 851 of 2023 prevents local governments from banning data center development. The law does not prevent local governments from adopting rules that create delays or significant restrictions with data center projects. The cities of Fayetteville and Little Rock have approved more stringent data center development rules. The development of data centers nationwide and in Arkansas has become controversial, with pushback often resulting from local grassroots efforts. Concerns include the potential for massive water use, rising utility rates, excessive noise, and groundwater pollution. The state of New York recently implemented a one-year moratorium on data center construction. According to reporting from CNBC and other outlets, more than 500 local governments nationwide have enacted bans, moratoriums, and other restrictions on data centers. âData centers sit at the intersection of economic development, energy policy and state fiscal health,â according to a report from the National Conference of State Legislatures. âWhile 38 states currently offer dedicated tax incentives to attract data centers, lawmakers across the country are working to balance economic development priorities with sustainable development goals. These capital-intensive projects can generate significant tax revenue for localities, yet data centers also contribute to surging energy demand across the country.â

artigo.texto: Plano de Supervisão de IA de Connie Chan Entra em Choque com Scott Wiener sobre Expansão de Data Centers Connie Chan transformou a supervisão de IA em uma linha divisória na corrida congressional de San Francisco ao exigir uma moratória nacional sobre novos data centers. Seu adversário, o senador estadual da Califórnia Scott Wiener, rejeitou essa suspensão abrangente durante o debate entre os dois em 1º de outubro. Ele argumentou que regras operacionais rígidas oferecem mais influência do que interromper a construção no país. O confronto foi mais do que uma divergência sobre desenvolvimento industrial. Chan quer que o Congresso desacelere a infraestrutura que sustenta a IA avançada até que existam padrões nacionais econômicos, ambientais e de segurança. Wiener quer que os data centers continuem se expandindo sob regras exigíveis que cubram segurança, custos de serviços públicos, uso de água e localização dos projetos. Ambos os democratas defendem uma regulamentação mais forte para a IA. A discussão diz respeito ao ponto em que a regulamentação deve intervir. Chan restringiria nova capacidade computacional enquanto os legisladores estabelecem proteções. Wiener regulamentaria empresas e instalações sem restringir amplamente essa capacidade. Essa diferença oferece aos eleitores uma escolha concreta sobre a estratégia de IA dos Estados Unidos. Ela também expõe um problema de política nacional que vai muito além de uma eleição em San Francisco. O Que Mudou Durante o Debate sobre IA em San Francisco O debate transformou um amplo apelo por regulamentação de IA em uma escolha direta entre pausar a infraestrutura e governar sua construção contínua. Chan e Wiener se encontraram na KQED em 1º de outubro, durante a campanha pelo 11º Distrito Congressional da Califórnia. O distrito inclui a maior parte de San Francisco, colocando a disputa próxima de muitas empresas que desenvolvem sistemas de IA de fronteira. O debate foi organizado pela KQED e pelo San Francisco Chronicle. Segundo a programação publicada do debate, ele abordou tecnologia, custo de vida, economia, imigração e política externa. Sobre IA, os candidatos partiram de premissas semelhantes. Ambos disseram que a tecnologia precisa de mais supervisão pública. Ambos rejeitaram uma abordagem que deixa as empresas fiscalizarem a si mesmas. Suas prescrições, então, se separaram de forma acentuada. Chan pediu uma moratória sobre data centers, maior supervisão das empresas de IA e uma desaceleração no desenvolvimento da superinteligência. Superinteligência descreve um sistema hipotético que supera as capacidades humanas em uma ampla gama de tarefas intelectuais. Wiener se opôs a uma moratória geral sobre data centers. Em vez disso, enfatizou a legislação de segurança de IA que aprovou na Califórnia e prometeu buscar proteções comparáveis em nível federal. A cobertura do debate também registrou a crítica central de Chan a Wiener. Ela argumentou que a medida de segurança aprovada por ele era mais fraca do que um projeto anterior vetado pelo governador Gavin Newsom. Wiener defendeu a lei aprovada como um compromisso viável. Ele disse que ela criou um modelo que outros governos podem adaptar, em vez de esperar por uma estrutura federal ideal. Essa troca importa porque nenhum dos candidatos defendeu o status quo regulatório. A disputa foi entre duas estratégias de intervenção, e não entre regulamentação e desregulamentação. A estratégia de supervisão de IA de Connie Chan começa com uma restrição temporária à infraestrutura. Sua lógica é que os data centers criam compromissos físicos e econômicos antes que as comunidades recebam proteções exigíveis. A estratégia de Wiener começa com regras para desenvolvedores e operadores de infraestrutura. Sua lógica é que uma pausa na construção poderia realocar investimentos sem reduzir a demanda subjacente por computação de IA. O debate, portanto, combina duas camadas de política pública que autoridades frequentemente discutem separadamente. Uma camada governa modelos de IA, práticas de segurança, comunicação de incidentes e denunciantes. A outra governa a eletricidade, a água, o terreno e os equipamentos necessários para treinar e operar esses modelos. Conectar essas camadas mudou o debate. Os eleitores já não ouviam apenas alertas abstratos sobre futuras capacidades da IA. Eles ouviam propostas concorrentes para os edifícios, sistemas de energia e custos locais que tornam essas capacidades possíveis. Por Que a Supervisão de IA de Connie Chan Começa com Data Centers Chan trata a infraestrutura computacional como o ponto de pressão em que o governo pode desacelerar a expansão da IA e negociar proteções mais fortes. Chan apoia uma moratória nacional sobre novos grandes data centers voltados à IA até que o Congresso estabeleça regras abrangentes. Essas regras tratariam dos efeitos econômicos, ambientais e de segurança da tecnologia. Sua posição reflete uma observação simples. A IA avançada não é apenas software distribuído a partir de servidores comuns de escritório. Treinar e disponibilizar modelos amplamente utilizados exige capacidade computacional concentrada, extensa infraestrutura elétrica, sistemas de refrigeração e conexões de rede. Uma moratória visaria essa capacidade antes que ela se tornasse operacional. Ela daria aos legisladores tempo para decidir quais instalações deveriam prosseguir e quais obrigações seus proprietários deveriam cumprir. Em um questionário anterior para candidatos, Chan disse que os Estados Unidos poderiam continuar líderes em IA sem transferir os custos para trabalhadores e comunidades. Sua posição completa, resumida pela Mission Local, vinculou a pausa na construção a regras nacionais, e não a uma proibição por prazo indeterminado. Essa distinção é importante. Chan não apresenta a moratória como uma política completa de IA. Ela a apresenta como instrumento de pressão para obtê-la. Sua abordagem se baseia em três preocupações interligadas. Primeiro, novos data centers podem aumentar
