artigo.texto: Grid-forming capabilities support multiple grid-restoration functions The project plays an important role in supporting voltage and frequency stability at a key point in Cambodia's central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. Its grid-forming capabilities were put through a series of demanding system-restoration scenarios, demonstrating how energy storage can take on a more active role in supporting the power system. Key highlights include: - Large-scale black start from zero voltage: 516 grid-forming PCS units successfully energized the entire plant from zero voltage, establishing stable voltage and frequency across the system. - Restoration of a 240 km transmission network: The system supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations, while maintaining stable operation as the network was progressively restored. - Support for multiple generation sources: The system supported the start-up and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant, before the restored network was operated together with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, energy storage and loads. - Stable operation under challenging grid conditions: During restoration, the system remained stable through five transformer energization events, including a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stability when synchronizing different power sources under a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees, demonstrating its ability to handle challenging conditions during system recovery. - Extended islanded operation: The system operated independently for 3.5 hours, demonstrating that the energy storage system could continue supporting the local network even when separated from the main grid. - Seamless transitions: The project completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, with voltage deviation kept below 2% and transient frequency fluctuation within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. "This project demonstrates that the value of grid-forming energy storage goes far beyond storing electricity.When a power system faces disturbances or loses normal grid support, grid-forming technology can help establish and maintain stable voltage and frequency, support system restoration and keep the grid operating reliably," said Michael Ruan, Regional Director of Sungrow Southeast Asia and South Asia. "Through projects like this, Sungrow is helping turn energy storage into a more active grid-support asset and bringing proven grid-forming capabilities to the evolving power systems of Southeast Asia." Reducing Technical Risk and Ensuring Timely Delivery Faced with strict test protocols, complex power system scenarios, a compressed construction schedule and rainy‑season working conditions with ambient temperature up to 40°C, Sungrow's cross‑functional team covering pre-sales, on‑site delivery and R&D collaborated closely to deliver high‑quality project outcomes: - 20-day commissioning and testing: The on‑site team worked relentlessly under hot and humid conditions for two consecutive months. The team wrapped up hot commissioning plus three rounds of performance tests within 20 days to guarantee timely grid‑connection. - End‑to‑End Service Solution: Sungrow provides full‑lifecycle and one‑stop services spanning integrated design of storage and monitoring systems, EPC‑related support, equipment design, commissioning and O&M services, enabling the customer to fulfill customized grid‑level requirements with reduced management overhead. As Southeast Asia advances its energy transition, Sungrow will continue to bring proven energy storage technologies and solutions to the region, helping customers build more reliable and sustainable power infrastructure. artigo.texto: Webinar "Data Centers no Brasil: Oportunidades, Incentivos e Desafios para Novos Investimentos" Incentivos, aspectos regulatórios e requisitos para projetos de instalação, modernização e expansão de data centers no país estão entre os temas debatidos no webinar. terça-feira, 6 de outubro de 2026 Atualizado às 13:44 Os grupos Tributário, Meio Ambiente e Energia do Trench Rossi Watanabe promovem, no dia 9/10, das 10h às 11h, o webinar "Data Centers no Brasil: Oportunidades, Incentivos e Desafios para Novos Investimentos". O encontro ocorre em meio ao cenário de crescimento da computação em nuvem, da IA e da demanda por processamento e armazenamento de dados, que vem ampliando o interesse por investimentos em data centers no Brasil. O evento será dedicado à análise das principais oportunidades e dos desafios jurídicos, tributários, regulatórios, ambientais e operacionais relacionados a projetos de instalação, modernização e expansão de data centers no país. Entre os temas que serão abordados está a recente instituição do REDATA, que ampliou os incentivos tributários para o setor e estabeleceu requisitos de energia renovável, eficiência hídrica, sustentabilidade, pesquisa e desenvolvimento e oferta de capacidade ao mercado doméstico. A proposta é discutir o novo cenário sob diferentes perspectivas e contribuir para que investidores, operadores e fornecedores possam avaliar os impactos das recentes mudanças, os requisitos aplicáveis aos projetos e os principais pontos de atenção para novos investimentos no setor. Participam como speakers do Trench Rossi Watanabe os sócios Clarissa Machado, Giovani Tomasoni, J. Roberto Martins, Reinaldo Ravelli e Thales Stucky, e a consultora Alessandra Machado. O evento é gratuito e aberto ao público, mediante inscrição prévia. Clique aqui e faça sua inscrição!

artigo.texto: Suzuki utilises BYD’s battery to launch Japan’s most affordable Kei-car EV Suzuki unveiled its first passenger Kei-car EV, the “e-Sky.” With a starting price of 2.12 million yen (13,400 USD), the model aims to become the most affordable Kei-car EV in Japan. While Suzuki has long dominated the Japanese Kei-car market, the e-Sky marks the company’s formal entry into the electric segment. Strategic pricing To achieve its competitive price point, Suzuki collaborated with BYD, utilising the Chinese giant’s battery technology. According to Suzuki, the e-Sky is built on a newly developed dedicated EV platform and features a proprietary “e-Axle” drive system. The vehicle is powered by a 26 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, delivering a WLTP range of 310 km. By comparison, the entry-level BYD Racco, with a 22.4 kWh LFP battery, offers a WLTC range of 210 km, while higher-spec models feature a 35.84 kWh LFP battery and a WLTC range of 320 km. The difference in the two cars’ range is due to their different weights. The Suzuki e-Sky weighs 1,030 kg, while the Racco weighs 1,160 kg with a 22.4 kWh battery and 1,220 kg or 1,230 kg with the 35.84 kWh version. The e-Sky measures 3,395 mm in length, 1,475 mm in width, and 1,625 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 2,460 mm. The Racco measures 3,395 mm long, 1,475 mm wide and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 2,520 mm. Market positioning Suzuki is offering three versions of the e-Sky. The entry-level model, designed primarily for corporate clients, is built-to-order and omits features like fast charging to keep costs low. Suzuki aims for a combined monthly sales volume of 1,000 units across all three trims. With Japanese government subsidies of 568,000 yen (3,600 USD), the effective purchase price for consumers can drop to as low as 1.55 million yen (9,800 USD). This undercuts key rivals, including the BYD Racco (starting at 1.99 million yen after subsidies) and the Nissan Sakura (starting at 1.86 million yen after subsidies). Even without subsidies, the Suzuki e-Sky is still 20,000 yen (126 USD) cheaper than the BYD Racco, making it Japan’s cheapest kei car EV. In 2025, Suzuki sold 556,632 petrol-powered kei cars. Since its July launch, the BYD Racco has sold 1,800 units, and the company plans to enter the Sri Lankan and Macao markets.

artigo.texto: Créditos Fiscais de Data Centers da Meta Transformam Infraestrutura de IA em uma Disputa Tributária de US$ 6 Bilhões A Meta teria reduzido sua conta de impostos federais em quase US$ 6 bilhões após tratar novos data centers de IA como “modelos-piloto” experimentais. Os créditos fiscais dos data centers da Meta abrangeram chips especializados e equipamentos relacionados adquiridos durante 2024 e 2025. Esse tratamento transforma um boom de infraestrutura em um teste de alto risco para a política federal de pesquisa. A disputa não trata de saber se a Meta realiza pesquisa. Ela diz respeito a se campi de computação em escala de produção e seu hardware caro se qualificam como despesas de pesquisa experimental. A Meta afirma que o Congresso criou o crédito para incentivar investimentos domésticos como os seus. Críticos dizem que a empresa está reclassificando infraestrutura empresarial essencial como pesquisa, mesmo enquanto usa essa infraestrutura para operar produtos comerciais. A divergência continua sem solução. O Internal Revenue Service não anunciou publicamente que a Meta violou a lei nem emitiu uma decisão final rejeitando essas reivindicações. No entanto, os próprios registros regulatórios da Meta identificam créditos de pesquisa entre suas posições fiscais incertas mais relevantes. Essa divulgação torna a estratégia mais do que um argumento teórico de política pública. A Meta Transformou Data Centers de IA em Modelos-Piloto A mudança relatada não é um novo incentivo fiscal, mas uma aplicação extraordinariamente ampla de um crédito de pesquisa já existente. Segundo uma investigação sobre créditos fiscais, a Meta categoriza determinados data centers de IA como modelos-piloto para fins tributários federais. Essa classificação permite que a empresa inclua alguns custos de equipamentos no cálculo de seu crédito de pesquisa. Um modelo-piloto é uma representação ou modelo usado para avaliar um produto ou processo novo ou aprimorado. Ele pode se qualificar quando sua construção e uso fazem parte de uma experimentação genuína. A interpretação da Meta supostamente aplica esse conceito a grandes instalações de computação repletas de caros chips de inteligência artificial. A empresa diferencia esses campi de data centers convencionais que sustentam operações estabelecidas de armazenamento, publicidade e redes sociais. Os benefícios fiscais reportados chegaram a cerca de US$ 2 bilhões em 2024 e US$ 3,9 bilhões em 2025. Juntos, isso representa quase US$ 6 bilhões em dois anos. Esses valores descrevem benefícios fiscais federais reivindicados, não uma subvenção em dinheiro do governo. Eles também continuam sujeitos a análise, ajustes e possível litígio. A abordagem da Meta importa porque a infraestrutura de IA está se tornando uma das maiores exigências operacionais do setor de tecnologia. Aceleradores, sistemas de rede, equipamentos de resfriamento e infraestrutura de energia agora determinam com que rapidez as empresas podem treinar e implantar modelos avançados. Os créditos de pesquisa tradicionalmente se concentram em salários qualificados, suprimentos e pesquisa contratada. A estratégia da Meta supostamente coloca muito mais infraestrutura física de computação dentro do cálculo. A empresa não negou o uso do crédito de pesquisa. O porta-voz da Meta, Andy Stone, afirmou que a empresa é uma grande investidora americana em pesquisa e utiliza incentivos criados pelo Congresso para investimento doméstico. Essa defesa se baseia em um argumento direto. A Meta desenvolve novos modelos, sistemas, chips e projetos de data centers, portanto a infraestrutura que sustenta esses experimentos faz parte de seu programa de pesquisa. A questão sem solução é onde termina a experimentação e começam as operações empresariais comuns. Um campus de IA pode apoiar trabalho técnico incerto e, ao mesmo tempo, atender produtos usados por anunciantes, criadores e consumidores. Esse papel misto dá à Meta um argumento plausível, mas também cria a principal fragilidade de sua posição. Chamar um ativo de experimental não torna automaticamente todo custo associado uma despesa qualificada de pesquisa. O código tributário se concentra na atividade, finalidade, incerteza e experimentação envolvidas. Ele não pergunta simplesmente se uma empresa comprou equipamentos avançados para um negócio intensivo em pesquisa. Essa diferença explica por que as reivindicações reportadas atraíram escrutínio. A Meta está tratando a base física de sua estratégia de IA como parte do próprio experimento. Por Que os Créditos Fiscais dos Data Centers da Meta Enfrentam Escrutínio A disputa depende de saber se as instalações da Meta realizam experimentação qualificada ou se fornecem principalmente capacidade para um negócio comercial estabelecido. O crédito federal de pesquisa recompensa despesas qualificadas de pesquisa acima de um valor-base definido. Seu objetivo é incentivar trabalho técnico que as empresas talvez financiassem menos porque os resultados permanecem incertos. As regras de pesquisa do IRS aplicam uma estrutura de quatro partes. A pesquisa deve ser tecnológica, abordar incerteza, sustentar um componente empresarial aprimorado e envolver um processo de experimentação. Construir um sistema de IA pode satisfazer esses princípios. Pesquisadores não sabem antecipadamente qual arquitetura de modelo, método de treinamento ou configuração de hardware produzirá o resultado pretendido. A questão mais difícil diz respeito aos equipamentos usados durante esse trabalho. Empresas não podem transformar ativos empresariais padrão em despesas de pesquisa apenas conectando-os a projetos experimentais. O argumento da Meta parece tratar seus data centers de IA como sistemas experimentais integrados. Seus chips, redes, projetos de resfriamento e software operam juntos enquanto engenheiros testam novos modelos e métodos de infraestrutura. Críticos enxergam uma realidade econômica diferente. artigo.texto: O que a guerra na Ucrânia e a guerra no Irã têm em comum? Ataque de Kiev a um navio iraniano no mar Cáspio expõe uma rede densa de inteligência militar circulando entre os dois conflitos. Gerando resumo Ao menos uma pessoa morreu e outras seis ficaram feridas após um ataque da Ucrânia com cerca de 650 drones contra a capital da Rússia na madrugada desta terça-feira, 6. Trata-se do segundo maior ataque com esses artefatos nos últimos dois anos contra a região de Moscou, localizada a centenas de quilômetros da fronteira ucraniana. Além da vítima fatal, um jovem de 20 anos, e dos feridos, várias casas foram atingidas pelo bombardeio, detalhou o governador regional Andrei Vorobyov. O Ministério da Defesa da Rússia afirmou que suas tropas atingiram quatro centros de processamento de dados em cidades da Ucrânia. Segundo a pasta, os alvos — Parkovyi, Ukrtelecom, Giga e Podolsky — seriam instalações estratégicas das Forças Armadas ucranianas. O ataque foi realizado com drones da brigada Varyag, de acordo com informações da agência estatal russa RIA. Tanto a Ucrânia quanto a Rússia intensificaram, nos últimos meses, os ataques com mísseis contra alvos civis e industriais incluindo infraestruturas de energia, transporte e portuárias, bem como embarcações no Mar Negro. A Rússia já declarou que pretende aumentar ainda mais ataques contra infraestruturas energéticas, inclusive em Kiev, à medida que o inverno se aproxima. /AFP

artigo.texto: Nevada AG Aaron Ford holds Boulder City town hall on data centers, utility bills LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford discussed data centers and their impact on utility costs in Boulder City. Ford, who is running for governor, held a town hall on Sunday in Boulder City focused on data centers’ impact on affordability and his plan as governor to protect Nevada families from higher utility bills. He also outlined his plan to protect taxpayer dollars and state resources. Ford has said he plans to pause new tax abatements and stop attempts to build data centers on federal land. He has also said he will audit data centers to verify whether they have delivered on their commitments. In a release sent to News 3, Ford's campaign claims, "Data Center Joe 'wholeheartedly' supports data centers and has handed them more than $240 million in taxpayer dollars while Nevadans struggle to afford to live in his failed economy. Meanwhile, Joe Lombardo’s campaign has taken $2 million from MAGA data center and Flock billionaires." News 3 reached out to Governor Lombardo's campaign for comment and is awaiting a response.

artigo.texto: Trending MARQUETTE -- From 6-7:30 p.m. on Thursday, the Lake Superior Community Partnership will be hosting a community informational session on data centers in the basement room at Peter White Public Library. "Join us for an informational session about what communities should know about data centers and how to prepare if a project comes your way," said the event description. "Hear from experts, learn about potential benefits and challenges, and have the opportunity to ask questions." Featured speakers at the event will be Ron Akers of the Charter Township of Van Buren and Dakota Baker of the Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance. Van Buren, a township in Macomb County, recently became home to a Google data center project. In a May 11 article by MLive titled "Google pitches Michigan on a different kind of data center. Some don't buy it," Akers is quoted as saying that the Google data center project was "the most extensively researched and evaluated site that I've ever worked on." MLive reports that while Akers and other township representatives have stressed that the project has been heavily vetted and regulated, many Van Buren residents continue to have concerns about certain aspects of the project, such as the non-disclosure agreement Akers and other township officials signed while the project was in its infancy. The full MLive article can be read here: https://www.mlive.com/news/2026/05/google-pitches-michigan-on-a-different-kind-of-data-center-some-dont-buy-it.html. The Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance describes itself on their website as "elevating and advancing local business." Their focus is on advocating for rural business-forward policy at the legislative level. Baker is their director. The Northern Michigan Chamber Alliance has participated in past public information sessions on data centers in other parts of Northern Michigan. "(Thursday's) session is intended to provide information and context around data centers, including potential opportunities, considerations and impacts associated with this type of development," said LSCP in a press release about the event. "The goal of the event is not to advocate for or against data centers, but to create a space where community members can become better informed and engage in the conversation." "As Marquette County's local economic development organization, we have a responsibility to help our community understand the issues and opportunities that could impact our economy," said Natalie Chmiko, CEO of the Lake Superior Community Partnership. "Our role with this event isn't to advocate for or against data centers. It’s to provide an opportunity for community members and municipal leaders to learn more and ask questions.” Those interested in attending Thursday's LSCP event can register for free on LSCP's website at https://members.marquette.org/ap/Events/Register/v5FJw2BUKCyCm. Doors for the event open at 5:30. Annie Lippert can be reached at 906-228-2500, ext. 550. Her email address is alippert@miningjournal.net.

artigo.texto: Residents in Arkansas, Missouri unite against proposed Oregon County data center MAMMOTH SPRING, Ark. (KAIT) - A lot just outside of Thayer, Missouri, and minutes from Mammoth Spring State Park and the Arkansas state line, is open to potential data center development, prompting opposition from residents on both sides of the border. No developer has taken on the site yet, currently owned by Charles McCullough. Jeremiah Read, a protest organizer, said the area needs to be protected. He led a protest in Mammoth Spring Saturday against the potential data center investors. “Why should you care? I mean, we have an obligation to protect this beauty and not contaminate it for our children and future generations and for ourselves,” Read said. The proposed site sits about five minutes north of Mammoth Spring State Park, across the Arkansas-Missouri state line in Thayer. Read says that if a data center were to draw water from this state park, especially given the lower water table numbers due to the extended drought, it could put the state park in real danger. Thomas Sallings and Magic Keller, Alton residents and local business owners in Missouri, have been doing advocacy work opposing the data center in Oregon County. “This is a chance to use that momentum for people’s voices to be heard and for us to take a more active role in creating the world that we want,” Sallings said. A data center could have a major influence on the county based on the revenue it brings in, and those interests are not in the hands of the residents living close to it. “They’ll basically own 90% of the county and be able to make all the decisions for us,” Sallings said. “We want all the people’s voices to be heard, to develop our economy the way we want it to be developed.” Sallings and Keller propose maximizing taxes on potential developers, and inputting stricter pollution laws, many of which data centers would not meet. They said they hope these moves will keep potential investors away. Keller adds that many proponents tout the investment and value data centers bring to an area don’t amount to benefit for the local community. “The landowner, Charles McCullough, he’s been pretty straightforward,” Keller said. “He’s said—he’s just come out and said, like, this facility will bring in less than 10 jobs.” Romona Hampton, 72, lives minutes from the proposed site and owns a small farm nearby. “The water and the noise has got me bothered more than anything because it would direct me, I mean, it would affect me directly as close as I live to the farm that’s proposed,” Hampton said. Hampton believes the noise could disrupt her and her family, as well as local animal populations with a constant sound that can reach up to 105 decibels—the equivalent of a jet flyover. Additionally, she said a center could potentially heat up water drawn from the spring, which typically runs about 50°F, to temperatures 30-50 degrees higher. Hampton said she took to protesting not only because she feels like these centers are putting profits over people, but because she wants to make sure the future has a fair shake, too. “I have children and grandchildren, Hampton said. ”And I look at all these young people and I think, ‘Oh dear God, it’s up to us to protect them.’ It really is." artigo.texto: China has presented a goal of bringing all-solid-state batteries to an early stage of scaled application by 2030. However, CATL, the world's largest battery maker, is taking a cautious view, saying cost and mass-production technology issues remain and wider adoption will take more time. According to InsideEVs and other outlets, seven government bodies including China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology announced the "15th Five-Year Plan for the New Battery Industry". The plan includes a goal of realising early scaled application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030 and making breakthroughs in core technologies such as advanced electrode materials and new electrolytes. While the government is accelerating efforts to foster the industry, CATL is cautious about the commercialisation timeline. CATL Chairman Robin Zeng (쩡위췬) in June rated the technology maturity of all-solid-state batteries at level 4 out of 9. With level 9 representing mass-producible capability, he said a large technology gap remains. CATL is aiming for small-scale production and vehicle validation in 2027. However, Zeng forecast that "the possibility of scaling all-solid-state batteries to the point of being applied to millions of vehicles is very low before 2030". That is because manufacturing stability and cost, as well as performance, must be solved at the same time. LG Energy Solution offered a similar view. Robert Lee (로버트 리), head of LG Energy Solution in North America, said, "There are still difficulties in mass-producing large all-solid-state cells," adding that they are more likely to be commercialised first in smartphones or specialised uses before expanding to electric vehicles. Market forecasts are also cautious. BloombergNEF projected that "all-solid-state batteries will account for about 10 percent of global demand for electric-vehicle and energy-storage batteries even in 2035." In China, vehicles equipped with semi-solid-state batteries have already appeared, but it is difficult to view this as full-fledged commercialisation of fully all-solid-state batteries. Meanwhile, the Chinese government plans to foster next-generation technologies simultaneously, including sodium-ion and flow batteries, as well as long-life lithium batteries, in addition to all-solid-state batteries. It also set a goal of increasing the charge-discharge cycle life of long-life lithium batteries to 15,000 cycles by 2030.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Two transmission-connected energy storage projects are slated to receive awards in the first round of the Maryland Next Generation Energy Act energy storage procurement, the state public service commission said on Thursday. - The finalists are Flatiron Energy’s 400 MW/1,600 MWh Chalk Point Storage Project in south-central Maryland and REV Renewables’s 40 MW/160 MWh Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in the far western part of the state. Both will receive flat pricing for 15-year terms at a combined cost of 6.98 cents/month for the average Maryland residential customer, the public service commission said. - The award will help address the PJM Interconnection’s capacity woes, which Federal Energy Regulatory Commission chair Laura Swett last week called a “mess.” The grid operator faces a capacity shortfall of 6.8 GW for the 2028-2029 delivery year, up 300 MW from the previous period, as capacity prices remain at the $325/MW-day cap. Dive Insight: Passed in 2025, the Next Generation Energy Act requires Maryland to conduct at least two solicitations for a combined 1.6 GW of energy storage capacity. Eligible projects must be designed to discharge at full power for at least four hours. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced the awards for the first solicitation round on Thursday, the statutory deadline. By law, it must open bidding for the second round by Jan. 1, 2027, and announce project awards by Oct. 1, 2027. Evan Vaughan, executive director of the regional clean energy group MAREC Action, said Thursday’s selections will help mitigate the effects of PJM’s high capacity prices. “These projects can help meet growing electricity demand while reducing exposure to volatile capacity prices that ultimately affect customers’ bills,” Vaughan said in a statement. Also known as the Mid-Atlantic Renewable Energy Coalition, MAREC Action consists of more than 50 developers and manufacturers serving the region’s utility-scale solar, wind and battery storage industry. Flatiron Energy and REV Renewables are both members. Flatiron’s project will be located at NRG’s oil- and gas-fired Chalk Point power plant in the southeastern corner of Prince George’s County, according to the Maryland Public Service Commission. REV will site its project on a portion of a reclaimed coal mine in mountainous Garrett County, near Maryland’s border with West Virginia and Pennsylvania. The commission said it chose not to award the 500-MW/3,000-MWh Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project nor a 135-MW/540-MWh expansion Flatiron requested for the Chalk Point project in a revised filing after the first-round application window closed. The commission said Flatiron could reapply for the Chalk Point expansion and “invited [Oystercatcher] to consider participating” in round two, citing the “desirable electric grid location and characteristics” of the project’s northeastern Maryland site while noting “the need for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County if the project is pursued further.” In addition to near-term cost pressures due to PJM’s capacity crunch, Maryland has ambitious clean energy goals, including a statutory 2045 target for statewide net-zero emissions and a 2035 goal for 100% carbon-free electricity set by gubernatorial order. In a statement, Maryland Public Service Commission Chair Kumar Barve called the first-round award a milestone in the state’s effort to meet its energy policy goals, while acknowledging its relatively modest contribution. “While we are disappointed that these awards are below our 800-MW target for Round 1, our Round 2 solicitation is expected to attract many more offers due to a pool of over 40 additional energy storage projects from PJM’s Cycle 1 interconnection process,” Barve said.

artigo.texto: Panasonic Holdings plans to begin manufacturing humanoid robots by 2029, using its battery technology to power machines designed for factories and warehouses. Panasonic Holdings will enter the humanoid robot market by 2029, Chief AI Officer Akira Sakakibara told Nikkei Asia in an interview in Osaka. The Japanese electronics giant plans to deploy the machines in its own plants and warehouses first, drawing on its battery business to solve the power constraints that have limited robot mobility. Sakakibara said the company's battery technology gives it an advantage in developing robots that can operate for extended periods without tethering. Current humanoid prototypes from competitors typically run for two to three hours on a charge. Panasonic aims to exceed that significantly, though the company declined to specify target runtimes. The move places Panasonic alongside a growing cohort of Japanese manufacturers pursuing humanoid automation. Kawasaki Heavy Industries has said it will field a fully autonomous humanoid by 2030. Mitsubishi Motors plans to build humanoids for its auto factories. Toyota has committed to deploying 400,000 robots alongside factory staff. Japan's robotics push comes as the country faces a shrinking workforce. The working-age population has fallen 13% since its 1995 peak, according to government data. Companies are racing to automate tasks that conventional industrial robots cannot handle — jobs requiring two-legged movement, balance, and fine motor skills in spaces designed for humans. Panasonic's strategy differs from pure-play robotics startups. Rather than selling robots as standalone products, the company intends to integrate them into its own manufacturing and logistics operations first, then offer them to external customers. This mirrors the path Fanuc and Yaskawa took decades ago, when they automated their own factories before becoming the world's largest industrial robot makers. The humanoid market remains nascent. Goldman Sachs estimates global shipments will reach 1.4 million units annually by 2035, up from fewer than 10,000 in 2024. Most current deployments are pilots. Tesla's Optimus, Figure AI's Figure 02, and Agility Robotics' Digit have demonstrated warehouse tasks but have not reached volume production. Battery life remains a primary bottleneck. Humanoid robots carry their power source, adding weight that demands more power — a vicious cycle. Panasonic's energy division, which supplies batteries to Tesla and other automakers, produces cells with energy densities above 300 watt-hours per kilogram. Sakakibara said the robotics team is working directly with battery engineers to design custom packs shaped to the robot's torso and limbs. "We are not just buying batteries off the shelf," Sakakibara said. "We are co-developing the power system with the robot architecture." Panasonic has not disclosed investment figures for the humanoid program. The company spent 420 billion yen ($2.8 billion) on research and development in the fiscal year ended March 2024, about 4% of revenue. Robotics accounts for a small but growing share. Analysts say Panasonic's vertical integration — batteries, motors, sensors, and AI software all developed in-house — could accelerate development cycles. Competitors often rely on third-party suppliers for key components, creating integration delays. The first Panasonic humanoids will likely handle material transport and machine tending in the company's battery and electronics factories. Warehouse picking and packing will follow. Sakakibara said the robots must meet the same safety and reliability standards as Panasonic's industrial equipment before any external sales. "We have the luxury of being our own first customer," he said. "That lets us iterate fast without promising specs we can't meet." Panasonic shares rose 1.2% in Tokyo trading Monday following the Nikkei report. The stock has gained 18% this year, outperforming the Topix index's 9% rise. Source:asia.nikkei.com

artigo.texto: CIP invests over â¬270 million in Kilmarnock South battery storage project in Scotland Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners has taken the final investment decision for Kilmarnock South, a 350 MW, 1,400 MWh system. Under construction in southern Scotland, the site is due to enter service in early 2028. Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), through its fourth flagship fund Copenhagen Infrastructure IV, has taken the final investment decision for Kilmarnock South. The 350 MW, 1,400 MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) is located in South Ayrshire, southern Scotland. Construction has begun, and commercial operations are expected in the first quarter of 2028, the company said. A commitment of over â¬270 million CIP says the project represents an investment commitment of more than â¬270 million. UK Energy Minister Michael Shanks, for his part, refers to a battery worth GBP 232 million. With a four-hour duration, Kilmarnock South would become the longest-duration asset in CIP's UK storage portfolio. The system would store surplus Scottish wind power that would otherwise go unused and release it to the grid when the network has capacity. Such projects are part of a market where storage operators are multiplying across Europe, as illustrated by the energy storage contracts secured by ML System in Poland worth â¬4.1 million. Company Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners: company profile Four Scottish projects in total Kilmarnock South is CIP's fourth investment in transmission-connected BESS projects in Scotland. It joins Coalburn 1, which reached commercial operations in August 2026, as well as Coalburn 2 and Devilla. Once all four projects are fully commissioned, their combined storage capacity would reach 4.4 GWh, which CIP describes as the equivalent of almost a third of Great Britain's operational battery storage today. CIP's Scottish portfolio would have a total power capacity of 1.85 GW. According to the company, this capacity would match the electricity demand of over 5.5 million households over a two-hour period. Statements from officials Nischal Agarwal, Partner at CIP, says well-sited storage projects bring flexibility to the power system. In his view, they allow the full benefits of low-cost renewables to be captured, strengthen security of supply and help cut and stabilise consumer bills. Michael Shanks notes that a former coal mine at Coalburn is now home to one of Europe's largest batteries. artigo.texto: EMEA Data Center Expansion Faces a Delivery Test Power limits are pushing development beyond FLAP-D, but grid access, construction capacity, and community support will decide which projects get delivered. Power constraints are pushing data center development beyond Europe’s established hubs, but emerging markets now face the challenge of turning ambitious project announcements into operating facilities. Grid connections, construction capacity, and community support will determine how much of the next wave gets built. These were among the key takeaways from DC Byte’s latest EMEA analysis, which tracks 93 GW of IT capacity across operating facilities, construction, committed projects, and early-stage developments. Nearly a quarter of that total sits in Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin – the FLAP-D markets – although land and power constraints are encouraging expansion elsewhere. The figures describe a development landscape rather than available supply. Oscar Gomez Comellas, research manager for EMEA at DC Byte, said roughly 60% of the region’s pipeline remains at an early stage. “There are a number of things that need to take place before we consider it ‘realistic’,” he told Data Center Knowledge, noting that power availability is the principal obstacle to delivery. Beyond FLAP-D: Nordics Lead; Milan and Madrid Catch Up The Nordics are currently bringing capacity online fastest because development began earlier than in markets such as Milan and Madrid, Gomez Comellas said. He added that this lead could narrow over the next 12 months as projects in Milan and Madrid become ready for service. Michael Winterson, secretary general of the European Data Centre Association (EUDCA), said he expects Europe’s roster of markets with more than 1 GW installed to expand from five to between 12 and 14. “This is due to … increasing national demand married with lower risks of new deployments,” Winterson told Data Center Knowledge. “This is further driven by energy issues and other planning issues, driving development to markets with capacity.” Nevertheless, the established hubs retain advantages in connectivity and customer demand. New markets must demonstrate that their infrastructure can support successive projects, not just an initial campus. Winterson said EUDCA forecasts roughly 15% compound annual growth over seven years, taking deployed commercial capacity above 30 GW. Supply chain limitations and shortages of skilled design and construction workers constrain an industry seeking growth above 20%. That European commercial-capacity forecast is distinct from DC Byte’s broader EMEA tally, which includes projects at multiple development stages. AI Rewrites Site Selection AI training is giving developers greater freedom to choose sites based on the availability of electricity. “The majority of AI projects we see today are driven by AI training workloads, which require large amounts of power and don’t necessarily need to be near population centers or connectivity hubs, freeing developers and operators to be more flexible with location,” Gomez Comellas said. That flexibility could diminish as demand shifts toward inference, where models deliver responses to users. Gomez Comellas said he expects inference to become the main growth driver in the medium term, increasing demand near population centers and well-connected metropolitan markets. Operators, therefore, need to consider how a location’s appeal might change as customers’ workloads change. A power-rich site suited to training may offer a different proposition for services sensitive to latency. Grid Access and Local Opposition Make or Break Projects National grids are adding generation and transmission capacity, Gomez Comellas said, but whether those additions can keep pace remains uncertain. “The question is whether this increase, along with the already existing capacity in the new hubs, will be enough to satisfy accelerating demand,” he explained. Electricity is only part of the development challenge. Gomez Comellas identified expanding regulation and local opposition as factors that can undermine announced projects. “There is increasing awareness of data center projects among local communities, which can come with pushback, sometimes resulting in projects being abandoned,” he said. Winterson pointed to the Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact and the EU Energy Efficiency Directive’s reporting and labeling framework as benchmarks for environmental performance. He said the industry’s commitments increasingly extend beyond facility efficiency. “On top of water and energy efficiency, we are now measuring and targeting net new renewables, grid support, heat reuse, and biodiversity initiatives,” Winterson said.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de comutadores de fibra óptica até 2035: demanda de data centers impulsiona o crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de comutadores de fibra óptica entra em uma fase de expansão estrutural, sustentado pelo crescimento incessante da interconexão de data centers (DCI), pelas atualizações de redes de telecomunicações e pela mudança arquitetural em direção a sistemas ópticos abertos e desagregados. Os comutadores de fibra óptica — dispositivos eletro-ópticos ou optomecânicos que encaminham sinais ópticos sem conversão elétrica — são essenciais para gerenciar largura de banda, reduzir a latência e viabilizar redes definidas por software. A demanda se divide entre comutadores de alta confiabilidade e muitos recursos para redes de nível de telecomunicações e comutadores otimizados em custo e com alto número de portas para data centers de hiperescala. O controle sobre plataformas proprietárias de integração fotônica, como MEMS, PLC e fotônica de silício, determina desempenho e custo, enquanto a montagem e o encapsulamento continuam sendo gargalos. As compras são dominadas por relações diretas de design-in com fabricantes de sistemas ópticos, o que torna o sucesso dependente de roteiros tecnológicos plurianuais e de longos ciclos de qualificação. À medida que provedores de nuvem e operadoras buscam maior automação e programabilidade, o mercado migra de componentes isolados para soluções de subsistemas habilitadas por software. Este relatório analisa essas dinâmicas e apresenta uma previsão até 2035, com foco na demanda final, na lógica da cadeia de suprimentos e no posicionamento competitivo. O cenário-base para o mercado de comutadores de fibra óptica até 2035 pressupõe crescimento contínuo do tráfego global de dados, da computação em nuvem e da implantação de 5G/6G, impulsionando a demanda por comutação óptica tanto em telecomunicações quanto em data centers. Espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta anual (CAGR) de 8,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 220 (2025=100) em 2035. Essa perspectiva é sustentada pela transição em curso para redes ópticas abertas e desagregadas, que amplia o número de pontos de comutação e exige maior programabilidade. Nas telecomunicações, a implantação de CDC-ROADMs e OXCs sustentará a demanda por comutadores MEMS com alto número de portas, enquanto os operadores de data centers adotarão cada vez mais comutadores de circuito óptico para reduzir consumo de energia e latência. Regionalmente, a Ásia-Pacífico continuará sendo o maior mercado, impulsionada pela infraestrutura de telecomunicações da China e pelos data centers de hiperescala, enquanto América do Norte e Europa registrarão atualizações constantes. Restrições na cadeia de suprimentos, especialmente de ferramentas especializadas de fabricação e wafers eletro-ópticos, podem moderar o crescimento, mas as expansões de capacidade em andamento devem aliviar os gargalos. A pressão sobre os preços persistirá nos segmentos de menor número de portas, mas o valor migrará para subsistemas integrados com controle por software. O cenário-base não pressupõe mudanças tecnológicas disruptivas, e sim melhorias evolutivas na fotônica de silício e na confiabilidade dos MEMS. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Aumento da demanda por interconexão de data centers (DCI), impulsionado por cargas de trabalho de nuvem e IA - Atualização de redes de telecomunicações para 400G/800G e além, exigindo comutação óptica avançada - Migração para redes ópticas abertas e desagregadas, ampliando os pontos de comutação - Necessidade de menor latência e menor consumo de energia em data centers - Iniciativas governamentais de expansão de banda larga e implantação de 5G - Crescimento da computação de borda e da IoT, impulsionando arquiteturas de rede distribuídas Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Altos custos de qualificação e longos ciclos de design-in para comutadores de nível de telecomunicações - Gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos de componentes fotônicos especializados e ferramentas de fabricação - Erosão de preços nos segmentos de comutadores de baixo número de portas e de uso geral - Desafios técnicos para escalar a fotônica de silício para grandes números de portas - Tensões geopolíticas que afetam o comércio e o acesso à tecnologia, sobretudo entre EUA e China Estrutura da Demanda por Setor de Uso Final Telecomunicações (participação estimada: 40%) As operadoras de telecomunicações estão modernizando suas redes de transporte para lidar com o aumento do tráfego gerado por 5G, fibra até a residência e serviços corporativos. Os comutadores de fibra óptica são essenciais em nós ROADM e OXC para o roteamento dinâmico de comprimentos de onda, viabilizando grades flexíveis e arquiteturas incolores, sem direção e sem contenção (CDC). Até 2035, a demanda será impulsionada pela necessidade de maior número de portas, menor perda de inserção e velocidades de comutação mais rápidas. A transição para 400G/800G e, eventualmente, 1,6T exigirá comutadores com desempenho superior. Além disso, a busca por redes abertas e desagregadas aumentará o número de pontos de comutação, à medida que as operadoras procuram evitar a dependência de fornecedores. artigo.texto: - Jocelyn Benson and John James squared off in the first of two Michigan gubernatorial debates - Benson, for the first time, called for a suspension of Michigan’s gas tax to provide relief to motorists - James said he would not push for a statewide moratorium on data centers, countering his campaign’s past statements GRAND RAPIDS — Michigan gubernatorial nominees John James and Jocelyn Benson traded barbs while making some notable policy shifts on data centers and gas taxes Tuesday night during their first televised debate. The meeting between James, a Republican member of the US House, and Benson, the state’s Democratic secretary of state, was mostly cordial. But sparks flew during exchanges over affordability, the Iran war and more. Related: - Gubernatorial candidates’ plans for Michigan’s most pressing issues - Benson’s record: Election fights, faster DMV visits, transparency flop - James says he delivers results. What does his record show? The debate at WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids is the first of two between James and Benson ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. The next will be held at WDIV-TV in metro Detroit Oct. 15, although absentee voting is already underway and more than 201,000 Michiganders have already cast ballots. Read on for takeaways and fact checks from the first debate. James backtracks on moratorium A statewide moratorium on data centers is no longer on the table if James is elected governor, he told reporters after the Tuesday debate. “This will be led by the locals and not by Lansing,” James said. “As a conservative, I don’t like bans or mandates.” James’ stance had been somewhat opaque since August, when his campaign had told The Detroit News he was in favor of a moratorium until standards for local control, electricity use and environmental protections are put in place. After the debate James made it clear he believes local governments should decide the fate of the facilities and he does not favor a statewide block. “If free people decide (a data center is) what they want to do, then the government should get the heck out of their way,” James said. “The moratorium should be imposed on Lansing, not the people.” Fact check: Did James vote against local control? During an exchange over data centers, Benson claimed James “voted four times to block the ability of local communities to have a voice or a say in whether data centers can come to those communities.” As a member of Congress, James didn’t vote for any standalone bills to limit local control on data centers. But he did vote for an early version of the “Big, Beautiful Bill” that included a section called the “Artificial Intelligence and Information Technology Modernization Initiative,” which would have barred state and local jurisdictions from creating laws to regulate artificial intelligence. A bipartisan group representing state legislatures warned the provision would also “circumvent their authority to regulate the permitting, construction and operation of data centers within their borders.” It was not included in the final law. Benson shifts on gas tax Benson said Tuesday night she is “open” to suspending Michigan’s 52-cent gas tax to help motorists facing high prices. That was a shift for Benson, who had previously called for the federal government to suspend its own 18-cent tax but had argued against a state gas tax holiday, suggesting it could “potentially blow in the state budget.” Republican House Speaker Matt Hall has said calls to suspend the state tax are unrealistic given its importance to a bipartisan road funding deal negotiated last year with Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. James made a factual error on the issue during the debate, claiming Michigan could afford a gas tax holiday if Democrats hadn’t “blown” through the state’s “rainy day” savings account the past eight years. In reality, the Budget Stabilization Fund has nearly doubled under Whitmer’s tenure. This year, Senate Democrats proposed withdrawing $350 million to plug budget holes, but House Republicans opposed it, and that plan did not pass the full Legislature. Fact check: Did James vote for Iran war? During the gas tax debate, Benson responded to James: “You voted six times in support of a war in Iran that has directly led to the increase in these gas prices.” James didn’t vote to start the war, but he has voted against six resolutions to try to end it, most recently on Sept. 15, when he opposed a measure to end the conflict unless Congress explicitly authorized a declaration of war. The resolution James voted against directed Trump “to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran, other than those elements of the Armed Forces that may be necessary to defend the United States or an ally or partner of the United States from imminent attack.” James did not deny opposing the resolutions, saying in the debate that “I struggle with that vote.” But, he argued, “Iran must not have a nuke.” Fact check: Can Benson erase Canadian tariffs? During an exchange on President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, Benson claimed tariffs are costing the average Michigan household $5,600. That figure comes from a study by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation which estimated the total cost of all Trump tariffs, not just Canadian ones. Benson claimed she could end those costs: “On day one in office, I will call Canada and negotiate a contract between Michigan and Canada to eliminate the tariffs and the costs in Michigan,” she said. That’s likely not possible under the US Constitution, which only gives Congress the power to levy tariffs and approve formal treaties with foreign governments. States can create subnational agreements with other governments, but they historically have not been able to overrule federally imposed tariffs. artigo.texto: I visit the hospital rooms of my family and church elders relatively regularly. I have never been to the hospital to visit any of my young cousins, but that changed a week ago. As a heat dome covered Memphis and the Mid-South, my 21-year-old cousin, Ra’Kelle Miller, was struggling to breathe after five minutes outdoors and was rushed to the emergency room. Neither her nebulizer nor asthma pump worked to open her airways. She lives a few miles away from Colossus I and only a couple of miles away from the Valero Oil Refinery. The pollution from these facilities, and the power plant with the illegal gas turbines in neighboring Southaven, are having a real impact on our community’s health now. Politicians and talking heads are leaving the people impacted by hyperscale data centers behind when discussing the “economic development” they think data centers can bring. Memphis is becoming a testing ground for the future of artificial intelligence. But before we rush into that future, we need to pause and ask: What will it cost the people who live here? SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center arrived in Memphis under the cover of NDAs and secret meetings that never included people from the community. That rush to secrecy and to market has led to tons of harmful pollutants being emitted into our air and lungs. SpaceXAI is raking in billions of dollars a month, and all we have to show for it is $30M in city and county tax revenue and temporary construction jobs filled by people from out of town. The tax money is a pittance compared to SpaceXAI’s value and profits. We should be ashamed, not celebrating how we are being treated. SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center has put extraordinary demands on Memphis for electricity, water and other infrastructure. To power those demands, SpaceXAI’s founder, Elon Musk, has relied on dozens of methane gas turbines that emit nitrogen oxides and other pollutants with well-documented health risks. The full health and environmental consequences for Memphis residents continue to worsen. The Memphis City Council has an opportunity to help us learn from this colossal mistake by pausing to think, learn and act in the best interest of the people of Memphis. The council is scheduled for a third reading and vote on Ordinance 5982 on Tuesday. The ordinance proposes pausing new large-scale data center development for 12 months to give Memphis time to study the impact of facilities like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, allow for community input on where they are built, and develop regulations that protect our air, water, land and jobs. There’s more than enough reason to pause and research this before expanding the existing facilities or allowing more. The environmental concerns are substantial. A recent Reuters report found that Musk’s company has installed many more gas turbines than it claimed, and without proper permitting. The majority of those turbines are in neighboring Southaven, near predominantly Black communities of Whitehaven and Westwood that already face elevated rates of respiratory illness. The five-mile affected area extends across the state line into Memphis, including John P. Freeman Middle School. The Reuters report calculated that 30 methane gas turbines with available emissions data could produce nearly 2,500 tons of nitrogen oxides, 4,000 tons of carbon monoxide, and 22 tons of formaldehyde annually, assuming they operate continuously at 80% capacity. The report says that the EPA states that these turbines typically operate around the clock at 80% capacity or more. The American Lung Association states that nitrogen dioxide, one of the nitrogen oxides produced by these turbines, increases toxic smog, which is proven to reduce lung capacity and increase airway inflammation, coughing and wheezing. Toxic smog also worsens asthma and can cause asthma in children, leading to hospital and emergency room visits. Carbon monoxide deprives the body of oxygen, and formaldehyde is a human carcinogen. Cancer rates in South Memphis are already more than 4 times the federal cancer limit. Memphis has become the sacrifice zone for a billionaire’s wealth and profit. An investigative report by ProPublica exposes that this highly elevated cancer rate is due to cancer-causing pollution from industrial sites. Beyond the proposed economic effects of this industrialization are the effects on the lives of the people living in Memphis. People like my cousin, Ra’Kelle. Further, Memphis residents are being asked to not only put themselves in harm’s way for these and future data centers, but also to accommodate this massive land use without the necessary regulation. The current Unified Development Code doesn’t specify regulations for these massive data centers that so heavily consume our water, burden our electrical infrastructure, and threaten our health. The real question isn’t whether Memphis should participate in the AI economy. It’s whether we should allow this unprecedented data center growth to continue under rules written before this technology existed and its adverse health effects were known. We need courage from our City Council to put people at the forefront of these policy decisions. Our lives matter more than hyper-scale data centers. I urge the council to pass Ordinance 5982, which identifies the regulatory gaps and would impose a temporary 12-month moratorium on specified permits for new and expanded data-center development while the city studies and develops permanent regulations. Tennessee is not alone in its quest to understand the impacts of these large-scale facilities before granting permits. Last month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared a halt on new data center construction until the state can conduct an audit of energy and water use and the burden on Texas’ electricity grid. Across the country and across party lines, 65% of Americans are opposed to the construction of new large-scale data centers in their communities. artigo.texto: Ford CEO Jim Farley has pushed back against concerns surrounding the automaker’s relationship with China-based CATL, whose lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery technology Ford has agreed to license. The arrangement has drawn scrutiny over potential national security implications, but Farley has dismissed the growing controversy, urging critics to “stop the drama” and indicating that Ford has no intention of backing away from the partnership. Ford has expanded its ties with Chinese companies beyond its EV battery operations. The automaker works with CATL on electric vehicle batteries, while its new Ford Energy business will focus on battery energy storage systems. The American automaker also announced a partnership with Hangzhou-based Geely Automobile Holdings in July to establish a joint venture focused on the European market. The venture will operate from Ford’s Valencia plant in Spain, which currently produces the Kuga compact SUV for European and other global markets. According to the Detroit Free Press, Ford’s agreement with CATL gives the automaker access to battery technology it will use to produce EV batteries at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall. However, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy raised concerns about Ford’s growing dependence on overseas suppliers for key manufacturing components. In a letter to Farley that Duffy’s team shared, he specifically pointed to China and other countries that the administration considers foreign adversaries as sources of critical parts for the Dearborn-based automaker. The letter stated that Duffy was writing to express “the profound concern of the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) regarding the strategic trajectory of Ford Motor Company (Ford or Company), specifically as it pertains to American national automotive manufacturing integrity, supply chain exposure, and reliance on technologies of foreign adversaries.” Farley responded to the letter, saying Ford will partner with and compete against Chinese suppliers. He said: “We’re going to partner with the Chinese and we’re going to compete with them. Both can be totally fine, they are not mutually exclusive. “So, stop the drama. Just get on with designing good vehicles, great software, great experiences, a great relationship with your owners and suppliers — and we can compete.” Addressing the BlueOval Battery Park in Michigan, where the LFP batteries will be made, Farley said, “That’s our factory,” but noted that CATL is a leader in battery production, so the partnership was a good solution. He added: “It’s American jobs. We’re learning. We’re working with them. We’re solving problems together. It’s better than importing batteries.”

artigo.texto: Americans have a lot of concerns about AI data centers, but two keep rising to the top. First, the process for approving data centers is very secretive, and the developers are concealing even basic details about their projects from the public. Second, the environmental impacts could be significant, from energy use and bills to water use to noise. In his recent MinnPost Voices commentary, Lindsay Mark Lewis tries to portray the proposed Pine Island, Minnesota, data center as an example of a project that “went through the process” and should therefore be built. But I wonder if Lewis has read any of the documents in the Pine Island “process.” I have, and there simply isn’t enough information in them to evaluate the potential environmental impacts. Key facts were not included in the documents, including how much energy the facility would use and what that might mean for the energy grid or electricity bills; why the facility needs 55 million gallons of water per year and what impact that might have on water resources; how many diesel generators the facility might need on site and what air quality impacts those generators could have; and how much noise or light pollution the facility might cause. The study also neglected to do a required cumulative impact analysis, looking at whether there are other proposed similar facilities nearby and what the cumulative impact of multiple AI data centers might be. Related: The Pine Island blueprint: How Minnesota is setting the standard for data centers The developers have claimed that they didn’t know these details at the time, not that they were deliberately withheld under the non-disclosure agreements they signed with local officials. I don’t know which one is true. But from the perspective of the law, and the residents who wish to know what is being proposed in their town, the result is the same — the environmental study doesn’t include information that the public needs to evaluate and comment on the project. Ironically, Google’s news release about their involvement and anticipated clean energy investments, which was released after the city had voted to approve the project, contained more details about the project than the environmental study. So let’s dig in a bit further to those energy issues, because this is the primary claim at Pine Island — that they are a model of clean energy investment. But the environmental study is silent on the topic of energy demand and clean energy investments. Google doubled down on this secrecy strategy in its recent filings at the Public Utility Commission, where it claimed this information was trade secret and must be withheld from the public. With regard to how much energy the facility would use, here is a direct quote from their filing: “The facilities are anticipated to bring an electrical load of [TRADE SECRET DATA BEGINS TRADE SECRET DATA ENDS] to the Company’s Minnesota system.” Community Voices: Pine Island data center project is far from a gold standard Did that answer your questions? Or are you curious about Google’s plan to build new energy resources? Here is what Google has to say: “At full load ramp and with all resources online, these assets are expected to produce at least [TRADE SECRET DATA BEGINS TRADE SECRET DATA ENDS] of the capacity and [TRADE SECRET DATA BEGINS TRADE SECRET DATA ENDS] of the energy required by the facility.” As long as this veil of secrecy is held around these facilities, this will never be a transparent and democratic public process. Nor can we fully assess this project and its potential impacts. Lewis points to the 2025 law passed in Minnesota on data centers as evidence that we have strong safeguards in place already. That law did have good provisions, such as a requirement that utilities create separate terms of electric service, or “tariffs” for data centers to avoid putting costs onto ratepayers. But we still have significant outstanding issues to address, including nondisclosure agreements, environmental review, and the cumulative impacts of multiple AI data centers on our air, water, and land, among other things. And contrary to Lewis’s claims about clean energy, the law does not prevent our utilities from building fossil fuel plants to service AI data centers, as is happening all around the country right now. There is, in short, a lot more to do. Lewis’s original question about whether it is possible to build and regulate at the same time, the answer is an unequivocal yes. Minnesota is doing it all the time. In its most recent report on permitting efficiency, the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency currently manages air, water, and land permits at over 26,000 facilities across the state. Last year, 99% of the permits submitted met the timeliness requirements set forth by the Minnesota Legislature. Related: In pausing data centers, Minnesota courts did what local officials wouldn’t And yes, there are large, controversial projects that are outliers, including AI data centers. Some folks like to point to these examples to make it seem like all facilities are litigated and challenged. In reality, the vast majority of projects in Minnesota go through environmental review and permitting in a timely manner and are never challenged in court. AI data centers are moving quickly and quietly into the state. They are moving so quickly and under so much secrecy that, without judicial review, communities would have few, if any, tools to protect themselves. The courts do have a role to play in enforcing our bedrock environmental laws, and the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy’s litigation is intended to ensure that these facilities undergo the same process as every other facility in Minnesota. The real question is, who will decide whether these facilities are right for this state — Minnesotans, or the massive technology companies behind these developments? A transparent process is the first step toward putting this decision back where it belongs — in the hands of Minnesotans. Kat

artigo.texto: ROX Capital Group Launches ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform Targeting UAE and Oman ROX Capital Group, a UAE-headquartered investor and developer of real assets, has introduced the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform, which will focus on utility-scale and commercial storage schemes across the UAE and Oman while also assessing prospects for regional assembly and manufacturing. The platform intends to assess multiple storage technologies, among them vanadium redox flow, lithium iron phosphate and sodium-ion batteries, plus long-duration options such as CO2 batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage. ROX aims to build alliances with chosen technology suppliers, judging them on their record of delivering large-scale storage projects, long-duration storage know-how where applicable, financial and operational strength, and ownership or control of core technology intellectual property. According to the company, preference will go to suppliers offering bankable systems, proven manufacturing capabilities and the capacity to provide long-term technical support, performance guarantees and warranties. Together with its partners, the platform will chase forthcoming energy storage tenders and evaluate local assembly or manufacturing prospects where commercially feasible. Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group, said the Gulf is developing some of the world's biggest solar projects, and the next hurdle is making sure clean power stays available after sunset and through peak demand periods. He observed that no single technology can satisfy every requirement, and that the platform is designed to pair the appropriate technology with each project's needs while, where feasible, backing the growth of local manufacturing capability. Antony further stated that lithium-ion batteries have reshaped energy storage and will continue to be a key part of the answer. Nevertheless, he noted that the Gulf's climate, load profile and energy-security priorities call for a wider mix of technologies. High summer temperatures can drive up cooling needs, while solar-heavy systems demand storage over longer stretches after dark. artigo.texto: Alabama regulators to decide how data center power deals protect customers MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WBMA) — As Alabama works to attract massive data centers, state regulators are preparing to answer a question that could eventually matter to every Alabama Power customer: Who pays for the electricity and infrastructure those facilities require? The Alabama Public Service Commission is scheduled Tuesday to consider new procedures for reviewing electric-service contracts between Alabama Power and large data centers. The proceeding does not decide whether a particular data center can be built. Instead, the PSC is establishing how it will review the power contracts for some of the state's largest electricity users — including whether the data center is paying the additional costs created by its demand and whether the agreement benefits other Alabama Power customers. The commission received 19 sets of initial comments and 10 sets of reply comments before developing the procedures scheduled for consideration Tuesday. What qualifies as a large data center? Under a new Alabama law, the process applies to a "large load data center customer" with an expected peak electricity demand of at least 150 megawatts at one or more contiguous parcels and meeting other requirements in state law. That threshold is important because the PSC says its existing process for reviewing special electricity contracts was developed long before today's large-scale data centers. Alabama Power's current Flexible Contract Rate, known as Rate FCR, dates to 1996 and applies to qualifying commercial and industrial customers. Under that process, contracts are deemed approved 10 days after filing unless the PSC disapproves them. The commission acknowledged in July that large data center contracts may require more time to review because they can require significantly more electricity capacity and energy than the types of customers contemplated when the existing system was established. Why should an Alabama Power customer care? At the center of the new law is a consumer protection. Before approving one of these contracts, the PSC must determine that its pricing and terms are expected to recover from the data center the incremental costs of providing its electric service and promote positive benefits for other retail customers. Incremental costs include additional expenses involving electricity generation, transmission and distribution that would not have been incurred without the data center, along with fuel costs and taxes. Put more simply: The regulatory framework is intended to determine whether a large data center pays the additional electric costs associated with serving it instead of shifting those costs to existing customers. State law also directs regulators to consider whether a data center agreement could lower costs for other customers, improve the efficiency of the power system and contribute to economic growth in the community where it is located. The PSC's action Tuesday does not itself change residential electric rates. More time to review contracts The PSC proposed in July replacing the existing process for qualifying data center contracts with a dedicated review system. Under the initial proposal, Alabama Power would have to provide regulators with the complete proposed contract and supporting information showing how the agreement complies with the new law. That would include evidence addressing the data center's incremental costs, effects on other customers' costs, power-system efficiency and economic-development benefits. The Alabama Attorney General would also receive an unredacted copy of the filing and supporting documents. PSC staff and the attorney general could then ask Alabama Power questions and request additional information. The proposed formal review period would increase from 10 days to 60 days. However, the original proposal contains an important provision: If the PSC does not issue an order rejecting the contract within those 60 days, the contract would be automatically deemed approved. No affirmative commission vote or approval order would be required. Whether that provision remains in the final procedures is one issue to watch Tuesday. Alabama Power says reviews already happen before contracts are filed Alabama Power told the commission in July that the existing 10-day approval period does not represent the entire review process. The company said it historically works with PSC staff before formally filing a contract and triggering the approval clock. According to Alabama Power, its most recent pre-filing review lasted nearly 60 days, while each of the two proposed contracts before it underwent review for several months. The company said that during the 30 years Rate FCR has existed, it has consistently waited to formally file a contract until it understood PSC staff had enough information to demonstrate that the proposal satisfied the existing criteria. Alabama Power temporarily agreed this summer to extend the formal review period for qualifying data center contracts from 10 to 45 days while the PSC developed permanent procedures. Those temporary changes lasted until the new state law took effect Oct. 1. How much will customers be allowed to see? Transparency also became an issue during the PSC proceeding. The commission's original proposal called for Alabama Power to file a public version of each proposed contract, with information redacted when necessary, while providing unredacted information to regulators and the attorney general. The PSC specifically asked commenters to address what information should be publicly available and what should remain confidential. Regulators also sought input on whether they should monitor contracts after approval to determine their actual effects on other customers and Alabama Power's system. One Alabama resident and ratepayer, Arie Lucille Kimble-Foster, urged the PSC to protect genuinely sensitive infrastructure information while keeping other information available

artigo.texto: Sand Batteries From Finnish Startup Offer New Renewable Energy Storage Option Polar Night Energies sand-filled silos show promise for load-balancing heating systems Builders are preparing the way to fill 2,400 tons of local sand into a silo under construction off a rural route between two large lakes in southern Finland in what will be, when finished, the second heat-storage battery for renewable energy operating in the region. Currently designed to power local district heating networks, the ‘sand battery’ is the brainchild of startup company Polar Night Energy. It now has two utility partners in the region deploying the technology. One sand battery has operated since 2025 in the town of Pornainen; the second is under construction about an hour’s drive away in the larger town of Vääksy. A sand battery is a large silo filled with an inert, non-combustible material that absorbs and retains heat from superheated air. The air circulates through a network of pipes and ducts coiled through the silo. This heat energy can come courtesy of excess electric power from renewable sources such as wind or solar. That power often arrives at the wrong time, creating a use-it-or-lose-it problem. This issue has stalked renewables for decades, spurring a hunt to develop creative energy-storage solutions. A sand battery uses electricity to power resistance elements (like a toaster, only bigger) that heat air flowing into the battery. The sand inside—or in the case of the Pornainen battery, the crushed soapstone recycled from a local fireplace manufacturer—can hold that heat. Internal temperatures can reach 500° to 600°C, or 930° to 1,100°F. The stored heat is then dispatched, on demand, via a heat exchanger. The output can be heated air, water, or steam, explains Annette Höglund-Dönnes, chief commercial officer at Polar Night Energy, based in nearby Tampere. The sand battery components include steel, piping, an electric fan and resistors, insulation, and a steel carriage. The idea came to Tommi Eronen and Markku Ylönen, now Polar Night Energy’s chief executive and chief technology officers, respectively, when they were students in the early 2010s. They developed it in a backyard. By 2022 they had a pilot battery running, successfully boosting runoff from a data center for heating purposes. Looking for quick answers on construction and engineering topics? Try Ask ENR, our new smart AI search tool. Ask ENR → That same year the utility Loviisan Lämpö, which is owned by a private equity firm, bought the heating business from a utility serving Pornainen’s 5,000 people. That’s when the town's mayor, Antti Kuusema, got a call. If the town was willing, Lämpö intended to install a 2,000-ton, 1 MW/100 MWh sand battery unit. It was in place by 2025, replacing the oil-and-wood-chip boiler the town used, along with biomass, to operate its district heating network. “Our experience has been very good. The idea for us as a small municipality has been to try to reduce carbon emissions in all operations,” Kuusela says. So far it’s meant a 60% to 70% reduction in carbon emissions in its district heating, and no more oil burning. District heating networks are specific environments: they are common in Scandinavia, less so elsewhere, but there are about 2,500 in the United States (including the steam tunnel system in Manhattan). They distribute heat from a central source, be it fossil, geothermal, or nuclear, through a spaghetti network of insulated pipes into surrounding residential or industrial areas. As of July 2026, the foundation was in place at the Vääksy sand battery site, which will be a 2MW/250 MWh facility, and construction was moving ahead for spring 2027 operation. Polar Night Energy recently inked a distribution deal to expand its reach into the Baltic states, partnering with US investors Solsiden Wangard Family Office and SIA Soldag, a construction firm based in Latvia. Plans call for the next sand battery to be even larger—perhaps 10 MW. The sand batteries are now being used for heat in cold weather, but the technology is not strictly tied to that, Höglund-Dönnes says. They could find industrial uses at a shipyard, university campus or in dairies for pasteurization. “You just need to have the need for heat,” she says.
