artigo.texto: Godawari Power Gets Green Light For 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System In Maharashtra Godawari Power's subsidiary, Godawari New Energy, has received key environmental clearance from Maharashtra's SEAC-3 for a 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System building in AURIC. This critical milestone follows a cumulative capex of ₹501 crore already deployed into the BESS segment as of June 2026 and the recent incorporation of a dedicated clean energy EPC subsidiary. Market snapshot: Godawari Power & Ispat Limited's wholly owned subsidiary, Godawari New Energy Private Limited, has received fresh environmental clearance to construct an industrial building for its upcoming 20 GWh Battery Energy Storage System. The greenfield facility is being developed at the AURIC Bidkin Industrial Area in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar, Maharashtra, signaling major progress in the company's strategic pivot toward clean energy technology. Data Snapshot - Incurred ₹501 crore in capital expenditure for the BESS project as of June 30, 2026. - Subscribed to ₹150 crore in equity shares on a rights basis on July 3, 2026, taking total investment in subsidiary Godawari New Energy to ₹600 crore. - Reported Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue of ₹1,750.47 crore and a consolidated net profit of ₹222.37 crore. - Offered a 31.45-acre industrial plot at AURIC Bidkin Industrial Area for setting up its downstream Cold Rolling Mill project on September 24, 2026. What's Changed - GPIL's transition from cyclical steel manufacturing to a structural green energy platform is accelerating. The environmental clearance for Godawari New Energy's industrial building in AURIC clears the regulatory path for physical construction of the 20 GWh BESS facility. Parallelly, GPIL incorporated Godawari Energy Solutions on October 1, 2026, establishing a dedicated, in-house EPC and O&M vehicle to manage turnkey execution and capture integrated project margins. Key Takeaways - Environmental Clearance Secured: Godawari New Energy received environmental clearance from Maharashtra's SEAC-3, enabling structural construction of the 20 GWh battery storage facility in Chhatrapati Sambhaji Nagar. - Robust Financial Backing: GPIL has already deployed ₹501 crore in BESS capex as of June 30, 2026, and scaled its equity investment in the subsidiary to ₹600 crore to fund project development. - Synergistic Land Infrastructure: Alongside the BESS facility, GPIL's downstream CRM project has secured a 31.45-acre land allotment at the same AURIC master-planned smart city, consolidating downstream manufacturing operations in Maharashtra. - EPC Ecosystem Integration: The newly incorporated Godawari Energy Solutions arm expands GPIL's capabilities to manage utility-scale clean energy installation and operations internally. SAHI Perspective GPIL's transition strategy is structured to build a highly captive energy storage value chain. By utilizing Godawari New Energy for battery integration and Godawari Energy Solutions for in-house EPC, the group is mitigating execution leakages. Securing environmental clearance for the 20 GWh BESS building is a crucial de-risking milestone that ensures civil works can proceed on schedule for a planned Q1 FY28 commercial launch. Furthermore, opting for AURIC—a master-planned smart city with ready plug-and-play utilities—bypasses the historical infrastructure and water allotment delays that have slowed the company's steel expansions in Chhattisgarh. Market Implications The clearance provides immediate medium-term visibility on GPIL's growth pipeline, which is key as traditional steel divisions remain subject to commodity price cycles. Investors are likely to react favorably to this tangible execution milestone, which validates the feasibility of GPIL's long-term clean energy initiatives. However, core profitability will remain driven by iron ore pellet realizations in the immediate quarters, with the BESS segment requiring further working capital deployment before generating meaningful margins in FY28. Trading Signals Market Bias: Bullish The regulatory clearance for the 20 GWh BESS building substantially de-risks GPIL's clean energy capex pipeline. With ₹501 crore already spent as of Q1 FY27 and the project on track for Q1 FY28 commissioning, GPIL is positioned as a rare first-mover in utility-scale industrial storage. Overweight: Clean Energy, Power Infrastructure, Industrial Engineering Trigger Factors: - Commencement of physical civil construction at the AURIC BESS site. - Operational setup and bagging of first EPC projects by Godawari Energy Solutions. - Formal registration and execution of land deeds for the 31.45-acre CRM plot at AURIC. Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months) Industry Context India's clean energy landscape is experiencing massive grid-scale storage mandates to balance renewable power supply. State and central agencies are aggressively bidding out gigawatt-hour battery storage contracts. GPIL's 20 GWh manufacturing facility—utilizing large-format Grade-1 LFP cells secured via supply deals with EVE Power—positions it strategically to capture early-stage tenders. The integration of its own CRM steel output into structural battery container manufacturing represents a compelling vertical integration play. Key Risks to Watch - Supply Chain Volatility: Dependance on imported lithium-ion cells from global partners exposes the project to geopolitical trade barriers and component pricing shifts. - Execution Timelines: Achieving the target Q1 FY28 commercial launch depends on smooth civil works execution and tech transfers without further regulatory bottlenecks. - Capex Pressure: While backed by solid cash generation (net profit of ₹222.37 crore in Q1 FY27), the overall transition is highly capital-intensive and could strain balance sheet liquidity if steel margins deteriorate. artigo.texto: Resumo - LG firmou contrato plurianual de 'chillers' para data centers de IA nos EUA - Empresa fecha acordo com a AIR Control Concepts, da Virgínia - Projetos somam mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade; valor não foi revelado - Ação da LG Electronics subiu até 8,8% no pregão em Seul - Nova fábrica na Virgínia deve começar a produzir no 1º semestre de 2027 - Encomendas anuais podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até fim de 2026 Fornecer soluções de refrigeração para data centers voltados à inteligência artificial é o objetivo de um contrato de longo prazo que a unidade norte-americana da LG Electronics selou, conforme a empresa divulgou nesta terça-feira (6). Do outro lado do negócio está a AIR Control Concepts, operadora de data centers com sede na Virgínia, cujos projetos somam capacidade superior a 5 gigawatts. Diante do anúncio, as ações da fabricante avançaram até 8,8% na bolsa de Seul. As partes não revelaram o valor do contrato. A fabricante sul-coreana afirma, no entanto, que esse entendimento de vários anos impulsiona sua expansão no mercado mundial de refrigeração destinado à infraestrutura de IA. O salto das ações em Seul quase representou o maior movimento registrado em um único dia nos últimos dois meses. Apelidados de ‘chillers’, tais sistemas de refrigeração industrial se tornaram alvo de expansão acelerada na LG. Por trás disso está a multiplicação de data centers pelo planeta, cuja disseminação fez disparar a demanda por formas eficazes de controle térmico, necessárias para manter funcionando as cargas de inteligência artificial. Expansão para além dos Estados Unidos Além dos acordos fechados recentemente em território norte-americano, a companhia afirma que tem avançado também em iniciativas relevantes na Indonésia e no Oriente Médio. Ainda neste mês, a companhia havia anunciado a intenção de expandir a fabricação de ‘chillers’ nos Estados Unidos e também na Coreia do Sul. O plano prevê erguer uma unidade na Virgínia, voltada a atender a demanda dos data centers americanos, cuja produção deve começar no primeiro semestre de 2027. Na Coreia, por sua vez, a LG quer ampliar a capacidade das fábricas de Changwon e Pyeongtaek, que já estão em operação. Meta de receita antecipada As projeções da companhia são ambiciosas. Tendo garantido US$ 426 milhões já no primeiro semestre, a LG estima que, até o encerramento de 2026, os pedidos anuais de resfriamento voltados a data centers cheguem à casa dos vários bilhões de dólares. Segundo a empresa, a meta de 2027, US$ 680 milhões em receita com ‘chillers’, deve ser alcançada antes do previsto.

artigo.texto: Rox wagers on the Gulf’s storage gap Rox Capital Group, a Dubai-based asset manager focused on sustainability, is in talks with potential partners for a new energy-storage platform targeting utility-scale and commercial projects in the UAE and Oman, founder Robin Antony tells EnterpriseAM UAE. Rox’s plans will focus on storage technologies ranging from lithium-ion, flow, and sodium-ion batteries to longer-duration options such as thermal, gravity, and compressed-air storage, according to a press release. The plan includes jointly submitting bids for upcoming storage tenders. Depending on the project, Rox could invest directly, co-develop with partners, or broker contracts between technology providers, investors, and project owners, Antony said. The pitch is that Gulf projects need a mix of technologies: Summer heat raises cooling needs for batteries, and solar-heavy grids need storage that lasts longer after dark, Antony argues. Demand is building: Masdar and EWEC are developing a USD 6.1 bn Abu Dhabi plant that pairs 5.2 GW of solar with 19 GWh of storage, and Masdar’s Ibri III project is Oman’s first solar-plus-storage plant. Still no specifics: Rox hasn’t named partners, projects, or target tenders, and Antony declined to give a capital target or timeline. Following up on A:5 (xNF>AF) A UAE delegation was in Washington last week pushing for deeper tech ties, including follow-through on the US decision to ease export controls on the UAE. The trip was led by Omran Sharaf, assistant minister for advanced science and technology at the Foreign Affairs Ministry, according to a ministry statement. The delegation met White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios and Under Secretary of State for Economic Growth Jacob Helberg. Talks covered AI, cybersecurity, space, quantum computing, and post-quantum encryption. With the Commerce Department, the agenda covered trade facilitation and export management. BACKGROUND- Washington moved the UAE into Country Group A:5, its allies-only export tier, in July. That lets G42 and other approved firms buy advanced chips without a license, as we’ve reported. But G42’s access lapses in April 2027 unless it’s extended, and G42 is reportedly in exploratory talks about selling a majority stake to US firms to secure access beyond that date. The two countries are working together on a 5 GW UAE-US AI campus in Abu Dhabi, anchored by the 1 GW Stargate UAE cluster.

artigo.texto: Grid-forming capabilities support multiple grid-restoration functions The project plays an important role in supporting voltage and frequency stability at a key point in Cambodia's central power grid, including transmission corridors that import electricity from Vietnam. Its grid-forming capabilities were put through a series of demanding system-restoration scenarios, demonstrating how energy storage can take on a more active role in supporting the power system. Key highlights include: - Large-scale black start from zero voltage: 516 grid-forming PCS units successfully energized the entire plant from zero voltage, establishing stable voltage and frequency across the system. - Restoration of a 240 km transmission network: The system supported the energization of approximately 240 km of transmission lines and five substations, while maintaining stable operation as the network was progressively restored. - Support for multiple generation sources: The system supported the start-up and synchronization of the 60 MW Kamchay Hydropower Plant, before the restored network was operated together with the 135 MW CIIDG coal-fired power plant, energy storage and loads. - Stable operation under challenging grid conditions: During restoration, the system remained stable through five transformer energization events, including a transformer rated at up to 100 MVA. It also maintained stability when synchronizing different power sources under a phase-angle difference of up to 15 degrees, demonstrating its ability to handle challenging conditions during system recovery. - Extended islanded operation: The system operated independently for 3.5 hours, demonstrating that the energy storage system could continue supporting the local network even when separated from the main grid. - Seamless transitions: The project completed three transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, with voltage deviation kept below 2% and transient frequency fluctuation within 0.15 Hz during grid separation. "This project demonstrates that the value of grid-forming energy storage goes far beyond storing electricity.When a power system faces disturbances or loses normal grid support, grid-forming technology can help establish and maintain stable voltage and frequency, support system restoration and keep the grid operating reliably," said Michael Ruan, Regional Director of Sungrow Southeast Asia and South Asia. "Through projects like this, Sungrow is helping turn energy storage into a more active grid-support asset and bringing proven grid-forming capabilities to the evolving power systems of Southeast Asia." Reducing Technical Risk and Ensuring Timely Delivery Faced with strict test protocols, complex power system scenarios, a compressed construction schedule and rainy‑season working conditions with ambient temperature up to 40°C, Sungrow's cross‑functional team covering pre-sales, on‑site delivery and R&D collaborated closely to deliver high‑quality project outcomes: - 20-day commissioning and testing: The on‑site team worked relentlessly under hot and humid conditions for two consecutive months. The team wrapped up hot commissioning plus three rounds of performance tests within 20 days to guarantee timely grid‑connection. - End‑to‑End Service Solution: Sungrow provides full‑lifecycle and one‑stop services spanning integrated design of storage and monitoring systems, EPC‑related support, equipment design, commissioning and O&M services, enabling the customer to fulfill customized grid‑level requirements with reduced management overhead. As Southeast Asia advances its energy transition, Sungrow will continue to bring proven energy storage technologies and solutions to the region, helping customers build more reliable and sustainable power infrastructure. Contact: Luly Wang, luly.wang@sungrow-hq.com Source: Sungrow Power

artigo.texto: LG Electronics fecha contrato nos EUA para resfriamento de data centers de IA As ações da LG Electronics avançaram depois que a companhia fechou um novo contrato plurianual para fornecer sistemas de resfriamento a data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos. A gigante sul-coreana de eletrônicos de consumo vem expandindo rapidamente o negócio de equipamentos de refrigeração industrial, conhecidos como “chillers”, impulsionada pelo boom global de data centers, que aumenta a demanda por soluções eficientes de gestão térmica para infraestrutura de IA. A LG informou nesta terça-feira (6) que sua subsidiária nos EUA firmou um acordo de longo prazo com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia, para fornecer “chillers” a data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. A empresa não revelou o valor do contrato, mas afirmou que o acordo acelera a expansão da LG no mercado global de resfriamento para data centers de IA. Em Seul, as ações da LG Electronics chegaram a subir 8,8% no início do pregão, caminhando para a maior alta diária em cerca de dois meses. A LG disse que, apoiada por vitórias recentes na América do Norte, também está ampliando presença em projetos relevantes de data centers no Oriente Médio e na Indonésia. No início deste mês, a empresa anunciou que vai aumentar a produção de “chillers” tanto nos EUA quanto na Coreia do Sul. A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia para atender à demanda crescente de data centers americanos, com início de produção previsto para o primeiro semestre de 2027. Paralelamente, pretende elevar a produção em unidades já existentes em Changwon e Pyeongtaek, na Coreia. Segundo a LG, as novas encomendas anuais de soluções de resfriamento para data centers podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após a companhia garantir US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A empresa também afirmou esperar atingir antes do prazo a meta de 2027 de US$ 680 milhões em receita no negócio de “chillers”.

artigo.texto: A corrida pela inteligência artificial está criando uma infraestrutura gigantesca. Empresas de tecnologia estão investindo bilhões de dólares em data centers, chips, memória, redes e sistemas de energia para atender ao crescimento da IA. Agora, uma projeção coloca em perspectiva o tamanho desse movimento. Para sustentar o nível de investimento esperado nos próximos anos, o mercado de inteligência artificial precisaria chegar perto de US$ 6 trilhões em receita anual até 2031. O valor é uma estimativa baseada no ritmo projetado de expansão da infraestrutura, e não significa que US$ 6 trilhões serão gastos na construção de data centers. Investimento pode chegar a US$ 1,5 trilhão por ano A projeção considera que os gastos anuais com infraestrutura de IA podem alcançar US$ 1,5 trilhão em 2031. A conta inclui novos data centers, capacidade computacional e atualizações de equipamentos já instalados, como GPUs, memória e sistemas de rede. A estimativa utiliza uma hipótese de que os investimentos representariam cerca de 25% da receita do setor. Nesse cenário, uma infraestrutura anual de US$ 1,5 trilhão exigiria aproximadamente US$ 6 trilhões em receitas para ser sustentada. Boa parte dessa receita ainda não existe O problema apontado pela análise está na diferença entre o mercado que já existe e o tamanho necessário para sustentar a infraestrutura projetada. Aplicações voltadas ao consumidor, incluindo assinaturas e publicidade, poderiam gerar entre US$ 200 bilhões e US$ 400 bilhões por ano em 2031. Já soluções empresariais baseadas em produtividade e automação poderiam representar entre US$ 1 trilhão e US$ 1,4 trilhão. Juntos, esses mercados chegariam a algo entre US$ 1,2 trilhão e US$ 1,8 trilhão. Isso deixa cerca de US$ 4,2 trilhões que precisariam surgir de novas aplicações e mercados. Robôs e carros autônomos podem ajudar Entre as possibilidades estão veículos autônomos, automação industrial, robótica e outras aplicações conhecidas como IA física. Também aparecem áreas como descoberta de medicamentos, desenvolvimento de novos produtos, simulações e gêmeos digitais. A expectativa é que essas tecnologias criem mercados capazes de gerar receitas que ainda são pequenas ou inexistentes atualmente. Isso significa que o futuro financeiro da IA não depende apenas de chatbots e ferramentas de produtividade. Seria necessário que a tecnologia encontrasse aplicações comerciais muito maiores. Data centers estão ficando cada vez maiores A expansão também acontece em escala física. Segundo a projeção, o tamanho e o custo das principais instalações de IA estão crescendo rapidamente, com capacidade e investimento podendo dobrar em intervalos de aproximadamente 12 a 16 meses. O consumo de eletricidade acompanha esse movimento. A expectativa é que o consumo global dos data centers mais do que dobre até 2030, chegando a aproximadamente 945 TWh por ano. A inteligência artificial aparece como um dos principais motores desse crescimento. A conta depende do sucesso comercial da IA A projeção não afirma que o setor necessariamente alcançará US$ 6 trilhões em receita. O número representa o tamanho anual que o mercado precisaria atingir para sustentar o nível de investimento previsto dentro das premissas utilizadas. A questão central, portanto, não é apenas quantos data centers serão construídos. É também descobrir quais aplicações conseguirão transformar toda essa capacidade computacional em valor econômico. Nos próximos anos, a resposta deverá depender da capacidade da indústria de transformar a atual corrida por infraestrutura em produtos e serviços que encontrem demanda suficiente em larga escala. artigo.texto: GlobalFoundries brings massive solar array, battery storage online in Essex Junction ESSEX JUNCTION, Vt. (WCAX) - A massive new solar array and battery storage system are now online at GlobalFoundries’ Essex Junction campus to offset demand on the power grid and lower electric bills. With the flip of the ceremonial breakers, GlobalFoundries’ new on-site solar array and 16-megawatt battery energy storage system are now online, marking a milestone for the Green Mountain State. “It’s the largest battery ever installed in Vermont, right here behind our own meter,” said GlobalFoundries’ Dan Colello. The battery goes hand in hand with the solar array, which sits on more than 30 acres of already developed but underutilized land that includes an old parking lot and brownfield. The energy from the panels is then stored in the four-hour, or 16-megawatt-hour, battery energy storage system. Related Story: “The battery is positioned to be able to reduce peak. Over that four hours of duration, it will discharge to reduce the consumption by the facility in its footprint on the regional grid,” said Rory Jones, co-founder of Lightshift Energy. Gov. Phil Scott joined in on the celebration Monday, commending the project on saving Vermonters money. “In fact, it should reduce costs by more than $40 million over the next 25 years. That’s real money. The savings is important to GlobalFoundries, and the Vermonters that work here. It’s also important for all of us as ratepayers,” Scott said. The project, part of GlobalFoundries’ net-zero goals, won’t disrupt the company’s energy needs for manufacturing. “The project demonstrates how battery storage can be integrated into advanced manufacturing, while maintaining the quality our operations require. And it provides a valuable lesson about future projects across the whole of GlobalFoundries,” said GlobalFoundries’ CEO Tim Breen. Copyright 2026 WCAX. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Data centers, Flock cameras discussed in city council meeting adopting 2027 budget EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - City council members approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center development Monday night, pausing all related construction while officials study its potential impact on the city. City leaders say the pause gives them time to research effects on infrastructure, utilities and neighborhoods, and to finalize zoning rules before any new projects move forward. The moratorium can be extended if officials need more time. Council President, Ben Trockman said the decision followed sustained public pressure. “We had multiple conversations — I’ve heard in council quite frequently, and I think something that we see in our inboxes quite often as well, is that there is concern,” Trockman said. $152 Million Budget Approved for 2027 Council also adopted the city’s 2027 budget, totaling more than $152 million. Major allocations include: - ~$6 million for restoring 27 miles of city roads - ~$20 million for parks and recreation - ~$30 million for water and sewer projects - $182,000 for Flock Safety cameras — a line item that drew criticism from residents Flock Camera Funding Sparks Privacy Concerns Some residents like Philip Elpers say the automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras amount to an invasion of privacy and argue they were installed without public input. “There has to be a commitment in the budget that actually stops all of this in the future until we say it’s okay,” Elpers said. Police Chief Defends Flock Camera Use Evansville Police Chief Philip Smith addressed the concerns directly at Monday’s meeting, saying the department has strict procedures in place to prevent misuse. He pointed to the cameras’ role in solving crimes, including a 2022 child kidnapping case. Smith said the technology has not been found unconstitutional and defended the department’s track record. “Not one time, in not one courtroom in the United States has ALPR been ruled as a violation of the 4th Amendment,” Smith said. “We’ve had Flock here since 2021, and we’ve not had one officer violate the policy or procedure of Flock usage in Evansville, Indiana.” Officials say even though the budget was adopted, they can still bring up flock cameras in future meetings if needed. artigo.texto: In response to Dwayne Yancey’s “Data centers are creating blue-collar jobs. Are Democrats on the wrong side politically of these workers?”, September 29, 2026. Dwayne Yancey is right that the Munters plant in Botetourt County is making real things for real wages, and right that a moratorium would reach workers nobody in the moratorium debate is thinking about. He is also right that this is more complicated than a bumper sticker. I want to take that last point further than the column does, because the jobs number is softer than it looks and the rest of the ledger rarely gets added up. Start with where the numbers come from. The PwC study Yancey cites was commissioned by the Data Center Coalition, the industry’s trade association, and published on a website the Coalition runs. Those are the sources available, which is the problem. Read it as a party’s filing rather than a finding. The JLARC number is more interesting than either side has noticed. Yancey reports about 50 jobs for each 250,000-square-foot facility, citing JLARC’s 2024 study. What the study says is that “several data center representatives indicated” that figure, and that about half of them are contract workers: electricians, pipefitters, security. Fifty is also the number the statute asks for. To claim Virginia’s sales tax exemption a data center must invest $150 million and create 50 jobs at 150 percent of the local average wage, with lower thresholds in distressed localities. Virginia is not observing that data centers employ fifty people. Virginia is observing that they employ the number Virginia told them to employ. Then the measurement. No series publishes union membership annually for a single trade in a single metropolitan area, so far as I could find, so I built one from sixteen years of federal filings signed under penalty of perjury. Inside electrical construction membership in hyperscale data center metros grew 17.3 percent faster than in comparable metros through 2025. Covered employment in those same places, on the government’s own count, grew 9.1 to 11.9 percent faster. Both numbers are real and they are not the same claim. Some of what reads as job creation is a trade organizing work that was already there. That is a good thing for those workers, and it is different from hundreds of new jobs, and anyone arguing either side of a moratorium should know which one they are holding. Now Botetourt, since that is where the column starts. Google bought 312.55 acres of the county’s flagship business park at Greenfield in June 2025 for $14,055,406.37, plus $4 million for county initiatives, on an option signed the previous October. Eight weeks after that signature the county added “data center” to the permitted uses of the only zoning district that could host one and called it housekeeping. The staff report on the accompanying rezoning said “no use or concept is identified at this time.” The county had been hosting Google site visits since January 2024 under the code name Project Raspberry. The performance agreement caps the company’s effective equipment tax rate at $2.40 per $100 for twenty years per building. It binds the county and its development authority, on a records request reaching Google’s confidential information, to notify the company and help narrow or resist it. It assigns Google “all media and press relation services” concerning its involvement with the county. And it promises $1 billion and 50 jobs for each data center built. Fifty again. A local government signed away its own ability to talk about the largest transaction in its history. The noise standard it will hold the finished campus to asks only whether the sound is clearly audible fifty feet from the property line. None of that appears in a jobs count. Neither does the transmission. When a 765-kilovolt line is built in PJM, Schedule 12 splits the cost two ways: half by a zone’s share of regional load, half by a flow calculation. Neither half asks where the towers go. Dominion’s zone carries about 45 percent. The farmer whose fields the line crosses is not a stakeholder in any sense the proceeding recognizes. Once the line is certificated he is a landowner facing condemnation if he says no. Water is its own accounting. The Department of Environmental Quality simulated a three-million-gallon-a-day withdrawal, the published upper end for a hyperscale campus on evaporative cooling, at nine locations spanning the coastal plain. All nine failed the permitting criteria. That is the closest thing the commonwealth has to an answer about whether the eastern half of the state can physically host what it is approving. Then there is the subsidy, which is the part that should trouble anyone who cares what the money could otherwise do. Virginia’s exemption cost the commonwealth about $1.94 billion in forgone revenue in fiscal 2025 by operator self-reporting, or about $1.6 billion by state audit. JLARC’s own incentives table puts the return at 48 cents in state revenue for every dollar spent, against 41 cents for the average Virginia incentive, and says that on the state’s side of the ledger it does not pay for itself. The same table credits the exemption with 84 jobs per million spent against 58 for the average, which is the industry’s best card and a real one. It beats the average incentive on jobs and still loses money. What has never been measured for Virginia is how much of the investment the exemption actually caused. Georgia measured its own. The Carl Vinson Institute at the University of Georgia found that 30 percent of Georgia’s data centers could be attributed to the exemption, and that the other 70 percent would exist without it. The broader incentives literature points nearer 25 percent. Virginia is finally getting a number of its own. The Joint Subcommittee on Tax Policy, revived in this summer’s budget compromise and meeting in August for the first time since 2024, reports December 15. Six weeks after the election. artigo.texto: A tática da Rússia envolve o uso de drones para atacar centros de dados e redes de telecomunicações ucranianas. Os ataques de drones russos contra centros de dados e telecomunicações ucranianos estão exercendo uma pressão significativa sobre as capacidades de defesa aérea e as redes de conectividade da Ucrânia. De meados de setembro ao início de outubro, as forças russas lançaram uma série de ataques contra importantes centros de dados e redes de telecomunicações na Ucrânia . Essa ofensiva marcou um aumento no uso de veículos aéreos não tripulados (VANTs) movidos a jato, representando um desafio significativo para a infraestrutura de tecnologia da informação e a rede de defesa aérea de Kiev. Alvos e frequência de ataques com drones a jato Na manhã de 27 de setembro, ataques de drones russos atingiram a sede da Kyivstar em Kiev, a maior operadora de telefonia móvel da Ucrânia. No mesmo dia, o Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou um ataque a um centro de dados da rede de telecomunicações ucraniana Vodafone. Anteriormente, em 15 de setembro, o centro de dados da BeMobile foi afetado por um ataque aéreo, interrompendo diversos serviços que operavam na plataforma UCloud. Em 23 de setembro, a infraestrutura de dois provedores de rede, UTELS e Pavutyna, foi danificada, deixando aproximadamente 100.000 residências em Kiev e arredores sem conectividade à internet. Em 25 de setembro, o centro de dados da Datagroup em Solomianskyi, Kiev, também sofreu danos após um ataque com drone, obrigando a empresa a manter as operações a partir de locais de backup. O Ministério da Defesa russo afirmou que essas instalações foram alvejadas por desempenharem um papel no processamento e transmissão de dados de inteligência militar para a Ucrânia. Em contrapartida, o Ministro das Relações Exteriores ucraniano, Andrii Sybiha, rejeitou essa alegação, enfatizando que se tratava de infraestrutura civil essencial para a transmissão de alertas de mísseis e drones ao público. A campanha prosseguiu em 30 de setembro, quando a Rússia anunciou um ataque ao centro de dados De Novo, em Kiev, seguido por um ataque a um centro de dados em Odessa, em 4 de outubro. De acordo com a ex-vice-ministra da Defesa da Ucrânia, Kateryna Chernohorenko, a intensidade dos ataques com drones, incluindo os da série Shahed, contra instalações de dados, aumentou drasticamente. Você também pode gostar Limitações da infraestrutura em nuvem e da construção subterrânea Desde os estágios iniciais do conflito, a Ucrânia descentralizou proativamente sua infraestrutura digital. Em 17 de fevereiro de 2022, o Parlamento ucraniano aprovou a Lei de Serviços em Nuvem e, posteriormente, emitiu resoluções permitindo que órgãos estatais colocassem sistemas de informação e registros públicos em serviços de nuvem estrangeiros durante períodos de lei marcial. Por meio do dispositivo de armazenamento Snowball da Amazon Web Services (AWS), mais de 10 petabytes de dados de 42 agências governamentais e 24 universidades foram migrados para a nuvem. O PrivatBank, que atende aproximadamente 40% da população da Ucrânia, também concluiu a migração de seus sistemas para a nuvem. Embora o backup de dados no exterior ajude a minimizar o risco de perda permanente de dados caso a infraestrutura seja atingida, as soluções de computação em nuvem não podem substituir a infraestrutura física local. Redes de fibra óptica, fontes de energia e estações de retransmissão locais continuam sendo elos vulneráveis, fazendo com que os usuários percam a conectividade quando as estações de retransmissão são destruídas. A realocação de data centers inteiros para o subsolo também apresenta inúmeros desafios técnicos. Essas instalações exigem sistemas de alimentação de energia de alta capacidade, mecanismos de refrigeração especializados e manutenção contínua, o que torna a construção subterrânea dispendiosa e demorada. Por outro lado, análises de código aberto (OSINT) da Dnipro Osint indicam que a Rússia também está acelerando a construção de uma instalação subterrânea de produção de drones com uma área estimada em aproximadamente 42.000 m² na Zona Econômica Especial de Alabuga, no Tartaristão. A capacidade de interceptar drones e o desafio da manutenção do F-16. As variantes de UAVs movidas a jato apresentam maiores desafios de engenharia em comparação com os UAVs tradicionais movidos a hélice. Graças aos seus motores a jato, essas armas atingem velocidades mais altas e tetos de voo mais elevados do que os modelos Shahed convencionais. Você também pode gostar O presidente Volodymyr Zelensky afirmou que, durante o ataque de 28 de setembro, 90 dos mais de 120 drones russos utilizados eram movidos a jato. A taxa de interceptação apenas para esse grupo de alvos foi de aproximadamente 57%, significativamente inferior à média de 70% para drones convencionais. Para superar essa diferença, a Ucrânia está acelerando o desenvolvimento de aeronaves interceptoras especializadas e a produção nacional de motores a jato. O caça F-16 é considerado um dos interceptores anti-drones mais eficazes disponíveis atualmente em Kiev. No entanto, os procedimentos técnicos para a manutenção dessa frota enfrentam obstáculos logísticos. Segundo o Wall Street Journal, a inspeção técnica de rotina de um F-16 a cada 300 horas de voo pode levar até 40 semanas nas instalações belgas, em comparação com 2 a 6 semanas em condições normais. O porta-voz do Ministério das Relações Exteriores da Ucrânia, Heorhii Tykhyi, e a empresa belga Sabena Engineering afirmaram que os prazos de entrega estão sendo acelerados e que os relatos sobre uma prontidão de combate criticamente baixa são imprecisos. Embora a Bélgica, a Espanha e outros parceiros continuem comprometidos com a entrega de mais caças F-16 e munição, a pressão para manter as horas de voo, peças de reposição e pessoal técnico permanece crucial para a proteção eficaz de data centers contra as novas táticas de ataque da Rússia.

artigo.texto: Beaufort County commissioners holding public hearing & vote on data center moratorium The above video is our WITN+ livestream and may not reflect the content in this story. BEAUFORT COUNTY, N.C. (WITN) - Tonight, Beaufort County commissioners will hear public input and vote on a moratorium for data center developments. The public hearing on the one-year moratorium was originally scheduled for last month but was postponed so the community could have an additional opportunity to share input. Commissioners will then vote on the proposal following the hearing. The moratorium would pause building or expanding large computer facilities used to power artificial intelligence. The commissioners offered an informal hearing during last month’s meeting, where several residents spoke in favor of the moratorium. Residents voiced concerns about noise pollution, emissions and electricity costs from potential data centers. Several residents said they support a moratorium lasting longer than one year. The commissioners’ meeting will start at 5:30 p.m. at 136 W. Second Street in Washington. County commissioners say a public hearing sign-up sheet will be placed on the podium before tonight’s meeting. Copyright 2026 WITN. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Mercado Voluntário de Carbono alarga metodologias para projetos florestais O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) passou a contar com duas novas metodologias para projetos de Reflorestação e de Gestão Florestal Melhorada, juntando-se à já existente para Novas Florestações. A informação consta de um comunicado do Ministério do Ambiente e Energia (MAEN), que considera este alargamento uma forma de aumentar as possibilidades de investimento privado em projetos de sequestro de carbono em Portugal. Com estas alterações, ficam disponíveis três metodologias de carbono destinadas a diferentes tipos de intervenção florestal. Segundo o comunicado do MAEN, a medida pretende também incentivar práticas de gestão sustentável que produzam benefícios climáticos, ambientais e territoriais, reforçando a capacidade de geração de créditos de carbono no país. “Estamos a criar condições para que mais proprietários, entidades e empresas possam investir na floresta e na ação climática”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho, citada no comunicado do MAEN. A governante acrescenta que o alargamento das metodologias pretende reforçar a credibilidade e o crescimento do MVC e mobilizar financiamento privado para projetos relacionados com a neutralidade carbónica e a resiliência das florestas. A plataforma tem atualmente dois projetos registados, ambos na categoria de Novas Florestações, enquanto um terceiro se encontra em validação inicial. Estão disponíveis para venda 977 créditos de carbono e estão registados 29 utilizadores. O comunicado do MAEN indica ainda a existência de 10 verificadores qualificados, responsáveis pela validação inicial e pela verificação periódica dos projetos. Para Maria da Graça Carvalho, o mercado está a ganhar “escala e maturidade”. De acordo com o MAEN, estão já a ser desenvolvidas novas metodologias relacionadas com o carbono azul e as pradarias marinhas, com o objetivo de abranger também os ecossistemas costeiros no âmbito da ação climática e da valorização do capital natural.

artigo.texto: Noah Berger/Getty Images via Amazon Web Services Over the next five years, Amazon will invest more than $1 billion in education, energy and water conservation, as well as in infrastructure in communities that host their data centers, the company said last week. As part of its “Built Together” framework, residents of Amazon’s data center communities will receive free community college and hands-on workforce training to prepare them for in-demand career fields, such as HVAC, IT, health care, education, public safety and advanced manufacturing. When the initiative launches in a few months, Amazon will cover all out-of-pocket expenses that remain after a student receives financial aid. The company anticipates that the program will help some 300,000 students access degree programs over the next five years. In addition, Amazon is expanding the network of physical training facilities at and near its data centers. These facilities provide free skilled trade certification programs and direct pathways to jobs with Amazon and its construction partners. The company projects that by the end of 2028, they will train 100,000 workers a year “for real jobs in their hometowns—fully funded by Amazon,” Matt Garman, CEO of Amazon Web Services, wrote in the announcement. The announcement comes amid growing backlash against the AI-fueled proliferation of data centers over the past few years. According to a recent Gallup poll, 70 percent of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their area, citing strained natural resources, cost-of-living increases, noise pollution and job losses, as well as general negative views about AI. But Amazon, which has at least 900 data centers across 50 countries, claimed in the announcement that many of those concerns stem from “misinformation” and “outright lies,” and that the United States can’t afford to fall behind on building more data centers. “There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it in the short and long run,” Garman said. “The choices we make today will determine that outcome, and a lapse in our nation’s focus or resolve could put us behind, and potentially irreparably so.”

artigo.texto: Quando se fala em projetos REDD+, a discussão costuma começar, e muitas vezes terminar, nas toneladas de carbono. Quantas emissões foram evitadas? Quantos créditos foram gerados? Qual foi a redução do desmatamento? Essas são perguntas essenciais. Afinal, o objetivo central do REDD+ é reduzir as emissões provenientes do desmatamento e da degradação florestal. Mas olhar apenas para o carbono deixa de fora uma parte importante daquilo que pode determinar o sucesso de um projeto no longo prazo. Uma floresta não permanece em pé simplesmente porque existe uma meta de carbono associada a ela. Conservá-la exige presença territorial, monitoramento, prevenção de incêndios, instituições capazes de tomar decisões, recursos para enfrentar pressões externas e, em muitos casos, alternativas econômicas compatíveis com a manutenção da área. Por isso, quando bem estruturados, projetos REDD+ podem produzir benefícios que vão além das toneladas de CO₂ evitadas. A própria estrutura internacional de salvaguardas do REDD+ reconhece a importância da governança florestal, dos direitos e da participação de povos indígenas e comunidades locais, da biodiversidade e dos benefícios sociais e ambientais associados à conservação. Proteger a floresta exige infraestrutura Grandes áreas florestais precisam ser acompanhadas continuamente para identificar abertura de estradas, invasões, focos de incêndio, extração ilegal de madeira, garimpo, novas áreas de ocupação e outros sinais de pressão. É nesse contexto que recursos provenientes de projetos REDD+ podem financiar sistemas de monitoramento por satélite, equipamentos, capacitação de equipes locais e ações de vigilância em campo. A tecnologia permite acompanhar mudanças na cobertura vegetal em grandes extensões territoriais. O trabalho em campo, por sua vez, acrescenta uma dimensão que o satélite sozinho não oferece: compreender o que está acontecendo, quem está entrando no território, quais áreas são mais vulneráveis e como responder às ameaças. A combinação entre instrumentos tecnológicos, conhecimento territorial e capacidade de atuação local transforma monitoramento em proteção. Governança também é conservação Projetos florestais são implementados em territórios onde já existem pessoas, organizações, conhecimentos, direitos, relações sociais e estruturas próprias de decisão. Por isso, uma das questões mais importantes em REDD+ é quem decide o que será feito com os recursos gerados pela conservação. As prioridades podem ser construídas por meio das estruturas de governança da própria comunidade: assembleias, associações, lideranças, conselhos ou outras formas legítimas de representação. Esse processo pode fortalecer organizações locais, ampliar sua capacidade administrativa e financeira e criar mecanismos mais estruturados para planejamento, execução de recursos, prestação de contas e tomada coletiva de decisões. Gerar renda sem derrubar florestas Talvez uma das maiores possibilidades dos projetos REDD+ esteja na capacidade de conectar conservação com desenvolvimento econômico local. Em muitas regiões amazônicas, isso significa fortalecer atividades que dependem da floresta em pé. Açaí, castanha-do-brasil, óleos, sementes, frutas, artesanato e outros produtos da sociobiodiversidade podem compor cadeias econômicas baseadas na manutenção dos recursos florestais. No entanto, fortalecer uma cadeia produtiva exige mais do que financiar a coleta. É possível investir em beneficiamento, armazenamento, equipamentos, boas práticas de produção, logística, organização de cooperativas, acesso a mercados e agregação de valor. Nesse contexto, a lógica econômica começa a mudar. A floresta deixa de ser percebida apenas como uma área que não pode ser convertida e passa a fazer parte de uma atividade econômica cuja continuidade depende da conservação florestal. É preciso evitar a explicação simplista de que comunidades desmatam apenas porque possuem baixa renda. Os vetores do desmatamento são muito mais complexos e incluem mercados de commodities, ocupação irregular de terras, infraestrutura, exploração ilegal de recursos naturais, fragilidade institucional e diferentes incentivos econômicos. A lição é relevante: conservar floresta exige olhar para décadas, não só para o próximo ciclo de emissão de créditos. Proteção além da fronteira do projeto Há outro desafio fundamental: uma área pode estar protegida enquanto seu entorno continua submetido às mesmas forças que provocam o desmatamento. Nesse cenário, existe o risco de que determinada atividade simplesmente se desloque. É o chamado leakage ou vazamento de emissões. Se um projeto impede o desmatamento em determinada área, mas a atividade responsável por aquela pressão migra e derruba floresta em outro local, parte do benefício climático pode ser anulada. Metodologias atuais de REDD+ tratam esse risco de maneira explícita. É nesse ponto que benefícios sociais, produtivos e climáticos começam a convergir. Quando um projeto investe exclusivamente dentro dos seus limites, existe a possibilidade de parte das pressões simplesmente migrar para regiões próximas. Quando combina conservação com alternativas de renda, recuperação produtiva, assistência técnica, engajamento de comunidades vizinhas e fortalecimento da governança territorial, cria condições para atacar alguns dos fatores que poderiam provocar o leakage. Estrutura maior A tonelada de CO₂ é a unidade utilizada para medir o resultado climático de um projeto REDD+. Mas ela não descreve tudo o que precisa acontecer para que essa quantidade de dióxido de carbono deixe efetivamente de ser emitida. Esses elementos não devem ser considerados automaticamente como prova de integridade climática. Um projeto continua precisando demonstrar adicionalidade, utilizar uma linha de base robusta, contabilizar incertezas e leakage e verificar de forma independente suas reduções de emissões. artigo.texto: Hermantown council unanimously passes AUAR review for proposed data center HERMANTOWN, Minn. (Northern News Now) - The Hermantown city council voted unanimously on Monday to approve an Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for the proposed Google data center. Read: Heated data center debate results in pause to Hermantown city council meeting An AUAR is a state-authorized environmental review process used to study how different development scenarios could affect the environment before construction begins. The 2,700-page AUAR for the proposed Google Data Center includes comments from five government agencies and more than 200 residents. Public concerns listed in the AUAR include environmental impacts, wetlands and transparency to the public. Many data center opponents over the past year have pushed back on the AUAR, arguing it is not as comprehensive as an Environmental Impact Statement. Project leaders who presented at the meeting, including Kimley Horn and Mortenson Construction, said they addressed the public’s concerns in the AUAR. “Many of those items are the direct result of the public process the city facilitated through the AUAR, and demonstrate Google’s commitment to incorporating public input in the development of the project,” said Chris Bates with Mortenson. Public Comment Supporters at the meeting agreed, arguing that Google is acting in good-faith by making these changes, and that the AUAR is a comprehensive framework for the city. They also emphasized the economic benefits of the data center. “One thing I appreciate about the AUAR process is that it allows us to be excited about economic development while also doing the necessary work to understand its impacts,” said Hermantown Chamber of Commerce President Kim Parmeter. On the other hand, opponents of the data center pushed back on the AUAR, asking the city to instead do an Environmental Impact Statement, which they view as a more comprehensive review that would bring in an outside entity to complete it. “They can’t make promises for what’s happening in 5 years,” said Duluth resident Jim Klukkert. “How long has Google been in existence, and they want to tell you that they understand they are making a commitment of 20-25 years?“ MN DNR Letter Another big topic of conversation from both the public and presenters Monday night was the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. The DNR sent a letter to the city in August asking for clarification and revision on the AUAR. That included mitigation plans and additional monitoring for impacts to wetlands from this project. Presenters on Monday said they made changes based on these letters, and that the DNR never formally objected to the environmental review Vote on Thursday The environmental review for Minnesota Power’s transmission line, which would power the data center, was also up for vote on Monday night. However, city leaders announced that due to the long public comment period on the AUAR vote, they moved for council to reconvene this Thursday. artigo.texto: City of Ozark, Mo., passes an ordinance that imposes restrictions on data center development OZARK, Mo. (KY3) - It’s about to be a lot tougher for data center developers to build in Ozark. On Monday night, the city’s board of aldermen voted unanimously to add more hurdles to data center development. Additions to the city ordinance tackle issues like water use and noise regulations, and others point to public input and transparency. “They would have to hold a mandatory neighborhood meeting for surrounding residents to allow residents to voice their opinions with regard to the development. They would have to submit ongoing noise monitoring and, in fact, maintain a public website,” said Ozark’s Mayor Pro Tem, Chris Aiken. “They will have to document and make public all complaints that they receive as well as their responses to those complaints.” Ozark resident Justin Wisdom says water consumption is towards the top of his list of concerns when it comes to data centers. “They do take a lot of water, and I’ve heard that water rights kind of get a little restricted when data centers are in your vicinity,” said Wisdom. “So, I mean, that’s kind of a pretty big worry.” Aiken says that the board of aldermen believes these changes to the city ordinance also address citizen concerns over potential data centers’ water and electricity consumption. “We’ve included design requirements within our ordinance to make sure that if there is a data center here, it’s using the most efficient cooling systems available,” said Aiken. “They actually have to submit a report from the utility company analyzing the impact that the facility would have on our electrical infrastructure.” Aiken says the city chose to add restrictions to the existing ordinance rather than impose a moratorium or outright ban on data centers. “I think our city determined that, legally, that was maybe a little more risky and that we’d be better off getting out ahead of these developments, placing reasonable restrictions on them so that they’re not going to constitute a nuisance for the people of Ozark,” said Aiken. “I think that’s a good strategy,” said Wisdom. “Make the companies just not even want to come around due to the restrictions and stuff. I think that’s honestly a good way to go.” To read the full ordinance, click here. The ordinance begins on page 105; new additions are in red. artigo.texto: Maryland Conditionally Selects Two Energy Storage Projects Totaling 440 MW in First Round Maryland's Public Service Commission conditionally selects Chalk Point (400 MW) and Jade Meadow III (40 MW), below the 800 MW target set for the first round. A second call for applications is due by January 1, 2027. The Maryland Public Service Commission announced on October 1, 2026 that it has conditionally selected two transmission-connected energy storage projects. They will receive Energy Storage Capacity Credits under the first round of procurement required by the state's Next Generation Energy Act. The sector is also seeing other deals, such as Usva Energia's sale of a 100 MW battery storage project in Finland to Enlight and the â¬37.9 million secured by Qair for two solar-plus-storage plants in Chad. According to the commission, the credits help large projects obtain financing by hedging against price uncertainty in the PJM Interconnection capacity market, through a more stable revenue stream. Two projects selected for 440 MW The commission selected the 400 MW Chalk Point Storage Project in Aquasco, Prince George's County, and the 40 MW Jade Meadow III Battery Storage Project in Barton, Garrett County. Together they would provide 440 MW of potential storage capacity, with four-hour durations and flat 15-year award terms. The awards remain subject to the commission's approval conditions and obligations. The combined estimated cost of the two projects is 6.98 cents per month for a typical Maryland residential customer, according to the commission. The Chalk Point project would be located at the site of the existing power plant of the same name. Jade Meadow III would be a combined solar-and-storage facility on a reclaimed coal mine in Western Maryland. A framework set by the 2025 law Enacted during the Maryland General Assembly's 2025 legislative session, the law directs the commission to conduct at least two solicitations for a cumulative 1,600 MW of front-of-the-meter, transmission-connected storage with a minimum four-hour duration. The first solicitation, which sought 800 MW, was issued through a Request for Applications on December 24, 2025. Five applicants submitted proposals in Round 1. The commission, assisted by its consultant Power Advisory LLC, found all five applications administratively complete and eligible. It then evaluated and ranked them using qualitative and quantitative criteria, including cost-effectiveness and potential ratepayer impacts. Two applicants subsequently withdrew: the 300 MW Fourth Quarter Battery Energy Storage System project in Montgomery County and the 135 MW Pulaski Energy Storage Project in Baltimore County. Decision after the summer hearings After a public hearing on July 30, 2026, and evidentiary hearings involving multiple parties from August 4 to 6, 2026, the commission determined that Chalk Point and Jade Meadow III were the most cost-effective and highest-ranked remaining proposals. It did not select the 500 MW Oystercatcher Energy Storage Project in Harford County, citing its lower ranking and considerations of cost-effectiveness and ratepayer impacts. The commission nonetheless recognized the project's desirable grid location and characteristics, and invited the applicant to consider Round 2. It also noted the need for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County. The commission also denied Chalk Point's proposed increase from 400 MW to 535 MW for Round 1. It said the revised capacity was offered after the application window closed and was not evaluated through the competitive solicitation process. The project may submit its expanded proposal in Round 2. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 % Next steps ahead of Round 2 "These awards are an important milestone for Maryland in our efforts to meet state energy policy goals set by the legislature in recent years," said Commission Chair Kumar Barve. He added that the commission is disappointed the awards fall below the 800 MW target for Round 1. He expects the Round 2 solicitation to attract many more offers, owing to a pool of over 40 additional storage projects from PJM's Cycle 1 interconnection process. The developers of Chalk Point and Jade Meadow III will have to apply to the commission for construction approval. That step will involve additional public and evidentiary hearings on non-financial aspects, including safety, siting and environmental impacts. The commission will continue the capacity credit awards process through a second Request for Applications, which is due to be issued by January 1, 2027.

artigo.texto: Spain is Raising its Stake in Utility-Scale Battery Storage Renewable energy developers Zelestra and EDP have signed two long-term power purchase agreements (PPA) that will expand their combination of utility-scale solar energy and battery storage brought together for the first time in Spain’s grid history. The companies announced Tuesday that the two new PPAs would add about 462 MWh of battery storage to 181 MW of direct-current solar capacity across the portfolio. The new PPAs are built on an original 2025 agreement which detailed the hybrid solar and storage project in the Trujillo, Extremadura region. Altogether it brings the EDP-Zelestra partnership to four Spanish projects totaling more than 500 MWh of renewable capacity with four-hour duration storage. Portuguese utility and global renewables project developer EDP will be the off-taker for both power generation resources. “Zelestra and EDP have built something together that is unique in the Spanish market: a commercial partnership that is unlocking large-scale storage capacity that will benefit the wider energy system,” Jaime Burguete, CEO of Zelestra in Spain, said in a statement. “These four hybrid projects show that energy storage is bankable in Spain, and we expect this segment of the market to be the main growth area in the years ahead. It also means that every megawatt-hour moved into the evening or early morning is clean power the system would otherwise have had to find elsewhere.” Earlier this year, Zelestra and EDP moved to hybridize an existing solar energy plant in Cáceres. The plans for the developing 160 MWh of battery energy storage is intended to balance and complement the 50-MW Pizarroso solar facility which began operations in 2023. “We are continuously developing new solutions that combine technology, market expertise and flexibility assets to unlock greater value from clean energy,” said Pedro Neves Ferreira, CEO of global energy management at EDP. “By integrating storage with renewable generation, we can enhance system resilience, improve efficiency and accelerate the electrification and decarbonization of the economy.” Spain’s electricity planners are increasingly adopting renewable energy resources. Low-carbon energy accounts for about 75% of the nation’s electricity resource mix, led by solar, wind, nuclear and hydropower. Spanish grid operator Red Eléctrica has tallied the installed battery energy storage capacity at nearly 200 MW across the country. While far below the battery capacity in the U.S., Spain’s installed energy storage has grown nearly 600% in the past year. artigo.texto: Data centers are a hot-button issue right now, but many executives in Northern Virginia are looking beyond the controversy. Related stories - Despite skyrocketing rates, real estate agent says DC-area homebuyers still have ‘upper hand’ - How Alexandria hopes to transform Duke Street into a more unified corridor - From napkin drawing to final product, this Fairfax business helps inventors through the process A majority of D.C.-area business leaders now believe the centers will have a positive impact on the regional economy, according to a survey. A survey from the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce and Pinkston found 53% of top executives view data centers positively while 34% have doubts. One in eight leaders, 13%, had no opinion. “A majority of them see data centers as a positive economic force, but there is some concern,” Julie Coons, president and CEO of the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce, told WTOP News. “I believe that what business leaders see is that our economy today, and as it evolves into the future, the toehold we have here in Northern Virginia and the greater DMV is so important,” she said. “And data centers do enable those industries that we want to continue to keep here and attract here — cybersecurity, commercial space, quantum of the future. So they’re critical to our economic standing today and certainly in the future.” While many business leaders in the Northern Virginia region are embracing data centers, Tim Tkacz is a bit more guarded. The CEO of Blue Sky Innovators, a Reston-based defense and national security company, said he is “whole hog optimistic” about the technology behind data centers. “We need these,” Tkacz said. “But at the same time, we have to be responsible about the impact that they have on the local communities that they go into.” This was the first time the Northern Virginia Chamber of Commerce and Pinkston asked about the economic impact of data centers in their quarterly survey. They surveyed 169 CEOs, executives and business owners from companies based in Fairfax, Loudoun, Arlington and Prince William counties as well as the cities of Fairfax, Falls Church and Alexandria. Growing doubts about the economy The survey also found growing pessimism among business leaders about the economy, both nationally and locally. Thirty-six percent of executives expect the regional economy to grow in the next six months, down from 40% in the second quarter. Some 23% believe the local economy will decline slowly or significantly in the coming months. Coons said business leaders expressed a level of caution. “While they maintain high, high confidence in their own business capacity,” Coons said. “They do see regional headwinds.” Pessimism has swelled about the national economy in recent months too, with 47% of leaders now downbeat about the national landscape. That’s up from 38% in the second quarter. Only 34% are optimistic about the national economy. Almost half business leaders, 49%, said their companies are being hurt by President Donald Trump’s foreign policy decisions, led by international trade, tariffs and the war in the Middle East. Hiring and spending plans Two-thirds of business leaders are optimistic about their own company’s outlook. While strong, that’s still down from 77% in the last survey. This rise in pessimism about the local economy has business leaders moving cautiously as they plan for 2027. Some 40% do not plan to change their spending plans in the next six months while 37% plan to increase spending slightly. Only 6% plan to increase spending significantly. As for hiring, a third of business leaders in Northern Virginia, 32%, plan to increase their payrolls and add positions heading into the new year. Almost three in five, 58%, plan to keep staffing about the same. “Let’s watch how things go over the next year or so,” Coons said. artigo.texto: Juniper Green Cosmic, a subsidiary of Juniper Green Energy, has commissioned 100.64 MWh of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity under the Bikaner Phase II project in Rajasthan. The commissioning took place at the project site after the facility completed trial operations and received approval from the Northern Regional Load Despatch Centre. The addition has increased the aggregate commissioned BESS capacity of Juniper Green Cosmic from 100.64 MWh to 201.28 MWh. It has also taken the aggregate operational capacity of Juniper Green Energy and its subsidiaries to approximately 2,725 MWp of renewable energy capacity and 600 MWh of BESS capacity. Juniper Green Energy commissioned its first merchant BESS project in Bikaner in January 2026. The 100 MWh facility was fully commissioned through Juniper Green Cosmic and marked the company's initial operational merchant storage project. The company has also started commissioning a firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE) project under the applicable FDRE guidelines. The project combines 259 MWp of solar capacity, 280 MW of wind capacity and a 200 MWh BESS spread across Rajasthan and Gujarat. The solar component began commercial operations in March 2026, while the BESS started commercial operations in April 2026. The project was awarded through a tender floated by SJVN under its FDRE scheme. Juniper Green Energy entered into a 200 MW power purchase agreement with SJVN, which has a back-to-back power sale agreement with Haryana Power Purchase Centre for supplying electricity to the state. artigo.texto: The partnership will also assess advanced battery technologies for telecom applications Cygni Energy and Indus Towers have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore collaboration on sourcing energy storage solutions for telecom infrastructure in India. Under the proposed collaboration, the companies will evaluate establishing Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) manufacturing capacity of up to 1.5 GWh to meet the evolving energy requirements of telecom infrastructure. The partnership will also assess advanced battery technologies for telecom applications, with a focus on improving reliability, energy efficiency, and sustainability of telecom operations. Venkat Rajaraman, Founder & CEO, Cygni Energy, said the initiative will focus on building manufacturing scale, technology capabilities, and readiness to support the energy requirements of large-scale telecom infrastructure. Cygni Energy plans to develop capacity of up to 2 GWh, while expanding its battery portfolio from existing 100Ah solutions to higher-capacity 314Ah systems and emerging battery technologies, Rajaraman said. Prof. Ashok Jhunjhunwala, Institute Professor, IIT Madras, and Chairman, ITEL Foundation, said collaboration between users, startups, manufacturers, and technology institutions can support the development and adoption of energy storage solutions in India. The collaboration comes as telecom operators and infrastructure providers increasingly look for reliable and efficient energy storage systems to support India’s expanding digital infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Amazon ends secret data center pacts and pledges $1 billion to host towns — AWS promises 30,000 home efficiency retrofits amid 100 proposed bans It will also invest more than $1 billion over five years in communities hosting its facilities. Amazon will no longer require nondisclosure agreements (NDA) with government agencies involved in its data center projects and will adhere to its new Data Center Commitment program designed to address mounting opposition to AI infrastructure, it disclosed on Friday in a blog post. The company also unveiled plans to invest more than $1 billion over five years in communities hosting its facilities. The announcements come as more than 100 data center moratoriums are being considered across the U.S., so AWS wants to make data centers more attractive to locals. No NDAs Amazon's decision to no longer require NDAs from government officials working with it is part of the company's newly announced Data Center Commitment program aimed at making data center building more transparent and somewhat less unpleasant to people living nearby. Among other things, the company vows to hold community open houses, disclose information about projects as early as possible, and listen to local concerns as development proceeds. Amazon also vows annual disclosure of its energy consumption and efficiency, water consumption and efficiency, and the proportion of electricity supplied by carbon-free sources. Speaking of power usage efficiency (PUE), Amazon reports a global PUE of 1.14 for 2025, compared with an industry average of 1.25 and 1.63 for on-premises enterprise data centers. It also says its facilities were 7x more water-efficient than the industry average and that it had reached 75% of its goal to become water-positive by 2030. Many concerns Also, new sites will use backup generators compliant with EPA Tier 4 emissions standards. While Amazon emphasizes that new sites will use backup generators meeting EPA Tier 4 emissions standards, the commitment is somewhat ambiguous in general, as the specification limits vary by engine power and generator classes, whereas Amazon does not specify the generator classes it intends to deploy. The company says an average U.S. data center consumes around 170,000 gallons of water per day, whereas an average Amazon facility uses less than 13,000 gallons, equivalent to 42 U.S. households. However, Amazon does not distinguish between the water consumption of a typical AWS data center designed for general-purpose cloud workloads and newly built AI data centers packed with power-hungry AI accelerators, which certainly have substantially different cooling requirements. In general, Amazon is trying to counter concerns about the resource requirements of data centers, although some of its comparisons remain rather ambiguous. When it comes to energy efficiency, the new Built Together initiative will add more than $1 billion to Amazon’s existing community spending. The company expects to provide more than 300,000 students with access to free community-college education over five years. It currently operates three Modular Training Centers, has six more under development, and plans another 16. Each facility can train roughly 2,000–4,000 people annually, with Amazon targeting as many as 100,000 trained workers per year by the end of 2028. Separately, more than 65 contracted water projects are expected to return over 8 billion gallons annually, more than twice the water Amazon says its data centers consumed in 2025. artigo.texto: SAN FRANCISCO — As food delivery workers on e-scooters whizzed past a hulking tour bus parked next to Anthropic’s headquarters in downtown San Francisco on Monday afternoon, software engineers returning from their lunch breaks snapped pictures of a brash slogan bursting out of the bus’ idyllic Americana artwork of farmhouses and fields of grain. “AI Data Center Revolt,” the bus’ detailed wrapping declared, proclaiming its mission to rally communities against wanton data center construction efforts across the country. The bus and its small crew of conservative activists from a group called Humans First had just completed an over 8,000-mile whistle-stop marathon of a road trip on perhaps the most uniting theme today: anti-data-center sentiment. “This technology is being shoved down people’s throats,” said Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, admiring the bus’ artwork from a nearby sidewalk. She said the group aimed to push back against AI giants and their assumption that they can build billions of dollars of AI infrastructure without residents’ input. “That’s not the American way,” she said. Founded this year as a coalition of left- and right-wing activists who worry that the rush to embrace AI is being spearheaded by tech oligarchs steamrolling Americans’ ability to steer the technology, Humans First has since morphed into a conservative-only effort led by Kremer to advocate for better guardrails on data center construction and AI in general. Kremer, a veteran conservative organizer who played noted roles in the tea party and the organization that helped create the rally preceding the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol attack, has spearheaded cross-country bus trips to extol MAGA talking points and deny the outcome of the 2020 election. Composed of Kremer, her husband, her daughter and her dog, Lovie — “He’s been with me the entire trip,” Kremer said — along with staffers and security guards, the Humans First squad has made more than 35 stops in communities across the country over the past five weeks. The trip culminated in Monday’s visits to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta and Nvidia — widely regarded as the world’s largest and most influential AI companies. Kremer and her daughter, Kylie Jane Kremer, fielded questions from reporters about the tour’s goals and its accomplishments. FOR SUBSCRIBERSLatino voters feel buyer’s remorse in battleground Texas FOR SUBSCRIBERSWhat’s on the Supreme Court’s docket this term? “I want Big Tech to actually include the American people and allow them to have a seat at the table,” said Kylie Jane, a senior adviser at Humans First. She highlighted the organization’s Data Center Policy, a 13-point charter that emphasizes community control over data center planning, rejects data centers’ role in increasing electricity prices and decries any use of American data centers for unconstitutional surveillance, among other issues. “We’re not anti-AI, we’re not anti-tech, we’re not even anti-data center,” Kylie Jane said. Instead, the team touts a proud populist message: AI development must prioritize Americans, and the historic infrastructure buildout must benefit the communities hosting data centers humming with billions of dollars of business. Yet, during the monthlong tour, much of the nation’s AI discourse shifted dramatically from worries about data centers’ guzzling water to fears that the technology might wipe out billions of people — or the entire species — in the next decade. Recent worries about such risks were catalyzed by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s warning on X that leading AI companies are recklessly speeding toward technological disaster. Amy Kremer said AI’s potential existential threats had clearly struck a nerve with Middle America, with growing numbers of people at Humans First rallies bringing up AI’s risks to society beyond immediate data center impacts. “People across the country are definitely paying attention to the existential risk and what is coming out about that,” Kremer said. On Sunday, Kremer participated in a panel at a gathering of AI luminaries in nearby Berkeley, where she laid out the future of conservative AI approaches to mitigate such potential outcomes. Kremer said she vehemently disagreed with some of the conference’s participants about the idea that AI systems could ever be conscious or have a soul — a belief some Anthropic employees acknowledge as possible. “Personally, I think it’s demonic,” she said, looking toward the Anthropic headquarters. “We are human beings, and we all have souls. And you cannot put a soul in a machine. Part of me feels sad for them that that’s how empty and soulless their lives are.” Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Kremer and her cadre have found thousands of Americans fed up with large AI companies’ setting up data center projects under shady shell companies or under the protection of nondisclosure agreements. She pointed to a tour stop in Jonesburg, Missouri, a small town in a county of 12,000 people. Google and Amazon have announced they will invest a combined $25 billion in data centers in the county over the coming years. “That is a David-versus-Goliath story,” she said. “How do you ever fight that alone?” The journey hasn’t been without its bumps. Kremer has received death threats, some from staunchly pro-AI people, her husband said. And sometimes the road has been too rough for the bus itself — one gravel road in Wakarusa, Kansas, proved impassable and forced the team to ask the owners of a nearby house whether they could hold their rally there instead of farther down the road. “Word got to the people down the dirt road, and then all of a sudden, before you know it, here they come,” Kremer said. “It was like ‘Field of Dreams.’ They just kept coming, the cars and the people.
