artigo.texto: City council meeting erupts into chaos after planned data center vote postponed See more of our coverage in your search results. Chaos erupted at the end of a Tennessee city council hearing when officials postponed a vote on Elon Musk’s data centers, sparking a fistfight and protesters taking over the meeting hall. A mob of enraged protesters harassed members of the Memphis City Council Tuesday night after they had just voted to delay the vote on a moratorium of data centers in the city. Councilors voted 7 to 5 Tuesday night to table the remaining items on the agenda for a later date before the meeting devolved into a loud disarray of shouting between council members and the residents. One protester broke out a bullhorn and began to lead a chant of “ain’t no power like the power of the people.” Council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen Washington had called for a recess to the meeting and ordered police officers to clear out the hall, according to a livestream. The frenzied mob worked its way to the dais and began shouting at the city councilors who were huddled around. The protesters accused the elected officials of being “sellouts,” according to video from KWAM News Radio. Officers had successfully removed the protesters from the meeting hall as the mob continued to shout “this is our city” and “show me what democracy looks like.” At least two women engaged in a fight near the exits during the chaotic meeting, but no arrests were made, WREG reported. Roughly 100 protesters had attended the meeting for the scheduled final vote on the data centers that sit south of the city on the Memphis, Tenn.-Southaven, Miss. border. Two large data center facilities, named Colossus and Colossus 2, are run by Musk’s artificial intelligence company SpaceXAI. The original Colossus facility was built to serve X’s Grok AI bot but was later part of an agreement in May that will see Anthropic use the full computing power of the facility The delayed motion was rescheduled to October 20, Action News 5 reported. If passed, a 12-month moratorium would be enacted on data centers to allow for a study on the impact the facilities have on the city’s health, engineering, power and water infrastructure. City council infighting occurred amid the chaos as one councilor accused another of confusing people. “That’s all he does; he brings up mess, he… that’s all you do, JB Smiley, confuse the people over, over, over and over! Anytime there is an election,” Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, according to Action News 5. Councilman Smiley, who voted against delaying the vote, called for a civilized discussion on the subject instead of the shouting and fighting. “When the community shows up, we just have to listen to them. I’m disappointed that we didn’t listen with ears, okay, I hear you, I understand. Let’s figure out how we can do what you want, but also what we believe would be in the best interest of the community,” said Smiley, who was the lead sponsor on the moratorium proposal. Councilman Jeff Warren, an opponent of any moratorium, warned that the year-long pause would give incentive to companies to not do business with the city and find another area to build the complexes. “If we pass a moratorium, there’s not reason for them to think they need to come here. They get the same benefit from going to Desoto County, Crittenden County, Fayette County, Tipton County,” said Councilman Jeff Warren Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - Business and economic experts told members of the Ohio Valley’s business community that data centers would be beneficial to the economic future of the community. Data centers, a hot topic in the region, was discussed at length Tuesday morning at the annual Economic Outlook Conference sponsored by the Wheeling Area Chamber of Commerce. The conference was held at the Wheeling Island Hotel-Casino-Racetrack. David H. McKinley, president and chief investment officer at McKinley-Carter Wealth Services, supported construction of data centers locally, pointing out the financial success in Loudoun County, Virginia. There are 234 data centers located in the county, and the collective property tax on them comes in at $1.8 billion, according to McKinley. This accounts for 38-40% for the county's tax base. "Technology investments are huge. We take them all for granted," he said. "The ramp up is significant and not to be overlooked. "I'm disappointed there is so much negativity about data centers." Former Delegate Erikka Storch, R-Ohio, now external affairs manager for American Electric Power, and James Bailey, a member attorney at Spilman, Thomas and Battle, participated in a panel discussion pertaining to the energy industry in the state that was led by John Deskins, assistant dean at the WVU John Chambers College of Business and Economics. both Storch and Bailey indicated support for data centers. "From our perspective, data centers operating in our area would help our customers," Storch said. "It would give us a larger population in which to spread our costs, and we would welcome them. "It would send the message that it would diversify the economy when there are opportunities, and it would increase tax revenue." The money has been "very transformational” for counties that already have data centers or are building them, such as in Putnam County, she added. Google is developing a multi-billion-dollar hyperscale data center campus in Buffalo, West Virginia. "There are incredible opportunities, but unfortunately there are tons of misinformation out there," said Bailey, whose law firm represents those wanting to build a data center in Ohio County. "The water use isn't nearly what you hear. These things are self-contained now." Newer technology allows the water at the plant to be recycled and it uses about the same amount of water as any industrial facility, he explained. "You never hear from people who are for something. You only hear from people who are against it," Bailey said. Deskins provided a statewide economic outlook, and said that West Virginia needs more working-age adults in the workforce and a more diversified business climate if it is to grow economically. Deskins predicts there will be economic growth in West Virginia in the coming years, though it will happen at a slower rate than is typical. "We still have uncertainty ... over tariff policy, the war in Iran," he said. "Certainly, we have uncertainty around interest rates, but that uncertainty has diminished and that's a good thing. "Here in West Virginia, we think the state is going to remain stable over the next five years. There will be growth in some regions, but stability overall statewide." West Virginia has many successes, but they are "too concentrated geographically," Deskins noted. These are occurring in Jefferson and Berkeley counties in the Eastern Panhandle, and in Putnam County near Charleston and Kanawha County. "We have a lot of regions that are stagnant, and we need to find ways to have growth in those regions that are healthy to broaden out geographically," he continued. Despite the fact that West Virginia has low unemployment rates and people are working, the state continues to rank last in the number of adults actively participating in the workforce. The national workforce participation rate is 64%, while West Virginia continues to lag at 54.5%. "It is the biggest economic challenge we face," Deskins said. "There is no way West Virginia can achieve the prosperity we hope for until we get more people in the workforce. It is virtually a mathematical impossibility to imagine that West Virginia would have some form of economic prosperity on par with the nation... and have mathematically the smallest share of adults in the workforce. "It should be our biggest economic development challenge, and it should be our biggest priority. But fixing this is very hard." Among West Virginia counties, Wetzel County has the lowest workforce participation rate at 47.9%, according to U.S. Census statistics. This reflects a measurement of people between the ages of 16 and 64 who are not in school. Sharon Campbell, executive director of the Wetzel-Tyler Chamber of Commerce, suggested workforce participation in the region is lower because of a lack of any childcare facilities there and a lack of public transportation. These factors particularly affect women in the workforce, she added. The area also has been hit hard with drug addiction issues, Campbell noted. Deskins noted the years West Virginia has outperformed the nation in gross domestic product growth were when oil and gas industries performed strongly. The healthcare industry, led by WVU Medicine, also has been growing in the state, he added, as has the information industry. More diversification among businesses located in the state would lead to more economic growth, Deskins said. He also suggested the state should make more effort to retain and attract people to increase population. West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack spoke about "how inefficient state government is," and how when a bad decision is made, "government keeps going on." "West Virginia is at a crossroads, and this demand is being brought to us by the demand for electricity nationwide," he explained. "Most of it is needed by AI (artificial intelligence and data centers). "America cannot produce that electricity for West Virginia. They have to have us." artigo.texto: Ukraine will receive $16.2 million to develop renewable energy and energy storage systems The Board of the Climate Investment Funds (CIF) has approved Ukraine’s $16.2 million investment plan. The funds will be directed toward the development of renewable energy, cross-border power interconnections, and energy storage systems. According to the minister, this funding is part of the “Renewable Energy Integration” (REI) program. “This will help accelerate the integration of the Ukrainian power grid into the European energy network and will also strengthen the transformation of the Ukrainian energy sector,” Shmyhal said. The implementation of the approved program involves both public and private sectors. As Denys Shmyhal noted, as part of the public sector component, an investment package with an estimated value of $200 million has been put together in collaboration with the World Bank and NPC “Ukrenergo.” It includes a number of important projects to strengthen the Ukrainian power grid. Specifically, the following are planned: - construction of the 400 kV Chernivtsi–Suceava cross-border interconnector; - the creation of additional transmission capacity of 880 MW toward Ukraine and 445 MW toward European power grids; - the modernization and reinforcement of five high-voltage substations; - providing engineering support for the implementation of investment projects; - modernizing the IT, telecommunications, and operational infrastructure of NPC “Ukrenergo.” The implementation of these measures is expected to contribute to the further strengthening of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and its integration with the European power system. The second component of the program focuses on attracting private investment into modern energy infrastructure. According to Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal, this component is being developed by the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Specifically, the plan includes: - support for private investment in energy storage systems; - the development of autonomous BESS systems, which are expected to provide 610 MW of battery storage capacity; - implementation of renewable energy generation projects in combination with energy storage systems; - the implementation of other distributed energy solutions. Thus, the investment plan approved by the CIF is intended to simultaneously support the development of renewable generation, electricity storage, and the expansion of Ukraine’s capacity to exchange electricity with European countries. This was announced on October 6 by Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal. As a reminder, Ukraine and Germany plan to expand cooperation in the energy and transportation sectors. Among the agreements are potential purchases of German equipment to restore the power grid and locomotives for Ukrzaliznytsia, which are intended to help offset losses caused by Russian attacks. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi announced this following a conversation with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Ukraine and Germany have signed a series of agreements in the energy sector totaling more than 155 million euros. The agreements concern the restoration of damaged infrastructure, the supply of critical equipment, and the development of distributed generation. Separately, Germany announced a contribution of 250 million euros to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund.

artigo.texto: Data center emissions dispute prompts Virginia trip by Spartanburg officials Environmental group says public was misled on data center’s cancer-causing emissions SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - The Southern Environmental Law Center is asking the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services to reconsider its decision involving the Valara data center project in Spartanburg County, arguing the public did not have an opportunity to review updated information about the facility’s formaldehyde emissions. SELC sent a letter to DES on Oct. 1 asking the agency to reopen the public comment period for Valara’s air permit. Emissions estimates changed The dispute centers on formaldehyde emissions from natural gas-fired turbines planned for the data center. In its permitting documents, DES previously calculated controlled formaldehyde emissions at less than 10 tons per year. DES’ September permit sets a federally enforceable limit of less than 10 tons per year for any individual hazardous air pollutant, including formaldehyde. The permit also limits total hazardous air pollutants to less than 25 tons per year. SELC argues updated calculations put Valara’s controlled formaldehyde emissions at 10.58 tons per year. Frank Holleman, a senior attorney with SELC, said Valara’s original application relied on an emission reduction associated with technology the company was not using. “They reduced the estimates of that by using a reduction based on a technology they were not using and is no longer marketed,” Holleman said. DES later acknowledged that an incorrect emission factor had been used, according to SELC. The agency reviewed additional information provided by Valara and recalculated the emissions before issuing the permit. Holleman said the public has not been given enough information to independently review the updated calculation. “They also say they had some industry information that Valara provided, but they didn’t give the numbers. They didn’t show how they calculated it. And we’ve got this black box of additional information, all done behind closed doors,” Holleman said. DES says its permitting staff reviewed the application, supplemental information and public comments before issuing the Sept. 18 permit. The agency says it is required by law to issue the permit if an application demonstrates compliance with applicable state and federal regulations and the conditions of the permit. Why the 10-ton limit matters The permit places a limit of less than 10 tons per year on any individual hazardous air pollutant. Exceeding a permit limit could put the facility out of compliance and subject it to enforcement. Formaldehyde is classified as a known human carcinogen. Holleman said DES should give the public more information about how the updated emissions figure was calculated. “And what we’re saying is, no, no, no. The law doesn’t allow that. Simple fairness doesn’t allow it,” Holleman said. SELC is asking DES to reopen the public comment period. FOX Carolina reached out to DES for a response. The agency said it would answer questions the following day. Valara is also facing at least two active lawsuits, both led by the Southern Environmental Law Center. Valara had not responded as of the report. Spartanburg County officials travel to Virginia’s Data Center Alley The dispute comes as several Spartanburg County Council members and county officials travel to Loudoun County, Virginia, an area known for its concentration of data centers. According to a county travel notice, council members Monier Abusaft and Paul Abbott are traveling to Loudoun County from Sunday, Oct. 4, through Tuesday, Oct. 6. They are joined by county staff and others to learn from community leaders, utility executives and industry experts about Loudoun County’s experience with data center development. Monday’s schedule included a data center industry tour, discussions with Loudoun County supervisors and board members, a meeting with Amazon data center representatives and a session with other data center industry representatives. Tuesday’s schedule includes meetings with Loudoun Water, Loudoun County Economic Development and a state delegate. Loudoun County is about an hour and a half drive northwest of Washington, D.C. FOX Carolina reached out to county officials for comment but no one was available for an interview. Holleman, whose organization was told about the trip when it was announced Friday night, said he believes county leaders should hear from people who have raised concerns about data center development. “It really is yet another disgrace. And here they have county councilmen traveling up to Virginia. And if you look at their agenda, they’re meeting with one industry representative after another. Why are they not meeting with environmental advocates, community advocates, people who are concerned? Who do they represent? Do they represent the people of Spartanburg? Or do they represent the data center operators, owners, and investors and hedge funds in major corporations?” Holleman said. What Loudoun County says about data centers Loudoun County officials point to the tax revenue generated by the data center industry as a major economic benefit. According to Loudoun County, data centers generated $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue during fiscal year 2026, representing 39% of the county’s overall budget. The county’s adopted fiscal year 2027 budget projects $1.3 billion in data center revenue, or about 40% of the total budget. Loudoun County also says more than 17,000 direct and indirect data center-related jobs have been created. Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. artigo.texto: During their first face-to-face debate, candidates for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, Democrat William Lawrence and incumbent Republican Tom Barrett, faced off on immigration policy, the Iran war and data center development. Throughout the debate on Tuesday, Barrett continually referenced old statements posted by Lawrence on social media, while Lawrence repeatedly took a stance of connecting Barrett to President Donald Trump. A 'humane' immigration policy Upon being asked about budgeting for the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Lawrence said border security and ICE personnel should be regarded as separate. Lawrence said he supported a “secure border” paired with a “humane, efficient and orderly” immigration system. The congressional hopeful referenced the deaths of two Minneapolis, Minnesota, residents, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during Operation Metro Surge in January, saying the current immigration system is “un-American.” “We need to remember the words on the Statue of Liberty, which call us to our high values and remind us that we should welcome immigrants because we are immigrants,” Lawrence said. Barrett also established a desire for a “humane” system of immigration that is also “firm” and “fair.” He further advocated a need for a “secure border,” saying current border security legislation has reduced fentanyl overdose rates. The Department of Homeland Security's renewed focus on immigration enforcement under the second Trump administration led to a 31% decrease in the number of hours spent on fentanyl-related criminal investigations, according to a recent DHS Office of the Inspector General report. “We have to start with the border security first policy,” Barrett said. “Then we can have a conversation about the remaining immigration questions that are out there that we need to continue to work on.” Barrett also referred to Lawrence’s old social media posts advocating for “free and open migration” and “amnesty to all 12 million illegal immigrants in the country,” saying Lawrence’s plan would make “communities less safe.” Lawrence said they were “hypothetical statements" and later said he has since changed his mind. Future data center development Data centers have been a bipartisan source of strain in the Greater Lansing Area, with residents concerned about the hyper-scale projects' toll on the environment and the job market. Barrett said local governments should be in charge of data center development projects. The incumbent Republican candidate disparaged the pursuit of the Green New Deal due to it “taking away local control" from future development. “I've been on the side of local control,” Barrett said. “I've been on the side of local residents for this.” Lawrence, who co-founded the Sunrise Movement, championed his “nationally recognized” fight against data centers and advocacy for “safe AI.” He referenced past appearances at local council meetings where Lawrence condemned data center development, calling out Barrett’s lack of presence in such areas. “Residents across the political spectrum — Democrats, Independents, Republicans — have been fighting back and saying, ‘No, we don't want this in our communities,’” Lawrence said. The Iran War Barrett said he was “one of the very first Republicans” to vote against continuing the war in Iran. He said this “continued vote” was not of "convenience" but "conviction,” advocating for "separating" himself from Trump with regard to the nation’s part in the war. “Our national leaders, whether it's the president or anybody else, (have) to be contemplating the downstream effects of every decision that we make,” Barrett said. While Lawrence also supported an end to the conflict, he emphasized the economic impacts, saying, “We can’t afford for this war to continue.” Lawrence also criticized Barrett’s initial support of Trump, condemning his decision to “arm the Israeli government.” Support student media! Please consider donating to The State News and help fund the future of journalism. “We have got to put a stop to this,” Lawrence said. “I am a strong supporter that we should bring our money home, stop arming Israel and stop these endless wars that are not making us any safer.” Lawrence called for Barrett to “condemn the president for his words” in reference to recent comments suggesting that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if cleared to develop nuclear weaponry. While Barrett agreed that this language “wasn’t acceptable,” he fired back, challenging Lawrence to denounce leftist streamer Hasan Piker’s remarks that “Americans deserved 9/11.” Lawrence denounced Piker's comments, saying, “It was a despicable statement.” The event was livestreamed through WKAR’s YouTube channel on Tuesday and will air on Oct. 7 at 7 p.m. through local news outlets.

artigo.texto: KUALA LUMPUR – The deferment of Malaysia’s carbon tax implementation will give the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry (NRES) more time to finalise the regulatory and policy framework needed before emission caps are enforced. Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup said the decision to postpone the tax, which was initially scheduled to be introduced this year, was also influenced by global geopolitical developments that had contributed to energy price volatility. Speaking during a Concorde Club dialogue session at Wisma Bernama here today, he said the delay would provide industries with additional time to adjust while the government strengthens the legal framework governing carbon emissions. He said this included the National Carbon Market Policy and the proposed Climate Change Act, which he hoped could be tabled soon. “(The postponement) is also right because we need to have the proper framework and all that in place first. That’s why we’ve been successful in launching the National Carbon Market Policy and I hope that we can table the Climate Change Act soon. “Once that is up, then we have the framework and the policies all clearly in place, including the regulation, enforcement, the regulatory powers to give us to set the emission ceiling, and then we can know anything above the ceiling, then the carbon tax will come into place as a penalty to the polluters. “So, we’re not looking at this year for the carbon tax,” he said. On exemptions under the Clean Air Regulations, Arthur said industrial plants would only be considered for extensions if their operators could demonstrate concrete efforts to adopt the necessary technologies. He said the ministry would not issue further blanket exemptions, adding that operators whose existing exemptions expire by January next year would need to demonstrate progress towards compliance. He said 2030 remained the final deadline for all industries to achieve full compliance. “We had the Clean Air Regulations, which came into force in 2014, where plants, factories are not allowed to pollute above the 600 milligram per cubic meter…that was the regulation set…however, they’ve been enjoying exemptions up to this year. “So when I came in as the Minister, I decided that I will not be issuing any more exemptions because the technology is available, the technology is accessible and if we are to meet our target of net zero emissions by 2050, we need to have all this in place and we definitely need the cooperation from the industries as well,” he said. Arthur said operators would still be given sufficient time to conduct feasibility studies and carry out necessary modifications, but they would have to demonstrate meaningful progress to qualify for any temporary extension. The session, titled “Building A Resilient Malaysia: Environment, Climate And Our Future”, was moderated by Malaysian National News Agency (Bernama) chairman Datuk Seri Wong Chun Wai. Also present were Bernama chief executive officer Datin Paduka Nur-ul Afida Kamaludin and members of the local and foreign media based in Malaysia. - October 5, 2026 The post Carbon tax deferment gives NRES time to finalise regulatory, policy framework: Arthur appeared first on Scoop.

artigo.texto: Tecnologia criada na FEEC utiliza células cilíndricas, eletrólito aquoso e circulação interna por turbina, elimina mangueiras e bombas externas e pode evoluir para sistemas estacionários de armazenamento conectados à rede Pesquisadores da Faculdade de Engenharia Elétrica e de Computação da Unicamp (FEEC) desenvolveram uma nova arquitetura de bateria de fluxo voltada ao armazenamento estacionário de energia em larga escala, com aplicação potencial em sistemas associados à geração solar e eólica. A solução chama atenção por abandonar parte da configuração tradicional dessas baterias. Em vez de placas empilhadas, mangueiras e bombas externas para movimentação do eletrólito, a tecnologia desenvolvida na Unicamp utiliza eletrodos cilíndricos, células seladas individualmente e uma pequena turbina instalada dentro da própria bateria. - Brasil já tem 35 GW em energia eólica, concentra 90% das turbinas no Nordeste e agora enfrenta o gargalo que pode limitar a expansão até 2035 - China coloca em operação nova unidade de 660 MW em Zhongwei para dar estabilidade a base de 13 GW de energia renovável no deserto de Tengger e levar eletricidade até Hunan - Europa inaugura complexo híbrido com 242 MW de energia solar e bateria de 773 MWh na Bulgária e prepara expansão com mais 250 MW em turbinas eólicas - Nordeste já produz energia solar e eólica para exportar ao restante do Brasil, mas expansão esbarra em falta de armazenamento, gargalos na transmissão e impactos sobre fauna, flora e comunidades Nos ensaios realizados em laboratório, o equipamento alcançou aproximadamente 400 ciclos de carga e descarga, além de cerca de 98% de eficiência de carga e 82% de eficiência energética. O projeto nasceu no grupo Brazilian Renewable Energies (BREnergies) durante o doutorado do engenheiro eletricista João Pedro Aguiar dos Santos, sob orientação de César Pagan e coorientação de Hudson Zanin, ambos da FEEC. A arquitetura já resultou em um pedido de patente depositado no Instituto Nacional da Propriedade Industrial (INPI), com estratégia conduzida pela Agência de Inovação Inova Unicamp. Eletrodos cilíndricos substituem pilhas de placas Nas baterias de fluxo convencionais, os eletrodos normalmente são organizados em placas empilhadas. O eletrólito circula por tubos e mangueiras ligados a bombas externas. Essa arquitetura funciona, mas aumenta o número de conexões hidráulicas e, consequentemente, os pontos em que podem surgir falhas ou vazamentos. A proposta desenvolvida pela Unicamp parte de outra geometria. Cada célula é selada individualmente e utiliza dois eletrodos posicionados de forma concêntrica: um deles forma um anel maior, enquanto o outro ocupa a região interna. Essas células podem ser ligadas em série sem necessidade de formar uma pilha convencional. A mudança não é apenas geométrica. Ela altera também a maneira como o eletrólito se movimenta dentro do sistema. Pequena turbina dentro da bateria elimina bombas e mangueiras externas Um dos diferenciais centrais da tecnologia está no sistema de circulação interna. Uma pequena turbina instalada dentro da própria bateria movimenta o eletrólito. Com isso, o projeto dispensa parte das bombas e tubulações externas utilizadas em sistemas convencionais. A ideia é reduzir componentes hidráulicos e simplificar a arquitetura. Esse foi também um dos maiores desafios do trabalho. Segundo João Pedro Aguiar dos Santos, a equipe não encontrou equipamentos comerciais capazes de atender à configuração pretendida. Foi necessário construir praticamente toda a estrutura experimental. “Durante os estudos, percebi que não existia nenhum tipo de design ou setup experimental que pudéssemos comprar para montar a bateria. Isso foi um grande desafio, porque tivemos que montar desde as células até os reatores maiores para fazer os experimentos no laboratório.” O pesquisador também destaca que o desenvolvimento exigiu conhecimentos de diferentes áreas. “Foi um sistema multidisciplinar, unindo engenharia mecânica, eletrônica e eletroquímica, e tivemos que construir tudo do zero.” Bateria chegou a aproximadamente 400 ciclos sem aditivos Nos testes de carga e descarga, a bateria de fluxo giratório chegou a aproximadamente 400 ciclos sem a utilização de aditivos no eletrólito. Segundo os pesquisadores, esse desempenho superou referências de sistemas semelhantes avaliados sob condições comparáveis, que alcançaram cerca de 100 ciclos. Um dos problemas encontrados nesses sistemas é o crescimento de dendritos. Essas estruturas podem se formar durante os processos eletroquímicos e, em determinados casos, provocar curto-circuitos e comprometer a bateria. No protótipo da Unicamp, o ensaio não terminou por falha eletroquímica. A interrupção ocorreu devido a uma limitação mecânica no anel coletor responsável pelo contato elétrico do eletrodo interno. Esse detalhe importa porque indica que a limitação observada não estava diretamente relacionada à química da bateria. A próxima etapa será justamente aprimorar esse componente. Pesquisadores querem superar 3 mil ciclos A equipe trabalha agora com a perspectiva de melhorar a durabilidade do sistema. Além da mudança no mecanismo de contato elétrico, o projeto prevê a utilização de aditivos no eletrólito. A expectativa dos pesquisadores é superar 3 mil ciclos de operação. Nos testes já realizados, a bateria apresentou aproximadamente 98% de eficiência de carga e 82% de eficiência energética. Em uma demonstração prática, o sistema conseguiu operar durante duas horas alimentando LEDs e um ventilador. O objetivo dessa etapa ainda não era demonstrar uma aplicação comercial em grande escala, mas verificar o comportamento integrado da bateria durante a operação. Sistema eletrônico acompanha até pH e formação de dendritos Os pesquisadores também precisaram criar um sistema próprio de gerenciamento. A solução reúne uma placa eletrônica e software responsáveis por acompanhar diferentes parâmetros durante o funcionamento. Entre eles estão: - tensão; - corrente; - tem

artigo.texto: Data Center Power Demand to Grow 24% Annually by 2030: McKinsey Power constraints are pushing operators toward on-site generation, but uncertainty beyond 2030 raises questions about how much infrastructure to build. Data center electricity demand could grow at a compound annual rate of 24% through 2030, but the availability of power infrastructure will determine how much computing capacity developers can bring online, according to McKinsey’s Global Energy Perspective 2026. The projection places data centers among the most consequential sources of new electricity demand while highlighting uncertainty over how that demand will evolve beyond the decade. For developers, the immediate challenge is securing sufficient power to meet computing requirements. Longer-term investment decisions must also account for improvements in AI efficiency and the possibility that demand develops differently than anticipated. “From now to 2030, our most likely scenarios all have power supply lower than IT compute demand,” Sam DeFabrizio, a partner at McKinsey, told Data Center Knowledge. Power Supply Sets the Pace McKinsey’s projections combine monthly tracking of CPU and GPU purchase commitments and hyperscaler capital spending announcements with assessments of how quickly power infrastructure can be delivered. On the supply side, the model considers interconnection approvals, permitting, moratoriums, transformer lead times, and the availability of turbines, reciprocating engines, and fuel cells. Engineering, procurement, and construction capacity is another limiting factor. Faster expansion would require improvements across those constraints, rather than a stronger demand for computing alone. DeFabrizio said greater construction and turbine manufacturing capacity, alongside faster interconnection approvals and permitting, could allow power supply to grow more quickly than expected. Conversely, limited construction capacity or stronger-than-expected efficiency gains could pull electricity demand below the baseline. Those gains could come from AI models, data center buildings, or greater flexibility in when computing workloads consume power. The report’s broader conclusion is that inexpensive generation cannot support electrification unless transmission, storage, and reliable capacity are ready to deliver it. On-Site Generation Adds Speed and New Bottlenecks Developers seeking faster access to power are turning to gas engines and turbines, fuel cells, and battery storage. Those options can reduce dependence on utility construction schedules, but they introduce infrastructure requirements of their own. “Natural gas is often viewed as the fastest path to adding firm power capacity and generation, but competition for pipeline infrastructure could cause delays in building gas-powered generation,” DeFabrizio said. That applies to both generation supplying the grid and facilities operating behind the meter. Projects requiring redundant pipeline connections to meet reliability requirements face additional complexity. Locating closer to gas-producing basins can reduce the need for new pipeline infrastructure, DeFabrizio said. Securing rights-of-way for pipeline construction can otherwise be difficult within the short development schedules that operators are targeting. Battery storage offers another way to manage electricity costs and improve flexibility. However, DeFabrizio cautioned that storage introduces reliability trade-offs when not paired with generation. Grid Connections Still Matter On-site power does not necessarily mean a permanent departure from the grid. DeFabrizio said more than 60% of operators now view their strategy as combining on-site generation with grid access. “Eventually, many data centers that build on-site generation will retain it post-grid connection, becoming flexible grid assets,” he said. Under that approach, generation initially installed to power a facility could later provide backup and occasional support once utility service becomes available. Running those assets less frequently could reduce local emissions while preserving reliability. DeFabrizio said he also expects a more diverse supply mix beyond 2030. Growing demand and additional grid connections could support expanded solar and wind development, sometimes paired with batteries or other storage technologies. Integrating data center loads into the wider system, he argued, provides opportunities to spread the benefits of investment beyond individual campuses. Planning Beyond the Current Boom For data center developers and utilities, an approach considering multiple energy futures will become particularly important after 2030, when the demand pipeline is less certain. DeFabrizio suggested developers align capital deployment with indicators of market evolution, negotiate contractual protections with creditworthy customers, and maintain a portfolio of power solutions that can support the grid. He noted community engagement also belongs in that planning process, emphasizing the need to ensure local benefits outweigh potential burdens, alongside managing construction, contractual, and demand risks. From DeFabrizio’s perspective, it will be critical for developers to secure scarce power quickly enough to meet near-term computing demand while retaining options if efficiency improvements or changes in AI adoption alter the longer-term outlook. “The leaders across the value chain will likely be those who combine early access to scarce power resources with thoughtful risk management,” he said.

artigo.texto: Kinesis, a specialist project developer in the field of renewable energy, and NEDE, a developer of hybrid and sector-coupled energy projects, are planning the Afferde-Ost wind and solar park in Hameln-Afferde for the hybrid generation of renewable energy. At the end of September 2026, the Hameln City Council’s Administrative Committee approved the drafting of a project-specific local development plan for the project; the Afferde Local Council and the Hameln Urban Development Committee had previously also unanimously welcomed the project. About the planned Hamelin-Afferde hybrid energy site At the “Unter dem Schecken” site, a hybrid energy park is to be built, comprising two wind turbines with a hub height of 199 metres and a combined capacity of 13.6 megawatts, as well as two photovoltaic fields with a combined capacity of 24 megawatts. To make optimum use of the electricity generated and to buffer peak loads, a battery energy storage system (BESS) is also to be added to the park. The relevant land has been secured by the investors. A company has been set up by the project initiators to handle the project planning and operation. "This means our recently established partnership with NEDE is now gaining momentum," says Dr Janis Meyerhof, Managing Director of Kinesis, with delight. He continues: "The hybrid energy site planned here is very well thought out in its design, which has been approved by the local authorities. The combined generation of green energy from solar and wind power, together with integrated storage, forms a sustainable concept." Evan Gilroy, Managing Director of NEDE, on the project in Hameln-Afferde: “Now that the resolution to initiate the planning process has been passed, the next step is an early stage of public consultation for the preparation of the project-specific development plan. We anticipate that, once the resolution on the planning regulations has been passed, the project can be completed by our partners and ourselves within around 30 months.”

artigo.texto: A capital paulista recebe, entre os dias 6 e 8 de outubro de 2026, a edição de estreia do Data Center World Brasil, conferência internacional voltada à infraestrutura crítica de tecnologia da informação. Conforme anunciado pela organizadora Informa Markets, o congresso ocorre nas instalações do São Paulo Expo, funcionando em paralelo às atividades do evento Futurecom. O encontro reúne mais de 2.500 executivos e cerca de 300 congressistas com o objetivo de discutir os rumos da capacidade de processamento em larga escala no território nacional. Segundo informações divulgadas pela promotora, a agenda prioriza os impactos decorrentes da rápida expansão dos ecossistemas de inteligência artificial sobre a malha operacional brasileira. A programação foi estruturada para contrapor a crescente demanda por poder computacional aos desafios técnicos de suprimento elétrico, conectividade em hiperescala e segurança jurídica. A entidade promotora sustenta que os debates ocorrem em uma conjuntura na qual decisões regulatórias e logísticas moldarão a atratividade do país perante o fluxo global de capital intensivo voltado à computação em nuvem. Competitividade tributária e regime especial para infraestrutura De acordo com a programação detalhada pela Informa Markets, a rodada de abertura do congresso concentra-se nos instrumentos de atração de capital produtivo, com ênfase no debate sobre o Redata — regime especial de tributação formulado especificamente para o setor de processamento de dados. A organizadora aponta que o painel inaugural visa mapear os efeitos dessa política sobre a competitividade fiscal brasileira em um horizonte estimado entre cinco e dez anos. Especialistas escalados para a plenária avaliam como o alinhamento de diretrizes entre o Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) e as alíquotas estaduais de ICMS incide sobre a viabilidade financeira das construções civis e da importação de insumos tecnológicos de ponta. A promotora assinala que a discussão tributária transcende o escopo contábil e assume caráter geopolítico. Países vizinhos na América Latina disputam aportes de provedores globais conhecidos como hyperscalers, tornando a clareza nas regras de incentivo e desoneração de bens de capital um diferencial competitivo relevante. O cronograma do evento prevê a participação de lideranças do Ministério das Comunicações, do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES), da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação (Brasscom) e da gestora Patria Investments para abordar entraves de funding, modelos de garantias e arquitetura de crédito de longo prazo. Restrições energéticas e viabilidade de suprimento elétrico A disponibilidade de potência elétrica desponta como o principal gargalo estrutural identificado pelos organizadores do congresso. De acordo com a Informa Markets, a transição para clusters computacionais dedicados a modelos generativos de inteligência artificial multiplicou o consumo por metro quadrado útil nos centros de processamento. A programação técnica inclui mesas dedicadas à análise da intermitência da matriz limpa, modelos de autoprodução de energia e sistemas avançados de armazenamento para garantir que as instalações sustentem contratos de nível de serviço com operação contínua e ininterrupta. O debate abrange as variáveis determinantes na seleção de sítios imobiliários industriais para a instalação dessas estruturas físicas. Conforme destacam os documentos informativos da organização, contratantes corporativos examinam indicadores de performance que exigem equilíbrio milimétrico entre proximidade dos anéis de transmissão, redundância de subestações e proximidade dos grandes polos consumidores para evitar perdas de transmissão e oscilações de voltagem. A busca por áreas com capacidade de expansão modular de megawattagem tornou-se premissa mandatória nos planos de negócios do segmento. - Segurança de suprimento: análise de interconexões com a Rede Básica do Sistema Interligado Nacional. - Contratos de longo prazo: estruturação de acordos bilaterais de compra de energia renovável certificada. - Sistemas de contenção de falhas: implementação de usinas de geração de backup e módulos de baterias químicas. - Arquitetura de missão crítica: redundância elétrica baseada em tolerância a falhas sem paradas programadas. Transformação da arquitetura térmica e expansão do resfriamento líquido A Informa Markets relata que a evolução de processadores gráficos e aceleradores de tensores provocou uma ruptura nos padrões tradicionais de engenharia predial. O diretor do Data Center World Brasil, Leonardo Benedicto, declarou na apresentação do fórum que a inteligência artificial exige repensar integralmente o ecossistema dos edifícios dedicados, articulando fornecimento energético, controle microclimático e flexibilidade modular para acomodar atualizações tecnológicas contínuas ao longo do ciclo de vida dos empreendimentos. Conforme sustentam os relatórios técnicos que embasam os painéis, a densidade energética por rack ultrapassou patamares históricos, forçando o abandono gradual dos sistemas convencionais de resfriamento exclusivamente por ar comprimido. O congresso programou demonstrações sobre o avanço de soluções de resfriamento líquido direto no chip (liquid cooling ou direct-to-chip) e tecnologias de imersão total. Essa migração técnica reduz substancialmente o indicador de eficácia no uso de energia (PUE), permitindo elevar a capacidade de cálculo instalada no mesmo espaço físico sem sobrecarregar os limites térmicos dos componentes semicondutores. artigo.texto: Yesterday morning we launched our National Data Center Tracker, and within hours we had a major new project to add to it, as well as legislation aimed at preventing projects like it from being built on federal public lands. The ground is moving fast. NPR reported Wednesday that nuclear startup Valar Atomics is proposing a massive data center complex on more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land near Price, Utah. The project, called Project Beehive, would include data centers powered by roughly 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and facilities for storing nuclear waste. According to company documents reviewed by NPR, the reactors would collectively produce around 9.6 gigawatts of electricity for the data centers, plus additional thermal energy for other industrial uses. Utah currently produces around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average, though its peak generating capacity can reach roughly 10 gigawatts during the summer. At almost the same time, Oregon Senator Ron Wyden introduced legislation that would prohibit the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands for new data centers and associated infrastructure nationwide. Project Beehive Valar’s federal proposal is still at the beginning of the process. BLM’s Utah office confirmed to NPR that it has received the company’s application and is reviewing it for completeness. The agency said that if the application moves forward through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, the public will have opportunities to weigh in. Valar is already laying out a timeline. Company documents call for non-nuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. The 9,000-plus acres of BLM land are only part of the project. Utah state records show that Valar also sought a special-use lease covering roughly 640 acres of state trust land in Carbon County. The Trust Lands Administration Board unanimously approved the lease on September 17, according to KSL. The federal application is much larger. Project Beehive would spread across more than 9,000 acres near Price and combine the data centers, hundreds of reactors, nuclear fuel production and nuclear waste storage in a single proposed complex. And we’d already come across Valar before any of this surfaced. We’ve Seen Valar Before Our tracker already contained another Valar project near Green River, Utah. The company had applied for roughly 10,200 acres of BLM land for a data center co-located with small nuclear reactors before deciding not to pursue the site. We kept it in the tracker as withdrawn. That history looks a little more important today. A roughly 10,200-acre Valar proposal near Green River appeared in the federal record and was later dropped. Now another Valar proposal has surfaced near Price involving more than 9,000 acres of BLM land and hundreds of nuclear reactors. The Public Lands Fight Is Already Bigger Than Valar Our Public Lands tracker now has 16 data center sites sitting on land the public owns, each tied to a public document placing it there. South of Boise, Rhea Data’s Blacks Creek Campus would put a four-million-square-foot data center campus on 3,226 acres of BLM land beside Blacks Creek Reservoir. In Nevada, Copia Digital’s Bergen Data Center is proposed on 744 acres of BLM land north of Las Vegas. In Arizona, the Frontier Data Center would occupy 620 acres of BLM land in Pinal County, while the Harquahala Data Center would occupy another 275 acres in Maricopa County. All three remain proposed. The tracker also includes public-land projects that are much further along or have already run into trouble. Townsite Solar 2 outside Boulder City, Nevada was proposed on 89 acres of BLM land about 1.6 miles from Lake Mead National Recreation Area. Its approval was challenged, and BLM later asked the Interior Board of Land Appeals to set aside the agency’s own approval so the application could undergo additional review. Federal land controlled by other agencies is part of the buildout too. The tracker includes proposed or active data center projects at Energy Department sites in Kentucky, Ohio and South Carolina, along with projects on state-owned land and other BLM applications scattered across the West. And the 16 mapped sites still don’t capture everything sitting in the federal pipeline. BLM records also contain applications that don’t yet have enough public location information to map, including a Prometheus Hyperscale proposal in Wyoming involving rights-of-way for a road, telecommunications line and water pipeline, and another Valar nuclear-powered data center proposal in Utah whose public record still doesn’t disclose its size or exact location. The federal push behind these projects is coming from the top. President Trump’s July 2025 executive order directed federal agencies to make appropriate federal sites available for qualifying data center projects, and our tracker shows Interior later telling BLM state directors to identify public lands that could take data centers. Now there’s movement in the other direction. Wyden’s new legislation would prohibit the development, sale or transfer of federally owned public lands for new data centers and associated infrastructure. His office said the bill followed reporting that more than 17,000 acres of public land across Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, Idaho, Wyoming and Utah were being considered for data center development. None of that changes the law today. Valar’s application is still before BLM, the other proposed projects remain in various stages of the process, and Wyden’s legislation has only been introduced. But one day after launching the tracker, there’s already another 9,000-plus-acre project to follow and another major federal response to add to the record. We’ve added Project Beehive and will keep following what happens next. Explore the National Data Center Tracker. Search your ZIP c

artigo.texto: AI Energy Parks: From Speed to Power to Power That Lasts Why This Matters Up to 10 years. That's how long a large new grid connection can take in North America. So developers are chasing time-to-power, and they should be. But a site that gets power first and gets the architecture wrong has only traded one bottleneck for another. Every shortcut taken to energize on schedule becomes technology debt, and the bill comes due when the load changes, the technology moves, and the site has to be rebuilt while the data center is running. The alternative is the AI Energy Park. Think of it as a microgrid built for AI: a large, optimized, behind-the-meter power system designed for the scale, density, and dynamic load of AI data centers. It integrates grid supply, on-site generation, storage, power distribution, and controllable demand into one coordinated, software-enabled campus. But speed to power can’t be the only objective. Sites designed only to hit an energization date lock in today's assumptions: boundaries drawn around the first equipment, bespoke software, interfaces that fit one configuration. Over a multi-decade lifecycle, generation technologies, market rules, utility capacity, and AI load profiles will all change. An AI Energy Park should be treated as long-term infrastructure, not a temporary bridge to utility service. The goal is not to predict the next 20 years perfectly, but to build an architecture that can evolve without costly rip-and-replace cycles. So how do you get both: power on a credible schedule and an architecture built to last? Stop designing every site from scratch. A Repeatable Model for Speed and Certainty Custom designs add engineering effort, integration complexity, cost, and execution risk. They also force each project to repeat key decisions about system boundaries, operations, protection, procurement, and commissioning. Repeatability speeds delivery. Standard power blocks, controls, cybersecurity zones, data structures, and commissioning methods can be validated once and adapted to each site. This allows for earlier procurement and lets engineers focus on site-specific needs. Four principles make that model scalable and future-ready: - Connectivity links assets and systems, reducing integration effort and speeding commissioning. - Interoperability allows systems from different vendors to work together, preserving choice and simplifying expansion. - Visibility gives operators a real-time view of system health, capacity, risk, and performance. - Optimization uses that visibility to balance cost, reliability, emissions, and grid services. Design for Lifecycle Value Over a 20-year horizon, generation technologies, utility capacity, power density, market rules, software platforms, and renewable economics will all evolve. A future-ready design preserves options so the site can respond without rebuilding its core power architecture. That means designing for change through configuration and modular expansion. Standards-based interfaces, clear system boundaries, repeatable building blocks, and shared digital capabilities allow technologies and vendors to change without redesigning the entire system, reduce dependence on any single supplier, and allow capacity to be added as demand becomes firm. The objective is not a static design that is frozen on day one, but a durable framework that can absorb innovation over time. Reliability for AI Workloads A flexible Energy Park can operate in grid-connected, islanded, or hybrid modes; add generation, storage, and renewables without rebuilding supervisory controls; and actively manage demand. For AI workloads, coordinated controls across UPS, batteries, generation, and the grid provide load smoothing and fault ride-through. This protects compute uptime while preventing rapid load changes and grid disturbances from cascading across the campus. Reliability depends on coordinated system behavior, not just redundant equipment. The controls must detect changing conditions, protect critical loads, manage transitions between operating modes, and support predictable recovery. Validated sequences and clear visibility into available capacity help operators act before asset limits become campus-wide disruptions. Value Beyond the Fence Line A well-designed Energy Park can operate as a grid asset rather than an isolated private power plant: a flexible participant that can support both the anchor load and the broader energy system. For utilities, measurable curtailment, load shifting, and self-supply create more flexible interconnection options and can defer infrastructure during constrained periods. For communities, purpose-built infrastructure can strengthen local reliability, support future electrification, and provide measurable grid services. Community acceptance will depend on making those benefits tangible and transparent, while addressing concerns about local cost, reliability, land use, noise, emissions, water, and construction. Where market rules and utility agreements allow, these capabilities can also support demand response, reserve services, renewable balancing, and restoration. These remain secondary; the primary mission is reliable power for the data center. Power That Lasts Speed to power delivers the first megawatt. Power that lasts protects the investment over the decades that follow. A purpose-built Energy Park must absorb volatile AI loads, ride through grid disturbances, adapt as supply options and technologies change, and contribute measurable value beyond the fence line. A repeatable reference design and delivery model is how an Energy Park delivers both: power on a credible schedule, and an architecture built to last. artigo.texto: Council moves to extend Lexington's pause on data center development, restart zoning process In a lengthy public hearing, Council heard from dozens of residents who pressed for more time to get Lexington data center regulations right. Following a lengthy public hearing Tuesday, Lexington’s Urban County Council moved to extend Fayette County’s pause on data center development until October 31, 2027, as the body continues working to regulate them. Spurred on by the sale of a former Lexmark property to a data center developer, Council has spent the last few months studying the facilities, along with their environmental and electrical grid impacts. In June, the body unanimously passed a moratorium – or temporary pause – on their development in Fayette County, effective through October 31, 2026. Council had also directed the Planning Commission to develop a zoning ordinance text amendment (updates to Lexington’s zoning laws) so it could modernize its regulation of data centers. Councilmembers discussed the Planning Commission’s recommendations Tuesday after a public hearing that lasted for several hours and saw nearly 60 residents and individuals sign up to address the Council. From representatives of Lexington’s business community to members of the Bluegrass Democratic Socialists of America, their message was clear: Lexington needs more time to properly regulate data centers, including determining where they should go and what types of restrictions they should have. Most speakers opposed data centers or wanted much stricter limits on the facilities. Many in the room called for a ban on hyperscale data centers (those with an energy capacity exceeding 25 megawatts) and some supported a complete ban on new data centers in Fayette County. Speakers raised several concerns about data centers’ potential land use impacts, from electricity and water consumption to higher utility bills, strains on the electrical grid, noise, pollution, waste heat and potential negative health effects for nearby residents. Representatives of Commerce Lexington, banks, telecommunications companies, and the University of Kentucky stressed that smaller data centers and server rooms already exist in Lexington and support local businesses and institutions here, particularly those that rely on data storage and processing, from hospitals to schools. They cautioned against overly broad restrictions that could hurt Lexington’s economic development. The deciding motions came from District 1 Councilmember Tyler Morton and District 4 Councilmember Emma Curtis. Morton successfully moved to remove most of the Planning Commission’s recommendations for data centers and server rooms from the draft zoning ordinance text amendment (ZOTA), allowing the Council to move forward with its own approach to regulating data centers in Fayette County. Morton had previously questioned the fairness of the recommendations, which proposed allowing smaller-scale data centers in Lexington’s industrial and commercial zones – which are concentrated in District 1 and on the city’s northside. Morton also successfully moved to advance a resolution launching a new zoning ordinance text amendment process that will look at creating a separate zoning category for data centers. The new process will not be under the tight timeline Lexington’s Planning Commission faced to deliver its recommendations to Council, and it will include more opportunities for residents to engage, Morton told CivicLex in an interview after the hearing. Curtis moved to advance a resolution extending the current data center moratorium through to October 31, 2027. Morton and Curtis’ resolutions will move through Council’s regular legislative process, with final votes expected at an upcoming Council meeting.

artigo.texto: Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) has issued an 800 MW/3,200 MWh standalone Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) tender to select Battery Energy Storage System Developers (BESSDs). The projects will be developed under the Build, Own and Operate (BOO) model. It has sought online bids till October 30, 2026. The developer is required to install, operate and maintain the BESS to provide the Buying Entity with the facility to discharge the BESS on an “on-demand” basis. The tender carries an application fee of Rs. 50,000 plus applicable GST, which is to be submitted through NEFT/RTGS transfer to SECI’s account along with the response to the tender. The tender also carries a bid processing fee of Rs. 20,000/MW, plus applicable GST, for the quoted capacity, subject to a maximum of Rs. 20,00,000 plus applicable GST. An Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of Rs. 7,18,400/MW/project is also required, which must be submitted in the form of a Bank Guarantee, Payment on Order Instrument (POI), or Insurance Surety Bond along with the response to the tender. The developer is required to arrange charging power for the BESS project, with at least 51% of the energy used for charging being procured from renewable energy sources. The discharging of the BESS system will be under the scope of the Buying Entity. Scope of Work A bidder is required to submit a single bid offering a minimum cumulative project capacity of 50 MW/200 MWh and a maximum cumulative project capacity of 800 MW/3,200 MWh. The project capacity is to be quoted for four hours of charging and four hours of discharging in one cycle. The procurement would be in energy (kWh) terms. The Buying Entity would schedule the discharge from the BESS for any four hours starting at 17:00 Hrs. on a given day and ending at 11:00 Hrs. the following day. There will be no discharging from the BESS by the Buying Entity between 11:00 Hrs. and 17:00 Hrs. on a day. The Buying Entity would also intimate the hours during which it intends to draw energy from the BESS on a day-ahead basis. It would select the four hours such that there is continuous discharge from the BESS for at least one hour. The BESS would also be designed to provide a maximum of four hours of discharging capacity. The BESSD would guarantee a minimum system availability of 85% monthly. In case of a shortfall, the BESSD shall pay liquidated damages and remit the amount to SECI, which will subsequently remit the amount to the Buying Entity(ies) under the Power Sale Agreement (PSA). The liquidated damages would be equivalent to twice the PPA tariff for the discharge energy that was not made available during the month.

artigo.texto: Raleigh leaders voted to put a pause on developing new, larger data centers for six months, as community advocates push for a 32-month pause to study the impacts and give residents more say. The measure passed in a 7-1 vote, with councilmember Christina Jones voting against the moratorium. A group advocating for a longer moratorium expressed frustration after the moratorium passed, saying it wasn't long enough. Other WRAL Top Stories The moratorium is shorter than the 12-month pause Apex approved in April and the 18-month pause Cary adopted in August. Raleigh’s draft sets aside 60 days for research and drafting rules, followed by 120 days to move proposed changes through the legislative process. Mary Black, who served on Raleigh City Council from 2022 to 2024 and is now a community organizer for the Raleigh Anti-Data Center Coalition, says that leaves too little time to involve people who could live near the facilities. “What we want is transparency and input in the process, and that’s going to take more than six months,” Black said. WRAL contacted Mayor Janet Cowell and every council member on Monday and Tuesday morning to ask why six months was chosen, whether that would be enough time, and whether they would support an extension if new guidelines were not ready. They had not responded as of publication. Why six months? The draft ordinance says Raleigh needs time to address the development, infrastructure, and environmental impacts of larger data centers. It identifies potential concerns, including electricity and water demand, noise, light pollution and heat islands. While Raleigh has general industrial development rules, the draft says it lacks standards specific to larger data centers. It also warns that infrastructure needed to serve those facilities could create significant burdens for the city’s water utility and its ratepayers. During the first 60 days, staff would study impacts, draft proposed changes and examine how other communities regulate data centers. A team of staff experts would coordinate that work. The final 120 days would be used to propose code amendments and follow the legislative adoption process. The draft calls that six-month period necessary to complete the work. It does not explain why Raleigh’s schedule is shorter than those in Cary and Apex. Black said adopting regulations within six months may be possible, but meaningful community engagement would take longer. She said the coalition’s request for 32 months would allow more time for research, rulemaking and public involvement. In September, Cowell told WRAL the pause would allow a conversation about an issue that had become highly emotional. She also said Raleigh wanted to protect residents while preserving its role as a technology and research hub. “This is a tech center,” Cowell said. Neighboring towns have longer timelines Cary unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium Aug. 27 to study power demand and grid capacity, water consumption, noise and vibration, site design and buffering. Staff will provide progress updates, with a decision on an ordinance expected in February 2028. Cary’s schedule includes technical studies, community engagement and regional coordination through spring 2027, followed by draft ordinance review that summer and public hearings and board consideration before a council decision. Apex unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on April 14 after a developer withdrew a proposed data center near the Shearon Harris Nuclear Plant. Mayor Jacques Gilbert previously told WRAL the pause would allow more research into water and electricity use and potential costs to residents. Pushback over neighborhood impacts and transparency Raleigh’s debate follows substantial opposition to a proposed data center near Jones Sausage and Rock Quarry roads in Southeast Raleigh. In August, 30 of the 32 people expected to speak at a public hearing had signed up in opposition, according to a sign-up sheet WRAL obtained. The developer subsequently withdrew its annexation request. Mayor Pro Tem, Jane Harrison, said in August that she wanted residents to better understand the approval process and wanted more notice when larger projects came before the Board of Adjustment. “I just want to make sure that we all understand how this process currently works,” Harrison said. Black said public hearings alone do not provide enough opportunity to reach residents and understand their concerns. She wants council members to engage people where they live, work and play. Supporters point to jobs, tax revenue and innovation Data center supporters say the facilities can generate investment and tax revenue while supporting the technology behind modern services and artificial intelligence. During a recent visit to Duke Energy’s Roxboro coal plant in Person County, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright described data centers as “intelligence factories” and linked their growth to the Trump administration’s economic agenda. “So we can spur economic growth, generate revenues for local communities, drive up wages for workers,” Wright said. “To do that, you need more energy, not less energy.” In a statement to WRAL, the Data Center Coalition, an industry group representing companies including Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta, urged local leaders to pursue regulations instead of moratoriums. “Rather than enacting moratoriums, which will discourage investment and send signals that the community is closed for business, local leaders should work with the industry and all stakeholders to establish reasonable regulatory frameworks that meet the needs of the community without deterring the industry and the benefits it can bring,” said Christy Tarallo, the group’s Southeast director of government affairs. artigo.texto: Romania’s renewable energy associations have called on the country’s energy regulator, ANRE, to slash the required financial guarantee for standalone battery projects sixfold, from EUR 30,000 per MW of installed capacity to EUR 5,000 per MW. They claim the “excessive” guarantee amount hinders investment in energy storage amid increasing flexibility needs. The current regulation, issued by the Romanian Energy Regulatory Authority (ANRE) this summer, treats energy storage projects and new power generation plants equally, despite considerable differences in investment profile, revenue structure, and economic risks, according to the Romanian Wind Energy Association (RWEA) and the Romanian Photovoltaic Industry Association (RPIA), Economica reported. “Independent (standalone) electricity storage facilities have a distinct technical and functional specificity compared to electricity generation capacities. Consequently, the investment profile, revenue structure, and related economic risks differ considerably and require a proportionate approach in terms of the financial guarantee related to the issuance of the establishment authorization,” according to RWEA and RPIA. Battery projects would face a disproportionate financial burden if treated equally as power generation plants The uniform treatment creates an unequal financial burden for standalone storage projects, which may affect their economic viability and create an additional barrier to their development, amid the increased need for flexibility and at a time when more and more investors plan to install large-scale batteries, they claim. The two associations have sent an amendment to ANRE calling for the required financial guarantee for standalone battery energy storage projects to be set at EUR 5/kW of installed capacity, down from EUR 30/kW. Romania has tightened the rules for energy projects in an attempt to filter out “serious” investors from “speculators.” Other measures include raising the financial guarantee for grid connection from 5% of the connection fee to 20% and introducing auctions to allocate grid capacity. Romania’s total battery storage capacity currently stands at about 2.31 GWh and is expected to reach 4 GWh by the end of 2027, according to Economica’s report.

artigo.texto: Finlândia interrompe construção de data centers do Google pelo impacto ambiental De acordo com a Agência de Supervisão Finlandesa, mais de 300 hectares de floresta foram cortados sem avaliação de impacto A Agência de Supervisão Finlandesa (LVV) ordenou nesta terça-feira, 6, que o Google suspenda a construção de novos ‘data centers’ em dois municípios da Finlândia até no máximo 23 de outubro de 2026, à espera de uma avaliação de seu impacto ambiental. Estes projetos fazem parte de um investimento de 13 bilhões de euros (R$ 72,7 bilhões) anunciado na Finlândia, o maior investimento da gigante tecnológica americana na Europa no âmbito da inteligência artificial. Durante uma visita na semana passada à cidade de Muhos, uma jornalista da AFP observou o ir e vir de retroescavadeiras. Em frente à fazenda de um dos moradores com quem conversou, a floresta tinha desaparecido de um terreno adquirido pelo Google. A agência finlandesa de supervisão exigiu, em um comunicado, que sejam suspensas “todas as medidas preparatórias suscetíveis de modificar de forma significativa o meio ambiente no âmbito dos projetos de ‘data centers’ previstos em Muhos e Kajaani”, no noroeste do país. A agência abriu uma investigação pela suspeita de que a empresa Tuike Finland, que representa o Google, cortou mais de 300 hectares de floresta em Muhos sem realizar previamente a avaliação de impacto ambiental. As obras devem ser interrompidas até que seja feita esta avaliação, detalhou a agência. “Entendemos as preocupações expressas e reconhecemos que, neste caso concreto, não estivemos à altura de nossos próprios padrões, que são elevados”, admitiu Sondre Ronander, porta-voz do Google, em uma mensagem enviada à AFP. “Estudaremos as conclusões da agência e seguiremos suas recomendações”, acrescentou. Graças a um clima ameno, uma eletricidade relativamente estável e barata, produzida majoritariamente mediante energia nuclear, além de uma ampla capacidade eólica e hidrelétrica, a Finlândia experimentou recentemente um auge dos investimentos em ‘data centers’. (com AFP)
