artigo.texto: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries The Chinese company is making liquid-solid hybrid cells to pack more power into products like electric cars and cargo ships. WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The company’s semi-solid-state cells could improve safety and offer greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries to power electric cars, boats, and drones. From the EVs that carry commuters home to the ships that transport goods across countries, more and more vehicles around us are powered by batteries. Lithium-ion batteries are commonly used to power personal devices and vehicles today. But as the need for batteries surges, there’s a growing appetite for cells that can store more energy on a single charge. Also, in lithium-based batteries the electrolyte, which facilitates ion transfer, uses a flammable liquid that can create a fire hazard. Several companies, including WeLion New Energy, are working to make solid-state cells, which use a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. This could increase the energy density of batteries, as well as improve their safety. Fully solid-state cells are extremely difficult to manufacture, though. So WeLion currently focuses on developing and producing semi-solid-state cells, which have a part-liquid, part-solid electrolyte. On that front, they have made steady progress. In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack in partnership with Shanghai-based EV-maker Nio, best known for its battery-swapping technology. The pack had an energy density of 360 watt-hours per kilogram (wh/kg), significantly higher than the 200 wh/kg average for lithium-ion packs today. That translated to a range of over 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). However, only about 200 of the battery packs were manufactured due to their high production cost, but they are still being used by Nio, WeLion says. WeLion has also built batteries to power cargo ships and ferries through a subsidiary. And the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density too. WeLion’s engineers made a semi-solid-state battery that achieved a remarkable energy density of 824 wh/kg during testing in 2025, more than three times that of a standard lithium-ion battery available today. Key indicators - Industry: Energy storage - Founded: 2016 - Headquarters: Beijing, China - Notable fact: WeLion’s cofounders include Chen Liquan, a scientist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who led the development of the country’s first all-solid-state battery back in 1988. Potential for impact China emits more carbon dioxide than any other country, and its transportation sector accounts for around 10% of that total. Scaling up the production of safer, higher-capacity batteries could help switch more vehicles away from fossil fuels. Batteries that power electric ships could be especially helpful—the carbon dioxide emissions from vessels that move goods along China’s lakes, canals, and rivers are projected to grow by around 25% in this decade alone, reaching 18.7 million metric tons by 2030. Caveats One big challenge WeLion faces is scaling up production of its semi-solid-state batteries and competing on cost in a crowded battery market. WeLion says that its semi-solid-state batteries are more expensive than conventional lithium-ion batteries made by larger Chinese battery companies such as CATL. And while laboratory tests showing high energy density are impressive, it can be difficult to translate laboratory results to the real world. The company declined to give more details about the experimental results from its 2025 prototype, which it says is far from commercialization. Key details remain unclear, including how many times the cell can be charged and discharged and how capacity degrades over its lifetime. Next steps WeLion plans to bring a new semi-solid-state battery for drones to market with an energy density of 410 wh/kg by the end of this year. It also intends to introduce its first all-solid-state battery for cars in 2027, which is expected to have an energy density of 400 wh/kg. Two inland cargo ships powered by WeLion’s batteries are expected to launch in October 2026 in Huzhou, a city in eastern China. The battery pack of each of these ships will be able to carry nearly 4,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough for them to sail for up to 250 kilometers (155 miles), the company says. Today, WeLion has an annual manufacturing capacity of 11 gigawatt-hours (GWh) spread between four production bases in China. Two additional plants with a combined yearly capacity of 18 GWh are under construction. What’s behind this summer’s heat, and why 2027 could be worse El Niño? Climate change? All of the above? The global gold rush for underground stores of hydrogen fuel continues. But researchers are still sorting out how much of the stuff there is. artigo.texto: Mercado global de baterias avançadas: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de baterias avançadas até 2035: demanda por armazenamento estacionário deve acelerar o crescimento Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Baterias Avançadas, o setor inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta regionalmente mais diversificada. O mercado global de baterias avançadas entra em uma nova fase de expansão e deixa para trás a dependência exclusiva da adoção de veículos elétricos. Passa a operar com uma arquitetura de demanda multipolar, na qual os sistemas estacionários de armazenamento de energia voltados a serviços de rede e à integração de renováveis se consolidam como um pilar estruturalmente relevante e de crescimento mais rápido. À medida que os sistemas elétricos absorvem parcelas maiores de geração renovável variável, a necessidade de capacidade de armazenamento flexível e de resposta rápida redefine prioridades de compra, fluxos de investimento e alocação de capacidade fabril em toda a cadeia de valor. A resiliência da cadeia de suprimentos, e não mais a simples minimização de custos, tornou-se o principal vetor estratégico. Mudanças geopolíticas e de política comercial forçam a reconfiguração do fornecimento de materiais, da fabricação de componentes e da montagem final de células em ecossistemas regionais distintos. A diversificação tecnológica além das químicas dominantes de lithium-ion se acelera, impulsionada pela busca de perfis de segurança superiores, materiais de menor custo e características de desempenho adequadas a aplicações de armazenamento de longa duração. Essa diversificação impõe novos prazos de qualificação e altera a dinâmica competitiva entre fornecedores de tecnologia consolidados e emergentes. A viabilidade econômica dos projetos de armazenamento em baterias já não depende apenas do custo da célula por quilowatt-hora. O custo total do sistema — que abrange componentes de balanceamento, sistemas de conversão de potência, gestão térmica, instalação e operação e manutenção contínuas — é o que agora determina a bancabilidade do projeto e o retorno dos desenvolvedores. Capacidades de integração de sistemas e de controle por software despontam como diferenciais críticos e fontes de margem, abrindo uma brecha entre fornecedores de hardware básico e provedores de soluções completas. Segurança e certificação deixaram de ser meros requisitos técnicos para se tornar pré-condições comerciais centrais, com financiadores e seguradoras de projetos impondo exigências rigorosas a projeto de sistema, testes de terceiros e protocolos operacionais. O cenário competitivo se estratifica em arquétipos distintos: gigantes verticalmente integrados, inovadores tecnológicos especializados, desenvolvedores de projetos e produtores independentes de energia, além de integradores de sistemas e empresas de EPC. O sucesso exige posicionamento estratégico claro dentro desse ecossistema, pois competir em todas as camadas se torna cada vez mais insustentável. Os modelos de compra se bifurcam: o armazenamento em escala de utilidade privilegia a relação direta com fabricantes ou a intermediação de integradores de sistemas, com ênfase em garantias de longo prazo e de desempenho. Este relatório oferece uma análise estruturada e comercialmente fundamentada do mercado global de baterias avançadas, cobrindo a evolução histórica de 2012 a 2025 e cenários prospectivos até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado global de baterias avançadas até 2035 projeta expansão robusta, sustentada pela implantação acelerada de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias para serviços de rede, integração de renováveis e energia de reserva. Com o avanço da participação solar e eólica, riscos de curtailment e preocupações com a estabilidade da rede levam concessionárias e produtores independentes de energia a investir em ativos de armazenamento flexíveis, impulsionando a demanda por soluções de baterias avançadas. Espera-se que o mercado cresça a uma taxa composta de crescimento anual de 18,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 520 em 2035, tendo 2025 como base 100. Essa trajetória de crescimento reflete não apenas o aumento de volume, mas também um deslocamento de valor em direção à integração de sistemas, aos controles por software e às capacidades de armazenamento de longa duração. O cenário-base pressupõe apoio contínuo de políticas públicas a energias renováveis e mandatos de armazenamento nas principais economias, além de melhorias graduais na resiliência da cadeia de suprimentos conforme os ecossistemas fabris regionais amadurecem. O ritmo de crescimento, porém, varia por região e aplicação, com a Ásia-Pacífico mantendo a maior fatia das implantações, seguida pela América do Norte e pela Europa. Espera-se que o segmento de armazenamento estacionário supere a demanda por baterias de veículos elétricos em termos de crescimento relativo, embora este último continue sendo um importante vetor de volume. A diversificação tecnológica prosseguirá, com o lithium iron phosphate e químicas de nova geração ganhando participação em aplicações específicas, enquanto os requisitos de segurança e certificação se tornam cada vez mais rigorosos. A perspectiva de mercado é positiva, mas os agentes precisam navegar por gargalos de cadeia de suprimentos, volatilidade de preços de matérias-primas e cenários regulatórios em evolução para capturar as oportunidades emergentes. artigo.texto: Key points: Will the development of global solid-state batteries use patents as a yardstick to determine the endpoint of each country's technology roadmap? Currently, the global competition is characterised by China leading in quantity, while Japan and South Korea hold key patent positions. China is pursuing a dual-track approach, with solid-liquid batteries already in mass production and all-solid-state batteries catching up; Japan is doubling down on sulphide, South Korea is targeting dual markets, and Europe and the US are adopting technology introduction plus local manufacturing. 2027-2028 is a critical window, with patents, industrialisation speed, and lithium sulphide capacity deciding the outcome. SMM has recently reviewed the future of solid-state batteries and compiled a ten-year outlook series. Using the current development of the lithium battery industry as a reference, especially the intertwined rivalry between LFP and ternary routes, which has written an epic chapter over the years. In the long history of conventional liquid lithium batteries, solid-liquid and solid-state batteries will take the stage, outlining a new generation of high-specific-energy battery world. The ten-year series will be divided into nine parts: introduction, westward movement, industry chain structure, industry-wide involution, Cinderella moment, ternary becoming great again, patent shadow war, investment clock, and conclusion. Introduction: Dreams will surely shine into reality: why we need to re-understand the industrial logic of solid-state batteries - the gap between ideal and reality, and the result is that dreams shine into reality Part 1: Will it replicate the westward movement of liquid batteries: the logic of western concentration - will solid-state batteries replicate the "westward movement" of liquid lithium batteries? Part 2: A good opportunity to correct the distorted power structure of the industry chain: power structure of the industry chain - upstream windfall profits, midstream squeezed, downstream delayed payments? Part 3: Warning of PV-style industry-wide involution: will solid-state batteries enter PV-style industry-wide involution? Part 4: Cinderella's comeback in technology routes: the "Cinderella moment" of solid-state batteries - which technology route will follow the comeback path of LFP? Part 5: Ternary may become great again: can ternary batteries "become great again" with the help of solid-state batteries? Part 6: Global competitive landscape - the "patent shadow war" and industrialisation race among China, Japan and South Korea Part 7: Entering the market early will show you yourself ten years later: investment clock - the "five-stage model" of solid-state battery industrialisation Conclusion: A brand-new track: solid-state batteries are not a "simple sequel" to liquid lithium batteries This article is Part 6 of the series on the global competitive landscape of solid-state batteries - the "patent shadow war" and industrialisation race among China, Japan and South Korea, reviewing the patents of LFP, a process full of twists and turns . China broke through the overseas patent barriers of LFP with a policy package: first, it initiated patent invalidation domestically, and in 2011 declared the core patent of Hydro-Québec invalid, clearing local obstacles; overseas, it broke the deadlock through settlement, licensing and acquisition, such as Dynanonic and Wanrun New Energy obtaining licences from the LiFePO4+C alliance, and Wanxiang acquiring A123 to directly obtain core patents; at the same time, it insisted on original technology, with the team of Chen Liquan from the Chinese Academy of Sciences using sodium doping and other approaches to circumvent the original patents. Finally, it waited for the basic patents to expire in 2017 and the carbon coating patents to expire in 2022, then went global comprehensively with cost and scale advantages, ultimately dominating the global LFP market. Review of the previous article, the sixth of nine articles in the ten-year solid-state battery series: can ternary batteries "become great again" with the help of solid-state batteries? Ternary has been structurally squeezed by LFP in the liquid lithium battery stage, and its share is unlikely to return to the mainstream. Solid-state batteries catalyse its "second positioning": high-nickel ternary and lithium-rich manganese-based materials are naturally compatible with solid-state systems, and solid-liquid batteries provide transitional growth. Scenarios such as eVTOL, humanoid robots, and high-end EVs that have rigid demand for energy density and are price-insensitive will become a solid foundation for the high-end specialised path of ternary. Part 6: Global competitive landscape - the "patent shadow war" and industrialisation race among China, Japan and South Korea I. Patent landscape: the quality gap behind the quantity lead The global competition in solid-state batteries is first and foremost a patent shadow war. The most counter-intuitive feature of this shadow war is that China has already won in quantity, but is still encircled in quality. In March 2026, Ouyang Minggao, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, disclosed at an expert and media exchange meeting of the China EV100 that China's newly published patents for all-solid-state batteries had accounted for 44% of the global total, surpassing Japan to rank first worldwide. China's patent applications in the field of solid-state lithium batteries reached 3,341, ranking alongside Japan (3,225) as the top two globally, each accounting for nearly 20%. But the patent war has never been about who has the thicker stack of documents. On indicators that better represent the quality of technological innovation, the landscape reverses. artigo.texto: SOUTH BRUNSWICK, N.J. — Intense backlash facing the Princeton Nurseries Data Center grew after plans for 20 diesel-fueled generators were raised at a contentious air pollution permit hearing. As a result, the public comment period for the permit has been extended until Nov. 9 — a permit which claims that the twenty generators to be placed in the data center are “minor sources” of pollution despite pushback from residents. The backlash follows an ongoing lawsuit in South Brunswick against the data center’s development, and several other townships in the state banning data centers completely. At the center of the backlash is a 341,000 square-foot data center less than a mile from University research facilities. In 2024, Princeton University sold 143 acres of its Princeton Nurseries site for nearly $22 million to WRV Nurseries South Brunswick Owner, LLC, a company that is now building the data center. The final tenant is unknown, and following the completion of the sale of the property, the University has had “no connection to it since that time,” according to a statement from University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss. Students, faculty, and Princeton residents are now rallying against the construction of the data center, mainly citing potential environmental concerns. Construction for the data center is on track to be completed by the end of 2026. The timeline of the data center The Princeton Nurseries data center sits on a historic site that formerly housed a section of the country’s largest commercial plant nursery, which at its height spanned 1,200 acres across New Jersey. In 1986, Princeton Nurseries and the Flemer Family sold a 271-acre chunk of land to the University, which remained its sole owner until the 2024 sale. The University sold the land to the developmental consortium WRV Nurseries South Brunswick Owner, LLC, and made almost $22 million from the sale. The data center is also known as the Sentinel Data Center, as the real estate company Sentinel will be developing the site. Sentinel did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the ‘Prince.’ This August, a case went to trial over the data center. The lawsuit against South Brunswick Township and WRV Nurseries South Brunswick Owner, LLC was filed by South Brunswick residents Mark and Katherine Smith in 2025 a year after plans for the data center were first announced in March 2024. The Smiths alleged that the process behind the data center’s plan was inconsistent with the Township’s Master Plan — a design document for the whole county used to guide the future physical, economic, and social development of South Brunswick. On Sept. 2, the lawsuit against the data center was ruled in favor of South Brunswick. The lawsuit is currently being appealed and has the potential to stop the construction of the data center, if successful. On Sept. 23, the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection hosted a public forum on an air pollution permit allowing the construction of 20 large diesel-fired emergency generators at the Sentinel site. The meeting did not concern approval for the project, which was already confirmed to proceed in May 2025. “The public has not been properly informed,” Jill Feldman, a Princeton resident, argued to the NJ DEP at the data center’s air pollution permit hearing on Sept. 23. “If the out-of-state corporation didn’t need permission to release particulate matter that is classified as air toxins into the air of Central New Jersey, it’s likely that we and our neighbors would never have known about the construction of this data center,” Feldman said. One comment came from Cyndi Shattuck, a Kingston resident, who said she developed skin cancer as a result of returning to work shortly after 9/11 under the government’s advice. “I’m asking for you to not use all of us as an experiment to see how much we can tolerate before there’s a class action lawsuit. You were supposed to protect us from this,” she said. “What happened in Vineland is embarrassing, and it could easily happen here,” Mary Saudargas, a Princeton resident and a member of Food and Water Action NJ, said at the hearing. On Sept. 22, Gov. Mikie Sherrill issued a $1.07 million fine against a data center in Vineland for violating the Air Pollution Act. “I encourage the NJ DEP to reconsider the models that [it] used for this permit, and reclassify it as a major source of pollution,” Saudargas added. At the Undergraduate Student Government senate meeting on Sunday, the senate passed “A Statement in Opposition to Data Center Development in South Brunswick, N.J.,” which initially scheduled the letter to be sent to the NJ DEP and Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Tuesday. The statement specifically targets the air pollution permit the site needs to install the 20 diesel-fired generators on the site. In addition to concerns from the University community, New Jersey residents and Princeton Municipality officials have also spoken out against the data center. “We strongly urge DEP to take every possible measure to ensure that this data center does not become an environmental blight on our region,” the Princeton Mayor and council wrote in an Oct. 1 statement. Students, faculty, residents speak out Princeton Mayor Mark Freda addressed concerns about air pollution at a Princeton Council meeting hosted on Sept. 28 at a hotel near the data center, stating, “We should officially go on the record and put a comment in also being opposed to this ... Having diesel generators in today’s day and age makes absolutely no sense. They’re doing everything they can to just have the worst air possible.” On Tuesday, David Cohen, a councilmember for the Princeton Council who is currently running for reelection to the Council, said that there was no “need for Council to take action” on the data center at a general candidate forum. “We did … consider passing an ordinance not to have data centers in Princeton” Cohen said. “Land is too expensive in Princeton anyway for anybody to want to buil

artigo.texto: Energia se Torna o Maior Gargalo para a Expansão de Data Centers: Quais Ações de Energia Valem a Pena Acompanhar? A economia da IA depende fundamentalmente de uma infraestrutura física robusta, sendo a energia elétrica o seu principal gargalo estrutural. À medida que o consumo de data centers e a potência por rack aumentam rapidamente, gargalos na geração, transmissão e distribuição elétrica tornam-se restrições críticas para os investimentos. O ciclo de expansão energética da IA abrange desde fontes como gás e energia nuclear até equipamentos de gestão térmica e distribuição, beneficiando fornecedores com pedidos verificáveis e forte capacidade de entrega. A valorização do setor dependerá da superação dessas limitações físicas e da conversão da demanda em receitas reais. TradingKey - Quando o CEO da Nvidia (NVDA) discutiu a inteligência artificial no G20, ele não se concentrou em GPUs ou nos chips mais recentes, mas apresentou uma estrutura mais fundamental: a economia da IA é como um "bolo de cinco camadas", com a energia na base, seguida sequencialmente por chips, terrenos e infraestrutura de data centers que abrigam o sistema, modelos e, por fim, dados e aplicações que geram valor comercial. Essa definição muda a perspectiva sobre os investimentos em IA. A IA não se resume a serviços de software em nuvem, mas é uma cadeia altamente integrada de infraestrutura física: sem energia elétrica estável, acessível e escalável, nem mesmo os chips mais avançados podem ser convertidos em poder computacional. Hoje, o suprimento de energia para data centers está se tornando uma variável crítica para definir se as despesas de capital em IA poderão ser implementadas dentro do cronograma. A Primeira Camada da IA: Por Que a Energia Passou de um Custo para uma Restrição O conceito de Jensen Huang de "energia se transformando em computação" aponta para o fato físico mais simples e frequentemente negligenciado da computação de IA: tanto o treinamento quanto a inferência consomem, fundamentalmente, energia elétrica. À medida que a potência por rack continua a subir, os data centers não são mais apenas grandes consumidores de eletricidade, mas sim novas cargas incrementais que estão reformatando o planejamento das redes elétricas, a matriz de geração e a oferta e demanda de equipamentos em nível regional. De acordo com previsões da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA), o consumo global de eletricidade por data centers deve quase dobrar, alcançando cerca de 945 terawatts-hora até 2030. Projeções de diversas instituições também apontam para a mesma tendência: servidores otimizados para IA estão elevando significativamente a intensidade do consumo elétrico dos data centers. Essa mudança na demanda não se limita ao volume total, estando ainda mais relacionada à sua concentração e velocidade de atendimento — projetos em regiões de alta demanda frequentemente precisam assegurar energia na escala de gigawatts em um ou dois anos, enquanto a transmissão de energia, novas subestações e grandes transformadores normalmente exigem vários anos para serem construídos e entregues. Isso também explica a avaliação enfatizada pelo CEO da Berkshire Hathaway, Greg Abel, de que a energia continua sendo uma "grande limitação" para a rápida expansão dos data centers de IA. Em sua visão, a Berkshire enxerga não apenas um desafio, mas também uma oportunidade de longo prazo, desde que a nova demanda dos data centers não repasse custos aos atuais clientes das concessionárias de serviços públicos e que os locais dos projetos consigam suportar seu impacto sobre recursos públicos, como a água. Energia não é apenas sobre 'geração', é também sobre entregar energia aos racks Nos últimos dois anos, a trajetória de rotação da narrativa de IA nas ações americanas tem sido relativamente clara: chips, servidores, armazenamento, redes e resfriamento líquido ocuparam sucessivamente o centro das atenções no mercado. A singularidade do tema de energia reside no fato de que não se trata de uma escassez cíclica de um componente de hardware específico, mas sim de uma questão sistêmica que abrange a geração de energia, a conexão à rede, a transmissão e distribuição, e o suprimento de energia no nível do rack. À medida que as filas de conexão à rede elétrica se prolongam, alguns hyperscalers começaram a avaliar a geração no próprio local (on-site) ou o suprimento nas proximidades. Turbinas a gás, células de combustível, contratos de aquisição de energia (PPAs) nuclear de longo prazo e armazenamento de energia correspondem a diferentes prazos de entrega, confiabilidade e estruturas de custo. A lógica central que impulsiona seus retornos reside na demanda real dos data centers por energia confiável e um comissionamento mais rápido. A eletricidade gerada também precisa ser transmitida até o campus e, em seguida, convertida e distribuída para servidores e sistemas de resfriamento. Prazos de entrega estendidos para grandes transformadores, equipamentos de manobra (switchgear), disjuntores e equipamentos de subestações tornaram-se restrições rígidas para o comissionamento de projetos. Alterações nos pedidos e nos backlogs de provedores de equipamentos e serviços de engenharia, como Eaton e Quanta Services, são, portanto, vistas pelo mercado como indicadores antecedentes para monitorar o capex de energia para IA. À medida que a potência por rack de IA evolui dos níveis tradicionais para centenas de quilowatts ou até mais, a eficiência no fornecimento de energia e a gestão térmica passam a determinar conjuntamente a capacidade computacional disponível. O suprimento de energia em corrente contínua em alta tensão (HVDC), nobreaks (UPS), armazenamento de energia, transformadores de estado sólido (SST) e resfriamento líquido não são independentes entre si: a cada avanço na densidade computacional, a capacidade de distribuição de energia, o projeto de redundância e a capacidade de dissipação de calor precisam ser atualizados em sintonia. artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov Oligarch Series on Oligarchy and the Historical Economics of Energy Storage Stanislav Kondrashov on oligarchy and energy storage The historical relationship between oligarchy and energy storage can be examined through a recurring economic question: who possesses the infrastructure, technical knowledge, manufacturing capacity, and organizational reach required to preserve usable energy for a later moment? Long before modern batteries, societies developed ways to retain energy indirectly through elevated water, mechanical systems, thermal methods, and other forms of storage. Modern electrical technologies have greatly expanded those possibilities. Key takeaway: energy storage matters economically because it changes the relationship between availability and time. Across history, technologies capable of preserving usable energy have required different combinations of infrastructure, engineering, manufacturing, specialist expertise, and coordination. Those requirements can influence where economic influence becomes concentrated and where new specialized participants can emerge. The Stanislav Kondrashov Oligarch Series examines this relationship without treating storage as a single technological category. Its history is instead a progression of methods for separating two moments that would otherwise need to occur close together: the moment when energy becomes available and the moment when it is needed. That ability has economic consequences. What Connects Oligarchy With the History of Energy Storage? The connection lies primarily in infrastructure, specialization, and scale. Storage technologies can require significant technical capabilities and extensive supporting systems. When those capabilities become concentrated among relatively few economic actors, storage can become part of a wider pattern of concentrated economic influence. The relationship is not automatic. Different storage technologies create different economic structures. Some depend heavily on large infrastructure. Others can operate at much smaller scales. Some require sophisticated manufacturing. Others depend more strongly on engineering, software, installation, maintenance, or integration with existing electrical networks. For this reason, the economics of storage cannot be understood simply by looking at the storage device. The surrounding system matters just as much. Energy Storage Existed Before Modern Batteries The basic principle of storage is much older than contemporary electrical technology. One of the simplest examples involves gravity. Water moved to a higher elevation contains potential energy that can later be converted into useful mechanical or electrical output as it moves downward. Mechanical systems provide another historical model. Energy can be retained through movement, pressure, or physical configuration and released later. Thermal storage follows a similar principle through temperature differences. The technologies differ considerably, but they share a common economic characteristic: they create a bridge between availability now and usefulness later. That bridge can be valuable whenever timing matters. Why Does Time Matter Economically? Electricity is unusual because generation and consumption traditionally require close coordination. Storage modifies that relationship. Electricity can become available during one period and contribute to activity during another. The economic importance of this capability becomes clearer when viewed through time rather than through the device itself. Storage can absorb electricity. It can retain it. It can release it later. This sequence creates flexibility. “The economic significance of storage begins with a remarkably simple transformation: something available at one moment can acquire additional usefulness because technology allows its availability to be shifted toward another moment,” Stanislav Kondrashov says. Time consequently becomes part of the infrastructure. Large Infrastructure Historically Favored Concentration Some forms of storage naturally operate at substantial scale. Large installations can require complex engineering, extensive construction, specialized equipment, and long-term maintenance. These requirements can favor organizations capable of coordinating numerous technical and industrial activities simultaneously. That is where the connection with oligarchic economic structures becomes particularly interesting. Economic concentration does not need to originate in the storage technology itself. It can emerge around the capabilities necessary to create and operate the wider system. Engineering expertise may become strategically important. Manufacturing can become highly specialized. Infrastructure can require substantial organizational capacity. Maintenance creates long-lasting technical relationships. The relevant economic structure therefore extends far beyond the physical storage installation. Batteries Changed the Geography of Storage Modern batteries introduced a particularly important characteristic: modularity. A storage installation does not necessarily need to exist at only one scale. Battery systems can appear in relatively compact configurations or become part of much larger electrical installations. This creates a different economic geography. Storage can exist closer to consumption. It can be integrated with buildings. It can support industrial facilities. It can participate within broader electrical networks. Different scales can coexist. That flexibility complicates traditional patterns of concentration. Large organizations may remain important in manufacturing and extensive infrastructure, while smaller specialized firms can participate in installation, engineering, software, maintenance, and technical services. artigo.texto: The U.S. power system ended 2025 with 43.6 gigawatts of utility-scale battery storage online. In just the first six months of 2026, operators added another 8.3 gigawatts, pushing total capacity to nearly 52 gigawatts. Over the prior three years, EIA data shows an annual average growth rate of 70 percent. Few segments of the energy industry are growing this fast, and few are being built on contract templates this unsettled. That gap between deployment speed and legal infrastructure is where the real risk sits right now, for developers, for the utilities and data centers buying storage capacity, and for the lenders financing it. What’s Actually Driving 52 Gigawatts Storage is being built for two different reasons that happen to be converging at the same time. The first is the traditional pairing with intermittent renewables, storage smooths out solar and wind output and lets a project sell power when prices are higher rather than only when the sun happens to shine. The second, newer driver is data centers. Standalone battery projects are increasingly being sited to manage congestion and reliability challenges tied to rapid data center load growth, particularly in interconnection markets that are already constrained. The industry expects roughly 24 gigawatts of new storage capacity in 2026 alone. A meaningful share of that is being financed and sited specifically around data center clusters, with ERCOT’s Dallas and Houston-area projects a leading example, positioned to capture both merchant revenue and behind-the-meter offtake arrangements with co-located facilities. The Revenue Structure Isn’t the Same in Every Market A storage contract that works in one market can be the wrong structure entirely in another, because the underlying revenue mechanics differ by region. ERCOT runs an energy-only market, so a battery there earns most of its money from arbitrage, charging when power is cheap and discharging when it’s expensive, with no guaranteed capacity payment underneath that strategy. California’s Resource Adequacy framework works differently: contracted capacity payments can represent 30 to 40 percent of a storage project’s annual revenue, a floor ERCOT projects don’t have. PJM’s recent capacity price spike signals its own acute need for dispatchable resources, changing the math again. A financing agreement or offtake contract built around one market’s structure doesn’t transfer cleanly to another. The Regulatory Gap FERC Is Still Closing The clearest sign that the legal framework hasn’t kept pace with deployment is a specific finding FERC made about PJM, the grid operator covering all or part of 13 states and the District of Columbia. FERC determined that PJM’s own tariff lacked sufficient rates, terms, and conditions of service governing co-located generation and load arrangements, the exact structure many storage-plus-data-center deals are built on. FERC ordered PJM to file a compliance filing by February 17, 2026, spelling out the specific terms an interconnection customer must follow to serve a co-located load, including how to designate the eligible customer that takes transmission service on the load’s behalf. That’s a regulator telling one of the country’s largest grid operators, mid-buildout, that its existing rules don’t actually cover the arrangements companies are already signing. Storage developers and their counterparties negotiating co-location deals in PJM territory right now are working against a rulebook that was still being written as of early this year. The FEOC Problem Nobody Priced In Two Years Ago Foreign entity of concern restrictions now affect eligibility for the investment tax credit and the Section 45X manufacturing credit that much of the storage industry’s financing model depends on. Battery supply chains run heavily through a small number of international manufacturers, which means FEOC compliance documentation has become a real part of deal timing and cost, not a formality. Industry guidance for 2026 now treats FEOC documentation protocols as something that needs to be ready at signing, not something to work out after a customer relationship is already underway. Companies that priced financing models two or three years ago, before FEOC rules were finalized, are discovering that the compliance framework underneath their tax credit assumptions has changed since the deal was structured. That’s the kind of gap that surfaces during due diligence on a financing round or an acquisition, not before. What This Means for Anyone Building or Buying Storage Four things are worth checking against current deals rather than assuming they were handled correctly when signed. Does the revenue structure match the market the project actually sits in, since an ERCOT arbitrage assumption built into a PJM capacity deal is a mismatch that eventually shows up in the financials. Do co-location and interconnection terms reflect the grid operator’s current tariff, not a template drafted before FERC forced operators like PJM to fill gaps in their own rules. Is FEOC documentation actually in place and current, given how much of the industry’s tax credit eligibility now depends on it. And have safety and siting requirements been checked against the newest state rules, since incidents at storage facilities have pushed several states toward new requirements that can affect permitting mid-project. The Pace Isn’t Slowing Down Nothing in the current data suggests this growth curve is flattening. Illinois enacted a wide-ranging energy law this year addressing battery storage payment structures and consumer protection requirements, one example among several states actively legislating in this space right now, and grid operators including the Southwest Power Pool have separately reformed their own interconnection queue processes to accommodate storage. artigo.texto: The Union Cabinet, an India-based executive body chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has approved the third phase of the Green Energy Corridor, known as GEC-III. Under this scheme, 50 GWh of BESS will be deployed, and INR 50,000 crore (~ $5.19 billion) has been allocated to it. These batteries will be placed at renewable energy generator ends and at other locations of importance for grid flexibility. There, they are expected to ease intermittency, congestion and peak-hour curtailment, and to meet demand during non-solar hours. Alongside the storage, INR 1,36,378 crore (~ $14.15 billion) will be spent on intra-state transmission that is designed to evacuate up to 135 GW of renewable energy. Together, the two components bring the total outlay to INR 1,86,405 crore (~ $19.34 billion), with completion targeted for FY 2032-33. India's Union Cabinet approves 50 GWh of BESS under the GEC-III scheme Under the Green Energy Corridor Phase III scheme, which the Union Cabinet has approved, India will deploy 50 GWh of BESS backed by INR 50,000 crore (~ $5.19 billion). artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 6 de outubro de 2026, às 07:19 As ações da LG Electronics avançaram depois que a companhia fechou um novo contrato plurianual para fornecer sistemas de resfriamento a data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos. A gigante sul-coreana de eletrônicos de consumo vem expandindo rapidamente o negócio de equipamentos de refrigeração industrial, conhecidos como “chillers”, impulsionada pelo boom global de data centers, que aumenta a demanda por soluções eficientes de gestão térmica para infraestrutura de IA. A LG informou nesta terça-feira (6) que sua subsidiária nos EUA firmou um acordo de longo prazo com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia, para fornecer “chillers” a data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. A empresa não revelou o valor do contrato, mas afirmou que o acordo acelera a expansão da LG no mercado global de resfriamento para data centers de IA. Em Seul, as ações da LG Electronics chegaram a subir 8,8% no início do pregão, caminhando para a maior alta diária em cerca de dois meses. A LG disse que, apoiada por vitórias recentes na América do Norte, também está ampliando presença em projetos relevantes de data centers no Oriente Médio e na Indonésia. No início deste mês, a empresa anunciou que vai aumentar a produção de “chillers” tanto nos EUA quanto na Coreia do Sul. A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia para atender à demanda crescente de data centers americanos, com início de produção previsto para o primeiro semestre de 2027. Paralelamente, pretende elevar a produção em unidades já existentes em Changwon e Pyeongtaek, na Coreia. Segundo a LG, as novas encomendas anuais de soluções de resfriamento para data centers podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após a companhia garantir US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A empresa também afirmou esperar atingir antes do prazo a meta de 2027 de US$ 680 milhões em receita no negócio de “chillers”. Fonte: Dow Jones Newswires. *Conteúdo traduzido com auxílio de Inteligência Artificial, revisado e editado pela Redação do Broadcast, sistema de notícias em tempo real do Grupo Estado. Veja também

artigo.texto: A cidade suíça de Laufenburg passou a ocupar posição de destaque num dos maiores projetos europeus de armazenamento de energia elétrica. A iniciativa prevê a instalação de uma gigantesca bateria subterrânea capaz de acumular grandes volumes de eletricidade (mais de 2,1 gigawatts por hora) para utilização em momentos de alta demanda ou instabilidade no sistema energético. O projeto pertence à empresa FlexBase, que aposta na região como ponto estratégico para integração das redes elétricas do continente. Para acomodar a estrutura principal, foi escavada uma enorme área subterrânea abaixo da cidade com cerca de 27 metros de profundidade, criando um espaço planejado para receber equipamentos de armazenamento em larga escala. O empreendimento não se limita apenas à bateria. O plano inclui um centro tecnológico multifuncional de 20 mil m² com laboratórios, escritórios, infraestrutura digital e um centro de processamento de dados voltado à inteligência artificial. Crédito: Divulgação/Flexbase A proposta busca unir tecnologia, eficiência energética e reaproveitamento de recursos dentro de um mesmo ecossistema operacional. O sistema utilizará baterias de fluxo redox, tecnologia diferente das tradicionais baterias de lítio presentes em celulares, computadores e veículos elétricos. Nesse modelo, a energia fica armazenada em líquidos especiais mantidos em reservatórios separados. Crédito: Divulgação/Flexbase Quando necessário, esses líquidos passam por módulos eletroquímicos capazes de converter energia química em eletricidade para abastecer a rede. Uma das principais vantagens apontadas pelos especialistas envolve a durabilidade do sistema e a facilidade de ampliar a capacidade de armazenamento sem necessidade de mudanças estruturais complexas. Crédito: Divulgação/Flexbase Outro aspecto destacado pela empresa responsável está relacionado à segurança. Os líquidos utilizados no processo possuem características menos inflamáveis do que parte das tecnologias convencionais, fator considerado importante em instalações subterrâneas de grande porte. Crédito: Divulgação/Flexbase Além disso, o projeto pretende oferecer respostas extremamente rápidas às oscilações do sistema elétrico europeu, com uma agilidade que viabiliza a injeção ou absorção imediata de carga e estabiliza as flutuações de redes alimentadas por fontes de energia solar e eólica. Crédito: Farah Almazouni/Unsplash A localização escolhida possui importância histórica para o setor energético europeu. Desde o século passado, Laufenburg funciona como um dos pontos centrais de conexão entre redes elétricas de diferentes países da Europa. Essa tradição motivou o plano de conectar a usina à rede nacional de alta tensão por meio da operadora Swissgrid, estabelecendo uma referência de infraestrutura inédita no país. Crédito: Wikimedia Commons/Campiana Nos últimos anos, o avanço das fontes renováveis aumentou a preocupação de governos e operadores de rede com o armazenamento de energia. Como parques solares e eólicos dependem das condições climáticas, tornou-se necessário desenvolver sistemas capazes de guardar excedentes produzidos em determinados horários e redistribuí-los quando o consumo aumenta. Crédito: Pexels/Jakub Zerdzicki Grandes baterias estacionárias passaram então a ocupar espaço estratégico nas políticas energéticas internacionais. A previsão é que a estrutura suíça entre em funcionamento até o fim da década, após investimentos estimados entre 1 bilhão e 5 bilhões de francos suíços financiados pela iniciativa privada. Crédito: Imagem gerada por IA O polo tecnológico planeja abrir 300 postos de trabalho e canalizar o calor residual dos servidores de dados para uma rede de aquecimento doméstico regional, o que deve evitar a emissão de 75 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂) ao longo de três décadas. Crédito: Imagem gerada por IA A iniciativa ganha força em um período de forte pressão sobre o abastecimento e alta nos custos tarifários no continente europeu. A opção por edificar a estrutura em subsolo otimiza a ocupação do espaço urbano da cidade e integra todos os serviços em um ecossistema focado na eficiência. Crédito: Reprodução A evolução da obra acompanha uma tendência de mercados globais que tentam mitigar os desequilíbrios gerados por variações climáticas súbitas na geração. Mesmo em estágio de desenvolvimento, as proporções gigantescas anunciadas para o complexo de Laufenburg já colocam o projeto na vanguarda dos maiores sistemas de armazenamento de energia subterrâneos do planeta. artigo.texto: Energia Mercado de baterias elétricas dispara no Brasil e vendas chegam a 504 MWh em seis meses Por Redação - Em 06/10/2026 às 12:50 PM O mercado brasileiro de sistemas de armazenamento de energia vive um período de forte expansão. Somente no primeiro semestre de 2026, as vendas e contratações de baterias elétricas chegaram a 504 MWh no País, aproximando o setor de um novo recorde anual. Os dados são de levantamento da consultoria Greener. Em 2025, o volume comercializado alcançou 730 MWh, resultado superior ao registrado, de forma acumulada, nos cinco anos anteriores. O avanço ocorre principalmente fora dos grandes projetos de infraestrutura. Sistemas menores vêm ganhando espaço em indústrias, estabelecimentos comerciais, condomínios e residências, muitas vezes associados à geração solar instalada em telhados. Conhecidos pela sigla BESS, os sistemas permitem armazenar eletricidade para utilização posterior e vêm sendo considerados uma alternativa importante para dar maior flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico. Atualmente, a capacidade acumulada de baterias instaladas no Brasil chega a aproximadamente 1,9 GWh. Empresas como WEG e Grupo Moura estão entre as companhias que vêm direcionando investimentos para esse mercado. A trajetória é comparada à expansão da energia solar distribuída. Hoje, o País possui mais de 53 GW de capacidade nesse modelo, que reúne principalmente sistemas instalados em telhados e pequenas unidades de geração. A geração solar centralizada, por sua vez, soma 23,6 GW, de acordo com dados da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). Leilão pode contratar ao menos 8 GWh Paralelamente ao crescimento das instalações menores, o governo federal prepara para dezembro um leilão destinado à contratação de grandes sistemas de armazenamento. A expectativa é de contratação de pelo menos 2 GW de potência, com capacidade para operar durante quatro horas por dia. Na prática, isso representaria cerca de 8 GWh de armazenamento, embora integrantes do mercado avaliem que o volume possa ser ainda maior. O Ministério de Minas e Energia também prevê leilões anuais de reserva de capacidade até 2029, nos quais as baterias poderão disputar espaço com outras tecnologias, como termelétricas, hidrelétricas e usinas reversíveis. Fontes renováveis A ampliação da capacidade de armazenamento ganha relevância à medida que fontes como solar e eólica ocupam uma parcela maior da matriz elétrica brasileira. Como a produção dessas fontes varia de acordo com as condições climáticas, as baterias permitem guardar energia em períodos de maior oferta e disponibilizá-la quando a demanda aumenta. A tecnologia também pode contribuir para reduzir episódios de curtailment, quando usinas precisam limitar ou interromper a geração diante de excesso de oferta ou restrições na rede elétrica. Apesar das perspectivas de crescimento, o leilão previsto para dezembro ainda enfrenta indefinições regulatórias, principalmente em relação à divisão dos custos dos projetos. A atual legislação prevê o rateio entre empresas de geração, modelo que vem sendo questionado por agentes do setor e pode resultar em disputas judiciais. Enquanto essa discussão avança, o mercado distribuído segue puxando a expansão das baterias no Brasil e começa a transformar o armazenamento em uma nova frente de investimentos no setor elétrico.

artigo.texto: China’s next EV power play: Beijing targets solid-state battery scale by 2030 Elon Musk has scale, capital and a global EV brand. China has something harder to replicate: a vast, vertically integrated battery ecosystem now backed by a national plan to push all-solid-state batteries from the lab towards "initial large-scale" use by 2030. Beijing’s latest roadmap aims to extend China’s existing lithium-ion advantage into the next battery era — where longer range, faster charging and safer cells could reset the electric-vehicle race. Get it: Fast, verified news for FREE ... download the Gulf News app — simply click here China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other government bodies issued a 2026–2030 plan that makes battery technology a national industrial priority. It calls for breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials, as well as initial large-scale deployment of all-solid-state batteries by 2030. The roadmap does not merely identify a destination. It targets the technical bottlenecks holding solid-state batteries back: ionic conductivity, battery-cycle stability, electrode-electrolyte contact and manufacturing capability. It also promotes production equipment — including isostatic presses — and calls for industrialisation technologies that can bring costs down while improving consistency. China is also pursuing a broader battery portfolio, centred on lithium-ion cells but supplemented by sodium-ion, lithium-ion phosphate and flow batteries. That matters because the future market will not be exclusively about EVs: the government’s strategy spans grid storage, ships, aviation, low-altitude aircraft, intelligent robots and heavy machinery. Conventional lithium-ion batteries use a liquid electrolyte, whereas a true all-solid-state battery replaces it with a solid material. In theory, this can enable higher energy density, quicker charging, longer service life and a lower fire risk — attributes especially valuable for electric vehicles, aviation and high-performance storage. But the promise remains ahead of mass-market reality. The EV and clean-energy revolutions do not need to wait for solid-state batteries, according to technology disruption think-tank RethinkX. The organisation, co-founded by Stanford University strategist Tony Seba and James Arbib, argues that existing battery technologies are already capable of driving a rapid transformation of transportation and electricity markets. Its thesis challenges the increasingly common industry narrative that solid-state batteries are essential for the next major phase of EV adoption. RethinkX instead points to both lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and emerging sodium-ion batteries as technologies capable of delivering the lower costs and scalability required for mass adoption. LFP batteries have become increasingly important because they avoid cobalt and nickel, are generally safer and offer long cycle life. RethinkX sees the LFP chemistry as particularly important for stationary energy storage, where energy density is less critical than cost, durability and safety. Sodium-ion batteries could further accelerate the transition, Seba has argued. Sodium is more abundant than lithium and does not require some of the critical minerals used in conventional lithium-ion chemistries. Solid-state cells can fail where the solid electrolyte meets the electrodes; they also need much better ionic conductivity, stable interfaces and a manufacturing process capable of producing millions of reliable cells at competitive prices. China’s plan recognises these constraints explicitly. This is why it sets “initial large-scale application” rather than claiming blanket mass-market deployment by 2030. Tesla remains one of the most influential EV companies in the world, but it does not control a national battery supply chain. China does — not through one company, but through a dense network of cell makers, materials processors, EV manufacturers, equipment suppliers, researchers and state agencies. China manufactured more than 80% of the world’s batteries in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). It also accounted for about 85% of global lithium-ion battery production and more than 70% of global electric-car production, giving Chinese firms unmatched scale in materials procurement, cell manufacturing and deployment that competitors are still trying to match, according to the agency. That base gives companies such as CATL and BYD an advantage in testing new chemistries, building pilot lines, securing supply chains and lowering unit costs as production grows. BYD has said it aims to begin mass manufacturing solid-state batteries for EVs by 2030, though it expects the technology to complement — not immediately replace — existing lithium-ion and LFP batteries. The Lion's share of global battery manufacturing in 2025 took place in China, but that didn't happen overnight. It reached this critical level through deliberate government policy, investments, clustering or "hubs" of battery manufacturing sites and ruthless domestic competition. The result: Existing factories, suppliers and skilled labour can speed scale-up. 85% of global lithium-ion production China has experience in high-volume cell production and cost reduction. National 2026–2030 battery roadmap Policy, research, industrial standards and investment are aligned behind commercialisation and exports. Large domestic EV and storage markets Manufacturers can test and deploy new technologies at home before expanding abroad. Creating global champions (including CATL and BYD) China has global-scale battery and EV champions positioned to commercialise breakthroughs, as per the International Energy Agency. Beijing’s plan is a statement of intent, not proof that solid-state batteries have been solved. artigo.texto: Eastern Nebraska village becomes first to permanently ban data centers By Noelle Annonen , Multimedia Reporter Oct. 5, 2026, 6 a.m. · Nehawka, a village in Cass County, recently became the first known village in Nebraska to set in place a permanent ban against data centers. A local leader said the idea might be spreading to other villages. Chad Krueger, co-chair of the Nehawka Village Board of Trustees, said data center developers were seeking to buy up land, and the optioned land was getting closer and closer to Nehawka. “One of our residents said, ‘Maybe we should do something about it,’” Krueger said. Cass County approved a data center moratorium, which is a temporary ban on data centers that will buy the county time until regulations around the projects can be drafted, but Krueger said it doesn’t help Nehawka. Cass County’s jurisdiction only covers up to the edge of Nehawka’s extraterritorial jurisdiction, he said, which includes the village itself and a one-mile buffer zone. This is standard for small Nebraska villages, Krueger said, and the village has zoning authority over what happens within that boundary. “Obviously we could always rewrite our (zoning) code again later in the future,” Krueger said. “But at this point, it’s an all-out-ban of data centers in our territory.” Only one Nehawka resident cautioned the board about broadly banning development, according to Krueger, but the majority of residents who weighed in were all in favor of the plan. “The last thing they wanted was a big data center or a natural resources vacuum near our village,” Krueger said. At least 19 counties now have moratoriums, typically ranging from six months to a year, against data centers. The counties are Box Butte, Butler, Cass, Custer, Dundy, Furnas, Gage, Garfield, Hayes, Harlan, Howard, Johnson, Kearney, Logan, Otoe, Rock, Saline, Seward and Sioux Counties. Other counties have drafted regulations controlling how data centers will interact with their natural resources. For instance, Buffalo County approved data center regulations in August and required any development that uses water for cooling to use a closed-loop system. This addresses a common concern that data centers continually pull from the regional water supply, with some fearing that a center could take up to 5 million gallons a day. Closed-loop systems will still use water for cooling but only take in water one time and recycle it. Lincoln County also approved regulations in August, following a controversial denial of a moratorium. These regulations require closed-loop or recycled-water cooling systems as well as protections for public power customers by prohibiting any costs associated with electric service to the data center from being passed on to residents. Noise pollution, electricity use, protection of wildlife and especially water resources were all key factors for Nehawka residents, Krueger said. “Nehawka has been in a slight drought for a good while now,” Krueger said. “We have ponds that used to exist around our village that no longer exist because the water table has dropped down so far the springs don’t feed (them) anymore. Our villagers are always concerned with water and with our natural resources.” Krueger said the village has been getting calls from village clerks across the state looking for information on Nehawka’s ban. L. Lynn Rex, executive director of the Nebraska League of Municipalities, said her organization is unaware of any villages outside of Nehawka banning data centers.

As contribuições poderão ser apresentadas entre 8 de outubro e 9 de novembro. A principal questão em discussão é a forma de distribuir os custos da contratação. Em parecer elaborado em agosto, a área técnica da agência apontou como alternativa preferencial o rateio do encargo entre todos os geradores de energia elétrica, com valores diferentes conforme o Índice de Flexibilidade (IF) de cada usina. Pelo modelo proposto, os geradores com maior flexibilidade arcariam com 25% do encargo, enquanto aqueles com menor flexibilidade pagariam 100%. Para a área técnica, essa opção oferece o “melhor equilíbrio” entre a finalidade do encargo, a estabilidade do custeio, a objetividade técnica e a viabilidade regulatória. A definição desse mecanismo ocorre em meio a uma controvérsia sobre o rateio. Há projetos de lei no Congresso que pretendem derrubar a previsão de distribuição dos custos. A Lei nº 15.269/2025, que trata da modernização do setor elétrico, estabeleceu que as despesas relacionadas à contratação de baterias sejam rateadas exclusivamente entre os geradores de energia elétrica, sem participação dos consumidores no financiamento. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O modelo em análise poderá ser aplicado aos sistemas de armazenamento que forem contratados nos dois leilões de baterias previstos para dezembro de 2026, descritos como inéditos. Relator do processo, o diretor Gentil Nogueira afirmou que a proposta corresponde à chamada “norma perene”. Caso seja aprovada, ela poderá servir de referência para definir o custeio dos sistemas de armazenamento contratados no leilão previsto para dezembro. Nogueira destacou, porém, que o edital do próprio leilão ainda precisa ser aprovado e poderá estabelecer regras específicas para o custeio. artigo.texto: LG lands multibillion dollar deal to cool North American AI data centers LG Electronics will supply chillers for 5 gigawatts of AI data center capacity under a long-term agreement with U.S.-based AIR Control Concept. From top left, Don Kwack, chief executive of LG Electronics' North America; James Lee, president and head of LG Electronics' Eco Solutions business; and, from bottom left, Chris Ahn, president of LG Electronics USA’s Air Conditioning Technology division, and Hayden Bland, president of AIR Control Concept (AIR), and other AIR executives pose for a photo at the signing ceremony for a long-term chiller supply contract between LG and AIR. The location and date of the photo are unspecified. LG ELECTRONICS LG Electronics has won a long-term contract to supply chillers for AI data centers (AIDC) in North America, with a total capacity of 5 gigawatts. The company's U.S. subsidiary said Monday that it recently signed a long-term supply agreement with AIR Control Concept (AIR), a North American infrastructure platform company. The contract value was not disclosed, but an LG Electronics spokesperson said it was worth several trillion won, or several billion dollars. LG will supply chillers and other cooling equipment in phases for AIDCs totaling 5 gigawatts. AIR designs and builds data centers in the United States and Canada and also handles public procurement and aftermarket services. It executes large projects through its data center subsidiary, AIR Mission Critical, and counts major data center operators worldwide as clients. LG said the long-term contract, which guarantees large volumes, shows that its products meet the technical and reliability standards of hyperscale data centers. Cooling has become one of the main constraints in building AI data centers. AI servers rely on high-performance GPUs, which consume far more power and give off far more heat than conventional servers. Overheated chips slow down or fail, which is why chillers are a central piece of equipment in most data center cooling systems. Traditional data centers mostly use air cooling, which blows cold air across the servers. As power density per rack rises, air alone is often not enough, and operators are increasingly adding liquid cooling, which brings cold water or other coolant close to the chips to absorb heat directly. In such systems, a coolant distribution unit (CDU) manages the flow and temperature of the coolant that reaches the chips. LG and AIR are discussing expanding the supply to include CDUs. LG is also broadening its portfolio to cover thermal management for both air and liquid cooling. The cooling business is expected to grow as AI drives demand for more data center capacity. Worldwide data center power capacity is expected to grow by 108 gigawatts in a single year, from 226 gigawatts in 2026 to 334 gigawatts in 2027, according to market researcher Omdia. LG's AIDC cooling orders topped 600 billion won ($446.4 million) in the first half of this year, and the company expects cumulative orders to reach several trillion won by year-end. It also expects to reach its target of 1 trillion won in chiller sales ahead of the original schedule of the end of 2027. LG began supplying and installing cooling equipment this year for a large North American AIDC project it won last year. It has also won deals for major data centers elsewhere in the world, including the Middle East and Indonesia. "Based on our differentiated technologies, including high-efficiency chillers and high-performance liquid cooling solutions, and our experience supplying rapidly expanding large-scale data centers, we will lead the global AIDC cooling market," said James Lee, president and head of LG Electronics' global heating, ventilation and air conditioning and AI data center thermal management operations. BY LEE JAE-LIM [lee.jaelim@joongang.co.kr]

artigo.texto: Governor and Representatives Ocasio-Cortez and Ryan Hold Roundtable in Dutchess County With Farmers and Community Stakeholders To Discuss Impacts of Potential Data Center Development Governor Highlighted Key Policies from Data Center Moratorium and AI Safety Regulations Governor Kathy Hochul and U.S. Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan today toured Fishkill Farms, a family-owned, multigenerational farm in East Fishkill, Dutchess County and held a roundtable discussion with several local farmers, advocates and businesses to discuss the impacts of hyperscale data centers. Today’s discussion highlighted New York’s nation-leading moratorium on hyperscale data center construction, which is helping to protect local communities amid concerns over water and land use, energy costs, and proposed data center development, including in East Fishkill. New York State is experiencing an unprecedented surge in proposals for data center development driven by artificial intelligence and other computing operations that could require massive amounts of energy and water to run and cool thousands of computer servers. This summer, Governor Hochul signed an Executive Order hitting pause on new hyperscale data center development. This action has temporarily paused discretionary State environmental permits for up to one year in order to build a regulatory framework that will protect ratepayers, the environment, the energy grid and communities across the state. By pausing discretionary state environmental permits for new hyperscale data center construction for up to one year and imposing strict new rules that hold data center developers accountable and ensure benefits for local residents, Governor Hochul’s moratorium is addressing the ongoing concerns being raised by communities statewide. “As artificial intelligence grows more powerful and transforms our world as we know it, I’m standing up for New York’s farmers, small businesses and families — ensuring they aren’t left behind,” Governor Hochul said. “I enacted a nation-leading data center moratorium to protect our communities and hold developers accountable because I believe New Yorkers deserve a say in the decisions that affect their future. I’m proud to stand with Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pat Ryan as we deliver a government that’s committed to fighting for working families across New York.” Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, “Across the country, Silicon Valley billionaires are trying to impose data centers on communities that don’t want them. Today, Governor Hochul, Representative Ryan, and I heard directly from Hudson Valley farmers on the impacts these data centers have on the farming communities in New York State. This is a fight that transcends so many of the divides in our country right now because we’re all united in putting our community ahead of corporate profits. From our town boards, to the Governor’s nation-leading moratorium, to urgently needed action at the federal level, we’re going to continue our fight to ensure that we the people are the ones to decide what happens in our lives and in our communities.” State Senator Michelle Hinchey said, “Tech companies are racing to profit off the AI boom, building data centers wherever they can and leaving communities to bear the costs through increased pressure on water supplies, energy infrastructure, and utility bills. artigo.texto: PIERCE TOWNSHIP, Ohio — A new data center proposal in Pierce Township turned what was scheduled to be a regular Zoning Commission meeting into an hour-long referendum on how the controversial facilities should be regulated Tuesday. People packed the Locust Corner Elementary School gymnasium to get their turn telling Zoning Commission members what they'd like to see done to limit the potential impact on utility rates, water consumption, noise levels, lighting and more. To get inside, just about everyone had to pass through a net of Pierce Township residents passing out fliers against them being welcomed to town. Kathy Cummins told us she was against the facilities being built in Pierce Township for many reasons, but the location of Crane Data Center's 300-acre proposal directly across US 52 from the now-closed Walter C. Beckjord Generating Station, still contaminated with toxic coal ash, was the most concerning. "That's what makes this site particularly challenging," Cummins told us before the meeting began. WATCH: Pierce Township residents pack a meeting on data center rules with a proposal looming A Crane representative told us after their presentation to Pierce Township Trustees that they had considered building on the Beckjord site, but ruled against it due to the ongoing contamination. We asked another member of the group passing out fliers, Bruce Cummins, what he thought about a deal allowing Crane to move in if they agreed to clean up Beckjord. "If the site was remediated, the coal ash was removed, I think that's a different conversation," he said. Bob Hucker told us he attended the meeting because he was against any new large-scale data center construction. "People need to know about this," Hucker said. Zoning Commission Chairman Jeff Stitt told the crowd before public comment began that they have been tasked with establishing data center rules for the entire township, and no official application had been submitted. Therefore, he said there was no specific project they could address directly. When asked about Crane's proposal, Stitt said that was not a formal submission they could review. "There is no one who has submitted an application, so there is no area planned," he said. "That was just an area someone expressed concern in." That sentiment was echoed weeks earlier when Pierce Township Trustee Allen Freeman talked with our I-Team. "It's basically a sales pitch, but it was not a proposal. It wasn't a zoning request. It doesn't even rise to that level, so we're not entertaining it," he said. At Tuesday's meeting, Freeman pledged transparency as the Zoning Commission built data center regulations and the trustees considered them. "This stays open. This stays transparent. Anything that we discuss, you're not going to see an NDA (non-disclosure agreement) that's going to block it," he said. Stitt urged patience as the process could take months to complete. "We don't want to make a snap decision because we live here," he said. Pierce Township has a moratorium on data center construction through May 31, 2027. Stitt said if the rules aren't prepared by the time the moratorium expires, it could be extended. Click here to see Crane's full presentation.

artigo.texto: The Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI) has issued a Request for Selection (RfS) for setting up 800 MW/3,200 MWh of standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) under tariff-based competitive bidding. The tender, identified as SECI-ESS-IV, is aimed at strengthening India’s energy storage capacity and supporting the reliable integration of renewable energy into the power system. The RfS, issued on October 1, 2026, carries tender reference number SECI/C&P/IPP/15/0010/26-27 and ISN-ETS Tender Search Code SECI-2026-TN000032. The projects will be developed under the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model and will supply stored electricity on an on-demand basis. SECI will act as the Intermediary Procurer under the arrangement. It will enter into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with successful BESS Developers and subsequently sign back-to-back Power Sale Agreements (PSAs) with the Buying Entities. The selection process will follow a single-stage, two-envelope e-bidding system, followed by an electronic reverse auction. The BESS projects will be technology-agnostic and can be connected to the Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) or State Transmission Utility (STU) network. For ISTS connectivity, the minimum voltage level is 220 kV. Developers will also be required to ensure that at least 51% of the energy used for charging the storage system is sourced from renewable energy. A single bidder, including its group companies, can bid for a minimum capacity of 50 MW/200 MWh and up to the entire tendered capacity of 800 MW/3,200 MWh. The minimum project size is therefore set at 50 MW/200 MWh. The tender requires bidders to submit an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of ₹7.184 lakh per MW per project. Selected developers will be required to provide a Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG) of ₹17.96 lakh per MW before signing the PPA. Permitted security instruments include bank guarantees, Payment on Order Instruments from PFC or REC, and insurance surety bonds, subject to the tender conditions. The RfS document carries a non-refundable fee of ₹50,000 plus GST, while the bid processing fee is ₹20,000 per MW, capped at ₹20 lakh, plus GST. Successful BESS Developers will also be required to pay a success charge of ₹1 lakh per MWh plus GST and a payment security deposit of ₹5 lakh per MWh. The PPA will have a tenure of 20 years from the Scheduled Commissioning Date (SCD) or full project commissioning, whichever is later. Developers must obtain final connectivity at the selected substation with a start date on or before April 30, 2027. The projects are required to achieve 100% financial closure four months before the SCD. The full project capacity must be commissioned by April 30, 2027. Part commissioning is allowed in up to three installments, with the first installment requiring at least 50 MW capacity. Micro and Small Enterprises with valid Udyam registrations have been exempted from document fees, bid processing fees, and EMD. All bidding submissions and e-reverse auction activities will be conducted through the ISN-ETS portal. Discover more from SolarQuarter Subscribe to get the latest posts sent to your email.

CATL also said the platform is designed to support a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometer service life for heavy-duty truck applications. Cooperation with DHL Group CATL said it also signed a memorandum of understanding with DHL Group at the show. The companies plan to develop green freight corridors across Europe and work with vehicle manufacturers and other partners on electric-vehicle pilot deployments.
