artigo.texto: UKIAH, CA., 10/6/26 — Mendocino County’s ban on new data centers will run until August 2028, with an exception about the size of a shipping container. The ban was put in place while a committee works with staff on a permanent ordinance that would govern how and whether the county permits data centers in the future. Supervisors voted 4-1 Tuesday to extend the moratorium they adopted Sept. 1 by 22 months and 15 days, to Aug. 21, 2028, the longest stretch state law allows. They also narrowed the terms. As Supervisor Ted Williams described the change to the board, facilities that draw less than 3 megawatts of electricity are no longer subject to the moratorium. The ad hoc committee of Williams and District 3 supervisor John Haschak met with county staff over lunch, worked out the change, and the board adopted it the same afternoon. Supervisor Maureen Mulheren voted no, calling the threshold “not fully developed.” “This idea that we’re having three megawatts coming up during a meeting as a path forward,” she said, was something she would’ve wanted staff and the community to work out first. The first version of the moratorium, a 45-day urgency ordinance, was set to expire Oct. 16. Deputy County Counsel Matthew Kiedrowski told the board the next meeting would’ve fallen outside the 45-day limit. Why 3 megawatts Williams, reporting for the board’s two-supervisor ad hoc committee of Haschak and himself, said 3 megawatts is roughly what PG&E will deliver through standard service before a project needs its own transformers or a substation. “3 megawatts would allow a data center the size of a shipping container,” he said. The point, he said, was to let local businesses use small data projects without tripping over the ordinance while the county spends the next 20 months writing a permanent rule, and still keep out “gigawatt-size facilities.” Richard Angley, the interim director of Planning and Building Services, said he believed the ordinance his staff has been drafting uses 20 megawatts as a threshold, a figure drawn from other jurisdictions. “The three megawatts came up today,” he said. Supervisor Madeline Cline said she was “not particularly in love with this arbitrary setting” of a number, but preferred allowances to a blanket ban. Williams, who proposed the figure, said it was “still somewhat arbitrary.” The board took the item up at 9:33 a.m. and couldn’t finish it before lunch break. Williams and Cline wanted a power threshold so telecommunications facilities wouldn’t be caught by the ban. Mulheren said she wouldn’t vote for any megawatt figure that day. “I do not know what that should be,” she said. “From a politics standpoint, a ban on data centers is great politics,” Cline said. As actual policy, she said, a flat-out ban is problematic. A two-year clock The board also asked whether two years was too long. Interim CEO Sara Pierce said Planning and Building is short-staffed and anything sooner than two years “would be stretched.” Later in the same discussion, senior planner Mark Cliser said the permanent ordinance “is just about done,” and a first draft could reach the Planning Commission in six or seven months. However, in the afternoon, Angley said 10 months was possible “in an absolute perfect world,” but “the likelihood of that is very slim.” Supervisor John Haschak said these things can take a while, explaining that the county has worked on an ordinance for low-intensity camping, the Hipcamp model, for about five years and still doesn’t have one. Adam Gaska, executive director of the Mendocino County Farm Bureau, told the board the bureau opposed the blanket ban. “We believe a ban is a knee-jerk reaction stemming from fear and not out of a real and actual present threat,” he said. Eileen Russell of Mendocino Forest Products, who asked the board in September to leave room for a data center at the Ukiah sawmill, said in the morning that “people have stopped the conversation” about investing here since word of the moratorium got out. In the afternoon, after the 3-megawatt change, she said a data center the size of a storage container is “not really allowing the type of development or innovation that could take Mendocino Forest Products into the next generation.” She described a power plant burning forest residuals next to the sawmill, selling its power to a data center. Doug Stewart, president of the Anderson Valley Winegrowers Association, said he wanted a limit, not a two-year moratorium. After the change, he said it “did address what I came here to discuss.” Dolly Riley, chair of the Redwood Valley Municipal Advisory Council, supported the full extension. “Mendocino County does not have the water to spare,” she said. What else changed over lunch The lunch rewrite made two other changes. The ordinance had exempted ordinary office, retail, school, hospital and industrial computer equipment. Williams said that under that wording a large retailer could have built a data center for its own operations. That exemption is gone. Hospitals and healthcare facilities are now exempted as public safety and emergency facilities, and the requirement that those be owned and operated by a public agency was dropped, because the county’s hospitals aren’t. The ordinance doesn’t name a project. It says the county “anticipates receiving” inquiries and applications. The moratorium can end sooner than 2028. Kiedrowski said the board can terminate it once it adopts a permanent data center ordinance. Haschak moved the amended ordinance with two conditions: a report back to the board every four months, and a new ad hoc committee to work with staff on the permanent ordinance. Chair Bernie Norvell named Cline and Williams to it. Mulheren said she assumed that committee would take up the question she voted no over. “If three megawatts is too small, what isn’t too small?” she asked.

artigo.texto: The second-generation BYD Seagull (or ‘Dolphin Surf’ in the UK) has been unveiled in China with a raft of major changes, including a rear-mounted 127bhp motor, a 94-litre frunk, and rumoured compatibility with BYD’s ultra-rapid Flash charging network. New BYD Dolphin Surf exterior design The BYD Dolphin Surf’s design has undergone several key changes, and it now has a more grown-up appearance than the outgoing car. While the Dolphin Surf’s upright stance remains, BYD appears to have introduced a set of new front headlamps, along with a less angular front bumper, a new tailgate, a rear diffuser, and a roof spoiler. In line with the Chinese Government’s ban on flush door handles, these have been replaced by semi-hidden mechanical units. The 16-inch, four-spoke alloy wheels and 205/60 R16 tyres are also new, giving the Dolphin Surf a wider, more purposeful stance. In general, BYD’s designers have toned down the previous version’s wedgy, unorthodox design. Interior design Inside, the changes continue. The previous BYD Dolphin Surf’s unorthodox air-conditioning controls have been replaced by a more conventional, physical button arrangement in the centre of the dashboard beneath the air vents. The infotainment screen is now fixed, and a lightbar runs the width of the cabin. Based on images issued by BYD in China, the material quality used throughout appears to be vastly superior to the first-gen car, as do the screen’s graphics. A two-spoke steering wheel, plus an optional massaging driver seat is a new addition, too. New BYD Dolphin Surf tech and performance BYD has tweaked the new Dolphin Surf’s underpinnings and has replaced the supermini’s rear torsion beam with an independent, multi-link setup. In the Chinese market, power is up by almost 50% from 73bhp to 127bhp. Paired with BYD’s decision to move the electric motor from the front to the rear axle, the extra horses should make the new Dolphin Surf more engaging to drive than its predecessor. This configuration change also brings it closer to its main rival, the rear-wheel-drive (RWD) Geely EX2 supermini, which is China’s best-selling car. Test versions of the new Dolphin Surf have been spied charging at BYD’s ‘Flash’ charging stations, prompting suggestions that it will be compatible with the company’s 1,500-kilowatt charging network. BYD, however, still has to confirm full battery specs, charging rates, and times. Other test cars in China have also been seen fitted with a roof-mounted LiDAR pod supporting BYD’s God’s Eye B, Level 2 driving-assistance package, which introduces automated highway and urban navigation, lane-change assist, obstacle avoidance, and automated parking. Pricing For now, the new BYD Dolphin Surf is only on sale in China, where pricing has yet to be confirmed. Given the new tech and technical changes, it is expected to cost more than the current model’s 69,900 – 85,900 yuan (around £7,900 to £9,700) price tag. With BYD currently the second most-popular carmaker in the UK, the new Dolphin Surf is expected to arrive here soon. EV Powered has reached out to BYD UK for confirmation and an arrival date. Pricing for the current model starts at £21,975 for the entry-level ‘Boost’ trim, and increases to a Renault 5-bordering £23,975 for the range-topping Comfort.

artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series on the United States and the Evolution of Energy Storage Stanislav Kondrashov on American Style energy storage The relationship between the United States and energy storage stretches across several generations of technological development. Long before contemporary battery installations became part of the electrical landscape, American engineers and industries were already exploring ways to preserve usable energy through mechanical, gravitational, thermal, and electrochemical methods. Electrification gradually gave storage a different role: it could become an active component of increasingly complex electrical networks. Key takeaway: the American history of energy storage is fundamentally a history of timing. Generation and consumption do not always occur at the same moment, and storage creates a technological bridge between them. As American electrical infrastructure expanded, that bridge became increasingly sophisticated, combining physical equipment with manufacturing, electronics, software, monitoring, and specialized engineering. The Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series examines this progression as more than the history of the battery. Energy storage includes several technological families. What connects them is a simple objective: retain useful energy in one form and make it available later. That principle has remained remarkably consistent even as the technologies surrounding it have changed. How Did Energy Storage Develop in the United States? Energy storage in the United States developed alongside industrialization and electrification, progressing through mechanical systems, elevated-water methods, electrochemical batteries, thermal techniques, and increasingly sophisticated electrical storage installations. More recently, electronics and software have added a digital layer to storage infrastructure. The historical sequence was not a straight replacement of one technology by another. Different storage methods solved different problems. Some were suited to large infrastructure. Others became useful in relatively compact applications. Modern electrical networks can contain several approaches simultaneously. This diversity is central to understanding the American storage landscape. Storage Began With a Problem Older Than Electricity The fundamental challenge of storage predates electrical networks. Energy may become available at one moment but become useful at another. Mechanical systems provided early answers. A moving component could preserve kinetic energy. Compressed systems could retain energy for later release. Elevated water could preserve potential energy through gravity. Thermal methods could retain useful differences in temperature. These approaches differ technically, but each introduces flexibility between availability and use. That flexibility became increasingly important as industrial systems grew more sophisticated. Electrification Changed the Storage Question Electricity introduced a distinctive challenge. Electrical generation and consumption need close coordination. As American electrification expanded, engineers needed increasingly sophisticated ways to manage changing patterns of demand and generation. Storage offered one possible response. It could absorb electricity at one moment and make electricity available at another. The significance of this capability increased as electrical networks became larger. “The history of storage becomes especially revealing when electricity enters the picture, because engineers are no longer thinking only about preserving energy; they are also thinking about how timing can become an active part of an interconnected electrical system,” Stanislav Kondrashov says. Storage was becoming part of network architecture. Elevated Water Introduced Storage at Large Scale One historically important approach uses gravity and water. Electricity can be used to move water upward. The elevated water represents stored potential energy. When electricity is needed later, the water can move downward through generating equipment. The concept is straightforward. Its implementation requires substantial engineering. Reservoirs, turbines, pumps, electrical equipment, transmission connections, and monitoring systems must operate together. This illustrates an important feature of energy storage history. Storage is rarely just the medium retaining energy. It is the complete system that makes storing and recovering that energy practical. Batteries Created a Different Kind of Flexibility Electrochemical storage changed the possibilities considerably. Batteries could be manufactured as discrete units. They could be installed in different places. They could operate across different scales. They could serve applications far removed from large gravitational infrastructure. This introduced modularity. Modularity is historically significant because it allows capacity to be assembled from multiple units rather than requiring every storage installation to follow a single physical model. As manufacturing developed, batteries became relevant across an expanding range of applications. Portable Storage Changed Everyday Technology One important chapter in American storage history occurred far from large electrical infrastructure. Portable batteries allowed electrical energy to travel with devices. This changed the relationship between electricity and location. An electrical product no longer always needed an immediate connection to fixed infrastructure while operating. Stored electricity could accompany the device. That principle became increasingly important as electronics expanded into professional and everyday activities. Portable storage therefore represents another historical dimension of the American relationship with energy storage: mobility. artigo.texto: Cisco's Jeetu Patel: AI Agents Are Coming, and Data Centers Are a National Security Issue Jeetu Patel is bullish on AI, especially AI agents. He also thinks the technology brings real national security stakes. Patel is Cisco's president and chief product officer. He was in Austin for WebexOne, Cisco's major user conference, where the company showed off its next wave of AI tools. Cisco has a significant presence in Austin, including an innovation hub. "One of the most seismic shifts in history" Patel says AI is moving fast. He believes it can help solve some of the world's biggest problems, including disease, poverty, and education. "This technology is one of the most seismic innovations and shifts that we have experienced in the history of humanity," Patel said. "But it also has a meaningful amount of risk that we have to make sure that we mitigate." His outlook is optimistic, with a clear view of the downsides. "I am, on balance, a net optimist," he said. "I feel like this is going to be one of the most amazing technologies that allows us to do things we could never dream of doing before. But I don't wear rose-colored glasses." ALSO| This vest simulates getting shot in the line of duty so officers can train for it before What are AI agents? Patel says the next big wave is AI agents. These are tools that take on tasks, make decisions, and do more work on our behalf. Cisco sits on the front lines of cybersecurity, and Patel says the company is working to reduce the risks that come with that shift. As agents get more powerful, he says, they create new challenges. One is network strain. "Agents consume about five times more network bandwidth for conducting the same exact task as a human does," Patel said. The data center debate Data centers have become a hot topic across Texas. Patel says the stakes go beyond the economy and changing the landscape. His warning is that if the country does not keep up with demand for computing power, it could face a national security problem as AI agents and bad actors multiply their capabilities. "You're going to have trillions of agents around the world, and they can start attacking critical infrastructure if we're not careful," Patel said. "That could cost lives. The only way you can defend against it is by making sure that your defenses are also at machine scale." Machine-scale defense takes computing power, and computing power takes data centers. "So I feel like for the safety and security of humanity, data centers are actually a very essential ingredient," he said. "It's not something that's an elective that we can either choose to do or not do, because it actually won't keep us safe." Texas and the AI buildout Patel says Texas is well positioned for the AI buildout. He adds that the country as a whole will need more power, computing capacity, network bandwidth, and security to keep pace.

artigo.texto: Micron versus SanDisk: À medida que o boom dos data centers de IA continua a se aquecer, qual ação de memória é a melhor compra? A expansão global de data centers impulsionada pela inteligência artificial impulsiona o superciclo de memórias, beneficiando fabricantes do setor. A Micron Technology destaca-se pela diversificação e portfólio full-stack (DRAM, HBM e NAND), oferecendo maior estabilidade e previsibilidade de receitas através de acordos estratégicos. Em contrapartida, a SanDisk atua focada exclusivamente em NAND, apresentando alta alavancagem operacional e sensibilidade direta às flutuações de preços. Enquanto a Micron atrai investidores em busca de segurança e resiliência estrutural, a SanDisk atrai aqueles dispostos a assumir maiores riscos cíclicos em troca de elevado potencial de valorização. TradingKey - A expansão da infraestrutura de IA nos EUA está entrando em uma fase de crescimento sem precedentes. À medida que as empresas de tecnologia continuam a expandir a capacidade computacional para atender às crescentes demandas por treinamento, inferência e cargas de trabalho de agentes de inteligência artificial, tanto o número de data centers de grande escala quanto os volumes de investimentos planejados vêm disparando conjuntamente. De acordo com um relatório do The Kobeissi Letter, os EUA contam atualmente com aproximadamente 90 data centers operacionais com capacidade de energia superior a 100 megawatts, atingindo uma máxima histórica; se todos os projetos planejados atualmente se concretizarem, esse número poderá chegar a cerca de 280 até 2030. Dados de mercado mostram que a expectativa é de que as empresas de tecnologia invistam cerca de US$ 7 trilhões em data centers até 2030; Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet e Meta assinaram mais de US$ 1,5 trilhão em contratos de aluguel de data centers desde o início do boom da IA, incluindo compromissos que ainda não entraram em vigor. O alcance dos projetos de construção há muito tempo ultrapassou os próprios provedores de nuvem hyperscale, com empresas de semicondutores, equipamentos de rede, servidores, energia, sistemas de resfriamento e operadoras de data centers expandindo a capacidade para atender a demandas computacionais cada vez maiores. Na cadeia de suprimentos de data centers de IA, o armazenamento é um elo insubstituível. Os aceleradores de IA exigem memória de alta largura de banda para transferência de dados, enquanto os sistemas de treinamento e inferência precisam de DRAM de alta capacidade e SSDs corporativos para armazenar modelos, dados e resultados intermediários. Entre elas, a Micron (MU) atua nos segmentos de DRAM, HBM e NAND; já a SanDisk (SNDK) aposta principalmente em memória flash NAND e armazenamento para data centers corporativos. Ambas as empresas se beneficiam da demanda por armazenamento para IA, mas o que os investidores realmente precisam avaliar é: esta é uma plataforma diversificada mais adequada para alocação ou uma ação cíclica pura de NAND com maior elasticidade? Qual é o papel da Micron e da SanDisk na cadeia de armazenamento de IA? A Micron é uma das principais fabricantes de chips de memória do mundo, adotando um modelo IDM verticalmente integrado com um portfólio de produtos que abrange DRAM, HBM e NAND. DRAM e HBM atendem principalmente a servidores, aceleradores de IA e computação de alto desempenho, com a HBM impactando diretamente a eficiência da transmissão de dados de GPUs; já a NAND é mais utilizada em SSDs corporativos, dispositivos clientes e outros equipamentos de armazenamento. A SanDisk, por outro lado, é uma fabricante focada exclusivamente em NAND (pure-play) que voltou a ter ações negociadas de forma independente após sua cisão da Western Digital, focando em SSDs corporativos, armazenamento para data centers e armazenamento na borda (edge). A empresa garante seu suprimento de wafers por meio de um sistema de fabricação em joint venture com a Kioxia, combinando-o com encapsulamento e testes internos, controladores e soluções de produtos para formar um modelo de fabricação de "wafers em joint venture + produtos proprietários". Em comparação com a abordagem IDM full-stack da Micron, a SanDisk carrega um encargo de despesas de capital relativamente menor, mas sua concentração de negócios é maior: a precificação da NAND, a demanda de clientes corporativos e os pedidos de data centers determinarão de forma mais direta o seu desempenho financeiro. O superciclo de memória de IA pode durar? A chave está na oferta, não apenas na demanda O mercado agora já aceitou de forma ampla que a IA impulsionará uma maior demanda por memória e armazenamento, mas o que realmente determina a sustentabilidade dos lucros das duas empresas não é o número de data centers em si, mas se a oferta de armazenamento conseguirá acompanhar o ritmo em tempo hábil e se a nova demanda poderá se traduzir em condições contratuais e de preços favoráveis. A lógica de oferta da Micron está mais voltada para produtos de ponta. HBM, DRAM para servidores de IA e SSDs corporativos de alta capacidade impõem exigências mais elevadas em tecnologia de processo, encapsulamento, validação e colaboração com clientes, levando a ciclos mais longos de expansão de capacidade. A empresa revelou ter assinado diversos acordos estratégicos com clientes que cobrem cerca de 20% das remessas de DRAM e aproximadamente um terço das remessas de NAND, com alguns acordos incluindo compromissos financeiros por parte dos clientes. Se esses acordos forem executados conforme o planejado, a visibilidade da receita futura da Micron poderá ser superior à dos ciclos tradicionais de memória, embora ao custo de exigir investimentos de capital iniciais significativos. As principais mudanças da SanDisk residem em sua estrutura de clientes e modelos de contrato. A proporção da receita proveniente de data centers cresceu rapidamente, e oito acordos NBM oferecem suporte de base para as remessas futuras. artigo.texto: Cabinet Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Deborah Barasa speaking during the launch of the Kenya Guide for Strategic Engagement in Carbon Markets 2026./KNA Kenya has moved to strengthen its participation in global carbon markets with the launch of a new guide aimed at attracting high-integrity climate investments while protecting communities, ecosystems and the country’s national climate targets. Cabinet Secretary for Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Deborah Barasa said the Kenya Guide for Strategic Engagement in Carbon Markets 2026 would provide a framework for ensuring that carbon-market investments generate genuine environmental benefits and lasting value for Kenyans. The guide was officially launched in Nairobi on Monday in the presence of Environment and Climate Change Principal Secretary Dr Eng Festus Ng’eno and senior representatives from Switzerland, South Korea, the European Union, the United Kingdom and Norway. Barasa said the guide marked a critical milestone in making Kenya’s engagement in carbon markets more strategic, transparent and aligned with national interests. “Kenya is open to responsible and high-integrity carbon investment. We are seeking quality, integrity and lasting development value,” she said. She noted that carbon markets presented a major opportunity to mobilise private capital into renewable energy, forestry, agriculture, waste management and clean cooking, while creating jobs, supporting innovation and facilitating technology transfer. However, she cautioned that such investments must not come at the expense of communities or the environment. The guide is expected to provide greater clarity and predictability for investors, project developers and communities, while complementing ongoing reforms, including the establishment of the National Carbon Registry and strengthening of Kenya’s legal framework for implementing Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Barasa called for partnerships that deliver measurable climate benefits, strong environmental and social safeguards and equitable sharing of benefits generated by carbon projects. She said the government’s priority was now to translate the new policy framework into concrete action and position carbon markets as a credible pathway towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient and inclusive economy. Environment and Climate Change Principal Secretary Dr Eng. Festus Ng’eno said Kenya was moving beyond viewing carbon markets as a future opportunity and was positioning itself as a key player in shaping the emerging global carbon trading system. “For years, carbon markets were discussed as a future opportunity. That future is now here,” Ng’eno said, noting that international trading frameworks under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement were becoming operational. He said the new guide would strengthen Kenya’s strategic, transparent and high-integrity participation in international carbon markets. A key provision of the guide is a 10 million-tonne cumulative ceiling for international transfers of carbon dioxide equivalent between 2025 and 2030. Ng’eno said the ceiling would help safeguard Kenya’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets and minimise the risk of the country overselling its carbon credits. He said Kenya’s carbon-market strategy was anchored on four principles: predictability, uncompromising integrity, putting people before carbon, and creating value beyond carbon. Under the framework, carbon projects will be expected to provide tangible benefits to local communities through equitable benefit-sharing, technology transfer, skills development, employment and local value creation. The government said the approach would ensure that carbon markets contribute to national development without undermining Kenya’s climate commitments or the rights and livelihoods of communities hosting carbon projects. The launch brought together Switzerland’s Ambassador to Kenya Mirko Giulietti, South Korean Ambassador Kang Hyung-shik, EU Deputy Ambassador Ondrej Simek, British Deputy High Commissioner and Development Director Diana Dalton, and Norwegian Minister Counsellor and Deputy Head of Mission Christian Gahre. Kenya is now expected to focus on implementing the new framework as it seeks to attract climate finance while maintaining strong safeguards against environmental degradation, inequitable benefit-sharing and risks to the country’s carbon budget.

artigo.texto: Amazon to invest $1B into data center communities amid backlash against data center rollouts Published 3:03 pm Monday, October 5, 2026 NEW YORK — Amazon is investing more than $1 billion over the next five years into communities where it operates data centers for education, job training, water and energy preservation projects and other local priorities as it reacts to a growing backlash from politicians and consumers to the tech industry’s rollout of the massive buildings. According to a blog post on Friday by Matt Garman, Amazon’s CEO of its cloud computing arm, Amazon has already spent more than $1 billion in communities with a large data center presence over the past three years. Garman also said that Amazon is no longer using nondisclosure agreements with government agencies it works with on its projects, and it said it hosts open houses in communities where it operates to share information about what it’s doing. He also warned against the spread of what he believes is misinformation about data centers’ impact on the environment and energy rates — and he cited the dangers of over 100 moratoriums against these centers being considered across the country. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” he wrote. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position. There is urgency to this data center build out because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security.” Garman’s pledge comes as data centers, which power artificial intelligence and cloud computing, have become a hot political issue heading into the midterms as tech giants race to invest more money in expanding these infrastructures. Small, under-the-radar data centers have been around for decades. But the explosion of artificial intelligence chatbots has resulted in data centers that are bigger than anything just about any town has ever seen. Some of them dwarf football stadiums and factories and consume more energy than small cities. By 2030, data centers will account for nearly 3% of the world’s projected electricity use, with 935 trillion watt-hours, according to a United Nations University report released in June on these buildings’ environmental footprint. Amazon said in July that it now expects to spend $220 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, including on data centers and other technology investments. That’s up from its prior estimate of $200 billion. President Donald Trump has embraced the building of more data centers, but there is growing wariness from voters. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans. And a majority of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.

artigo.texto: A diretoria da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) decidiu, nesta terça-feira (6/10), abrir consulta pública de 30 dias para o aprimoramento da proposta de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), na modalidade de reserva de capacidade. A consulta ficará aberta de 8 de outubro a 9 de novembro de 2026. A área técnica da agência apontou, em parecer de agosto, que a melhor alternativa para os custos da contratação de baterias é o rateio entre todos os geradores de energia. Contudo, a proposta é que o pagamento seja modulado em função do chamado Índice de Flexibilidade (IF). Com esse critério, aquelas usinas com maior flexibilidade pagariam menos (25% do encargo), enquanto aquelas com menor flexibilidade pagariam 100%. A alternativa, ainda de acordo com a área técnica, apresenta o “melhor equilíbrio entre aderência à finalidade do encargo, estabilidade do custeio, objetividade técnica e viabilidade regulatória”. O tema é controverso, especialmente porque há projetos de lei no Congresso buscando derrubar essa previsão de rateio dos custos. A Lei nº 15.269/2025, de modernização do setor elétrico, previu expressamente que os custos decorrentes da contratação de baterias sejam rateados apenas entre os geradores de energia elétrica, excluindo a possibilidade de custeio pelos consumidores. Os dois leilões de baterias, inéditos, estão previstos para dezembro deste ano. O diretor Gentil Nogueira, relator, comentou que a proposta em discussão trata da “norma perene”, que, se aprovada, poderá ser utilizada para o custeio dos sistemas de armazenamento que devem ser contratados no leilão de baterias marcado para dezembro. No entanto, ele salientou que o próprio edital do leilão, ainda a ser aprovado, pode trazer disciplina para esse custeio específico. O edital precisa ser aprovado até o fim de outubro, de maneira a cumprir a regra de publicação com 30 dias de antecedência. Por Renan Monteiro e Luciana Collet

artigo.texto: Data Centers: Dalton Utilities details water usage, power costs, citizens repeat pause request Published 3:01 am Wednesday, October 7, 2026 City officials said Monday night that work is continuing behind the scenes to examine issues surrounding data centers and other large power users, while Dalton Utilities offered new details about the financial safeguards and revenue associated with serving the rapidly growing industry. The discussion came amid repeated calls from some residents for the city to impose a six-month moratorium on new data center development while it considers regulations specifically governing the facilities. Before the public comment portion of Monday’s meeting, Mayor Sams said city staff are continuing work the council has requested involving large power users. “I want to make [clear] that our staff are continuing to work on doing their due diligence as we have asked of them as it relates to large power users, which would include but not be limited to data centers,” Sams said. Sams did not announce a decision on a moratorium or a data center-specific ordinance. City Administrator Andrew Parker said he had invited Dalton Utilities CEO John Thomas to speak because of the amount of public comment council members have heard about data centers during recent meetings. Parker cautioned that the utility’s role represents only one part of the broader discussion and that some issues surrounding large power users and data centers fall outside Dalton Utilities’ purview. “We’ll continue to provide more information as we move forward,” Parker said. Water use Thomas addressed water use, electricity supply and rates, financial protections for other utility customers and revenue generated by data center customers. On water, Thomas said the large data center being developed in Whitfield County is being built with a closed-loop cooling system in which water is initially added and then recirculated rather than continuously replaced. Thomas said some water can be lost through evaporation or other means but said the amount is expected to be small. “It’s not expected to use really much more water than a restaurant, two restaurants or so that you might think of around town,” Thomas said. Thomas also said Dalton Utilities has water capacity available because its industrial customers now use about one-third as much water as they once did. Power and protecting other customers Thomas said Dalton Utilities has always purchased some of its electricity from the regional wholesale market and has never supplied its entire electric load solely from resources it owns. As population, manufacturing and other economic activity grow across the Southeast, increased demand can constrain that regional market and put upward pressure on wholesale electricity costs, he said. Thomas emphasized that electric providers do not all have the same mix of owned and purchased power and therefore may experience those pressures differently. When Dalton Utilities serves a data center directly, Thomas said, the utility uses several measures intended to protect its other customers from financial exposure created by the enormous electric loads involved. Data center customers are subject to what Thomas described as exceptional deposit requirements. They also pay a fixed monthly demand charge tied to the amount of electric capacity available to them, regardless of whether they use that full capacity during a particular month. Dalton Utilities’ largest data center customer is treated differently still. Thomas said the customer is billed weekly for electricity rather than monthly and maintains a prepaid account. Each week, the customer pays for the amount of electricity Dalton Utilities expects it to consume during the following week. Data center customers also pay upfront for local infrastructure Dalton Utilities must construct to connect their facilities to the electric grid, Thomas said, rather than leaving the utility to recover those costs through rates over time. Millions in revenue Thomas also put numbers Monday night to the financial benefits Dalton Utilities says data centers provide. According to Thomas, the utility’s two largest data center customers generated just under $5 million in state and local sales tax revenue in 2025. Data center revenue has also substantially increased the amount Dalton Utilities transfers annually to the city’s general fund, according to Thomas. Dalton Utilities transfers 5% of its revenue to the city. Thomas said that in each of the past four years, the annual transfer would have been approximately $3.5 million to $4 million lower without revenue from data center customers. The city’s adopted 2026 General Fund budget includes $15.55 million from the Dalton Utilities transfer, compared with $9.1 million in budgeted property-tax revenue. Councilmember Steve Farrow noted that the utility transfer reduces the amount of revenue the city must raise through property taxes. Parker said the city’s 2026 budget includes approximately $15.5 million from Dalton Utilities transfer payments, compared with approximately $9.1 million in budgeted property tax revenue. Resident renews call for moratorium The presentation did not resolve the broader questions that have brought residents to recent city and county government meetings. During public comment, Carmen Shuler again asked the city to adopt a six-month moratorium on data center development while officials develop a data center-specific ordinance. Shuler said a group of concerned residents has submitted a proposal seeking the moratorium and argued that a temporary pause would give the city time to research standards and best practices. “A moratorium is a pause, not a ban,” Shuler said. She asked whether city officials have made decisions on either the requested moratorium or development of a data center ordinance and questioned whether the city has sought consultants or impact studies to help evaluate future development. artigo.texto: The Real Story – A Column On Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at 6:00 PM, the Hillsboro City Council will convene at the Civic Center for the first reading of Ordinance No. 6521 (Case File No. CDCA-004-26). This new Data Center / Artificial Computing and Energy Storage System code will, for the first time ever, define these uses and place restrictions on where they can go. After months of passionate testimony on these matters, the City of Hillsboro took the bold, necessary step of putting a 120 Day Moratorium in place, initially called for by Councilor Kipperlyn Sinclair. Meaningful Guardrails Are Necessary Before we get into this, let’s give credit where credit is due. Hillsboro residents showed up all year to express their concerns. That was followed by the City Council and City staff working through an ever-expanding list of concerns and impacts, and they took significant time to review it. Work sessions and open council debate sent the list of concerns to the Planning Commission, which approved this proposed ordinance. As mentioned above, the City also took an important and commendable step by enacting a temporary 120-day moratorium to address explosive data center and battery storage expansion. Hillsboro urgently needs firm rules, clear acreage caps, and enforceable buffers that protect schools and residential neighborhoods. However, the draft ordinance heading to Council this Tuesday contains significant loopholes and procedural vulnerabilities that could undermine those good intentions. If the City rushes to adopt an incomplete or legally vulnerable code, the ordinance risks being challenged or overturned at the Land Use Board of Appeals (LUBA)—potentially expiring the moratorium and leaving Hillsboro with zero protections in place. The Loopholes in Ordinance No. 6521 Before Council votes, residents should urge leadership to address three critical concerns: Unvetted “Transfer Offsite” Rights (CDC 12.40.145.D.2) While the City is publicizing strict caps on primary data centers (215 acres in I-P and 310 acres in I-S), the draft code creates an untested backdoor. Section 12.40.145.D.2 allows “accessory” compute capacity to be transferred offsite to an “affiliated location” anywhere in an industrial zone. - The Risk: The term “affiliated location” is completely undefined anywhere in the code definitions. Without strict boundaries or cumulative caps on the receiving site, operators could shuffle large server footprints across town into zones where primary data centers were supposed to be prohibited. On July 21, Council directed staff to study transfer rights in Phase 2, not rush them into Phase 1. In Fact, this transfer clause opens the door to placing data centers where they were previously not allowed. This code section is a mess right now. Broad Accessory Uses Across 12 Base Zones The draft code officially prohibits standalone data centers across commercial and mixed-use corridors, but quietly permits them as an “Accessory Use with Limitations” across 12 different base zones—including Commercial General (C-G) and Urban Center Neighborhood Center (UC-NC). Tight, clear parameters are essential to ensure “accessory” rules do not become an end-run around local base zoning. Again opening the door to zones not previously open to Data Centers. These two loopholes technically open up more land to Data Centers and AI computing than exists as of this article’s writing. These two loopholes actually grow the land base open for these uses in a way that vastly expands the current base and totally negates any benefits of the acreage restrictions outlines herein. These two rules also open up all of the restricted lands in Jackson-East North and South and the Meek Road Industrial areas. From our review, this new code could be used to make those areas buildable for data centers and AI Computing via these transfer and accessory use rights, it looks once again like a Trojan horse purposefully put in the code for this reason. Protecting Due Process and Correcting Notice Defects Because of a City Staff-acknowledged mapping error, 34 industrial properties (19 property owners) never received notice of the August Planning Commission hearing. The City mailed corrective notices only on September 9. To ensure any ordinance Council passes survives LUBA review, Council must ensure all affected property owners and residents are fully heard on the record. Behind the Scenes: The Changing Rules of the Public Record When community members track land-use policy, clear procedures are essential. In the handling of Case File No. CDCA-004-26, the administrative process has raised significant questions. On August 26, the Planning Commission formally voted to close the public hearing. When asked on the record whether citizens could continue to submit evidence, staff confirmed the hearing was closed and that deliberations would focus on testimony already received. However, during the two-week continuance before the Commission’s September 9 vote, staff accepted late filings from corporate and utility stakeholders—including PGE, the Washington County Chamber of Commerce, the Technology Association of Oregon, and the Westside Economic Alliance. Staff incorporated those submittals into Staff Report No. 5 and uploaded them just hours before the final vote. When residents attended the September 9 meeting to address those additions, the dais took public testimony off the table. When formal objections were raised regarding the closed hearing, omitted property notices, and unvetted code additions, City staff provided the following written clarification: “Dirk, Staff will address some of your concerns in the October 6 staff report and presentation. In the meantime, attached is a copy of the revised public notice that was sent in the Special Industrial District I-P zone for your information. artigo.texto: To Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian, the debate over data centers starts with the boom in capital investment and property tax revenue the developments promise to the state. Creating regulatory guardrails on issues such as water usage and power are necessary but shouldn’t risk the potential return, Christian told the Fort Worth Report after appearing on a data centers panel Sept. 26 at the Texas Tribune’s annual TribFest conference in Austin. “I think you can learn from previous problems from data centers that have shown problems in the past,” said Christian, who doesn’t regulate data centers but has increasingly spoken on related questions about natural resources. “And what you do as an educated public is you fix the problems, you regulate to make sure it doesn’t happen again. But you don’t stop and turn down billions, billions of free market dollars.” Data centers — and their massive potential economic return — have careened into the intersection of the free market and community concerns about their environmental impact. The Texas Legislature is set to take up the debate over regulation in the 2027 session. The accompanying statistics highlight the choices and problems data center developers and operators face. Demand nationally for development of data centers — the buildings that house the digital infrastructure necessary for processing daily transactions worldwide for everything from paying water bills to buying airline tickets — is surging, according to research by the JLL commercial real estate firm. Seventy-nine percent of Americans support U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence, but only 14 percent support “data centers in our community,” according to research by JLL, Gallup and Reuters published by JLL in August. JLL declined a request by the Report for an interview for this story. Communities are experiencing the conundrum. In Fort Worth, property tax revenue makes up about 60% of the city’s general fund budget, which pays for most basic city services. But residential revenue — 63% of the tax base, compared to commercial — has turned soft in recent years because of protests and litigation, plus the Tarrant Appraisal District’s policy of reappraising every two years. Fort Worth struggled to close a $94 million budget shortfall for 2027 as a result. The city estimated this spring it received $83 million in gross property tax revenue from four data centers in the city over the last five years. In 2024, Fort Worth’s property tax revenue from data centers equaled the same revenue from 8,378 average-valued single family homes, the city estimated. “That’s a huge impact to a school district as well,” Jesica McEachern, an assistant city manager, told council members June 2 in presenting a report on proposed regulation. By 2030, including the existing data centers and phases of planned facilities the city projects will launch by then, the proportion of property tax taken up by commercial property could move more toward half, driven by the hubs, she estimated. It would take an estimated 22,718 average-valued single family homes in fiscal 2031 to generate the same projected property tax as data centers for that year, she added. McEachern maintained the economic benefit of data centers isn’t the “decision point” on whether to accept them. City officials have debated water, power, noise, land use, neighborhood encroachment, setbacks and other questions. Christian takes another view on the matter of decision points. Capital investment by investors in Texas artificial intelligence and data center projects now rivals investments in oil and gas, he noted. Some cities are now actively recruiting data center development. “Now, digest that total amount of money,” Christian said. “What that would do for future generations, for Texas, and for opportunities in half the state that’s literally dying. Here’s opportunities for families to have money, businesses, opportunities for the American dream to be expanded.” Looking ahead to what the Legislature may decide, Fort Worth City Council members in August unanimously approved the first move toward implementing a 90-day moratorium on the construction of data centers. Council members have struggled with the issue as throngs of residents have shown up at meetings to protest data center development. “Data centers can add significantly to the tax base, even if they create fewer permanent jobs than some other uses,” council member Michael Crain told the Report this week. “That’s why we need to evaluate each proposal on its merits — its long-term tax revenue, jobs, infrastructure demands and impact on nearby neighborhoods — and determine whether it’s the right fit for our community.” Data center developers and operators have descended on Texas, which has now overtaken Virginia as the nation’s top state for such projects, because of its business-friendly approach, low energy cost, faster permitting, incentives and abundance of land close to power infrastructure, Fort Worth city staff told council members at the June 2 meeting. Such projects also have low impact on city services and infrastructure, the staff said. After the staff presented the property tax comparison of data centers to single-family homes at the meeting, council member Macy Hill asked for information on the costs of providing infrastructure to homes compared to data centers. Whether to offer economic incentives, as the city often does in cases where major investment is being offered, has quickly become a flashpoint. “These are not desirable land uses,” council member Elizabeth Beck said at the meeting. “I think what makes them desirable is their tax base. So by giving that up to get them I think is a ridiculous policy. If they’re so needed, then they’ll come. And if they’re so needed and they need an incentive, they can go somewhere else.” Industry estimates on data center valuations for property tax purposes are significantly higher than for other potential commercial land uses. artigo.texto: Actis adds 244MW / 1,141MWh battery storage portfolio to Polish platform within three months of launch - Transaction advances Actis’ 1.5GW wind, solar, and BESS target for new Central & Eastern Europe platform - Actis has committed more than US$1.1 billion across three platforms in CEE LONDON, 6 October 2026: Actis, a leading growth market investor in sustainable infrastructure, today announced it is acquiring two battery energy storage system (BESS) projects as it rapidly scales its recently launched Polish renewable energy platform. The projects are being acquired from DRI, with one 112MW / 518MWh project in Kozienice already acquired and ready for construction by Actis, and the other – a 132MW / 623MWh project in Trzebinia – signed and set to complete once operational. These projects will represent some of the first utility-scale BESS projects to reach commercial operation in Poland, with a total 244MW of power capacity and 1,141MWh of four-hour plus duration energy storage. Both assets benefit from a secured revenue base through a 17-year inflation-indexed capacity market contract. Building on Actis’ acquisition of Klara Renewables – a 171MW onshore wind portfolio with approximately 275MW of hybridisation potential, signed in July 2026 – these two assets support Actis’ integrated approach, combining renewable power generation with BESS to create a system-level portfolio that aims to mitigate volatility and maximise value capture across the power system while increasing Poland’s grid flexibility and renewable energy integration capability. With Poland expected to retire approximately 18GW of coal while adding 50GW of renewables and 14GW of gas capacity by 2040, the country’s structural transition away from coal offers significant growth opportunities for assets like BESS, particularly given electricity demand is forecast to more than double by 2050 due to industrial and transport electrification and economic growth. This transformation is underpinned by attractive financial mechanisms, including a strong capacity market providing long-term and stable cashflows, alongside robust corporate PPA demand. Jaroslava Korpanec, Head of Central & Eastern Europe at Actis, commented: "The CEE region has historically been underinvested in, and the need to drive decarbonisation and invest in independent energy supply is, in our view, absolutely crucial. Poland is a major European power market but a carbon-intensive one that needs to transition from coal to renewables while keeping the grid steady. These two projects will help build the grid flexibility required and in doing so support Poland in managing its energy transition, energy competitiveness and resilience.” Murat Cinar, Chief Executive Officer of DRI, said: “Battery storage is expected to play an increasingly important role in Poland’s energy system as the share of renewables continues to grow. We believe Kozienice and Trzebinia are strong projects that can provide significant flexibility to the grid and we are pleased to see them moving into their next stage with Actis. This transaction also reflects the strength, in our view, of DRI’s capability to develop and advance meaningful energy projects in Europe’s most important growth markets.” ENDS RELATED ARTICLES The statements contained herein, including those made by Jaroslava Korpanec are as of 6 October 2026 and represent the views of Actis which is not research and should not be treated as research. artigo.texto: A gigante sul-coreana LG Electronics assinou um contrato de longo prazo para fornecer sistemas de refrigeração industrial a data centers de inteligência artificial nos Estados Unidos. O acordo, que impulsionou as ações da empresa em Seul, visa atender à demanda crescente por infraestrutura térmica eficiente para o boom de IA no mundo. As ações da LG Electronics avançaram no mercado financeiro depois que a companhia fechou um novo contrato plurianual para fornecer sistemas de resfriamento a data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos. A gigante sul-coreana de eletrônicos de consumo vem expandindo rapidamente o negócio de equipamentos de refrigeração industrial, conhecidos como "chillers", impulsionada pelo boom global de data centers, que aumenta a demanda por soluções eficientes de gestão térmica para infraestrutura de IA. Pontos-chave sobre o contrato - Contrato plurianual firmado com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia. - O acordo prevê o fornecimento de "chillers" para data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. - As ações da LG subiram 8,8% no início do pregão em Seul, marcando a maior alta diária em dois meses. - A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia, com início da produção no primeiro semestre de 2027. - Encomendas anuais podem chegar a bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A LG informou nesta terça-feira (6) que sua subsidiária nos EUA firmou um acordo de longo prazo com a AIR Control Concepts, plataforma de data centers com sede na Virgínia, para fornecer "chillers" a data centers de IA com mais de 5 gigawatts de capacidade. A empresa não revelou o valor exato do contrato, mas afirmou que o acordo acelera a expansão da LG no mercado global de resfriamento para data centers de IA. Em Seul, as ações da LG Electronics chegaram a subir 8,8% no início do pregão, caminhando para a maior alta diária em cerca de dois meses. A LG disse que, apoiada por vitórias recentes na América do Norte, também está ampliando sua presença em projetos relevantes de data centers no Oriente Médio e na Indonésia. Expansão industrial e metas de receita No início deste mês, a empresa anunciou que vai aumentar a produção de "chillers" tanto nos EUA quanto na Coreia do Sul. A LG planeja construir uma nova fábrica na Virgínia para atender à demanda crescente de data centers americanos, com início da produção previsto para o primeiro semestre de 2027. Paralelamente, pretende elevar a produção em unidades já existentes em Changwon e Pyeongtaek, na Coreia do Sul. Segundo a LG, as novas encomendas anuais de soluções de resfriamento para data centers podem chegar a vários bilhões de dólares até o fim de 2026, após a companhia garantir US$ 426 milhões no primeiro semestre. A empresa também afirmou esperar atingir, antes do prazo, a meta de 2027 de US$ 680 milhões em receita no negócio de "chillers".

artigo.texto: U.S. data center capacity growth projections appear to be on track for 2026 and 2027 despite mounting opposition to projects that support the build-out of artificial intelligence technologies. Goldman Sachs now projects that total U.S. data center capacity will reach 64 gigawatts by year’s end, an increase in its prior forecast by 5 gigawatts. But the financial services firm also decreased its 2027 forecast by 5 gigawatts, expecting it to reach 90 gigawatts in that year. U.S. capacity stands at about 62.7 gigawatts, according to energy data firm Cleanview. The latest big development announcements include plans in Virginia by LG Electronics to build its first U.S. plant focused on production of chillers for data center cooling. On the investment side, facility operator Sabey Data Center Properties reported a significant new commitment from global equity firm Ares Management Corp. to support expansion. Nearly 400 U.S. cities and towns, along with at least 14 states, are considering moratoriums or other restrictions on data center development. This comes as more than 1,500 data center projects are in various stages of planning nationwide, according to the Pew Research Center. “While U.S. data center development faces increasing political and community opposition, project data and our updated capacity estimates suggest that the U.S. data center growth outlook through 2027 remains largely unchanged,” Goldman analysts said in a research note issued Sunday. Goldman’s 2026-2027 projections are based on its forecast of a 38% increase in U.S. power demand in 2026 and another 38% rise in 2027, much of it driven by data centers. A single gigawatt is roughly enough to power up to around 1 million homes, based on energy industry standards. Power consumption plays a big part in nationwide opposition to data centers, with communities concerned about energy, water and land usage amid worries that projects could also drive up utility bills for residents and businesses near the facilities. Several technology and energy firms have pledged to pay costs for needed utility upgrades as states and cities seek to put those policies into law. Data center projects increasingly include on-site power generation facilities designed to prevent taking power from regional grids, but those components add considerably to development costs. Goldman previously projected that U.S. capital investment in data centers and related AI support systems would hit $765 billion for 2026 alone. The firm expects cumulative global capital spending to reach $7.6 trillion by 2031. More companies boost investment Much of the current and future spending is coming from the largest tech company “hyperscalers,” such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Facebook parent Meta. Multiple other data center operators, investors and suppliers are responding to the AI build-out. LG Electronics, a division of the South Korean industrial giant, said it is expanding its global chiller manufacturing capacity with its first facility in the U.S., planned for a 43-acre site near Windsor in southeastern Virginia. Production is scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027 at a 350,000-square-foot industrial building completed in 2025 by developers of the Shirley T. Holland Intermodal Park, according to an LG statement and regional reports. The new plant is expected to employ more than 150 people and is part of LG Electronics’ strategy to "expand production capacity for advanced cooling technologies and better serve the rapidly expanding customer base in North America,” Don Kwack, CEO of LG Electronics North America, said in the statement. LG plans to invest more than $100 million in the new U.S. facility and expansions of two existing South Korean factories to meet North American demand, the company said. Its first U.S. chiller factory “is addressing the growing need for advanced cooling solutions for data centers across the country,” said Chris Ahn, president of LG Electronics USA’s air conditioning technology division. In another transaction, leaders of Sabey Data Center Properties, the operator of more than 4 million square feet of U.S. data centers, announced on Monday an expanded investment by minority owner Ares Management Corp. That takes the equity firm’s stake to more than $500 million since the first investment was announced in July. Sabey Data Center Properties is majority-owned by Seattle-based Sabey Corp. and National Real Estate Advisors LLC of Washington, D.C. A statement from the two companies and Los Angeles-based Ares said new funding will go toward planned U.S. capacity expansion by Sabey Data Center Properties. Sabey’s development pipeline would take its data center computing capacity from its current 275 megawatts to a planned 737 megawatts by 2033, company officials said. A single megawatt powers up to about 1,000 homes, according to industry standards.

artigo.texto: There’s a growing need for long-duration storage to meet energy demand and balance out renewables on the grid. Energy Dome uses compressed carbon dioxide gas in its massive grid batteries, which can deliver power for up to 24 hours. As the world races to meet growing electricity demand, solar and onshore wind power have become the cheapest and quickest-to-deploy sources to install on the grid. But, despite their upsides, both are subject to variations in weather patterns, which means supplies can be intermittent. Energy Dome is using stored carbon dioxide to help smooth out gaps between supply and demand. Advertisement The key component of an Energy Dome plant is a huge white dome that covers an area about the size of seven soccer fields and holds about 2,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide. When energy is available—say, from a connected solar farm—compressors squeeze the gas, turning it into a liquid that’s then stored in carbon-steel tanks. That process generates heat, which the system holds in a proprietary thermal storage material. Then, when the grid needs power, the carbon dioxide is released from the tanks and warmed with the stored heat, turning it back into a gas. That gaseous carbon dioxide then passes through a turbine to generate electricity and flows back into the dome, ready to begin the cycle again. This story is only available to subscribers. Don’t settle for half the story. Get paywall-free access to technology news for the here and now. Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new—utilities have been using compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades. But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world. Energy Dome turned on its first commercial plant in Sardinia, Italy, in 2025. The facility has a capacity of 200 megawatt-hours. That’s enough to power about 18,000 Italian homes for 10 hours. Key indicators Industry: Energy storage Founded: 2020 Headquarters: Milan, Italy Notable fact: Energy Dome has plans for 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of projects across five continents. Potential for impact Cheaper energy storage could help wind and solar meet more of the world’s electricity demand. Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate new installations for short-duration applications of up to four hours. But the economics aren’t competitive for longer durations: A lithium-ion system that provides eight hours of storage at the same power output requires doubling the number of cells. Energy Dome estimates that its technology is roughly 10% to 15% cheaper than lithium-ion batteries for an eight-hour system, and that the economics are even better for longer-duration systems of up to 24 hours. The company says its ability to scale bigger and faster than lithium-ion boils down to the fact that its design uses existing commercially available equipment like compressors and storage tanks. Its plants that are either operational or under contract have eight or 10 hours of capacity. Caveats Energy Dome only has one commercial project that’s operational. It’ll need to build many more to provide the 30 gigawatt-hours of storage it has planned. The technology also isn’t quite as efficient as lithium-ion. Overall, Energy Dome’s process can return about 70% of the electricity it stores to the grid (a measure known as roundtrip efficiency). Lithium-ion batteries average roughly 90%. But some other long-duration storage techniques clock in lower; some iron-air batteries, for example, are around 50%. Advertisement Energy Dome’s plants may not all be benign from a planet-warming perspective. The company offers a version of its system that pairs its carbon dioxide battery with natural gas turbines. That version replaces internal heat storage with waste heat from the gas turbines to help evaporate carbon dioxide. That helps the plant run more efficiently but ultimately results in greenhouse-gas emissions from the natural gas turbines. Next steps Energy Dome has a pipeline of about 30 gigawatt-hours’ worth of plants in the works around the world, and many of these projects could come online by the end of the decade. Because the company uses off-the-shelf components, the time from a signed contract to delivered capacity is only two years. In June 2026, for example, it signed a deal with Google to build a 200 MWh plant in Ireland, which is expected to come online in 2028.

artigo.texto: New data center development in Anne Arundel County is on hold while county leaders decide how to regulate the rapidly growing industry. The Anne Arundel County Council voted 7-0 Monday night to approve an amended version of Bill 63-26, establishing a temporary moratorium on new data center development. The moratorium will run until Jan. 31, 2028, or until the county adopts comprehensive data center legislation, whichever comes first. The measure differs significantly from the bill as originally introduced. Council members initially considered banning new privately operated data centers in the county, then unanimously amended the proposal in September to replace the ban with a temporary moratorium. Projects already in the development process will generally be allowed to continue. The amended measure also includes future phases of existing data centers on adjacent or adjoining properties. During the moratorium, the county will establish a work group to study data center development and recommend permanent regulations to the county executive and County Council. The group is expected to consider energy and water use, utility infrastructure, noise, air quality, environmental impacts, and economic development. The debate comes as data centers continue to expand in Anne Arundel County. Microsoft, which is developing a data center campus at Annapolis Junction Business Park, previously testified against the original ban. The company said it supported developing regulations and creating a work group, but wanted existing campuses to continue development. The legislation also calls for repealing a personal property tax assessment reduction for qualified data storage centers. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates. artigo.texto: Zelestra and EDP have signed two new power purchase agreements (PPAs) to hybridise operational solar plants in Spain with battery energy storage systems (BESS), taking their partnership to four hybrid projects and more than 1 GWh of contracted storage capacity in the country. The long-term agreements cover Zelestra’s operational Pedroso solar plant in Seville and Valkyria solar plant in Castilla-La Mancha. Under the agreement, Zelestra will develop a 25 MW BESS with approximately 100 MWh of storage capacity at the 31 MWdc Pedroso solar plant. At the Valkyria project, a 90.45 MW BESS with approximately 362 MWh of storage capacity will be integrated with the 150 MWdc solar plant. Both battery systems will have a four-hour duration. EDP, which is already the offtaker for both solar plants, is expanding its role in the Spanish battery storage market through the new agreements. The latest PPAs bring the companies’ Spanish hybridisation partnership to four projects. In 2025, EDP and Zelestra signed what they described as Spain’s first combined solar and BESS PPA, covering 170 MWdc of solar capacity and 400 MWh of storage at a project in Trujillo, Extremadura. Earlier in 2026, the companies signed an agreement to hybridise an operational solar plant, adding a 160 MWh BESS to the 50 MW Pizarroso solar plant in Cáceres. Across the four projects, the partnership now represents more than 1 GWh of contracted battery storage capacity. The companies said hybridising existing operational solar plants can provide a faster route to increasing grid flexibility, as the projects already have land, grid connections and renewable generation infrastructure in place. Pedro Neves Ferreira, CEO of Global Energy Management at EDP, said the company is developing solutions that combine renewable generation with flexibility assets to improve the value and efficiency of clean energy. He added that integrating energy storage with renewable generation can strengthen system resilience and support electrification and decarbonisation. Jaime Burguete, CEO of Zelestra in Spain, said the partnership is enabling large-scale storage capacity in the Spanish market and described energy storage as a growing segment of the country’s renewable energy sector. artigo.texto: JUWI GmbH, based in Wörrstadt, has recently signed contracts with three leading companies in the energy sector for the technical operation, servicing and maintenance of six further battery energy storage systems (BESS). The facilities are currently under construction and are due to be commissioned within the next six months. For more than five years, the JUWI Group’s O&M experts have been managing battery storage systems in Germany and Belgium. With these newly secured contracts, JUWI is expanding its portfolio of managed battery storage systems to around 700 megawatt-hours of storage capacity. The new projects are being carried out for three different companies and involve storage capacities ranging from 4 to 100 megawatt-hours. JUWI’s services include technical operations management as well as servicing and maintenance for the first few years of the plants’ operational phase. The new contracts underscore the growing importance of battery storage systems for a secure and flexible energy supply, as well as market participants’ confidence in JUWI’s long-standing expertise in operations management and service provision. Oliver Otte, Head of O&M at JUWI GmbH, explains: “We are delighted that three renowned companies in the energy sector have chosen us as their O&M partner for the servicing, maintenance and technical operation of their battery storage systems. With our many years of experience in operating battery storage systems, we create real added value for investors and operators. Our aim is to operate the systems reliably, safely and cost-effectively throughout their entire life cycle.” By further expanding the BESS portfolio, JUWI is strengthening its position as an experienced operations management and service partner for battery storage and renewable energy systems in Europe.

artigo.texto: Indiana has heard plenty about the data center boom: billions in proposed investment and construction jobs. The more consequential question is whether the benefits will extend beyond the project site and be shared by all Hoosier families and businesses. One early answer is coming from Indiana Michigan Power, which has proposed a rate reduction plan to the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission. The proposal would reduce Indiana customer bills by about $59 million in 2027, freeze all rates on the monthly bill for three years and, by I&M’s estimate, save its average residential customer about $100 annually. I&M explains why: “This rate decrease is made possible by the load growth and increased revenue it is experiencing from large customers including data centers.” I&M’s proposal offers a concrete early indication of how the economics can work. Large customers bring more than new demand. Their steady, substantial revenue can create room for utilities to invest in transmission, substations and the technology that makes the grid stronger. That means more capacity, fewer and shorter outages, and a system prepared for the factories, homes and businesses that will need dependable electricity in the years ahead. South Bend Mayor James Mueller called the proposal “the power of growth and getting more for less.” It is a concise description of how growth can work for the people of Indiana. Indiana is only beginning to see these investments reach the system. As projects move to construction and operations, the benefits of growth should become easier to recognize: stronger infrastructure, greater capacity and, if I&M is a guide, lower bills for Hoosier households. Data center investment can generate significant local tax revenue to help communities pay for schools, police and fire protection, infrastructure and amenities. A larger tax base can also mean less pressure to raise property tax rates on homeowners and businesses. Water use is changing, too. A new data center planned for Lebanon will use a water-efficient closed-loop system designed to use zero water for most of the year. The developer says a typical AI-optimized data center using this kind of system uses less water annually than two full-service restaurants. Just as important is the people side of this growth. Last month, Indianapolis celebrated the first graduating class of Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy. Indiana is one of four states in the initial pilot for Meta’s $115 million nationwide initiative, which trains people for the skilled trades needed to build and maintain digital infrastructure, power generation and grid modernization. Participants need no prior experience. They are paid while completing the program and graduate with industry credentials and a guaranteed job with a Meta partner. Ethan Blake, a graduate from Fishers, put its value more directly: “They gave me an on ramp to success in a way, and they gave me the tools that I needed to be able to navigate this new workforce. They gave me the knowledge that I needed to be able to navigate the new workforce, and they gave me a job.” That is why this moment matters. Indiana has abundant energy resources, a skilled manufacturing tradition, strategic location and workers ready to build. The data center boom can create jobs for electricians, fiber technicians, equipment operators, construction workers and the many local businesses that support them. It can also catalyze the grid improvements that help every employer and family. I&M’s proposed rate reduction is not the end of the conversation. It is a promising early sign of what Indiana can achieve through new investment, a growth-oriented mindset, and confidence in ourselves and the future. Jim Merritt of Carmel is a former Indiana state senator.

artigo.texto: Jupiter Wagons Limited (JWL), through its energy business arm JEM Energy, has strengthened its presence in India’s battery energy storage system (BESS) market by securing a 41 MW/102.5 MWh standalone BESS project in Uttarakhand in partnership with Madhav Infra Projects Limited. The joint venture emerged as the L1 bidder for Cluster C of the Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited (UPCL) tender issued under the Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) mechanism. The project includes the supply and commissioning of BESS systems with an estimated value of approximately ₹100 crore. The award marks JEM Energy’s entry into the Uttarakhand energy storage market. JWL has also received a formal Letter of Award (LoA) from the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (WBSEDCL) for a 50 MW/200 MWh standalone BESS project. The project will be located at the Jeerat 132 kV substation in North 24 Parganas, West Bengal. JWL had originally secured the project in August 2026, while the latest LoA formalizes the award. Together, the two projects represent a combined BESS capacity of 91 MW/302.5 MWh and strengthen JEM Energy’s pipeline in the rapidly expanding energy storage segment. The company’s expansion comes as India accelerates investments in battery storage to support renewable energy integration and improve grid flexibility. The Union Cabinet’s approval of the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III includes plans to add 50 GWh of battery energy storage capacity along with the development of stronger intra-state transmission infrastructure. Substation-level storage projects such as those being developed in Uttarakhand and West Bengal are expected to support this broader grid modernization strategy. Vivek Lohia, Managing Director of Jupiter Wagons Limited, said that winning the Uttarakhand project and receiving the formal award for the Jeerat project represent important milestones in scaling JEM Energy into a significant energy storage business. The company has set a target of building a BESS order book of approximately ₹1,000 crore by FY27. JWL also expects its electric mobility business to turn EBITDA positive in the third quarter of FY27 and achieve profitability by FY28. JEM Energy plans to continue a disciplined bidding strategy for utility-scale as well as Commercial and Industrial (C&I) energy storage opportunities across India. The company’s growing presence in BESS reflects JWL’s broader strategy of diversifying beyond its traditional railway and mobility operations and participating in high-growth segments linked to India’s energy transition.
